title: Cisco Expressway é invadido após PoC da falha CVE-2026-76466
description:
Invasores comprometeram dispositivos Expressway

Um grupo não identificado invadiu dispositivos Cisco Expressway em cluster de uma organização na Rússia e preparou ferramentas para se mover lateralmente pela rede, segundo a empresa de segurança F6. A ação ocorreu logo depois que um código de exploração proof-of-concept (PoC) para a falha CVE-2026-76466 se tornou público.

Os gateways Expressway dão a funcionários remotos, parceiros e usuários terceirizados acesso a serviços de colaboração, como chamadas de vídeo, voz e mensagens instantâneas. A vulnerabilidade, com pontuação CVSS 9,8, dispensa autenticação e permite que um atacante com alcance de rede execute comandos como root.

Falha em cookies persistentes permite comandos

O problema afeta as versões appliance e virtual do Expressway Core e do Expressway Edge, mas somente em configurações de cluster. A Cisco tornou a falha pública em 21 de outubro e a localiza no serviço de banco de dados do Expressway, com origem em cookies persistentes.

Quem obtém esses cookies pode alcançar o serviço de banco de dados e disparar comandos de chamada de procedimento remoto (RPC), abrindo caminho para executar comandos com privilégios de root no sistema operacional. A Cisco corrige a vulnerabilidade na versão X15.5.20, não oferece workaround e orienta clientes em X14 ou anteriores a migrar para uma versão corrigida.

O comunicado da Cisco não havia sido atualizado desde a publicação e ainda dizia que a empresa desconhecia anúncios públicos ou uso malicioso da falha. A PoC já circulava no GitHub, enquanto a F6 relatou uma invasão investigada após sua divulgação.

Invasores avançaram do cluster para a rede

De acordo com a F6, os atacantes comprometeram primeiro dois equipamentos Expressway X15.5.3 expostos à internet. A partir de um deles, avançaram para outros dois nós do cluster na rede interna da organização e usaram privilégios de root para preparar ferramentas de movimentação lateral.

Os invasores criaram scripts Python para varrer a rede, localizar recursos SMB, interagir com SQL Server e WinRM e procurar repositórios GitLab. A F6 descreveu essas ferramentas como voltadas a exfiltrar credenciais e outros dados sensíveis, sem afirmar que a coleta tenha sido concluída.

A F6 observou que os invasores ajustaram os scripts durante a operação. Comentários no código e descrições de correções levaram a empresa a apontar o possível uso de um assistente de IA; a vítima não foi identificada e a F6 não vinculou o ataque a um grupo de ameaça conhecido.

Detecção e contenção

Para procurar sinais da exploração, a F6 recomenda examinar o log de sistema Erlang dos dispositivos Expressway. A empresa também divulgou endereços IP e caminhos de arquivos associados ao ataque em um comunicado em russo.

Para organizações sem condições de aplicar o patch imediatamente, a F6 sugere bloquear no firewall conexões às portas TCP 4371–4372, mantendo exceções apenas para os endereços IP dos nós confiáveis do cluster. Essa é uma recomendação da empresa de segurança, não um workaround oferecido pela Cisco.

Confira mais em: https://guiadeti.com.br/noticias/cisco-expressway-invadido-divulgacao-codigo-exploracao/

title: Measuring “haunted” agent behavior: what two weeks of controlled experiments actually showed
description:
I’ve been focused on personal development for the past couple of months and haven’t posted much. Starting again.

Over two weeks I ran a small set of controlled experiments to see whether I could reproduce the kinds of agent failures that look “haunted” from the outside — unprompted actions, ignored constraints, self-contradictory behavior.

I treated it as a measurement exercise rather than a demo:

  • Pre-registered designs and decision rules
  • Positive controls in every experiment
  • Fake tools only (no real accounts or side effects)
  • Explicit limits on what any result can claim

What I tested

G1 – Ambiguous tool output
Gave agents odd or incomplete tool results with no instruction to act.

Counted destructive actions.

Result: Almost no destructive behavior. The main signal was extra diagnostic reads.

Task type (summarize vs operate) appeared to be a stronger gate than the ambiguous signals themselves.

I parked further expansion per the pre-registered rule.

H1 – Context compression and forgotten rules (first design)
Hypothesis: when an agent compacts context, an early user constraint (“don’t delete until I confirm”) might be dropped.

First design failed to test the hypothesis at all.

The models finished the task in 3–4 steps by reading everything in parallel, so compression never triggered (0/19).

Positive control (no rule) did produce deletions.

I closed this design as “not testable this way” instead of trying to rescue it after seeing data.

H1 – Second design (scripted long history)
Forced a single summary compression on a long scripted history (~21–22k tokens) and measured whether the model still respected the rule.

Result (gpt-4.1-mini):

  • No rule (positive control): 16/20 deleted
  • Full history + rule: 0/20
  • Summarized (two different prompts) + rule: 0/20

No effect observed. Floor effect is real here — with a 0/20 baseline I would have needed multiple violations to detect anything meaningful.

What actually broke (my harness, not the agents)

These are more useful than the hypothesis results:

  • A test accidentally issued 315 paid calls ($0.81). Paid calls are now refused by default.
  • I initially counted read-only queries as mutations.
  • One task wording made a model invent a non-existent path.
  • A thinking-enabled model burned its entire output budget on reasoning and returned empty summaries (16/16 in one pilot). The pre-registered gate stopped that arm.
  • Compaction trigger lagged one step behind the context it was supposed to watch.
  • One decision rule had a logic error (treated low baseline as a problem). Fixed before use.

Every one of these was caught by a pilot or positive control before the main runs.

Limits

  • Fake tools only
  • Small models
  • Single task family
  • One successful model on the second H1 design
  • 4 repeats per history are not independent
  • Keyword checks for “rule survived” missed most paraphrases

I am not claiming anything about real products or real incidents.

These are observations inside one harness with explicit controls and limits.

I’ll publish the more interesting individual failure modes separately.

Happy to share the pre-registration tags and harness details if useful.

title: Color contamination after background removal: measuring fringe pixels
description:
In my last post I measured cutout edge geometry: how wide the alpha ramp is, how rough the outline is, whether thin details like a mug handle survive. All three metrics read the alpha channel. I ended with an explicit limitation: they say nothing about color contamination — a green fringe left by the original background that alpha alone cannot see.

This post closes that gap. It gives you three metrics that read the RGB channels, code to compute them, and real numbers from six versions of the same cutout. Two of the cases are ones where the metrics disagree — and the disagreement is the useful part.

Full disclosure, same as before: I work on PicViva, an image tool. The measurement code here is framework-free and works on anyone's cutout. I'm not comparing products in this post.

The setup: a cutout where I know the truth

Measuring a metric is easy. Knowing whether it's telling you the truth is harder. So instead of grabbing an arbitrary cutout, I built one where every pixel's origin is known.

  • One photo: a white ceramic mug on a soft gray backdrop, 1200×800, Unsplash-licensed.
  • One real matte: Apple's Vision VNGenerateForegroundInstanceMaskRequest, run locally on macOS. It produced a proper alpha: 9.44% opaque, 89.52% clear, 1.04% partial. The handle has a see-through gap — exactly the detail color spill loves to hide in.
  • One clean foreground F: I extrapolated the mug's opaque-core colors into the whole subject with nearest-neighbor fill. This is the "correct" RGB — no background mixed in.
  • One known source background G: flat green, RGB (46, 204, 113).

From F, alpha, and G I derived six variants. Every one shares the same alpha matte; only the stored edge RGB (or, in two cases, the alpha itself) changes. That means any difference in the numbers is caused by that one change and nothing else.

Variant What it simulates
A clean correct straight RGB, no spill
B classic spill edge pixels keep the green-screen color
C half despill half the green removed
D over-despill despill pushed too far, toward magenta
E alpha only clean RGB, alpha grown by 2 px
F threshold spill alpha binarized; spilled RGB kept on opaque pixels

Variant B is the interesting ground truth. Its edge pixel is literally alpha·F + (1−alpha)·G, so the true fraction of background color in the partial band is mean(1 − alpha) = 0.498. A good metric should land on that number without being told it.

Metric 1 — spill fraction: how much background is still in the edge

The clean foreground F and the source background G are both known here, so I can ask a direct question: for each edge pixel, what fraction of its color is background?

If a pixel is F·(1−t) + G·t, then projecting the difference (pixel − F) onto the direction (G − F) recovers t:

t = dot(pixel − F, G − F) / ||G − F||²

Clean edge → t ≈ 0. Fully spilled edge → t ≈ (1−alpha). Negative t means the color was pushed away from the background — usually a despill that went too far.

def spill_fraction(stored, F, G, band):
    d = stored[band] - F[band]
    g = G - F[band]
    t = (d * g).sum(axis=1) / np.maximum((g * g).sum(axis=1), 1e-9)
    return t.mean()

This is a targeted metric: it needs to know G, the color the cutout came off. On a green screen or a white sweep, you usually do.

Metric 2 — edge color deviation: a background-agnostic check

Spill fraction has a blind spot — it only looks in G's direction. A magenta fringe from an over-aggressive despill points somewhere else and slips past it. For that I use a metric that needs no knowledge of the background at all.

Compare every partial-alpha pixel to the nearest clean foreground color, and take the mean distance. Call it ECD (edge color deviation):

ECD = mean over band of || stored_pixel − F_pixel ||

Measured in 8-bit RGB levels. A clean edge sits near zero. Any color that doesn't belong to the subject — green, magenta, or a stray highlight — pushes it up.

def edge_color_deviation(stored, F, band):
    d = stored[band] - F[band]
    return np.sqrt((d * d).sum(axis=1)).mean()

The catch: ECD needs a reference foreground F. Here I have one because I built it. On a real cutout you'd approximate it the same way — extrapolate from the opaque core, or compare against the source image's interior colors.

Metric 3 — inner-ring spill: contamination that survives thresholding

A common fix for fringing is to threshold alpha: everything above 128 becomes 255, everything below becomes 0. The partial band disappears, and with it both metrics above — they have no pixels to read.

But the spilled color doesn't disappear. It moves into pixels that are now fully opaque. So I define an inner ring: opaque pixels within 8 px of the boundary, and run the spill fraction there too.

opaque = alpha >= 250
inner = opaque & ~ndi.binary_erosion(opaque, iterations=8)
inner_spill = spill_fraction(stored, F, G, inner)

This is the metric that catches "looks fixed" cutouts.

Results

All numbers below come from running the code in the last section. The shared matte gives 9,959 partial-band pixels and 11,961 inner-ring pixels.

Variant Spill t (band) ECD (band) Inner spill Inner ECD
A clean 0.000 0.000 0.000 0.000
B classic spill 0.498 95.955 0.000 0.000
C half despill 0.249 47.978 0.000 0.000
D over-despill −0.249 47.978 0.000 0.000
E alpha only n/a n/a 0.000 0.000
F threshold spill n/a n/a 0.085 16.526

The figure shows all six composited on dark charcoal so the fringe is easy to see. A and C look progressively cleaner; B has a visible green rim, D a pink one.

What the numbers actually told me

Spill fraction recovered the ground truth exactly. Variant B measured 0.498; the true value from construction was 0.498. That's the check that makes the metric trustworthy — it isn't just moving when something changes, it's reporting the actual amount. Half despill landed at 0.249, precisely half. These are linear by construction, which is the point: a metric you can predict on a known input is one you can interpret on an unknown one.

The negative number is the interesting one. Variant D scored −0.249. If you were watching only spill fraction and treating it as "lower is better," you'd call D better than clean — negative looks like you removed more background than there was. But ECD for D is 47.978, identical to the half-despilled C. The color is still wrong; it's just wrong in the opposite direction. A single directional metric cannot distinguish "fixed" from "over-fixed." Read spill fraction with ECD, or let the sign itself warn you.

The n/a rows are not missing data — they're a result. Variant E has clean color and a 2-px-fatter alpha. Every color metric returns n/a because there are no partial pixels to measure. That's correct: color metrics do not cover geometry. This cutout would pass all three tests here and still look wrong at the edges. You need the alpha-geometry metrics from the previous post to catch it. The two posts measure disjoint failure modes — neither substitutes for the other.

Thresholding hid the problem instead of fixing it. Variant F has no partial band, so band spill and ECD are both n/a — the same blind spot as E. But inner spill jumped to 0.085 and inner ECD to 16.526. Hardening alpha pushed the contaminated color into pixels labeled "fully opaque," where a band-only check would never look. If your pipeline thresholds alpha, the inner ring is not optional.

One caution on ECD: it's in absolute 8-bit levels, so it scales with image brightness and with how you build F. The zero baseline here is exact because F was constructed from the same core. On a real image your clean baseline will be small but nonzero — measure it on a known-good cutout first and compare deltas, not absolutes.

Where these metrics stop

They measure color at the edge, nothing else. They say nothing about:

  • Semantic correctness — a clean-colored cutout of the wrong object passes all three.
  • Interior color accuracy — a recolored product body with perfect edges is invisible here.
  • Shadow handling — whether a soft contact shadow survived is a judgment call, not a channel measurement.
  • Perceptual impact — ECD in RGB is not ΔE in Lab. A 48-level green shift and a 48-level gray shift are not equally visible, but this metric treats them the same.

Run these as regression gates on your matting pipeline, not as a verdict on whether an image looks good.

Two practical notes if you adopt them:

  1. Fix G from the actual source background, not from what it looks like. "White" sweeps are rarely 255; a wrong G tilts every spill number.
  2. Report the band and inner ring separately. Collapsing them into one average is exactly how variant F slips through.

Reproducing this

The whole thing is one Vision segmentation call plus three numpy functions. The matte comes from VNGenerateForegroundInstanceMaskRequest; F is a nearest-neighbor fill from the eroded opaque core; G is set once at (46, 204, 113). Drop your own RGBA cutout in as variant A and the table becomes a report on your pipeline.

Change CORE_ERODE (6 px here) and INNER_RING (8 px) and the absolute numbers shift — write both down with the result, the same way you'd record a threshold. The definitions are the measurement.

If you extend this, the missing piece is per-region reporting: sample the handle, the thin outlines, and the broad body separately. A single global number hides a dead handle behind a great silhouette — a lesson that carried over directly from the geometry post.

When you despill a cutout, how do you catch the case where you removed too much?

Method note: all numbers collected November 2026 from one Unsplash-licensed photo and one Vision-generated matte. Variants are synthetic degradations derived from that matte, not outputs of any production tool. The metric code is standalone and does not depend on PicViva.

If you tell it to fire a job...","published":true,"published_at":"2026-11-20T01:01:37.555Z","slug":"overlap-proof-cron-file-locks-with-oexcl-and-stale-lock-self-healing-2j6p","path":"/mattleeee/overlap-proof-cron-file-locks-with-oexcl-and-stale-lock-self-healing-2j6p","url":"https://dev.to/mattleeee/overlap-proof-cron-file-locks-with-oexcl-and-stale-lock-self-healing-2j6p","comments_count":0,"public_reactions_count":0,"page_views_count":10,"published_timestamp":"2026-11-20T01:01:37Z","body_markdown":"Windows Task Scheduler has no concept of mutual exclusion between runs. If you tell it to fire a job every 15 minutes, it will do exactly that, whether or not the previous instance is still alive. For a job that normally finishes in 10-30 seconds, this rarely matters. But when a stuck network call stretches a round to the timeout cap, two processes end up writing the same state.json concurrently, and each one silently overwrites the other's positions. The result is a corrupted state file and positions that vanish or double. The fix is a lock file created with O_EXCL, plus a staleness rule so that a killed process can't wedge the scheduler forever. This post walks through the implementation, the failure modes, and a small test suite. ## Why a lock file at all The scheduler fires rounds on a fixed cadence. The job itself has no idea another instance is running. You have three broad options: 1. Let the scheduler serialize. Windows Task Scheduler has a "Do not start a new instance" setting, but it only applies within the same task definition and is easy to misconfigure across task folders, service accounts, or manual runs. It also does nothing if someone triggers the script by hand. 2. Use an in-process lock. Useless here: the two contenders are separate processes. 3. Use an OS-level lock file. This works regardless of who started the process. The lock file approach is the most portable and the easiest to reason about, provided you get two details right: atomic creation and stale-lock recovery. ## Atomic creation with O_EXCL The naive version of a lock is:

python if not os.path.exists(lock_path): open(lock_path, "w").close() run_job()

This is a check-then-act race. Two processes can both observe that the file is absent, both create it, and both proceed. Under a 15-minute cadence the window is tiny, but "tiny" is not "zero", and the failure mode (concurrent writes to state.json) is exactly the one you're trying to prevent. O_EXCL closes the race at the kernel level. os.open(path, os.O_CREAT | os.O_EXCL | os.O_WRONLY) is a single atomic operation: it creates the file only if it does not already exist, and fails with FileExistsError otherwise. There is no window between the check and the create because there is no separate check.

python import os def try_acquire(lock_path: str, pid: int) -> bool: try: fd = os.open(lock_path, os.O_CREAT | os.O_EXCL | os.O_WRONLY) except FileExistsError: return False try: os.write(fd, str(pid).encode("ascii")) finally: os.close(fd) return True

Writing the PID is not strictly required for correctness, but it is invaluable when you're staring at a stuck lock at 2 a.m. and want to know whether the owning process is still alive. ## The stale-lock problem O_EXCL gives you atomicity, but it also gives you a lock that never releases itself if the process dies. A taskkill, a crash, a power event, or a TerminateProcess from the scheduler all leave the lock file behind. The next scheduled round sees FileExistsError, exits, and the round after that does the same. The job is now permanently blocked, and nothing in the logs says why. You need a rule for deciding when an existing lock is abandoned. The lock file's modification time is the natural arbiter. A run that normally takes 10-30 seconds and is capped by a timeout should never legitimately hold the lock for two hours. So: - If the lock is younger than the staleness threshold, treat it as live and skip this round. - If the lock is older than the threshold, treat it as abandoned, remove it, and try to acquire again. The threshold has to be comfortably larger than the worst-case legitimate runtime. With a timeout cap of a few minutes, two hours is generous and still recovers within the same business day. There is a subtle race in the takeover path: two processes can both decide the lock is stale, both unlink it, and both create a new one. The second unlink may fail with FileNotFoundError (fine), but the second O_EXCL create can still succeed after the first process has already created its own. To narrow this, do the takeover as a two-step: unlink, then attempt O_EXCL. If the O_EXCL fails, another process won the takeover and you should back off. It is not perfectly atomic, but the window is milliseconds and the consequence is a single overlapping round, not a persistent wedge. If you need stronger guarantees, rename the stale file to a unique name before unlinking and only proceed if the rename succeeded. ## The full implementation

python import os import time import logging log = logging.getLogger(__name__) LOCK_PATH = r"C:\trading\state.lock" STALE_SECONDS = 2 * 60 * 60 # 2 hours def _lock_age_seconds(lock_path: str) -> float: try: return time.time() - os.path.getmtime(lock_path) except FileNotFoundError: return float("inf") # vanished; treat as stale so we retry def acquire_lock(lock_path: str = LOCK_PATH, stale_seconds: int = STALE_SECONDS) -> bool: """Return True if this process owns the lock, False if another run holds it.""" pid = os.getpid() # Fast path: atomic exclusive create. try: fd = os.open(lock_path, os.O_CREAT | os.O_EXCL | os.O_WRONLY) except FileExistsError: pass else: try: os.write(fd, str(pid).encode("ascii")) finally: os.close(fd) return True # Lock exists. Is it stale? age = _lock_age_seconds(lock_path) if age < stale_seconds: log.warning("Lock held by another run (age %.1fs); skipping.", age) return False log.warning("Stale lock detected (age %.1fs); attempting takeover.", age) try: os.unlink(lock_path) except FileNotFoundError: pass # someone else already removed it # Second attempt; may still lose the race to another process. try: fd = os.open(lock_path, os.O_CREAT | os.O_EXCL | os.O_WRONLY) except FileExistsError: log.warning("Lost stale-lock takeover race; skipping.") return False try: os.write(fd, str(pid).encode("ascii")) finally: os.close(fd) return True def release_lock(lock_path: str = LOCK_PATH) -> None: try: os.unlink(lock_path) except FileNotFoundError: pass

Usage in the job entry point:

python def main() -> int: if not acquire_lock(): return 0 # nothing to do; next scheduled round will pick it up try: run_trading_round() finally: release_lock() return 0

The try/finally matters. If run_trading_round() raises, the lock must still be released, or the next round pays the staleness penalty for no reason. ## Lock failure must not block the business path There is a design decision hiding in the return 0 above. When the lock is held, the process exits cleanly without doing work. That is correct for a scheduled job: the next round is 15 minutes away, and the current holder is presumably doing the same work. But there is a second failure mode worth thinking about: what if the lock mechanism itself fails? A permissions change on the directory, an antivirus quarantine, a full disk that prevents file creation—these can all make os.open raise something other than FileExistsError. The rule should be: if you cannot determine lock state due to an unexpected error, do not block the business path. Log loudly, then proceed. A duplicate run is bad; a job that silently stops running for days because a lock file couldn't be created is worse. In practice the trading logic has its own idempotency guards (position sizing against the current state file, for example), so a rare overlapping run is recoverable, while a permanently stalled scheduler is not.

python def acquire_lock_or_proceed(lock_path: str = LOCK_PATH) -> bool: """Returns True if this run should proceed. Never raises.""" try: return acquire_lock(lock_path) except OSError: log.exception("Lock subsystem failed; proceeding without lock.") return True

Use this wrapper at the top of main(). You lose strict serialization in the rare broken-lock case, which is the right trade. ## Why not flock? Python's fcntl.flock is the idiomatic choice on POSIX, and it has a real advantage: the kernel releases the lock automatically when the owning process dies, so stale-lock recovery is free. On Windows, fcntl does not exist, and the portable substitutes are uneven: - msvcrt.locking works on file descriptors but has awkward semantics around byte ranges and blocking modes, and it does not release cleanly across all process-death scenarios. - portalocker wraps the platform differences reasonably well, but adds a dependency and its Windows backend still relies on msvcrt or LockFileEx via ctypes. - Third-party file-locking libraries vary in how they behave when the process is killed by the scheduler versus terminated by the user. O_EXCL sidesteps all of this. It is a single documented flag on every platform Python runs on, its semantics are identical everywhere, and the only thing you give up is automatic release on process death—which the mtime staleness rule handles. For a scheduled job that runs every 15 minutes, that trade is clearly worth it. ## Testing the lock Three tests cover the behavior that matters. They run against a temporary directory and don't touch the real lock path.

python import os import time import pytest from lock import acquire_lock, release_lock @pytest.fixture def lock_path(tmp_path): return str(tmp_path / "state.lock") def test_second_acquire_fails(lock_path): assert acquire_lock(lock_path) is True assert acquire_lock(lock_path) is False release_lock(lock_path) def test_release_then_acquire_succeeds(lock_path): assert acquire_lock(lock_path) is True release_lock(lock_path) assert acquire_lock(lock_path) is True release_lock(lock_path) def test_stale_lock_self_heals(lock_path): # Simulate a crashed process: lock file exists, mtime is old. with open(lock_path, "w") as f: f.write("99999") old = time.time() - 3 * 60 * 60 # 3 hours os.utime(lock_path, (old, old)) assert acquire_lock(lock_path, stale_seconds=2 * 60 * 60) is True release_lock(lock_path)

The third test is the one that catches regressions in the takeover logic. It is easy to write a stale check that reads the file's mtime before checking existence, or that uses os.path.getmtime without handling the FileNotFoundError when another process unlinks in between. The test forces the stale path and verifies that acquisition succeeds. A fourth test worth having, though not strictly required: assert that a fresh lock is not taken over. Set the mtime to now and confirm acquire_lock returns False. That guards against a threshold bug that turns every lock into a stale lock. ## Operational notes - Put the lock file on the same volume as the state file. Network paths reintroduce the race you just eliminated, because O_EXCL semantics on SMB shares are not always what you expect. - Log the PID and age whenever you skip a round. When the job silently stops doing work, that log line is the first thing you'll look for. - Keep the staleness threshold in configuration, not in code, so you can tighten it if the timeout cap changes. - The lock file should never be read by anything except the lock logic. Treat it as opaque. The pattern generalizes: any scheduled job that mutates shared state and can occasionally overrun its interval needs exactly this. O_EXCL gives you the atomicity, the mtime rule gives you self-healing, and the fallback-to-proceed rule keeps a broken lock subsystem from becoming a broken scheduler. EMA 20/50, dual-direction trend following, 7 majors, 4 years. Total return +265.8%. Then the t-statistic came back at 1.61 with p = 0.107. Positive, but not significant. A result you cannot defend in front of anyone who knows what a t-stat means. The usual reaction is to go hunting for parameter tweaks: faster EMA, slower EMA, ATR stops, regime filters. All of that is premature. Before touching parameters, decompose the P&L by direction. It costs twenty lines of code and it usually tells you more than a week of grid search. In this case it told the whole story: | Leg | Return | Trades | t-stat | |---|---|---|---| | Long-only | +295.7% | 298 | — | | Short-only | -37.9% | 140 | -1.61 | | Combined | +265.8% | 438 | 1.61 | The short leg did not just underperform. It carried the same magnitude of t-statistic as the combined system, with the opposite sign, and it dragged the aggregate from something you could argue about into the noise floor. The short book was not dead weight. It was actively destroying the evidence that the long book worked. ## Why Decompose by Direction First A dual-direction system is two strategies stapled together with a shared parameter set. The entry logic is symmetric on paper — golden cross long, death cross short — but the return distributions on either side of zero are not symmetric at all. Aggregating them hides that asymmetry behind a single equity curve. Decomposition is the cheapest diagnostic you have. If one leg has a positive expectancy and the other has a negative one, the combined t-stat is a blend of two different processes and means very little. You are not testing "does trend following work." You are testing "does trend following work, averaged over two markets with different structural properties, weighted by trade count." That is a question nobody asked. The fix is not to re-weight or re-optimize. It is to measure each leg on its own, then decide what the evidence actually supports. ### Implementation: Same Engine, Filter by Sign The key discipline is that you do not write a second backtester for the long-only variant. You run the exact same engine, record every trade with its direction, and slice the trade log afterward. This guarantees the two legs are directly comparable — same fills, same costs, same sizing.

python from dataclasses import dataclass import numpy as np import pandas as pd @dataclass class Trade: symbol: str direction: int # +1 long, -1 short entry_time: pd.Timestamp exit_time: pd.Timestamp entry_px: float exit_px: float size: float # notional at entry def trade_pnl(t: Trade, fee_bps: float = 5.0) -> float: gross = t.direction * (t.exit_px - t.entry_px) / t.entry_px fees = 2 * fee_bps / 1e4 return t.size * (gross - fees) def run_engine(prices: dict[str, pd.DataFrame], fast: int = 20, slow: int = 50) -> list[Trade]: """Dual-direction EMA crossover. One position per symbol at a time.""" trades = [] for sym, df in prices.items(): ef = df["close"].ewm(span=fast, adjust=False).mean() es = df["close"].ewm(span=slow, adjust=False).mean() state = 0 entry_px = entry_t = None for ts, f, s, px in zip(df.index, ef, es, df["close"]): sig = 1 if f > s else -1 if state == 0: state, entry_px, entry_t = sig, px, ts elif sig != state: trades.append(Trade(sym, state, entry_t, ts, entry_px, px, size=1.0)) state, entry_px, entry_t = sig, px, ts return trades

Now the decomposition itself. This is the part worth institutionalizing — put it in a shared module so every strategy report includes it by default.

python def leg_stats(trades: list[Trade]) -> pd.DataFrame: rows = [] for leg, sign in [("long", 1), ("short", -1)]: pnls = [trade_pnl(t) for t in trades if t.direction == sign] if len(pnls) < 2: continue arr = np.array(pnls) tstat = arr.mean() / (arr.std(ddof=1) / np.sqrt(len(arr))) rows.append({"leg": leg, "n": len(arr), "total": arr.sum(), "mean": arr.mean(), "t": tstat}) allp = np.array([trade_pnl(t) for t in trades]) rows.append({"leg": "combined", "n": len(allp), "total": allp.sum(), "mean": allp.mean(), "t": allp.mean() / (allp.std(ddof=1) / np.sqrt(len(allp)))}) return pd.DataFrame(rows).set_index("leg")

Two notes on the statistics. First, per-trade t-stats are not the same as a daily-returns t-stat on the equity curve; they answer slightly different questions. Per-trade is fine for a diagnostic like this, but if you want to publish a number, compute the t-stat on the daily P&L series of each leg and let the trade-level view stay a screening tool. Second, if trades overlap across symbols, the independence assumption behind the t-stat is violated. For 7 majors running the same signal, correlation is high enough that the effective sample is smaller than 438. That makes the combined p = 0.107 optimistic, not pessimistic — another reason the original result never deserved the benefit of the doubt. For completeness, the long-only variant is not a new engine. It is the same loop with the short branch suppressed:

python def run_long_only(prices, fast=20, slow=50): trades = [] for sym, df in prices.items(): ef = df["close"].ewm(span=fast, adjust=False).mean() es = df["close"].ewm(span=slow, adjust=False).mean() in_pos, entry_px, entry_t = False, None, None for ts, f, s, px in zip(df.index, ef, es, df["close"]): if not in_pos and f > s: # golden cross enters in_pos, entry_px, entry_t = True, px, ts elif in_pos and f < s: # death cross exits, no reverse trades.append(Trade(sym, 1, entry_t, ts, entry_px, px, 1.0)) in_pos = False return trades

Golden cross enters, death cross exits, flat in between. No reverse, no short. The trade count drops from 438 to 298 — exactly the long leg of the dual-direction run, which is the check that your filter is doing what you think it is. ## Why Shorting a Trend Follower Is Structurally Hard Here The short leg was not unlucky. It was fighting three structural forces at once, and none of them show up in a parameter sweep. *Upward skew in the underlying.* Crypto majors over a four-year window spent most of their time in a positive drift regime. A trend follower's short entries cluster right after a death cross — that is, after a decline has already happened. In a market with positive drift, the expected value of being short immediately after a drawdown is negative even if the signal has some genuine momentum content. You are systematically selling after the move and buying back into the mean reversion. *Wick-heavy pops.* Crypto has no circuit breakers and thin books on the way up. Short positions get stopped or squeezed by single-bar wicks that leave no trace on a close-to-close backtest if your fills assume the close. The asymmetry is brutal: a long position caught in a wick-down is a drawdown, a short position caught in a wick-up is often a liquidation event at a price worse than any bar's close. Backtests systematically flatter shorts because they fill at benign prices. *Negative carry.* Funding on perpetuals is positive in bullish regimes, which means shorts pay to hold. Over four years that is a persistent bleed on top of the directional loss. If your backtest does not model funding, your short leg looks better than it is. If it does, the -37.9% is the honest number and it likely understates the real-world drag. Put together: the short side of a symmetric crossover is short a positively skewed, wick-prone, negative-carry asset class using a signal that enters late. That is not a parameter problem. No combination of 15/60 or 25/80 fixes the structure. This is why the correct response to a failing leg is usually deletion, not repair — the search space for "repair" is mostly overfitting in disguise. ## The Discipline of Shipping Only What Passes Deleting the short leg raised the return to +295.7% on 298 trades. It did not raise the t-statistic into significance. Long-only is still positive-but-not-significant, and pretending otherwise would be the same mistake in a new costume. So the label on the dashboard changed. The strategy is not promoted to live. It is downgraded to observation tier: a paper-trading observer that runs the long-only logic, logs every signal, and reports the same statistics on a rolling basis until the evidence accumulates. The dashboard text says exactly that — no green badge, no "live" tag, just the numbers and the tier. The rule that makes this work is mechanical, not judgment-based:

python def tier(t_stat: float, n: int, min_n: int = 200) -> str: if n < min_n: return "observation" # not enough evidence either way if abs(t_stat) >= 2.0: return "live-eligible" if t_stat > 0: return "observation" # positive but unproven return "retired" def dashboard_row(leg: str, stats: pd.Series) -> dict: return { "leg": leg, "n": int(stats["n"]), "total_pct": round(100 * stats["total"], 1), "t": round(float(stats["t"]), 2), "tier": tier(float(stats["t"]), int(stats["n"])), "note": "positive but not significant" if stats["t"] < 2 and stats["t"] > 0 else "", }

Three properties matter here. The threshold is pre-registered, so you cannot move the goalposts after seeing the result. The tier is a pure function of the stats, so the dashboard cannot disagree with the data. And "observation" is a real state with real work attached — the observer keeps logging, and the strategy can only graduate by accumulating evidence, not by someone deciding it feels ready. Parking the short leg as a paper observer rather than deleting it entirely is the second half of the discipline. You keep the measurement running at zero cost. If the regime shifts — funding flips persistently negative, or the market develops sustained downtrends — the short leg's stats will show it, and you will have four more years of honest data instead of a hunch. What you do not do is force it live because the long book needed a hedge, or because a symmetric strategy looks more elegant in a slide. ## What Actually Changed The final state: one engine, two legs measured separately, one leg deleted from live consideration, the survivor labeled honestly as unproven and parked in observation tier. The headline number went from +265.8% with a misleading aggregate t-stat to +295.7% with a clear statement that it is still not significant. That is a worse-looking result than the original backtest and a much better one to build on. The decomposition did not find alpha. It found the reason the alpha was invisible, and then it refused to pretend the remainder was more than it was. DSR came out at 1.000. Coin-block Monte Carlo showed a 0% ruin rate across hundreds of randomized pool combinations. Split-half stability was positive in both halves of the trade sequence. I shipped it, and the strategy was garbage, because the backtest that produced those numbers had a lookahead bug that leaked future candle data into the entry decision. The uncomfortable lesson: all three layers evaluate the statistical properties of one trade sequence. They assume that sequence was generated honestly. None of them audits how trades were generated. A poisoned sequence can be perfectly well-behaved statistically — in fact, a lookahead bug usually makes it more well-behaved, because the strategy is effectively peeking at the answer. High DSR, zero ruin, clean split-half — that's exactly what a leak looks like. This post is the four-layer design I run now, with the code signatures and a table of what each layer actually catches. The fourth layer is the one that would have saved me. ## Layer 1: Deflated Sharpe Ratio The DSR (Bailey & López de Prado) adjusts an observed Sharpe ratio for the number of trials you ran, and for the non-normality of returns. If you tried 40 parameter sets and kept the best, the DSR asks: given 40 trials, skew, and kurtosis, is this Sharpe still distinguishable from the maximum you'd expect from noise?

python import numpy as np from scipy.stats import norm def deflated_sharpe_ratio( returns: np.ndarray, n_trials: int, sr_variance: float | None = None, periods_per_year: int = 252, ) -> float: """ Returns the probability that the true Sharpe exceeds zero, after deflating for n_trials and return non-normality. returns: per-period (e.g. daily) strategy returns, chronological n_trials: number of configurations you actually evaluated sr_variance: variance of Sharpe across your trials; if None, use the estimator below (conservative for small n_trials) """ r = np.asarray(returns, dtype=float) r = r[np.isfinite(r)] n = r.size if n < 30 or n_trials < 1: return 0.0 mu, sd = r.mean(), r.std(ddof=1) if sd == 0: return 0.0 sr = mu / sd # per-period Sharpe g1 = ((r - mu) ** 3).mean() / sd**3 g2 = ((r - mu) ** 4).mean() / sd**4 # Variance of the Sharpe estimator under skew/kurtosis sr_var = (1 - g1 * sr + (g2 - 1) / 4 * sr**2) / (n - 1) if sr_variance is None: # Expected max of n_trials draws from N(0, sr_var) e_max = np.sqrt(sr_var) * ( (1 - np.euler_gamma) * norm.ppf(1 - 1 / n_trials) + np.euler_gamma * norm.ppf(1 - 1 / (n_trials * np.e)) ) else: e_max = np.sqrt(sr_variance) * norm.ppf(1 - 1 / n_trials) z = (sr - e_max) / np.sqrt(sr_var) return float(norm.cdf(z))

Two things matter operationally. First, n_trials must be honest — every grid point, every filter variant, every "quick check" counts. Second, the DSR is only as good as the return series you feed it. It has no opinion on whether that series is real. ## Layer 2: Coin-Block Monte Carlo I don't bootstrap individual trades. Trades cluster — volatility regimes, correlated entries, streaks. So I resample in blocks with random block boundaries, and I randomize the pool composition across hundreds of runs: which assets or sub-strategies are included, in what weights, drawn from the eligible universe. The output I care about is the ruin rate — the fraction of simulated paths that breach a drawdown or capital threshold.

python def coin_block_monte_carlo( trade_pnls: np.ndarray, n_sims: int = 500, mean_block: int = 10, ruin_dd: float = 0.25, initial_capital: float = 1.0, rng: np.random.Generator | None = None, ) -> dict: """ Resample the trade sequence in random-length blocks and measure the fraction of paths that breach ruin_dd. trade_pnls: per-trade PnL as a fraction of capital, chronological mean_block: average block length (geometric block lengths) ruin_dd: drawdown threshold as fraction of peak equity """ rng = rng or np.random.default_rng(7) pnl = np.asarray(trade_pnls, dtype=float) n = pnl.size ruins, finals = 0, np.empty(n_sims) for s in range(n_sims): path, i = [], 0 while len(path) < n: blk = max(1, int(rng.geometric(1.0 / mean_block))) start = rng.integers(0, n) idx = (start + np.arange(blk)) % n # wrap-around blocks path.extend(pnl[idx]) i += blk eq = initial_capital + np.cumsum(np.array(path[:n])) peak = np.maximum.accumulate(np.concatenate([[initial_capital], eq])) dd = 1.0 - eq / peak[1:] if dd.max() >= ruin_dd: ruins += 1 finals[s] = eq[-1] return { "ruin_rate": ruins / n_sims, "median_final": float(np.median(finals)), "p05_final": float(np.percentile(finals, 5)), }

This layer answers: given this sequence's dependence structure, how fragile is the equity path? It does not answer whether the sequence could have been produced by the strategy in the first place. If the sequence is a fabrication, the Monte Carlo is resampling fiction with great rigor. ## Layer 3: Split-Half Stability The simplest and most brutal check: split the trade sequence in two, require positive expectation in both halves. I also require the halves to be roughly comparable in magnitude — a strategy whose entire edge lives in the first 30% of trades is a regime artifact, not a strategy.

python def split_half_stability( trade_pnls: np.ndarray, min_trades_per_half: int = 30, max_decay_ratio: float = 0.5, ) -> dict: """ Require positive mean in both halves and that the second half retains at least max_decay_ratio of the first half's mean. trade_pnls: per-trade PnL, chronological """ pnl = np.asarray(trade_pnls, dtype=float) n = pnl.size if n < 2 * min_trades_per_half: return {"pass": False, "reason": "insufficient trades"} h1, h2 = pnl[: n // 2], pnl[n // 2 :] m1, m2 = h1.mean(), h2.mean() ok = m1 > 0 and m2 > 0 and m2 >= max_decay_ratio * m1 return { "pass": bool(ok), "mean_h1": float(m1), "mean_h2": float(m2), "decay_ratio": float(m2 / m1) if m1 > 0 else float("nan"), }

Split-half catches overfitting to a specific time window, edge decay, and single-regime dependence. It cannot catch a leak, because a leak inflates both halves. My lookahead bug made the second half look better than the first, and I read that as "edge improving." ## The Blind Spot Here's the thing all three layers share: they take trade_pnls as an axiom. Every one of them is a function of the sequence, not of the process that generated it. The DSR deflates for how many sequences you tried, not for whether each sequence was built from legal information. The Monte Carlo reshuffles the sequence. Split-half cuts it. None of them opens the strategy code and asks: at the moment of this entry decision, what data was visible? My bug was mundane. The feature pipeline computed a rolling statistic with center=True on a window that extended past the decision timestamp, then joined features to signals on bar index. The backtest engine was happy to serve it. Every trade was entered with a few bars of future information baked into the feature. The resulting sequence had a Sharpe that survived 40 trials, zero ruin across 500 block simulations, and positive expectation in both halves. DSR = 1.000. Ruin = 0%. Both halves positive. All three green, all three meaningless. The failure mode is structural: statistical validation is orthogonal to implementation correctness. You can have a flawless validation stack and a broken data path, and the stack will report success with total confidence. ## Layer 4: Replay Testing The fix is to stop trusting the backtest's trade sequence and instead force two independent code paths to agree on the same history. Replay testing drives the production trading code — the same signal generator, the same risk module, the same order logic that runs live — over real historical candles, bar by bar, with the data feed truncated at each decision timestamp. Then it diffs the resulting trades against the backtest's trades. Any divergence is a bug in one of the two, and the diff tells you where.

python from dataclasses import dataclass from typing import Callable, Iterable @dataclass class Candle: ts: int open: float high: float low: float close: float volume: float @dataclass class Trade: ts: int side: str qty: float price: float def replay_production( candles: Iterable[Candle], on_candle: Callable[[list[Candle]], list[Trade]], warmup: int = 200, ) -> list[Trade]: """ Drive production code over history with a strictly causal feed. on_candle receives ONLY candles visible at the current timestamp. Returns the trade list the production code would have produced. """ history: list[Candle] = [] trades: list[Trade] = [] for c in candles: history.append(c) if len(history) <= warmup: continue # The engine must never see beyond `history` here. trades.extend(on_candle(history)) return trades def compare_trade_streams( backtest: list[Trade], replay: list[Trade], ts_tolerance: int = 0, qty_rel_tol: float = 1e-6, ) -> dict: """ Diff two trade streams. Any mismatch is a validation failure, regardless of what layers 1-3 said. """ if len(backtest) != len(replay): return {"match": False, "reason": "trade count differs", "backtest_n": len(backtest), "replay_n": len(replay)} mismatches = [] for i, (b, r) in enumerate(zip(backtest, replay)): if abs(b.ts - r.ts) > ts_tolerance or b.side != r.side: mismatches.append({"i": i, "kind": "timing_or_side", "backtest": b, "replay": r}) continue rel = abs(b.qty - r.qty) / max(abs(b.qty), 1e-12) if rel > qty_rel_tol: mismatches.append({"i": i, "kind": "qty", "backtest": b, "replay": r}) return {"match": not mismatches, "mismatches": mismatches[:20], "n_mismatches": len(mismatches)}

The critical property is causality enforcement. The replay harness hands the production code a list that ends at the current bar — there is no future data in the object, so a center=True bug becomes a crash or an obviously wrong feature, not a silent edge. If the production code needs a warmup window, it gets only the past. If it tries to index forward, it raises. Two practical notes from running this: 1. Diff at the trade level, not the signal level. Signals can diverge harmlessly due to float ordering. Trades — timestamp, side, quantity — must match. A single-trade mismatch is worth a full investigation. 2. Run replay on the same candles the backtest used, byte for byte. If the backtest reads from a research store and replay reads from a production feed, you're testing data plumbing, not strategy logic. Pin one dataset. When I added this layer, the lookahead bug surfaced in minutes. The replay trade stream diverged from the backtest at the first signal after warmup, and the diff pointed straight at the feature join. The first three layers had been reporting success on a sequence the production code could never have generated. ## What Each Layer Catches | Layer | Catches | Does not catch | |---|---|---| | DSR | Multiple-testing inflation, non-normal Sharpe, selection bias across trials | Lookahead, data leakage, execution mismatches, regime fragility | | Coin-block Monte Carlo | Path fragility, drawdown/ruin risk under dependence, pool-composition sensitivity | Whether the trade sequence is achievable by production code | | Split-half | Edge decay, single-regime dependence, time-window overfitting | Leaks (they inflate both halves), implementation divergence | | Replay | Lookahead, engine/production divergence, data-path bugs, timestamp handling | Overfitting, multiple testing, ruin risk, regime dependence | The layers are complementary, and the order matters less than the coverage. Layers 1–3 audit the statistics of the sequence. Layer 4 audits the provenance of the sequence. You need both, and the provenance check is the one that's cheap to skip and expensive to omit. The general principle: every validation layer should be tested against a deliberately broken strategy. Feed your DSR a known-leaky sequence — it should pass, and now you know its blind spot. Feed your replay harness a strategy with a one-bar peek — it should fail loudly. A validation layer you've never seen fail is a layer you don't understand. You...","published":true,"published_at":"2026-11-06T08:30:51.347Z","slug":"anti-overfitting-for-retail-backtests-few-rules-fewer-trades-more-skepticism-5e4o","path":"/mattleeee/anti-overfitting-for-retail-backtests-few-rules-fewer-trades-more-skepticism-5e4o","url":"https://dev.to/mattleeee/anti-overfitting-for-retail-backtests-few-rules-fewer-trades-more-skepticism-5e4o","comments_count":0,"public_reactions_count":0,"page_views_count":10,"published_timestamp":"2026-11-06T08:30:51Z","body_markdown":"## Why the Fifth Rule Is Usually Noise Every discretionary backtest dies the same death. You start with a simple idea — buy the pullback, exit on a failed retest. It returns something mediocre. So you add a filter: skip trades when volatility is too high. The equity curve improves. You add another: only take longs when the trend filter agrees. Better. One more: require volume confirmation. Now the curve looks great, and you have five conditions, each of which was chosen because it made the past look better. That is the entire failure mode in one sentence. Each added rule is a new degree of freedom, and every degree of freedom is a chance to fit noise rather than signal. A retail backtest with ten boolean conditions and a parameter grid is not a strategy; it is a compression algorithm for historical data. The compression is excellent. The generalization is not. The defensive doctrine here is short enough to memorize: - Few rules over many. Every added condition must survive its own audit. - Fewer trades with clear invalidation over many marginal ones. A trade you cannot invalidate is not a trade, it is a hope. - Distrust any edge that only appears after tuning. If it needs the search to exist, the search created it. - Re-test on unseen data before believing anything. Including your own improvements. Below is how to apply that in code and process. ## The Rule That "Improved" the Backtest by Rejecting 52 Trades A concrete case. The base strategy took ~400 trades over several years and had a modest expectancy. Adding a filter — "skip entries when the 20-day realized volatility is above its 80th percentile" — removed 52 trades and lifted the profit factor from 1.18 to 1.41. Tempting. Ship it. But that filter was not proposed in advance. It was proposed after looking at the losing trades, noticing they clustered in high-volatility regimes, and encoding that observation as a rule. That is a hypothesis generated from the same data used to test it. The 52 rejected trades are not out-of-sample evidence; they are the training set for the filter. The fix is an A/B audit of the rule itself, treated as a separate hypothesis with its own test:

python import numpy as np import pandas as pd def ab_audit(trades: pd.DataFrame, filter_mask: pd.Series, n_perm: int = 5000, seed: int = 7) -> dict: """ trades: one row per trade with columns ['pnl', 'entry_time']. filter_mask: True where the filter would REJECT the trade. Question: is the rejected subset's mean pnl meaningfully worse than the kept subset, beyond what random rejection of the same size gives? """ rng = np.random.default_rng(seed) pnl = trades["pnl"].to_numpy() rejected = filter_mask.to_numpy() k = rejected.sum() observed_gap = pnl[~rejected].mean() - pnl[rejected].mean() gaps = np.empty(n_perm) for i in range(n_perm): idx = rng.choice(len(pnl), size=k, replace=False) mask = np.zeros(len(pnl), dtype=bool) mask[idx] = True gaps[i] = pnl[~mask].mean() - pnl[mask].mean() p_value = (gaps >= observed_gap).mean() return { "n_trades": len(pnl), "n_rejected": int(k), "observed_gap": round(observed_gap, 4), "p_value": round(p_value, 4), }

If the p-value is not small — and with 52 trades out of 400, it usually is not — the filter is not evidence of a regime effect. It is a random subset that happened to contain losers. The honest outcome is to drop the rule and keep the simpler system. There is a second, cheaper audit: does the rule survive on a holdout period it never saw? Split by time, not randomly. Random splits leak regime information across the boundary; time splits mimic what you will actually face.

python def time_split_ab(trades: pd.DataFrame, filter_mask: pd.Series, split_frac: float = 0.6) -> pd.DataFrame: trades = trades.sort_values("entry_time").reset_index(drop=True) filter_mask = filter_mask.loc[trades.index] cut = int(len(trades) * split_frac) rows = [] for name, sl in [("in_sample", slice(0, cut)), ("holdout", slice(cut, None))]: sub = trades.iloc[sl] rej = filter_mask.iloc[sl] rows.append({ "period": name, "pf_all": profit_factor(sub["pnl"]), "pf_kept": profit_factor(sub.loc[~rej, "pnl"]), "n_rejected": int(rej.sum()), }) return pd.DataFrame(rows) def profit_factor(pnl: pd.Series) -> float: wins = pnl[pnl > 0].sum() losses = -pnl[pnl < 0].sum() return round(wins / losses, 3) if losses > 0 else float("inf")

A rule that lifts profit factor in-sample but does nothing in the holdout is a rule you invented, not one the market gave you. ## The Multiple-Comparisons Trap in Parameter Sweeps Parameter sweeps are where retail backtests quietly become data mining. Run 12 variants of a stop-loss, 8 of a take-profit, 5 of a trend filter — that is 480 configurations. The best one will look good even if every configuration is pure noise. The maximum of 480 random draws is not a discovery; it is the expected maximum of 480 random draws. You can quantify this. Under the null hypothesis of no edge, the best in-sample Sharpe across N independent trials has an expected value roughly on the order of sqrt(2 * ln(N)) times the standard error of a single trial. That is why "I tested 500 combos and found one with Sharpe 2.1" is not impressive. Two practical defenses: *1. Correct the significance threshold.* If you test N configurations and want a family-wise error rate of α, require each individual result to beat a Bonferroni-style threshold of α/N. Crude, but it kills most false discoveries outright.

python def sweep_report(results: pd.DataFrame, alpha: float = 0.05) -> pd.DataFrame: """ results: columns ['config_id', 'sharpe', 'n_trades', 'p_value'] p_value: from a permutation test of that config's expectancy vs zero. """ n = len(results) threshold = alpha / n out = results.copy() out["bonferroni_threshold"] = threshold out["survives"] = out["p_value"] < threshold return out.sort_values("p_value")

*2. Count your trials honestly.* Every variant you ran and discarded is a trial. If you cannot remember how many you ran, your effective N is larger than you think, and your best result is weaker than it looks. Keep a log.

python import json, datetime def log_trial(path: str, config: dict, metrics: dict) -> None: with open(path, "a") as f: f.write(json.dumps({ "ts": datetime.datetime.utcnow().isoformat(), "config": config, "metrics": metrics, }) + "\n")

The log is uncomfortable to keep precisely because it makes the search visible. That is the point. ## Honest Metrics Most retail backtests report the wrong numbers. Total return and win rate are the worst offenders — win rate in particular rewards strategies that take many small wins and one catastrophic loss. Report these instead: ### Expectancy net of fees Per-trade expectancy after realistic costs, including slippage. If your edge disappears at 2x your assumed fees, it was never an edge.

python def expectancy(pnl: pd.Series, fees_per_trade: float) -> float: net = pnl - fees_per_trade return round(net.mean(), 4)

### Profit factor Gross wins over gross losses. Above ~1.3 net of costs is worth a second look; below 1.1 is noise territory. But profit factor alone hides path dependence — pair it with drawdown. ### Monthly consistency Bucket returns by calendar month. A strategy that makes all its money in three months out of forty-eight is a regime bet, not a system.

python def monthly_consistency(returns: pd.Series) -> pd.DataFrame: monthly = (1 + returns).resample("ME").prod() - 1 return pd.DataFrame({ "month": monthly.index.strftime("%Y-%m"), "return": monthly.round(4), "positive": monthly > 0, })

Look at the fraction of positive months and the worst month. If 80% of the total return comes from the top 10% of months, you are not running a strategy; you are waiting for a handful of lucky regimes and paying fees the rest of the time. ## The Person Who Built It Cannot Approve It This is the cultural rule, and it matters more than any code above. The person who tuned the parameters has a vested interest in the curve. They have seen every variant. They know which filter "works." That knowledge is contamination, and it does not wash off. The fix is procedural, not technical: the backtester must never be the approver. Someone else — a partner, a friend, a second account with a written checklist — reviews the out-of-sample report without seeing the parameter search. They get the final config, the holdout results, and the trial count. Nothing else. If the strategy only convinces the person who built it, it does not convince anyone. A minimal approval checklist: - Rule count is small and each rule has an A/B audit with a p-value. - The trial log exists and the best result survives a multiple-comparisons correction. - Expectancy is positive after 2x assumed fees. - Profit factor and monthly consistency hold on the holdout period. - A second person, who did not tune it, signed off. If any line fails, the strategy goes back to the simplest version that passed. Usually that is the version with two rules and a lot of skipped trades — which is exactly the version most people discard on the way to a prettier curve. It has a schedule. Understanding that schedule is the difference between a pullback filter that protects you and one that quietly starves your strategy. The four phases look like this: *Accumulation.* Price ranges tight, often for days. On low timeframes you see repeated sweeps of the same high with no follow-through. Volume is thin and inconsistent. The operator is absorbing supply and building a position without moving price. Retail sees a boring chart. *Markup.* This is where the structure breaks. Price leaves the range in continuous legs — impulse, shallow dip, impulse, shallow dip. The dips are engineered to be just deep enough to shake out weak hands and just short enough that anyone waiting for a "proper" retracement never gets filled. Volume expands on the legs and contracts on the dips. This is the phase most pullback strategies are built for, and the phase where they fail. *Distribution.* The operator needs exit liquidity. The buy-side liquidity created by the markup — stop orders above highs, breakout traders, FOMO limit orders — is the target. Price often pushes one final leg into that liquidity, then stalls. Ranges form near the highs. The dips get deeper and the recoveries get weaker. By the time a textbook pullback signal prints, you are buying into the distribution, not the trend. *Collapse.* Once the operator is out, the bid disappears. The same continuous legs that went up go down, faster, because there is no absorption underneath. The critical point: the markup and the distribution look similar on a single candle and completely different across a sequence. Your pullback filter has to distinguish them, and most don't. ## Why Pullback Quality Degrades in Pump Regimes A classic pullback entry says: wait for three consecutive red candles, a retracement to a moving average or a Fibonacci level, then buy the first green confirmation. This works in liquid, mean-reverting markets where participants are numerous and independent. In an orchestrated pump, it breaks for structural reasons: 1. The dips are too shallow. A continuous-leg markup might retrace 15–25% of the prior leg on the 15m chart. A three-candle pullback filter calibrated on BTC or ETH expects 40–60%. You get no entries during the entire profitable body of the move. 2. The dips are too fast. When the operator does allow a deeper dip, it happens in one or two violent candles, not a clean three-candle sequence. Your filter sees a single red candle followed by a green one and rejects it as "not enough confirmation." 3. The liquidity is manufactured. The pullback itself creates the buy-side liquidity the operator needs to distribute into. A pullback that looks clean on the chart is, in this regime, often the signal that distribution is starting. The filter is not just late — it is systematically inverted at the top. 4. Volatility is non-stationary. The same coin can have a 2% average true range during accumulation and a 12% ATR during markup. A fixed pullback depth threshold is meaningless across those regimes. The result in backtests is a filter that rejects the middle of the move (too shallow) and accepts the top (deep enough, but for the wrong reason). It looks conservative. It is actually selective in the worst possible way. ## What the Backtest Data Showed I ran a simple momentum strategy on a basket of mid-cap altcoins over eighteen months, tagging each entry by phase using a manual label set (accumulation / markup / distribution / collapse) derived from volume and range behavior. The strategy had two variants: - Strict: require a three-candle pullback with a retracement of at least 38% of the prior leg, plus a volume contraction on the pullback. - Relaxed: require a single-candle dip below the prior leg's midpoint, no volume condition, with a hard invalidation below the leg low. The strict variant produced roughly 40% of the trade count of the relaxed variant. More importantly, the distribution of returns was inverted relative to expectation: | Variant | Trades | Win rate | Avg R (markup) | Avg R (distribution) | |---|---|---|---|---| | Strict | 112 | 51% | +0.9 | −1.4 | | Relaxed | 287 | 44% | +1.3 | −1.1 | The strict filter missed most of the markup entries because the dips were too shallow, and it still got caught in distribution because the deeper dips near the top satisfied its retracement threshold. The relaxed version took more trades, won less often, but captured a larger share of the markup body and — critically — its invalidation cut losses faster in distribution. The conclusion was not "loosen everything." It was: the confirmation step was doing the wrong job. It was supposed to filter out bad entries, but in this regime the confirmation was filtering out good ones and letting bad ones through. The invalidation step was doing almost none of the work. ## The Practical Response Three changes, applied together. None of them is optional if you want the others to work. ### 1. Relax the confirmation Stop requiring a multi-candle pullback. In a continuous-leg markup, the entry signal is the resumption, not the depth of the dip. A single candle that dips below the prior leg's midpoint and closes back above it is enough. You are trading the operator's need to keep the leg going, not a textbook retracement.

python def pullback_entry(df, leg_lookback=8, dip_frac=0.5): """ df: OHLCV DataFrame with columns open, high, low, close, volume. Returns a boolean Series: True on bars where a relaxed pullback entry triggers. """ # Identify the most recent impulse leg: highest high over lookback vs lowest low before it leg_high = df["high"].rolling(leg_lookback).max() leg_low = df["low"].rolling(leg_lookback).min() leg_mid = leg_low + (leg_high - leg_low) * dip_frac # Dip below midpoint and close back above it on the same bar dipped = df["low"] < leg_mid reclaimed = df["close"] > leg_mid green = df["close"] > df["open"] # Require the leg to be an actual impulse: range expansion vs prior window prior_range = (df["high"] - df["low"]).rolling(leg_lookback * 2).mean().shift(leg_lookback) impulse = (leg_high - leg_low) > 1.5 * prior_range return dipped & reclaimed & green & impulse

The impulse condition matters. Without it, you are buying every dip in every range. With it, you are only buying dips inside a leg that has already shown range expansion. ### 2. Tighten the invalidation Because the confirmation is weaker, the invalidation must be harder. Place it below the leg low, not below the pullback low, and make it a hard stop with no discretion. In a pump regime, a break of the leg low is the operator telling you the markup is over. Respect it immediately.

python def apply_invalidation(df, entries, leg_lookback=8): """ For each entry, set stop at the low of the impulse leg. Returns a Series of stop prices aligned to entry bars (NaN elsewhere). """ leg_low = df["low"].rolling(leg_lookback).min() stops = leg_low.where(entries) return stops def position_size(equity, entry_price, stop_price, risk_frac=0.005): """ Size down: risk_frac is deliberately small because regime certainty is low. """ risk_per_unit = entry_price - stop_price if risk_per_unit <= 0: return 0.0 return (equity * risk_frac) / risk_per_unit

Note the risk_frac=0.005. That is half a percent of equity per trade, not the 1–2% you might use in a liquid market. The reason is in the next section. ### 3. Size down because regime certainty is lower The relaxed confirmation raises your trade count and lowers your per-trade edge. The tighter invalidation caps your loss per trade but also increases the frequency of stops — you will get shaken out of legs that continue. Both effects mean your estimate of the win rate is noisier and your drawdowns are more frequent. The correct response is not to compensate with leverage. It is to reduce risk per trade and let the larger sample of trades do the work. A strategy with a 44% win rate and a 1.3R average winner is profitable, but only if you survive the losing streaks. Half a percent per trade gives you room for a 15-trade losing streak without a 10% drawdown.

python def regime_adjusted_risk(phase, base_risk=0.005): """ phase: 'accumulation' | 'markup' | 'distribution' | 'collapse' Scale risk by how much you trust the regime label. """ scale = { "accumulation": 0.5, # low volatility, but no trend yet "markup": 1.0, # the regime the strategy is built for "distribution": 0.3, # structure is degrading, cut exposure "collapse": 0.0, # do not trade } return base_risk * scale.get(phase, 0.0)

The phase label can be approximate. You don't need a perfect classifier; you need a coarse filter that stops you from sizing up in distribution. Volume contraction on legs, weakening recovery highs, and range compression near the top are enough to flag it. ## What Changes in Practice The strict pullback filter felt safe. It was not. It rejected the body of the move and accepted the top, because it was measuring the wrong thing — depth of retracement instead of continuation of structure. The fix is a trade-off, not a free lunch. You take more trades, win less often, and rely on a hard stop and smaller size to keep the tail controlled. In a pump-driven market, that is the honest shape of the edge: you are not predicting the operator's next move, you are participating in the leg while it lasts and getting out when the structure breaks.
