A monitoring server had nine scheduled tasks, each firing hourly. The machine stays logged in permanently—it runs a dashboard that needs an interactive session. That detail matters, because it meant every task launched a console window on the desktop. Nine tasks, hourly, each flashing a black CMD rectangle over whatever was on screen. Unacceptable for a machine someone actually looks at.

The tasks did real work: pulling metrics, rotating logs, syncing a couple of directories. They were created over time by different tools—some by hand with `schtasks`, some by a third-party installer, one by an old deployment script. That mix turned out to be the source of the second problem.

## Diagnosis: Why `schtasks /change` Failed

The obvious fix is to flip each task to run whether the user is logged on or not, which suppresses the window:

```batchfile
schtasks /change /tn "\Metrics\HourlyPull" /ru "SYSTEM"
```

That failed with a parameter error:

```plaintext
ERROR: The parameter is incorrect.
```

No further detail. The task existed, the name was right, the quoting was right. I checked the XML with `schtasks /query /tn "\Metrics\HourlyPull" /xml` and the task definition looked normal. The failure was not in my command.

The real cause is in how `schtasks.exe` is built. It is a thin command-line parser sitting on top of the Task Scheduler COM API (the `ITaskService` interface family). When you run `/change`, it reads the existing task, mutates a few properties, and writes it back. Tasks created by other tools—installers, deployment frameworks, anything that talks to the COM API directly—often carry property combinations that the `schtasks` parser does not expect. In this case, the offending task had a principal block with a logon type the CLI did not know how to round-trip. The COM call inside returned `E_INVALIDARG`, and `schtasks.exe` surfaced it as the generic "parameter is incorrect."

The lesson: when a task was not created by `schtasks`, do not try to fix it with `schtasks`. Go to the same API layer the creating tool used.

### PowerShell Reaches the Same API Without the Parser

`Set-ScheduledTask` and `Get-ScheduledTask` are PowerShell cmdlets that wrap the identical COM interface. They do not re-parse a command line, so they do not choke on properties the CLI does not understand. The same mutation that failed above worked immediately:

```powershell
$t = Get-ScheduledTask -TaskName "HourlyPull" -TaskPath "\Metrics\"
$t.Principal.LogonType = "S4U"
$t.Principal.RunLevel = "Highest"
Set-ScheduledTask -InputObject $t
```

`S4U` (service-for-user) runs the task without storing a password and without an interactive session, which is exactly the behavior needed to suppress the console window. `Highest` avoids the elevation prompt path.

But this only solved part of the problem. Switching every task to `S4U` changes the security context, and a couple of the tasks depended on the interactive user's mapped drives and environment. Rewriting all nine tasks was more invasive than necessary. There is a lighter, more surgical pattern.

## The VBS Wrapper Pattern

The window appears because the task action is `cmd.exe` or `powershell.exe`, and those are console applications. When Task Scheduler launches a console application in an interactive session, Windows creates a console window. You can suppress that at the launch site rather than by changing the task principal.

The launch site is `wscript.exe`. It is a GUI-subsystem host: it has no console of its own. When it starts a child process, it can ask the shell to run that child with a hidden window. That is the entire trick.

### The Two-Line Runner

Create `silent_runner.vbs`:

```vbscript
Set sh = CreateObject("WScript.Shell")
sh.Run "cmd /c """ & WScript.Arguments(0) & """", 0, False
```

Line by line:

- `CreateObject("WScript.Shell")` gives us the shell automation object.
- `sh.Run` takes three arguments: the command line, the window style, and whether to wait.
- Window style `0` means hidden. This is the parameter that kills the black rectangle.
- `False` means do not wait for the child to exit. The task returns immediately; the actual work runs detached.

The command line is `cmd /c "target.bat"`. The double quotes inside the VBS string are escaped by doubling them, so the final command is `cmd /c ""`. The `cmd /c` wrapper is there so the batch file runs in a proper command interpreter with its own environment, and exits when done.

Two lines, no dependencies, works on every Windows version since XP.

### Wiring It Into Task Scheduler

Each task action changes from:

```plaintext
Program:   C:\Scripts\metrics_pull.bat
Arguments: (none)
```

to:

```plaintext
Program:   wscript.exe
Arguments: "C:\Scripts\silent_runner.vbs" "C:\Scripts\metrics_pull.bat"
```

That is the whole change. The task still runs as the same user, in the same session, with the same environment. Only the window is gone.

### The PowerShell Loop

Nine tasks, done in one pass. This script rewrites the action of every task under a given path:

```powershell
$runner = "C:\Scripts\silent_runner.vbs"
$path   = "\Metrics\"

Get-ScheduledTask -TaskPath $path | ForEach-Object {
    $task = $_
    foreach ($action in $task.Actions) {
        # Only rewrite actions that launch a console host directly.
        if ($action.Execute -match '^(cmd|powershell|pwsh)(\.exe)?$') {
            $target = $action.Arguments
            if ($target -match '^/c\s+(.+)$') { $target = $matches[1].Trim('"') }

            $action.Execute   = "wscript.exe"
            $action.Arguments = "`"$runner`" `"$target`""
        }
    }
    Set-ScheduledTask -InputObject $task | Out-Null
    Write-Host "Rewrote $($task.TaskName)"
}
```

A few things worth noting:

- `Get-ScheduledTask -TaskPath` returns the task objects, and `Set-ScheduledTask -InputObject` writes them back through the COM API. No CLI parsing, no `E_INVALIDARG`.
- The `Execute` check is a guard. If a task already runs a non-console program, leave it alone.
- The regex `^/c\s+(.+)$` strips a leading `/c` from the arguments, which is how `schtasks` stores a `cmd /c` invocation. If the arguments are empty, `$target` stays empty and the rewrite is skipped by the guard—handle that case if your tasks vary.
- `Out-Null` keeps the pipeline quiet; `Set-ScheduledTask` returns the updated task object otherwise.

If you want to be more conservative, add a `-WhatIf` style dry run first by printing `$action.Execute` and `$action.Arguments` before mutating.

## Verification

Two checks, both fast.

First, confirm the task definition changed:

```powershell
(Get-ScheduledTask -TaskName "HourlyPull" -TaskPath "\Metrics\").Actions |
    Format-List Execute, Arguments
```

Expected output:

```plaintext
Execute   : wscript.exe
Arguments : "C:\Scripts\silent_runner.vbs" "C:\Scripts\metrics_pull.bat"
```

Second, confirm the behavior. Run the task on demand and watch the desktop:

```powershell
Start-ScheduledTask -TaskName "HourlyPull" -TaskPath "\Metrics\"
```

No window should appear. Then check that the work actually happened—the log file, the output directory, whatever the batch file produces. A hidden window that fails silently is worse than a visible one, so verify the side effects, not just the absence of the window.

If the task still flashes a window, the usual cause is that `wscript.exe` is not the actual launcher. Some tasks are configured with an "action" that is a script host already, or a task created by a tool that wraps the action in its own launcher. Query the raw XML to see what is really stored:

```powershell
Export-ScheduledTask -TaskName "HourlyPull" -TaskPath "\Metrics\"
```

Look at the `` block. If `` is not `wscript.exe`, the rewrite did not take.

## When This Pattern Is the Right Choice

The VBS wrapper is not the only way to hide a task window. The alternatives and their trade-offs:

- **Run as `S4U` or `SYSTEM`**: suppresses the window because there is no interactive session, but changes the security context. Breaks tasks that depend on mapped drives, user environment variables, or interactive credentials.
- **Use `pythonw.exe` instead of `python.exe`**: works if your task is a Python script, but not if it is a batch file or a PowerShell script. Also changes how stdout and stderr behave.
- **Set the task to "Run whether user is logged on or not"**: same security-context change as `S4U`.
- **The VBS wrapper**: keeps the same user, same session, same environment, same stdout/stderr behavior. Only the window is hidden. This is the least invasive option, which is why it was the right one here.

The pattern generalizes. Any time you need to launch a console process without a console window—from Task Scheduler, from a startup script, from another automation tool—`wscript.exe` plus a two-line VBS is the smallest possible shim. It has no runtime dependency, no installation, and it survives Windows updates because it uses an API that has been stable for two decades.

## Adapting It to Python

If you prefer to keep everything in Python, you can generate the VBS and the task definitions from a script. This is useful when you have many tasks to convert or when the task list changes:

```python
import subprocess
from pathlib import Path

RUNNER = Path(r"C:\Scripts\silent_runner.vbs")
RUNNER.write_text(
    'Set sh = CreateObject("WScript.Shell")\n'
    'sh.Run "cmd /c """ & WScript.Arguments(0) & """", 0, False\n',
    encoding="ascii",
)

def rewrite_task(task_name: str, task_path: str, target_bat: str) -> None:
    """Point an existing task at the silent runner."""
    ps = (
        f"$a = (Get-ScheduledTask -TaskName '{task_name}' "
        f"-TaskPath '{task_path}').Actions[0]; "
        f"$a.Execute = 'wscript.exe'; "
        f"$a.Arguments = '\"{RUNNER}\" \"{target_bat}\"'; "
        f"Set-ScheduledTask -TaskName '{task_name}' -TaskPath '{task_path}' "
        f"-Action $a | Out-Null"
    )
    subprocess.run(["powershell", "-NoProfile", "-Command", ps], check=True)

for name in ("HourlyPull", "HourlyRotate", "HourlySync"):
    rewrite_task(name, r"\Metrics\\", rf"C:\Scripts\{name}.bat")
```

The Python layer is just orchestration. The actual suppression still happens in the VBS, because that is the only place the window style can be set.

## Summary

The failure mode was specific: `schtasks /change` returned a generic parameter error on tasks created by other tools, because the CLI's parser could not round-trip properties the COM API produced. The fix was to stop using the CLI and use PowerShell's `Set-ScheduledTask`, which reaches the same API without the parsing layer. The window suppression was a separate concern, solved by routing each task action through `wscript.exe` and a two-line VBS that runs the real command with window style `0`. Nine tasks, one loop, no more black rectangles.

```plaintext
2024-03-11 09:14:02 INFO  worker started (pid 18432)
2024-03-11 09:14:02 INFO  worker pid 18432 exited with code 0
2024-03-11 09:14:02 INFO  restarting worker...
2024-03-11 09:14:02 INFO  worker started (pid 19004)
2024-03-11 09:14:02 INFO  worker pid 19004 exited with code 0
2024-03-11 09:14:02 INFO  restarting worker...
```

A tight restart loop with no error. The child processes were being created and immediately killed. No Python exception, because the kill happened at the OS level before the interpreter could raise anything.

The culprit was Sangfor aTrust, the endpoint security suite that ships with a lot of enterprise environments. It hooks process creation and, depending on policy, blocks or silently terminates child processes that don't match an allowlist. A daemon that spawns workers looks exactly like the kind of behavior a security product is built to stop. The watchdog made it worse: every restart attempt was another blocked `CreateProcess` call, which is why the loop was so tight.

You can confirm this pattern quickly. Run a trivial spawner and see whether the child ever gets to execute:

```python
import subprocess
import sys

# If this prints nothing, the child never ran.
# That is a security-policy block, not a Python bug.
proc = subprocess.Popen(
    [sys.executable, "-c", "print('child alive')"],
    stdout=subprocess.PIPE,
    stderr=subprocess.PIPE,
)
out, err = proc.communicate(timeout=10)
print("returncode:", proc.returncode)
print("stdout:", out)
print("stderr:", err)
```

If `returncode` is non-zero and both streams are empty, the child was killed before it could write anything. That's the signature.

## Why Task Scheduler Survives Where Daemons Don't

The key insight is that Task Scheduler is not a user process. It's a Windows service (`Schedule`) running in session 0, and the processes it launches are created by the service host, not by your Python interpreter. Sangfor aTrust and similar suites generally allow this path because:

1. **The parent is a trusted system service.** Process-creation hooks are usually scoped by parent identity. `svchost.exe` running the Schedule service is on the allowlist; `python.exe` spawning `python.exe` is not.
2. **Task Scheduler is a documented management surface.** Enterprise security products are designed not to break the OS's own scheduling. Blocking it would break Windows Update, backup agents, and half the management stack. So it stays open.
3. **No persistent parent process.** There's nothing long-running to kill. Each task run is a short-lived process, launched, executed, and reaped by the service. The "daemon" is the scheduler itself, which you don't have to keep alive.

That last point is the real architectural win. Instead of building a process that stays up and supervises itself, you hand the supervision to the OS. The OS is very good at it and the security suite leaves it alone.

## Mapping Jobs to Tasks

Once I accepted the model, the migration was mechanical. Each recurring job becomes one scheduled task with four things defined: a trigger, a working directory, a timeout, and a result convention.

### Trigger

Triggers replace your `while True: sleep(...)` loop. For a job that runs every five minutes, use a daily trigger with a repetition interval. For a job that runs once at 06:00 on weekdays, use a weekly trigger with the day set. The scheduler handles the clock; you don't need `time.sleep` at all.

### Working Directory

This is the most common source of "it works in my terminal but not in the task." Task Scheduler defaults the working directory to `C:\Windows\System32`. Any relative path in your script breaks. Always set an explicit working directory, and make your script resolve its own paths rather than relying on `os.getcwd()`:

```python
from pathlib import Path

# Anchor everything to the script location, not the process cwd.
BASE_DIR = Path(__file__).resolve().parent
LOG_DIR = BASE_DIR / "logs"
STATE_DIR = BASE_DIR / "state"
LOG_DIR.mkdir(exist_ok=True)
STATE_DIR.mkdir(exist_ok=True)
```

### Timeout

Task Scheduler has a per-task execution time limit. Set it. A hung job that holds a database connection or a lock file forever is worse than a failed job. For a job expected to run in under two minutes, set the limit to ten. The scheduler terminates the process and records a failure, which you can see.

### Result Convention

The scheduler records the process exit code. Use it. A script that always exits 0 is invisible to the scheduler's history. Exit non-zero on failure so the last-run result is meaningful:

```python
import sys
import logging

logging.basicConfig(
    filename=str(LOG_DIR / "job.log"),
    level=logging.INFO,
    format="%(asctime)s %(levelname)s %(message)s",
)

def main() -> int:
    try:
        run_job()
    except Exception:
        logging.exception("job failed")
        return 1
    return 0

if __name__ == "__main__":
    sys.exit(main())
```

## Creating Tasks from Python

You can register tasks by hand in the GUI, but that doesn't scale and it isn't reviewable. I keep a single `setup_tasks.py` that registers every job idempotently. It shells out to `schtasks.exe`, which is present on every Windows install and needs no extra dependency.

```python
import subprocess
from pathlib import Path

PYTHON = r"C:\Python311\python.exe"
BASE = Path(r"C:\jobs")

TASKS = [
    {
        "name": "QuantJob_Fetch",
        "script": BASE / "fetch.py",
        "schedule": "MINUTE /MO 5",
        "timeout_min": 10,
    },
    {
        "name": "QuantJob_Report",
        "script": BASE / "report.py",
        "schedule": "DAILY /ST 06:00",
        "timeout_min": 30,
    },
]

def register(task: dict) -> None:
    cmd = [
        "schtasks", "/Create",
        "/TN", task["name"],
        "/TR", f'"{PYTHON}" "{task["script"]}"',
        "/SC", *task["schedule"].split(),
        "/RL", "LIMITED",          # run with normal user rights
        "/F",                       # overwrite if it exists
    ]
    subprocess.run(cmd, check=True, capture_output=True, text=True)

    # Set working directory and execution time limit separately.
    # schtasks has no direct flag for cwd, so use XML for full control.
    set_task_xml(task)

def set_task_xml(task: dict) -> None:
    # Export, patch, re-import. This is the reliable way to set
    # WorkingDirectory and ExecutionTimeLimit.
    name = task["name"]
    xml = subprocess.run(
        ["schtasks", "/Query", "/TN", name, "/XML"],
        check=True, capture_output=True, text=True,
    ).stdout

    xml = xml.replace(
        "",
        f"{BASE}",
    )
    xml = xml.replace(
        "PT72H",
        f"PT{task['timeout_min']}M",
    )
    # StartWhenAvailable: if the machine was off at trigger time,
    # run the task as soon as it comes back.
    if "false" in xml:
        xml = xml.replace(
            "false",
            "true",
        )

    subprocess.run(
        ["schtasks", "/Create", "/TN", name, "/XML", "-", "/F"],
        input=xml, check=True, capture_output=True, text=True,
    )

if __name__ == "__main__":
    for t in TASKS:
        register(t)
        print(f"registered {t['name']}")
```

The XML round-trip is the part people skip and then wonder why their working directory is `System32`. `schtasks` doesn't expose `/WorkingDirectory` or `/ExecutionTimeLimit` as command-line flags, so you export the task, edit the XML, and re-import. It's ugly but it's stable and it's scriptable.

## Operational Wins You Get for Free

The migration wasn't just about surviving the security suite. Three things got better immediately.

### Reboot survival

A daemon dies on reboot and you need a service wrapper, a startup shortcut, or a login script to bring it back. A scheduled task just runs on its trigger. If the trigger is a repetition interval, the task resumes on the next interval after boot. If you need it to catch up, `true` makes the scheduler run a missed task as soon as the machine is back. That single flag replaced an entire startup-recovery code path in my old daemon.

### Built-in retry

Task Scheduler has a native retry policy. If a task fails, you can configure it to retry every N minutes for M attempts. That's the watchdog pattern, implemented by the OS, and it doesn't spawn child processes from your interpreter so the security suite has nothing to object to. You set it in the task's Settings tab, or in XML:

```xml

  PT5M
  3

```

### Last-run result codes

Every task records its last run time and result code. You can query them without any custom instrumentation:

```python
import subprocess
import csv
from io import StringIO

def last_results() -> list[dict]:
    out = subprocess.run(
        ["schtasks", "/Query", "/FO", "CSV", "/V"],
        check=True, capture_output=True, text=True,
    ).stdout
    rows = list(csv.DictReader(StringIO(out)))
    return [
        {
            "name": r["TaskName"],
            "status": r["Status"],
            "last_run": r["Last Run Time"],
            "result": r["Last Result"],
        }
        for r in rows
        if r["TaskName"].startswith("\\QuantJob_")
    ]

for row in last_results():
    print(row)
```

`Last Result` is the process exit code. `0` means success, anything else means the job failed and you can look at your log file. That's a free health dashboard for every job on the machine. I pipe this into a small status page and I haven't written a single line of process-monitoring code since.

## What I'd Do Differently

Two things. First, I'd set explicit working directories from day one instead of debugging `FileNotFoundError` for an afternoon. Second, I'd design every job to be idempotent and short-lived. The scheduler model rewards jobs that start, do one thing, and exit. If your job needs to hold state between runs, write it to a file or a database rather than keeping it in memory. The process is gone when it's done; that's the point.

The daemon pattern isn't wrong in general. It's wrong on a locked-down corporate machine where you don't control the process-creation policy. Task Scheduler is the platform's own answer to "run this on a schedule," and in that environment, using the platform's answer is the shortest path to something that actually stays running.

title: How to Get Product Prices and Stock from Shopify and WooCommerce Stores (Python and No-Code)
description:
Competitor price tracking, product research and catalog migrations all start with the same question: how do I get every product of a store, with prices and stock, without copying it by hand? For the two most common e-commerce platforms you usually do not need to parse HTML at all.

Option 1: WooCommerce's public Store API in Python

Most WooCommerce stores answer at /wp-json/wc/store/v1/products (the Store API that WooCommerce's block-based cart and checkout use). It needs no key, returns up to 100 products per page, and includes prices, stock and categories.

import json
import urllib.request


def get(url):
    req = urllib.request.Request(url, headers={"User-Agent": "Mozilla/5.0 (price-check-script)"})
    with urllib.request.urlopen(req) as r:
        return json.load(r)


def woo_products(store, pages=2):
    out = []
    for page in range(1, pages + 1):
        items = get(f"https://{store}/wp-json/wc/store/v1/products?per_page=100&page={page}")
        if not items:
            break
        for p in items:
            pr = p["prices"]
            unit = 10 ** pr["currency_minor_unit"]  # prices come in cents as strings
            out.append({
                "name": p["name"],
                "price": int(pr["price"]) / unit,
                "regular_price": int(pr["regular_price"]) / unit,
                "currency": pr["currency_code"],
                "in_stock": p["is_in_stock"],
                "url": p["permalink"],
            })
    return out


for p in woo_products("woocommerce.com", pages=1)[:5]:
    print(p["price"], p["currency"], "|", p["name"], "|", "in stock" if p["in_stock"] else "out of stock")

Two details that trip people up: prices are strings in the currency's minor unit (cents), and product names come HTML-escaped (– and friends), so unescape them with html.unescape before you compare titles.

Shopify: products.json, and the 429 wall

Every Shopify store serves its catalog at /products.json?limit=250&page=N: title, handle, vendor, product type, tags, images and a variants list with price, compare_at_price, sku and available. For a single collection, use /collections/<handle>/products.json.

The catch is rate limiting. While writing this post, four different Shopify stores answered 429 Too Many Requests to the very first request from my own connection. Once you scrape more than a few stores, you need retries with back-off, pauses between pages, and ideally a different network than your laptop.

Other things you will end up handling:

  • Which platform is it? A list of competitor domains does not tell you whether a store runs Shopify or WooCommerce.
  • Variants: a T-shirt is one product with many sizes and colors, each with its own price, SKU and stock.
  • Sale prices: compare_at_price on Shopify and regular_price vs price on WooCommerce.
  • Change tracking: to know what changed since yesterday, you have to keep yesterday's prices.

Option 2: a ready-made Actor that also tracks changes

I packaged all of that as an Apify Actor: Shopify & WooCommerce Products Scraper. You paste store domains or URLs, it detects the platform, and it returns one clean row per product. A real item from a run (shortened):

{
  "store": "www.beardbrand.com",
  "platform": "shopify",
  "title": "Bold Fortune Classic Beard Bundle",
  "brand": "Beardbrand",
  "productType": "Bundles",
  "url": "https://www.beardbrand.com/products/bold-fortune-classic-beard-bundle",
  "currency": "USD",
  "price": 119.85,
  "compareAtPrice": 141,
  "onSale": true,
  "available": false,
  "variantCount": 1,
  "change": null
}

What it adds:

  • Filters for keywords, excluded words, minimum and maximum price, in stock only and on sale only
  • Variants with their own price, SKU and stock, and the product description as plain text, when you turn them on
  • Return only changes: schedule it daily and each run returns only new products and products whose price or stock changed, with previousPrice and previousAvailable
  • Export to JSON, CSV or Excel, or send results to Google Sheets, Slack or a webhook

From code:

from apify_client import ApifyClient

client = ApifyClient("YOUR_APIFY_TOKEN")
run = client.actor("webobsidians/shopify-woocommerce-products-scraper").call(
    run_input={"stores": ["www.beardbrand.com", "woocommerce.com"], "maxProductsPerStore": 100, "onlyOnSale": True}
)
for p in client.dataset(run["defaultDatasetId"]).iterate_items():
    print(p["store"], "|", p["title"], "|", p["price"], p["currency"])

It costs $1.00 per 1,000 products plus $0.00005 per run start, with platform usage included, and Apify's free plan includes monthly credit to try it.

Which one should you use?

  • One WooCommerce store, once: the Python script above.
  • Many stores, Shopify at scale, or daily price-change alerts: the Actor.

Either way, you are reading catalogs that the stores publish for every visitor, so keep request rates polite.

title: How to Scrape Job Listings from Greenhouse, Lever and Ashby Career Pages (Python and No-Code)
description:
If you want the open jobs of a list of companies (for a job board, market research, a recruiting tool or your own job search), you do not need to scrape HTML career pages one by one. Most companies host their career page on an applicant tracking system (ATS), and several of them publish the open jobs as public JSON.

This post shows the three easiest ones in Python, the catches you will hit after that, and a no-code option for when you need many companies and many systems.

Option 1: public job board APIs in Python

Greenhouse, Lever and Ashby each have a public, read-only endpoint per company. You only need the company's board name, which is usually in its careers URL (boards.greenhouse.io/stripe, jobs.lever.co/palantir, jobs.ashbyhq.com/ramp).

import json
import urllib.request


def get(url):
    # some job boards reject Python's default User-Agent, so send a normal one
    req = urllib.request.Request(url, headers={"User-Agent": "Mozilla/5.0 (job-list-script)"})
    with urllib.request.urlopen(req) as r:
        return json.load(r)


def greenhouse(board):
    data = get(f"https://boards-api.greenhouse.io/v1/boards/{board}/jobs")
    return [{"title": j["title"], "location": j["location"]["name"], "url": j["absolute_url"]}
            for j in data["jobs"]]


def lever(board):
    data = get(f"https://api.lever.co/v0/postings/{board}?mode=json")
    return [{"title": j["text"], "location": j["categories"].get("location"), "url": j["hostedUrl"]}
            for j in data]


def ashby(board):
    data = get(f"https://api.ashbyhq.com/posting-api/job-board/{board}")
    return [{"title": j["title"], "location": j.get("location"), "url": j["jobUrl"]}
            for j in data["jobs"]]


for name, jobs in [("stripe", greenhouse("stripe")), ("palantir", lever("palantir")), ("ramp", ashby("ramp"))]:
    print(name, len(jobs), "open jobs, e.g.", jobs[0]["title"], "-", jobs[0]["location"])

That is enough for a handful of companies on these three systems. Things to know before you scale it:

  • Full descriptions are optional. Greenhouse returns them with ?content=true; Lever includes descriptionPlain; Ashby has descriptionPlain and, with ?includeCompensation=true, salary ranges when the company publishes them.
  • Every system has its own shape. Locations, departments, remote flags, dates and salaries live in different fields, so you will write a normalizer per system.
  • You first have to know which ATS a company uses. A list of company names does not tell you whether to call Greenhouse or Workday.
  • Workday is the hard one. Large companies often use Workday, which has no simple per-company feed: each company has its own tenant, data center number and site name, and the job list is a paged POST endpoint.
  • Monitoring needs state. To get "only jobs that are new since yesterday", you have to remember what you already saw.

Option 2: a ready-made Actor for many companies and systems

I packaged all of that as an Apify Actor: ATS Jobs Scraper. You paste company names, domains or careers URLs, and it finds the system behind each one (Workday, Greenhouse, Lever, Ashby, Workable, SmartRecruiters, Recruitee, Personio and Breezy) and returns one clean row per job:

{
  "company": "Linear",
  "ats": "ashby",
  "title": "Senior / Staff Fullstack Engineer",
  "department": "Product",
  "team": "Engineering",
  "location": "Europe",
  "isRemote": true,
  "workplaceType": "remote",
  "employmentType": "Full-time",
  "salary": null,
  "url": "https://jobs.ashbyhq.com/linear/d3bc1ced-3ce4-4086-a050-555055dbb1ff",
  "applyUrl": "https://jobs.ashbyhq.com/linear/d3bc1ced-3ce4-4086-a050-555055dbb1ff/application",
  "descriptionText": "At Linear, we're building the product development system for teams and agents. ..."
}

On top of the script above it gives you:

  • Filters for title keywords (or keywords in the description), excluded words, locations, remote only, departments and "posted within the last N days"
  • Salary in one format (min, max, currency, interval) when the company publishes it
  • Return only new jobs: schedule it daily and each run returns only the jobs that earlier runs did not return
  • Export to JSON, CSV or Excel, or push results to Google Sheets, Slack or a webhook with Apify integrations

From code, use the Apify client:

from apify_client import ApifyClient

client = ApifyClient("YOUR_APIFY_TOKEN")
run = client.actor("webobsidians/ats-jobs-scraper").call(
    run_input={"companies": ["stripe", "linear.app", "palantir"], "keywords": ["engineer"], "remoteOnly": True}
)
for job in client.dataset(run["defaultDatasetId"]).iterate_items():
    print(job["company"], "|", job["title"], "|", job["location"], "|", job["url"])

It costs $1.00 per 1,000 jobs plus $0.00005 per run start, with platform usage included, and Apify's free plan includes monthly credit to try it.

Which one should you use?

  • A few companies on Greenhouse, Lever or Ashby: the Python script.
  • Many companies, Workday, a daily "new jobs" feed, or a spreadsheet for a non-developer: the Actor.

Either way, you are reading job posts that the companies publish for everyone, so keep request rates reasonable.

title: How PERT Estimation Assists in Better Project Planning
description:
Project planning is a crucial component for the successful execution of any project, be it a website, a product development or a management task. Sufficient planning would involve breaking down all the tasks to be handled and estimating the time you would take in completing each of them. But this isn't necessarily an easy task to do!

That's where PERT comes in. PERT - which is short for Program Evaluation and Review Technique - is a project management technique that involves predicting task durations based on three separate duration estimates as opposed to a single estimate or guess. https://projecttimecalculator.com/pert-calculator/

What is PERT Estimation?

PERT calculation considers three different values for the tasks: Optimistic; Pessimistic; and Most Likely.

The longest realistic time the job should take.

The specified time that a task will probably take when performed normally.

Pessimistic estimate (P): The upper time limit within which the task will be completed when faced with unforeseen difficulties.

With these three estimates, project managers will be able to plan a schedule more realistically and help plan for delay.

How to Calculate Expected Project Time

The PERT formula is simple and gives more weight to the most likely estimate.

Expected Time = (O + 4M + P) ÷ 6

A website development project can be estimated with three values: an optimistic estimate of 5 days, a most likely estimate of 8 days, and a pessimistic estimate of 17 days.

Using the formula:

Expected Time = (5 + 4 × 8 + 17) ÷ 6

Expected Time = 54 ÷ 6 = 9 days.

This is an estimate of the length of time it will take for team members to complete a specific task.

Why Is PERT Important for Project Managers?

Project managers are regularly faced with uncertain time frames for completing projects, evolving expectations for project deliverables and unexpected difficulties during the life cycle of a project. PERT (Program Evaluation Review Technique) provides a method of reducing the uncertainty associated with developing a schedule for a project through the development of numerous estimates.

This software helps teams determine which tasks require additional time, allocate resources more efficiently, and make better decisions regarding project deadlines. It is especially beneficial for projects that include multiple sequential tasks.

A PERT (program evaluation and review technique) calculator can help you calculate the expected time for a project to be completed, its variability, the standard deviation of its completion time, and how likely it is that you will finish the project before your deadline.

Estimation Techniques that Improve Projects Schedules

In developing timelines for projects, realistic estimates should always be considered. There is no need to make estimates under the assumption of idealistic situations. It's important to think about the possible problems, availability of necessary resources, and complexity of tasks to be accomplished.
The splitting up of a large task into manageable small parts can assist with the estimate as well. After all of the manageable small parts have been estimated for the amount of time required to accomplish them, then the total will give you the estimate of completing the large task.

Conclusion

PERT (Program Evaluation & Review Technique) may be a great tool for project managers in developing better schedules and dealing with uncertainty of project deadlines. After making an evaluation of the best, the most probable, and the worst case scenarios, the project manager can get a better schedule and be closer to meeting project deadlines.

There would be much more organization and effectiveness in project management if there were proper estimation techniques and identifying of potential unknowns.

title: How to get every job from a company's careers page as JSON (Greenhouse, Lever, Ashby and 7 more)
description:
If you are building a job board, a hiring-signal tool for sales, or a "tell me when Company X posts a data role" alert, you do not need to scrape LinkedIn or fight anti-bot walls. Most companies run their careers page on an applicant tracking system (ATS), and every major ATS publishes the open jobs through a public feed that the careers page itself reads.

Here is how to use those feeds directly, what breaks when you do it at scale, and a shortcut if you would rather not maintain ten parsers.

Step 1: find out which ATS the company uses

Open the company's careers page and click any job. The link usually gives it away:

If the job link goes to The ATS is Company identifier
boards.greenhouse.io/airbnb/... Greenhouse airbnb
jobs.lever.co/spotify/... Lever spotify
jobs.ashbyhq.com/ramp/... Ashby ramp
jobs.smartrecruiters.com/BoschGroup/... SmartRecruiters BoschGroup
apply.workable.com/huggingface/... Workable huggingface

If the job opens on the company's own domain, view the page source and search for greenhouse, lever, ashby, workable or smartrecruiters: embedded boards load a script that contains the identifier.

Step 2: call the feed 

import requests

def greenhouse(company):
    r = requests.get(f"https://boards-api.greenhouse.io/v1/boards/{company}/jobs", params={"content": "true"}, timeout=30)
    r.raise_for_status()
    return [{"title": j["title"], "location": j["location"]["name"], "url": j["absolute_url"],
             "department": ", ".join(d["name"] for d in j.get("departments", []))} for j in r.json()["jobs"]]

def lever(company):
    r = requests.get(f"https://api.lever.co/v0/postings/{company}", params={"mode": "json"}, timeout=30)
    r.raise_for_status()
    return [{"title": j["text"], "location": j["categories"].get("location"), "url": j["hostedUrl"],
             "team": j["categories"].get("team")} for j in r.json()]

def ashby(company):
    r = requests.get(f"https://api.ashbyhq.com/posting-api/job-board/{company}", params={"includeCompensation": "true"}, timeout=30)
    r.raise_for_status()
    return [{"title": j["title"], "location": j.get("location"), "url": j.get("jobUrl"),
             "salary": (j.get("compensation") or {}).get("compensationTierSummary")} for j in r.json()["jobs"]]

print(len(greenhouse("airbnb")), "Airbnb jobs")
print(len(lever("spotify")), "Spotify jobs")
print(len(ashby("ramp")), "Ramp jobs")

That is enough for a weekend project. A November 2026 run returned about 200 jobs for Airbnb, 90 for Spotify and 180 for Ramp, each in under a second.

The feed URLs for all ten ATS (including Workable, Recruitee, Personio, Teamtailor, Gem and Breezy HR), with what each returns, are in this reference repo: ats-job-feeds.

Step 3: what breaks at scale

Once you follow a few hundred companies, the work moves from fetching to normalising:

  • Ten formats. Greenhouse and Ashby return JSON objects, Lever a JSON array, Personio XML, Teamtailor RSS. Dates come as ISO strings, epoch milliseconds or RFC 822.
  • Locations and remote work. "Remote (US)", "Hybrid - London", a list of offices, or a separate workplaceType field, depending on the ATS.
  • Salary. Ashby gives a structured range for about half of jobs; Lever only when the employer fills it in; Greenhouse not at all in the public feed. When pay is written in the description, you need text parsing or an LLM to get numbers out.
  • Paging. SmartRecruiters returns 100 postings per page; large employers have thousands.
  • Only new jobs. For alerts you have to remember which IDs you already sent, per company and per filter set.
  • Identifiers that are not the company name. Ubisoft2 on SmartRecruiters, case-sensitive slugs on Lever.

The shortcut

I got tired of maintaining this and packaged it as an Apify Actor: Company Careers Jobs API. You paste careers pages, board URLs or plain company names; it finds the ATS, reads the public feed and returns one format for ten ATS (Greenhouse, Lever, Ashby, SmartRecruiters, Workable, Recruitee, Personio, Teamtailor, Gem, Breezy HR). It has an "only new jobs" mode for scheduled runs and optional AI fields (visa sponsorship with the quote, normalised salary, seniority, skills).

from apify_client import ApifyClient

client = ApifyClient("<YOUR_APIFY_TOKEN>")
run = client.actor("sandy_cornfield/company-jobs-api").call(run_input={
    "companies": ["https://www.figma.com/careers/", "lever:spotify", "ashby:ramp"],
    "keywords": ["engineer"],
    "onlyNew": True,
})
for job in client.dataset(run["defaultDatasetId"]).iterate_items():
    print(job["companySlug"], "|", job["title"], "|", job["workplaceType"], "|", job["url"])

It costs $2 per 1,000 jobs, with no monthly fee. If you only need one ATS, there are single-ATS versions for Greenhouse, Lever and Ashby.

Disclosure: I built those Actors. The feeds in steps 1 and 2 are free to use on their own; be polite with them (cache, a few requests per second at most).

title: GPT-6.2 Astra vs. Sol in Kilo: The Great Pyramid Test
description:
From ancient wonders to artificial intelligence: we asked the latest Astra and Sol to build a pyramid

OpenAI just released GPT-6.2 Astra and GPT-6.2 Sol. Astra is the new frontier model for the hardest projects. Sol is the fast, versatile model for everyday work.

We wanted to see the difference on a real task, not just on a chart. So we gave both models the same big prompt: build an interactive 3D scene where workers construct a pyramid, with boats bringing stones along a river. Then we put the results side by side.

This post covers what OpenAI announced, what we saw, and how you can run the same test yourself in Kilo Desktop, including on the ChatGPT plan you already pay for.

Meet Astra and Sol

Astra costs $8 per million input tokens and $40 per million output tokens. Sol costs $2 and $10. Both are built to get better results on demanding tasks with fewer output tokens, so you get more done within your usage limits.

These are standard API rates. Higher rates apply above 272K input tokens.

  • Astra's price dropped. Its input and output token prices are 20% lower than GPT-6 Astra's, with a 60% discount on cached input.

  • Sol's price held. It keeps GPT-6.1 Sol's rates.

  • Where to find them. Both are in ChatGPT Work and Codex for Plus, Pro, Enterprise and Edu users, and in the API as gpt-6.2-astra and gpt-6.2-sol. Ultrafast is available for both at launch.

What OpenAI says they can do

The headline claim: Sol gets close to Astra at a fraction of the cost. On FrontierCode 2.0, which checks whether changes to real codebases meet maintainers' merge standards, Sol comes within 0.5 points of Astra at about one-fifth the cost (both at max).

For Agents' Last Exam, OpenAI notes that its Fable 5.2 results leave out nine tasks that used a fallback model.

The AA-3D result is the one that made us curious. OpenAI says Astra and Sol can turn a written brief into an interactive browser experience, and that Astra builds frontends that look and work better, particularly for websites, gaming and 3D design. A pyramid-building scene is a good way to test that.

The test: build a pyramid

One of my colleagues, Marius Wichtner, built a pyramid benchmark for fun. It gives each model the same prompt and shows the finished apps side by side.

The prompt asks for a polished, interactive 3D scene of ancient Egyptian workers building a pyramid, with boats delivering materials along a river. Workers have to coordinate heavy loads. Boats have to dock, unload and keep materials flowing. The model picks the tech, the style and the building method.

We ran it with GPT-6.2 Astra and GPT-6.2 Sol, both through Kilo. Both models chose Three.js, Vite and TypeScript, and both built a pyramid of 204 stones.

This is one run per model, so treat it as a first vibe look.

Astra looks like a film set. Sol looks like a strategy game.

Both models finished the job: 204 of 204 stones placed, all 8 courses built. The difference is in how they got there.

Astra pyramid building in progress

Sol pyramid building in progress

On looks alone, Astra wins clearly. Up close, the sledge, the ropes and the dock planks hold up. Sol's scene is simpler, but its panel tells you exactly what every crew is doing, which makes the work easy to follow.

That fits what OpenAI says about the two models: Astra for the work where quality matters most, Sol for everyday use. It is one run each, though. Run it a few times on your own tasks before you pick.

Run the test yourself in Kilo Desktop

Kilo Desktop is now generally available, and it is a good place for this kind of comparison. Every task gets its own session, and each session can run in its own git worktree, so two models never fight over the same files.

  1. Download Kilo Desktop and open an empty project.

  2. Start a session and give it its own git worktree. Pick GPT-6.2 Astra.

  3. Start a second session in a new worktree. Pick GPT-6.2 Sol.

  4. Paste the prompt below into both.

  5. When they finish, open each result in the built-in browser and compare.

Here is the prompt:

Build a polished, interactive 3D scene that simulates ancient Egyptian workers constructing a pyramid, supported by boats delivering materials along a river.

Choose the technical approach, visual style, layout, construction methods, and animation techniques yourself. Focus on meeting the requirements below rather than following a prescribed design.

Core Requirements

- Show construction from the beginning through to a finished, explorable pyramid.
- Workers must perform meaningful work and coordinate intelligently. Heavy loads should be handled collectively, with believable assignments and movement.
- Boats should travel convincingly, stop at suitable docking or anchor points, unload, and support a functional flow of materials to the builders.
- Include different useful wares, not only stones. Their delivery and use should matter to construction.
- Build the entrance, tunnels, and burial spaces as part of the simulation. Workers must construct them, rather than simply revealing a prebuilt interior.
- The finished pyramid should function as a believable virtual tomb with a connected, walkable interior.
- Draw inspiration from plausible ancient Egyptian engineering. Use judgment where historical methods are uncertain.

Experience and Quality

- Make the building, hauling, unloading, and underground work animations convincing, including when viewed up close.
- Different wares should have appropriate handling for their material, weight, and purpose. Avoid generic or cheap-looking motion, floating loads, unexplained transformations, and obvious clipping.
- Provide transparency and first-person buttons that remain available during construction.
- Transparency should make internal and underground work easy to inspect.
- First-person mode should offer a pleasant, responsive walking experience around accessible areas and through the finished interior.
- Keep the ordinary HUD minimal, retaining compact speed, reset, transparency, and first-person controls.
- Make underground information and navigation attractive and useful without cluttering the view.
- Ensure stable geometry and rendering, particularly inside the pyramid. Avoid flickering walls, visible gaps, and clunky movement.
- Use free tools and assets without requiring paid services.

Workflow and Delivery

- Build from scratch and stay in the current worktree.
- Implement and test the solution yourself, including the complete construction flow and exploration.
- Keep testing and iteration fast. Avoid endless analysis, repeated long benchmarks, or waiting through construction in real time for every check.
- Finish with a working application, start it, open the preview, and briefly report the results and any remaining limitations.

A few tips for a fair comparison:

  • Use the same Kilo Desktop version and settings for both models.

  • Run each model at least three times. One run can flatter or hurt either side.

  • Write down time and plan usage per run, so you can compare cost as well as looks.

  • Check the prompt's own requirements: boats docking, workers hauling together, a walkable interior, working transparency and first-person buttons.

Bring your ChatGPT plan to Kilo

You don't need an API key to try these models. With Sign in with ChatGPT, you pick "Continue with ChatGPT" in Kilo, and your requests draw on the Codex and ChatGPT Work usage included in your plan instead of per-token API billing.

  • Works across Kilo. Desktop, VS Code, JetBrains, the CLI, Cloud Agents, Code Reviews and the mobile app.

  • You stay in control. Per OpenAI, connecting an app adds no new allowance, and you can cap how much of your weekly plan Kilo uses in ChatGPT settings under Usage.

  • Your chats stay yours. Using your plan does not give Kilo access to your ChatGPT conversations or memories.

  • Switch freely. Use your plan's OpenAI models next to the 500+ models in the Kilo Gateway, from the same model picker.

For teams

Kilo now supports ChatGPT Business plans too. Admins enable "Use ChatGPT plan" for Kilo under Tenant settings, then External access in the OpenAI admin console, and can set a workspace-wide limit on how much of each member's included allowance approved services can use. Usage shows up in the OpenAI dashboard like any other connected app.

OpenAI's Sign in with ChatGPT docs list eligible plans (Go, Plus, Pro and Business) and the full admin steps.

Which one should you use?

Start with Sol for everyday work. It costs a quarter of Astra per token, and OpenAI's own FrontierCode result puts it within 0.5 points of Astra at about one-fifth the cost. Reach for Astra when quality matters most: 3D and visual work, long projects, and the hardest problems. In our pyramid test, that is where it pulled ahead.

The best answer depends on your tasks, and Kilo makes it easy to find out. Run both on the same job, compare the diffs, and keep the one you would merge. If you'd rather not choose, Auto Efficient picks the least expensive model proven capable of the task.

Download Kilo Desktop, connect your ChatGPT plan, and try the new Astra and Sol today. Then tell us what you build.

title: From Flaky Cypress Tests to a Maintainable Playwright Strategy
description:
From Flaky Cypress Tests to a Maintainable Playwright Strategy

Changing the testing framework was only part of the solution. The bigger challenge was building automation we could actually trust.

When Rerunning Tests Becomes Normal

If you've worked with automated testing long enough, you've probably experienced this:

A test fails in CI.

You investigate, rerun it, and suddenly everything is green.

Problem solved, right? 😅

Unfortunately, not really.

During my journey into QA and test automation, I've learned that flaky tests are more than just an annoying technical problem. They slowly affect how much confidence developers and QA engineers have in their test results.

When failures become normal, people eventually stop taking them seriously.

And that's a dangerous place for a regression suite to be.

Why We Started Moving Away from Cypress

We had been working with Cypress for our end-to-end testing, but as our automation grew, we started looking at how we could improve reliability, maintainability, and the overall testing architecture.

Playwright became our choice for moving forward.

It offered useful capabilities such as automatic waiting, powerful locators, browser tracing, and cross-browser testing.

But one thing became clear:

Migrating from Cypress to Playwright wouldn't magically fix our testing problems.

We could easily recreate the same issues in a different framework if we continued writing and maintaining tests the same way.

The framework was only one part of the equation.

Building a Strategy, Not Just Migrating Tests

Instead of simply rewriting Cypress tests into Playwright, we wanted to rethink how our automation should work.

A few things became particularly important.

1. Make tests independent

Tests should not rely on another test having executed successfully beforehand.

Each test needs a predictable starting point, so failures are easier to reproduce and investigate.

2. Stop relying on arbitrary waits

Waiting three seconds and hoping an element is ready isn't exactly a reliable testing strategy.

We want tests that wait for meaningful conditions rather than guessing how long an application needs.

3. Establish shared conventions

As more engineers contribute to automated tests, consistency becomes increasingly important.

How should we structure tests? How should we handle test data? When should we use API setup, and when should a test remain entirely UI-driven?

Having clear conventions helps prevent every engineer from inventing a different approach.

4. Make failures easier to investigate

A failed test should provide useful information.

Screenshots, traces, logs, and clear assertions can help us understand whether we're dealing with a real application bug or a problem in the automation itself.

The Real Challenge Is Maintaining Trust

One lesson I've taken from this experience is that test automation isn't just about increasing coverage.

You can have hundreds of automated tests, but if developers don't trust the results, how valuable are they?

A reliable regression suite should help teams make decisions.

When something fails, we should investigate it rather than automatically press rerun.

And when everything passes, we should have confidence that the tests actually verified meaningful behavior.

Final Thoughts

Moving from Cypress to Playwright has been an important part of improving our test automation approach.

But the biggest lesson wasn't about choosing one framework over another.

It was about recognizing that good test automation requires more than good tools. It requires good engineering practices.

Playwright gives us useful capabilities, but architecture, consistency, and maintainability are what make an automation strategy sustainable.

And let's be realistic: a new testing framework won't save us from writing bad tests. 😅

I'm curious how other teams have approached this.

Have you migrated from Cypress to Playwright? Did it improve test reliability, or did you discover that the bigger challenges weren't related to the framework at all?
