title: I Built a Claude Code Plugin Because I Was Becoming a Rubber-Stamp Reviewer
description:
My development team has two members: me and AI. And lately, I've been feeling like I'm becoming the less useful member of the team.

I've been using AI coding agents for years. Claude Code, and plenty of other tools. They're incredible at what they do, but somewhere along the way, my development process started looking like this:

Me: "Implement this feature."

AI: "Done! Changed 27 files, added 3,400 lines, refactored two modules. All tests passed."

Me: "LGTM."

Narrator: He did not, in fact, look.

The code gets written. Features get shipped. Productivity looks great. But here's what bothers me: Am I actually reviewing the code anymore, or am I just approving whatever the AI tells me?

And if I'm not making the technical decisions, what exactly is my role as a developer?

The problem isn't that AI writes code

I don't think developers need to manually write every line of code. That's not the point. The problem is that we're slowly outsourcing something much more important than typing: our judgment.

Think about how often this happens. The AI makes an architectural decision without asking you. It assumes a requirement that was never specified. It changes something outside the original scope. Then it confidently reports that all tests passed, and you trust the summary because reviewing everything yourself would take too long.

None of this necessarily means the AI is bad at coding. It means our development workflow hasn't caught up with how much code AI can produce.

I wanted a workflow where AI could do most of the implementation without quietly taking ownership of the decisions. I also didn't want to become an unpaid project manager, manually breaking everything into tiny tasks and supervising every step.

So I built human-rights.


GitHub: https://github.com/kiduki77/human-rights

AI writes the code. Humans own the decisions.

human-rights is an open-source Claude Code plugin built around a simple idea: Don't make humans review every line. Make sure they understand and approve the decisions that matter.

The requirements. The architecture. The risks. The acceptance criteria. And the evidence that the implementation actually works.

But there's an obvious problem with this approach. If every tiny change requires a design document, three approvals, and a meeting with yourself, nobody is going to use it.

So the workflow adapts to the task.

  1. Not every change deserves the same process

human-rights classifies development requests into four levels, from simple edits to high-risk changes.

Level

Example

Workflow

L0 — Direct

Center a login card

Make the change and check it

L1 — Focused

Add input validation hints

Short plan and targeted tests

L2 — Planned

Add Google authentication

Investigate, design, and review

L3 — Governed

Modify safety-critical control logic

Human approvals, integration tests, and final verification

The classification considers ambiguity, scope, architectural impact, risk, verification difficulty, and dependencies. A small UI change shouldn't require the same process as modifying authentication or controlling physical hardware.

For larger changes, the agent investigates the existing code, asks questions that could change the design, and creates a testable implementation plan. If the request is too large, it first breaks the work into smaller features that can be reviewed and verified independently.

The human decides what should happen. The AI figures out how to implement it.

  1. The AI cannot simply approve its own work

This was one of the most important design decisions. I didn't want to rely entirely on instructions like "Always ask the user for approval." An AI agent following a prompt is not the same thing as an enforced workflow.

So human-rights has two parts: a Claude Code skill that decides what process a task needs, and a deterministic Python runtime that enforces state transitions, approvals, test evidence, and failure handling.

Design approvals are tied to the approved plan, while final approvals are tied to the code being verified. If the plan changes, the previous design approval becomes invalid. If the code changes, the final approval becomes invalid too.

A test result is not accepted just because the agent says it passed. The runtime records the execution result and associates it with the relevant code version.

The goal is simple: stop trusting the AI's description of what happened and start requiring evidence of what actually happened.

  1. Then I realized something worse: humans can still blindly approve everything

Even with all those safeguards, there's a fundamental weakness in the system.

The human.

You can build the most carefully controlled approval system in the world, and I can still click "Approve" without reading anything.

So I added a feature called Red Pill Mode.

Here's how it works. When enabled, the system occasionally introduces a deliberately incorrect item into the review material. The developer is supposed to notice it before approving the work.

For example, suppose the original requirement says:

The system must support four simultaneous drone connections.

But the review table contains:

TEST-010: Verify that two simultaneous drone connections work correctly.

Would you notice the difference? Or would you just approve?

If you catch the incorrect item, the system records the catch and explains why it was wrong. If you blindly approve, the approval is blocked.

And yes, it makes fun of you:

You didn't really review this, did you, human? Keep approving like that and the AI really will take your job. lol.

It's intentionally a little ridiculous, but the underlying problem is serious. An approval button means nothing if the person clicking it isn't paying attention.

The planted mistakes never modify the actual implementation plan or executable code. They exist only in the review material, so they cannot accidentally become part of the software being built.

Red Pill Mode is optional and off by default. It also supports adaptive difficulty, so the review exercises can become harder as you successfully identify mistakes.

I find this particularly interesting because we're entering a world where developers may spend more time reviewing AI-generated work than writing code themselves. If that's where we're heading, shouldn't we be actively improving our review skills instead of letting them deteriorate?

  1. Bigger requests are split before implementation

Another issue I kept encountering was asking an agent to implement something too large. It would produce an enormous plan, and I'd be expected to approve the whole thing.

That's not meaningful review. That's just outsourcing a massive amount of work and hoping the result is correct.

So compound requests are split into independently verifiable features. The human approves the feature list before implementation starts, and each feature gets its own workflow, decisions, and verification.

After those features are implemented, the system checks that they work together. Independent tasks can also run in parallel using isolated Git worktrees, while conflicting tasks are kept sequential.

The idea isn't to slow down AI development. It's to gain the speed of AI agents without giving up control of the overall design.

  1. You can try it

The project is currently at v0.5.0 and is open source under the MIT license. It runs as a Claude Code plugin with a Python 3.8+ standard-library runtime.

Install it in Claude Code:

/plugin marketplace add kiduki77/human-rights

/plugin install hrs@human-rights

Initialize it in your project:

/hrs:init

Then start a task:

/hrs:new add Google authentication

Or, if you want to see whether you're actually paying attention during reviews, try:

/hrs:redpill on 5 adaptive

The repository includes an automated test suite, but this is still an early-stage project. Some integrations, including live GitHub adapter operation and real concurrent sub-agent execution, still need field validation.

GitHub: https://github.com/kiduki77/human-rights

Where this could go

Right now, human-rights focuses on individual development workflows, but I think the underlying problem could become much more important for engineering teams.

As AI generates more code, how do we know that code was meaningfully reviewed? How do we distinguish a real technical decision from a rubber-stamp approval? And how do we help developers improve at finding problems instead of gradually losing that skill?

Imagine an engineering team where AI generates most of the code. A developer approves a pull request without noticing that an important requirement was missed. Another developer catches the same issue immediately.

Today, we can track who approved a pull request, but that doesn't necessarily tell us how thoroughly it was reviewed. What if we could help developers identify the types of mistakes they tend to miss, practice reviewing realistic changes, and improve over time?

I think there's an opportunity to build something that doesn't just manage AI-generated code, but helps humans become better reviewers of it.

That's a longer-term idea, not something I'm claiming the current plugin already solves.

For now, I'm starting with the problem I experience every day: making sure I still understand and control the software I'm building.

I'd love to hear what other developers think

I'm especially curious whether other developers have noticed themselves reviewing AI-generated code less carefully over time. Would enforced approval gates help, or would they just become another form of bureaucracy? And would you actually enable something like Red Pill Mode in your own development workflow?

I don't have all the answers, and I'm sure there are things I've overlooked. That's why I'm releasing this as open source and looking for feedback from developers who are experiencing the same problems.

I built this because I don't want to stop using AI.

I just don't want to stop being a developer while using it.

human-rights — AI writes the code. Humans own the decisions.

https://github.com/kiduki77/human-rights

title: Send Your Updated APIs to DocStar Without Signing In

title: AI Agent Deployment Gates: How to Scale Productivity Without Losing Control
description:
AI agents can already complete parts of multi-hour tasks, but their performance remains uneven. Businesses need deployment gates that combine measurable outcomes, restricted access, and human escalation.

AI adoption in business is entering a new phase. The question is no longer simply whether employees use chatbots. Increasingly, organizations are working with agents that can analyze information, write code, monitor processes, and complete tasks that previously required several hours of human effort.

Yet the latest research material points to an important conclusion: AI progress is uneven. An agent may perform strongly in one part of a workflow while still requiring close human supervision in another. A mature deployment model should therefore be built around controlled gates rather than unrestricted automation.

Agent capabilities are uneven

OpenAI’s research acceleration report shows that agent performance varies significantly by task. Agents now complete nearly half of tasks estimated to require two to four hours of human work, but the results depend heavily on the nature of the task.

For example, the reported success rate was 79 percent for monitoring training runs, 35 percent for launching them, and 25 percent for writing code for inference and serving systems. A single measure of “AI automation” can therefore be misleading. Organizations need to evaluate specific actions, not just the technology label.

The practical lesson is straightforward: break a workflow into individual tasks and assign each one its own level of trust.

Three deployment gates for business

1. The outcome gate

The first gate defines what the agent is expected to achieve and how quality will be assessed. This should not be an abstract promise of productivity. It might be a shorter analysis cycle, less manual coding, or faster preparation of a management proposal.

The Sumitomo Life case shows why usage volume alone is not enough. The company tracks how employees use ChatGPT, which parts of their work it supports, and how usage relates to reported time savings. The company reports an overall estimated ROI of 203 percent and an estimated 524 percent ROI among employees using the tool at least 101 times per month. These figures are based on employee-reported time savings and should not be treated as a universal promise, but they illustrate why organizations should measure practical impact.

2. The access gate

The second gate defines what the agent can see and change. The Codex sandbox approach relies on restricting access to the filesystem and network. This allows an agent to perform useful work while limiting the potential impact of mistakes or unwanted data transfers.

In a business environment, this means an agent does not automatically need administrator privileges. It may be allowed to read selected documents, work inside a project area, or prepare changes for review while leaving the final action to a person.

3. The escalation gate

The third gate defines when the agent must stop and hand the task back to a human. This is especially important in finance, legal work, customer service, and software development.

The frontier AI risk framework emphasizes defense in depth. During research and training, organizations use sandboxes, virtual machines, network restrictions, and monitoring. During internal and external deployment, behavioral testing, monitoring, and safeguards against misuse become increasingly important.

For a business, the principle can be stated simply: the greater the agent’s access and potential impact, the more independent layers of control are required.

Leadership matters more than one-time training

Technology adoption does not happen simply because employees receive accounts. The Sumitomo Life case suggests that executives and managers helped move the organization from a pilot to broader adoption by using the technology themselves and encouraging employees to try it.

Leadership, however, should not mean pressuring teams to use AI everywhere. A stronger signal is to explain where the tool creates value, what data must not be shared, and when human review is mandatory.

What does a mature first project look like?

A good initial project has limited scope, a defined outcome, and measurable risk. For example, a planning team can use an agent to review public sources and prepare an initial proposal structure. Experts can then verify the findings and add firsthand context.

Another example is using AI to draft statistical analysis code. Analysts can accelerate the preparatory work while checking the assumptions, data, and calculation logic before using the result. The agent speeds up the workflow without taking responsibility for the final decision.

Control is not the opposite of productivity

AI discussions often move between two extremes: giving agents maximum autonomy or avoiding them because of potential risk. The research material suggests a more practical path. Agent capabilities are already sufficient for some tasks, but performance remains uneven and risk depends on access and context.

Business advantage will therefore belong not necessarily to the organization that automates everything first, but to the one that best connects three elements: a measurable outcome, limited access, and continuous evaluation. This allows AI use to expand gradually while preserving the ability to understand, verify, and stop an agent’s actions when necessary.

Conclusion: AI agent deployment should be managed as an architecture of access and trust. Each new level of autonomy should be supported by measured results, safe boundaries, and a clear escalation rule. This reduces risk and helps turn productivity gains into a sustainable operating model.

Originally published at insights.aisys.lt/di-agentu-diegimo-vartai-kaip-auginti-produktyvuma-neprarandant-kontroles.

title: Reject Duplicate JSON Keys Before Mapping a Stock Update
description:
A JSON object can contain the same property name twice. Python's default decoder retains the last value, so an upstream ambiguity can disappear before a stock update reaches schema validation.

Reject duplicates while pairs are still visible

Use object_pairs_hook to inspect each object's ordered key-value pairs. The hook below rejects an exact repeated key, including inside nested objects. It preserves arrays and permits the same key in separate objects.

import json

def unique_object(pairs):
    result = {}
    for key, value in pairs:
        if key in result:
            raise ValueError("duplicate JSON key: " + key)
        result[key] = value
    return result

def read_update(text):
    return json.loads(text, object_pairs_hook=unique_object)

assert json.loads('{"quantity":2,"quantity":9}') == {"quantity":9}
assert read_update('{"sku":"A","quantity":2}') == {"sku":"A","quantity":2}
assert read_update('[{"sku":"A"},{"sku":"B"}]')[1]['sku'] == 'B'
assert read_update('{"SKU":1,"sku":2}') == {"SKU":1,"sku":2}
for text in ['{"quantity":2,"quantity":9}', '{"item":{"sku":"A","sku":"B"}}', r'{"a":1,"\u0061":2}']:
    try:
        read_update(text)
    except ValueError:
        pass
    else:
        raise AssertionError("duplicate accepted")
print("7 checks passed")

Why this belongs before mapping

A Shopify 3PL adapter may receive a quantity update before shopify fulfillment work is prepared. If two quantity properties disagree, choosing the last one silently is an accidental policy. Rejecting the ambiguous object gives the sender a specific correction to make.

The same issue can occur in a drop shipping file handover or a china fulfillment stock feed. A china 3PL mapping layer should receive one unambiguous value before deciding its business meaning. International Fulfillment for Folligen is used here only as a hypothetical enquiry label for such a data handover, not a customer relationship or a tested integration.

Checks and limits

The example exercises seven assertions or rejection cases: default last-value behavior, a normal object, separate objects in an array, case-distinct keys, top-level duplication, nested duplication and an escaped spelling of the same key. Run it locally with Python; no store, warehouse or API is contacted.

This is an exact decoded-key rule. Case normalization, required fields, numeric ranges, non-standard number constants, document size and nesting limits require separate validation. The hook does not make arbitrary JSON safe or authorize a stock change.

Python's JSON documentation describes object_pairs_hook and the default handling of repeated names. For operational context, the integration overview describes the handover questions; this example is an isolated parser check.

Computer workstations and printing equipment in a warehouse.

title: Why Android apps behave differently on x86 emulators: ARM translation and native libraries explained
description:
Updated November 2026

Android apps behave differently on x86 emulators because native code is compiled for one CPU architecture at a time. Kotlin and Java run on ART and don’t care. Native .so libraries do. An x86 emulator runs either the app’s x86 libraries, which ARM phones never use, or ARM libraries translated to x86 inside the app’s process. Testing on ARM hardware, physical or cloud-hosted, closes both gaps.

What are Android ABIs?

An ABI (application binary interface) is the contract between compiled code and the CPU and system it runs on. Android’s NDK docs describe one ABI per combination of CPU and instruction set. It covers the instruction set, calling conventions, the binary format (always ELF on Android) and endianness (always little-endian).

The NDK supports four ABIs today:

  • armeabi-v7a: 32-bit ARM, with Thumb-2 and Neon

  • arm64-v8a: 64-bit ARM (AArch64)

  • x86: 32-bit Intel and AMD

  • x86_64: 64-bit Intel and AMD

Older ABIs like armeabi and MIPS were removed in NDK r17.

Every device reports which ABIs it can run, primary first:

bash
adb shell getprop ro.product.cpu.abilist

The primary ABI matches the machine code of the system image itself. Any others listed are secondary ABIs the image also supports. That one line tells you more about a test device than its model name.

On the app side, native libraries live inside the APK at lib/<abi>/lib<name>.so. A “fat” APK carries a folder for each ABI it supports. Since an APK is a zip file, you can check this in seconds:

bash
unzip -l app.apk 'lib/*'

At install time, the package manager looks for libraries under the device’s primary ABI first. If it finds none, it tries the secondary ABIs. It copies the best match into the app’s native library directory and ignores the rest.

That detail drives most of what follows.

What happens when an ARM-only app runs on an x86 emulator?

It depends on the system image. On an image without ARM translation, an ARM-only app usually won’t install. On an image with translation, it installs and runs, with the ARM code translated to x86 inside the app’s process.

Here’s the background. In March 2020, Google announced Android 11 emulator system images for x86 that can run ARM binaries. Before that, you had two options for ARM-only apps on an x86 computer. You could use a full ARM emulation image, which Google describes as much slower, or test on a physical device.

How the translation works, per that Android Developers Blog post:

  • The whole system runs as x86, with normal hardware virtualization.
  • When an app’s process needs an ARM binary, only that binary is translated to x86, inside that process.
  • Everything else in the process, including ART and graphics libraries like libGLES and libvulkan, keeps running natively as x86.
  • The translator skips low-level, hardware-specific libraries to avoid a performance hit.

Two conditions matter for teams. The translation ships only on Google APIs and Play Store system images. It’s also licensed for development and debugging on your own machines, on-premises servers and cloud environments you procure yourself, not for commercial hosted services.

Without translation, the package manager finds no library folder matching any ABI on the image. You’ll usually see INSTALL_FAILED_NO_MATCHING_ABIS and “Failed to extract native libraries” in the install output.

What if the APK also ships x86 libraries?

Then translation never happens, and that’s the trap worth knowing about. The emulator’s primary ABI is x86 or x86_64, so the package manager picks the x86 libraries first. Your test passes on code no ARM phone will ever run.

Usually that’s fine. The x86 and ARM builds come from the same source. But compiler flags, intrinsics, hand-written assembly and third-party SDKs can differ per ABI. A bug that lives only in the ARM build won’t show up on the emulator.

You can push the emulator toward the ARM build on a translation-capable image. Android’s docs describe forcing an ABI at install time on devices that support more than one:

bash
adb install --abi arm64-v8a app.apk

Now you’re testing the ARM library through the translator. That’s closer to what users run, but still not the same as ARM silicon.

On ARM hosts, the picture changes again. Google’s Apple silicon emulator preview ran ARM64 system images through ARM64 hardware virtualization, with no translation involved. Your library then runs as ARM code, but on a laptop CPU inside an emulator, not on a phone’s chipset and vendor build.

What did the test show?

[WRITER: one sentence on the setup. Suggested: “On [date], I installed three apps with native libraries on an x86_64 emulator ([image: API level, Google APIs or Play] on [host CPU]) and on an ARM device ([model, Android version, physical or cloud]).”]

*When is ARM hardware worth it for testing?
*
When native code is part of what you’re testing. If your app is pure Kotlin or Java and every dependency ships x86 builds, an emulator covers most of your day-to-day work. Once native libraries enter the picture, an ARM run before release earns its place.

It’s worth it when:

  • A dependency ships ARM only. Many third-party SDKs never build x86, so on the emulator you’re always testing through translation.
  • You ship x86 libraries too. The emulator runs those by default, so it never touches your ARM build.
  • Native code is performance-sensitive. Games, video, audio, image processing and crypto behave differently under translation, and frame timings on an x86 laptop say little about a phone.
  • Crash reports come only from ARM devices. Reproduce them where they happen.
  • It’s a release candidate. One pass on ARM hardware, the way users install from the store, catches packaging mistakes like a missing ABI folder.

Google’s own advice in the translation announcement points the same way. It still recommends publishing both x86 and ARM variants and treating translation as a testing convenience.

*Where do you get ARM devices?
*
Most teams mix these:

  • Physical phones. The real thing, with sensors, SIM and vendor builds. They need a desk, cables and someone to keep them charged.
  • Device farms. Services like Firebase Test Lab and BrowserStack host physical devices you test on per session. Good for broad coverage and CI. Devices reset between sessions.
  • Cloud phone providers. Persistent Android devices in a data centre that you keep and reach over the network. Multilogin, a cloud Android phone platform for multi-account management, is one example: each cloud phone runs on its own real ARM Android device. It offers 30+ device types across 12 brands, Android versions selectable per profile, APK upload and full ADB access, so the commands above work as-is. Its cloud phones can’t receive SMS or calls, and they need a reliable connection. GeeLark, DuoPlus and VMOS Cloud also offer cloud phones.
  • ARM hosts running ARM64 emulator images. No translation, but still an emulator, not a phone.

Whichever you pick, run getprop ro.product.cpu.abilist first. It’s the quickest way to know what you’re actually testing on.

FAQ

What’s the difference between ARM and x86 Android emulators?
An x86 emulator runs an x86 system image. ARM native libraries run there only through translation, and only on images that include it. An ARM64 image on an ARM host runs ARM code directly. Neither is a phone, but only the second runs your ARM libraries as ARM code.

Why does my app crash only on the emulator?
Check which library it loaded. If the APK has x86 libraries, the emulator runs those, so the crash may sit in your x86 build. If it’s ARM-only, the crash may come from code the translator handles differently. adb logcat -b crash -d shows the native stack, including the library path.

Do I need ARM hardware if my app is pure Kotlin or Java?
Rarely for day-to-day work, because ART runs your bytecode on any ABI. Check your dependencies with unzip -l app.apk 'lib/*'. If a lib/ folder shows up, you have native code after all.

Can I use the emulator’s ARM translation in a hosted testing service?
Not as a commercial service. Google’s announcement limits it to development and debugging on your own machines, on-premises servers and cloud environments you procure. It isn’t meant for providing commercial hosted services.

Is a cloud-hosted ARM device the same as a physical phone for testing?
For native code, it runs ARM binaries on ARM hardware, as a phone does. Other details depend on the provider, such as device models, Android versions, SIM and sensors. Multilogin’s cloud phones, for example, offer full ADB access but can’t receive SMS or calls.

title: Your AI tool changed this week. Would your team know?
description:
Most teams version-pin their dependencies, read changelogs and get a pull request when a library bumps. Then they hand a chunk of their daily work to an AI service that can change under them with no version bump at all.

This week the Ada Lovelace Institute published a feature called Running up that bill? (Charlie Grossman, 16 November 2026). It catalogues how AI subscriptions have changed what they deliver while the price stayed put. It's written about consumer plans, but it says organisations on business plans "remain exposed to practices like plan repricing or changes to how usage is counted."

Here's the engineering version, and a small fix.

What the feature documents

Some of the examples from the past 15 months, as the feature reports them:

  • Anthropic cut Claude Code's weekly limits by 17% after a temporary increase.
  • A new Anthropic tokeniser produced up to 35% more tokens for the same text.
  • OpenAI cut the reasoning time behind GPT-5.2 Thinking's "standard" setting and kept the name.
  • OpenAI's GPT-5 router sent some requests to less capable model variants.
  • OpenAI acknowledged an issue that applied the wrong usage limits to 40,000 accounts.

It isn't only pricing games

Two older data points matter more to engineers, because they're about quality, not allowances.

In 2023, Chen, Zaharia and Zou compared the March and June versions of GPT-3.5 and GPT-4. On identifying prime numbers, GPT-4 fell from 84% accuracy to 51%. GPT-3.5 improved on the same task. Their conclusion was that the same named service can change a lot in a short time and needs continuous monitoring.

In September 2025, Anthropic published a postmortem of three infrastructure bugs that intermittently degraded Claude's output between August and early September. At the worst hour, one routing bug hit 16% of Sonnet 4 requests. Anthropic said plainly these were bugs, not demand-based cuts. The bit I'd underline is its admission that "we relied too heavily on noisy evaluations."

If the provider's own evals missed it, "the model feels off today" in Slack is not a detection strategy.

My inference: treat the AI service like a dependency you can't pin

This is my mapping onto engineering work, not something the sources prescribe.

You probably can't pin a consumer chat plan. You can still do the three things you'd do for any upstream you don't control:

  1. Record the contract. Plan, model names, stated limits, reasoning setting, price. Write it down on the day you adopt the tool.
  2. Run a canary. A fixed set of your own tasks, run on a schedule, scored the same way every time.
  3. Keep a change log. One table where canary results and provider announcements sit side by side.

Build the canary set in an afternoon

  • Pick 10 to 20 tasks from real work: a function with existing unit tests, a SQL query with a known result set, a log excerpt with a known root cause, a diff with a known bug.
  • Prefer tasks with a mechanical pass mark. Tests pass, query matches, bug found. Skip anything that needs a long debate to grade.
  • Fix the prompt, settings and context. Store them in the repo next to the expected answers.
  • Run it weekly, same day, and record pass count, wall-clock time and tokens where the API reports them. The feature notes that API responses come back with a token count, which consumer web apps don't show.
  • Expect noise. The feature cites a 2026 study where the most expensive run of the same coding task typically used around twice the tokens of the cheapest. Look for a shift that holds across two runs, not one bad Tuesday.

If you're on the API, pin a dated model version where the provider offers one, and treat a version change like a dependency upgrade: run the canary before you switch.

The artefact: an AI service change log

Copy this into your repo as ai-service-log.md. The rows are labelled examples to show the shape. They are not measurements from the sources.

| Week | Tool / plan / model | Canary pass (of 20) | Median time | Tokens (API) | Provider change seen | Our change | Action |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| EXAMPLE 2026-W45 | Assistant X, team plan, default model | 18 | 41s | 212k | None | None | Baseline recorded |
| EXAMPLE 2026-W46 | Assistant X, team plan, default model | 18 | 44s | 260k | Changelog: new tokeniser | None | Watch token use, check allowance |
| EXAMPLE 2026-W47 | Assistant X, team plan, default model | 14 | 63s | 255k | None found | Longer system prompt | Revert prompt, rerun before blaming vendor |
| EXAMPLE 2026-W48 | Assistant X, team plan, default model | 14 | 61s | 250k | None found | Prompt reverted | Raise ticket with vendor, attach W45 vs W48 |

Two columns do the real work. "Our change" stops you blaming the vendor for your own prompt edits. "Provider change seen" forces someone to actually read the changelog and status page each week.

What to ask before you renew

Take these to your next renewal:

  • How much notice do we get before models, limits, reasoning settings or usage counting change?
  • Can we export usage data per user and per request?
  • What credit applies if a bug drains our allowance?

Consumer plans give weak answers to all three, the feature argues. Business contracts are where you can get better ones.

Sources

  • Running up that bill?, Charlie Grossman, Ada Lovelace Institute, 16 November 2026.
  • How is ChatGPT's behavior changing over time?, Chen, Zaharia and Zou, arXiv, July 2023.
  • A postmortem of three recent issues, Anthropic, 17 September 2025.

Has your team ever caught an AI tool getting worse with actual numbers, or was it gut feel every time?

title: Engineering Staffing Services: Helping Businesses Hire Skilled Engineering Professionals
description:
Engineering plays an important role in modern business development, infrastructure, manufacturing, and technological innovation. Companies across industries require qualified engineers to manage technical operations, develop innovative solutions, and complete projects successfully. However, finding professionals with the right technical knowledge and experience can be challenging due to talent shortages, increasing competition, and changing workforce requirements.

Engineering staffing services provide an effective solution by helping businesses connect with qualified engineering professionals for different roles and projects. From permanent hiring to temporary and contract-based recruitment, these services offer flexible workforce solutions. Talentiqo helps organizations identify suitable engineering talent and simplify their recruitment processes to support business growth.
What Are Engineering Staffing Services?
Engineering staffing services are recruitment solutions that help companies find and hire skilled professionals for technical and engineering positions. These services involve understanding job requirements, sourcing candidates, evaluating technical skills, conducting initial screening, and coordinating interviews.

Engineering staffing providers work with businesses to identify candidates who match their specific qualifications, experience, and project requirements. They support recruitment across multiple engineering disciplines, including mechanical, civil, electrical, electronics, software, and industrial engineering.

Whether an organization needs engineers for a short-term assignment, a specialized project, or a permanent position, engineering staffing services help make the hiring process more organized and efficient.
Benefits of Engineering Staffing Services

  1. Access to Qualified Engineering Talent Finding engineers with relevant technical expertise can be time-consuming. Engineering staffing providers help businesses access a wider talent pool of qualified professionals. This makes it easier to identify candidates with suitable educational backgrounds, practical experience, and industry knowledge.
  2. Faster Recruitment Process Technical recruitment often requires detailed candidate evaluation and multiple interview stages. Staffing providers support candidate sourcing, screening, and interview coordination, helping companies reduce recruitment delays and identify suitable professionals more efficiently.
  3. Flexible Hiring Solutions Business requirements can change depending on project schedules, workload, and operational priorities. Engineering staffing offers permanent, temporary, contract, and project-based hiring options. Companies can select the recruitment model that best suits their workforce requirements.
  4. Better Recruitment Cost Management Hiring involves expenses related to job advertising, candidate sourcing, interviews, and internal HR resources. Engineering staffing services help organizations manage recruitment activities more effectively and reduce the workload associated with finding suitable candidates.
  5. Support for Specialized Projects Some engineering projects require professionals with specific technical skills or industry experience. Staffing providers help businesses identify specialists for particular assignments, allowing organizations to strengthen their existing teams when additional expertise is required.
  6. Focus on Core Business Activities Managing recruitment internally can take considerable time from HR teams and business managers. Outsourcing recruitment support allows organizations to concentrate on project management, production, customer service, and other important business operations. Types of Engineering Staffing Solutions Different organizations have different hiring needs. Engineering staffing providers offer several recruitment models to support these requirements.

Permanent Engineering Staffing: Helps businesses recruit engineers for long-term positions. It is suitable for organizations looking to build stable technical teams and develop internal capabilities.

Contract Engineering Staffing: Connects companies with engineering professionals for a fixed period or specific assignment. It provides flexibility when additional technical expertise is needed.

Temporary Engineering Staffing: Supports short-term workforce requirements, seasonal workloads, and temporary operational needs.

Project-Based Engineering Staffing: Helps organizations recruit professionals with specific skills required to complete particular projects within planned timelines.

Specialized Engineering Recruitment: Focuses on hiring professionals with expertise in areas such as automation, product design, structural engineering, quality management, and industrial processes.
Engineering Positions Covered by Staffing Services
Engineering staffing solutions support recruitment across various technical disciplines and industries. Common positions include:

  • Mechanical Engineers
  • Civil Engineers
  • Electrical Engineers
  • Electronics Engineers
  • Software Engineers
  • Design Engineers
  • Structural Engineers
  • Quality Engineers
  • Production Engineers
  • Project Engineers
  • Automation Engineers
  • Process Engineers
  • Industrial Engineers
  • Manufacturing Engineers The exact positions depend on business requirements, project complexity, and the technical qualifications needed. How Does the Engineering Staffing Process Work? A structured recruitment process helps organizations find professionals who match their technical and business requirements.

Step 1: Understanding Hiring Requirements

title: Test-Time Compute: Why Spending More Compute at Inference Beats Training a Bigger Model
description:
For most of deep learning history, the recipe for a better model was simple: train a bigger one. More parameters, more data, more training compute, better results. That recipe still works, but it has a rival. Instead of spending compute once, up front, during training, you can spend it every time the model answers a question. Let the model think longer, try several answers, check its own work, and pick the best one. This is test-time compute, and in the last two years it has quietly become one of the most effective ways to improve a model you already have.

The intuition is older than the term. A student who spends ten minutes on a hard exam question usually does better than one who rushes the first answer that comes to mind. Language models behave the same way. A single greedy forward pass is the rushed answer. Given more time, the same model, with the same weights, can produce substantially better answers.

Two ways to spend compute at test time

Test-time compute comes in two flavours, and understanding the difference matters, because they scale differently and fail differently.

Sequential scaling makes one attempt longer. The model generates a chain of thought, revises it, backtracks from a dead end, and tries another approach inside a single long output. This is what "reasoning models" do when they produce thousands of tokens of internal deliberation before answering. The benefit is that later tokens can correct earlier ones: the model can notice a contradiction, re-derive a step, or verify a calculation.

Parallel scaling makes many attempts and selects among them. Sample N independent answers, then pick the best. The simplest selector is majority vote, known as self-consistency: if 32 samples mostly agree on an answer, that answer is probably right. A stronger selector is a verifier, a second model that scores each candidate. Best-of-N with a good verifier often beats majority vote, because the verifier can recognise a correct answer even when it is in the minority.

In practice the two combine. A common strong recipe is to generate many long chains of thought and then verify them, or to run a search procedure, such as beam search or Monte Carlo tree search, over the model's own reasoning steps.

Why it works: the maths of repeated tries

Suppose a model answers a given question correctly with probability p on a single attempt, and that attempts are roughly independent. The chance that at least one of N attempts is correct is:

1−(1−p)N

Even a modest p becomes a near-certainty as N grows. If p is 0.3, then N = 10 gives about a 97% chance that at least one sample is correct. This is the raw power behind parallel scaling. The hard part is not generating a correct answer somewhere in the pile; it is identifying it. That is why the verifier, not the sampler, is usually the bottleneck.

A useful way to think about the total compute budget is to split it between training and inference. Let C be the total compute available. Training a model of size M on D tokens costs roughly 6MD FLOPs, while answering one query with a model of size M costs roughly 2M FLOPs per generated token. Test-time compute shifts the balance: a smaller model, run for longer at inference, can match a larger model run once, at least on tasks where verification is easy.

This trade-off was made precise in a 2024 study by Snell and colleagues, who compared scaling test-time compute against scaling model parameters. On easy and medium-difficulty problems, scaling inference compute beat scaling parameters. On the hardest problems, the larger pretrained model still won, because a small model simply never samples a correct answer, no matter how many tries it gets. That asymmetry is the key result: test-time compute helps most where the base model is already close.

The verifier problem

Every selection method needs a way to judge candidates, and the choice of judge shapes everything.

Outcome verifiers check only the final answer. They are cheap and reliable when the answer is checkable, as in maths problems with a single numeric answer or code that can be run against tests. This is why test-time compute has shown its largest gains on maths and coding benchmarks.

Process verifiers score each intermediate step. They can catch a reasoning error early, before it poisons the rest of the chain, and they support search: keep the promising partial solutions, discard the rest. But they are expensive to train, because they need step-level labels, and a process verifier that is itself imperfect can systematically prefer fluent-looking but wrong reasoning.

Generative verifiers are just the same language model asked to critique its own output. This works better than it sounds, because judging is often easier than generating, but it inherits the model's blind spots. A model that cannot solve a problem usually cannot reliably tell a wrong solution from a right one either.

The practical consequence is a rule of thumb: test-time compute pays off when answers are verifiable. Maths, code, and formal logic are the sweet spots. Open-ended writing and judgement calls are not, because there is no reliable way to pick the best of N essays.

A minimal implementation

The simplest useful version of test-time compute is self-consistency with majority vote. It needs no extra model and no training. Here is the core idea in Python:

from collections import Counter

def self_consistent_answer(model, prompt, n=16, temperature=0.7):
    samples = [
        model.generate(prompt, temperature=temperature)
        for _ in range(n)
    ]
    answers = [extract_final_answer(s) for s in samples]
    most_common, count = Counter(answers).most_common(1)[0]
    confidence = count / n
    return most_common, confidence

A few details matter. Sampling temperature must be high enough for diversity, but not so high that the answers degenerate; 0.6 to 0.8 is a common range. The extraction step must be reliable, since a vote is only as good as the parser that reads each sample. And the confidence estimate, the fraction of samples agreeing, is genuinely useful: it tells you when to spend more compute. If 15 of 16 samples agree, stop. If the vote is split 9 to 7, sample more, or escalate to a verifier.

Best-of-N adds a scoring step:

def best_of_n(model, verifier, prompt, n=16):
    samples = [model.generate(prompt, temperature=0.8) for _ in range(n)]
    scores = [verifier.score(prompt, s) for s in samples]
    return samples[scores.index(max(scores))]

The cost is N generations plus N verifier calls. When the verifier is much smaller than the generator, this is cheap. When the verifier is another large model call, the budget doubles, and you should ask whether the extra verification is worth more than extra samples.

When test-time compute fails

Test-time compute is not a free lunch, and its failure modes are worth naming.

Verification collapse. If the verifier is wrong, more samples make things worse, not better. Best-of-N optimises the verifier's score, and with enough samples it will find an answer that games the verifier while being wrong. This is reward hacking at inference time, and it gets worse as N grows. The fix is a better verifier or a cap on N, not more sampling.

The base model ceiling. If the model never produces a correct answer in N samples, selection cannot help. On problems far beyond the model's capability, test-time compute is wasted. The Snell study's finding, that pretraining wins on the hardest problems, is the formal version of this.

Cost and latency. Test-time compute converts a fixed training cost into a per-query cost. Generating 32 samples costs 32 times as much per answer. For a service answering millions of queries, that trade is often unaffordable, and a larger model run once may be cheaper. The economics depend on how many queries you expect to serve.

Diminishing returns. The curve 1−(1−p)N flattens fast. Going from 1 to 8 samples is usually a large gain; going from 32 to 128 is usually small. Adaptive compute, spending more only on hard or uncertain queries, captures most of the benefit at a fraction of the cost.

The takeaway

Test-time compute reframes the scaling question. Instead of asking how big a model you can afford to train, ask how much compute you can afford to spend on each answer. For verifiable tasks, and for models that are already close to the answer, spending compute at inference is often the cheaper and faster route to better performance. It does not replace pretraining, and it cannot rescue a model that is fundamentally out of its depth. But it is the reason the same model can look mediocre on a one-shot benchmark and impressive when you let it think.

title: @Data on a JPA Entity Gave Us a False `equals()` and 18,000 Duplicate Rows
description:
The nightly import had been running for months without a complaint. Then a report came back with customers listed twice, and a count of the staging table showed roughly 18,000 rows more than the source file contained. The import code had a deduplication step, it was three lines long, and it looked impossible to get wrong.

Set<Customer> toSave = new HashSet<>(existingCustomers);
toSave.addAll(importedCustomers);
customerDao.saveAll(toSave);

A HashSet deduplicates by equals and hashCode, and the entity had both, because it was annotated with Lombok's @Data. That is the part everyone trusted and nobody read.

@Data generates equals and hashCode from every field of the class, and on a JPA entity every field includes the primary key. A customer loaded from the database carried an id. The same customer parsed from the import file had not been persisted yet, so its id was null. Two objects describing the same person, with the same external reference and the same email, were not equal to each other, because one of them had an id and the other did not. The set kept both, saveAll inserted the second one, and the deduplication step had been quietly doing nothing for as long as the id had been part of the comparison.

The same generated method has a second failure mode that is easier to hit and harder to see. Because the id participates in hashCode, an entity's hash changes the moment it is persisted and the database assigns a value. An object placed in a HashSet before the flush lands in one bucket, and after the flush the set looks for it in another. The object is in the collection and the collection says it is not there. Any code that holds entities in a set or uses them as map keys across a flush boundary is exposed to this, and it fails intermittently, which is how it survives review.

The fix was to stop deriving identity from the database. The import records had a natural key already, a source system and an external id, unique by contract and never changed after creation, so equals and hashCode were written by hand against those two fields and nothing else. Identity became a property of the record rather than of its row, which means it is the same before the insert, after the insert and after a detached object is merged back.

@Override
public boolean equals(Object o) {
    if (this == o) {
        return true;
    }
    if (!(o instanceof Customer other)) {
        return false;
    }
    return sourceSystem == other.sourceSystem && externalId.equals(other.externalId);
}

@Override
public int hashCode() {
    return Objects.hash(sourceSystem, externalId);
}

When there is no natural key to lean on, the usual alternative is a UUID assigned in the constructor rather than by the database, which gives the same stability without requiring the business to supply one.

There is a smaller reason to keep @Data away from entities, and it shows up in logs rather than in data. The annotation also generates toString across all fields, including lazily loaded associations, so printing an entity can trigger a query per association, or a LazyInitializationException outside a session. The usual compromise, if Lombok is going to stay on the class, is @Getter and @Setter rather than @Data, with equals, hashCode and toString written.

The broader point is that an entity has two identities, the row it maps to and the thing it represents, and they are not available at the same moments in its lifecycle. A generated method cannot know which one you meant. Ours picked the row, in a set that was asking about the thing.

title: So sicherst du einen MCP-Server mit codex sandbox ab
description:
MCP-Server in der Codex-Sandbox ausführen: Berechtigungsprofile für stdio-MCP-Server

Um einen MCP-Server in der Codex-Sandbox auszuführen, definierst du ein Berechtigungsprofil in ~/.codex/config.toml und setzt dann das command des Servers auf codex sandbox --permission-profile <name> --, gefolgt vom ursprünglichen Befehl. Codex sandboxt stdio-MCP-Server standardmäßig nicht – ohne diesen Wrapper läuft ein npx-Server mit deinen vollen Benutzerberechtigungen.

Probiere Apidog heute aus

OpenAIs Engineering-Beitrag Inside the Codex sandbox vom 18. November 2026 bringt es auf den Punkt: Codex kann nicht zuverlässig erraten, welche Dateien oder Netzwerkdienste ein Server benötigt, deshalb lässt es den Startbefehl des Servers unangetastet. Jeder MCP-Server, den du mit npx -y hinzufügst, kann deinen Home-Ordner lesen, überall schreiben, wo du schreiben kannst, und jeden Host im Internet aufrufen.

Im Folgenden erstellst du ein Profil für den Apidog MCP Server, bindest es bei abgeschaltetem Netzwerk an eine lokale OpenAPI-Datei, weist mit codex sandbox nach, dass das Profil funktioniert, und übergibst die Routinearbeit dann über die Apidog CLI an deinen Coding-Agenten.

Warum Codex stdio-MCP-Server ohne Sandbox lässt

Ein stdio-MCP-Server ist ein lokales Programm, das Codex startet und mit dem es über Standard-Ein- und -Ausgabe kommuniziert. Codex sandboxt die Shell-Befehle, die sein Modell ausführt, aber nicht den Befehl, der einen MCP-Server startet, weil es nicht erkennen kann, welche Dateien oder Hosts dieser Server benötigt. Der Server erbt deine vollen Benutzerberechtigungen.

Befehle, die das Modell ausführt, erhalten das eingebaute :workspace-Profil: Schreibzugriff nur innerhalb des Workspace, .git und .codex schreibgeschützt, umfangreiche Lesezugriffe, kein Netzwerk. Ein MCP-Server unter [mcp_servers] bekommt davon nichts.

Diese Lücke ist relevant, weil MCP-Server fremder Code sind, den du erst beim Start herunterlädst. Eine typische Konfiguration sieht so aus:

[mcp_servers.memory]
command = "npx"
args = ["-y", "@modelcontextprotocol/server-memory@1.0.0"]

npx -y lädt das Paket herunter und führt es ohne Rückfrage aus. Ist dieses Paket kompromittiert, kann es deine .env-Dateien und SSH-Schlüssel lesen und an beliebige Orte senden. Unser Leitfaden zu MCP-Sicherheitsrichtlinien behandelt das übergeordnete Bedrohungsmodell; dieser Beitrag schließt das eine Loch in deinem Codex-Setup.

So funktioniert ein Codex-Berechtigungsprofil

Ein Berechtigungsprofil ist eine benannte Sammlung von Dateisystem- und Netzwerkregeln unter [permissions] in config.toml. OpenAIs Beitrag und die Codex-Dokumentation zu Berechtigungen beschreiben drei Dateisystemstufen:

Wert Auswirkung
read Nur Lesezugriff
write Lese- und Schreibzugriff
deny Überhaupt kein Zugriff

Drei Schlüssel erledigen den Großteil der Arbeit:

  1. ":root" = "read" gewährt umfangreiche Lesezugriffe, die Node.js und npm benötigen, um ihre eigenen Dateien zu laden.
  2. Ein Pfad wie "~/.npm" = "write" gewährt Schreibzugriff ausschließlich auf diesen Ordner.
  3. Eine ":workspace_roots"-Tabelle wendet Regeln relativ zu jedem Workspace-Root an. "**/*.env" = "deny" blockiert jede .env-Datei darunter.

Beim Netzwerk gibt es drei Modi: aus, über Codex' Proxy mit einer Domain-Allowlist geleitet oder voller Zugriff.

Die Open-Source-Codex-CLI setzt diese Regeln über das Betriebssystem durch: Seatbelt unter macOS, bubblewrap plus seccomp unter Linux und auf kompatiblen Windows-Geräten Microsofts MXC. Kindprozesse erben die Limits, sodass alles, was der Server startet, in derselben Box bleibt.

Schritt 1: Den sichersten Modus für den Apidog MCP Server wählen

Der Apidog MCP Server (apidog-mcp-server auf npm, derzeit Version 0.0.18) läuft in zwei Modi:

  • Projektmodus: mit --project-id=<id> und einem APIDOG_ACCESS_TOKEN ruft er deine API-Dokumentation über das Netzwerk aus einem Apidog-Projekt ab.
  • OAS-Modus: mit --oas=<url-or-path> liest er eine Swagger- oder OpenAPI-Datei direkt.

Der OAS-Modus mit einer lokalen Datei braucht überhaupt kein Netzwerk. Das ist das strengste Profil, das du schreiben kannst, deshalb ist es hier das Hauptbeispiel. Die Apidog CLI hält die Spec von außerhalb der Sandbox aktuell (Schritt 5).

Wir haben das Paket in Version 0.0.18 analysiert, um herauszufinden, was der Server schreibt: Er legt Daten in ~/.apidog-mcp-server ab (oder im Ordner aus APIDOG_DATA_LOCATION) und ruft im Projektmodus https://api.apidog.com auf, sofern du nicht --apidog-api-base-url übergibst.

Schritt 2: Das Berechtigungsprofil definieren

Füge Folgendes zu ~/.codex/config.toml hinzu:

[permissions.apidog-mcp.filesystem]
# Broad reads so Node.js and npm can load their own files.
":root" = "read"
"~/.npm" = "write"
"~/.apidog-mcp-server" = "write"

[permissions.apidog-mcp.filesystem.":workspace_roots"]
"**/*.env" = "deny"

[permissions.apidog-mcp.network]
enabled = false

Der Server kann die Spec lesen und in zwei Cache-Ordner schreiben. Er kann keine .env-Datei im Workspace öffnen und hat kein Netzwerk.

Schritt 3: Den Serverbefehl in codex sandbox einbetten

Ersetze nun den einfachen npx-Start durch codex sandbox. Das Flag -C legt das Arbeitsverzeichnis fest, das zugleich der Workspace-Root ist, auf den die .env-Regel angewendet wird:

[mcp_servers.pets-api-docs]
command = "codex"
args = [
  "sandbox",
  "--permission-profile", "apidog-mcp",
  "-C", "/Users/you/code/pets-api",
  "--",
  "npx", "--offline",
  "apidog-mcp-server@0.0.18",
  "--oas=/Users/you/code/pets-api/openapi.json"
]

Drei Details sind wichtig:

  • Version pinnen. @0.0.18 bedeutet, dass ein neues Release den Code nicht unter dir austauschen kann.
  • npx --offline verwenden. Bei abgeschaltetem Netzwerk muss npx das Paket im Cache finden.
  • Absolute Pfade verwenden. Codex reicht args ohne Shell direkt durch, daher wird ~ nicht expandiert.

Die Apidog-README empfiehlt, den Server nach der API zu benennen, die er dokumentiert, etwa „Pets API Documentation“, damit das Modell weiß, wann es ihn einsetzen soll.

Schritt 4: Das Paket vorab cachen und nachweisen, dass das Profil funktioniert

Die Sandbox kann in den Cache-Ordner schreiben, ihn aber nicht anlegen, und sie kann nichts herunterladen. Führe Folgendes einmal außerhalb der Sandbox aus:

mkdir -p ~/.apidog-mcp-server
npx -y --package=apidog-mcp-server@0.0.18 -c true

Teste das Profil dann, bevor du ihm vertraust. codex sandbox führt jeden beliebigen Befehl unter einem Profil aus und ist damit ein schneller Testrahmen:

cd /Users/you/code/pets-api

# 1. A .env file in the workspace is unreadable
codex sandbox --permission-profile apidog-mcp -- cat .env
# cat: .env: Operation not permitted

# 2. Writes outside the allowed folders fail
codex sandbox --permission-profile apidog-mcp -- bash -c 'echo x > /tmp/probe.txt'
# bash: /tmp/probe.txt: Operation not permitted

# 3. The allowed cache folder is writable
codex sandbox --permission-profile apidog-mcp -- touch ~/.apidog-mcp-server/probe
# (no output, exit 0)

# 4. No network
codex sandbox --permission-profile apidog-mcp -- curl -sS https://api.apidog.com/
# curl: (6) Could not resolve host: api.apidog.com

Das sind die Ergebnisse, die wir unter macOS erhalten haben. Prüfe anschließend, ob der Server noch funktioniert, indem du ihm einen MCP-Handshake sendest:

printf '%s\n' \
 '{"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":1,"method":"initialize","params":{"protocolVersion":"2025-06-18","capabilities":{},"clientInfo":{"name":"t","version":"1"}}}' \
 '{"jsonrpc":"2.0","method":"notifications/initialized"}' \
 '{"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":2,"method":"tools/list"}' \
| codex sandbox --permission-profile apidog-mcp -- \
  npx --offline apidog-mcp-server@0.0.18 --oas=$PWD/openapi.json

Bei abgeschaltetem Netzwerk antwortete der Server mit drei Tools: eines, das die OpenAPI-Spec liest, eines, das von $ref referenzierte Dateien liest, und eines, das die Spec aktualisiert. Mehr braucht Codex nicht, um Code gegen deine API zu schreiben.

Unter macOS kannst du jedem codex sandbox-Aufruf --log-denials hinzufügen, um die Seatbelt-Verweigerungen nach dem Beenden des Befehls auszugeben. Das ist der schnellste Weg, einen Ordner zu finden, den der Server legitim benötigt.

Schritt 5: Die Spec mit der Apidog CLI aktuell halten

Ein Offline-Server liest eine Datei, also muss irgendetwas diese Datei aktualisieren. Übergib diese Aufgabe mit der Apidog CLI an deinen Coding-Agenten. Sie läuft außerhalb der MCP-Sandbox unter den normalen Befehlsregeln von Codex, und der MCP-Server benötigt nie einen Token.

Einrichtung (einmalig):

npm install -g apidog-cli
apidog auth login --with-token <your-access-token>

Wenn du die CLI noch nicht in Codex eingebunden hast, folge So verwendest du die Apidog CLI in Codex.

Prompt für deinen Agenten:

Export the OpenAPI 3.1 spec for Apidog project 1234567 to ./openapi.json,
then run test scenario 637132 in environment 358171 against it and give me
a CLI summary. Don't touch any .env file.

Befehle, die der Agent ausführt (Flags aus apidog export --help und apidog run --help, CLI 2.2.12):

apidog export --project 1234567 --format openapi --oas-version 3.1 --output ./openapi.json
apidog run -t 637132 -e 358171 -r cli,junit --out-dir ./apidog-reports

export überschreibt die Datei, die der gesandboxte Server liest, sodass der nächste MCP-Aufruf die neuen Endpunkte sieht. run führt dein Testszenario aus und schreibt einen JUnit-Bericht für CI. Füge --upload-report hinzu, wenn du den Lauf in der Apidog-App überprüfen möchtest. Der Free-Plan von Apidog deckt bis zu 4 Benutzer ab.

Wenn der Server Netzwerk braucht: die Domain-Allowlist

Der Projektmodus muss api.apidog.com erreichen. Codex' Antwort darauf ist der Netzwerk-Proxy: Setze enabled = true, liste die erlaubten Domains auf und aktiviere das Feature network_proxy. Das ist die dokumentierte Form aus OpenAIs Beitrag, angepasst an Apidog:

[permissions.apidog-mcp-live.filesystem]
":root" = "read"
"~/.npm" = "write"
"~/.apidog-mcp-server" = "write"

[permissions.apidog-mcp-live.filesystem.":workspace_roots"]
"**/*.env" = "deny"

[permissions.apidog-mcp-live.network]
enabled = true

[permissions.apidog-mcp-live.network.domains]
"api.apidog.com" = "allow"

[features]
network_proxy = true

Ein explizites deny hat Vorrang vor allow, und der Proxy löst einen Hostnamen erst auf, nachdem eine Regel ihn erlaubt hat – denn selbst eine DNS-Abfrage kann Daten preisgeben. OpenAI warnt, dass breite Wildcards weiterhin DNS-basierte Exfiltration erlauben können; liste deshalb exakte Hosts auf.

Eine Warnung aus unserem eigenen Test. Auf unserem Mac startete der Proxy und injizierte HTTP_PROXY und Co. in die Sandbox, antwortete aber bei jedem Host mit 403 und x-proxy-error: blocked-by-allowlist – auch bei den erlaubten. Unser Rechner leitet DNS über eine lokale Proxy-App, was der Grund dafür sein könnte. Führe codex sandbox --permission-profile apidog-mcp-live -- curl -sS https://api.apidog.com/ auf deinem eigenen Rechner aus, bevor du dich auf dieses Profil verlässt. Wenn der erlaubte Host fehlschlägt, falle auf den OAS-Modus aus Schritt 1 zurück.

Welches Profil solltest du verwenden?

Servertyp Netzwerk Schreibzugriffe im Dateisystem Beispiel
Liest nur lokale Dateien enabled = false npm-Cache + eigener Datenordner Apidog MCP Server mit --oas
Ruft eine bekannte API auf Proxy + exakte Domains npm-Cache + eigener Datenordner Apidog MCP Server mit --project-id
Braucht offenes Internet Vermeiden oder in einer VM isolieren So eng wie möglich Web-Browsing-Server

Wenn du Codex im Team einsetzt, können Administratoren mit allowed_permission_profiles in requirements.toml festlegen, welche Profile Benutzer auswählen dürfen. Und falls du versucht bist, die Sandbox stattdessen einfach abzuschalten: Lies nach, warum du beim Umgehen der Codex-Sandbox genau diesen Schutz aufgibst.

FAQ

Sandboxt Codex MCP-Server standardmäßig? Nein. OpenAI stellt klar, dass Codex den Befehl nicht sandboxt, der einen in config.toml konfigurierten stdio-MCP-Server startet. Du fügst die Sandbox selbst hinzu, indem du den Server über codex sandbox --permission-profile <name> -- startest.

Warum npx --offline statt npx -y verwenden? Bei network.enabled = false kann npx nichts herunterladen. --offline weist es an, die Kopie zu verwenden, die du mit npx -y --package=<pkg>@<version> -c true gecacht hast, und das Pinnen der Version verhindert, dass ein neues Release den Code ersetzt.

Schützt die Sandbox meine API-Schlüssel? Sie blockiert, was du verweigerst. Das :workspace-Profil erlaubt umfangreiche Lesezugriffe, also ergänze deny-Regeln für .env-Dateien und Secret-Ordner. Bei abgeschaltetem Netzwerk kann der Server außerdem nichts senden, was er liest.

Funktioniert das unter Linux und Windows? Ja. Dasselbe Profil gilt überall; Codex setzt es unter Linux mit bubblewrap und seccomp und auf kompatiblen Windows-Geräten mit einer MXC-basierten Sandbox durch. Teste jeden Rechner mit codex sandbox, da sich Pfade und DNS-Setups unterscheiden.

Kann ich andere MCP-Server auf dieselbe Weise sandboxen? Ja. Jeder stdio-Server funktioniert: Finde heraus, in welche Ordner er schreibt und welche Hosts er aufruft, gib ihm ein Profil, umhülle den Befehl, cache das Paket vorab und teste. OpenAIs eigenes Beispiel sandboxt @modelcontextprotocol/server-memory mit Schreibzugriffen nur auf ~/.npm und ~/mcp-data.
