title: Calling Claude, GPT-6, Gemini, and DeepSeek with Native Protocols Behind One API Key
description:
Most multi-model AI API gateways make a convenient shortcut: they wrap every upstream model behind a single /v1/chat/completions translation layer.

While that works for basic chat prompts, it starts breaking down in real coding agents and production pipelines:

  • Anthropic Claude relies on native /v1/messages content blocks (thinking, tool_use, tool_result) and prompt cache controls (cache_control).
  • OpenAI GPT-6 / xAI Grok increasingly target the Responses API (/v1/responses), which uses input, output_text, text.format, and named SSE events like response.output_text.delta rather than choices[0].delta.
  • Image and video models require dedicated /v1/images/generations, /v1/images/edits (multipart), and async /v1/videos endpoints—not text completions.

DeepClub is built around a protocol-first gateway model: one account, one API key, and pay-as-you-go billing, while routing each model family through its recommended protocol.

1. Protocol Selection at a Glance

Model Family Primary Endpoint SDK Base URL Fallback / Notes
Claude (claude-opus-5-5, claude-sonnet-5-5, claude-fable-5-1/5-2) POST /v1/messages https://deepclub.net /v1/chat/completions available for legacy clients
GPT Text & Grok (gpt-6.1-sol, gpt-6-astra, gpt-6-luna, gpt-6.1-terra, grok-4.7) POST /v1/responses https://deepclub.net/v1 /v1/chat/completions available for compatibility
DeepSeek, Gemini Text, GLM, Kimi, Qwen POST /v1/chat/completions https://deepclub.net/v1 GLM also exposes /v1/responses
Images (gpt-image-2*, gemini-3-pro-image, nano-banana-*) POST /v1/images/generations, POST /v1/images/edits https://deepclub.net/v1 Dedicated Images API
Videos (Seedance-2.0-Fast/Mini, MiniMax-H3) POST /v1/videos + polling https://deepclub.net/v1 Async task ID polling + content download

2. Two-Line Migration in Python

Claude via Anthropic SDK (Root URL — no /v1) 

import os
from anthropic import Anthropic

client = Anthropic(
    api_key=os.environ["DEEPCLUB_API_KEY"],
    base_url="https://deepclub.net",
)

msg = client.messages.create(
    model="claude-sonnet-5-5",
    max_tokens=1024,
    messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "Explain SSE event parsing in 3 bullets."}],
)
print(msg.content[0].text)

GPT-6 / Grok via OpenAI Responses SDK (/v1) 

import os
from openai import OpenAI

client = OpenAI(
    api_key=os.environ["DEEPCLUB_API_KEY"],
    base_url="https://deepclub.net/v1",
)

resp = client.responses.create(
    model="gpt-6.1-sol",
    input="Compare Responses API and Chat Completions for structured outputs.",
    store=False,
)
print(resp.output_text)

3. Coding Agents (Claude Code, Cursor, Cline, Roo Code)

  • Claude Code: Export ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL=https://deepclub.net and ANTHROPIC_API_KEY=<YOUR_KEY> (full setup at Claude Code custom ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL setup).
  • Cursor / Cline / Roo Code: Override the OpenAI-compatible Base URL to https://deepclub.net/v1 and use exact model IDs from the live LLM API pricing catalog (see Cursor setup and Cline & Roo Code setup).

4. Billing & Privacy Guarantees

  • Pay-as-you-go: Text models bill per million tokens (with separate prompt caching read/write pricing where supported); image and video models bill per successful generation.
  • Global & Asian Payment Options: Visa/Mastercard, Alipay, and WeChat Pay—no monthly subscription lock-in.
  • Zero Data Retention (ZDR): Prompts and completions are not stored persistently or used for training.

If you are building with AI coding tools or multi-model pipelines, you can inspect live endpoints, machine-readable pricing (/llms.txt), and per-family guides on the DeepClub English API Gateway Portal and Python & Node.js SDK Guide.

title: Your Go MJML and Liquid libraries fail on hostile templates. I tested them all.
description:
While auditing the security of Notifuse, a self-hosted email platform I maintain in Go, I asked AI to generate hostile templates and ran them against every MJML library and every Liquid library I could find for the language.

Notifuse users write their own email templates, in MJML for the layout and Liquid for the personalization, and my server compiles whatever they paste in. Anyone with an account can paste in something written to hurt the server.

What broke

One MJML library crashes the whole process when two emails render at the same time. Another turns an escaped " back into a raw quote, so data that was escaped correctly still adds an onclick attribute to the HTML. With 1 MB of inline styles, the libraries that accept the template take between one and five minutes to render it.

For Liquid I used four templates: a loop of a billion iterations, a string doubled 40 times, a billion bytes of output, and 100,000 nested blocks. The Go library whose output is closest to Shopify's has no limits at all, so each of the four runs it out of time or memory. The best of the others stopped three.

The Go MJML libraries didn't match MJML's output well either. The best produced the same HTML as MJML on 82.4% of my test documents, and Outlook punishes anything that drifts from it.

So I wrote two engines

I want both to be the best implementations in the world, in any language: safe-mjml for MJML and liquidgo for Liquid. That is a big claim, and the rest of this post is how I measure it.

safe-mjml is an MJML compiler in pure Go. It started from gomjml, Preslav Rachev's Go port, which gave me a big head start. Version 1.1 follows MJML 5.4.1 and writes identical HTML on 99.3% of 8,093 test documents. Most of the remaining differences are on purpose, such as MJML writing NaN as a width.

For hostile templates, a panic comes back as an error. Nesting depth is limited, the HTML output is capped at 16 MB, and attribute values are always escaped.

liquidgo is a port of Shopify's Ruby gem, done file by file so that each Shopify release can be carried over. It stops all four hostile templates, as Shopify's own gem does, and a template never reads your Go values by reflection. Its output is identical to Shopify Liquid's on 94.2% of 963 templates, and the rest are differences I chose and wrote down. A newsletter template that loops over 50 products renders in 53 µs, against 368 µs for Shopify Liquid on Ruby 3.3 with YJIT.

Try them 

go get github.com/Notifuse/safe-mjml/mjml
go get github.com/Notifuse/liquidgo/v5

Both are MIT licensed and pure Go.

Where this runs: Notifuse 44

Both engines render every email in Notifuse 44, which came out on November 19. It is the largest release so far, with 194 changelog entries. I rebuilt almost every screen of the console on a new design system, and the editor now writes MJML 5. The release post has the screenshots.

There is a live demo, and the code is on GitHub. If one of your templates makes safe-mjml or liquidgo disagree with the reference implementation, open an issue with it and I'll fix it.

title: Your Release Process Should Fail Closed
description:
Your Release Process Should Fail Closed

Last week our Obsidian plugin disappeared from its store listing. Nothing was wrong with the code. The plugin's manifest said version 1.3.0, but no matching release existed — so the listing dropped. A human checklist had every step on it. One step just quietly didn't happen, and every other step reported success anyway.

That is what failing open looks like: a check that errors, times out, or gets skipped counts as done. Most release processes fail open, because they're built from checklists, and checklists don't execute themselves.

So we built the opposite and shipped it: release-gate, a single 245-line Python script (standard library only, nothing to install) whose whole design is that the default answer is no.

The five checks

Give the gate a directory of release artifacts and it runs, in order:

  1. SCAN — the directory exists and contains at least one artifact.
  2. INTEGRITY — no artifact is zero bytes. A truncated or placeholder upload fails here, by name.
  3. EXPECTED — every artifact you named with --expect is actually present.
  4. SEAL — SHA-256 hashes of every artifact are written to SHA256SUMS in the release directory.
  5. VERIFY (with --verify) — every artifact is re-hashed and compared against the seal. A changed byte, a missing file, or a file that was never sealed is a failure.

Every run, pass or fail, is appended to a hash-chained ledger: each entry records the hash of every artifact and chains to the previous entry, so a PASS is bound to the exact bytes that were checked. Change one byte afterwards and the old PASS no longer describes your release.

The part that matters: there is no override flag

No --force. No --skip-checks. A check that throws an error is recorded as a FAIL, not skipped. Sealing is refused if any earlier check failed. The exit code is the entire contract: 0 means every check ran and passed, 1 means do not publish.

That sounds strict until you've watched the alternative ship a broken release because somebody was in a hurry and the checklist "basically passed."

Watch it catch one byte

Real output, from running the shipped v1.0 today. Seal a two-file release:

$ python3 release_gate.py ./my-release --expect app-linux.tar.gz --expect app-windows.zip
RELEASE GATE v1.0 — SEAL — /tmp/rg-demo/my-release
  SCAN: PASS
  INTEGRITY: PASS
  EXPECTED: PASS
  SEAL: PASS
  sha256 9a3719788de597c4…  app-linux.tar.gz
  sha256 774640a50264d6f7…  app-windows.zip
VERDICT: PASS — ledger entry #1 (hash-chained) in ./rg-demo/ledger.jsonl

Append a single byte to one file — the smallest corruption there is — and verify:

$ python3 release_gate.py ./my-release --verify
RELEASE GATE v1.0 — VERIFY — /tmp/rg-demo/my-release
  SCAN: PASS
  INTEGRITY: PASS
  VERIFY: FAIL
  sha256 9cd6e59bd2a37184…  app-linux.tar.gz
  sha256 774640a50264d6f7…  app-windows.zip
  detail: VERIFY: app-linux.tar.gz: checksum mismatch
VERDICT: FAIL — ledger entry #2 (hash-chained) in ./rg-demo/ledger.jsonl

Exit code 1. The release does not ship, and the output names the check and the file instead of leaving you to guess.

The gate's own test suite makes the same point sixteen ways — good release, tampered release, stale checksums, a zero-byte artifact, a missing expected file, an unsealed release — asserting the exit code and the named failed check each time. I re-ran it today before writing this: 16/16 checks passed.

The second rule the incident taught us

The gate proves the bytes. It doesn't prove the publish happened the way the success message claims — so our second rule is: verify on the authoritative surface, never from the success response. When release-gate itself shipped (public repo, November 16), the push wasn't trusted until all 11 files were read back and compared byte-for-byte against the local package, and the v1.0 release wasn't called live until its page said so.

A gate that fails closed, plus a read-back that doesn't take anyone's word for it. Neither is clever. Together they've ended the class of incident that cost us a listing: the step that silently didn't happen.

Facts in this post, checkable on the repo linked above: release-gate v1.0, commit 6e9d39c, 11 files, MIT licensed; the self-test output and the seal/verify demo above were run on 2026-11-20 against the shipped code, and the demo hashes are from that run — yours will differ, the verdicts shouldn't.

title: How to build your MVP’s UI in a week: a Figma kit, React code and an AI agent
description:
Most MVPs lose their first weeks to UI that isn't the product. This is the week I'd plan with a Figma kit, React code and an AI agent. Disclosure: I run mebius.design, which sells kits like this, but the plan works with any kit that ships both Figma and code.

To build an MVP’s UI in a week, start from a UI kit with Figma screens and matching React code. On mebius.design, 19 kits ship both: design your flows in Figma, install the code with the shadcn CLI or an AI agent, then wire your backend, auth and payments.

What does mebius.design cover when you build an MVP?

The UI only: the Figma file and the React front end.

mebius.design covers an MVP’s UI and nothing behind it. Each mebius.design code kit gives you a Figma file and a React front end in the same style. The backend, database, auth, payments and hosting stay yours to build or buy.

Every mebius.design code kit includes sign-in, onboarding, settings and billing blocks. They are screens, not services: the sign-in form creates no accounts until you connect an auth provider.

Code UI kits on mebius.design at a glance

  • Kits with code: 19 of 35 kits, for dashboards, mobile apps and websites
  • Screens: A Figma file per kit, e.g. 161 screens in Arcline
  • Components: 2,046 React components across the code kits
  • Blocks: 1,061 React blocks, with sign-in, onboarding, settings and billing in every kit
  • Code stack: React 19, TypeScript and Tailwind CSS v4, in shadcn registry format
  • Install: shadcn CLI, or the mebius MCP in Claude Code, Cursor and VS Code
  • Scope: The UI only. The backend, database, auth and payments are yours.
  • License: Single license, client work included. The Agency license adds handing the files to clients, white-label and resale.
  • Price: $19 once per kit, or $259 for all items. No subscription.
  • Counts as of: 19 Nov 2026, live from the catalog

What does a one-week plan for an MVP’s UI look like?

Seven days, one kit, one AI agent.

This plan for a mebius.design code kit assumes a small team and Claude Code or Cursor. Days 5 and 6 bring in your own backend.

  1. Day 1: pick the kit and list the screens. Write down the MVP’s three to five core flows, such as sign-up and the main dashboard, and match each to the kit’s screens. Cut the rest.
  2. Day 2: make the Figma file yours. Copy the screens you need to a new page and change the logo, colors and copy. Build any missing screen from the kit’s own components, since the code matches them. Or skip Figma and go straight to code.
  3. Day 3: set up the project and the theme. Create a React 19 + Tailwind v4 app with Next.js or Vite, run shadcn init, add the @mebius registry and install the kit’s theme on its own.
  4. Day 4: install the blocks. Add the blocks for your flows with the shadcn CLI, or ask your AI agent to add them over the mebius MCP, then lay them out as pages.
  5. Day 5: connect auth and data. Wire the sign-in block to your auth provider and replace the blocks’ sample data with calls to your API.
  6. Day 6: connect payments and email. Point the billing block at your payment provider’s checkout and send receipts from your email service.
  7. Day 7: test and ship. Sign up as a new user, check every empty state, deploy, and show the MVP to its first users.

How do you choose a UI kit for an MVP?

By the core screen, not by the screen count.

Choose the mebius.design kit whose screens are closest to your product’s main flow. A kit that already has your core screen saves the most days.

  • Code first: 19 of the 35 mebius.design kits ship React code. Owners of the Figma-only kits get the code free once it ships.
  • Platform: dashboard kits are desktop web apps, most with mobile layouts. Mobile app kits’ code is React for the web, not React Native.
  • Niche: the niche guides compare the kits for CRM, finance apps and AI assistant apps, among others.
  • Shortlist: the picks for SaaS, fintech and AI MVPs are in Best UI kits for building an MVP.

How do you install a mebius.design kit with the shadcn CLI?

Theme first, then items, from the @mebius registry.

mebius.design code installs with the shadcn CLI 4.x into a React 19 + Tailwind v4 project that uses shadcn’s @/ aliases, with Next.js or Vite. Run init once if the project has no components.json:

Terminal:

npx shadcn@latest init

Create a token in Settings › Tokens and add the @mebius registry to components.json:

components.json:

{
  "registries": {
    "@mebius": {
      "url": "https://www.mebius.design/r/{name}.json",
      "headers": {
        "Authorization": "Bearer ${MEBIUS_TOKEN}"
      }
    }
  }
}

.env.local:

MEBIUS_TOKEN=mbs_your_token

Install the kit’s theme on its own first, then items with --overwrite so shared parts take the kit’s version. For a SaaS MVP on Arcline, the sign-in, settings and billing blocks are:

Terminal:

npx shadcn@latest add @mebius/arcline-theme
npx shadcn@latest add @mebius/arcline-login-and-sign-up @mebius/arcline-settings-page @mebius/arcline-billing-overview --overwrite

Every CLI command and error message for the @mebius registry is in the shadcn MCP and CLI guide.

How do Claude Code and Cursor add mebius.design items over MCP?

A hosted server with browser sign-in.

The mebius.design MCP server lets an AI agent list a kit’s items, read their source and usage docs, and get the exact install commands. It runs at https://www.mebius.design/api/mcp and signs in through the browser, so there is no token to copy. In Claude Code:

Terminal:

claude mcp add --transport http mebius https://www.mebius.design/api/mcp

Run /mcp, choose Authenticate and approve in the browser. Cursor takes the same URL in .cursor/mcp.json. Then ask for a flow, for example “Add the Arcline login and sign-up block to this app.” The agent runs the shadcn CLI commands the server returns, theme first.

A free mebius.design account covers the free charts and forms, so you can sign up and test the whole setup before you buy a kit.

How do you wire the backend, auth and payments to a mebius.design kit?

Your stack, the kit’s screens.

mebius.design kits include no backend, so this part of the MVP depends on the stack you pick. The blocks are React components with sample data, easy to connect to any provider.

  • Auth: connect the sign-in and sign-up block to an auth service or your own server, and guard the app routes.
  • Data: replace each block’s sample data with props or fetch calls to your API.
  • Payments: send the billing block’s upgrade buttons to your payment provider’s checkout.
  • Email: sign-up codes, receipts and alerts come from your email service.

Ask your AI agent to do this wiring one block at a time, and keep your data logic in your own files.

What are the other ways to build an MVP’s UI?

Checked on each product’s own site on 19 Nov 2026.

AI app builders and shadcn block libraries solve the same problem from other sides. Each fact links to its source.

  • v0 by Vercel turns prompts, screenshots or Figma files into code and full-stack apps, works with Next.js, shadcn/ui and Tailwind, and deploys on Vercel. Pricing: Free at $0 with a 7-message daily limit; Plus at $30 per user a month with $30 of monthly credits; Business at $100 per user a month.
  • Lovable builds full-stack web apps from plain-language prompts, with frontend, backend, database and auth, as editable code you can sync to GitHub. Pricing: Free at $0 with 5 daily credits; Pro at $25 a month with 100 monthly credits; Business at $50. Its FAQ says you own your code.
  • Shadcnblocks sells 2,697+ blocks and 2,241+ components for shadcn/ui, installed with the shadcn CLI and searchable over shadcn’s MCP. Pro is $149, Premium $299 and Elite $399, paid once ($89, $179 and $239 in a sale that day); Premium and Elite add 22 templates and a Figma kit. One user, unlimited end products for you and your clients.

An AI builder is quickest when the look can wait. A block library suits teams that design in code. A mebius.design kit suits founders who want a designed product in Figma and React from day one.

FAQ

Can you build an MVP’s UI in a week?

Yes, if the MVP has a few core flows and you start from a UI kit with code. Design and install take four days; the backend, auth and payments take the rest, or longer. mebius.design covers the UI only.

Does mebius.design include a backend, auth or payments?

No. mebius.design covers the UI: the Figma file and the React front end. Every code kit has sign-in, onboarding, settings and billing screens, but connecting them to an auth provider, a database and a payment provider is your work.

Which AI coding tools work with the mebius.design MCP?

Claude Code, Cursor and VS Code sign in through the browser. Tools that can’t open a browser send a token from Settings › Tokens. The shadcn CLI installs the same items without any AI tool.

How much does a mebius.design kit cost for an MVP?

$19 per kit, paid once, or $259 for all items. Every purchase covers client work; the Agency license adds handing the files to clients, white-label and resale. The free charts and forms need only a free account.

Is v0 or a UI kit better for an MVP?

It depends on what the MVP needs first. v0 and Lovable generate working apps from prompts, which suits testing an idea fast. A UI kit gives you designed screens and code in one style. v0 can start from a Figma file, so the two can work together.
