Standard coding agents shell out to raw git commands and hope nothing collides. Dx introduces the world's first GitHarness implementation—native version-control orchestration built directly into the harness for safe, structured agentic workflows.

  1. Rust-Native RLM + 15–90% Token Savings

Most context-compression and retrieval layers drag in a heavy Python runtime or flood the context window with verbose JSON tool definitions. Dx includes a built-in Rust RLM (zero Python bloat) paired with tool-schema optimizations that ship 20+ full tools at near-Pi token overhead, cutting token usage by 15–90% across real coding sessions.
How Dx Compares Against 9 Top AI TUIs

It is day one, so there may still be a few rough edges and glitches—the goal is building a radically better developer experience.

Rethinking the TUI experience. Try it, break it, and tell me what you think: https://dx.essencefromexistence.com

title: NestJS for Spring Boot developers: a TypeScript backend that will feel familiar
description:
If your team writes Spring Boot and is about to build something in TypeScript (a new service next to a frontend that's already in TypeScript, a backend for a product that's moving off the JVM, or just a team that wants one language), the Node.js world can look like a pile of small libraries you're expected to assemble yourself. Express, a validation library, a DI container someone picked, a folder structure someone invented. That's the part that usually puts Spring developers off, and it's fair.

Nest is the framework that takes that decision away. Its architecture came from Angular rather than from Spring, but the two ended up close, because they solve the same problem: a container that creates your classes and wires them through constructors, controllers and services in layers, decorators that read like annotations, and first-party modules for configuration, validation, security, scheduling, health checks and OpenAPI. Most of what you know carries over.

This post is the tour I'd give a Spring team on day one: the tools, the structure, each Spring feature and its Nest counterpart with code on both sides, how it ships, and the differences that will actually bite.

The short version

Spring Boot Nest
Spring Initializr, Maven or Gradle nest new, npm
@Service, @Component @Injectable() classes, listed in a module
@Configuration + @Bean a factory provider (useFactory)
@Qualifier an injection token and @Inject()
@PostConstruct, @PreDestroy onModuleInit(), onApplicationShutdown()
@RestController, @GetMapping @Controller(), @Get()
Servlet filters, HandlerInterceptor middleware, guards, interceptors
Bean Validation a validation pipe, with class-validator or Zod
@RestControllerAdvice an exception filter
Spring Security @nestjs/authentication and @nestjs/authorization
application.yml, profiles, @ConfigurationProperties @nestjs/config
Spring Data JPA TypeORM (@nestjs/typeorm) or Drizzle (@nestjs/drizzle)
@Scheduled, ShedLock @nestjs/schedule, @nestjs/locks
@EventListener @nestjs/event-emitter
RestClient, WebClient @nestjs/http-client
Resilience4j @nestjs/resilience
Actuator health @nestjs/terminus
springdoc-openapi @nestjs/swagger
@WebMvcTest, @SpringBootTest @nestjs/testing with Supertest

Every row has its own section below. The docs have the same mapping as a reference page, with a link to the full chapter for each row: Coming from Spring Boot.

Your tools, translated

Before any code, here's what replaces the things around it:

Spring world Nest world
JDK Node.js (a current LTS release)
Maven or Gradle, pom.xml npm, package.json
Maven Central the npm registry
Spring Initializr npx @nestjs/cli new
mvn spring-boot:run, DevTools npm run start:dev, which restarts on every save
mvn package, a fat jar npm run build (the TypeScript compiler, or SWC for speed), a dist/ folder plus node_modules
javac tsc
JUnit and Mockito Vitest, with its own mocks
Lombok not needed: constructor parameter properties replace the boilerplate
Jackson nothing: JSON is the language's native format
IntelliJ IDEA WebStorm, or VS Code
A multi-module build a Nest workspace: nest generate app and nest generate library

npm run start:debug starts the app with the Node inspector attached, and both editors above connect to it the way IntelliJ connects to a JVM debug port.

Project layout

nest new orders-api gives you a small src/ folder and asks two questions: ES modules or CommonJS (ESM is the default, with Vitest; CommonJS uses Jest), and whether to set up NestJS Observe for monitoring. As the app grows, the convention is one folder per feature, each with its module, and tests next to the code they test rather than in a parallel tree:

src/
  main.ts                    # the main class
  app.module.ts              # the root module
  orders/
    orders.module.ts
    orders.controller.ts
    orders.controller.spec.ts
    orders.service.ts
    order.entity.ts
    create-order.dto.ts
  payments/
    payments.module.ts
    ...
test/
  app.e2e-spec.ts            # end-to-end tests

nest g resource orders generates the orders/ folder above with CRUD routes filled in, which is the fastest way to see the structure with your own names in it.

The entry point is the counterpart of your @SpringBootApplication class:

@SpringBootApplication
public class OrdersApplication {
  public static void main(String[] args) {
    SpringApplication.run(OrdersApplication.class, args);
  }
}

// main.ts
async function bootstrap() {
  const app = await NestFactory.create(AppModule);
  await app.listen(process.env.PORT ?? 3000);
}
await bootstrap();

Beans are providers, and you list them

A Spring service and the same service in Nest:

@Service
public class OrdersService {
  private final OrdersRepository ordersRepository;

  public OrdersService(OrdersRepository ordersRepository) {
    this.ordersRepository = ordersRepository;
  }
}

@Injectable()
export class OrdersService {
  constructor(private readonly ordersRepository: OrdersRepository) {}
}

Constructor injection, no @Autowired, and private readonly declares and assigns the field in one go. The one real difference is that there's no component scanning. Every provider belongs to a module, and the module lists it:

@Module({
  controllers: [OrdersController],
  providers: [OrdersService, OrdersRepository],
  exports: [OrdersService],
})
export class OrdersModule {}

That looks like boilerplate at first, and I'd argue it's the best part. A module is a boundary Spring's application context doesn't have: OrdersRepository isn't exported, so no other module can inject it. In a big Spring codebase you rely on package conventions and ArchUnit tests for that. In Nest the container enforces it, and you can read what a feature exposes from one file. A module that needs OrdersService adds OrdersModule to its imports.

If a dependency can't be resolved, the app fails at startup with an error naming the class, the missing dependency and the module, much like Spring's "unsatisfied dependency" failure.

@Configuration and @bean

A @Bean method builds something you don't own, or something that needs setup:

@Configuration
public class StorageConfig {
  @Bean
  public S3Client s3Client(StorageProperties properties) {
    return S3Client.builder().region(Region.of(properties.region())).build();
  }
}

In Nest it's a factory provider. inject lists what gets passed to the factory, in order, and the factory can be async:

@Module({
  providers: [
    {
      provide: S3Client,
      useFactory: (config: ConfigService) =>
        new S3Client({ region: config.getOrThrow<string>('AWS_REGION') }),
      inject: [ConfigService],
    },
  ],
  exports: [S3Client],
})
export class StorageModule {}

And the starters? There's no auto-configuration. A package ships a module, and you import and configure it: ConfigModule.forRoot(), TypeOrmModule.forRootAsync(), ScheduleModule.forRoot(). Nothing turns on because it's on the classpath, which I think is the right trade for a language where "the classpath" is node_modules.

Interfaces and @Qualifier

This is the first thing that trips Spring developers up. In Java you inject PaymentGateway, the interface, and the container finds the implementation. TypeScript interfaces are erased when the code compiles, so there's nothing left for the container to look up. Use an abstract class as the contract: it exists at runtime, so it doubles as the injection token.

export abstract class PaymentGateway {
  abstract charge(orderId: string, amountInCents: number): Promise<void>;
}

@Module({
  providers: [{ provide: PaymentGateway, useClass: StripePaymentGateway }],
  exports: [PaymentGateway],
})
export class PaymentsModule {}

// anywhere that imports PaymentsModule
constructor(private readonly paymentGateway: PaymentGateway) {}

Where you'd use @Qualifier("primary") to pick one of several beans of the same type, Nest uses a string or Symbol token and @Inject(TOKEN) on the parameter.

Scopes and lifecycle

Spring Nest
singleton (the default) Scope.DEFAULT (the default)
@Scope("prototype") Scope.TRANSIENT
@RequestScope Scope.REQUEST
@PostConstruct onModuleInit()
ApplicationRunner onApplicationBootstrap()
@PreDestroy onModuleDestroy(), onApplicationShutdown()

The defaults match, and you should keep them: almost every provider should be a singleton. Request scope works differently from Spring's, which I'll come back to under "What's actually different".

Controllers you can read without a guide 

@RestController
@RequestMapping("/orders")
public class OrdersController {
  private final OrdersService ordersService;

  public OrdersController(OrdersService ordersService) {
    this.ordersService = ordersService;
  }

  @GetMapping
  public List<Order> findAll(@RequestParam(defaultValue = "0") int page) {
    return ordersService.findAll(page);
  }

  @GetMapping("/{id}")
  public Order findOne(@PathVariable String id) {
    return ordersService.findOne(id);
  }

  @PostMapping
  @ResponseStatus(HttpStatus.CREATED)
  public Order create(@Valid @RequestBody CreateOrderRequest request) {
    return ordersService.create(request);
  }

  @DeleteMapping("/{id}")
  @ResponseStatus(HttpStatus.NO_CONTENT)
  public void remove(@PathVariable String id) {
    ordersService.remove(id);
  }
}

@Controller('orders')
export class OrdersController {
  constructor(private readonly ordersService: OrdersService) {}

  @Get()
  findAll(@Query('page', new ParseIntPipe({ optional: true })) page = 0) {
    return this.ordersService.findAll(page);
  }

  @Get(':id')
  findOne(@Param('id') id: string) {
    return this.ordersService.findOne(id);
  }

  @Post()
  create(@Body() dto: CreateOrderDto) {
    return this.ordersService.create(dto);
  }

  @Delete(':id')
  @HttpCode(204)
  remove(@Param('id') id: string) {
    return this.ordersService.remove(id);
  }
}

Small things:

  • Route parameters are :id.
  • A POST answers 201 without being told; @HttpCode() changes any status.
  • Query and path parameters arrive as strings. ParseIntPipe does what Spring's type conversion does, and answers 400 for ?page=abc.
  • Handlers return Promises (or plain values), and Nest awaits them and serializes the result as JSON.
  • There's no ResponseEntity. You return the body, set headers with @Header(), and throw NotFoundException, ConflictException and friends for error statuses. They play the role of ResponseStatusException.

Filters, interceptors and AOP

Spring gives you servlet filters, HandlerInterceptors and aspects. Nest has a fixed set of components around each route handler, run in this order:

Nest When it runs Spring counterpart
Middleware before routing, with the raw request a servlet Filter
Guards after routing: may the handler run? the authorization part of the security filter chain
Interceptors around the handler, with its result HandlerInterceptor, @Around advice
Pipes on each argument type conversion and validation
Exception filters when anything above throws @ControllerAdvice

Each can be bound to one handler, a whole controller or the entire app. An interceptor that logs how long each request took, the way you'd write an @Around aspect:

@Injectable()
export class TimingInterceptor implements NestInterceptor {
  private readonly logger = new Logger(TimingInterceptor.name);

  intercept(context: ExecutionContext, next: CallHandler): Observable<unknown> {
    const started = performance.now();
    const handler = `${context.getClass().name}.${context.getHandler().name}`;
    return next
      .handle()
      .pipe(tap(() => this.logger.log(`${handler} took ${Math.round(performance.now() - started)} ms`)));
  }
}

next.handle() is your joinPoint.proceed(), as an RxJS stream of the handler's result. The difference from AOP: interceptors wrap route handlers (and message and event handlers), not arbitrary methods of any bean. More on that below.

Validation is explicit, and that's the first gotcha

Bean Validation:

public record CreateOrderRequest(
  @NotBlank String customerId,
  @NotEmpty List<@Valid OrderItem> items,
  @Size(max = 500) String note
) {}

The closest Nest equivalent is a DTO class with class-validator decorators and a global ValidationPipe:

export class CreateOrderDto {
  @IsString()
  @IsNotEmpty()
  customerId: string;

  @ArrayNotEmpty()
  @ValidateNested({ each: true })
  @Type(() => OrderItemDto)
  items: OrderItemDto[];

  @IsOptional()
  @MaxLength(500)
  note?: string;
}

app.useGlobalPipes(new ValidationPipe({ whitelist: true, transform: true }));

whitelist drops fields the DTO doesn't declare, and transform turns the body into an actual CreateOrderDto instance. An invalid body gets a 400 listing every failed rule.

If you'd rather not write classes, Nest 12 also takes a Zod (or any Standard Schema) schema per parameter, and the type is inferred from it:

export const createOrderSchema = z.object({
  customerId: z.string().min(1),
  items: z.array(z.object({ productId: z.string(), quantity: z.int().positive() })).min(1),
  note: z.string().max(500).optional(),
});
export type CreateOrderDto = z.infer<typeof createOrderSchema>;

@Post()
create(@Body({ schema: createOrderSchema }) dto: CreateOrderDto) {
  return this.ordersService.create(dto);
}

Here's the gotcha. In Java, Jackson builds the class you declared, so a request body is at least the right shape before validation even runs. TypeScript types are erased when the code compiles. Without a pipe, @Body() dto: CreateOrderDto is whatever JSON the client sent, with whatever fields it felt like sending. Register a validation pipe globally on day one and you never think about it again. Forget it and the compiler won't warn you.

@ControllerAdvice becomes an exception filter

Spring 6 with ProblemDetail:

@RestControllerAdvice
public class ApiExceptionHandler {
  @ExceptionHandler(OrderNotFoundException.class)
  public ProblemDetail handle(OrderNotFoundException exception) {
    return ProblemDetail.forStatusAndDetail(HttpStatus.NOT_FOUND, exception.getMessage());
  }
}

The same thing in Nest. @Catch() names the exception types, like @ExceptionHandler:

@Catch(OrderNotFoundError)
export class OrderNotFoundFilter implements ExceptionFilter {
  constructor(private readonly httpAdapterHost: HttpAdapterHost) {}

  catch(exception: OrderNotFoundError, host: ArgumentsHost) {
    const { httpAdapter } = this.httpAdapterHost;
    const response = host.switchToHttp().getResponse();
    httpAdapter.setHeader(response, 'Content-Type', 'application/problem+json');
    httpAdapter.reply(
      response,
      { type: 'about:blank', title: 'Not Found', status: 404, detail: exception.message },
      404,
    );
  }
}

Register it app-wide as a provider in the root module, { provide: APP_FILTER, useClass: OrderNotFoundFilter }, and it can inject other providers like any bean. Exceptions nobody handles become a 500 with a generic body, and the stack trace goes to the log, not to the client.

Security that's closed by default

Spring Security's default is "everything requires authentication", and you open things up with permitAll(). @nestjs/authentication works the same way: the moment you register the module, every route answers 401 unless the request carries valid credentials, and @Public() opens a route. @CurrentUser() is your @AuthenticationPrincipal.

@RestController
public class MeController {
  @GetMapping("/me")
  public User me(@AuthenticationPrincipal User user) {
    return user;
  }
}

@Controller('me')
export class MeController {
  @Get()
  me(@CurrentUser() user: User) {
    return user;
  }
}

Where Spring has AuthenticationProviders, the package has credential providers: one reads the session cookie, another a bearer token, another an API key, and each loads the user through your code. The user is your own object, not a UserDetails. It also ships the flows Spring applications usually end up writing by hand: sign-up, password hashing, server-side sessions, email verification and password reset links, TOTP two-factor, OpenID Connect sign-in, rotating refresh tokens and API keys. State lives in your database through a store you implement against documented interfaces.

For @PreAuthorize, @nestjs/authorization uses policy classes. The check on a route is type-checked against the policy, so a typo in an ability name doesn't compile, which is more than a SpEL string gives you:

@PostMapping
@PreAuthorize("hasRole('STAFF')")
public Product create(@Valid @RequestBody CreateProductRequest request) { ... }

@Policy()
export class ProductPolicy {
  create(user: User | null) {
    return !!user?.roles.includes('staff');
  }
}

// in the controller
@Post()
@Can(ProductPolicy, 'create')
create(@Body() dto: CreateProductDto) { ... }

Its guard denies by default too, so a route that declares no check at all is closed, not open. Checks that depend on the record, the job you'd give @PostAuthorize, go in the service: authorizationService.authorize(OrderPolicy, 'view', user, order) throws when the policy says no.

Configuration and profiles

application.yml and profiles become .env files and environment variables through @nestjs/config. Real environment variables win over the files, which is what you want in a container:

# application.yml
orders:
  page-size: 20
  payments-url: https://payments.example.com

@Module({
  imports: [
    ConfigModule.forRoot({
      isGlobal: true,
      envFilePath: [`.env.${process.env.NODE_ENV ?? 'development'}`, '.env'],
      validationSchema: z.object({
        ORDERS_PAGE_SIZE: z.coerce.number().int().positive().default(20),
        PAYMENTS_URL: z.url(),
      }),
      load: [ordersConfig],
    }),
  ],
})
export class AppModule {}

There are no profiles as such. NODE_ENV picks the file, and the first file in envFilePath that defines a variable wins, so .env.production overrides .env the way application-prod.yml overrides application.yml. The schema is checked at startup, so a missing or malformed variable stops the deploy instead of failing the first request that reads it.

@Value("${...}") becomes config.get('PAYMENTS_URL'), or getOrThrow() for a value that must be there. @ConfigurationProperties becomes registerAs(), injected with its type:

export default registerAs('orders', () => ({
  pageSize: Number(process.env.ORDERS_PAGE_SIZE ?? 20),
  paymentsUrl: process.env.PAYMENTS_URL!,
}));

// in a service
constructor(@Inject(ordersConfig.KEY) private readonly config: ConfigType<typeof ordersConfig>) {}

And @ConditionalOnProperty has a cousin in ConditionalModule.registerWhen(FeatureModule, 'FEATURE_ENABLED'), which imports a module only when an environment variable allows it.

Spring Data becomes TypeORM (or Drizzle)

TypeORM is the closest thing to JPA in Node: entities are decorated classes, and each module registers repositories for the entities it uses.

@Entity
@Table(name = "orders")
public class Order {
  @Id @GeneratedValue(strategy = GenerationType.UUID)
  private String id;

  @Column(nullable = false)
  private String customerId;

  @Enumerated(EnumType.STRING)
  private OrderStatus status;
}

@Entity('orders')
export class Order {
  @PrimaryGeneratedColumn('uuid')
  id: string;

  @Column()
  customerId: string;

  @Column({ type: 'varchar', default: 'pending' })
  status: 'pending' | 'paid' | 'shipped';
}

@Module({
  imports: [TypeOrmModule.forFeature([Order])],
  providers: [OrdersService],
  controllers: [OrdersController],
})
export class OrdersModule {}

@Injectable()
export class OrdersService {
  constructor(@InjectRepository(Order) private readonly orders: Repository<Order>) {}

  findPending(customerId: string) {
    return this.orders.findBy({ customerId, status: 'pending' });
  }
}

Two things you'll miss. Derived query methods: findByCustomerIdAndStatus becomes findBy() with an object of conditions, and anything bigger goes through the query builder. And @Transactional: transactions are a callback that commits when it resolves and rolls back when it throws.

return this.dataSource.transaction(async (manager) => {
  const order = await manager.save(Order, { customerId: dto.customerId });
  await manager.insert(OrderItem, dto.items.map((item) => ({ ...item, orderId: order.id })));
  return order;
});

@InjectRepository(Order) names the entity for the same reason interfaces don't work as tokens: Repository<Order> and Repository<Customer> are the same class at runtime.

If you like jOOQ more than Hibernate, Drizzle is the other first-party option (@nestjs/drizzle): tables are plain TypeScript, queries look like SQL, and every result type is inferred from the schema, with no entity classes. MikroORM, whose unit of work and identity map are the closest thing to a JPA persistence context, Prisma and Mongoose all work too. Flyway or Liquibase migrations become the ORM's own migration tool, run as a separate step before the new version starts.

Scheduling, events and background jobs

@Scheduled becomes @Cron() from @nestjs/schedule. Same six fields, seconds first:

@Scheduled(cron = "0 0 2 * * *")
public void exportInvoices() { ... }

@Injectable()
export class InvoiceJobs {
  @Cron('0 0 2 * * *')
  @OnOneInstance({ key: 'invoices:export' })
  async exportInvoices() {
    // ...
  }
}

A Nest cron job runs on every replica, exactly like @Scheduled. The second decorator is the ShedLock part: @OnOneInstance() from @nestjs/locks takes a lease in a store every instance shares, so the job runs on one of them. fixedRate becomes @Interval(ms).

ApplicationEventPublisher and @EventListener become @nestjs/event-emitter:

// publishing
constructor(private readonly events: EventEmitter2) {}
this.events.emit('order.created', new OrderCreatedEvent(order.id));

// listening, in any provider
@OnEvent('order.created')
handleOrderCreated(event: OrderCreatedEvent) { ... }

@Async has no counterpart, and you won't miss it: database calls and HTTP requests in Node are already asynchronous, so an async method that awaits them doesn't hold a thread while it waits. Work that should leave the request entirely, like sending emails or building reports, goes on a queue with @nestjs/bullmq, which plays the role a JMS or RabbitMQ listener does in Spring.

Calling other services

RestClient and WebClient become HttpClient from @nestjs/http-client, built on Node's own fetch. Each upstream service gets a named client with its base URL and timeout:

@Module({
  imports: [HttpClientModule.register({ name: 'payments', baseUrl: process.env.PAYMENTS_URL, timeout: '5s' })],
  providers: [PaymentsClient],
})
export class PaymentsModule {}

@Injectable()
export class PaymentsClient {
  constructor(@InjectHttpClient('payments') private readonly http: HttpClient) {}

  async getStatus(orderId: string) {
    const { data } = await this.http.get<PaymentStatus>(`/payments/${orderId}`);
    return data;
  }
}

Resilience4j's timeouts, retries and circuit breakers become @nestjs/resilience. You describe each dependency once as a preset, and routes opt in with a decorator:

ResilienceModule.forRoot({
  presets: {
    carrier: {
      timeout: '2s',
      retry: { attempts: 2 },
      circuitBreaker: { failureRateThreshold: 50, minimumCalls: 10, openDuration: '30s' },
    },
  },
}),

// in a controller
@Get('quotes')
@Resilience('carrier')
getQuotes(@Query('orderId') orderId: string, @Signal() signal: AbortSignal) {
  return this.shippingService.getQuotes(orderId, signal);
}

@Signal() injects an AbortSignal that fires when the attempt times out; pass it to the HTTP call and the request is actually cancelled, not just abandoned. Retries only apply to safe methods like GET by default, so a retried POST never charges a card twice. Inside services, where decorators don't apply, the same presets are available as policy objects.

Health, logs and OpenAPI

Actuator's health endpoints become a controller using @nestjs/terminus, with separate liveness and readiness checks for Kubernetes:

@Public()
@Controller('health')
export class HealthController {
  constructor(
    private readonly health: HealthCheckService,
    private readonly db: TypeOrmHealthIndicator,
  ) {}

  @Get('live')
  @HealthCheck()
  live() {
    return this.health.check([]);
  }

  @Get('ready')
  @HealthCheck()
  ready() {
    return this.health.check([() => this.db.pingCheck('database')]);
  }
}

(@Public() because @nestjs/authentication closes every route, and probes don't sign in.)

For logging, private static final Logger log = LoggerFactory.getLogger(OrdersService.class) becomes private readonly logger = new Logger(OrdersService.name). The built-in ConsoleLogger writes JSON with json: true, which is what your log pipeline wants in production; pino and winston plug in if you already have a preference. For the metrics and traces Micrometer and an APM agent give you, nest new offers to set up NestJS Observe, which reports requests, jobs and errors in terms of your controllers and providers.

springdoc becomes @nestjs/swagger:

const config = new DocumentBuilder().setTitle('Orders API').setVersion('1.0').build();
SwaggerModule.setup('api', app, () => SwaggerModule.createDocument(app, config));

Swagger UI is at /api. Its compiler plugin reads property types and optionality from your DTOs at build time, so you don't put @ApiProperty() on every field, and Zod schemas describe the document too.

Testing

@WebMvcTest with @MockitoBean becomes a testing module with a fake provider, and MockMvc becomes Supertest:

@WebMvcTest(OrdersController.class)
class OrdersControllerTest {
  @Autowired MockMvc mvc;
  @MockitoBean OrdersService ordersService;

  @Test
  void returnsAnOrder() throws Exception {
    when(ordersService.findOne("42")).thenReturn(new Order("42", "c-1", OrderStatus.PENDING));
    mvc.perform(get("/orders/42")).andExpect(status().isOk()).andExpect(jsonPath("$.id").value("42"));
  }
}

describe('OrdersController', () => {
  let app: INestApplication;
  const ordersService = { findOne: vi.fn() };

  beforeAll(async () => {
    const moduleRef = await Test.createTestingModule({
      controllers: [OrdersController],
      providers: [{ provide: OrdersService, useValue: ordersService }],
    }).compile();
    app = moduleRef.createNestApplication();
    await app.init();
  });

  afterAll(() => app.close());

  it('returns an order', async () => {
    ordersService.findOne.mockResolvedValue({ id: '42', customerId: 'c-1', status: 'pending' });
    const response = await request(app.getHttpServer()).get('/orders/42').expect(200);
    expect(response.body.id).toBe('42');
  });
});

For a @SpringBootTest, import AppModule instead and swap individual providers with .overrideProvider(OrdersService).useValue(fake). And for a plain unit test you need no framework at all: a provider is a class, so new OrdersService(fakeRepository) works.

Shipping it

A Spring Boot service ships as a fat jar or an image built from one. A Nest service ships as compiled JavaScript plus its node_modules, almost always in a container. A production Dockerfile, built in one stage and run in another:

FROM node:24-slim AS build
WORKDIR /app
COPY package*.json ./
RUN npm ci
COPY . .
RUN npm run build && npm prune --omit=dev

FROM node:24-slim
ENV NODE_ENV=production
WORKDIR /app
COPY --from=build /app/package.json ./
COPY --from=build /app/node_modules ./node_modules
COPY --from=build /app/dist ./dist
USER node
CMD ["node", "--enable-source-maps", "dist/main.js"]

Three things to check that Spring handled for you:

  • Shutdown hooks. Spring runs @PreDestroy on SIGTERM without being asked. Nest runs onModuleDestroy() and onApplicationShutdown() only after app.enableShutdownHooks() in main.ts.
  • The process gets the signal. Use the exec form, CMD ["node", ...], not npm start, which doesn't reliably forward signals to Node.
  • Memory. Node's heap limit is a flag, like -Xmx. Set --max-old-space-size below the container's memory limit, so running out of memory is a JavaScript error with a stack trace instead of a silent OOMKilled.

Moving over without a rewrite

You don't have to move a Spring codebase to Nest to start using Nest. The pattern I'd recommend:

  • Start with a new service, not a port. The next service you need gets written in Nest, behind the same gateway or ingress, using the same database conventions and the same auth (a guard can verify the JWTs your Spring services already issue, for example with @nestjs/jwt).
  • Share the contract, not the code. springdoc already publishes an OpenAPI document for your Spring services; generate a TypeScript client from it for the Nest service, and the other way round with @nestjs/swagger.
  • Move existing endpoints only when you'd rewrite them anyway. A route that's being redesigned can move to the Nest service behind the gateway, one path at a time.

What's actually different

The syntax takes a week. These take longer, so I'd rather you hear them from me than find them in production.

One thread. Spring MVC gives each request a thread. Node.js runs all of your code on one thread with an event loop: while a request waits for Postgres, the others run. That's why a modest Node process handles thousands of concurrent connections without any pool tuning, the same promise WebFlux and virtual threads make. The flip side is that CPU-heavy work in a handler, like hashing a big file or a long synchronous loop, blocks every other request in the process. Push that work to a queue (@nestjs/bullmq) or a worker thread, and scale with more processes instead of more threads. If your service is mostly number crunching, the JVM is the better runtime, and I'd say so to anyone.

No ThreadLocal, and request scope is contagious. Per-request state goes in AsyncLocalStorage, which follows a request through every await. Don't reach for request-scoped providers to get the current user: Spring injects a request-scoped bean into singletons through a proxy, but Nest has no proxies, so a request-scoped provider makes everything that injects it request-scoped too, all the way up to the controller, rebuilt on every request. Keep providers singletons.

No proxies, no AOP. Nest's DI reads constructor types from metadata the TypeScript compiler emits, once, at startup. There's no bytecode generation and no proxy around your beans. You lose @Transactional, @Cacheable and @Retryable on arbitrary methods, and you also lose the self-invocation trap that comes with them. Cross-cutting concerns live in interceptors, guards and pipes around route handlers, and in decorators from packages like @nestjs/resilience (on handlers) and @nestjs/locks (on scheduled jobs).

Types are a compile-time check. Interfaces and generic type arguments don't exist at runtime, which is why injection uses abstract classes or tokens, and why a request body, a database row or a message from another service is only as typed as the code that validated it.

Decorators are functions. A Java annotation is passive metadata read by reflection. A TypeScript decorator runs when the class is defined, and Nest's decorators use that moment to record what Nest reads at startup. You'll rarely notice, but it's why a decorator can take any expression as an argument.

Numbers are doubles. There's no BigDecimal. Keep money in integer cents, or use a decimal library and your database's numeric type, which most drivers return as a string anyway.

ES modules. A new project imports local files with a .js extension, even from .ts files, because that's the name of the compiled file. It looks wrong for about a day.

When I'd stay on Spring

To be fair to Spring: if you have a large, healthy Spring codebase, a rewrite to get TypeScript is rarely worth it. If the work is CPU-bound, or depends on a JVM library with no Node equivalent, stay. And Spring's ecosystem for things like batch processing is deeper than anything in Node.

Nest is a good fit when the new thing is a new service, when the people building it also write the TypeScript frontend, or when you want one language from the browser to the database without giving up the structure you're used to.

Getting started 

npx @nestjs/cli new orders-api
cd orders-api
npm run start:dev

Then nest g resource orders, and you have a module, controller, service, DTOs and tests to compare against the Spring version in your head. The Coming from Spring Boot page in the docs keeps this mapping as a reference, with a link from each row to its full chapter.

If something there doesn't match how you'd do it in Spring, tell me. It's written for you, and it's easy to fix.

Coming from .NET instead? Here's the same tour for ASP.NET Core: NestJS for ASP.NET Core developers.

title: Motion that hurts visitors: reduced motion and layout
description:
Animation can make visitors dizzy or lock up a page. The common CSS motion mistakes, which WCAG criteria apply, and how to test reduced motion in DevTools.

Most animation bugs are invisible to the person who wrote the animation. It looks smooth on a fast laptop with the operating-system setting left at its default, so it ships. The people who pay for it are visitors whose inner ear reacts to large movement, visitors who cannot read a sentence while something beside it keeps sliding, and visitors on a phone that starts to stutter. This guide lists the motion mistakes that cause real harm, ties each to the guidance that names it, and ends with a test you can run in a browser in under a minute that can fail.

Read the full report on AISkills402: https://aiskills402.com/blog/css-motion-reduced-motion-mistakes?utm_source=devto&utm_medium=social

title: Technical Documentation That Gets Read
description:
Technical documentation fails in a specific and predictable way. Somebody writes a great deal of it during a quiet fortnight, the system changes, nobody updates it, and within a year the document is confidently wrong. At that point it is worse than nothing, because a reader who trusts it acts on information that no longer holds.

The usual response is a push to write more, which accelerates the same failure. The useful response is to write less and choose what, because the constraint is not authoring effort. It is maintenance.

The only durable test for whether a document should exist: will somebody notice when it becomes wrong? A deployment guide gets used and its errors surface immediately. A twenty-page description of a subsystem gets read once, and its errors surface eighteen months later when somebody acts on it. Documents nobody exercises rot silently, and those are the ones to leave unwritten.

Why It Goes Stale

Three mechanisms, and only one of them is laziness.

Documentation lives away from the thing it describes. A change to the code is not a change to a wiki page, so keeping them aligned depends on somebody remembering. That memory fails, reliably, and the further the document sits from the code the faster it goes.

It describes implementation rather than intent. A document explaining how a component currently works is invalidated by every refactor. One explaining why the component exists and what constraint it satisfies survives, because the reason changes far less often than the code.

Nobody owns it. Documentation owned by everybody is owned by no one, and there is no moment at which its accuracy is anybody's problem.

The fixes follow from the causes: keep it close to the code, write intent over mechanism, and give each document a named owner and a reason somebody exercises it.

The Technical Documentation Worth Maintaining

Four documents cover most of the value. Everything else should have to justify itself.

A README that gets you running. What this is, how to set it up, how to run the tests, how to deploy. Exercised constantly, so errors surface fast. This is the highest-return document in any repository and the one most often left as a project template nobody edited.

An architecture overview. What the major pieces are, how they communicate, and why they are separated. One page and a diagram, describing shape rather than detail. It changes rarely and answers the question every new engineer otherwise reconstructs by reading everything.

Decision records. Short notes capturing a decision, the alternatives considered and the reason. These are append-only, never need updating, and prevent the most expensive kind of repeated work: re-arguing a settled question badly because nobody remembers the constraint that settled it.

Runbooks for things that break. How to diagnose and fix the failures you have actually had. Written after an incident while it is fresh, and exercised at the next one. A runbook nobody has followed is a draft.

Notice that none of these is a description of how the code works. That is what the code is for, and any prose duplicating it becomes a second source of truth that will disagree with the first.

Write for Somebody Tired and in a Hurry

Most technical documentation is read under pressure, by someone with a specific question, often outside working hours. Write for that reader rather than for a leisurely one.

Answer first, explain after. The person reading your runbook at two in the morning needs the command, then the reasoning. Context before answer is a structure that suits the author and nobody else.

Be concrete. Real commands, real paths, real example values. "Configure the appropriate environment variables" is not instruction, it is a description of instruction.

Say what will go wrong. The failure modes and what they look like are frequently the most valuable content, because they are what the reader is actually experiencing.

Keep it short enough to stay true. Every sentence is a maintenance liability. A page that covers the common case and admits its own limits beats a document that covers everything and is wrong in three places.

The same discipline that makes a page quotable to a retrieval system makes it usable to a tired colleague, which is the point our guide to why content ranks but never gets cited makes about public writing.

Keeping It Alive

Put it in the repository. A document that travels with the code is changed in the same review as the code, which is the only mechanism that reliably keeps the two aligned.

Review it in code review. If a change makes a document wrong, that is a review comment like any other. This is the single highest-leverage habit available and it costs nothing.

Test what you can. Setup instructions that run in a pipeline stop being aspirational. If your README claims three commands produce a running system, have a job prove it.

Delete aggressively. A wrong document is worse than a missing one, because it is trusted. When something goes stale and nobody will fix it, remove it and note what was lost.

Date the things that expire. Anything with a version number, a price or an external dependency should carry a date, so a reader can judge whether to trust it.

What This Is Really For

Documentation is the mechanism by which knowledge stops depending on individuals. That is the entire benefit, and it is why the argument for writing it is a business one rather than an aesthetic one.

A system only one person can deploy has a recovery time equal to that person's availability. A component nobody can justify gets rebuilt or preserved on superstition. Both show up as findings in technical due diligence, both extend developer onboarding, and both are the same problem wearing different clothes.

Mecanik writes this as part of handover on every engagement, as part of our software development work. The document that gets used is nearly always shorter than the one that was requested.

Related reading

  • API Versioning: When to Break and How Not To
  • Database Performance: Finding the Query That Is Killing You
  • Software Testing Strategies That Survive Real Users
  • Postmortems That Actually Change Something

Frequently Asked Questions

Why does technical documentation go out of date?
Because it lives away from the code, so alignment depends on somebody remembering; because it describes implementation rather than intent, so every refactor invalidates it; and because nobody owns it, so its accuracy is never anybody's specific problem. Keeping it in the repository and reviewing it alongside code changes addresses all three.

What documentation should a software team maintain?
Four things cover most of the value: a README that gets the system running, a one-page architecture overview explaining shape and reasoning, append-only decision records capturing why choices were made, and runbooks for failures you have actually had. Descriptions of how the code works are not on the list.

What is a decision record?
A short note capturing a decision, the alternatives considered and the reason for the choice. Because it records a moment rather than a current state, it never needs updating, and it prevents settled questions being re-argued badly by people who no longer remember the constraint that settled them.

How should technical documentation be written?
For somebody tired, under pressure and looking for one specific thing. Answer first and explain afterwards, use real commands and real paths rather than descriptions of them, say what goes wrong and what it looks like, and keep it short enough that it stays true.

Should out of date documentation be deleted?
Yes, if nobody will fix it. A wrong document is worse than a missing one because a reader trusts it and acts on it. Delete it and note what was lost, and date anything containing a version number, a price or an external dependency so readers can judge it themselves.

title: The Key Expires in 24 Hours. The Retry Arrives on Monday.
description:
itsvicmoreno left a comment on my last piece about the crash between the key insert and the charge, and it named the hole my run never tested. My rig crashed the receiver between writing the key and charging the card, in both orders, and measured what each shape lost. But every retry in that run arrived seconds later, while the provider still held the key. itsvicmoreno asked about the retry that arrives after the key is gone.

The provider's own docs say an idempotency key can be pruned once it is at least 24 hours old. A retry that waits past that, a dead-letter replay after a weekend outage or a row reclaimed the next day, is treated as a brand-new request. The shape as I ran it never tested a retry outside the window. So I built the weekend: same event, same $29 payment for order ORD-1042, a crash after the first charge lands, and then the retry arriving 25 hours later, after the key has expired. Two candidate fixes, and one of them survives. The other one refuses the retry and leaves the order stuck.

My claim before the numbers: the retry-age cap would be the fix, because refusing a stale retry is simpler than teaching the retry to look anything up. I was wrong about which one holds.

Problem 1: the expired key charges twice, exactly as the docs say

The control arm is the shape most systems actually have. First attempt: the charge lands at the provider, then the receiver dies before marking it done. Twenty-five hours later the dead-letter queue replays it. The provider's key is 90,000 seconds old. The lifetime is 86,400. The provider no longer holds it, so the retry looks like a new request, and the provider charges again.

Two provider charges. $58.00 for a $29.00 order. One local charge on the books, one charge the customer sees twice and nobody on our side can explain from the local record alone, because the local record says the order was charged once. The retry returned 200, status processed, and nothing in that response says anything went wrong. The double charge is invisible until the customer finds it, which is the same asymmetry as the last piece: a false "already charged" costs one charge nobody sees, and a false "not charged" costs a double charge somebody sees. This one is the second kind, and it still took a customer to notice, because our side of the record looked clean.

I ran the whole thing twice, and both runs gave the same numbers in every arm. The double is not a flake. It is what the shape does.

Problem 2: the order-id lookup makes the provider's clock irrelevant

The second arm changes one thing. Before retrying, the receiver searches the provider by our own order id, ORD-1042, instead of asking by the key. The key is still expired. The lookup does not care. The provider finds the first charge under that order id, answers "already charged", and the retry stops there.

One provider charge. $29.00. The retry returns 200, status duplicate, detail "provider already charged (order-id lookup)", and nothing is charged a second time. The order lands in "done" on the local record, which is the part the other fix never manages.

itsvicmoreno said it first in his follow-up: search the provider by your own order id before retrying, and the provider's clock stops mattering. He was right, and the run proves it in the shape that matters most: the retry that arrives after the key is dead is exactly the retry the lookup saves. The key is a convenience for the first 24 hours. The order id is the record that outlives it. If your retry path only knows the key, it has a 24-hour memory and a weekend-long blind spot.

Problem 3: the age cap refuses in time, and abandons the order

The third arm is the fix I believed in before the run. The retry path refuses any retry older than a 23-hour cap, set below the provider's 24-hour lifetime. The replay arrives at 25 hours. The receiver refuses it with a 422: retry older than cap, needs manual reconciliation.

One provider charge. $29.00. No double. The money is safe. But look at the local record: the order is still sitting in "processing". Zero local charges. The customer was charged once, the order was never marked done, and the only thing standing between that row and a human is a dead-letter entry that says "needs manual reconciliation". The cap protected the money and abandoned the job. Somebody has to go and finish it by hand, and if nobody does, the customer paid for an order the system still thinks is unfinished.

That is the honest shape of the cap. It is a backstop, not a fix. It stops the bleeding and leaves the wound open. On a quiet week, one manual reconciliation is nothing. On a weekend outage with a queue full of replays, it is a Monday morning of manual work, and every row in that queue is a customer who already paid.

Problem 4: the two fixes are not symmetric, and the order matters

So which one holds? The lookup, and it is not close. The lookup finishes the order: one charge, done on the record, no human needed. The cap refuses the retry: one charge, processing on the record, human needed. Both keep the money at $29. Only one finishes the work.

The right shape is both, in this order: lookup first, cap as the backstop. The lookup handles the replay that arrives after the key is gone, which is the common case after an outage. The cap handles the replay the lookup cannot settle — the provider that cannot be searched by order id, the lookup that fails, the answer that comes back "unknown". The cap is the fence at the edge. The lookup is the road.

The limit I have to state plainly: the provider here is a second table in the same process, modelling exactly one property — an idempotency-key lookup with a 24-hour lifetime. It has no network failures, no provider-side timeouts, no partial provider state. The 25-hour gap was simulated by ageing the stored key in place, not by waiting a day. What the run proves is the shape of the three arms against a key that is gone, not the behaviour of any real provider's prune. And the lookup only works if the provider lets you search by your own order id. If yours does not, the cap is all you have, and you should know what it leaves behind.

What do you do with retries older than the key lifetime: cap them, look them up, or let them through? I would like to hear which one your system does, and whether you found out from the design or from the second charge.

P.S. Everything I write stays free — that part doesn't change. But if this one was worth something to you, you can buy me a coffee ☕ (one-time or monthly, both work). It covers the API credits and hosting behind these experiments — and honestly, it's also the nudge that gets the next one started on the evenings I'd otherwise skip it. — Salam

title: My MCP Scanner Scored 0 of 2 on a Real CVE. Here Is What Found It Instead
description:
sooperset/mcp-atlassian is an MCP server for Jira and Confluence with 6,139 stars on GitHub. Version 0.16.0 has two published CVEs, one of them critical. I maintain mcpscan, a static scanner for MCP servers, and back in September I extended its path traversal rule to cover file writes after reading about the critical one. This week I ran the scanner against the vulnerable release itself, and it found neither CVE.

TL;DR

  • mcpscan 0.21.0 reported 7 findings on mcp-atlassian v0.16.0. None was a real bug. It missed CVE-2026-27825 (file write, CVSS 9.1) and CVE-2026-27826 (SSRF).
  • The patched v0.17.0 got the same 7 findings, line for line.
  • Reading the code by hand, following each path parameter to the place it gets written, found the 4 sites upstream fixed in 0.17.0.
  • mcpscan 0.22.0, released today, flags the two vulnerable write sinks as HIGH and has no MCP007 finding on the patched release. It still does not see the SSRF, and it loses track of a path that passes through several functions.

The two CVEs

CVE Severity What Fixed in
CVE-2026-27825 Critical, CVSS 9.1 Arbitrary file write leading to code execution, through the unconstrained download path in confluence_download_attachment 0.17.0
CVE-2026-27826 High SSRF through the X-Atlassian-Jira-Url and X-Atlassian-Confluence-Url headers 0.17.0

The advisory range for the file write is <0.17.0. The fix calls validate_safe_path(...) before every download is written.

What mcpscan 0.21.0 reported

I scanned src/ of the v0.16.0 tag: 94 files, about 6 seconds, 30 rules, 7 findings.

Going through them one by one:

  • Two MCP005 "hardcoded secret" hits in utils/oauth.py:30 and :39. They are CLOUD_TOKEN_URL and DC_TOKEN_PATH, an OAuth endpoint URL and a path. The maintainers had already marked both # noqa: S105, the same complaint from their own linter.
  • Two MCP007 "path traversal" hits in utils/oauth_setup.py:141 and :149. Both are JavaScript window.open( calls inside an HTML page that Python builds as a string. My regex saw open( and fired.
  • Three MCP010 "TLS verification disabled" hits in utils/ssl.py:42, :43 and :69. That code only runs when the operator sets ssl_verify=false, so it is there by design.

Then I scanned v0.17.0, the release that fixes both CVEs. Same 7 findings, same files, same lines. Whatever the report was measuring, it was not the security of the download path.

What found it: a manual trace

The question I asked by hand was narrow. For every function that writes a file, where does the path come from, and does anything check that it stays inside a base directory before the write?

In src/mcp_atlassian/confluence/attachments.py on v0.16.0 the answer takes a few lines to find:

def download_attachment(self, url: str, target_path: str) -> bool:
    ...
    # Convert to absolute path if relative
    if not os.path.isabs(target_path):
        target_path = os.path.abspath(target_path)

    # Create the directory if it doesn't exist
    os.makedirs(os.path.dirname(target_path), exist_ok=True)

    # Use the Confluence session to download the file
    response = self.confluence._session.get(url, stream=True)
    response.raise_for_status()

    # Write the file to disk
    with open(target_path, "wb") as f:

target_path is a parameter. os.path.abspath makes it absolute and does nothing to limit where it points. os.makedirs creates whatever directory is missing. Line 198 writes the downloaded bytes there. jira/attachments.py has the same shape, with the write at line 50.

Following the callers turned up two more functions, download_content_attachments and download_issue_attachments, which take a target directory and write through those two. That makes 4 sites, and they are the same 4 that upstream patched in 0.17.0.

In download_attachment the upstream fix is one call after abspath:

    # Guard against path traversal (resolves symlinks)
    validate_safe_path(target_path)

validate_safe_path resolves the path, symlinks included, and raises ValueError unless the result is_relative_to the base directory, which defaults to the working directory.

Why MCP007 missed it

The September change added write sinks to MCP007, but the rule still only fired when the path was interpolated on the same line as the sink. It catches open(f"{base}/{name}", "w"). The vulnerable line here is with open(target_path, "wb") as f:. There is nothing on that line for a regex to object to. The danger is that target_path came in from the caller at the top of the function and nothing checked it in between, and a line-based rule has no view of that.

The fix in mcpscan 0.22.0

mcpscan 0.22.0 adds a small ast pass for each Python function, next to the existing line regex:

  1. Start from the function's parameters. Names assigned from a parameter p, from Path(p) or from os.path.abspath(p) count as the same value.
  2. Look for a write sink that receives one of those names: open with a w, a, x or + mode, write_text, write_bytes, shutil.copy, copy2, copyfile and move, and os.rename and os.replace.
  3. If the function has no boundary check, report it as HIGH. A boundary check is realpath or resolve followed by startswith, is_relative_to or commonpath, or a call to anything named like *safe_path* or *validate_path*.

It also stopped matching window.open(.

On v0.16.0, MCP007 now reports confluence/attachments.py:198 and jira/attachments.py:50 as HIGH. On v0.17.0 it reports nothing, and the total drops to 5: the unchanged MCP005 and MCP010 findings. The release has 8 new tests, the full suite passes 266 of 266, and mcpscan's scan of its own code is clean.

Getting that self-scan clean needed one suppression. drift.py writes mcpscan's own baseline file to a path that arrives as a parameter, which is exactly the shape the new check looks for:

with open(path, "w", encoding="utf-8") as fh:  # mcpscan: ignore[MCP007] baseline path is ours, not tool input

That is the noise the check will add elsewhere. In an MCP server, a path parameter often comes from a tool call, and an unchecked write to it is the bug. In a generic utility or a CLI that writes where its own user told it to, the same pattern is fine, and you will be suppressing it.

What it still cannot do

  • A path that passes through several functions before the write is not tracked. The pass looks at one function at a time. It flags the two functions that do the writing in mcp-atlassian, while the two download-all functions that pass a directory down to them get no finding of their own.
  • A check that lives in the caller is not recognised. If the caller validates the path and the writing function does not, 0.22.0 still reports the writing function.
  • The SSRF is still missed. 0.22.0 changed MCP007 and nothing else, so on this release it gets 1 of the 2 CVEs, the file write.
  • The "14 of 14, zero false positives" benchmark I published earlier measured synthetic fixtures I wrote myself. It says nothing about detection on real code, and this run shows the difference.

Where the scanner fits in a review

Automated MCP scanners are sold for about $0.25 per server on Apify. That price is fine for what a scanner does. In this case the review was the human trace: take every input a tool call controls, follow it to the file system, the network or a shell, and look for what stops it. The scanner is the second pass, useful for the code you did not get to and for catching the same mistake when it comes back.

mcpscan 0.22.0 is on PyPI as mcpscan-cli:

pip install -U mcpscan-cli
mcpscan ./path-to-an-mcp-server

If you run an MCP server and want that trace done before a release, I offer a free preflight.

title: How to Find and Highlight Text in a PDF with Java
description:
When you review a purchase agreement, the phrase “payment terms” might appear in the main contract and again in an addendum. A Java program can tell you which pages to check, pinpoint each match on the page, and save a highlighted copy to share with a reviewer.

The examples below use the same three-page PDF. You can run each one on its own, depending on whether you need page numbers, coordinates, or a marked-up document.

Set Up the Maven Project

Add this repository and dependency to your project's pom.xml.

<repositories>
    <repository>
        <id>com.e-iceblue</id>
        <url>https://repo.e-iceblue.com/nexus/content/groups/public/</url>
    </repository>
</repositories>

<dependencies>
    <dependency>
        <groupId>e-iceblue</groupId>
        <artifactId>spire.pdf</artifactId>
        <version>12.10.3</version>
    </dependency>
</dependencies>

Prepare a Sample PDF

Save a searchable PDF as purchase-agreement.pdf in the program's working directory. To reproduce the examples, put the following text on three separate pages and export the document as a PDF.

Page Sample text
1 Payment terms: invoices are due within 30 days of receipt. Any change to the payment terms must be agreed in writing.
2 The supplier must deliver the equipment by the agreed date.
3 Payment terms in the signed addendum take precedence.

All three examples use TextFindParameter.IgnoreCase, so both “Payment terms” and “payment terms” match.

Find the Pages That Contain a Keyword

To see which pages mention the phrase, create a PdfTextFinder for each page and call find(). The size of the result tells you how many matches that page contains. The program skips pages with zero matches and adds 1 to the zero-based page index before printing it.

import com.spire.pdf.PdfDocument;
import com.spire.pdf.texts.PdfTextFinder;
import com.spire.pdf.texts.TextFindParameter;

import java.util.EnumSet;

public class FindPdfKeywordPages {

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        String keyword = "payment terms";

        PdfDocument document = new PdfDocument();
        try {
            document.loadFromFile("purchase-agreement.pdf");
            int totalMatches = 0;

            for (int i = 0; i < document.getPages().getCount(); i++) {
                PdfTextFinder finder = new PdfTextFinder(document.getPages().get(i));
                finder.getOptions().setTextFindParameter(EnumSet.of(TextFindParameter.IgnoreCase));
                int matches = finder.find(keyword).size();

                if (matches > 0) {
                    System.out.printf("Page %d: %d%n", i + 1, matches);
                    totalMatches += matches;
                }
            }

            System.out.printf("Total matches for \"%s\": %d%n", keyword, totalMatches);
        } finally {
            document.dispose();
        }
    }
}

For the sample agreement, the console output looks like this.

Page 1: 2
Page 3: 1
Total matches for "payment terms": 3

Get the Page Coordinates of Each Match

Each match comes back as a PdfTextFragment. Its getPositions() method returns an array of points. A match that spans multiple lines can return more than one point, so the code prints every point for that match.

Coordinates are measured in points (pt) from the top-left corner of the page. The x-coordinate increases to the right, and the y-coordinate increases down the page.

import com.spire.pdf.PdfDocument;
import com.spire.pdf.texts.PdfTextFinder;
import com.spire.pdf.texts.PdfTextFragment;
import com.spire.pdf.texts.TextFindParameter;

import java.awt.geom.Point2D;
import java.util.EnumSet;
import java.util.Locale;

public class GetPdfKeywordPositions {

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        String keyword = "payment terms";

        PdfDocument document = new PdfDocument();
        try {
            document.loadFromFile("purchase-agreement.pdf");

            for (int i = 0; i < document.getPages().getCount(); i++) {
                PdfTextFinder finder = new PdfTextFinder(document.getPages().get(i));
                finder.getOptions().setTextFindParameter(EnumSet.of(TextFindParameter.IgnoreCase));
                int matchNumber = 0;

                for (PdfTextFragment match : finder.find(keyword)) {
                    matchNumber++;
                    for (Point2D position : match.getPositions()) {
                        System.out.printf(Locale.ROOT,
                                "Page %d, match %d: x=%.2f pt, y=%.2f pt%n",
                                i + 1, matchNumber, position.getX(), position.getY());
                    }
                }
            }
        } finally {
            document.dispose();
        }
    }
}

Here are the coordinates from the sample PDF. The values will vary with the layout of your file.

Page 1, match 1: x=72.00 pt, y=72.29 pt
Page 1, match 2: x=172.07 pt, y=96.29 pt
Page 3, match 1: x=72.00 pt, y=72.29 pt

Highlight All Matches in the PDF

Search each page as before, then call highLight(Color.YELLOW) on every match. Once all pages have been processed, save the document to a new file so you have a separate copy for review.

import com.spire.pdf.FileFormat;
import com.spire.pdf.PdfDocument;
import com.spire.pdf.texts.PdfTextFinder;
import com.spire.pdf.texts.PdfTextFragment;
import com.spire.pdf.texts.TextFindParameter;

import java.awt.Color;
import java.util.EnumSet;

public class HighlightPdfKeywords {

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        String keyword = "payment terms";

        PdfDocument document = new PdfDocument();
        try {
            document.loadFromFile("purchase-agreement.pdf");

            for (int i = 0; i < document.getPages().getCount(); i++) {
                PdfTextFinder finder = new PdfTextFinder(document.getPages().get(i));
                finder.getOptions().setTextFindParameter(EnumSet.of(TextFindParameter.IgnoreCase));

                for (PdfTextFragment match : finder.find(keyword)) {
                    match.highLight(Color.YELLOW);
                }
            }

            document.saveToFile("purchase-agreement-highlighted.pdf", FileFormat.PDF);
        } finally {
            document.dispose();
        }
    }
}

Open purchase-agreement-highlighted.pdf to see two yellow highlights on page 1 and one on page 3.

Common Issues

Why does the search miss text I can see on the page?

Try copying the phrase from your PDF viewer into a plain-text editor. If the page is an image-only scan, run OCR first to create a searchable text layer. If you can copy the text, check for extra spaces or line breaks in the copied phrase.

Why do the page numbers differ from the ones printed in the PDF?

The program counts from the first page in the file. If a cover page comes before the main text, the page labeled “1” in the footer may be page 2 in the search results.

Can I remove the highlights from the PDF viewer's comments panel?

highLight() writes the highlight into the page content. To give reviewers control over individual highlights in the comments panel, create PDF highlight annotations.

title: 三层数据交付策略：本地开发环境设置
description:
安全运营平台

Project Summary（6W 路演框架）

  • Who（目标客户与核心角色）：面向大型企业的安全运维团队，由 AI 全栈开发工程师主导核心架构与业务域研发。
  • What（核心产品与痛点解决）：企业级一体化安全运营管理平台，解决海量安全告警处理滞后及风险管控分散的痛点，提供网络安全监测、资产管控、漏洞治理与 AI 智能分析一体化能力。
  • Why（核心壁垒与竞争优势）：「定时任务 + Redis 缓存 + 未命中实时聚合回填」三层数据供给策略，将核心接口响应压至 50ms 以内；实现从风险识别到防护响应的全自动化闭环。
  • Where（应用场景与部署环境）：覆盖企业多场景安全运维、防火墙设备联动及域名安全监测，支持基于 Docker 容器编排的多环境隔离部署与数据源动态切换。
  • When（时效性与实时能力）：日均实时处理 10 万+ 条全网安全设备原始告警，支持 5 分钟级定时聚合与缓存刷新，150+ 表万级数据全表聚合任务耗时控制在 3 秒以内。
  • How（技术路径与交付机制）：基于微服务架构拆分业务模块、复用公共能力库，构建「Kafka + InfluxDB + 规则引擎」实时分析与设备自动化联动链路。

Business

  • AI：对接 AI Agent 实现攻击路径智能研判、系统/资产/漏洞三维风险评级及自动化整改建议生成。
  • 自动化：通过 IP 黑名单 AI 分析公开接口支撑防火墙设备拉取数据，实现从风险识别到防护响应全程自动化。
  • 高并发：支撑 150+ 张业务表及日均 10 万+ 条告警数据实时处理，核心监测接口响应由 2 秒+ 优化至 50ms 以内，纯 Redis 读取接口 QPS 承载量达 500+。
  • 高可用：缓存失效自动降级查库，保障系统 99.9% 高可用性。
  • 信创：实现达梦数据库 与 PostgreSQL 无缝切换。
  • 提效：通过微服务独立迭代及公共能力库复用大幅提升研发与交付效率。

Tech Stack

  • 后端：Spring Boot 3.2.6
  • 前端：Vue3
  • 数据库：InfluxDB
  • 缓存：Redis
  • 中间件：Kafka，PostgreSQL
  • 容器化：Docker

本指南将构建一个用于三层数据交付策略的工作级本地开发环境，该策略使用了定时聚合、Redis 缓存以及缓存未命中（cache miss）后的实时聚合与缓存回填。本示例使用 Spring Boot 3.2.6、Java 17、PostgreSQL、Redis、Maven 和 Docker Compose。

该本地应用程序暴露了一个安全告警摘要 API。定时处理任务会准备常用的摘要并将其存储在 Redis 中。常规请求直接从 Redis 读取已准备好的结果。如果键（key）不存在，服务将从 PostgreSQL 实时聚合当前数据，返回结果，并将其写回 Redis，以便下一次请求能够快速响应。

本指南特意仅限于本地开发环境。它不包含生产环境的验收标准或生产验收测试。

第 1 步：准备本地开发环境

安装以下软件：

  • Java Development Kit 17
  • Apache Maven 3.9 或更高版本
  • Docker Desktop 或带有 Docker Compose v2 的 Docker Engine
  • Git
  • HTTP 客户端，例如 curl、Postman 或 Bruno
  • IDE，例如 IntelliJ IDEA 或 Visual Studio Code

确认安装情况：

java -version
mvn -version
docker --version
docker compose version
git --version

预期的 Java 主版本是 17。Maven 必须报告它正在使用 Java 17 运行。在启动基础设施之前，必须确保 Docker 正在运行。

创建项目目录：

mkdir three-tier-data-delivery
cd three-tier-data-delivery
mkdir -p src/main/java/com/example/security/config
mkdir -p src/main/java/com/example/security/controller
mkdir -p src/main/java/com/example/security/domain
mkdir -p src/main/java/com/example/security/dto
mkdir -p src/main/java/com/example/security/repository
mkdir -p src/main/java/com/example/security/service
mkdir -p src/main/resources
mkdir -p src/test/java/com/example/security

最终的本地目录结构将包含 Spring Boot 应用程序、PostgreSQL 模式（schema）和种子数据、Redis 配置以及 Docker Compose 文件。

第 2 步：使用 Docker Compose 启动 PostgreSQL 和 Redis

在项目根目录下创建 compose.yaml：

services:
  postgres:
    image: postgres:16-alpine
    container_name: security-postgres
    environment:
      POSTGRES_DB: security_ops
      POSTGRES_USER: security_user
      POSTGRES_PASSWORD: security_password
    ports:
      - "5432:5432"
    volumes:
      - postgres_data:/var/lib/postgresql/data
      - ./src/main/resources/schema.sql:/docker-entrypoint-initdb.d/01-schema.sql:ro
      - ./src/main/resources/data.sql:/docker-entrypoint-initdb.d/02-data.sql:ro
    healthcheck:
      test: ["CMD-SHELL", "pg_isready -U security_user -d security_ops"]
      interval: 5s
      timeout: 3s
      retries: 20

  redis:
    image: redis:7.2-alpine
    container_name: security-redis
    command: ["redis-server", "--appendonly", "yes"]
    ports:
      - "6379:6379"
    volumes:
      - redis_data:/data
    healthcheck:
      test: ["CMD", "redis-cli", "ping"]
      interval: 5s
      timeout: 3s
      retries: 20

volumes:
  postgres_data:
  redis_data:

此 Compose 配置在端口 5432 暴露 PostgreSQL，在端口 6379 暴露 Redis。命名卷（Named volumes）在容器重启期间保留本地数据。PostgreSQL 仅在其数据卷首次初始化时运行模式和示例数据脚本。

创建 src/main/resources/schema.sql：

CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS security_alert (
    id BIGSERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
    tenant_id VARCHAR(64) NOT NULL,
    severity VARCHAR(16) NOT NULL,
    status VARCHAR(16) NOT NULL,
    source_ip VARCHAR(45),
    asset_id VARCHAR(128),
    detected_at TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL,
    updated_at TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP
);

CREATE INDEX IF NOT EXISTS idx_security_alert_tenant_detected
    ON security_alert (tenant_id, detected_at DESC);

CREATE INDEX IF NOT EXISTS idx_security_alert_tenant_severity_status
    ON security_alert (tenant_id, severity, status);

创建 src/main/resources/data.sql：

    ('tenant-a', 'MEDIUM',   'OPEN', '203.0.113.13', 'server-004', CURRENT_TIMESTAMP - INTERVAL '20 minutes'),

启动这两个服务：

docker compose up -d

检查它们的状态：

docker compose ps

这两个容器应该都变为健康状态 (healthy)。如果任一服务未启动，请检查日志：

docker compose logs postgres
docker compose logs redis

确认 PostgreSQL 数据：

docker exec -it security-postgres \
  psql -U security_user -d security_ops \
  -c "SELECT tenant_id, severity, status, COUNT(*) FROM security_alert GROUP BY tenant_id, severity, status ORDER BY tenant_id, severity;"

确认 Redis 连接：

docker exec -it security-redis redis-cli ping

Redis 的响应应该是 PONG。

第 3 步：创建 Spring Boot 应用程序

在项目根目录下创建 pom.xml：

         xsi:schemaLocation="http://maven.apache.org/POM/4.0.0 https://maven.apache.org/xsd/maven-4.0.0.xsd">

    <parent>
        <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>

</project>

创建 src/main/resources/application.yml：

server:
  port: 8080

spring:
  application:
    name: three-tier-data-delivery
  datasource:
    url: jdbc:postgresql://localhost:5432/security_ops

      maximum-pool-size: 10

本地缓存的存活时间（TTL）为 10 分钟。定时刷新每 5 分钟运行一次。每个摘要涵盖过去 24 小时内检测到的告警。调度器会刷新两个示例租户（tenant）的数据。

创建 src/main/java/com/example/security/SecurityApplication.java：

package com.example.security;

import org.springframework.boot.SpringApplication;

@SpringBootApplication
