title: How to Search Tweets with twitter-api-v2 in Node.js (2026)
description:
Searching Tweets with twitter-api-v2

twitter-api-v2 is the most popular Node.js/TypeScript client for the X (Twitter) API, and searching recent tweets is one of the first things most developers reach for. It's also where people hit the most friction: the method returns a paginator, not a plain array, so getting to the actual tweets (tweets.data.data) and paging through results trips up newcomers constantly

This guide walks through searching tweets with twitter-api-v2 end to end: authenticating, calling client.v2.search(), reading the results correctly, paginating, the query operators worth knowing, and the rate-limit/cost realities. At the end we look at a simpler alternative for when the official API's setup and pricing are more than your project needs

Installing and Authenticating 

npm install twitter-api-v2

Recent tweet search is app-only, so all you need is a Bearer token from the X developer portal. No user OAuth flow required:

import { TwitterApi } from 'twitter-api-v2';

// App-only client from a Bearer token
const client = new TwitterApi(process.env.X_BEARER_TOKEN);

// Use the read-only sub-client for search/lookups
const roClient = client.readOnly;

Two things to know up front:

  • Recent search covers the last 7 days only. The full-archive endpoint requires an elevated (Pro/Enterprise or Academic) access level
  • Your access tier determines your rate limits and how many tweets you can pull per month

Your First Search: client.v2.search() 

const results = await roClient.v2.search('javascript lang:en -is:retweet', {
  'tweet.fields': ['created_at', 'public_metrics', 'author_id'],
  max_results: 100, // 10-100 per page
});

The first argument is your query string (operators covered below). The options object mirrors the API's query params: tweet.fields, user.fields, expansions, start_time, end_time, and max_results (capped at 100 per request)

Reading the Results: the tweets.data.data Gotcha

client.v2.search() does not return an array of tweets. It returns a TweetSearchRecentV2Paginator. There are three correct ways to read it, and mixing them up is the single most common source of confusion:

// 1. Recommended - .tweets is every tweet fetched so far, as a flat array
for (const tweet of results.tweets) {
  console.log(tweet.id, tweet.text);
}

// 2. The RAW current-page payload - this is where "tweets.data.data" comes from
console.log(results.data.data);  // TweetV2[] for the current page
console.log(results.data.meta);  // { result_count, newest_id, next_token, ... }

// 3. Async iterator - automatically pages through results (mind rate limits)
for await (const tweet of results) {
  console.log(tweet.text);
}

Why does results.data.data have a double .data? The paginator's .data property is the raw API response, shaped like { data: Tweet[], meta: {...}, includes: {...} }. So .data.data is the tweet array nested inside that response. Stick with results.tweets in application code, and reach for results.data.data only when you need the raw page exactly as the API returned it

Guard against empty results. When a search matches nothing, result_count is 0 and results.data.data can be undefined:

if (!results.meta.result_count) {
  console.log('No tweets matched.');
} else {
  for (const tweet of results.tweets) console.log(tweet.text);
}

Pagination: Getting More Than One Page

Each request returns at most 100 tweets. The paginator handles the rest for you:

// Fetch one more page and merge it into results.tweets
await results.fetchNext();

// Keep fetching until you have ~1000 tweets (or the pages run out)
await results.fetchLast(1000);

console.log('Collected ' + results.tweets.length + ' tweets');
console.log('Exhausted?', results.done);

The async iterator (for await ... of results) pages automatically. That's convenient, but it will happily burn through your rate limit on a broad query, so cap it yourself

Search Query Operators Worth Knowing

The query string is where most of the power lives:

Operator Matches
from:username Tweets from a specific account
to:username Replies directed at an account
#hashtag A hashtag
"exact phrase" An exact phrase
-keyword Excludes a keyword
lang:en A specific language
-is:retweet Excludes retweets
is:reply / -is:reply Only / no replies
has:media / has:links Tweets containing media / links
url:"github.com" Tweets linking a domain

Combine them freely: from:vitalikbuterin (ethereum OR rollup) -is:retweet has:links

Rate Limits and the Cost Problem

This is where teams get stuck. Recent search on the X API v2 is rate-limited per 15-minute window and capped by a monthly tweet-pull quota tied to your plan. In practice:

  • The Basic tier runs $200/month and still caps how many tweets you can retrieve
  • Recent search only reaches back 7 days; historical work needs the pricier full-archive access
  • Hitting the ceiling means 429 responses and building backoff, queueing, and quota tracking around them

For a detailed breakdown see our guides on X API pricing and rate limits

Other Recipes You Will Need Next

Search is rarely the only call. These are the four that follow it in almost every project

Pull a user's timeline 

const timeline = await roClient.v2.userTimeline('44196397', {
  max_results: 100,
  'tweet.fields': ['created_at', 'public_metrics'],
  exclude: ['retweets', 'replies'],
});

for (const tweet of timeline.tweets) console.log(tweet.text);

Note that userTimeline takes a numeric user id, not a handle. Resolving the handle first costs you an extra call

Resolve handles to ids 

const user = await roClient.v2.userByUsername('elonmusk', {
  'user.fields': ['public_metrics', 'created_at', 'description'],
});
console.log(user.data.id, user.data.public_metrics.followers_count);

// Up to 100 at once
const many = await roClient.v2.usersByUsernames(['elonmusk', 'vitalikbuterin']);

Read followers 

const followers = await roClient.v2.followers('44196397', {
  max_results: 1000,
  'user.fields': ['public_metrics'],
  asPaginator: true,
});

Followers is one of the tightest limits on the official API: 15 requests per 15 minutes on most tiers, so a 100k-follower account takes hours to page through

Filter by engagement, and why it silently fails

This is the trap that costs people the most time:

// Looks right. Does NOT work on API v2.
const results = await roClient.v2.search('solana min_faves:100');

min_faves:, min_retweets: and min_replies: work in the web search box but are silently ignored by API v2. No error, no warning, just unfiltered results. Your options are to filter client-side after fetching (paying for every tweet you throw away), or to use a provider whose search speaks the full web operator set

Common Errors and Fixes

  • 401 Unauthorized: bad or missing Bearer token, or your app lacks read access. Regenerate the token and double-check the project's permissions
  • 403 Forbidden: your access tier can't use this endpoint (recent search needs Basic+, full-archive needs Pro/Academic)
  • 429 Too Many Requests: you're rate-limited. Read the x-rate-limit-reset header and back off with jitter
  • results.data.data is undefined: the search matched nothing, so check results.meta.result_count before indexing

A Simpler Alternative: XCROP

If the developer-app setup, the 7-day window, and the $200/month floor are more than your project needs, XCROP exposes the same tweet-search capability behind a single API key. No OAuth app, no Bearer-token juggling, and credit-based pricing that costs a fraction of the official API

curl -X POST https://xcrop.io/api/v2/search \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer xc_live_..." \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"query": "javascript lang:en", "count": 100, "sort": "latest"}'

The response is plain JSON: a data array of tweets plus a meta object with the cursor, so there is no paginator and no .data.data to unwrap:

const res = await fetch('https://xcrop.io/api/v2/search', {
  method: 'POST',
  headers: {
    'Authorization': 'Bearer ' + process.env.XCROP_API_KEY,
    'Content-Type': 'application/json',
  },
  body: JSON.stringify({ query: 'javascript lang:en', count: 100, sort: 'latest' }),
});

const { data } = await res.json();
for (const tweet of data) console.log(tweet.text);

You can sort by latest, engagement, or media, filter by min_likes / min_retweets / lang, and request up to 1,000 results in a single call. See every parameter in the interactive builder

Which Should You Use?

twitter-api-v2 (official) XCROP
Setup Developer app + Bearer token One API key
Auth OAuth / app-only token Bearer key in a header
Results shape Paginator (.tweets / .data.data) Plain JSON (data array + meta)
Search window 7 days (recent tier) Recent + trending coverage
Per-request cap 100 tweets Up to 1,000
Pricing From $200/mo (Basic) Free tier, then credit-based
Best for Deep X-native integrations Fast data pulls without the API-tier tax

If you're building a product deeply tied to the X platform, the official twitter-api-v2 library is the right tool. If you just need clean tweet data for a dashboard, a bot, research, or a side project, and you'd rather not wrestle with paginators, OAuth apps, and a $200/month minimum, XCROP gets you there in one curl

FAQ

What is tweets.data.data in twitter-api-v2?

It is the raw payload of the current page inside the paginator object. client.v2.search() returns a TweetSearchRecentV2Paginator, not an array: results.data is the API response and results.data.data is the TweetV2 array inside it. In application code you almost always want results.tweets instead, which flattens every page fetched so far

Why is data.data undefined after a search?

The search matched zero tweets. When nothing matches, result_count is 0 and results.data.data can be undefined, so check results.meta.result_count before you index into it

How far back can client.v2.search() go?

Seven days. Recent search only covers the last week; anything older needs full-archive search, which sits behind the Pro or Academic access tier

How many tweets can you get per call?

One hundred at most, set through max_results, then you paginate. Call results.fetchNext() for one more page or results.fetchLast(1000) to keep fetching toward a target count

Does twitter-api-v2 handle rate limits for you?

No. The library surfaces the rate-limit headers and throws on a 429, but the backoff is yours to write. Read x-rate-limit-reset and wait for the window rather than retrying immediately

Why does min_faves not work in API v2 search?

min_faves, min_retweets and min_replies work in the web search box but are silently ignored by API v2. There is no error, just unfiltered results, so you either filter client-side after fetching or use a provider whose search accepts the full web operator set

Originally published on the XCROP blog.

title: React UseCallBack Hook
description:
whenever a React component re-renders, the functions inside that component are normally recreated. To avoid unnecessary function reference changes, we can use useCallback.
useCallback is a React Hook that memoizes a function and returns the same function reference until its dependencies change.

import React, { useCallback, useState } from 'react'

function UseCallbackhook() {
    const[count,setCount] = useState(0);
    const[msg,setMsg] = useState("");
    function increase(){
        setCount(count+1);
    }
    // function fncallback(){
    //     console.log("hello world");
    // }
    const fncallback = useCallback(()=>{
        setMsg("hello world");
        console.log("hello world")
    },[]);
  return (
    <div>
      <h1>count : {count}</h1>
      <h1>message :{msg} </h1>
      <button onClick={increase}>+</button>
      <button onClick={fncallback}> show message</button>
    </div>
  )
}

export default UseCallbackhook

How does it work?
Initially, the component renders.
useCallback remembers the showMessage function reference.
When we click Increase, the count changes.
React re-renders the component.
Since the dependency array is empty, React returns the same function reference.

Advantages of useCallback

Helps avoid unnecessary function reference changes.
Useful when passing functions to memoized child components.
Helps optimize component rendering in suitable situations.
Useful when a function is a dependency of another Hook.

title: Why HTTP Status Codes Are Not Enough for Microservice Errors
description:
Why HTTP Status Codes Are Not Enough for Microservice Errors

HTTP status codes are essential to REST API design.

They tell us whether a request succeeded, failed because of a client problem, or encountered a server-side failure.

But when applications evolve into distributed systems, HTTP status codes become only part of the story.

Consider these questions:

  • What exactly caused the failure?
  • Which service owns the error?
  • Can the caller safely retry?
  • How should an unknown downstream error be handled?
  • How can operators trace the failure across services?

A 409 Conflict or 503 Service Unavailable cannot answer all of them.

While building NERV Exception, an open-source exception-handling library for Java and Spring Boot, I explored how a consistent error contract can address these limitations without tightly coupling independently deployed microservices.

Let's examine the problem from an API consumer's perspective.

1. The Same HTTP Status Can Mean Different Things

Imagine an e-commerce application with three services:

API Gateway
    |
    +-- Order Service
    |
    +-- Payment Service
    |
    +-- Inventory Service

Each service encounters a different failure.

Order Service

HTTP/1.1 409 Conflict

The order has already been processed.

Payment Service

HTTP/1.1 409 Conflict

The payment has already been captured.

Inventory Service

HTTP/1.1 409 Conflict

Inventory is reserved by another transaction.

All three return 409 Conflict.

But should clients handle them identically?

Probably not.

An already-processed order may require no further action.

An already-captured payment may require reconciliation.

An inventory reservation conflict may require refreshing availability.

If the response contains only:

{
  "status": 409,
  "message": "Conflict"
}

the consumer cannot reliably distinguish these conditions.

Add stable application error codes

Instead, return:

{
  "code": "ORDER_ALREADY_PROCESSED",
  "message": "The order has already been processed",
  "status": 409
}

For the payment failure:

{
  "code": "PAYMENT_ALREADY_CAPTURED",
  "message": "The payment has already been captured",
  "status": 409
}

And for inventory:

{
  "code": "INVENTORY_RESERVATION_CONFLICT",
  "message": "Inventory is reserved by another transaction",
  "status": 409
}

Now clients can identify each failure without parsing message text.

HTTP status codes classify failures. Application error codes identify them.

Both are useful, but they solve different problems.

2. Why Exception Messages Are Poor API Contracts

A common mistake is to use exception messages as machine-readable identifiers.

For example:

if ("Order has already been processed".equals(errorMessage)) {
    // Handle already-processed order
}

This is fragile.

Suppose someone changes the message:

Old:
Order has already been processed

New:
This order has already been completed

The underlying business condition hasn't changed.

But the consumer may stop recognizing it.

Messages can change because of localization, improved wording, security requirements, or ordinary refactoring.

A stable error code avoids that problem:

if ("ORDER_ALREADY_PROCESSED".equals(errorCode)) {
    // Handle already-processed order
}

The message remains useful for humans.

The code remains stable for software.

This introduces an important API design principle:

Application error codes should be treated as published contracts.

Renaming a code can break consumers even when the HTTP status and JSON structure remain unchanged.

3. Designing a More Expressive Error Response

A useful error contract should communicate more than an HTTP status and message.

For example:

{
  "code": "ORDER_ALREADY_PROCESSED",
  "message": "The order has already been processed",
  "status": 409,
  "retryable": false,
  "category": "BUSINESS",
  "traceId": "abc123",
  "spanId": "def456",
  "path": "/api/orders/123/process",
  "timestamp": "2026-11-20T08:30:00Z",
  "origin": {
    "service": "order-service",
    "instance": "order-service-1",
    "version": "1.0.0",
    "environment": "production"
  },
  "details": {}
}

This illustrates the response structure supported by NERV Exception's NervErrorResponse.

The business code, category, and example values are illustrative. Diagnostic fields depend on the application's configuration and available context.

Each field serves a purpose.

Field Purpose
code Stable application error identifier
message Human-readable explanation
status HTTP status
category General failure classification
retryable Recovery guidance
traceId Distributed tracing correlation
spanId Span correlation
path Request path
timestamp Response timestamp
origin Service-origin information
details Structured error-specific information

The goal isn't to expose as much information as possible.

It's to provide enough information for consumers to handle failures predictably while keeping sensitive internal details protected.

4. Modeling Application Errors in Spring Boot

Let's build a simplified example.

First, define an error response:

public record ApiError(
        String code,
        String message,
        int status,
        String category,
        boolean retryable
) {}

This is an educational example, not the full NERV Exception API.

Next, define an application exception:

public class OrderAlreadyProcessedException
        extends RuntimeException {

    public OrderAlreadyProcessedException() {
        super("The order has already been processed");
    }
}

Then handle it using Spring MVC:

@RestControllerAdvice
public class ApiExceptionHandler {

    @ExceptionHandler(OrderAlreadyProcessedException.class)
    public ResponseEntity<ApiError> handle(
            OrderAlreadyProcessedException exception
    ) {
        ApiError error = new ApiError(
                "ORDER_ALREADY_PROCESSED",
                "The order has already been processed",
                409,
                "BUSINESS",
                false
        );

        return ResponseEntity
                .status(HttpStatus.CONFLICT)
                .body(error);
    }
}

This produces a consistent response for that particular exception.

But there's an architectural problem.

What happens when you have 20 Spring Boot services?

If each application independently implements its own response DTO, exception handler, and error classification, inconsistencies eventually emerge.

One service includes an error code.

Another returns only a message.

Another exposes internal exception causes.

Another uses a different validation response structure.

This is where reusable exception-handling infrastructure becomes valuable.

A shared library can standardize the response contract and conversion mechanism while allowing applications to own their business errors.

5. HTTP Status, Category, and Retryability Are Different Concerns

A common shortcut is to derive retryability directly from HTTP status.

For example:

boolean retryable = status >= 500;

That is not a reliable rule.

A 500 response doesn't guarantee that repeating an operation is safe.

Likewise, a 409 may represent a permanent business conflict or a concurrency condition that could be resolved through a controlled retry.

Consider these illustrative examples:

Failure HTTP status Retryable
Invalid request 400 No
Resource not found 404 No
Already-processed order 409 No
Rate limit exceeded 429 Policy-dependent
Dependency unavailable 503 Potentially

The key distinction is that retryability describes a possible recovery strategy, not a guarantee of safe execution.

Applications still need to consider idempotency, unknown outcomes, retry limits, and backoff.

NERV Exception represents categories as strings, allowing applications to define classifications appropriate to their domains.

However, teams should establish conventions so that categories remain meaningful across services.

6. What Happens When One Microservice Returns an Unknown Error?

Consider a typical service-to-service interaction:

API Gateway
     |
     v
Order Service
     |
     v
Payment Service

Payment Service returns:

{
  "code": "PAYMENT_ALREADY_PROCESSED",
  "message": "Payment has already been processed",
  "status": 409,
  "category": "BUSINESS",
  "retryable": false
}

But Order Service doesn't recognize PAYMENT_ALREADY_PROCESSED.

What should happen?

There are three common approaches.

Option A: Replace the error

Order Service converts the response into a generic integration failure.

{
  "code": "DOWNSTREAM_SERVICE_ERROR",
  "message": "Unable to process order",
  "status": 500
}

This may be appropriate when the downstream failure should be hidden behind Order Service's public API.

But it can discard useful information.

Option B: Share every error code

Every microservice imports a common library containing all business error definitions.

This makes errors recognizable but introduces coupling.

When Payment Service adds a new code, other services may need dependency updates despite having no direct ownership of that business rule.

Option C: Preserve unknown codes

Services agree on the error response structure without requiring every application to register every downstream business code.

This allows independently deployed services to evolve more freely.

NERV Exception's Feign integration supports this approach using RemoteNervErrorCode.

For unknown downstream codes, it can preserve the remote code, message, response-body status, category, and retryability.

For codes registered locally, the local definition determines status, category, and retryability.

That distinction matters.

Registering a downstream error code locally can change how the receiving service interprets it.

A shared error contract improves interoperability, but it does not eliminate decisions about semantic ownership.

7. Error Propagation Is Not Always Transparent

Suppose Payment Service generates an error while handling:

POST /payments

Order Service receives that failure while handling:

POST /orders

Which request path should appear in the final error response?

The original downstream path?

Or the current request path?

Both describe useful but different contexts.

The same question applies to timestamps and tracing information.

In the reviewed NERV Exception implementation, the downstream exception retains supported remote information such as the message, origin, and details.

It does not retain the original downstream traceId, spanId, path, or timestamp for direct reuse.

When the receiving application generates a new HTTP response, those fields are populated from its current context.

This is why consistent error contracts and distributed tracing solve different problems.

An error contract identifies and classifies failures.

Distributed tracing helps reconstruct how those failures moved through the system.

Neither replaces the other.

8. Why HTTP 503 Doesn't Automatically Mean Retry

Consider a payment operation.

Order Service submits a payment request.

The payment provider processes it successfully.

But the response is lost because of a network interruption.

Order Service
     |
     | Submit payment
     v
Payment Service
     |
     | Payment succeeds
     v
Payment Provider
     |
     X Response lost

Order Service experiences a timeout.

Did the payment fail?

Or did it succeed without confirmation reaching the caller?

The caller doesn't know.

Retrying without idempotency protection could produce a duplicate payment.

Now consider this response:

{
  "code": "PAYMENT_PROVIDER_UNAVAILABLE",
  "message": "Payment provider is temporarily unavailable",
  "status": 503,
  "category": "DEPENDENCY",
  "retryable": true
}

The response communicates that retrying may be appropriate.

But the application must still decide whether the operation is safe to repeat.

NERV Exception's Feign decoder can wrap a retryable downstream failure in Feign's RetryableException.

However, the library does not automatically configure a retry policy.

Actual retry behavior depends on the application's Feign configuration.

There is another important consideration: after retry exhaustion, a generic exception handler may map the wrapper to an internal server error unless the application handles it explicitly.

Therefore:

Retry classification, retry execution, and final error presentation are separate responsibilities.

9. Error Contracts Are Also Compatibility Contracts

Consider an application that returns:

{
  "code": "PAYMENT_TIMEOUT",
  "retryable": false
}

Later, the service changes its response to:

{
  "code": "PAYMENT_TIMEOUT",
  "retryable": true
}

The JSON schema hasn't changed.

The error code hasn't changed.

But the semantics have.

Consumers may begin retrying operations they previously treated as final.

Similarly, changing an error code from CUSTOMER_DISABLED to CUSTOMER_INACTIVE can break consumers that rely on the original identifier.

This is why error contract compatibility should consider:

  • Error code stability
  • HTTP status mappings
  • Category semantics
  • Retryability changes
  • Unknown-code behavior
  • Diagnostic information exposure

A structurally compatible response is not necessarily behaviorally compatible.

10. What Should API Consumers Depend On?

Different fields serve different purposes.

A consumer should use the appropriate information for the decision it needs to make.

Consumer decision Relevant information
Determine the HTTP outcome HTTP status
Identify a specific business failure Application error code
Display an explanation Safe message
Classify the failure Category
Evaluate potential recovery Retryability and operation semantics
Investigate an incident Tracing and origin information
Handle validation failures Structured details

The goal is not to replace HTTP status codes.

It's to supplement them with application-level meaning.

11. Where NERV Exception Fits

NERV Exception provides reusable infrastructure for consistent error handling in Java and Spring Boot applications.

Its modules include:

Module Responsibility
nerv-exception-api Shared error contracts
nerv-exception-core Core exception and error-code behavior
nerv-exception-spring-web Spring Web exception handling
nerv-exception-spring-feign OpenFeign error decoding
nerv-exception-spring-boot-starter Spring Boot integration
nerv-exception-jpa Persistence-related support
nerv-exception-event Event-related support
nerv-exception-spring-kafka Kafka-related support

The library doesn't eliminate application-specific responsibilities.

Each service still needs to own its business errors, define appropriate recovery policies, and determine what information is safe to expose.

The objective is to standardize common infrastructure without centralizing every business decision.

Final Thoughts

HTTP status codes remain essential to REST API design.

They provide a standardized way to communicate the outcome of an HTTP interaction.

But microservice architectures require more information.

Consumers need to distinguish business failures, interpret downstream errors, evaluate potential recovery, and correlate failures across service boundaries.

Stable application error codes, meaningful classifications, retryability guidance, and diagnostic context help address these requirements.

HTTP status codes tell us how a request ended. A well-designed error contract tells us what the failure means.

Explore NERV Exception

NERV Exception is part of the open-source NERV ecosystem of reusable Java and Spring Boot libraries.

Explore the projects on GitHub:

https://github.com/czetsuyatech

For the canonical article and the rest of the NERV Exception series, visit:

https://www.czetsuyatech.com

title: Handling Payment Fumbles: ACH Return Codes and Recovery Logic
description:
Handling Payment Fumbles: ACH Return Codes and Recovery Logic

When Payments Go Wrong: Learning from Failure

In fintech, a failed payout isn't just frustrating—it's a data point. Every ACH return carries a specific code that tells you why the transfer failed. Just like a football team must analyze every turnover, a payment system needs to decode each return and route around it. This article walks through real ACH return codes and how to build logic that doesn't let a single failure break your payout flow.

The ACH Return Code Playbook

The National Automated Clearing House Association (Nacha) defines 85 possible return codes (R01–R85). Each maps to a specific rejection reason. Here are the most common ones you'll encounter:

Code Meaning Reversible? Retry Strategy
R01 Insufficient funds No Retry after 2–5 days or flag for manual review
R03 No account/unable to locate No Route to alternate rail or request new bank details
R04 Invalid account number structure No Request corrected account info from customer
R10 Unauthorized by account holder No Contact customer; may indicate fraud or dispute
R29 Corporate account closed No Update customer records; request new account

R01 (Insufficient Funds) fires when the receiver's account balance can't cover the debit. This is temporary—retry logic works here. Implement exponential backoff: retry at 24 hours, then 48 hours, then escalate to dunning (send a notification asking the receiver to top up).

R03 (No Account) means the account doesn't exist or the routing number is wrong. This is permanent. Don't retry. Instead, flag the receiver's account for manual review and ask them to verify their banking details.

R10 (Unauthorized) suggests the account holder disputed the transaction or blocked ACH debits. This requires human intervention—reach out to the customer directly.

Building a Return Handler

Here's a concrete pattern for handling returns programmatically:

async function handleACHReturn(returnData) {
  const { payoutId, returnCode, receiverId } = returnData;

  const returnLogic = {
    'R01': async () => {
      // Insufficient funds: retry after 48 hours
      await scheduleRetry(payoutId, 48);
      await notifyReceiver(receiverId, 'Please ensure sufficient funds.');
    },
    'R03': async () => {
      // No account: flag for manual review
      await flagForReview(payoutId, 'Invalid account number');
      await requestBankingDetails(receiverId);
    },
    'R04': async () => {
      // Invalid account structure: request correction
      await requestBankingDetails(receiverId);
      await markPayoutFailed(payoutId);
    },
    'R10': async () => {
      // Unauthorized: escalate to support
      await escalateToSupport(payoutId, 'Unauthorized by account holder');
    },
  };

  const handler = returnLogic[returnCode];
  if (handler) {
    await handler();
  } else {
    // Unknown code: log and alert
    await logUnexpectedReturn(payoutId, returnCode);
  }
}

Routing Around Failures

When an ACH return is permanent (R03, R04, R10), don't retry the same rail. Instead, offer an alternate:

  1. Check for a secondary account on file. Many customers link both checking and savings accounts.
  2. Route to RTP (Real-Time Payments) if available. RTP settles in seconds and has lower return rates (~0.1% vs. ACH's ~1%).
  3. Fall back to Visa Direct for card-based payouts (higher cost, but 99%+ success rate). 
async function routeAroundReturn(payoutId, returnCode) {
  const isPermanent = ['R03', 'R04', 'R10', 'R29'].includes(returnCode);

  if (isPermanent) {
    const receiver = await getReceiver(payoutId);

    if (receiver.secondaryBankAccount) {
      return await retryWithAccount(payoutId, receiver.secondaryBankAccount);
    }

    if (receiver.cardOnFile) {
      return await routeToVisaDirect(payoutId, receiver.cardOnFile);
    }

    return await escalateToSupport(payoutId);
  }
}

Reconciliation and Timing

ACH returns arrive 2–5 business days after the original debit. During that window, your payout status should be "pending" or "processing," not "complete." Once a return lands, update your ledger immediately and trigger the appropriate handler.

Track return rates by code and receiver bank. If one bank consistently returns R01, consider requiring a

Decoding ACH return codes programmatically? The ACH Return Codes API returns the full Nacha R01–R85 set with plain-language descriptions and handling guidance.

title: Understanding S3 Prefixes When Using Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases
description:
Introduction

While working with Amazon S3 as a data source for an Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Base, I came across a concept that seems simple but is important to understand correctly:

S3 folders do not work like folders on a traditional file system.

When you open an S3 bucket in the AWS Management Console, you can create folders, upload files into them, and navigate through a familiar folder structure.

However, Amazon S3 uses a flat object storage model. What looks like a folder is generally a prefix within an object's key.

This distinction becomes particularly important when connecting an S3 bucket to an Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Base.

The prefixes configured in the Bedrock data source determine which objects are included when the Knowledge Base ingests documents.

In this article, I'll explain how S3 prefixes work, how they relate to Bedrock Knowledge Base ingestion, and how I organized documents for the Daara Media AI Creative Content Assistant.

1. The misconception: S3 folders don't really exist

When people first work with Amazon S3, they often assume that its folder structure works like the directory structure on a Linux server or Windows computer.

For example, consider this structure:

daara-media-content/
│
├── brand-guidelines/
│   └── DAARA-Media-Brand-Guidelines.pdf
│
├── past-scripts/
│   └── DAARA-Media-Script-Bank.pdf
│
├── captions/
│   └── DAARA-Media-Caption-Bank.pdf
│
└── proposals/
    └── DAARA-Media-Client-Proposal-Template.pdf

In the S3 console, this looks like a bucket containing four folders, each holding a document.

But S3 does not store objects inside nested directories in the same way a traditional file system does.

Instead, each object has a key.

For example:

brand-guidelines/DAARA-Media-Brand-Guidelines.pdf

The entire string is the object's key.

The forward slash is simply part of that key. S3 uses the characters before it as a prefix that applications and the console can interpret as a folder-like hierarchy.

What S3 actually stores

Conceptually, the bucket contains objects like these:

Bucket: daara-media-content

Object 1:
Key = brand-guidelines/DAARA-Media-Brand-Guidelines.pdf

Object 2:
Key = past-scripts/DAARA-Media-Script-Bank.pdf

Object 3:
Key = captions/DAARA-Media-Caption-Bank.pdf

Object 4:
Key = proposals/DAARA-Media-Client-Proposal-Template.pdf

There is no requirement for S3 to create a physical directory called brand-guidelines before storing an object with that key.

The key itself contains the prefix.

This is why the more accurate way to describe S3 organization is through object keys and prefixes, rather than traditional folders and subdirectories.

2. Understanding an S3 object key and prefix

Let's break down one of the Daara Media object keys:

brand-guidelines/DAARA-Media-Brand-Guidelines.pdf

It contains two useful parts:

brand-guidelines/
        |
        v
      Prefix

DAARA-Media-Brand-Guidelines.pdf
        |
        v
    Object filename

The complete key is:

brand-guidelines/DAARA-Media-Brand-Guidelines.pdf

The prefix is:

brand-guidelines/

A prefix is simply the beginning portion of an object's key.

This means multiple objects can share the same prefix:

brand-guidelines/
│
├── brand-guidelines/brand-identity.pdf
├── brand-guidelines/logo-usage.pdf
└── brand-guidelines/brand-voice.pdf

All three objects have keys beginning with brand-guidelines/.

This is how S3 allows applications to organize and retrieve related objects without requiring a traditional directory structure.

3. Why prefixes matter when using Bedrock Knowledge Bases

Understanding prefixes becomes especially important when connecting an S3 bucket to an Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Base.

A Knowledge Base needs to know which documents it should ingest.

An S3 bucket might contain hundreds or thousands of objects, but not every object necessarily belongs in a particular Knowledge Base.

For example, a company might use one bucket to store:

  • Brand guidelines.
  • Marketing documents.
  • Customer support policies.
  • Financial reports.
  • Internal administrative files.
  • Archived documents.

If the Knowledge Base is intended to answer marketing questions, ingesting every object in the bucket may not be appropriate.

This is where inclusion prefixes become useful.

An inclusion prefix tells the Bedrock S3 data source which object keys should be included during ingestion.

Instead of treating the entire bucket as the document collection, you can restrict ingestion to selected key prefixes.

Example: Daara Media document organization

For the Daara Media AI assistant, I organized the source documents using four prefixes:


daara-media-content/
│
├── brand-guidelines/
│
├── past-scripts/
│
├── captions/
│
└── proposals/

Each prefix represented a category of company knowledge that the assistant could retrieve.

The data source needed to include these four categories rather than unrelated objects elsewhere in the bucket.

The intended ingestion scope was:

                 Amazon S3
                     |
                     v
          daara-media-content
                     |
          +----------+----------+
          |          |          |
          v          v          v
   brand-guidelines/ past-scripts/ captions/
          |
          v
      proposals/
          |
          v
    Bedrock Data Source
          |
          v
     Document Ingestion

The important part was not simply creating these folder-like paths in S3.

It was configuring the Bedrock data source to use the corresponding prefixes.

4. Configuring inclusion prefixes

When creating an S3 data source for a Bedrock Knowledge Base, you can specify the bucket and the prefixes that should be included.

A simplified example of the S3 data source configuration looks like this:

{
  "s3Configuration": {
    "bucketArn": "arn:aws:s3:::daara-media-content",
    "inclusionPrefixes": [
      "brand-guidelines/",
      "past-scripts/",
      "captions/",
      "proposals/"
    ]
  },
  "type": "S3"
}

The important part is:

"inclusionPrefixes": [
  "brand-guidelines/",
  "past-scripts/",
  "captions/",
  "proposals/"
]

Each entry identifies an S3 key prefix that the data source should include.

During ingestion, Bedrock uses these filters to determine which objects are within the configured scope.

Visualizing the selection

Imagine the bucket contains these objects:

daara-media-content/
│
├── brand-guidelines/
│   └── brand-identity.pdf
│
├── past-scripts/
│   └── campaign-script.pdf
│
├── captions/
│   └── caption-examples.pdf
│
├── proposals/
│   └── proposal-template.pdf
│
└── financial-reports/
    └── annual-report.pdf

If the inclusion prefixes are:

[
  "brand-guidelines/",
  "past-scripts/",
  "captions/",
  "proposals/"
]

The ingestion scope becomes:

                  S3 Bucket
                      |
          +-----------+-----------+
          |                       |
          v                       v
    Included Prefixes       Not Included
          |                       |
          v                       v
  brand-guidelines/          financial-reports/
  past-scripts/                    |
  captions/                        v
  proposals/                  Not ingested
          |
          v
   Bedrock Ingestion

The financial report is still stored in S3. It simply does not match any of the configured inclusion prefixes.

This is an important distinction: an object can exist in the bucket without being part of the Knowledge Base's ingestion scope.

5. Why the trailing slash matters

Consider these two prefixes:

brand

and:

brand-guidelines/

S3 prefix matching is based on the beginning of an object's key. It does not interpret the prefix as a directory name with special folder-boundary semantics.

For example, the prefix:

brand

could match keys such as:

brand-guidelines/brand-identity.pdf
brand-assets/logo.png
brand-archive/old-guidelines.pdf

All these keys begin with brand.

But if the intention is to include objects under the brand-guidelines/ path, specifying the trailing slash makes the intended scope clearer:

brand-guidelines/

It matches keys beginning with that exact prefix, such as:

brand-guidelines/brand-identity.pdf
brand-guidelines/logo-usage.pdf

It does not match:

brand-assets/logo.png
brand-archive/old-guidelines.pdf

This is why I recommend using the full folder-like prefix, including the trailing slash, when the intention is to target a specific category.

It makes the configuration easier to understand and reduces accidental matches.

6. What happens when the prefixes are incorrect?

This is where the concept becomes practical.

Imagine uploading documents into:

brand-guidelines/
past-scripts/
captions/
proposals/

But configuring the Bedrock data source with:

{
  "s3Configuration": {
    "bucketArn": "arn:aws:s3:::daara-media-content",
    "inclusionPrefixes": [
      "documents/"
    ]
  },
  "type": "S3"
}

The problem is that the configured prefix does not match the object keys.

The documents exist in S3, but their keys do not begin with documents/.

As a result, the data source will not include those objects through that inclusion filter.

This can create a confusing situation:

  • The S3 bucket contains the expected PDFs.
  • The folder-like paths are visible in the console.
  • The Knowledge Base exists.
  • The ingestion job may run.
  • But the expected documents are not ingested.

The problem may not be the PDF files, the embedding model, or the Knowledge Base itself.

It may simply be an incorrect inclusion prefix.

A useful troubleshooting checklist

When documents are not appearing in a Knowledge Base, check:

  1. Is the correct S3 bucket configured?
  2. Are the object keys spelled exactly as expected?
  3. Do the inclusion prefixes match the beginning of those keys?
  4. Are there accidental differences in capitalization?
  5. Are the required S3 permissions configured for the Knowledge Base execution role?
  6. Has the data source actually been synchronized after the documents were uploaded?

S3 keys are case-sensitive, so these two prefixes are different:

brand-guidelines/
Brand-Guidelines/

A small difference in capitalization can prevent an expected match.

7. How to inspect S3 object keys using the AWS CLI

The AWS Management Console provides a convenient visual representation of S3 objects, but the AWS CLI is useful when troubleshooting prefix problems.

To list all objects in a bucket:

aws s3api list-objects-v2 \
  --bucket daara-media-content \
  --region us-east-1 \
  --query 'Contents[*].Key' \
  --output table

This displays the actual object keys rather than relying on the folder-like presentation in the console.

To inspect objects under a specific prefix:

aws s3api list-objects-v2 \
  --bucket daara-media-content \
  --prefix brand-guidelines/ \
  --region us-east-1 \
  --query 'Contents[*].Key' \
  --output table

This limits the listing to keys beginning with brand-guidelines/.

You can repeat the command for the other prefixes:

aws s3api list-objects-v2 \
  --bucket daara-media-content \
  --prefix past-scripts/ \
  --region us-east-1 \
  --query 'Contents[*].Key' \
  --output table

The objective is to confirm that the actual object keys match the prefixes configured in the Bedrock data source.

For large buckets, remember that list-objects-v2 returns a limited page of results unless pagination is used. The AWS CLI normally handles pagination automatically, but options such as --no-paginate can change that behaviour.

8. Prefixes and Knowledge Base synchronization

Uploading a document to S3 does not automatically mean that it has been indexed by the Knowledge Base.

There is an important distinction between storing a document and ingesting it.

The process looks like this:

          Upload Document
                 |
                 v
             Amazon S3
                 |
                 v
          Object Stored
                 |
                 v
        Bedrock Data Source
                 |
                 v
         Start Ingestion Job
                 |
                 v
         Check Object Scope
                 |
                 v
          Process Documents
                 |
                 v
       Update Knowledge Base

The first synchronization processes the eligible content in the configured data source.

Subsequent synchronization jobs can detect added, updated, and deleted content and update the Knowledge Base accordingly.

This means that if a document is uploaded into an included prefix after the initial ingestion, you still need to synchronize the data source for the change to be reflected in the Knowledge Base.

For example:

Initial Ingestion
       |
       v
brand-guidelines/
       |
       v
brand-identity.pdf indexed
       |
       v
New document uploaded
       |
       v
logo-usage.pdf
       |
       v
Start another ingestion job
       |
       v
Knowledge Base updated

The prefix defines the scope of eligible objects. Synchronization is the process that discovers and processes changes within that scope.

9. Prefixes are not the same as access control

There is another important distinction worth understanding.

An inclusion prefix controls which S3 objects a particular Bedrock data source considers for ingestion.

It is not, by itself, an IAM security boundary.

For example, configuring:

"inclusionPrefixes": [
  "brand-guidelines/"
]

does not automatically prevent other AWS principals from reading objects under:

financial-reports/

Access to S3 objects is controlled separately through IAM identity policies, bucket policies, and other applicable access controls.

Similarly, once documents have been ingested, access to retrieved Knowledge Base content must be considered separately.

AWS warns that synchronized content can become available to principals with the relevant bedrock:Retrieve permissions, so ingestion scope should be designed with data access in mind.

The distinction is:

Mechanism Responsibility
S3 object prefix Identifies a portion of an object's key
Bedrock inclusion prefix Defines which matching objects are included in ingestion
IAM policy Controls permissions to perform AWS actions
S3 bucket policy Controls access granted through the bucket resource policy
Bedrock retrieval permissions Controls who can retrieve Knowledge Base content

This matters when a bucket contains documents with different sensitivity levels.

A well-organized S3 bucket does not automatically provide document-level authorization.

10. The architecture in the Daara Media project

The S3 document structure was part of the wider RAG architecture.

The original company documents were stored in S3. The Bedrock Knowledge Base used the configured data source to ingest eligible documents, process them, and make their content available for retrieval.

The overall flow was:

                 Company Documents
                         |
                         v
                    Amazon S3
                         |
             +-----------+-----------+
             |           |           |
             v           v           v
       Brand Guides   Past Scripts  Captions
             |           |           |
             +-----------+-----------+
                         |
                         v
                  Proposals
                         |
                         v
              S3 Inclusion Prefixes
                         |
                         v
             Bedrock Knowledge Base
                         |
                         v
                    Ingestion
                         |
                         v
                Searchable Knowledge
                         |
                         v
                 Application Retrieval
                         |
                         v
                  Claude Sonnet 4.5
                         |
                         v
                  Draft Response

The important point is that S3 and the Knowledge Base have different responsibilities.

Amazon S3 stores the original documents.

The Knowledge Base ingests eligible objects and prepares them for retrieval.

The application retrieves relevant information from the Knowledge Base and passes that context to the foundation model.

The prefix configuration connects the document organization in S3 to the ingestion scope of the Knowledge Base.

Conclusion

Understanding S3 prefixes is a small but important part of building a reliable RAG application with Amazon Bedrock.

What appears to be a folder in the S3 console is generally a prefix within an object's key. That prefix becomes important when configuring a Bedrock S3 data source because inclusion prefixes determine which objects are considered during ingestion.

In the Daara Media project, I used separate prefixes for brand guidelines, past scripts, captions, and proposals. This gave the Knowledge Base a clear document scope and made the source content easier to organize and maintain.

The biggest lesson is that storing documents in S3 and making them available to a Knowledge Base are two separate operations.

The objects must have the expected keys, the data source must include the correct prefixes, the Knowledge Base must have permission to access the objects, and the data source must be synchronized.

Once this distinction is understood, troubleshooting missing documents becomes much easier.

S3 stores objects using keys. Prefixes organize those keys. Bedrock uses the configured prefixes to determine which objects to ingest.

title: Do Not Flatten the Clusters: Connecting Kubernetes Across Clouds Without Merging Their Trust Boundaries
description:
The fastest way to connect two Kubernetes clusters in different clouds is also the most dangerous way: join them into one flat network, share service discovery, and let any pod in one cluster reach any service in the other. It demos well. It also means a compromised workload in the least protected cluster now has a network path into every cluster, and an outage or a bad route in one place can spread to all of them.

Multi-cloud Kubernetes is common for ordinary reasons. One cloud hosts the GPU training cluster, another hosts the customer facing services, a third was inherited or chosen for a specific managed service. The clusters need to talk. They do not need to become one cluster, and they should not become one trust zone.

Start with the flows, not with connectivity

Before choosing any tool, list the actual cross-cluster flows. In most estates the real list is short:

  • A named service in cluster A calls a named service in cluster B, on a known port, for a known reason.
  • A data job reads from or writes to a store that happens to live near the other cluster.
  • Operators need logs, metrics, and traces from both clusters in one place.

That list is the design. If a flow is not on it, it should not work by default. Connectivity products and mesh tools make it easy to connect everything first and restrict later, but later rarely arrives. Start restricted, with the named flows working, and add flows deliberately as teams request them with an owner and a reason.

This also settles the addressing argument early. Pod and service address ranges often overlap between clusters, especially when each cluster was built from the same tutorial defaults. Overlap only matters for flows that actually cross. A gateway pattern, described below, avoids renumbering every cluster just so that two services can talk.

Connect services through gateways, not networks through tunnels

Treat each cluster as its own network domain, with its own pod ranges, service ranges, policies, and failure modes. Between domains, place an explicit crossing point:

  1. Each cluster exposes only the services that other clusters are allowed to use, through a dedicated gateway or egress and ingress pair, not through direct pod to pod routing.
  2. Traffic crosses the private cross-cloud path between those gateways, so the path can be measured, encrypted, and audited in one place.
  3. Inside the receiving cluster, the gateway hands traffic to the target service only. It does not become a general router into the pod network.

The cost is a small amount of extra latency and one more component to run. The gain is large: each cluster keeps its own addressing, its own network policy, and its own blast radius. A route leak, a misconfigured policy, or a noisy workload inside one cluster stays inside that cluster, because there is no flat network for it to leak across.

It also makes the cross-cloud path honest. When all cross-cluster traffic passes through known gateways, capacity, errors, and latency on that path can be measured per flow. When traffic can cross anywhere, nobody can say which flows depend on the link until the link fails.

Identity should cross, addresses should not be trusted

On a flat network, teams quietly start trusting source addresses: allow traffic from the other cluster range. That trust is misplaced. An address says where a packet came from, not which workload sent it or whether that workload was allowed to call this service.

Use workload identity at the gateway and at the receiving service:

  • Each calling service presents a verifiable identity, issued per cluster and rotated automatically, rather than a shared secret copied between clusters.
  • The receiving service authorises the calling identity for that specific operation, not the source network for all operations.
  • Identity mappings are written down per flow, matching the flow list from the first section, so a reviewer can check who can call what without reading packet rules.

This is where many multi-cloud designs quietly fail. The two clouds issue identity differently, so teams fall back to network rules because they work everywhere. Resist that fallback for cross-cluster calls. Network rules can stay as a second layer, limiting which gateways can talk, while identity decides which workloads can.

Keep discovery local, publish a small directory

Shared global service discovery sounds convenient and creates a hidden dependency: when discovery breaks or returns stale answers, calls fail across every cluster at once, and a service that was only meant to be local becomes reachable everywhere because it was registered globally.

A safer pattern is boring. Each cluster keeps its own local discovery for its own services. For the small set of cross-cluster services, publish a small, explicit directory: name, owning team, gateway address, port, and the identity allowed to call it. That directory can be configuration in the gateway or a simple internal record, as long as it is reviewed like code and changes to it are visible.

When a cross-cluster service moves, only its directory entry changes. When a team wants a new cross-cluster dependency, adding the entry is the review point. That friction is a feature. Cross-cluster dependencies are architectural decisions, not accidents of discovery.

Plan for one cluster to be down, or untrusted

Two failure questions should be answered before the design ships:

First, if one cluster is down, what should the other cluster do? With gateway connections and local discovery, the answer can be per flow: queue the work, serve a cached answer, or fail that one feature. On a flat joined network, the failure tends to be global and surprising, because timeouts and retries cross the boundary in ways nobody listed.

Second, if one cluster is compromised, what can an attacker reach? The honest answer should be: the gateway, and only the services and operations that gateway was allowed to present, with identities that the compromised cluster cannot mint for other clusters. Test this. From a test workload in one cluster, try to reach a service that is not on the flow list, a pod address directly, and the other cluster API. All three should fail, and the attempts should be visible in logs.

Retries deserve a specific mention here. A calling service that retries aggressively across a slow cross-cloud path can turn a small problem in one cluster into a load problem in both. Set retry budgets and timeouts for cross-cluster calls separately from local calls, and make them stricter, because the path is longer and the shared resource, the link, is smaller.

A practical rollout order

For an estate connecting clusters that already exist, this order works without a flag day:

  1. Inventory the flows that already cross informally, including scripts, jobs, and operator access, not just application calls.
  2. Stand up the gateways on the private path and route one low risk flow through them, measuring latency and errors against the old route.
  3. Add identity checks for that flow, then remove the old network level permission for it.
  4. Move remaining flows one at a time, deleting the broad rule that made the informal route work only after the last flow has moved.
  5. Run the down cluster and untrusted cluster tests, and record the results with the flow list.

Notice what is not in that list: renumbering clusters, replacing the container network, or adopting a single control plane for every cluster. Those may be worth doing for other reasons, but they are not prerequisites for safe cross-cluster traffic, and tying them together turns a bounded network project into an open ended platform rebuild.

The design point

Clusters in different clouds need to cooperate, not merge. Keep each cluster as its own domain, cross between domains only at gateways, authorise workloads by identity rather than by address, publish only the services that are genuinely shared, and test what happens when one side is down or untrusted.

That kind of bounded, private multi-cloud design across AWS, Azure, Google Cloud, and Oracle estates is part of the work described at CloudVerg, where VergMesh covers multi-cloud networking and VergShield covers zero-trust security, alongside SOC 2 readiness support and managed services.

The test is simple. Pick any service in one cluster and ask what it can reach in the other, who approved that reach, and what happens if the other cluster disappears. If the team can answer from a short flow list, the clusters are connected well. If the answer is everything, they are not connected. They are flattened.
