title: Next.js `revalidatePath` vs `revalidateTag` in 2026: Choosing the Right Cache Invalidation Primitive at Scale
description:
Next.js revalidatePath vs revalidateTag in 2026: Choosing the Right Cache Invalidation Primitive at Scale

This article was written with the assistance of AI, under human supervision and review.

The Cache Invalidation Primitive You're Probably Using Wrong

Most Next.js developers reach for revalidatePath when a mutation happens. It is familiar, straightforward, and works immediately in development. The function invalidates everything under a path, ensuring users see fresh data after an update. This approach breaks down in production when applications scale beyond a single container or when cache entries multiply across dozens of routes.

The problem manifests when a product price changes. The developer calls revalidatePath('/products'), expecting the product list to refresh. The homepage also displays featured products, so they add revalidatePath('/'). The search page shows products too, so another call goes in. Within weeks, every mutation triggers a cascade of path invalidations, wiping caches that have nothing to do with the actual change.

Problem diagram showing revalidatePath invalidating unrelated cached data

Teams discover months later that a user profile update invalidates the product catalog because both routes sit under the same path prefix. Cache hit rates drop. Response times climb. Developers start questioning whether caching provides any benefit at all.

The solution requires understanding that Next.js offers two distinct primitives with fundamentally different invalidation semantics. revalidateTag targets specific cache entries by tag, leaving unrelated data intact. revalidatePath wipes everything under a URL path, regardless of whether the underlying data changed.

Solution diagram showing revalidateTag surgically invalidating only tagged data

This distinction determines whether a caching strategy scales or collapses under real traffic. The choice between these primitives shapes cache efficiency, deployment complexity, and the ability to reason about invalidation across a growing application.

Key Takeaways

  • revalidatePath invalidates all cached data under a URL path, often clearing unrelated entries and reducing cache hit rates in complex applications.
  • revalidateTag targets specific cache entries by tag, allowing surgical invalidation that preserves unrelated cached data.
  • Path-based invalidation requires no tagging infrastructure but becomes unmaintainable as applications grow and routes share data.
  • Multi-container deployments expose coordination failures with both primitives when using Next.js's default in-memory cache, requiring external cache adapters.
  • The correct primitive depends on data granularity, mutation patterns, and whether the application runs on a single instance or distributed infrastructure.

Understanding revalidatePath: Broad Strokes Invalidation

revalidatePath invalidates every cache entry associated with a URL path. When a Server Action or Route Handler calls revalidatePath('/products'), Next.js marks all cached data for that route as stale. The next request triggers fresh data fetches for the entire page, regardless of which specific piece of data changed.

This primitive exists for scenarios where precise tagging is impractical or impossible. A content management system might store dozens of content types across a single route. A dashboard might aggregate data from fifteen different sources. Tracking which tags to invalidate for each mutation becomes error-prone when the page composition changes frequently.

import { revalidatePath } from 'next/cache'

export async function updateProduct(productId: string, data: ProductData) {
  await db.product.update({
    where: { id: productId },
    data
  })

  // Invalidates all cached data for /products and its dynamic segments
  revalidatePath('/products')
}

The function accepts a second parameter controlling the scope. Setting it to 'page' invalidates only the exact path. Setting it to 'layout' invalidates the path and all nested routes. The default behavior matches 'page' in Next.js 15.3 as documented in the official revalidation guide.

Diagram showing revalidatePath invalidation scope through route hierarchy

The primitive works immediately in single-container deployments where all requests hit the same process. In-memory cache entries disappear synchronously when revalidatePath executes. Developers see instant feedback during local development and staging environments running on single instances.

The limitation surfaces when multiple routes depend on the same data but sit under different paths. A product appears on the homepage, search results, category pages, and its detail page. Invalidating the product requires calling revalidatePath for every path, or accepting stale data until the next scheduled revalidation.

Teams often solve this by calling revalidatePath('/') to invalidate the entire site. This approach sacrifices all caching benefits to avoid tracking which paths need invalidation. Response times climb as every page regenerates from scratch after any mutation.

Understanding revalidateTag: Surgical Cache Busting

revalidateTag invalidates cache entries that explicitly opt into a tag. Functions using the use cache directive call cacheTag('tag-name') to register their cache entry with one or more tags. Later mutations call revalidateTag('tag-name') to invalidate all entries with that tag, regardless of which routes or components created them.

This primitive scales to applications where many routes share the same underlying data. A product detail component might appear on five different pages. Tagging its cache entry with product:${id} allows a single revalidateTag call to invalidate the product everywhere it appears.

import { cacheTag } from 'next/cache'

export async function getProduct(id: string) {
  'use cache'
  cacheTag(`product:${id}`)

  return db.product.findUnique({
    where: { id }
  })
}

The tagging happens inside the cached function, not at the call site. This decouples cache invalidation from route structure. Components consume getProduct without knowing or caring about tags. Only the data layer manages cache semantics.

import { revalidateTag } from 'next/cache'

export async function updateProduct(productId: string, data: ProductData) {
  await db.product.update({
    where: { id: productId },
    data
  })

  // Invalidates the product everywhere it appears
  revalidateTag(`product:${productId}`)
}

The Next.js revalidation documentation recommends passing 'max' as the second argument to revalidateTag. This sets the stale-while-revalidate window to its longest duration, allowing stale content to serve while fresh data generates in the background. Users see instant responses while cache entries refresh asynchronously.

Diagram showing revalidateTag invalidating only tagged entries across routes

The tradeoff appears in infrastructure requirements. Tag-based invalidation requires a shared cache store in multi-container deployments. The default in-memory cache cannot coordinate tags across processes. Next.js 15.3 provides unstable_cache with pluggable backends, but custom cache adapters remain necessary for production distributed systems.

Tag naming conventions matter at scale. Prefixing tags by entity type prevents collisions. product:123 and category:123 represent different entities despite sharing an ID. Including version numbers in tags like api:v2:product:123 allows gradual cache migration during API changes.

The primitive also supports cache entry hierarchies. A product page might tag its cache with both product:123 and category:electronics. Invalidating category:electronics refreshes all products in that category without knowing their individual IDs. This pattern reduces coordination complexity when relationships change.

Direct Comparison: When Each Primitive Wins in Production

The choice between revalidatePath and revalidateTag determines cache efficiency and maintenance burden. Each primitive excels in specific scenarios while creating problems in others.

Aspect revalidatePath revalidateTag
Invalidation scope URL path and optionally nested routes Specific tagged cache entries only
Infrastructure requirement None (works with in-memory cache) Shared cache store for multi-container setups
Setup complexity Zero (immediate use) Requires tagging cached functions
Cache hit rate Drops as routes share data Remains high with proper tagging
Maintenance Simple initially, unmaintainable at scale Requires discipline but scales linearly
Cross-route invalidation Requires multiple calls or broad invalidation Single call affects all tagged entries

Path-based invalidation wins when routes operate independently. An admin dashboard with dedicated data for each page benefits from path invalidation. Each route fetches distinct data that never appears elsewhere. Invalidating /admin/users affects nothing else. No tagging infrastructure provides value here.

Comparison diagram showing when path invalidation works versus when tags work

Tag-based invalidation becomes essential when data appears across many routes. E-commerce applications display products on listing pages, detail pages, search results, recommendations, and cart summaries. A price change must invalidate the product everywhere. Tracking which paths contain which products quickly becomes impossible.

The difference compounds in applications with dynamic routes. A blog with /posts/[slug] might have thousands of post pages. Invalidating a single post requires either calling revalidatePath with the exact slug or invalidating the entire posts section. Tags allow revalidateTag('post:abc123') to target exactly one post regardless of its URL.

Mutation patterns influence the decision. Applications with frequent broad updates favor path invalidation. A stock market dashboard might refresh all displayed stocks every few seconds. Invalidating /dashboard once beats invalidating dozens of individual stock tags. The cache lifetime matters more than granular invalidation here.

Applications with infrequent, targeted mutations favor tags. A content management system might publish one article per day. Invalidating only that article's cache entries preserves every other cached page. Cache hit rates stay high even with daily updates.

Deployment architecture forces the decision in multi-container environments. Teams running on serverless platforms or container orchestrators must implement external cache coordination regardless of primitive choice. At that point, tag-based invalidation provides strictly more power for the same infrastructure cost.

Multi-container deployment diagram showing cache coordination challenges

The primitives combine in mature applications. Core shared data uses tags for surgical invalidation. Peripheral features with isolated data use paths. A product catalog relies on revalidateTag('product:*') while an admin settings panel uses revalidatePath('/admin/settings').

Real-World Code: Implementing Both With unstable_cache

Production applications require explicit cache control beyond Next.js automatic caching. The unstable_cache function provides programmatic cache management with support for both revalidation primitives. Despite its name, the API has remained stable since Next.js 14.0 as covered in Next.js caching patterns.

import { unstable_cache } from 'next/cache'

// Tag-based approach for shared data
export const getCachedProduct = unstable_cache(
  async (id: string) => {
    return db.product.findUnique({
      where: { id },
      include: {
        category: true,
        reviews: {
          take: 5,
          orderBy: { createdAt: 'desc' }
        }
      }
    })
  },
  ['product'],
  {
    tags: ['products', 'product:${id}'],
    revalidate: 3600
  }
)

// Path-based approach for isolated data
export const getCachedUserSettings = unstable_cache(
  async (userId: string) => {
    return db.userSettings.findUnique({
      where: { userId }
    })
  },
  ['user-settings'],
  {
    revalidate: 300
  }
)

The third parameter to unstable_cache accepts a tags array. These tags enable surgical invalidation through revalidateTag. The function also accepts a revalidate number setting time-based expiration. Combining both strategies provides defense in depth: tags for immediate invalidation, time-based revalidation as a safety net.

Server Actions coordinate cache invalidation with data mutations. The Next.js revalidation guide documents two timing options: revalidateTag for stale-while-revalidate semantics and updateTag for immediate expiration. Most applications prefer revalidateTag with its 'max' stale window.

'use server'

import { revalidateTag, revalidatePath } from 'next/cache'

export async function updateProduct(
  id: string,
  data: ProductUpdateInput
) {
  const product = await db.product.update({
    where: { id },
    data
  })

  // Tag-based invalidation for shared product data
  revalidateTag(`product:${id}`, 'max')
  revalidateTag('products', 'max')

  // Path-based invalidation for product detail page if needed
  // revalidatePath(`/products/${product.slug}`)

  return product
}

export async function updateUserSettings(
  userId: string,
  settings: UserSettingsInput
) {
  await db.userSettings.update({
    where: { userId },
    data: settings
  })

  // Path-based invalidation for isolated settings page
  revalidatePath(`/users/${userId}/settings`)
}

The pattern separates concerns effectively. Data fetching functions declare their cache behavior through tags and expiration. Server Actions handle mutations and trigger invalidation. Components simply consume the cached functions without knowing cache semantics exist.

Teams often create cache utilities to standardize tagging conventions and prevent duplicate cache keys:

// lib/cache-utils.ts
import { unstable_cache } from 'next/cache'

export function createProductCache<T>(
  fn: (id: string) => Promise<T>,
  cacheKey: string
) {
  return unstable_cache(
    fn,
    [cacheKey],
    {
      tags: ['products'],
      revalidate: 3600
    }
  )
}

export function withProductTag(id: string) {
  return [`product:${id}`, 'products']
}

// Usage in data layer
export const getCachedProduct = createProductCache(
  async (id: string) => {
    return db.product.findUnique({ where: { id } })
  },
  'product-detail'
)

This abstraction prevents tag typos and ensures consistent cache lifetimes across related functions. The utilities also provide a single place to change cache configuration when requirements evolve.

The key insight appears in production debugging. When a cache entry does not invalidate as expected, developers need to verify three things: the tags in unstable_cache match the tags in revalidateTag, the cache key remains consistent across calls, and the revalidation actually executes in the deployed environment.

Multi-Container Deployments: The Distributed Cache Problem

The revalidation primitives fail silently in distributed deployments when relying on Next.js default in-memory caching. A user updates a product on container A. The Server Action calls revalidateTag and invalidates the in-memory cache on container A. Container B still serves stale product data because its cache never received the invalidation signal.

This failure mode is subtle because it works perfectly during development. Local development runs a single Next.js process where all invalidations happen in the same memory space. Staging environments often use single containers for cost reasons, hiding the problem until production deploys multiple instances.

The failure compounds with load balancer behavior. Modern load balancers distribute requests across containers for fault tolerance and performance. A user might see fresh data on one request and stale data on the next, depending on which container handles the request. This creates a trust problem where users question whether their updates actually saved.

Diagram showing distributed cache invalidation failure across containers

The solution requires an external cache store that all containers share. Redis provides the standard choice for session stores and distributed caches. The Next.js runtime caching considerations document that serverless environments may not persist cache entries across invocations, requiring external storage for reliability.

Teams running on platforms like Google Cloud Run or AWS Lambda encounter this problem immediately. Each function invocation potentially runs in a fresh container with empty cache. The Payload CMS discussion on cache invalidation shows real production teams discovering this after deployment when users report seeing stale content.

Custom cache adapters bridge Next.js cache APIs to external stores. The adapter intercepts revalidateTag and revalidatePath calls, translating them to cache operations in Redis or another shared store:

// lib/cache-adapter.ts
import { Redis } from 'ioredis'

const redis = new Redis(process.env.REDIS_URL)

export async function revalidateTagInRedis(tag: string) {
  const keys = await redis.smembers(`tag:${tag}`)

  if (keys.length > 0) {
    await redis.del(...keys)
    await redis.del(`tag:${tag}`)
  }
}

export async function setCacheWithTag(
  key: string,
  value: unknown,
  tags: string[],
  ttl: number
) {
  await redis.setex(key, ttl, JSON.stringify(value))

  for (const tag of tags) {
    await redis.sadd(`tag:${tag}`, key)
  }
}

This implementation stores cache entries in Redis with standard expiration. Each tag maintains a Redis set containing all cache keys associated with that tag. Invalidating a tag looks up the set, deletes all associated keys, and removes the set itself.

The distributed coordination problem affects both primitives equally. revalidatePath and revalidateTag both require synchronization across containers. Path invalidation might seem simpler because it avoids tagging infrastructure, but the fundamental coordination challenge remains identical.

Teams sometimes attempt to solve this by broadcasting invalidation events through message queues or pub/sub systems. Each container subscribes to an invalidation channel and clears its local cache when messages arrive. This approach introduces race conditions and partial failure modes that make cache behavior unpredictable.

The correct solution accepts that distributed caching requires shared storage. Using Redis or another external cache eliminates the coordination problem entirely. All containers read and write the same cache store, so invalidation becomes instantaneous across the deployment.

Distributed cache architecture diagram showing Redis coordination

Serverless platforms often provide managed cache services that integrate with application code. Vercel's native edge caching handles this automatically for applications deployed on their platform. Teams deploying elsewhere must implement cache adapters manually or choose managed services that provide Next.js-compatible cache backends.

The infrastructure tradeoff becomes clear: single-container deployments avoid external cache dependencies at the cost of limited scalability. Multi-container deployments require shared cache stores but support horizontal scaling and fault tolerance. The revalidation primitive choice matters less than the cache storage architecture at this scale.

Decision Framework: Choosing the Right Primitive at Scale

The decision between revalidatePath and revalidateTag depends on data sharing patterns, mutation frequency, and deployment constraints. A systematic framework prevents premature optimization while identifying genuine scaling bottlenecks.

Start by mapping which routes share data. Applications where most data appears on a single route favor path invalidation. A landing page builder might have dedicated data for each page URL. Invalidating /pages/homepage never affects /pages/pricing. The routes share no data, so tags provide no benefit.

Applications where data appears across many routes require tags. E-commerce catalogs display products on listing pages, detail pages, search results, cart views, and recommendation widgets. Invalidating a product means invalidating entries across all these routes. Tracking paths becomes impossible while tagging the product once handles every location.

Decision framework flowchart for choosing revalidation primitive

Mutation patterns influence granularity requirements. Applications with bulk updates might invalidate entire sections. A news aggregator might refresh all articles in a category when the feed updates. Invalidating the category path once beats invalidating hundreds of individual article tags.

Applications with targeted mutations benefit from precise invalidation. A project management tool updates one task at a time. Invalidating only that task's cache entries keeps every other cached task fresh. Cache hit rates stay high even with constant updates.

Deployment architecture often makes the decision. Teams running on managed platforms with built-in distributed caching can use tags freely. The platform handles coordination across containers. Teams running on traditional infrastructure must weigh external cache implementation cost against path invalidation maintainability problems.

The framework suggests starting with path invalidation during early development. Routes typically contain isolated data while teams validate product direction. As applications mature and routes begin sharing data, migrate to tag-based invalidation. This evolution matches natural application growth.

Teams tracking cache hit rates gain concrete data for decisions. If path invalidation maintains hit rates above 80%, tags might be premature. If hit rates drop below 50% despite proper cache lifetimes, path invalidation likely invalidates too broadly. The metrics reveal whether the current approach scales.

The Next.js caching mental model provides context for how these primitives fit into the broader caching system. Revalidation represents only one part of cache strategy. Time-based expiration, stale-while-revalidate semantics, and cache warming also affect overall performance.

Frequently Asked Questions

When should teams use revalidatePath instead of revalidateTag?

Use revalidatePath when routes operate independently with dedicated data, such as admin dashboards where each page manages distinct resources. The primitive also works well during early development before data sharing patterns emerge. Teams should migrate to tags once multiple routes begin displaying the same underlying data.

How do revalidateTag and updateTag differ in production?

revalidateTag uses stale-while-revalidate semantics where old content serves while fresh content generates in the background. updateTag immediately expires cache entries, ensuring users see updated data on the next request. Use updateTag only in Server Actions where read-your-own-writes matters, such as after creating a new resource that must appear in a list immediately.

Can applications mix revalidatePath and revalidateTag in the same codebase?

Applications frequently combine both primitives. Core shared entities like products or users use tags for surgical invalidation. Peripheral features with isolated data like settings pages use path invalidation. The combination reduces maintenance burden while preserving cache efficiency where it matters most.

What happens to cache entries when neither primitive is called?

Cache entries remain valid until their time-based expiration triggers. The Next.js revalidation documentation explains that cacheLife profiles set expiration windows from 1 second to 1 year depending on data volatility. Entries expire and regenerate automatically even without explicit invalidation.

How do distributed deployments coordinate cache invalidation?

Distributed deployments require external cache stores like Redis or managed services that synchronize cache state across containers. Next.js default in-memory cache cannot coordinate across processes, causing silent failures where some containers serve stale data. Teams must implement custom cache adapters or use platforms with built-in distributed caching.

Building Maintainable Cache Invalidation Strategies

The difference between revalidatePath and revalidateTag determines whether cache invalidation remains manageable as applications grow. Path invalidation works immediately but collapses when routes share data. Tag invalidation requires upfront tagging discipline but scales linearly with application complexity.

Teams should start with concrete metrics. Track cache hit rates, response times, and invalidation frequency. Applications maintaining high hit rates with path invalidation should keep using it until metrics suggest otherwise. Applications with declining cache effectiveness need surgical tag-based invalidation.

The infrastructure decision matters more than the primitive choice at scale. Distributed deployments require external cache coordination regardless of invalidation strategy. Teams should implement shared cache storage early if multi-container deployment is planned. The Next.js 15 caching changes provide context for how the caching system evolved to handle these distributed scenarios.

The correct approach combines both primitives based on data sharing patterns. Tag shared entities for surgical invalidation. Use paths for isolated features. Measure cache performance to validate the strategy. Build external cache infrastructure before scaling beyond single containers.

title: A one-bag packing list for a weekend
description:
If you have read three pages about one cabin bag and still feel unclear, the reason is usually that the pages describe the product and not the situation. So this note is organised around the situation: an ordinary home, an ordinary week, and a shared space. The practical answer to whether a trip keeps the routine intact fits in a short list, and none of it requires a purchase.

Crossing time zones is easier if the routine moves with the first night, not the last.

A pouch in a backpack is more discreet than a case in a suitcase.

Leave the second item at home; you will not miss it.

For the broader context, the learning library collects the longer reads, and this duo set is the listing page where the same details are laid out in one place.

Write the decision down somewhere you will see it, because the point of a routine is not to think about it again.

LoveyDovey - body-safe intimate wellness, discreetly delivered across India. Questions: hello@lovedovey.com

title: How Do You Build a Fast, SEO-Friendly Landing Page with Next.js?
description:
To build a fast, SEO-friendly landing page with Next.js, render it as a Server Component, set metadata with the Metadata API, optimize images with next/image, add JSON-LD structured data, and keep client-side JavaScript to a minimum. Below is a practical setup using the App Router.

Why does Next.js suit landing pages?

Landing pages are mostly static content. The App Router renders Server Components to HTML on the server (or at build time), so crawlers and users get full content immediately, with little JavaScript to download.

How do you set metadata and a canonical URL?

Export a metadata object from app/page.tsx:

import type { Metadata } from "next";

export const metadata: Metadata = {
  title: "Acme Scheduler: Book meetings without back-and-forth",
  description: "A short, specific description of what the product does and who it is for.",
  alternates: { canonical: "https://example.com/" },
  openGraph: {
    title: "Acme Scheduler",
    description: "Book meetings without back-and-forth.",
    url: "https://example.com/",
    images: ["/og.png"],
  },
};

Give every page its own self-referencing canonical. A canonical pointing every subpage to the homepage can stop those pages from being indexed.

How do you keep images from hurting performance?

Use next/image with explicit dimensions and priority only for the above-the-fold hero image, and always write meaningful alt text:

import Image from "next/image";

<Image src="/hero.png" alt="Dashboard showing a weekly meeting calendar" width={1200} height={700} priority />

Explicit dimensions prevent layout shift (CLS).

How do you add structured data?

JSON-LD helps search engines and AI answer engines understand the page:

const jsonLd = {
  "@context": "https://schema.org",
  "@type": "SoftwareApplication",
  name: "Acme Scheduler",
  applicationCategory: "BusinessApplication",
};

export default function Page() {
  return (
    <>
      <script type="application/ld+json" dangerouslySetInnerHTML={{ __html: JSON.stringify(jsonLd) }} />
      {/* page content */}
    </>
  );
}

If you add an FAQ section, mark it up with FAQPage only when the questions are visible on the page.

How do you limit client-side JavaScript?

Keep components as Server Components by default. Add "use client" only to small interactive pieces such as a form or menu. Load third-party scripts with next/script and strategy="lazyOnload".

How do you add a sitemap and robots file? 

// app/sitemap.ts
import type { MetadataRoute } from "next";

export default function sitemap(): MetadataRoute.Sitemap {
  return [{ url: "https://example.com/", lastModified: new Date() }];
}

Then verify with Lighthouse or PageSpeed Insights and measure real results rather than assuming them.

FAQ

Do I need SSR for SEO? No. Static generation or server rendering both deliver crawlable HTML; what matters is that content is in the initial HTML.

Pages Router or App Router? The App Router's Metadata API and Server Components make this simpler for new projects.

How do I check it works? View the page source for your content, test with PageSpeed Insights, and inspect the URL in Google Search Console.

I'm Muhammad Afzal, a Python developer building web projects at INDUS Web Agency.

title: PostgreSQL 19 removes the MultiXact members wall. Reclamation still waits for template0.
description:
Between May 10 and May 17, 2025, Metronome had four outages that each lasted over an hour. Their dashboards showed "less than 50% utilization" of the configured MultiXact ID threshold (autovacuum_multixact_freeze_max_age = 400 million) on an Aurora PostgreSQL 13.18 cluster of more than 30 TB. The limit they actually hit was MultiXact member space. In their words, "PostgreSQL does not expose metrics for member space consumption". (Metronome RCA)

Member space is addressed by a 32-bit offset in every release through 18. PostgreSQL 19 widens it to 64 bits (commit bd8d9c9bd: "This eliminates MultiXactOffset wraparound and the 2^32 limit on the total number of multixid members. Multixids are still limited to 2^31").

I rebuilt the failure from scratch on PostgreSQL 18.7 and on 19.0, released on 19 November 2026, with 19 RC2 as a cross-check. 19.0 reproduced every RC2 count I reran exactly. Short version:

  • The member-offset stop is gone in 19; the 2^31 MultiXact ID stop is not. In a fast-forwarded lab cluster 18.7 refused writes with multixact "members" limit exceeded; 19.0 went past 2^32 member offsets without an error (3/3 runs on each of 18.7, 19 RC2 and 19.0).
  • The burn rate did not change. Same members per lock and the same member bytes on disk; only the offsets area doubles (8 bytes per MultiXact instead of 4).
  • pg_upgrade to 19 keeps one member per MultiXact. How much that shrinks depends on your lock pattern; in my k=64 runs on 19.0 the whole pg_multixact directory went from 107 MB to 8.2 MB (13x), the same as on RC2.
  • Reclamation did not change, and it is cluster-wide. On a fresh cluster where template0 had never been frozen, none of VACUUM, VACUUM (FREEZE) or vacuumdb --all --freeze freed a byte of member space on 18.7, 19 RC2 or 19.0, because truncation waits for the oldest datminmxid of every database and vacuumdb skips template0. One idle session that had taken a row lock before the workload, in a different database, stopped reclamation for the whole cluster.

FACT marks what I measured, INTERPRETATION what I conclude from it, and "source" what I read in the PostgreSQL code. Everything was measured on one VM; see "Method and limits" and "Reproduce". Scripts and raw data: https://github.com/firfircelik/pg-multixact-lab

1. What a MultiXact member is

When one transaction locks a row, PostgreSQL writes that transaction's ID into the row's xmax. When a second transaction locks the same row while the first is still open (SELECT ... FOR SHARE, or the FOR KEY SHARE lock that a foreign-key check takes on the parent row), the row needs to point at a set of transactions. That set is a MultiXact. Its ID goes into xmax; the list of transaction IDs (the members) is appended to pg_multixact/members. MultiXacts are immutable: when a third locker arrives, PostgreSQL creates a new MultiXact and copies in every member that is still running (plus a committed updater, if there is one), then adds the newcomer (MultiXactIdExpand in multixact.c).

So while lockers overlap, every new locker pays for all the others again.

2. Growth: member cost is quadratic in overlap

Setup. One row; k sessions lock it one after another, all transactions stay open, then all commit. 1,000 such episodes per run, 6 values of k, two lock types (explicit FOR SHARE and an FK insert into a child table), 3 repetitions, 18.7 and 19 RC2, fresh cluster per run, shuffled order (72 runs), then the same 36 cells on 19.0 the day it shipped. 108 runs.

Theory. Locker 2 creates a MultiXact with 2 members, locker 3 one with 3, ..., locker k one with k. Per episode: k-1 MultiXacts and k(k+1)/2 - 1 members. Metronome's RCA gives the same example: "locking a row with 5 transactions creates 4 MultiXacts containing a total of 14 members".

Result (FACT). The MultiXact count matched the formula exactly in 108/108 runs. The member count matched exactly in 36/36 runs on 19 RC2 and 36/36 on 19.0 (every count and file size identical to RC2), and was formula + 1 in 36/36 runs on 18.7 (18.7 skips offset 0 on the first allocation).

overlapping lockers k MultiXacts / episode members / episode
2 1 2
8 7 35
32 31 527
64 63 2,079

Two more facts from the same runs:

  • Each member costs about 5.0 bytes in pg_multixact/members on both versions (2,079,000 members = 10,412,032 bytes = 10.4 MB). So 2^31 members, where 18.x starts aggressive anti-wraparound work, is about 10.7 GB (10 GiB), and the 2^32 stop is about 21.5 GB (20 GiB). The PostgreSQL 18 docs give the same scale: "about 10GB" and "about 20GB" (routine vacuuming, 18).
  • 19 (RC2 and 19.0) writes 8 bytes per MultiXact in pg_multixact/offsets instead of 4 (507,904 vs 253,952 bytes for 63,000 MultiXacts). Same member bytes; offsets double.

Source note: a backend reuses a cached MultiXact when it needs exactly the same member set again (mXactCacheGetBySet in multixact.c). Repeating the same few sessions in the same order is therefore cheap; damage needs fresh combinations, which is what concurrent short writers produce.

3. Growth under real concurrency: the pause inside your transaction

Setup. pgbench, 20 s per run, transaction = BEGIN; INSERT INTO child(parent_id) ...; [\sleep 5 ms]; COMMIT;. Factors: 8/32/64 clients, 1 or 16 hot parent rows, 0 or 5 ms pause inside the transaction, both versions, 3 reps. 72 runs, fsync off (see Method). One run (64 clients, 16 hot rows, 5 ms, 18.7, rep 1) followed a 286 s box suspension and ran at half speed; I voided it and reran it under the load rule (242,906 transactions, 4.53 members per transaction, in line with its siblings).

clients hot parents pause in txn members / committed txn (18.7, median, fsync off)
8 1 0 ms 3.0
64 1 0 ms 9.6
8 1 5 ms 7.7
64 1 5 ms 60.7
64 16 5 ms 4.6
64 16 0 ms 1.5

Durable commits (control, FACT). I repeated the two 64-client, 1-hot-row cells with fsync, synchronous_commit and full_page_writes on (3 reps, both versions). With the 5 ms pause: 58.2 members per transaction on 18.7 and 58.3 on 19 RC2 (medians; fsync off: 60.7 and 60.6), at about 670k members/s. Without the pause: 20.8 and 21.4 (fsync off: 9.6 and 9.5), more than double. The pause cell is stable. The no-pause cell is not: commit latency itself keeps transactions open longer, which creates overlap (INTERPRETATION). Treat every number in this section as lab-relative.

FACT. With 64 clients and a 5 ms pause inside each transaction, each insert cost about 61 members. 19 RC2 was within run-to-run noise of 18.7 in every cell (one 19 RC2 run of the 64/1/5 ms cell was about 10% slower than its siblings; medians are reported). This grid, the cross-database grid (section 5) and the mitigations (section 7) ran on 18.7 and 19 RC2; nothing in multixact.c or ri_triggers.c changed between RC2 and 19.0.

INTERPRETATION. Each insert joins a MultiXact that already holds every other open inserter, so a pause inside the transaction (an HTTP call, a slow ORM flush, a sleep in a backfill) multiplies the cost. At the 741k members/s this box sustained with fsync off (about 670k with durable commits), an 18.x cluster would reach the 2^31 point in about 48 minutes and the 2^32 stop in about 1.6 hours if nothing reclaimed. Treat that as a ceiling for this box, not a production estimate; your rate is your transactions per second times members per transaction. The shape matches Metronome's description: a backfill with FK-heavy inserts on a few parent rows, running alongside other write-heavy jobs.

4. Reclamation: what actually frees member space

Two cluster-wide floors decide what can be released (source: multixact.c, vacuum.c):

  • Truncation floor. Member files are deleted only up to the minimum datminmxid over every database, template0 included.
  • Freezing floor. Vacuum cannot freeze MultiXacts newer than the oldest value in OldestMemberMXactId[] / OldestVisibleMXactId[]. A backend sets its entry when it first locks, updates or deletes a row in a transaction. The arrays have no database dimension.

Setup. k=32, 4,000 episodes in database app (124,000 MultiXacts, 2,108,000 members, 10,559,488 bytes = 10.6 MB of members). Then one of seven actions. 3 reps each on 18.7, 19 RC2 and 19.0, 63 runs. In the two "locker" arms a session in the same database app took a FOR SHARE lock before the workload and stayed idle in transaction.

action after the workload members after oldestMultiXid
nothing 10.6 MB 1
VACUUM parent 10.6 MB 1
VACUUM (FREEZE) parent 10.6 MB 1
vacuumdb --all --freeze 10.6 MB 1
same, with an idle-in-transaction locker 10.6 MB, also after the locker ended and vacuumdb ran again 1
autovacuum, autovacuum_multixact_freeze_max_age = 10000 0.86 MB (at most 1.65 MB in post-workload samples) 114,391 to 116,282
same, with an idle-in-transaction locker 10.6 MB for 120 s; 74 kB at the first poll (2 s) after it ended 1, then 124,001

Identical on 18.7, 19 RC2 and 19.0. Sizes are decimal (1 MB = 10^6 bytes, 1 kB = 10^3 bytes).

FACT (from pg_database). After vacuumdb --all --freeze, postgres, template1 and app moved to datminmxid 124,001. template0 stayed at 1, and so did oldestMultiXid.

Source. vacuumdb skips databases with datallowconn = false (vacuumdb.c), which is template0. Autovacuum does not check datallowconn and processes template0 once its MultiXact age passes the effective autovacuum_multixact_freeze_max_age. You can also do it by hand: ALTER DATABASE template0 ALLOW_CONNECTIONS true, VACUUM (FREEZE) in it, then set it back.

FACT (autovacuum arm). With the lab's 10,000 freeze age, the members directory was at most 1.65 MB in the samples taken right after the workload; there were no samples during it. All 9 runs ended at my 180 s poll limit with the oldest MultiXact about 8,000 to 10,000 behind the next one. At the end template0 held the lowest datminmxid in 5 of 9 runs, postgres in 2 (both 19 RC2), and template1 and app in one 19.0 run each. Two 19.0 runs in this section (one autovacuum, one autovacuum + locker) had a 7-minute box suspension inside the poll window. I kept them, flagged them and reran both: 0.86 MB, and 10.6 MB while pinned with 74 kB at the first poll after release, the same as every other run. INTERPRETATION: with a low freeze age, autovacuum keeps member space small during the workload, but template0 or another database still sets the floor.

INTERPRETATION. A fresh lab cluster is the extreme case: template0 had never been frozen. On a long-lived cluster template0 has been frozen before, but the rule is the same. Member files are released when the laggiest database, often template0, is processed. Manual VACUUM FREEZE on your hot table is necessary, not sufficient.

The blocker (FACT). In the "autovacuum + locker" arm, one session that took a FOR SHARE lock before the workload and went idle in transaction kept oldestMultiXid at 1 for the full 120 s while autovacuum was running. Vacuums meanwhile logged WARNING: cutoff for freezing multixacts is far in the past. In the lab that warning fired immediately because I set the freeze age to 10,000. At default settings (400 million, lowered on 18.x only once members pass 2^31) it fires only once the oldest MultiXact is past the effective freeze age, so treat it as a late alarm, not an early one.

5. Cross-database pinning

Metronome's RCA states that "even a single long-running transaction holding an old MultiXact alive prevents the vacuum from reclaiming newer, unused member spaces". It does not say whether that transaction must be in the same database. I tested that.

Setup. Same workload in app (k=32, 4,000 episodes), autovacuum on with autovacuum_multixact_freeze_max_age = 10000 so reclamation normally keeps up. Before the workload starts, a second session in a different database (other) opens one of four things. Poll for 90 s, release, poll 90 s. 5 arms, 3 reps, both versions, 30 runs.

session in database other, opened before the workload members after 90 s oldestMultiXid after release
none (control) 0.86 MB about 115,000 n/a
SELECT ... FOR SHARE on one of its own rows, then idle in transaction 10.6 MB 1 74 kB at the first poll (3 s)
open transaction with an assigned xid (pg_current_xact_id()), no row lock 0.60 to 0.86 MB about 115,000 same
REPEATABLE READ snapshot after a read, no row lock 0.60 to 0.86 MB about 115,000 same
row lock, but idle_in_transaction_session_timeout = 10s 0.60 to 0.86 MB about 115,000 the timeout ended the session about 10 s in, during the workload

Identical on 18.7 and 19 RC2 (6/6 runs per arm).

FACT. A session that took a FOR SHARE row lock in another database before the workload pinned MultiXact reclamation for the whole cluster. A plain open xid or a repeatable-read snapshot in another database did not pin it in my runs. With the 10 s timeout the session was killed during the workload and member space never accumulated.

Source-based extension. MultiXactIdSetOldestMember is called when a transaction first locks, updates or deletes a row (heapam.c), and records the next MultiXact ID at that moment in a shared array with no database dimension. By that code, any row lock, UPDATE or DELETE sets the same pin, and the pin covers every MultiXact created after the session took it. I only measured FOR SHARE.

INTERPRETATION. On a shared cluster, a forgotten psql session in a reporting database that ran SELECT ... FOR SHARE (or, by the source, FOR UPDATE) and stayed open can stall member reclamation for the busy OLTP database next to it. idle_in_transaction_session_timeout ended that in 6/6 runs. It does not cover prepared transactions, which keep their pin across restarts until COMMIT PREPARED or ROLLBACK PREPARED.

6. The danger zone: 18.7 vs 19 at the members stop

Reaching 2^32 real members takes about 21 GB and hours. I used a lab shortcut, so weigh the result accordingly:

  1. Pin the oldest MultiXact with an orphaned prepared transaction (prepared transactions survive restarts).
  2. Clean shutdown, then pg_resetwal -O moves the next member offset to 4,274,017,280, a segment boundary 20,897,664 members below the 18.7 stop point (2^32 - 52,352). The skipped range holds no data, but the server's limit arithmetic sees about 4.27 billion members in use.
  3. Run k=64 hot-row episodes on fresh rows until error, or until 24M members past 2^32.
18.7 (3 runs + 1 control) 19.0 (3 runs) 19 RC2 (3 runs)
outcome ERROR: multixact "members" limit exceeded after 20,897,624 members no error; next offset 4,319,755,280, past 2^32 same as 19.0
warnings before the error 31,729 occurrences of must be vacuumed before N more multixact members are used none of that kind none of that kind
vacuumdb --all --freeze while the pin is held (control) exit code 0, writes still failing n/a n/a
after ROLLBACK PREPARED + vacuumdb --all --freeze exit code 0, writes still failing, template0 datminmxid still 1 n/a n/a
writes back 12.2 to 15.3 s later in the 3 runs, 6.2 s in the control, once autovacuum had processed template0 n/a n/a

Details:

  • 18.7 stopped 40 members before the source-derived stop point (20,897,664): the next MultiXact needed 57 members and only 39 were left. The DETAIL line reads "This command would create a multixact with 57 members, but the remaining space is only enough for 39 members". After the first error the next offset still advanced by 35 members, so smaller MultiXacts kept being created. INTERPRETATION: small lockers keep working while the FK-heavy batch fails, which can make the incident look intermittent.
  • The warnings start 20 segments (1,047,040 members) before the stop and repeat for every new MultiXact. With k=64 that is about 1,047,040 / 2,079 x 63 = 31,728 MultiXacts, so the count depends on MultiXact size, not on time.
  • On 19, pg_get_multixact_stats() (new in 19, commit 97b101776) reported num_members = 4,319,755,279 and members_size of 21.6 GB, while the directory held 229 MB: only about 45.7 million members were really written, the rest is the fast-forward gap. On a real cluster that function is the metric Metronome said they did not have.

Fast-forward artifact. In the first runs on both versions the gap made MultiXact 1 look like it had about 4.27 billion members. Every VACUUM of the table holding it failed (18.7: invalid memory alloc request size; 19 RC2 and 19.0: MultiXact 1 has too many members), so those runs say nothing about vacuum behaviour under a pin. The control run fixed that: the gap sits behind MultiXact 2 on a table that is dropped before the test, all probes use fresh rows, and vacuumdb exit codes are recorded. The control logged 0 artifact errors and reproduced the same stop point, the same 31,729 warnings, and writes failing until template0 was processed.

7. Mitigations, measured

Setup. The worst cell from section 3 (64 clients, 1 hot parent, 5 ms pause inside the transaction) against four changes, one at a time. 20 s, 3 reps, both versions, 30 runs, fsync off. For a backfill of fixed size the useful metric is members per inserted row: total member cost = rows x members per row.

change members / row (18.7, median) rows / s members / s
baseline 59.7 12,076 721,155
cap the pool at 16 clients 14.9 2,979 44,489
no pause inside the transaction 10.6 71,299 750,496
10 child rows per transaction 6.1 118,457 727,444
spread over 16 hot parent keys 4.6 12,032 55,693

The baseline is a separate run set of the section 3 worst cell (59.7 here vs 60.7 there). 19 RC2 was within 1% of 18.7 on members per row in every arm; on members per second the largest gap was 2.05% (batch10: 727,444 vs 742,350).

FACT. Every change cut member cost per row by 4x to 13x in this lab. Batching and removing the pause also made the job faster, so the member rate stayed at about 0.72 to 0.75 million per second. Spreading the hot key was the only change that cut both cost per row and rate without costing throughput. The no-pause arm is the one most sensitive to fsync (in section 3 its members per transaction doubled with durable commits), so its advantage here is likely overstated; read all of these as lab-relative.

INTERPRETATION. A backfill of 100 million rows costs about 6.0 billion members at baseline and 0.6 billion batched. If reclamation is pinned, the batched job still reaches the stop after a similar wall-clock time; it just gets about 10x more rows done first. For a backfill: batch children per parent, keep slow work out of the transaction, and rate-limit on members, not on rows. On 18.x, next_multi_offset growth per minute is the number to throttle on.

8. Upgrading 18 to 19: pg_upgrade compacts member space

19 stores offsets as 64-bit, so pg_upgrade rewrites pg_multixact (multixact_rewrite.c at REL_19_0). It reads "only one member from each multixid: the one updating one, or if there was no update, arbitrarily the first locking xid", because lock-only members do not matter once no transaction can be running across the upgrade.

Setup. 18.7 cluster, k=64 hot-row episodes (1,000 / 10,000 / 30,000), no vacuum. The upgrade rewrites every MultiXact in the old cluster's [oldest, next) range; in these runs only the last MultiXact of each episode is still referenced by a row. pg_upgrade --link to 19 RC2 (and, for 10,000 episodes, to 19.0), then re-lock up to 2,000 of the old rows on 19 with 4 sessions (all 1,000 in the smallest run) and compare row counts and sums. 3 reps. Controls: 18.7 to 18.7 with 1,000 episodes, 18.7 to 19 RC2 with an empty cluster, and one 10,000-episode run with amcheck.

episodes members before (18.7) members before members after (19) members after pg_upgrade --link time
0 (control) 0 8 kB 0 8 kB 1.58 to 1.62 s
1,000 2,079,000 10.4 MB 63,000 0.32 MB 1.62 to 1.66 s
10,000 20,790,000 104 MB 630,000 3.2 MB 1.67 to 1.77 s
30,000 62,370,000 312 MB 1,890,000 9.5 MB 1.95 to 2.01 s
10,000, to 19.0 20,790,000 104 MB 630,000 3.2 MB 1.86 to 1.97 s

Rows without a version label are 18.7 to 19 RC2. All reps gave identical member counts and sizes, and 19.0 matched RC2 byte for byte (members 3,162,112 bytes, offsets 5,046,272 bytes, 10,010 rows matched after re-locking). The 19.0 upgrades took about 0.2 s longer than RC2 at the same size; I ran no 19.0 empty-cluster baseline and these runs were not load-gated, so I do not attribute that to the version.

FACT.

  • After the upgrade the member count equals the MultiXact count. For this workload that is a 33x reduction in members, which is (k+2)/2 at k=64, the members per MultiXact of a staircase episode. Your ratio is your own members per MultiXact; in my concurrent runs (section 3) the per-cell median ranged from 2.1 to 60.7.
  • The offsets area doubles (8 bytes per MultiXact), so the whole pg_multixact directory shrank less than members alone: 319.9 MB to 24.6 MB (13x) at 30,000 episodes on RC2, and 106.6 MB to 8.2 MB (13x) at 10,000 episodes on both RC2 and 19.0.
  • 18.7 to 18.7 kept all 2,079,001 members (1.55 to 1.58 s): the compaction comes from the 18 to 19 rewrite, not from pg_upgrade as such.
  • The rewrite added 0.0 to 0.4 s over the empty-cluster baseline, growing with size.
  • Re-locking worked and row counts and sums matched (1,010 / 10,010 / 30,010 rows). In the 10,000-episode control, amcheck (verify_heapam and bt_index_check) reported no corruption before the upgrade, after it, and after all 10,010 rows were re-locked by 4 sessions.

INTERPRETATION. If you are on 18.x with a large pg_multixact/members, the upgrade resets member usage to one per MultiXact in the retained range. It is not an emergency tool (it needs downtime and a clean shutdown), but it is worth knowing when you plan the 19 migration.

9. What I would do on Monday

Three monitoring queries (not benchmarked; on managed platforms, check privileges first):

-- Which database holds the MultiXact floor (template0 included)
SELECT datname, datallowconn, datminmxid, mxid_age(datminmxid) AS mxid_age
FROM pg_database ORDER BY mxid_age(datminmxid) DESC;

-- PostgreSQL 19+: returns NULLs unless the role has pg_read_all_stats
SELECT num_mxids, num_members, members_size, oldest_multixact FROM pg_get_multixact_stats();

-- Pinning candidates, cluster-wide (pg_stat_activity cannot show who holds a row lock)
SELECT pid, datname, usename, state, now() - xact_start AS xact_age, backend_xid, left(query, 80)
FROM pg_stat_activity WHERE state LIKE 'idle in transaction%' ORDER BY xact_start;
SELECT gid, database, owner, prepared FROM pg_prepared_xacts ORDER BY prepared;

The full set of seven queries, including per-table MultiXact age, member consumption since the last checkpoint and the members directory size, is in monitoring.sql.

On 18.x and earlier:

  1. Monitor member space, not just MultiXact age: the members directory size or next_multi_offset (about 5 bytes per member; 10.7 GB is the aggressive-vacuum point, 21.5 GB the stop), plus mxid_age(datminmxid) for every database including template0. [measured: sections 2, 4]
  2. Alert on long idle-in-transaction sessions and orphaned prepared transactions in every database, not just the busy one. Set idle_in_transaction_session_timeout; it does not end prepared transactions. [measured: section 5]
  3. Grep for cutoff for freezing multixacts is far in the past and must be vacuumed before ... multixact members. [source: vacuum.c, multixact.c; a late signal at default settings]
  4. Shape writes: no network calls or sleeps inside transactions that insert children of hot parents; batch children per transaction; spread hot keys. In my runs these cut members per row by 4x to 13x. [measured: section 7]
  5. Recovery order when it hits: end the pinning session or ROLLBACK PREPARED, then get every database including template0 past the old MultiXacts: wait for autovacuum, or temporarily ALTER DATABASE template0 ALLOW_CONNECTIONS true, run VACUUM (FREEZE) in it, and set it back. In my 18.7 runs autovacuum alone restored writes 6 to 15 s after the pin was released. [measured on 18.7: section 6; manual template0 path documented, not run]
symptom check action
multixact "members" limit exceeded (18.x) pg_prepared_xacts, idle-in-transaction sessions in every database end the pin, then freeze every database including template0
members directory keeps growing after VACUUM (FREEZE) mxid_age(datminmxid) per database the lowest database (often template0) needs processing
oldest_multi_xid does not move while autovacuum runs sessions open since before the growth started end them or set idle_in_transaction_session_timeout
high member rate during a backfill members per inserted row batch, remove pauses inside transactions, spread hot keys

On 19:

  • The member-offset stop is gone, so a member blow-up turns from "writes rejected" into "disk keeps growing at about 5 bytes per member". MultiXact IDs are still limited to 2^31, and that wraparound stop still exists. Points 1 to 4 still apply, and pg_get_multixact_stats() makes point 1 a single query.
  • Member pressure no longer launches anti-wraparound vacuum in 19 (commit 6aa2cefe11). It only makes vacuums that run anyway freeze more aggressively, scaled linearly from 2,000,000,000 members (MULTIXACT_MEMBER_LOW_THRESHOLD) to 4,000,000,000 (MULTIXACT_MEMBER_HIGH_THRESHOLD). With autovacuum disabled, nothing comes to clean up members for you.
  • 19 raises the MultiXact and XID wraparound warning distance to 100 million (commit 48f11bfa0).

Method and limits

  • Native builds of 18.7, 19 RC2 and 19.0 from the official tarballs, sha256 verified; gcc 14.2, Debian, Linux 6.12, 8 vCPU (the hypervisor reports "Intel(R) Xeon(R) Processor"), 15 GiB RAM, virtio disk of unknown media, single VM, no Docker.
  • fsync, synchronous_commit and full_page_writes off; autovacuum off unless the arm says otherwise. These settings do not affect deterministic counts (sections 2, 4, 5, 6 and 8 member and MultiXact counts, bytes per member). They can affect concurrency-dependent results (sections 3 and 7: members per transaction or row, and every rate), because commit latency changes how long lockers overlap. The fsync-on control in section 3 shows how much.
  • Counts come from pg_controldata after CHECKPOINT, file sizes in pg_multixact/, and pg_get_multixact_stats() on 19. Sizes are decimal (MB = 10^6 bytes) unless marked GiB.
  • Fresh cluster per run, shuffled run order with recorded seeds, 3 repetitions. The cross-database, mitigation and upgrade grids, and the control runs, were added after the original protocol; the upgrade and limit runs used a fixed order.
  • A load and suspension rule (load average below 2 before each run, void and rerun if wall-clock time and VM uptime disagree by more than 5%) was applied to the control runs only. Earlier runs had no such gate; I voided one run that followed a suspension (section 3).
  • The VM was reset once during the study. One limit-test attempt was cut off and discarded (raw file kept); the reclamation results were restored from a checksummed backup written before the reset.
  • The members-limit test fast-forwards the counter with pg_resetwal. The limit logic is real; the 4 billion members are not.
  • PostgreSQL 19.0 (tarball on ftp.postgresql.org on 19 Nov 2026, sha256 a89fd70e...e692d verified) was built and rerun the same afternoon for sections 2, 4, 6 and 8. Sections 3, 5 and 7 and the fsync-on control are from 19 RC2 (released 2026-11-12); between RC2 and 19.0 nothing changed in multixact.c, ri_triggers.c or the pg_upgrade MultiXact code. The 19.0 limit runs took 196 to 214 s for the same 22,000 episodes that took 176 to 179 s on RC2; that is wall time on a shared, ungated box, not a measured version difference.

Reproduce

Everything above comes from Python scripts that build fresh clusters on unix sockets, run one cell, and append one JSON line per run. The layout is:

scripts/      lab.py (cluster harness), grid_*.py, limit_ff.py, upgrade_rewrite.py, controls.py, analyze.py
results/      one .jsonl per grid, results/controls/ for the control runs
PROTOCOL.md   design, seeds, deviations, load rule, reset timeline

To rerun on your own machine: clone the repo, build PostgreSQL 18.7 and 19.0 (and 19 RC2 for the comparison) into install/pg-<version> with scripts/build_pg.sh (it includes contrib/amcheck for the upgrade control), create a Python venv with psycopg and matplotlib, then run for example python scripts/grid_growth.py g1 18.7,19.0, the other grid_*.py scripts, and python scripts/analyze.py. PROTOCOL.md lists every grid, its seed and its arguments.

Scripts, raw JSONL, charts and PROTOCOL.md: https://github.com/firfircelik/pg-multixact-lab (MIT; snapshot used for this article: commit 45f8d9d). Build steps, tarball checksums and the per-grid commands are in its README.

title: A Known-Data Check of Red and White Wine Domain Transfer
description:
A known-data check of red and white wine domain transfer

A model that looks useful on its own training source can still make worse per-record choices than a constant once it crosses to another source. I used the UCI Wine Quality files to make that gap visible with two small regressors, one trained on red wine records and one on white. The target is the sensory quality score from the source. This article records the saved run from November 4, 2026; publishing the article adds no new training.

The source files contain 1,599 red rows and 4,898 white rows, 6,497 in total. The UCI page summary of 4,898 instances describes white only. Each row has 11 physicochemical inputs and an ordered quality score from 0 to 10. The source names state that the score is the median of at least three expert evaluations. Individual chemistry units are not supplied in the files, so I keep the numeric scales as they appear. Treating that ordered score as an equally spaced number for MAE and MSE is a modeling assumption, not evidence that the score sits on an interval scale.

Before training, I assigned each record a role using only its 11 canonical feature values. I decimal-normalized the tokens, joined them, hashed the prefixed key with SHA-256, and used the integer modulo 10. Values 0 through 5 became a fit pool, 6 and 7 became a validation pool, and 8 and 9 became test. The same feature vector receives the same initial role in both colors, and quality and color are excluded from the key. That produces 5,318 unique groups among 6,497 rows and 1,179 duplicate-excess rows. Two exact input vectors appear in both colors. Exact vector identity is a duplicate control, not a producer or subject ID, and it does not prove that repeated rows are independent samples. Duplicate rows still enter the batch arithmetic, so they contribute repeated weight. Whether those repeated rows are ultimately independent measurements does not change that computational weighting.

The red source had 923 fit-pool rows, 335 validation-pool rows, and 341 test rows. The white source had 2,939 fit-pool candidates and 977 validation-pool candidates. I sampled 923 fit rows and 335 validation rows from white, leaving 2,016 fit candidates and 642 validation candidates unused. Tests were never downsampled, so the frozen test set is the full 341 red rows plus 982 white rows, 1,323 cases in total. Those same 1,323 cases are reused across three seeds in the paired comparison below.

Each source fit has 923 rows, 100 epochs, and batch size 64, giving 1,500 updates and 92,300 row visits per fit. The network is 11 inputs, 24 tanh units, and one linear output, 313 parameters. Seeds 17, 41, and 73 run for each source, giving six saved models. One initial parameter set per seed is shared between the red and white fits, three sets total; each set holds W1, b1, W2, and b2. Because each domain has its own train-only normalizer, a shared set does not necessarily define the same function on raw input scale. Validation and test rows never enter the normalizer statistics.

Checkpoint selection used each model's own 335-row validation set. I picked the earliest epoch with the strictly lowest MAE among all 100 checkpoints. Selected epochs were 31, 78, and 31 for red, and 52, 39, and 39 for white. Cross-domain evaluation never used the target color's validation set. An in-domain model's own source is also its target source, so that model did see the target-source validation set.

The aggregate MAE numbers are arithmetic means over three seeds, not ensembles and not confidence intervals.

Test domain Red-trained White-trained Red fit mean White fit mean Cases per seed
Red 0.476144 0.746975 0.647566 0.636872 341
White 0.649987 0.586350 0.748883 0.674610 982

The source-matched model has the lower mean error on both targets. The negative result sits inside that summary: the white-trained network is worse on the red holdout than its own fit-mean constant, 0.746975 versus 0.636872. Per seed, the three white-to-red MAE values are 0.657548, 0.732750, and 0.850627, each above that constant. The red-trained network beats the red constant on red, and the white-trained network beats the white constant on white. This is a specific cross-domain failure, not a statement that every neural model loses to every constant. The numbers also do not say that the white-trained model mostly emits its white training center, or that it learned no joint relation. They record that the aggregate error is worse than ignoring the inputs and returning the white fit mean.

The per-case view shows how much an average hides. Across 3,969 same-seed, same-case paired comparisons, the in-domain model had the larger absolute error in 1,585 pairs. By target domain, 321 of 1,023 red-target pairs and 1,264 of 2,946 white-target pairs went against the in-domain model. A negative value in the paired difference means the in-domain model was worse. These counts reuse the same 1,323 cases over three seeds. They are descriptive repetition, not 3,969 independent cases, and I did not run a significance test. The target-domain split is reported, but the denominators differ, and the repeated cases mean I cannot infer from those totals that one target domain explains the failures.

The fixed default case is red:0002. I selected it before any current-model test prediction as the lowest red test source ordinal. At seed 17, the red-trained model predicts 5.365765 and the white-trained model predicts 4.872778 for a true score of 5. The cross-domain model has the smaller error. I keep this case as a negative, not as a selected winner.

Figure: the actual study.png at 2015 by 1271 pixels, with all 600 own-source validation MAE points, the four seed-mean MAE bars and analytic fit-mean diamonds, and the full paired difference distributions. It is a descriptive known-data contrast, not a training-loss plot, screenshot, or causal diagram.

Equal rows, equal updates, and paired initial sets are computation controls. They do not isolate a source shift. The red fit pool contains all 923 red fit candidates. The white fit pool samples 923 from 2,939 white fit candidates. Train-only normalizers differ between the two pools. Feature support, quality distribution, own validation selection, and duplicate weighting differ at the same time. The source label is not the only thing that changes. A difference between the two training-pool feature means only shows that the pools differ. It does not prove that the white-to-red failure comes from a wrong center, a missing chemical relation, or another single mechanism.

Before assigning a mechanism, I would need separate runs that actually change the sampled training records under stated controls. One candidate would match the two pools by quality counts and overlapping feature support, keeping each domain's own normalizer and validation split, then check whether the white-to-red network still loses to its fit mean. Another would reweight duplicate rows down and see whether the headline errors move. Neither is part of this frozen run. The current result is a known-data descriptive comparison with the failures retained.

The fixed repository includes PROTOCOL.md, evaluation-001/results.json, and evaluation-001/paired-comparisons.json. Downloading only the static app page does not give you the complete set of research files. From the project root, after obtaining the fixed checkout at commit 2431a336acc4cef56f12b22a90bc77baed8c6863, the following Python 3 standard-library command recounts the headline numbers and the worse-pair split. It opens the two JSON files read-only. It does not download anything, install anything, fit anything, or write anything.

python3 - <<'PY'
import json, collections
r = json.load(open("evaluation-001/results.json"))
p = json.load(open("evaluation-001/paired-comparisons.json"))
for d in r["descriptive_seed_metric_means_not_ensemble"]:
    print("neural", d["target_domain"], d["trained_domain"], "mae", d["arithmetic_mean_seed_mae"])
for b in r["all_mean_baselines"]:
    print("mean", b["trained_domain"], "->", b["target_domain"], "mae", b["mae"])
c = collections.Counter((x["target_domain"], x["in_domain_worse"]) for x in p)
print("worse_split", "red", c[("red", True)], "white", c[("white", True)], "total", r["in_domain_worse_pairs"])
print("reuse_check", r["paired_rows"], "==", 3, "*", r["test_cases"], ":", r["paired_rows"] == 3 * r["test_cases"])
PY

The official space and the static demo load six saved forward models and two analytic constants. The demo is static, with no external API or browser storage. Edits entered in the page live in browser memory, so a refresh discards them. A deliberate export writes all eleven inputs, the six model outputs, the two mean baselines, normalizers, source matches, and provenance to a local JSON file; the file stays where the reader saves it. I state this so no one trusts unsaved work to survive. Input range checks are marginal bounds, not joint chemical support. An exact feature-key match is numeric consistency, not measurement provenance. Outputs are unrounded and unclipped, with no calibrated uncertainty or probability.

The original red and white CSV files and the derived weights, figures, and results retain attribution to Cortez, Cerdeira, Almeida, Matos, and Reis, UCI 186, DOI 10.24432/C56S3T, under CC BY 4.0. My code and documents are Apache 2.0. That split is recorded in NOTICE and LICENSES.md. The 2009 paper is cited as metadata; I did not read its full text, did not reproduce its model or scores, and did not use its results as my own. No tasting, health, certification, or future-vintage claim follows from this experiment.

English original.
