title: Why? Why do you need MongoDB?
description:
In applications, you can store data using a relational database.

The relational database already gives you the power to create complex relationships between data. Instead, you use a non-relational database.

Why? Why do you need MongoDB?

And if your argument is that MongoDB is a simple-to-use NoSQL database, so I prefer MongoDB, then actually, you don't understand the actual use case of MongoDB.

So, the use case starts when you build a social media application, a quick-commerce application, or an application where the attributes of a field are not fixed.

In this type of application, each product has different attributes, and for that, in a relational database, you need to create many optional fields so the table supports different types of product data.

This approach works, but after a certain level, it requires a heavily normalized design that supports all the products at a higher scale. This becomes more complex for querying and planning the database.

Whereas MongoDB has superpowers.

Because it uses documents to store data instead of records.

But what is a document?

Unlike relational databases, where all the details of a specific person or product are stored in a record, MongoDB stores information in documents in the form of a field-value structure. This gives you the ability to add any number of fields or unique fields to a document.

And the group of these documents is called a collection. A collection has different documents with different fields.

The problem that we face in relational databases is solved by this collection and document approach provided by MongoDB.

Now, this is one ability of MongoDB, and it has many other abilities.

Tell me in the comment section.

title: Ho tolto i miei file dal cloud e ho scritto un browser di file in un solo binario
description:
Sono l'autore del progetto, quindi leggete questo come un resoconto di costruzione, non come una recensione indipendente.

Il collo di bottiglia non era lo spazio, era l'anteprima

Il mio studio di design è piccolo: un NAS, una macchina con i file di lavoro e, più volte al giorno, la stessa richiesta — "mi mandi la versione più recente?". Il problema non è mai stato dove tenere i file. Era vederli prima di scaricarli. Nessuno vuole scaricare 400 MB per scoprire di aver preso il file sbagliato.

Quello che è uscito alla fine è un binario scritto in Go. Senza Docker, senza database, senza PHP, senza cron.

./banyan -headless

Stampa un indirizzo; lo apri nel browser di qualsiasi dispositivo sulla stessa rete. L'installazione finisce lì. Ci sono client nativi per Windows, macOS, Linux, FreeBSD e Android, e tutto il resto entra dal browser.

Cosa cambia ogni giorno

  • Anteprima di oltre 100 formati sul server: Office, PDF, DWG, video, immagini, archivi compressi, codice sorgente, font. Il file viene trasmesso, non scaricato.
  • Link di condivisione che il destinatario apre senza creare un account, con scadenza e contatore delle visite.
  • Modificare dall'anteprima salva direttamente nel percorso originale. Addio finale_v2_finale(2).psd.
  • Esportare in PDF con filigrana, firma e annotazioni nello stesso posto in cui il file già si trova.
  • Cifratura AES-256-GCM per cartella, nessun account, nessuna telemetria, e funziona offline dentro la rete locale.

Cosa non è (e perché vale dirlo)

  • Non è un client di sincronizzazione. Nessuna risoluzione dei conflitti, nessun mirroring. È un browser con anteprima, non un Dropbox.
  • Non esiste una versione ospitata. È self-hosted: TLS, dominio e reverse proxy sono affar tuo.
  • Il binario pesa ~65 MB perché porta dentro tutta la pipeline di anteprima.
  • L'interfaccia è in dieci lingue, ma la traduzione è stata generata automaticamente dal cinese: in italiano ci sono frasi che suonano strane e le sto correggendo a mano.

Perché un solo binario

L'alternativa abituale è montare Nextcloud o simili, cioè: Docker Compose, database, aggiornamenti, PHP, un pannello di amministrazione pieno di avvisi. Per "voglio vedere i miei file dal portatile nell'altra stanza" è troppo macchinario. Un binario che copi, esegui e dimentichi è più onesto per quel caso d'uso.

Il prezzo di questa scelta: nessun ecosistema di app, nessun mobile-first sincronizzato, e se vuoi collaborazione multiutente vera, questo non è il tuo prodotto.

Provalo e dimmi cosa si rompe

Pagina del progetto, con download per le sei piattaforme e documentazione in dieci lingue: https://banyan.ikootoo.com/?utm_source=devto&utm_medium=post&utm_campaign=banyan_it

Codice sorgente: https://github.com/nbmany-web/banyan

Se avete risolto il "scaricare per capire cosa è" in un altro modo, mi interessa sapere come.

title: Node.js SaaS Shipment Updates: Background Queue vs Cron for File, Email, Webhook Sync
description:
Short answer: for a Node.js SaaS that must fan out a shipment update, put each file processing, email sending, and webhook sync attempt behind a background job queue. Use cron to discover periodic work, such as a retry sweep. A clock can find work; it cannot remember which subscriber was delivered, which one timed out, or which side effect may have happened just before a crash.

Here is the small choice matrix I would start with:

Work Default Delivery reason
Process a file after an upload Queue job The job has one owner, attempt history, and a retry deadline
Send an email for a shipment update Queue job One slow recipient stays isolated from the fan-out
Sync a webhook subscriber Queue job Each endpoint needs its own backoff and idempotency key
Find work due at 02:00 Cron, then enqueue The schedule discovers records; a worker performs the effects
Remove expired temporary files Cron A later run can safely discover the same cleanup again

The easiest setup is usually a durable jobs table, one worker, and one scheduler. You do not need to start with a large messaging system to get the important guarantee. You do need durable state.

How should a beginner use a background job queue for file processing in a Node.js SaaS?

Start by naming the guarantee in plain English. For the shipment event shp_4821, the SaaS might need to attempt an email for subscriber sub_19, process a label PDF, and synchronize a webhook endpoint. Those are three jobs, even if one button created them. Each has a different destination, timeout, payload, and definition of success. Treating the fan-out as one function call hides the exact information an operator needs when a customer says, “the email arrived, but the partner system did not update.”

The useful promise is usually at-least-once processing with idempotent effects. Exactly-once delivery sounds tidy, but an external email or webhook can accept a request immediately before the worker loses power. The worker then cannot know whether repeating the request is safe. I would rather document that boundary than hide it behind a green status badge.

Keep these values with the job:

  • kind, payload, and the shipment event ID
  • attempts, nextAttemptAt, and a retry deadline
  • status, leaseUntil, and the last error category
  • a stable idempotency key for the logical side effect

The key should identify the effect, not merely the worker run. For example, shipment:shp_4821:subscriber:sub_19:webhook:v3 is more useful than a random UUID generated during a retry. A database uniqueness constraint can stop two workers from creating the same logical delivery record. The receiver still needs to honor a request key, or your system must accept that a crash can produce a duplicate.

Three words matter here: claim, effect, record. Claim a job for a limited lease. Perform one bounded effect. Record success only after the effect returns. If the process exits between the last two steps, the lease expires and the job becomes available again. That is the failure path your design has to explain.

RabbitMQ's consumer acknowledgement documentation describes the same handoff concern: an acknowledgement tells the broker that a consumer has handled a delivery, while an unacknowledged delivery can be made available again. The acknowledgement is useful state. It is not proof that an unrelated third-party side effect happened exactly once.

What delivery data belongs in the seven-day ledger?

Cron answers “when should I look?” It does not naturally answer “which of 18,000 subscribers is on attempt four, and which one is due in six hours?” A queue or durable job table can make that per-delivery state explicit.

This distinction matters for delayed messages up to 7 days. A retry due next week should have a stored deadline and a stored idempotency key. It should not depend on a Node.js process staying alive or on a cron script remembering local variables from last Tuesday.

Backoff should be bounded. A practical policy can use exponential delay with jitter, cap the delay at seven days, and move a permanently rejected job to a dead state. Classify errors before applying that policy. A timeout or transient network failure may be retryable. A malformed payload, invalid recipient, or authorization failure usually needs repair instead of twelve identical requests.

My test case includes a 409 from a deduplication constraint. I treat that as “the logical effect already exists,” not as a reason to send the email again. I'm not sure every provider uses that exact status or meaning, so the mapping belongs in the adapter for that provider, not in a generic worker.

The long delay also changes operations. Retain enough metadata to investigate a missed delivery without retaining secrets forever. Store a file reference instead of copying a large file into every job. Redact webhook credentials and email addresses in logs. A seven-day retry policy without a way to inspect or expire its payload is just a seven-day data-retention problem.

Can a cron workflow discover email and webhook work without owning it?

Make the scheduler a producer. It finds due work in bounded batches, inserts jobs with a uniqueness rule, and exits. Make the worker the owner of delivery. This division keeps a missed scheduled run recoverable and keeps a long webhook retry from turning into one enormous cron invocation.

The following TypeScript is deliberately an interface boundary. The database and queue implementations can change without changing the delivery rules.

type JobKind = "file.process" | "email.send" | "webhook.sync";

type DeliveryJob = {
  id: string;
  kind: JobKind;
  shipmentEventId: string;
  idempotencyKey: string;
  attempts: number;
  nextAttemptAt: number;
  expiresAt: number;
};

type JobStore = {
  claim(now: number, leaseMs: number): Promise<DeliveryJob | null>;
  markDone(id: string): Promise<void>;
  scheduleRetry(id: string, at: number, reason: string): Promise<void>;
  markDead(id: string, reason: string): Promise<void>;
};

type DeliveryEffect = {
  run(job: DeliveryJob): Promise<"done" | "retryable" | "permanent">;
};

async function processOne(store: JobStore, effect: DeliveryEffect): Promise<void> {
  const job = await store.claim(Date.now(), 60_000);
  if (!job) return;

  try {
    const result = await effect.run(job);
    if (result === "done") {
      await store.markDone(job.id);
      return;
    }

    if (result === "permanent" || Date.now() >= job.expiresAt) {
      await store.markDead(job.id, "delivery deadline reached");
      return;
    }

    const exponentialMs = Math.min(24 * 60 * 60 * 1000, 2 ** job.attempts * 1_000);
    const jitterMs = Math.floor(Math.random() * 1_000);
    await store.scheduleRetry(job.id, Date.now() + exponentialMs + jitterMs, "transient failure");
  } catch (error) {
    await store.scheduleRetry(job.id, Date.now() + 60_000, String(error));
  }
}

The adapter behind effect.run checks the idempotency key at the effect boundary. That matters because a lease can expire while a file processor is still finishing, allowing another worker to see the same logical job. A check only in the scheduler is too late.

Run the scheduler like this: select rows whose nextAttemptAt is due, insert a bounded batch, and let the uniqueness rule reject duplicates. GitHub Actions documents scheduled workflow triggers as a time-based mechanism; the same principle applies to any cron host. The scheduled process should not carry the delivery state in memory, and it should not report success until the discovered work is durable.

How can I benchmark the handoff before adding a broker?

Cron is a good fit for periodic, bounded work where lateness is acceptable and the next run can repair an omission. Expiring temporary files, reconciling a small table, and finding retryable rows are reasonable examples. A five-minute sweep can enqueue due delivery jobs without pretending that every subscriber is one five-minute task.

Measure it.

The catch is that cron alone is not suitable when subscribers have independent deadlines, rate limits, attempt histories, or dead-letter handling. It also becomes awkward when file processing takes longer than the schedule interval or when one failed email blocks later recipients in the same loop. Use a queue for that execution layer.

A queue can be the wrong first move, too. If the team cannot operate a broker and the workload is modest, a database-backed queue with polling may be easier to reason about. If the task has no meaningful recovery path and a missed run is harmless, adding durable per-item delivery state is configuration bloat. Keep the least complex mechanism that records the guarantee you actually need.

Do not choose by monthly price alone. Measure time to first call, queue age, p95 delivery latency, retry rate, dead-job count, and operator steps during a replay. I care about those numbers because a cheap queue that needs a custom script for every failure is not cheap in engineering time. There is a large difference between a job that is late for 30 seconds and one that is still pending after its subscriber's seven-day window; both can look like “the worker is running” in a shallow dashboard, while only the latter is a delivery incident. Your mileage may vary with traffic and latency targets.

What does the queue-versus-cron comparison say about low-stakes cleanup?

The failure drill belongs in this benchmark, not in a launch checklist nobody runs. Start two workers against the same job. Kill one after the outbound request returns but before markDone. Pause one webhook endpoint. Feed the file processor a large input. Advance the clock beyond the seven-day deadline.

The expected result is not “nothing runs twice.” The expected result is that repeated logical work is harmless or visible, the job can be traced by its idempotency key, and a permanent failure stops retrying. A green email response does not prove that the database update happened afterward.

Log the job ID, shipment event ID, attempt number, and outcome category. Do not log credentials or full webhook payloads by default. Alert on old pending jobs and an unusual retry rate, not only on a dead worker process. Those signals tell you whether delivery is drifting before a customer reports a missing update.

The decision rule is short: cron discovers time-based work; a background job queue owns independent delivery attempts. For a Node.js SaaS sending shipment updates to many subscribers, that boundary makes retries, idempotency, and delayed messages explicit without promising a guarantee the outside system cannot provide.

References

  • RabbitMQ consumer acknowledgements: https://www.rabbitmq.com/docs/confirms
  • GitHub Actions scheduled workflow triggers: https://docs.github.com/en/actions/using-workflows/events-that-trigger-workflows

title: Let your coding agent test the API it just wrote
description:
Coding agents are now fast at writing endpoints. What they are not good at, out of the box, is proving those endpoints still work after the fifth round of edits.

So the loop usually ends with a human: you open curl or an HTTP client, hit every route by hand, find the one that broke, and paste the error back into the chat.

We got tired of being that human. This post shows how we closed the loop so the agent tests its own work, using Ajiro API, a small MIT-licensed CLI we just open-sourced.


A moved route makes GET /todos/stats return 404. The fix makes all 34 tests pass again.

Why "just ask it to write tests" falls short

You can tell an agent to write tests. In practice you get:

  • Tests in whatever framework the agent picked that day, scattered across the repo
  • Failures printed for humans, so the agent has to guess which line to fix
  • Nothing that runs the same way in CI and on your laptop

What the agent needs is a fixed format to write, and failure output it can act on directly.

The idea: one YAML file per endpoint, next to your code

  1. scan reads your routes statically and writes one YAML file per endpoint
  2. You or the agent add expectations (status, body fields, values captured for later requests)
  3. test runs everything against your running server and returns failures with the response and handler location
  4. The agent fixes the code (or the test) and runs it again

We chose plain YAML over a custom format on purpose. Models write it reliably, diffs are readable in review, and it converts to and from OpenAPI.

Try it on a Hono app

The repo ships a small Hono TODO API in examples/hono-todo.

npx -y ajiro-api init     # detects Hono and the port
npx -y ajiro-api scan

+ POST /auth/login  api/auth/post-auth-login.yaml
+ GET /health  api/health/get-health.yaml
+ GET /todos  api/todos/get-todos.yaml
+ POST /todos  api/todos/post-todos.yaml
+ GET /todos/stats  api/todos/get-todos-stats.yaml
+ DELETE /todos/{id}  api/todos/delete-todos-id.yaml
+ GET /todos/{id}  api/todos/get-todos-id.yaml
+ PATCH /todos/{id}  api/todos/patch-todos-id.yaml
hono: 8 created, 0 updated, 0 unchanged (8 endpoints, 3 ms)

It's a single Rust binary, so there is no Node or Python runtime to manage. It is also on Homebrew (brew install niti-lab/tap/ajiro-api) and cargo.

Each file has a source block that scan owns and a tests list that is yours. Here is the stats endpoint with tests filled in:

# api/todos/get-todos-stats.yaml
id: todos.stats.list
depends_on: [todos.create, todos.update]
request:
  headers:
    Authorization: "Bearer {{ token }}"   # captured from the login test
  method: GET
  path: /todos/stats
source:
  framework: hono
  file: src/routes/todos.ts
  line: 26
tests:
  - name: returns counts
    expect:
      status: 200
      body:
        match:
          $.total: { $gte: 1 }
          $.done: { $gte: 1 }
          $.open: { $gte: 1 }
  - name: rejects a missing token
    request: { headers: { Authorization: "" } }
    expect:
      status: 401

Re-running scan after code changes updates source and leaves your tests alone. The login password stays in .env ({{ env.DEMO_PASSWORD }}), and tokens are masked as *** in output.

34 passed, 0 failed, 0 errors, 0 skipped (34 total) in 25ms

The part that matters: output an agent can act on

Here is a classic agent mistake. Asked to tidy up the routes, it moves GET /todos/stats below GET /todos/:id. Hono now matches stats as an id. Types still check, and handler-level unit tests still pass.

✗ todos.stats.list / returns counts (1ms)
    status: expected status 200, got 404
    body.match: $.total: path not found (expected >= 1)
    → api/todos/get-todos-stats.yaml
    → handler: src/routes/todos.ts:83

33 passed, 1 failed, 0 errors, 0 skipped (34 total) in 19ms

With --json, the agent gets the same failure with the request and the actual response:

{
  "endpoint_id": "todos.stats.list",
  "status": "failed",
  "request": { "method": "GET", "url": "http://localhost:3000/todos/stats",
               "headers": { "Authorization": "Bearer ***" } },
  "response": { "status": 404,
                "body": { "error": "not_found", "message": "Todo not found" } },
  "failures": [ { "check": "status", "expected": 200, "actual": 404 } ],
  "source": { "file": "src/routes/todos.ts", "line": 83 }
}

"Todo not found" on a stats route tells you right away that another handler swallowed the request. The agent opens line 83, restores the route order, re-runs, and it's back to 34/34.

Hand it to Claude Code

Install the plugin (skill + MCP server) from inside Claude Code:

/plugin marketplace add niti-lab/ajiro-api
/plugin install ajiro-api@ajiro-api

The skill kicks in whenever the agent adds or changes an endpoint: scan, write tests, run, read failures, fix, re-run. Two of its rules matter most:

  • Decide which side is wrong first. If the code contradicts the intent, fix the code. If the behaviour change is intended, fix the test. If unsure, ask the user.
  • Don't weaken assertions to get green. No deleting failing tests or loosening status checks.

The second one is the real fear with agent-written tests. Since the YAML lands in the same diff as the code, you can review what was checked, not just what changed.

Using Codex? Paste AGENTS.snippet.md into your AGENTS.md.

Using another MCP client? The server is listed in the official MCP Registry as io.github.NITI-Lab/ajiro-api (and on Glama). Point your client at npx -y ajiro-api mcp; it exposes scan, test, list, validate, get_endpoint and schema as tools.

Same tests in CI 

ajiro-api scan --check --ignore-lines        # fail if the YAML drifted from the routes
ajiro-api test --env ci --junit report.xml

A full GitHub Actions example is in examples/github-actions.

What else the same YAML gives you

  • ajiro-api mock: a mock server with switchable scenarios, so frontend work doesn't wait on the backend
  • ajiro-api docs: a single-file HTML API reference you can email to a client
  • ajiro-api openapi import/export, ajiro-api import postman/bruno: move in and out

Supported frameworks: Next.js Route Handlers, Hono, FastAPI, Express, and Go (net/http, chi, Echo). Nothing leaves your machine: no account, no cloud sync.

Where this fits

If you want to poke at an API by hand, keep using Postman, Bruno, or whatever you like. Ajiro API is for the other case: the agent writes the code, and the agent should prove it works.

Repo: https://github.com/NITI-Lab/ajiro-api

Issues about where the route scanner breaks on your codebase are the most useful feedback right now. Stars are welcome too.

title: Five Spring AI Agentic Patterns Every Java Developer Should Know
description:
Agentic systems are moving from demos into production, and Java teams are asking the same question: how do we structure them so they stay reliable, testable, and easy to change? Spring AI gives us the building blocks, but the building blocks alone do not make an agent. The design patterns do.

In this article I walk through five agentic patterns you can build with Spring AI: Router, Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG), Chain of Thought, Supervisor, and Guardrails & Validation. For each one I explain the problem it solves, when to use it, and a small Java example. The code is intentionally compact so you can see the structure rather than a full application.

This is the first in a series. The upcoming posts will explain each of the five Spring AI agentic patterns in depth, with complete projects you can run.

The Problem: LLM Calls Are Not Architecture

A single call to a language model is easy. A system that routes requests, looks up company knowledge, reasons through multi-step tasks, delegates work, and checks its own answers is much harder. Without structure, these concerns end up tangled inside one giant prompt and one giant service class.

Agentic patterns separate those concerns. Each pattern is a reusable shape for a specific kind of problem, and you can combine them. A production assistant often uses a router at the entry point, RAG for knowledge, and guardrails on the way out.

All examples below assume a Spring Boot application with a ChatClient bean, which Spring AI auto-configures from your chosen model provider:

@Configuration
class AiConfig {

    @Bean
    ChatClient chatClient(ChatClient.Builder builder) {
        return builder.build();
    }
}

Pattern 1: Router

The problem

Incoming requests vary widely. A customer asking about a refund should not reach the same logic as a developer asking about an API error. Sending everything to one general prompt makes answers vaguer and prompts longer.

The solution

A router inspects the request, classifies its intent, and dispatches it to a specialized handler. The classification step is itself an LLM call with a constrained output, so the router can only pick from known routes.

Java example 

enum Intent { BILLING, TECHNICAL, GENERAL }

@Service
class RouterService {

    private final ChatClient chatClient;
    private final BillingAgent billingAgent;
    private final TechnicalAgent technicalAgent;
    private final GeneralAgent generalAgent;

    RouterService(ChatClient chatClient, BillingAgent billingAgent,
                  TechnicalAgent technicalAgent, GeneralAgent generalAgent) {
        this.chatClient = chatClient;
        this.billingAgent = billingAgent;
        this.technicalAgent = technicalAgent;
        this.generalAgent = generalAgent;
    }

    String handle(String userMessage) {
        Intent intent = classify(userMessage);
        return switch (intent) {
            case BILLING -> billingAgent.answer(userMessage);
            case TECHNICAL -> technicalAgent.answer(userMessage);
            case GENERAL -> generalAgent.answer(userMessage);
        };
    }

    private Intent classify(String userMessage) {
        String label = chatClient.prompt()
                .system("""
                        Classify the user message into exactly one label:
                        BILLING, TECHNICAL, or GENERAL.
                        Reply with the label only.
                        """)
                .user(userMessage)
                .call()
                .content()
                .trim()
                .toUpperCase();

        try {
            return Intent.valueOf(label);
        } catch (IllegalArgumentException ex) {
            return Intent.GENERAL; // safe fallback for unexpected output
        }
    }
}

When to use it

Use a router when you have distinct domains with different tools, data sources, or system prompts. Always keep a fallback route, because the model will occasionally return something you did not expect.

Pattern 2: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG)

The problem

A model knows what it learned during training. It does not know your internal documentation, last week's policy change, or your product catalog. Asking it to answer from memory produces confident but wrong answers.

The solution

RAG retrieves relevant documents at query time and includes them in the prompt. The model answers based on that context. Spring AI provides VectorStore abstractions and advisors that wire retrieval into the chat flow.

Java example 

@Configuration
class RagConfig {

    @Bean
    ChatClient ragChatClient(ChatClient.Builder builder, VectorStore vectorStore) {
        return builder
                .defaultAdvisors(QuestionAnswerAdvisor.builder(vectorStore)
                        .searchRequest(SearchRequest.builder()
                                .topK(4)
                                .similarityThreshold(0.7)
                                .build())
                        .build())
                .build();
    }
}

@Service
class PolicyAssistant {

    private final ChatClient ragChatClient;

    PolicyAssistant(ChatClient ragChatClient) {
        this.ragChatClient = ragChatClient;
    }

    String ask(String question) {
        return ragChatClient.prompt()
                .system("Answer only from the provided context. If the context does not contain the answer, say so.")
                .user(question)
                .call()
                .content();
    }
}

Ingestion is a separate step. You split documents into chunks, generate embeddings, and store them in the vector store, typically on application startup or in a scheduled job.

When to use it

Use RAG whenever correct answers depend on data the model does not have, or data that changes often. Keep chunks focused, store metadata such as source and date, and instruct the model to refuse when the context is insufficient.

Pattern 3: Chain of Thought

The problem

Some tasks, such as calculating a loan schedule, comparing options against several constraints, or diagnosing a multi-step failure, produce unreliable results when the model jumps straight to a final answer.

The solution

Chain of Thought asks the model to break the problem into intermediate steps before answering. You can make the reasoning explicit in the prompt, or structure it into separate calls where each step's output feeds the next. The second approach is more controllable and easier to test.

Java example 

@Service
class RiskAnalysisService {

    private final ChatClient chatClient;

    RiskAnalysisService(ChatClient chatClient) {
        this.chatClient = chatClient;
    }

    String assess(String transactionDetails) {
        // Step 1: extract the facts
        String facts = chatClient.prompt()
                .system("Extract the factual fields from the transaction as a short bulleted list. Do not interpret them.")
                .user(transactionDetails)
                .call()
                .content();

        // Step 2: reason over the facts, one step at a time
        String analysis = chatClient.prompt()
                .system("""
                        Given these facts, reason step by step:
                        1. List the signals that increase risk.
                        2. List the signals that decrease risk.
                        3. Weigh them and state a risk level: LOW, MEDIUM, or HIGH.
                        """)
                .user(facts)
                .call()
                .content();

        // Step 3: produce the final, concise verdict
        return chatClient.prompt()
                .system("Summarize the analysis as a one-paragraph recommendation for a human reviewer.")
                .user(analysis)
                .call()
                .content();
    }
}

When to use it

Use this pattern when the task has a clear sequence of sub-problems. Splitting steps also makes each stage observable: you can log intermediate outputs, write tests for each stage, and see exactly where a wrong answer started. Keep in mind that every step adds latency and cost, so do not split a simple task.

Pattern 4: Supervisor

The problem

Some goals need several different skills. Writing a technical report might require research, drafting, and editing. One prompt that tries to do all of them tends to do none of them well, and the context window fills up quickly.

The solution

A supervisor agent receives the goal, decides which specialized worker agents to call, collects their results, and synthesizes a final answer. Each worker has its own system prompt, tools, and narrow responsibility. The supervisor coordinates; it does not do the work itself.

Java example 

@Service
class ReportSupervisor {

    private final ChatClient chatClient;

    ReportSupervisor(ChatClient chatClient) {
        this.chatClient = chatClient;
    }

    String produceReport(String topic) {
        // Worker 1: research
        String research = worker("""
                You are a research analyst. Return key facts, numbers, and sources as bullet points.
                """, topic);

        // Worker 2: drafting
        String draft = worker("""
                You are a technical writer. Turn the provided research into a structured draft
                with an introduction, three sections, and a conclusion.
                """, research);

        // Worker 3: editing
        String edited = worker("""
                You are an editor. Improve clarity and remove repetition. Keep the structure.
                """, draft);

        // Supervisor: final check and synthesis
        return chatClient.prompt()
                .system("""
                        You are the supervisor. Review the report for completeness against the topic.
                        Return the final report. If something is missing, add a short note at the end.
                        """)
                .user("Topic: " + topic + "\n\nReport:\n" + edited)
                .call()
                .content();
    }

    private String worker(String systemPrompt, String input) {
        return chatClient.prompt()
                .system(systemPrompt)
                .user(input)
                .call()
                .content();
    }
}

In a larger system, each worker would be its own Spring bean with its own ChatClient, tools, and memory. The supervisor can also decide dynamically which workers to call, rather than following a fixed sequence.

When to use it

Use a supervisor when the work naturally splits into roles and the sequence or selection of roles depends on the input. Keep the number of workers small at first. Every additional worker adds coordination cost and new failure modes.

Pattern 5: Guardrails & Validation

The problem

Model output is probabilistic. It can contain personal data it should not reveal, invented facts, unsafe instructions, or a format your code cannot parse. Trusting it directly in a business workflow is a risk.

The solution

Guardrails sit around the model. Input guardrails screen what goes in. Output guardrails verify what comes out. Validation can be deterministic, such as regular expressions and schema checks, or model-based, where a second model call judges the answer against a policy.

Java example 

@Service
class GuardedAssistant {

    private static final Pattern EMAIL = Pattern.compile("[\\w.+-]+@[\\w-]+\\.[\\w.]+");

    private final ChatClient chatClient;

    GuardedAssistant(ChatClient chatClient) {
        this.chatClient = chatClient;
    }

    String answer(String userMessage) {
        if (containsPersonalData(userMessage)) {
            return "Please do not share personal contact details in this chat.";
        }

        String draft = chatClient.prompt()
                .system("You are a customer support assistant. Answer briefly and politely.")
                .user(userMessage)
                .call()
                .content();

        // Deterministic check: never return personal data in the output
        if (containsPersonalData(draft)) {
            return "I cannot share that information.";
        }

        // Model-based check: a second call judges the policy compliance
        String verdict = chatClient.prompt()
                .system("""
                        Check the answer against these rules: no promises of refunds,
                        no legal or medical advice, no invented order numbers.
                        Reply with PASS or FAIL only.
                        """)
                .user(draft)
                .call()
                .content()
                .trim();

        return "PASS".equalsIgnoreCase(verdict)
                ? draft
                : "Let me connect you with a human agent who can help with this request.";
    }

    private boolean containsPersonalData(String text) {
        return EMAIL.matcher(text).find();
    }
}

For structured output, Spring AI can map the response to a Java record using .entity(...). Combined with bean validation, that turns a free-text answer into a typed object you can check before using it.

When to use it

Apply guardrails to every agent that talks to users or triggers actions. Start with deterministic checks because they are cheap, predictable, and easy to test. Add model-based checks where rules are semantic, and remember that the judging model can also make mistakes, so log its verdicts.

Combining the Patterns

These patterns work well together. A production flow might look like this:

  1. A guardrail screens the incoming message.
  2. A router classifies the intent.
  3. A RAG step retrieves policy or product documents for the selected domain.
  4. A supervisor coordinates workers when the task needs several skills.
  5. Chain of thought structures any multi-step reasoning inside a worker.
  6. A final guardrail validates the answer before it reaches the user.

Start with the smallest combination that solves your problem. A router and RAG cover many real assistants. Add supervisor and chain-of-thought steps only when a single agent cannot handle the task reliably.

Best Practices

  • Keep prompts in version control. Treat them as code, and review changes the same way.
  • Test each pattern in isolation. Mock the ChatClient for routing logic and use a fixed set of documents for RAG evaluation.
  • Log intermediate outputs. Routing decisions, retrieved chunks, and validation verdicts are the fastest way to debug an agent.
  • Set timeouts and limits. A supervisor that loops without a stop condition will drain your budget.
  • Prefer narrow agents. A worker with one clear job is easier to evaluate than a general-purpose one.
  • Measure quality. Build a small evaluation set of real questions and expected outcomes before tuning prompts.

What Comes Next

This article introduced the five patterns at a high level. In the next posts, I will explain each Spring AI agentic pattern in depth, one at a time, with complete Spring Boot projects, test strategies, and the trade-offs I have seen in real systems. If you are building agents in Java, follow along and tell me which pattern you want to see first.

Key Takeaways

  • Agentic systems need architecture, not just prompts.
  • Router sends each request to the right specialist.
  • RAG grounds answers in your own data.
  • Chain of Thought makes multi-step reasoning explicit and testable.
  • Supervisor coordinates specialized workers.
  • Guardrails & Validation keep outputs safe, accurate, and compliant.

Start small, measure everything, and add complexity only when the simpler pattern fails.

title: Tirei meus arquivos da nuvem e escrevi um navegador de arquivos em um único binário
description:
Sou o autor do projeto, então leiam como relato de construção, não como review independente.

O gargalo não era o armazenamento, era a pré-visualização

Meu escritório é pequeno: um NAS, uma máquina com os arquivos de trabalho e, várias vezes por dia, o mesmo pedido — "me manda a versão mais recente?". O problema nunca foi onde guardar os arquivos. Era ver antes de baixar. Ninguém quer baixar 400 MB só pra descobrir que pegou o arquivo errado.

O que saiu no fim é um binário em Go. Sem Docker, sem banco, sem PHP, sem cron.

./banyan -headless

Ele imprime um endereço; você abre no navegador de qualquer aparelho da mesma rede. A instalação acaba aí. Há clientes nativos para Windows, macOS, Linux, FreeBSD e Android, e o resto entra pelo navegador.

O que muda no dia a dia

  • Pré-visualização de 100+ formatos no servidor: Office, PDF, DWG, vídeo, imagem, arquivo compactado, código-fonte, fonte tipográfica. O arquivo é transmitido, não baixado.
  • Links de compartilhamento que o destinatário abre sem criar conta, com validade e contador de acessos.
  • Editar na pré-visualização grava direto no caminho original. Adeus, final_v2_final(2).psd.
  • Exportar para PDF com marca d'água, assinatura e anotação no mesmo lugar onde o arquivo já está.
  • Criptografia AES-256-GCM por diretório, sem conta, sem telemetria, funcionando offline na rede local.

O que ele não é (e por que vale dizer)

  • Não é cliente de sincronização. Sem resolução de conflito, sem espelhamento. É um navegador com pré-visualização, não um Dropbox.
  • Não tem versão hospedada. É self-hosted: TLS, domínio e proxy reverso ficam por sua conta.
  • O binário tem ~65 MB porque leva embutido todo o pipeline de pré-visualização.
  • A interface tem dez idiomas, mas a tradução foi gerada automaticamente a partir do chinês; o português tem trechos estranhos e eu estou corrigindo à mão.

Por que um único binário

A alternativa habitual é montar Nextcloud ou parecido, ou seja: Docker Compose, banco de dados, atualizações, PHP, painel de administração cheio de avisos. Para "quero ver meus arquivos do notebook no outro quarto", isso é aparelhagem demais. Um binário que você copia, roda e esquece é mais honesto para esse caso.

O preço dessa escolha: sem ecossistema de apps, sem móvel-first sincronizado, e se você quer colaboração multiusuário de verdade, este não é seu produto.

Testa e me conta o que quebra

Página do projeto, com downloads para as seis plataformas e documentação em dez idiomas: https://banyan.ikootoo.com/?utm_source=devto&utm_medium=post&utm_campaign=banyan_pt

Código-fonte: https://github.com/nbmany-web/banyan

Se você resolveu o "baixar pra saber o que é" de outro jeito, quero saber como.

title: When someone leaves, their API keys stay: how to offboard the access people create
description:
Most offboarding checklists stop at the same point: disable the login, collect the laptop, remove the person from the group chat. That handles the person. It doesn't handle what the person built.

Over a year or two, an engineer, analyst or ops lead creates access that isn't tied to their own sign-in. A service account for a nightly job. An API key pasted into a reporting script. An OAuth grant that lets a SaaS tool read the shared drive. And now, an AI agent connected to their mailbox or the ticketing system. Some of this breaks loudly when they leave. Most of it keeps running with nobody watching.

The quiet part is the risk. Verizon's 2025 Data Breach Investigations Report says credential abuse is still the most common way attackers get in, and that the median time to remediate leaked secrets found in a GitHub repository was 94 days. A key with no owner is a key nobody rotates.

This is the order I'd work in.

1. Start the list during the notice period

In the first week of notice, ask the person leaving for a written list: every service account, API key, token, webhook, scheduled job and AI tool they set up or connected. They know more than any scan will find. Make it a handover task with a due date, not a favour.

2. Check their list against what your systems show

Memory misses things, so verify. Look in:

  • Your identity provider (Okta, Microsoft Entra, Google Workspace): app grants and OAuth consents made by that user.
  • Cloud consoles (AWS, Azure, GCP): access keys, roles and service principals they created or last used.
  • Code repositories and CI/CD: secrets stored under their name, deploy keys, personal access tokens used by pipelines.
  • SaaS admin panels: integrations they installed, especially anything with "read all files" or "send as user" permissions.
  • AI tools: any agent or assistant connected through their account to mail, files, CRM or chat.

Anything the systems show that isn't on their list goes to the top of the review.

3. Give every item a named owner

A person, not a team. "The data team" owns nothing at 2 a.m. when a job fails. The new owner should know what the item does and be able to say whether it still needs to exist.

4. Decide: keep, move or retire

  • Keep it if it's needed and already runs on its own identity with narrow permissions. Change the owner and move on.
  • Move it if it runs on the departing person's own credentials. Create a dedicated service identity, give it only the permissions the job actually uses, switch the job over and confirm the next run succeeds.
  • Retire it if nobody can explain what it's for. Disable it rather than delete it, and wait two weeks to see if anything complains.

5. Rotate the secrets they could see

They probably had access to more secrets than they created: shared vault folders, .env files, config for tools they administered. Rotate those too. It isn't about trust. Former employees' laptops and password managers get compromised like anyone else's.

6. Disable the login on time, delete the account last

Cut interactive access on the last day as normal. Hold off deleting the account until steps 3 to 5 are done, because in some platforms deleting a user also removes or breaks what they owned. Then watch the logs for a week for failed authentications tied to the old account. Each one is something you missed.

7. Give AI agents their own line

Agents are where this gets harder each month. An agent connected "as me" inherits everything that person could do, and it may keep its own saved connections outside your identity provider. IBM's Cost of a Data Breach Report 2025 found that 13% of organisations reported breaches of AI models or applications, and 97% of those said they lacked proper AI access controls. For each agent the person connected, revoke its tokens in the source app (not only inside the agent), and if the work still matters, rebuild it under a dedicated identity with an owner.

8. Make sure the list exists next time

The real win is never having to rebuild this from memory again. Three habits cover most of it:

  • Every new service account, key or agent gets an owner and an expiry date when it's created.
  • Quarterly access reviews include non-human identities, not only people.
  • The offboarding checklist has a "things you created" section that both the manager and IT sign off.

You can do all of this with admin consoles and a spreadsheet. It's slower, and it depends on someone remembering every time, so it's worth automating the discovery step once you've done it by hand a couple of times. Whatever you use, the steps above are what matter: an owner, a decision and a rotation for everything a departing person leaves behind.

Originally published on my Substack: https://nurankhan.substack.com/p/when-someone-leaves-their-api-keys

title: Making a Trino lake as fast as a SQL database
description:
Photo by Joshua Kettle on Unsplash

Moving analytics data from a SQL database to a lake usually comes with a quiet assumption: you will pay for cheap, unlimited storage with slower answers. I tested that assumption end to end, with an AI agent that answers business questions over synced SaaS data, and the result surprised me. With four fixes, full answers on the lake took the same time as on the database. The biggest fix had nothing to do with Trino's speed.

The setup, in one breath

The data is CRM and accounting records, copied by a managed ingestion service into Iceberg tables on Azure storage (ADLS). Iceberg is an open table format: plain files plus a small "description file" per table saying which files make up the table right now. A hosted Polaris catalog keeps the list of where each table's description lives. Trino is the query engine that reads all of it. The comparison point is the same data in Azure SQL.

The agent doesn't run one query per answer. It runs five to seven: it lists tables, reads column names, samples a few values, then asks the real question. That detail turned out to matter more than anything else.

Out of the box, the lake lost badly

A small question touching four tables took about 2 seconds in Trino, against about 0.1 seconds in the database. A big accounting question that combines 25 tables took about 30 seconds, against about 6.

I expected the time to be in reading data. It wasn't. Trino splits its own work into stages, and most of the time sat in "analysis", the step before any data is read.

The catalog was the bottleneck

Trino asks the catalog about every table, in every query, with no memory between queries. Each ask is a network call. Our catalog sat in one region and the engine in another, so each lookup cost about half a second. Twenty-five tables, twenty-five calls, about 13 seconds of waiting before the engine did anything useful.

Think of a delivery driver who phones head office for the address of every stop, every single day, even though the addresses never changed.

The fix was to give the driver a notebook. Trino supports an Iceberg catalog stored in a plain Postgres database (the JDBC catalog in Trino's docs). "Registering" a table there is just writing one row: its name and the location of its current description file, which I read from the table's own $metadata_log_entries. No data is copied. Nothing is written to the lake.


Before and after: the engine stops phoning the catalog and reads a local address book instead.

The result was the clearest number of the whole project. Analysis on the 25-table question went from about 13 seconds to 0.8. On the small question it went from 1.5 seconds to 0.17. Answers were byte-for-byte identical.

The price is a job you now own. Every time new data lands, the notebook has to be updated with each table's new description file, or the engine reads yesterday's data.

What didn't help

A newer Trino setting, snapshot-loading-mode=REFS, asks the catalog for a shorter answer that leaves out old table history. Someone on another catalog measured a 6x faster lookup with it, but their tables had about 9,000 old versions. Mine had one. I tried it anyway: no gain. The time was the trip, not the size of the reply.

Trino's metadata cache was already on, and it caches description files, not the catalog lookup. Rewriting or compacting the source tables was off the table too, since the ingestion service owns them and would undo it on the next sync.

Precompute the heavy questions

Removing the lookups took the big accounting question from about 30 seconds to about 17. What remained was real work: about 8 seconds planning a query with hundreds of stages, and about 8 seconds running it.

So I stopped doing that work at question time. The accounting "model" (the recipe that turns 25 raw tables into one clean ledger) runs once after each sync and saves its result as a single table. A question like "income in March" then reads one small table instead of rebuilding the ledger.


The heavy combining happens once per data refresh, not once per question.

I tried the ready table in three places: in Trino's memory, in Postgres, and as an Iceberg table on the lake itself. All three answered in about 0.15 to 0.3 seconds, against about 6 seconds in the SQL database. Writing it to the lake took about 30 seconds. Writing it into Postgres took about 90, because rows go in one by one.

That last point matters if you worried, like I did, that precompute means "we're back to a database." The data stays in the lake. Postgres only holds pointers, and you can rebuild it from the catalog at any time.

Distance, twice

The engine first ran on a VM on the US west coast, with the data on the east coast. A single round trip across the country took 65 to 100 milliseconds, and each catalog call needed several. Moving the engine east cut a call from 0.21 to 0.40 seconds down to 0.06 to 0.16, and small questions got about twice as fast again, landing around half a second.

Then I made the mistake that taught me the most. I timed full answers with the app on my laptop.

Full answers on the lake averaged 53.7 seconds. On the SQL database, 44.3. Same correct answers, nine seconds worse. The engine was fine; the app was talking to it five to seven times per answer, across the internet, several round trips each time.

When I ran the app on the same machine as the engine, the lake averaged 42.5 seconds. Inside the noise of the database's 44.3.


Same engine, same questions. Only the app's location changed.

About 40 seconds of every answer is the AI thinking, on either system, and it swings by five seconds from run to run. Per-query benchmarks hid that. If you are timing a database for an agent, time the whole answer, and put the app where it will live in production.

The cache that worked and didn't matter

An answer cache in the app, keyed on the exact SQL text, did what it promised. A repeated 18-second question came back in under a millisecond, and by the third question in a session only the real query reached the engine.

It saved about a second per answer. I've seen caching cut query latency by 60% on a high-traffic payment system before, where queries were the whole cost. Here the AI is the whole cost, so the same trick barely registered. Worth keeping, not worth leading with.

Two other engines

StarRocks read the same catalog and the same storage with the VM's managed identity (the machine's own Azure login, no passwords) on the first try (its Azure auth docs cover it), and gave identical answers. With none of the fixes above, small questions took 0.4 to 0.7 seconds and the big accounting questions 7 to 10. That is faster than plain Trino out of the box, likely because it keeps table information between queries and shares repeated query blocks instead of planning each copy. The catch is a different SQL dialect, so every query the agent writes would need porting.

Apache Doris connected to the catalog and listed every table, then failed on the first read. Its Azure storage docs list account-key access only, and I wasn't going to hand a query engine a key to the whole storage account. If you use managed identities on Azure, check this before anything else.

What I'd tell you before you start

Profile the step before the data. On a lake, the slow part is often looking things up, not reading. Keep a local copy of the catalog's answers, precompute the few heavy models, and put the engine and the app next to the data. Then time whole answers, not queries.

The lake was never slow. It was asking for directions.

title: Saqué mis archivos de la nube y programé un navegador de archivos en un solo binario
description:
Soy el autor del proyecto, así que lean esto como un relato de construcción, no como una reseña independiente.

El cuello de botella no era el almacenamiento, era la vista previa

Tengo un estudio de diseño pequeño: un NAS, una máquina con los archivos de trabajo y, varias veces al día, el mismo pedido: "mándame la versión más reciente". El problema nunca fue dónde guardar los archivos. Era verlos antes de descargarlos. Nadie quiere bajar 400 MB para descubrir que eligió el archivo equivocado.

Lo que salió al final es un binario escrito en Go. Sin Docker, sin base de datos, sin PHP, sin cron.

./banyan -headless

Imprime una dirección; la abres en el navegador de cualquier dispositivo de la misma red. La instalación termina ahí. Hay clientes nativos para Windows, macOS, Linux, FreeBSD y Android, y todo lo demás entra por el navegador.

Qué cambia en el día a día

  • Vista previa de más de 100 formatos en el servidor: Office, PDF, DWG, vídeo, imágenes, archivos comprimidos, código fuente, tipografías. El archivo se transmite, no se descarga.
  • Enlaces para compartir que el destinatario abre sin crear cuenta, con caducidad y contador de visitas.
  • Editar desde la vista previa guarda directamente en la ruta original. Se acabó el final_v2_final(2).psd.
  • Exportar a PDF con marca de agua, firma y anotaciones en el mismo sitio donde ya está el archivo.
  • Cifrado AES-256-GCM por directorio, sin cuenta, sin telemetría, y funciona sin conexión si estás en la red local.

Lo que no es (y por qué importa decirlo)

  • No es un cliente de sincronización. No hay resolución de conflictos ni replicación. Es un explorador con vista previa, no un Dropbox.
  • No hay versión alojada. Es autoalojado: TLS, dominio y proxy inverso corren de tu cuenta.
  • El binario pesa ~65 MB porque lleva dentro todo el pipeline de vista previa.
  • La interfaz está en diez idiomas, pero la traducción se generó automáticamente a partir del chino; en español hay frases que suenan raras y lo estoy corrigiendo a mano.

Por qué un solo binario

La alternativa habitual para este problema es montar Nextcloud o similar, o sea: Docker Compose, base de datos, actualizaciones, PHP, un panel de administración lleno de avisos. Para "quiero ver mis archivos desde mi portátil en otra habitación", eso es demasiado aparato. Un binario que se copia, se ejecuta y se olvida es más honesto para ese caso de uso.

El precio de esa decisión: no hay ecosistema de apps, no hay móvil-first sincronizado, y si quieres colaboración multiusuario real, este no es tu producto.

Pruébalo y dime qué rompe

Página del proyecto, con descargas para las seis plataformas y la documentación en diez idiomas: https://banyan.ikootoo.com/?utm_source=devto&utm_medium=post&utm_campaign=banyan_es

Código fuente: https://github.com/nbmany-web/banyan

Si resolvieron el "descargar para saber qué es" de otra forma, me interesa saber cómo.

title: PSA: check auto_stop_mins on your SQL warehouses if you deploy with bundles
description:
If you create SQL warehouses through Declarative Automation Bundles and leave out auto_stop_mins, the default isn’t what you get in the UI. Bundles default to 10 minutes for Serverless and 120 for Pro/Classic. The UI defaults to 10 for Serverless and 45 for Pro/Classic.

Apparently someone deployed a Serverless warehouse with a bundle, didn’t set the field, and got 120 minutes instead of the 10 the docs list. That hurts if you have a bunch of short scheduled alerts, because each one wakes the warehouse up and then it just sits there until auto-stop kicks in.

A few other things from the same writeup:

The Serverless UI won’t go below 5 min auto-stop, but the API, CLI and bundles accept 1 (databricks warehouses edit --auto-stop-mins 1). Pro and Classic bottom out at 10.

A single slow or spilling query points to warehouse size. Queries waiting at capacity point to max clusters. Peak queued queries above zero doesn’t tell you which one on its own.

Power BI DirectQuery can send a query on every dashboard interaction. If the business only needs fresh data every few minutes, Import or Hybrid mode cuts a lot of that.

DBU rate alone is misleading. In one AWS US East example, Serverless is about $0.70/DBU, Pro $0.55 and Classic $0.22, but Pro and Classic bill infrastructure on top.

Is anyone running a 1-minute auto-stop on serverless for scheduled jobs? Do the cold starts bother you?

Full article : https://select.dev/blog/serverless-sql-warehouse-cost-optimization

title: 4 Repetitive Frontend & API Tasks You Can Automate in Seconds Without Installing Anything
description:
A lot of frontend engineering time gets eaten up by small, repetitive glue tasks: mocking a loading spinner without pulling in a 50KB icon library, translating an updated GraphQL schema into TypeScript interfaces, or checking character limits for UI copy.

Instead of installing single-use npm packages or spinning up local scripts for every micro-task, keeping a lightweight set of browser-native utilities in your bookmarks can shave minutes off every PR.

Here are four everyday workflows that run cleanly right inside your browser tab:

1. Shipping Zero-Dependency Pure CSS Loaders

Adding a spin animation shouldn't require importing an external GIF or a heavy UI component library. Pure CSS keyframe animations render on the GPU, scale cleanly at any DPI, and add almost zero bundle weight.

  • Workflow: Visually tweak spinner geometry, animation duration, and brand hex colors, then copy the self-contained HTML + CSS snippet directly into your component.
  • Tool: Pure CSS Loader & Spinner Generator

2. Turning GraphQL SDL Into Strict TypeScript Types

When backend teams update a GraphQL schema, manually rewriting interface and type definitions is tedious and error-prone—especially around nullable fields, arrays, and nested input types.

  • Workflow: Paste the raw GraphQL SDL block to immediately generate clean TypeScript definitions without uploading internal schemas to a remote server.
  • Tool: GraphQL Schema to TypeScript Generator (supports standard GraphQL SDL)

3. Generating Realistic Placeholder Copy & HTML Lists

Testing responsive grid layouts or card truncation with a single repeated sentence hides real-world overflow bugs. Generating variable-length paragraphs, exact word counts, or structured HTML bullet lists makes layout stress-testing much faster.

  • Workflow: Pick exact paragraph/word counts or toggle HTML tags, then copy in one click.
  • Tool: Lorem Ipsum & Dummy Text Generator

4. Instant Character, Word & Reading-Time Checks for UI Microcopy

Whether you're writing meta descriptions, localization strings, or documentation intros, keeping copy within strict character budgets prevents awkward ellipsis truncation in production.

  • Workflow: Paste draft text to check real-time character counts (with and without spaces), word counts, and estimated reading time locally.
  • Tool: Online Word & Character Counter

Keep Your Toolbox Light

All of these live inside MiniToolDesk, a free collection of client-side developer utilities and calculators built to load fast and run 100% locally in your browser.
