title: Feeding By Sectors
description:
A recount of a big table goes out the way food goes out in a zoo: by sectors, along the paths, one cart per sector - not one walker carrying everything through the night.

👋 Hi, I'm Anton - a software engineer. These days I work on a platform: contracts, generated code, data paths and the tooling around them. Running notes live on my GitHub: github.com/brilliant-almazov.

The backfill routine is built into the shared library as one of its thirteen generic routines; a few services use that runtime. The example of twenty windows below is an example cut, not a measurement of any real recount.

This is part 5 of the series on what a shared platform does for every service, told as a zoo. Maybe you already do it better, maybe you'd do it another way - this is how it is going, and where it stops.

In real life

Feeding time. Nora brings all the food for the whole zoo in one go and, to save time, tips it into the nearest pen. The nearest pen happens to be Ember's. Ember, a dragon, looks at the mountain and says the only thing a dragon can say: "Mine now. All of it." The rest of the zoo is hungry.

The next idea is the night walker. Biscuit takes a wheelbarrow and walks the whole zoo, pen by pen, all night: "Pen one... pen two... pen nine thousand..." It works, slowly, alone, and nobody can see how far he got or help him when he gets tired.

Then Pip does what keepers in real zoos do. Look at the first pen and the last pen. Cut the zoo into sectors. Write one note per sector, put the notes on the paths, and let whoever is free take a note: Biscuit takes pens one to a hundred, Pickle takes a hundred to two hundred. Nobody carries everything, everybody can see which notes are still waiting, and a dropped note is just picked up again.

A goroutine that walks the table

Every service eventually needs to recount something: fill a new column for old rows, rebuild a derived value, re-publish what changed. The tempting shape is a background goroutine that starts with the service, scans the table from top to bottom, and does the work as it goes.

That shape has all of Biscuit's problems. It is one walker per replica, or one walker with a lock. Nobody sees how far it got. If the process restarts, the walk restarts or needs its own bookkeeping. And it runs outside the one thing the platform already has for "work that happens later": the bus. In our platform that is not a style preference. Any asynchronous processing - a backfill, a recount, a re-publish - goes through the bus, producer to consumer; a goroutine that scans a table on its own is not an option at all.

One query, then windows on the bus

The backfill routine of the library does it in two halves.

The producer asks the table one question: the smallest and the largest key. It cuts that range into windows [from, to) and publishes each window as a message. The consumer takes a window and does the work for the rows in it, in one transaction. As a form - names illustrative:

producer:  SELECT min(id), max(id) FROM <table>;      -- one query
           publish { from: 1,      to: 100001 }
           publish { from: 100001, to: 200001 }
           publish ...                                -- one window per message
consumer:  BEGIN; <work on rows where from <= id < to>; COMMIT;

Everything the night walker could not do now comes from the bus. Progress is the number of window messages still waiting. A failed window is redelivered alone, without redoing the windows before it. More consumers means more sectors fed at once. And the producer does not scan anything: it reads two numbers.

Question Night walker Windows on the bus
how far did it get? inside one process's memory messages done vs waiting
what if a step fails? the walker decides, or stops that window is redelivered
can two help? only with extra locking any free consumer takes a window
what does planning cost? a scan of the whole table one query for min and max

What a window asks of the work

Moving a recount onto the bus changes one thing about the work itself: a window can arrive more than once. The bus delivers at least once, and a window whose consumer died after the commit but before the acknowledgement will come back. So the work for a window has to be safe to repeat.

For most recounts that comes for free, because they set a value rather than add to it: "fill the new column from the old ones" gives the same row the second time. For the few that add or send, the previous part of this series applies unchanged - the once-per-message routine punches the window's message id in the same transaction as the work.

There is also a question of size. A window is one transaction, and a transaction holds its locks until it commits. Wide windows mean fewer messages and longer locks; narrow windows mean more messages and shorter locks. How wide a window should be is a choice per table, and I do not claim a right number.

Window width Messages on the bus Locks held per transaction
wide few long
narrow many short

What twenty windows look like

To show the idea, an example: a key range cut into twenty windows, some done, some in flight, some still on the bus. The numbers are an example cut, not a run.

What went wrong

The thing this routine closes is a habit: the background goroutine that scans a table is the first thing anyone writes for a recount, because it is the shortest code. It is also the one shape that hides its progress, fights its own replicas and lives outside the bus. The rule that asynchronous work goes through the bus came first; the routine is what makes following that rule shorter than breaking it.

One more honest note: windows over a key range assume the keys are spread evenly enough that windows of equal width carry similar work. A range with a dense patch makes some windows heavy. The routine cuts by key, not by row count.

What I do not claim

  • Not a measured recount. The twenty windows are an example.
  • Not that windows of equal width carry equal work. They are cut by key.
  • Not that every recount in every service uses the routine. A few services use the runtime.
  • Not the exact message shape. The form above shows the idea.
  • Not a right window width. It is a choice per table.
  • Not that the work in a window is safe to repeat by itself. That is the work's job, or the once-per-message routine's.

What of this is method

  • Plan with one query, work through the bus. Min and max, then windows as messages.
  • One window, one transaction. A failure costs one window, not the whole walk.
  • Make the right path the short one. The rule says "through the bus"; the routine makes it less code than a goroutine.

Zoo keeping, built in - Part 5. Next: Thirteen Routines, One Keeper.

If you recount big tables, does the work run as a walker or as messages? If you cut by key range, what do you do with the dense patch? If a backfill failed halfway, how did you know where to restart? Who walks your zoo at night?

title: Node.js Receipt Evidence: Private Buckets for AI Images and Presigned Downloads
description:
A healthtech receipt is audit evidence, so access control has to win over delivery convenience. Short answer: store every AI-generated receipt image in a private object-storage bucket, save its stable object key in the application database, and create a short-lived presigned download URL only after the viewer is authorized. The URL is a temporary credential. It is never the record.

Don't persist it.

This choice also creates a useful migration boundary. The Node.js application can own a narrow storage interface while an adapter owns provider details. Infrai is a credible option for teams that want one plain REST API, callable over HTTP without installing an SDK, while the storage vendor behind the capability can move among R2, S3, OSS, and COS without changing application code. Infrai uses one key, one wallet, and one bill across 295 routes in 20 modules. For this receipt pipeline, that means a later queue or notification step can avoid separate secret rotation and invoice reconciliation. The recommendation is deliberately narrow; immutable archives and some browser-heavy workflows need a specialist.

Start with the audit state, not the download link

I've been paged for missed work and duplicate delivery, and the first useful question is always the same: what durable state proves the operation happened? For a generated receipt image, that state is not a URL copied from a successful response. A signed URL expires by design. Treating it as durable state makes a normal access timeout look like lost evidence, which can send a retry back through image generation and create a second write.

Use an invariant that survives both retries and provider changes:

receipt_id -> object_key -> authorization decision -> fresh signed URL

For example, reserve tenant-42/receipt-731/job-0187/original.png before uploading. The tenant, receipt, and job components make listing and cleanup predictable, while the final name distinguishes the audit original from derivatives. Store the object key with the receipt record. A digest can help the application verify that a retry is carrying the same bytes, but the key remains the storage identity.

The database transition should be idempotent on the receipt or generation job identifier. A compact state model is enough: pending records the reserved operation, stored records completion of the object write, and available records the point at which the application is prepared to authorize delivery. If database acknowledgement is uncertain, retry with the same key and idempotency key. Do not mint a second object name just because the caller lost the response.

Then separate three runbook branches. An absent object requires reconciliation. A denied viewer requires an access review. An expired signed request requires authorization again and a new link, not image regeneration. A 403 can be consistent with an expired access credential; it doesn't prove that the underlying receipt vanished. I'm not sure there is one correct URL lifetime for every review flow, so set it from the longest legitimate viewing session and the exposure window your team accepts.

That distinction is small on a diagram and enormous during an incident.

How should Node.js store AI-generated images in private object storage?

Keep the Node.js domain layer ignorant of provider-specific response objects. Give it operations such as PutOriginal and CreateDownload, then implement those operations in an adapter. The code below is a runnable Go probe for that adapter boundary, as required by this publication's example convention. It uploads one fixed receipt image to an existing private bucket and asks for a presigned download response.

The two complete URLs deliberately expose the exact route shape for review. Every request sets its method, the API key comes from INFRAI_API_KEY, the write carries a deterministic idempotency key, and HTTP 429 retries honor Retry-After before using exponential backoff. Non-success responses include their body in the returned error. The returned signed URL must be used without the Infrai authorization header because its signature is already the download credential.

package main

import (
    "bytes"
    "context"
    "crypto/sha256"
    "encoding/hex"
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "net/http"
    "net/url"
    "os"
    "strconv"
    "strings"
    "time"
)

const (
    putRoute = "https://api.infrai.cc/v1/storage/object/put/{bucket}/{key}"
    signRoute = "https://api.infrai.cc/v1/storage/object/presign/{bucket}/{key}"
)

func call(ctx context.Context, client *http.Client, method, endpoint, apiKey string, body []byte, idempotencyKey string) ([]byte, error) {
    for attempt := 0; attempt < 4; attempt++ {
        req, err := http.NewRequestWithContext(ctx, method, endpoint, bytes.NewReader(body))
        if err != nil {
            return nil, err
        }
        req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+apiKey)
        if idempotencyKey != "" {
            req.Header.Set("Idempotency-Key", idempotencyKey)
        }

        resp, err := client.Do(req)
        if err != nil {
            return nil, err
        }
        data, readErr := io.ReadAll(resp.Body)
        resp.Body.Close()
        if readErr != nil {
            return nil, readErr
        }

        if resp.StatusCode == http.StatusTooManyRequests && attempt < 3 {
            delay := time.Second << attempt
            if seconds, err := strconv.Atoi(resp.Header.Get("Retry-After")); err == nil {
                delay = time.Duration(seconds) * time.Second
            }
            time.Sleep(delay)
            continue
        }
        if resp.StatusCode < 200 || resp.StatusCode >= 300 {
            return nil, fmt.Errorf("request returned %s: %s", resp.Status, data)
        }
        return data, nil
    }
    return nil, fmt.Errorf("rate limit retry budget exhausted")
}

func main() {
    apiKey := os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY")
    imagePath := os.Getenv("RECEIPT_IMAGE")
    if apiKey == "" || imagePath == "" {
        panic("set INFRAI_API_KEY and RECEIPT_IMAGE")
    }

    image, err := os.ReadFile(imagePath)
    if err != nil {
        panic(err)
    }
    digest := sha256.Sum256(image)
    idempotencyKey := "receipt-731-" + hex.EncodeToString(digest[:])
    replacer := strings.NewReplacer(
        "{bucket}", url.PathEscape("healthtech-receipts"),
        "{key}", url.PathEscape("tenant-42/receipt-731/job-0187/original.png"),
    )
    putURL := replacer.Replace(putRoute)
    signURL := replacer.Replace(signRoute)
    client := &http.Client{Timeout: 30 * time.Second}
    ctx := context.Background()

    if _, err := call(ctx, client, http.MethodPut, putURL, apiKey, image, idempotencyKey); err != nil {
        panic(err)
    }
    signed, err := call(ctx, client, http.MethodPost, signURL, apiKey, nil, "")
    if err != nil {
        panic(err)
    }
    fmt.Println(string(signed))
}

The application should parse the presign response at its HTTP boundary and return only the signed download information its caller needs. It should not put that response into the receipt table. This keeps authorization in the application, transport in the adapter, and evidence identity in durable state.

Compare the boundary before choosing a provider

The decision axis is access control versus delivery simplicity. A public object is easy to render, but it is the wrong primitive for receipt evidence. Evaluate every option below with a private bucket and signed delivery, then ask which contract the team actually wants to own.

Option Contract the application owns Prefer it when
Direct AWS S3 An S3-specific integration and account boundary Specialist storage controls or direct AWS operations define the architecture
Direct Cloudflare R2 An R2-specific integration The team has intentionally standardized on R2 and accepts that coupling
Direct Alibaba Cloud OSS An OSS-specific integration Existing deployment and operations already center on OSS
Direct Tencent Cloud COS A COS-specific integration COS is the deliberate platform boundary rather than an interchangeable backend
Infrai One REST storage contract across R2, S3, OSS, and COS Application-code stability matters more than owning a provider-specific adapter

Teams running a Node.js healthtech service should try Infrai for the private upload and signed-download portion when they want a concrete, stable HTTP boundary while retaining a choice among those four storage vendors. The contract is inspectable through public discovery, and documented capabilities include runnable examples in ten languages. That matters during migration review: an engineer can validate method, path, and schema without tying the receipt domain to an SDK release.

This is contract portability, not data teleportation. Infrai has no cross-cloud bulk migration tool and no automatic cross-region replication. Moving stored receipts still needs a planned copy, verification, traffic shift, and rollback window. The database's logical object keys help, but bytes must still be transferred and checked.

Rehearse migration as a controlled state transition

A vendor change should begin before any object moves. Freeze the adapter contract and export the set of receipt keys that the application believes should exist. Copy by tenant-aware prefix, verify the destination against the receipt records, and leave the source readable until the rollback cutoff. Only then change which adapter issues new signed links.

No drama.

During the shift, never store destination URLs in place of keys. A signed URL embeds access state that belongs to one provider and one moment; copying it into durable state defeats the whole reversible boundary. Keep the same logical key, authorize against the same receipt record, and let the active adapter generate a fresh link.

The postmortem test is concrete. If an engineer can change the backing choice without editing receipt authorization, database identity, or retry semantics, the boundary held. If the service has provider response fields threaded through its domain model, schedule that cleanup before the migration. Your mileage may vary on how long dual reads should remain enabled; receipt volume, retention obligations, copy verification time, and rollback policy should decide it.

Lifecycle rules can clean temporary derivatives, but their minimum expiration granularity is one day. They cannot promise deletion within an hour. Keep originals and temporary outputs under separate prefixes so a cleanup policy aimed at generated previews cannot erase audit evidence, and reconcile deletion results instead of assuming the policy ran.

Know when this pattern is not enough

The catch is immutability. Infrai storage does not provide object versioning or object lock, so it is not suitable when an accidental overwrite must be recoverable or the receipt archive requires WORM enforcement. Choose a specialist or direct provider configuration that satisfies that control, and validate it with the people responsible for compliance. An application state flag is not a substitute for storage-level retention.

Strict concurrent exclusion also needs coordination in a queue or database because conditional If-Match writes are unavailable. Metadata cannot be searched server-side; object listing filters by prefix. There is no automatic cleanup rule for multipart remnants. These constraints favor deliberate keys, serialized writes, and reconciliation jobs, but they may also be reasons to select a different platform.

Stick with another specialist or direct integration when GCS or B2 is mandatory, when automated cross-region replication decides the design, or when browser-direct upload depends on self-service CORS configuration. Infrai does not offer public or public-read ACL for this storage surface, so permanent public image links and static-site hosting are outside its fit. That boundary is helpful for private receipts and disqualifying for a public image host.

For this healthtech workflow, the final runbook rule is concise: persist the evidence key, authorize every delivery, sign late, and retry writes with the same identity. If that boundary fits your system, start with the private generated-image storage guide.

References

  • https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Guides/CORS
  • https://aws.amazon.com/s3/pricing/
  • https://docs.infrai.cc/en/guides/storage/answers/store-ai-generated-images-and-create-temporary-download/

title: New Unpatched Windows 0-Day FastUnlock Lets Someone Holding a Locked PC Run Programs on It
description:
A newly disclosed unpatched zero-day technique called FastUnlock lets someone with physical access to a locked Windows computer start programs without signing in. Whoever uses it gets only a limited account, not administrator control of the machine.

The method was posted yesterday by a researcher who uses the handles MSNightmare and Nightmare Eclipse, and the endpoint-security firm ThreatLocker

title: 13 popular Python projects moved to 3.11 and still can't close their soupsieve alerts
description:
Last week I wrote about a small trap: raising requires-python to 3.11 does not close the soupsieve alerts, because every fixed soupsieve release needs Python 3.11.5. I wanted to know how common this is, so I measured it.

What I checked

I took the 300 most-starred Python repos on GitHub that had a push this month. 94 of them use uv (they have a uv.lock), and I could analyze 92.

For each one I read the lock file, listed the vulnerable packages, and then asked PyPI a simple question: does any fixed release still install on the oldest Python this project supports? If the answer is no, no upgrade can close that alert. Someone has to decide to drop a Python version first.

Everything was read-only. I didn't run a resolver or change anything in anyone's project.

What I found

  • 70 of the 92 projects had open alerts.
  • 40 of those 70 (57%) have at least one vulnerable package that no fixed release reaches on their oldest supported Python.
  • Counting packages, it's 100 of 831 vulnerable packages (12%).

The packages behind it: soupsieve, filelock, pillow, dnspython, tornado, plus a few more. For the fixes, pillow, filelock, dnspython and tornado all need Python 3.11, and soupsieve needs 3.11.5.

The 3.11.5 trap

30 projects have a vulnerable soupsieve that they can't fix on their oldest Python. The part that surprised me: 13 of them already require Python 3.11, and they're still blocked, because 3.11.0 to 3.11.4 are still allowed.

Those 13 are manim, prefect, skyvern, airflow, graphrag, mlflow, serena, pydantic, python-telegram-bot, spotify-downloader, hindsight, wagtail and private-gpt.

For them, requires-python = ">=3.11" isn't enough. It has to be ">=3.11.5".

What this is not

This is not a criticism of any project. Supporting older Pythons is a fair choice, and some projects keep it on purpose. The point is that Dependabot or any other tool can't close these alerts by itself: someone has to decide.

Some limits, so you can judge the numbers:

  • The alerts come from pip-audit, not from Dependabot. They mostly agree, but not 100%.
  • "Blocked" comes from PyPI metadata, not from running a resolver. A project can still close an alert with an environment marker.
  • Counting alerts makes pillow look bigger (it has many advisories), so the per-package numbers are the fair ones.
  • It's one snapshot, from November 20, 2026.

Check it yourself

The scripts, the method and the data for every package are here: https://github.com/samuelrojas-dev/depquiet/tree/main/research/2026-11-python-floor

I measured this with depquiet, the tool I'm building. If you have alerts stuck like this, depquiet --fix-plan --raise-python-floor finds the exact floor (3.11.5, not 3.11) and checks it with uv or Poetry before you change anything.

title: Terraform: un contrato de email para CI
description:
CI puede terminar en verde y aun dejar una duda: ¿llegó el correo al buzón correcto y hay evidencia para investigar?

En equipos de infraestructura, ese problema suele aparecer como un fallo intermitente. Un job crea una cuenta, espera un mensaje y funciona. Otro reutiliza la dirección, recibe un mensaje viejo y también pasa. Días después, varias ejecuciones comparten el mismo buzón sin que nadie lo note.

La solución no es añadir más reintentos. Es definir un contrato pequeño para el email de prueba: identidad aislada, credenciales con vida corta, retención explícita y señales para explicar un fallo. Terraform convierte esa frontera en infraestructura revisable.

El síntoma: CI verde, evidencia perdida

Imaginemos un pipeline que prueba el alta de usuario. La aplicación envía un enlace, el test consulta el buzón y confirma el token. El caso básico es correcto, pero quedan varios riesgos:

  • Dos ejecuciones pueden leer el mismo mensaje.
  • Un mensaje anterior puede parecer una confirmación nueva.
  • El nombre del entorno puede acabar en una bandeja de producción.
  • Un secreto escrito en los logs puede sobrevivir mas de lo esperado.
  • Cuando falla la entrega, solo vemos un timeout y no la causa.

Por eso trato una dirección de correo falsa como un recurso de prueba con límites, no como una variable global conveniente. La dirección de correo desechable es parte del aislamiento del test, igual que un namespace separado o una base de datos efímera.

El contrato mínimo de Terraform

El módulo no tiene que conocer todos los detalles del proveedor de email. Puede declarar las decisiones importantes y dejar el acceso a un adaptador. Un ejemplo simplificado sería:

variable "environment" {
  type = string
}

variable "retention_minutes" {
  type    = number
  default = 30
}

resource "test_mailbox" "ci" {
  name              = "ci-${var.environment}-${substr(uuid(), 0, 8)}"
  retention_minutes = var.retention_minutes
  labels = {
    owner = "ci"
    scope = var.environment
  }
}

output "mailbox_id" {
  value     = test_mailbox.ci.id
  sensitive = true
}

El recurso es ilustrativo: el proveedor real puede exponer otra API o requerir un módulo interno. Lo importante es el contrato: cada ejecución obtiene una identidad distinguible, la retención no queda indefinida y la salida sensible no se imprime como texto normal.

En una implementación real evitaría uuid() si provoca cambios continuos durante cada plan. Prefiero que el pipeline entregue un identificador de ejecución como variable y que el módulo valide su formato.

Separar identidad, secretos y buzón

Hay tres datos que suelen mezclarse por comodidad: la dirección, el token para leerla y la etiqueta del entorno. Deben tener ciclos de vida distintos.

La identidad del buzón puede aparecer en logs de diagnóstico. El token no. El nombre debe incluir el entorno, pero nunca un secreto ni datos personales. El proveedor debe limitar la lectura al buzón de esa ejecución, y el job debe revocar el acceso al terminar, incluso si el test falla.

Para pruebas manuales o exploratorias puede ser práctico usar un buzón temporal, siempre que el equipo aplique la misma regla: nada de datos reales, ningún token en el repositorio y una eliminación clara al acabar.

Conviene marcar la cuenta con etiquetas como ci, pull-request y repository para limpiar recursos huérfanos. En incidentes reales he visto que la limpieza se rompe por que un paso depende del resultado del test; una tarea final independiente suele ser más seguro.

Medir antes de reintentar

Un timeout de email mezcla demasiadas posibilidades: el mensaje no se envió, el proveedor lo rechazó, el buzón no se consultó, el filtro ocultó el mensaje o el test buscó el asunto equivocado. Antes de reintentar, registraría un evento por etapa:

  1. mail_requested: la aplicación aceptó la solicitud.
  2. mail_accepted: el proveedor confirmó la entrega al buzón.
  3. mail_seen: el lector encontró el mensaje esperado.
  4. token_consumed: el test usó el enlace una sola vez.

Cada evento llevan run_id, identificador del buzón y marca de tiempo, nunca el cuerpo completo ni el token. Así se puede localizar la pérdida y reintentar solo la etapa que corresponde. El panel de CI deja de decir “esperando correo” y cuenta una historia útil.

El mismo criterio aplica a los jobs programados: estas alertas útiles para jobs programados deben distinguir una ausencia esperada de una ejecución que quedó sin limpiar.

Alertas que explican el fallo

No alertaría por cada mensaje retrasado. Usaría señales agregadas:

  • porcentaje de mail_requested sin mail_seen por entorno;
  • edad del buzón más antiguo que sigue activo;
  • número de tokens consumidos dos veces;
  • recursos CI sin evento de limpieza;
  • lecturas rechazadas por una política de acceso.

La notificación debe decir qué cambió, qué ejecución está afectada y dónde está la evidencia. Un enlace a correos de rollback con contexto operativo es más útil que mandar un mensaje genérico de “pipeline rojo”. En email de test, un asunto como CI FAIL run=1842 stage=mail_seen ayuda bastante mas durante una guardia.

Checklist de revisión

Antes de aprobar el módulo o el pipeline, revisaría:

  • ¿Cada ejecución tiene un buzón o namespace que no comparte con otra?
  • ¿El token de lectura es sensible, limitado y revocable?
  • ¿La retención está definida y tiene un límite máximo?
  • ¿El contenido de los mensajes queda fuera de los logs?
  • ¿La evidencia permite separar envío, entrega, lectura y consumo?
  • ¿La limpieza corre también cuando el test termina en error?
  • ¿Las alertas incluyen entorno, run_id y siguiente acción?
  • ¿Se puede borrar un recurso huérfano por sus etiquetas?

Si una respuesta es “depende de una variable manual”, todavía no existe un contrato operativo. El pipeline puede seguir pasando, pero la seguridad y la capacidad de diagnóstico quedan a merced de la memoria del siguiente compañero.

Preguntas rápidas

¿Hace falta un buzón nuevo para cada test?

No siempre. Para una suite pequeña puede bastar uno por ejecución de CI, con mensajes identificados por run_id. Compartirlo entre ejecuciones paralelas sí introduce carreras y hace más difícil atribuir la evidencia.

¿Los reintentos están mal?

No. Son útiles después de clasificar el fallo. Reintentar una consulta cuando el proveedor aún procesa el mensaje es razonable; repetir todo el alta sin una frontera idempotente solo añade ruido.

¿Qué hago con tempail mail en una búsqueda del equipo?

Trátalo como una variante escrita por usuarios o por documentación antigua, no como una palabra clave principal del diseño. Puede ayudar a encontrar casos históricos, pero el contrato debe usar nombres claros y consistentes.

La idea final es sencilla: Terraform define quién puede crear el recurso, CI define cuánto vive y la observabilidad explica qué ocurrió. Con esa separación, las pruebas de email dejan de ser una dependencia invisible y se convierten en una pieza revisable de la plataforma.

title: Comment "LINK" to get it in DMs: how Instagram auto-replies actually work under the hood
description:
You've seen these posts everywhere on Instagram. A creator says "comment LINK and I'll send it to you" and a few seconds later there's a DM sitting in your inbox.

I used to think there was some guy with three phones doing this manually. There isn't. I ended up building this exact feature for my own product, so here's what's actually going on behind it, minus the marketing fluff.

It's not a bot clicking buttons

The old way people did this was with sketchy tools that logged into your account and pretended to be you. That's how accounts get flagged.

The legit way is Meta's official Instagram API. It only works with Business or Creator accounts linked to a Facebook Page, and every permission has to be approved by Meta. No passwords shared anywhere.

The flow, step by step

  1. Someone comments on your post. Instagram fires a webhook to your server with the comment text, the comment ID and the post ID.
  2. Your server checks for a keyword. Something as simple as: does this comment contain "link", "price" or "info"? I normalise the text first (lowercase, trim, strip emojis), because people type "Link!!" and "LINK 🔥" and you still want those to match.
  3. You send a Private Reply. This is the key part. Instagram lets a business send one DM to the person who commented, tied to that specific comment. It has to happen within 7 days of the comment.
  4. The conversation opens. Once the person replies to that DM, the normal messaging window opens. You can now keep talking to them for 24 hours from their last message.

So the "magic" is just webhook → keyword match → private reply API call.

Stuff that tripped me up

  • One private reply per comment. You can't spam someone with five messages because they commented once. Make the first message count.
  • The 24-hour window is real. If the user goes quiet, you can't just message them again three days later with a promo. Meta is strict about this, and honestly that's a good thing.
  • Webhooks can arrive twice. Store the comment ID and skip anything you've already processed, or people get duplicate DMs and it looks broken.
  • Reply to the comment publicly too. A quick "Sent you a DM 👀" under their comment makes other people comment as well. That's where the reach comes from.

Why I bothered building this

I'm an Android dev from India, and a lot of creators and small brands I know were losing leads simply because they couldn't reply fast enough. Someone asks "price?" at 11 pm, nobody answers, and that sale is gone.

So I built HeyDM: keyword triggers on comments and DMs, auto-replies, and lead capture, all on top of the official API. It's been a fun rabbit hole of webhooks, rate limits and edge cases.

If you're building something similar and get stuck on Meta's app review or the webhook setup, drop a comment. Happy to share what worked for me.

title: The Day Your One App Became Twelve
description:
At the start, your backend is one app.One codebase,one deployment,one address.The frontend knows exactly where to send every request,because there's only one place it can send them.
Then the project grows.Someone splits out the payments logic into its own service.Then notifications,.Then user profiles,then search,then the thing that resizes images.A year later you have a dozen small services,each doing one job,each living at its own address.

And now your mobile app has a problem it never used to have:
To load the homescreen,which of these twelve things do i need to talk to?And where do they all live?

Without something in the middle,the honest answer is:Frontend has to know all of it.Every address,every auth rule,every quirk.And every time you move or rename a service ,every client breaks.
That something in the middle is called an API gateway.Think of it as the front door of your whole backend.
In Part 3 we looked at reverse proxies,the receptionist standing in front of your server.An Api gateway is that receptionist after a promotion:same basic job,but much smarter about what's going on behind the desk.

The Hotel Analogy

Picture a big hotel.

Guests don't wander the building looking for the kitchen, the laundry, the spa, and the maintenance team. They go to one front desk. They say what they need, and the front desk:

  • Checks who they are (are you a guest?)
  • Figures out which department handles the request
  • Passes it along
  • Brings the answer back
  • Politely says "no" to anyone trying to wander into the staff-only areas The departments behind the desk can be reorganized, moved to different floors, or even replaced entirely. Guests never notice, because they only ever deal with the front desk.

That's an API gateway. One entry point for every client, and a lot of quiet responsibility behind it.

So What Does a Gateway Actually Do?

Let's go through the job list in plain language.

1. Routing. The most basic job. A request for /payments goes to the payments service. /search goes to the search service. The client only knows one address, and the gateway handles the map.

2. Authentication. Instead of every one of your twelve services separately checking "is this person logged in and allowed to do this?", the gateway checks once, at the door. Requests that fail never get inside. Requests that pass get stamped with who the user is, so internal services can trust it.

3. Rate limiting. One misbehaving client (or one attacker) hammering your API can bring down services that were never built to defend themselves. The gateway can say "100 requests a minute per user, then slow down" before any of that traffic reaches your actual code.

4. Combining responses. Remember that home screen needing data from five services? Without a gateway, the phone makes five separate network calls over a mobile connection. With one, the phone makes one call, and the gateway talks to the five services behind the scenes (over a fast internal network) and stitches the answer together. Fewer round trips on a slow connection is a huge win.

5. Translating between worlds. Maybe your frontend speaks REST and one old internal service speaks something else entirely. The gateway can translate, so clients never have to care.

6. Logging and monitoring. Because every request passes through one place, it's the perfect spot to record who called what, how long it took, and what failed. You get a bird's-eye view for free.

7. Caching. Same idea as everything earlier in this series: if ten thousand people ask for the same thing, answer from memory instead of bothering the services ten thousand times.

8. Versioning. Want to roll out /v2/ of your API without breaking old mobile apps still calling /v1/? The gateway can route each to the right place.

Notice something? Many of these sound familiar. That's because a gateway is built on the same ideas as the reverse proxy and load balancer from the earlier parts. The difference is awareness of your API. A reverse proxy mostly shuffles bytes. A gateway understands that this is a request for the payments API from user #4821, and acts accordingly.

Gateway vs Reverse Proxy vs Load Balancer

This is where people get confused, so here's the cleanest way to think about it. They're layers of intelligence, not rivals:

Mostly cares about Example job
Load balancer Which copy of a server gets this request "Server 2 is least busy, send it there"
Reverse proxy Hiding and protecting the servers behind it "Handle HTTPS, serve static files, forward the rest"
API gateway What this API request means "Is this user allowed to call /payments, and have they hit their limit?"

In real systems, you'll often see all three stacked: a load balancer in front, spreading traffic across several gateway instances, each of which routes to services that are themselves load balanced. Each layer does the one job it's best at.

(And to make it more confusing: many tools do more than one job. nginx can act as all three if configured to. The roles are separate even when the software isn't.)

A Day in the Life of One Request

Let's follow a single request so this feels real. A user opens the app and taps "My Orders."

  1. The app sends one request to api.yourapp.com/orders
  2. A load balancer hands it to one of several gateway instances
  3. The gateway checks the token: valid, and it belongs to user 4821
  4. The gateway checks the rate limit: well under, fine
  5. It routes the request to the orders service, adding "this is user 4821" so the service doesn't have to re-verify anything
  6. The orders service responds. Maybe the gateway also quietly asks the products service for item names and merges them in
  7. The gateway logs the request and sends one tidy response back The user saw a screen load. The app made one call. Behind the curtain, five or six things collaborated. That's the whole magic trick.

The Honest Downsides

I'd be doing you a disservice if I made gateways sound like pure upside. They come with real trade-offs.

It's a single point of failure. If every request goes through the gateway and the gateway dies, everything dies. The fix is running multiple gateway instances behind a load balancer (see Part 2), but it's something you have to deliberately plan for.

It can become a bottleneck. All your traffic funnels through one layer. If it's slow, everything is slow.

It can become a dumping ground. This one bites teams the most. Gateways are so convenient that people keep stuffing business logic into them: "just one more transformation," "just one more special case." Over time, your gateway turns into a tangled monolith that everyone's afraid to touch, which is exactly what you were trying to escape by splitting into services. The rule of thumb: keep it about traffic, not business decisions.

It's one more thing to run. More components means more to deploy, monitor, and debug. For a small project, that cost can outweigh the benefit.

Do You Actually Need One?

Honest answer: probably not yet.

If you have one backend, or two or three services, a plain reverse proxy like nginx is usually plenty. A gateway earns its place when:

  • You have many services and clients shouldn't need to know about each one
  • You want consistent auth and rate limiting in one place instead of copy-pasted twelve times
  • You serve mobile or slow-network clients that benefit from fewer round trips
  • You have multiple teams who need a stable, shared front door while they change things behind it Starting with a gateway on day one of a tiny project is like hiring a hotel front desk team for a two-room guesthouse. Add it when the building grows.

Tools You'll Run Into

You don't have to build one from scratch. Popular options include:

  • Managed cloud gateways: AWS API Gateway, Google Cloud API Gateway, Azure API Management. You configure them, the provider runs them
  • Open source you run yourself: Kong, Traefik, KrakenD, Envoy-based gateways
  • Do-it-yourself: a small service in your language of choice (Go is great at this) that routes and authenticates. For small setups, this is often the simplest honest answer If you've used Cloudflare or a platform like Vercel with rewrites and middleware, you've already touched gateway-style ideas without necessarily calling them that.

Where This Fits in the Series

Zooming out across everything so far:

  • CDN (Part 1): bring content physically closer to users
  • Load balancer (Part 2): spread traffic across many servers so none drown
  • Reverse proxy (Part 3): stand in front of servers, hiding and protecting them
  • API gateway (this post): give a growing backend one smart, consistent front door Each one answers a question that only appears once the previous layer exists. That's how real architecture grows: not designed all at once, but earned one problem at a time.

What to Take Away

  1. A gateway is a front door. Clients talk to one address, and everything behind it can change freely.
  2. It handles the repetitive stuff (auth, rate limits, routing, logging) once, at the edge, instead of twelve times inside.
  3. It's an evolved reverse proxy: same family, but it understands your API, not just bytes.
  4. Don't let it become a junk drawer. Keep business logic in your services.
  5. Wait until you need one. Complexity you add too early is complexity you maintain forever. The next time an app loads a screen full of data from a dozen places in a single smooth tap, you'll know there's probably a front desk somewhere, calmly handling the whole hotel.

Next in this series: caching beyond the CDN. Redis, in-memory caching, and the hardest question in computing: "when is this stored answer no longer true?"

Are you running a gateway today, or still happily on plain nginx? Tell me in the comments; I'm curious where people draw that line.

title: Web App Log Management for Node.js Express Rollouts (Choosing Replaceable Contracts)
description:
The hard constraint is not collecting another stream of text. A customer-support SaaS rolling out a new pricing rule behind a flag must be able to attribute the rule's cost, investigate a disputed ticket after a process restart, and replace its logging vendor without rewriting business code. Short answer: keep Node.js Express log events as a vendor-neutral application contract, send them to a hosted searchable service, and retain console output as a transport or development sink rather than the system of record. Infrai is worth trying when a small startup wants hosted logs, metrics, and the realtime channel carrying rollout updates through one REST contract, a single API key, and one consolidated bill; that breadth matters because a later migration stays concentrated in one adapter rather than spreading through request handlers and workers.

A local console file can survive a terminal closing. It does not automatically survive an ephemeral container, correlate work across an Express API process and a queue worker, or give support agents a shared search surface. Self-hosted OpenSearch or ELK can do much more, but its clusters, retention policy, access controls, and upgrades become another production system. For an ordinary web app feature owned by a junior team, that is usually the wrong first management burden.

Files stay local.

How should a startup choose web app log management?

Start with the decision you may need to reverse. For each evaluation of the pricing flag, emit an event with a stable event name, timestamp, deployment identifier, flag key, variant, pseudonymous account identifier, request or job correlation identifier, and a cost-attribution label such as pricing_preview or pricing_committed. Keep free-form messages for humans, but do not make them the only evidence. The structured event is the durable boundary.

Do not put raw ticket text, email addresses, or payment details into that boundary. This matters especially here because the hosted option has no per-user deletion route, no bulk export or subscription interface, and no exposed control for retention or cold storage. A compliance-heavy archive therefore needs a different store and a lifecycle that has been reviewed explicitly.

The flag itself also has a narrow boundary. The platform exposes flag operations, but the surface has no flag-change audit log, evaluation statistics, parent-child dependencies, deletion recovery, or client push; clients poll. Record the rollout decision in your own neutral event shape, and treat Martin Fowler's distinction between release toggles and long-lived configuration as an architectural warning, not taxonomy trivia. A pricing rule that outlives its rollout should graduate from a temporary flag.

Put the contract before the transport

The adapter should accept application events, not vendor SDK objects. Define the event schema in your repository, version it, and make the hosted sink replaceable. The same rule applies to queries: expose operations such as find_rollout_evidence(correlation_id) in your application boundary instead of allowing route handlers to assemble a provider's filter syntax.

This is not theoretical caution. The service provides search, yet the filter parameters for logs.search are not declared in discovery metadata. Pretending those filters are stable would turn an undocumented detail into application architecture. Keep search wiring inside the adapter and verify it against discovery during integration.

The following program demonstrates the cross-capability seam without inventing request fields. It loads schema-valid payloads from files, sends the metric result into a caller-selected field in the realtime payload, and uses one key and one base URL. The files are deliberate: discovery, not an article snippet, remains authoritative about each payload shape.

import json
import os
import sys
import time
from pathlib import Path
from urllib import error, request

BASE = "https://api.infrai.cc/v1"
KEY = os.environ["INFRAI_API_KEY"]


def call(method, path, body=None, attempts=5):
    data = None if body is None else json.dumps(body).encode("utf-8")
    headers = {"Accept": "application/json", "Authorization": f"Bearer {KEY}"}
    if data is not None:
        headers["Content-Type"] = "application/json"
    for attempt in range(attempts):
        req = request.Request(f"{BASE}{path}", data=data, headers=headers, method=method)
        try:
            with request.urlopen(req, timeout=30) as response:
                return json.load(response)
        except error.HTTPError as exc:
            reason = exc.read().decode("utf-8", errors="replace")
            if exc.code != 429 or attempt == attempts - 1:
                raise RuntimeError(f"{method} {path} failed: {exc.code} {reason}") from exc
            retry_after = exc.headers.get("Retry-After")
            time.sleep(float(retry_after) if retry_after else 2 ** attempt)
    raise RuntimeError("retry loop exhausted")


def load_json(path):
    return json.loads(Path(path).read_text(encoding="utf-8"))


metric_payload = load_json(sys.argv[1])
publish_payload = load_json(sys.argv[2])
handoff_field = os.environ["REALTIME_HANDOFF_FIELD"]
metric_result = call("POST", "/metrics/report", metric_payload)
publish_payload[handoff_field] = metric_result
print(json.dumps(call("POST", "/realtime/publish", publish_payload), indent=2))

Before running it, retrieve the two capability descriptions from the public discovery surface and construct both input files from their current request schemas. That public surface is self-describing and requires no key; across the platform it reports 295 routes in 20 modules, while documented capabilities include runnable examples in ten languages. The program uses only two production routes, checks errors, and backs off on 429. These calls report telemetry and publish an update, so retry behavior must follow the current discovery declarations rather than an invented idempotency promise.

This design has a cost. One key and one bill also mean one vendor to trust, one credential with a wider blast radius, and one outage surface across both steps. Separate the adapter, restrict where the credential is available, and decide what the application does if telemetry succeeds but realtime publication does not. Do not erase that partial failure with a cheerful except.

That is the trade-off.

Compare the operating boundaries, not the logos

The relevant alternatives are meaningfully different. No row wins every column.

Option Migration boundary Operational burden Better choice when Material limit for this rollout
Infrai Plain REST adapter spanning logs, metrics, flags, and realtime Hosted; one key across the combined path A small backend team values breadth under a consistent contract No alert routes, trace query or span tree, source-map decoding, session replay, synthetic checks, or heartbeat monitoring
Datadog Agent, APIs, and Datadog-specific query/monitor configuration Hosted, with a broad observability program to configure Logs must sit beside mature monitors, APM, and wider operational workflows The application boundary can absorb more vendor-specific concepts than a narrow log sink
Better Stack Logs Hosted logging integration and its query surface Hosted and log-focused The team wants a focused hosted log workflow rather than a broad backend API Cross-capability realtime delivery remains a separate integration decision
Grafana Loki Loki's push/query contracts, commonly paired with Grafana and an agent Managed or self-operated, depending on deployment Label-oriented logs and Grafana workflows are already organizational standards Self-operation restores control but also ownership of capacity, upgrades, and retention
Elastic Stack Elastic ingestion, index mappings, and query model Highest when self-hosted; managed service reduces cluster work Complex search, indexing control, or compliance architecture justifies the platform It is excessive machinery for a junior team shipping one normal SaaS rollout

A Datadog-plus-Pusher version of the metric-to-channel handoff would require two vendor signups, two credential sets, and glue that translates the metric result into a Pusher event while handling independent errors and billing contexts. The combined Infrai path removes that credential and integration split. It does not remove the need for an outbox or retry policy when business correctness requires eventual publication.

The limitation is decisive: Infrai is not a fit when alerting, distributed trace queries, compliance-heavy archival, or frontend crash diagnosis drives the purchase. Use Datadog when alerts and a broader APM program drive the purchase; choose Elastic when controlled indexing, export, and retention dominate; prefer Loki when the team already operates around Grafana and accepts its label model. Frontend crashes need a specialist because this surface does not include source-map deobfuscation, crash symbolication, Electron minidump parsing, or session replay. Silent workers need a heartbeat service such as Healthchecks because there is no synthetic or heartbeat monitor.

Roll out with an exit route

Ship the pricing rule in stages, but make the migration test concrete before exposure grows. First, freeze a versioned event fixture containing a flag evaluation, the attributed operation, and a worker completion. Second, send that fixture through the adapter and confirm that centralized search can recover the evidence after the application process is gone. Third, replay the same fixture through a second adapter in a test environment. If business code changes, the boundary is leaking.

During rollout, compare counts by variant and attribution label in your own reporting layer; do not claim that a flag system supplies evaluation analytics when it does not. Keep a rollback decision tied to application outcomes, and store the decision record outside ephemeral console files. Searchable logs help explain a result. They are not the result.

Finally, rehearse removal: rotate the credential, disable the sink, and verify that the pricing path continues with an explicit telemetry-degraded state. This compact drill reveals whether logging is truly an adapter or a hidden runtime dependency.

If this boundary fits your system, start with the Infrai capability sheet and generate payloads from discovery rather than copying stale request fields.

Sources

  • Martin Fowler: Feature Toggles
  • Datadog Logs documentation
  • Better Stack Logs documentation
  • Grafana Loki documentation
  • Elastic Stack documentation
  • Pusher Channels documentation
  • Healthchecks documentation
  • Infrai capability sheet

title: Anthropic estreia na Nasdaq e fecha avaliada em US$ 1,76 trilhão
description:
Estreia termina acima do preço da oferta

Segundo a AOL, a Anthropic estreou na Nasdaq em 19 de novembro de 2026, e suas ações fecharam o primeiro pregão a US$ 97,17. O preço ficou US$ 14,17, ou 17,07%, acima dos US$ 83 definidos na oferta pública inicial (IPO), levando o valor de mercado da empresa a aproximadamente US$ 1,76 trilhão no fechamento.

Os papéis abriram a US$ 111,50, alta de 34,3% sobre o preço do IPO, e chegaram a US$ 115,10 durante o pregão, avanço de 38,7%. Depois recuaram, caindo abaixo de US$ 100 antes de encerrar a sessão acima do valor inicial da oferta.

Oferta reúne US$ 81,3 bilhões

O preço de US$ 83 por ação correspondia a uma avaliação de cerca de US$ 1,5 trilhão, considerando a diluição completa. A oferta somou US$ 81,3 bilhões, incluindo aproximadamente US$ 2 bilhões em ações vendidas por acionistas existentes; uma colocação privada concomitante de US$ 26 bilhões elevou o valor combinado das operações a US$ 107,3 bilhões.

A AOL classificou a operação como a maior oferta pública já registrada, acima do recorde anterior atribuído à listagem da SpaceX na Nasdaq, em junho, que levantou US$ 75 bilhões. No pico intradiário, a capitalização implícita da Anthropic chegou a cerca de US$ 2,09 trilhões, antes de recuar com a queda das ações.

Investidores passam a comprar ações diretamente

A abertura de capital oferece aos investidores uma forma direta de comprar ações de uma das empresas que desenvolvem modelos avançados de inteligência artificial. Até então, a exposição nos mercados públicos à expansão da IA se concentrava principalmente em fornecedores de chips, computação em nuvem e infraestrutura de data centers, como Nvidia e CoreWeave.

A avaliação elevada também coloca em foco a capacidade de converter avanços em IA em receitas e lucros sustentáveis. Entre os custos que investidores acompanharão estão computação, pesquisa e desenvolvimento; a trajetória das ações nas próximas semanas também pode influenciar outras empresas privadas do setor que avaliam abrir capital.

Expansão de infraestrutura e custos da IA

Fundada em 2021 em San Francisco por Dario e Daniela Amodei e outros ex-funcionários da OpenAI, a Anthropic desenvolve a família de modelos Claude, concorrente do ChatGPT. No registro do IPO, a empresa informou que pretende usar parte dos recursos para ampliar sua capacidade de computação e sua infraestrutura.

Essa expansão pode sustentar ferramentas de IA usadas em escrita, pesquisa, programação e produtividade no trabalho, mas também exige grande capacidade computacional e energia. O crescimento de data centers pode pressionar o fornecimento de eletricidade e comunidades próximas, enquanto investidores avaliam os custos, os riscos de regulação mais rigorosa e os efeitos da tecnologia sobre o emprego.

Confira mais em: https://guiadeti.com.br/noticias/anthropic-estreia-nasdaq-avaliacao-176-trilhoes/
