title: IndexedDB in React: Offline-First Apps with WatermelonDB
description:
Originally published at muhammadmoiz.dev.

IndexedDB is the browser's built-in database. It is the right place to keep the data a React app needs to keep working when the network drops. You can use it directly through a small wrapper like idb for simple caching. If you need relations, reactive queries and two-way sync with a server, put WatermelonDB on top of it. This tutorial walks through both approaches, with code you can adapt.

I used WatermelonDB on browser storage to build the offline-first data layer of Oscar, a restaurant and retail POS. A POS can't stop taking orders just because the Wi-Fi went down. The patterns below are the ones I'd reach for again. If you want the product-level story first, read lessons from building an offline-first POS in React. This post is the hands-on developer version.

What is IndexedDB, and why not just use localStorage?

IndexedDB is an asynchronous, transactional object store that ships with every modern browser. You don't define tables with fixed columns. Instead you create object stores that hold JavaScript objects identified by a key. You add indexes on the fields you want to search by, and you read or write inside transactions. Anything the structured clone algorithm can copy, including Blobs and files, can be stored. It also works inside Web Workers, so heavy database work can stay off the main thread.

localStorage feels easier, but it has two problems for offline apps:

localStorage IndexedDB
API style Synchronous, blocks the main thread Asynchronous, event or promise based
Data Strings only Structured objects, Blobs, files
Querying Read by key only Indexes, key ranges, cursors
Size 5 MiB per origin A share of total disk (see below)
Transactions None Read-only and readwrite transactions

The 5 MiB figure comes from MDN's storage quota guide. A product catalogue, a few days of orders and some images will pass that quickly. IndexedDB quotas are far larger. Chromium browsers allow an origin up to 60% of total disk. Recent Safari versions (macOS 14 and iOS 17 onward) allow about 60% for browser apps. Firefox gives best-effort storage the smaller of 10% of the disk or 10 GiB.

How do you use IndexedDB in React without the boilerplate?

The raw API is built on request objects and onsuccess callbacks, which is awkward in modern code. The idb library by Jake Archibald wraps it in promises and adds TypeScript types. It is tiny, and version 8.0.4 was the latest on npm when I checked in November 2026.

npm install idb

Here is a small, typed data module for a list of orders:

// db.ts
import { openDB, type DBSchema } from "idb";

interface ShopDB extends DBSchema {
  orders: {
    key: string;
    value: {
      id: string;
      status: "pending" | "paid";
      total: number;
      updatedAt: number;
    };
    indexes: { by_status: string };
  };
}

export const dbPromise = openDB<ShopDB>("shop", 1, {
  upgrade(db) {
    const store = db.createObjectStore("orders", { keyPath: "id" });
    store.createIndex("by_status", "status");
  },
});

export async function saveOrder(order: ShopDB["orders"]["value"]) {
  const db = await dbPromise;
  await db.put("orders", { ...order, updatedAt: Date.now() });
}

export async function pendingOrders() {
  const db = await dbPromise;
  return db.getAllFromIndex("orders", "by_status", "pending");
}

A few things are worth knowing:

  • The schema only changes in upgrade. When you add a store or index, bump the version number and handle oldVersion inside upgrade. Never delete a store your users already have data in without migrating it.

  • Generate IDs on the device. crypto.randomUUID() lets you create records offline without asking the server for an ID. It also makes duplicate detection easy later.

  • Keep transactions short. A transaction closes once you stop giving it work, so don't await a network call in the middle of one.

In a component, read the data inside an effect and store it in state:

import { useEffect, useState } from "react";
import { pendingOrders } from "./db";

export function PendingOrders() {
  const [orders, setOrders] = useState<Awaited<ReturnType<typeof pendingOrders>>>([]);

  useEffect(() => {
    pendingOrders().then(setOrders);
  }, []);

  return <p>{orders.length} orders waiting to sync</p>;
}

This works well for caching and small offline features. It breaks down once your data has relations (an order with items, modifiers and payments) and many screens that must update the moment something changes. Then you are writing your own query layer, change tracking and sync protocol. That is what WatermelonDB already does.


Photo: imgix on Unsplash

Setting up WatermelonDB on top of IndexedDB

WatermelonDB is a reactive database for React and React Native. On the web it runs through its LokiJS adapter, which can save data incrementally to IndexedDB. The current npm release is 0.28.0.

npm install @nozbe/watermelondb

It uses decorators for models, so your bundler needs the Babel decorators and class-properties plugins. The installation guide lists them. Start with a schema:

// model/schema.ts
import { appSchema, tableSchema } from "@nozbe/watermelondb";

export const schema = appSchema({
  version: 1,
  tables: [
    tableSchema({
      name: "orders",
      columns: [
        { name: "status", type: "string", isIndexed: true },
        { name: "total", type: "number" },
        { name: "created_at", type: "number" },
      ],
    }),
    tableSchema({
      name: "order_items",
      columns: [
        { name: "order_id", type: "string", isIndexed: true },
        { name: "name", type: "string" },
        { name: "qty", type: "number" },
      ],
    }),
  ],
});

Then create the adapter and the database. The adapter options are where most of the production problems get solved, so don't skip them:

// database.ts
import { Database } from "@nozbe/watermelondb";
import LokiJSAdapter from "@nozbe/watermelondb/adapters/lokijs";
import { schema } from "./model/schema";
import { migrations } from "./model/migrations";
import { Order, OrderItem } from "./model";

const adapter = new LokiJSAdapter({
  schema,
  migrations,
  dbName: "shop",
  useWebWorker: false,
  useIncrementalIndexedDB: true,
  onQuotaExceededError: () => showStorageFullBanner(),
  onSetUpError: () => offerReloadOrLogout(),
  extraIncrementalIDBOptions: {
    // Another tab overwrote this tab's data: sync now, warn if offline
    onDidOverwrite: () => syncNow(),
    // The database was deleted in another tab (e.g. logout)
    onversionchange: () => window.location.reload(),
  },
});

export const database = new Database({
  adapter,
  modelClasses: [Order, OrderItem],
});

The multi-tab handlers matter more than they look. Staff often have the same app open in two tabs. If you ignore those callbacks, one tab can quietly overwrite what the other wrote.

Reading and writing records

Every write goes through database.write, which keeps changes consistent:

import { Q } from "@nozbe/watermelondb";

export async function createOrder(items: { name: string; qty: number }[]) {
  await database.write(async () => {
    const order = await database.get<Order>("orders").create((o) => {
      o.status = "pending";
      o.total = 0;
    });
    for (const item of items) {
      await database.get<OrderItem>("order_items").create((i) => {
        i.order.set(order);
        i.name = item.name;
        i.qty = item.qty;
      });
    }
  });
}

export const pendingQuery = () =>
  database.get<Order>("orders").query(Q.where("status", "pending"));

The real benefit is that queries are observable. Call pendingQuery().observe() (or use the withObservables helper) and any component reading it re-renders when a matching record changes, whether a cashier made the change or a sync did. You stop passing refresh callbacks around.

For synced apps, delete with markAsDeleted() so the deletion reaches the server. Use destroyPermanently() only for data that never leaves the device.

How does sync work between IndexedDB and your backend?

WatermelonDB's synchronize() function needs two things from you:

  1. pullChanges({ lastPulledAt }) calls your API and returns { changes, timestamp }. changes holds everything created, updated or deleted on the server since the last pull.
  2. pushChanges({ changes }) sends local changes to your API. It must reject if the server fails to apply them. 
import { synchronize } from "@nozbe/watermelondb/sync";

export async function syncNow() {
  await synchronize({
    database,
    migrationsEnabledAtVersion: 1,
    pullChanges: async ({ lastPulledAt, schemaVersion }) => {
      const res = await fetch(
        `/api/sync?since=${lastPulledAt ?? 0}&schema=${schemaVersion}`,
      );
      if (!res.ok) throw new Error("Pull failed");
      return res.json(); // { changes, timestamp }
    },
    pushChanges: async ({ changes, lastPulledAt }) => {
      const res = await fetch(`/api/sync?last_pulled_at=${lastPulledAt}`, {
        method: "POST",
        body: JSON.stringify(changes),
      });
      if (!res.ok) throw new Error("Push failed");
    },
  });
}

The changes payload is grouped by table, with created, updated and deleted lists. Deleted records are sent as IDs only, and fields use the raw column names from your schema. Your backend has to keep its side of the deal:

  • Track changes on the server. Add a last_modified column to every table and set it on every write. Pull returns rows where it is newer than lastPulledAt. Ignore any value the client sends for it.

  • Track deletions. Use a soft-delete flag or a table of deleted IDs. Otherwise devices never learn that a record is gone.

  • Make push all-or-nothing. Apply the whole batch in one database transaction. If anything fails, roll back and return an error. A half-applied order is worse than one that retries.

  • Reject stale pushes. If a record changed on the server after the client's lastPulledAt, fail the push. The client then pulls, resolves the conflict and pushes again. That's why the docs suggest retrying a failed sync once.

  • Never run two syncs at once. Guard syncNow() with a flag. Call it when the app starts, on the browser's online event and on a timer.

Production checklist for an offline-first React app

The tutorial code works on your laptop. These are the things that decide whether it survives real users:

  • Ask for persistent storage. By default, browser storage is "best effort" and can be evicted when the device is low on space. Call navigator.storage.persist() after the user has used the app for a while. Firefox shows a prompt. Chrome and Safari decide on their own based on how the user engages with the site.

  • Watch your usage. navigator.storage.estimate() gives a rough figure for usage and quota. Use it to prune old records before you hit QuotaExceededError.

  • Handle quota and setup errors in the UI, not just in the console.

  • Plan for Safari's 7-day rule. With tracking prevention on, Safari deletes script-written storage for an origin the user hasn't interacted with in the last 7 days of browser use. Treat the local database as a cache of the server, never as the only copy.

  • Remember that eviction is all-or-nothing. When an origin is evicted, its IndexedDB, Cache API and other storage go together. Sync often so there is little unsynced data at risk.

  • Write migrations from day one and never delete old ones. Users may open an app version that is months old.

  • Test the bad days. Turn off the network mid-order, open two tabs, fill the disk, log out in one tab. Those are the bugs real users will find.

Don't store secrets in IndexedDB: Anything in IndexedDB can be read by any script running on your origin, including a malicious third-party script. Keep auth tokens short-lived and never cache data the current user isn't allowed to see.

What this means if you own the app

Offline-first is a product decision before it is a technical one. If your users work in kitchens, warehouses, shops, field sites or anywhere with patchy signal, a "you're offline" screen costs you sales and trust. Building it properly means designing the data model and sync rules first, then the screens. Adding it to an existing app later is possible, but usually means reworking how every feature reads and writes data.

A rough guide:

  • Caching a few screens or drafts: IndexedDB with idb is enough.

  • The whole app must keep working offline, with relational data and multiple devices: use WatermelonDB (or a similar sync engine) and budget real time for the backend sync endpoints.

  • Not sure: start by listing what your users must be able to do with no connection. That list decides the architecture.

If you're planning an app that has to work offline, or your current one loses data when the connection drops, see how I approach offline-first app development. For point of sale systems specifically, there is also POS development.

Sources

  • MDN: IndexedDB API

  • MDN: Storage quotas and eviction criteria

  • idb on GitHub and npm

  • WatermelonDB: Installation

  • WatermelonDB: Setup (web adapter)

  • WatermelonDB: Create, Read, Update, Delete

  • WatermelonDB: Sync frontend

  • WatermelonDB: Sync backend

  • WatermelonDB on npm

  • Cover photo: Mohammad Rahmani on Unsplash

I'm Muhammad Moiz, a full-stack developer who builds web apps, SaaS and POS systems, and takes AI-built apps (Lovable, Bolt, Replit) to production. Get in touch.

title: GitHub Copilot cloud sandboxes start drawing from Actions compute on November 23
description:
Suppose a GitHub Team organization has already consumed USD 15.50 of its USD 18 compute allowance on CI. That leaves USD 2.50. At the assumed sizes below, 23 half-hour Copilot cloud sessions fit; the 24th crosses the allowance. CI and sandbox runtime draw from the same allowance, independently of model usage.

GitHub's November 19 changelog update gives November 23, 2026 as the billing start date without specifying a time or time zone. The following is a worked operating plan based on published rates, not a measured workload or bill.

01. Identify the environment and the account paying for it

Environment What is billed When to use it
Local No separate cloud sandbox runtime fee; model usage is separate Small changes and reviews that reproduce locally
Cloud GitHub-hosted isolated Linux; running CPU and memory, with retained snapshots metered separately Isolation or parallel work materially improves turnaround
Actions The rules for the selected Actions runner and repository A prescribed CI environment, Windows, specialized hardware, or a self-hosted runner is required

The sandbox owner pays, not necessarily the person who starts the session. For repository work, GitHub bills the account that owns the repositories, which must all share one owner in a given session. Without a repository, the selected organization or personal account pays; if none is selected, billing goes to the personal account. A developer can run an organization task and a personal experiment without drawing from the same allowance. Billing and ownership

02. Know which meters use included compute

Included compute is a monetary value, not a shared count of minutes. Eligible standard hosted runners for private and internal repositories share it with Cloud CPU and memory, with no priority between usage types. Eligible larger runners can also draw from it on Team and Enterprise Cloud. Standard hosted runners for public repositories and self-hosted runners are independently free under the Actions rules. That does not make public-repository Cloud sessions or public-repository larger runners free.

The included usage table lists USD 12 for both personal and organization Free, USD 18 for personal Pro and Team, and USD 300 for Enterprise Cloud. The allowance resets at the start of the billing cycle. These are GitHub account plans, not Copilot subscription levels.

Meter Measured as Rate (USD) Included compute
CPU Running seconds × allocated vCPU 0.000024 per vCPU-second Yes
Memory Running seconds × allocated GiB 0.000003 per GiB-second Yes
Snapshots Actual GiB-month kept after stop, until deletion 0.005 per GiB-month Separate
Model usage The applicable Copilot plan and usage meter Excluded here Separate

03. Find the boundary: 23 sessions versus 24

Running cost = running seconds × (allocated vCPU × 0.000024 + allocated memory GiB × 0.000003). For a 30-minute 2-vCPU, 4-GiB session, CPU costs USD 0.0864 and memory USD 0.0216, for USD 0.108. Low utilization does not reduce this allocated-resource meter. Count every session's running time rather than peak concurrency. Six 30-minute sessions total 180 session-minutes, or USD 0.648, whether they run in parallel or in sequence; turnaround can differ.

Assumed use in one billing cycle Sandbox runtime Including CI Above USD 18
20 sessions × 30 min USD 2.16 USD 17.66 USD 0
40 sessions × 30 min USD 4.32 USD 19.82 USD 1.82
20 sessions × 60 min USD 4.32 USD 19.82 USD 1.82

Worked Team example: $15.50 in eligible CI leaves $2.50 of the $18 allowance. Running overage and snapshot storage are calculated separately.

With CI fixed at USD 15.50, floor(2.50 ÷ 0.108) = 23. The 24th brings runtime to USD 2.592, exceeding the remaining allowance by USD 0.092. This assumes identical configurations, no other increase in eligible usage, a valid payment method, and no blocking budget. These estimates exclude taxes, model usage and snapshots.

04. Account for the cost after a session stops

Stopping ends CPU and RAM metering. A snapshot can be retained for resuming and is metered separately until deletion. Twenty actual 5-GiB snapshots held for one full month would be 100 GiB-month × USD 0.005 = USD 0.50. The 5 GiB refers to stored data, not the 4 GiB of RAM in the running example. Preserve any needed changes before deleting sessions you won't resume. GitHub's storage meter

05. Verify it in your team's billing account

  1. Before running: Find the billing owner, cycle and remaining entitlement. Reserve enough headroom for the CI you need before month-end. If headroom is tight, default small work to Local and use Cloud where warranted.
  2. Set the correct limit: Use a sandbox product budget or an applicable SKU budget. A Bundled AI credits budget cannot cap sandbox infrastructure spend. Hard limits block additional use when reached, not necessarily every active session immediately. Check for overlapping limits: capacity in one does not override a blocking limit in another. GitHub budget configuration
  3. After rollout: For each sampled session, record owner, UTC start/stop, allocated vCPU and GiB, and actual snapshot size and deletion status. Match estimates to the three Billing meters separately; if they disagree, check the time window, owner and running intervals before changing the budget. UULab has no measured account result to report here.

Decision: Compare the real turnaround improvement against runtime plus storage, not just model tokens. On a team with essential CI, treat the unspent allowance as shared headroom rather than a sandbox-only budget.

Official sources

  • GitHub Changelog: cloud experience rollout and November 19 billing-date update
  • GitHub Docs: cloud and local sandbox billing
  • GitHub Docs: cloud sandbox execution modes

title: 7,472 write bursts and 48,216 rows: what a prediction log can and cannot prove
description:
Every prediction platform eventually has to answer one question from a customer, a regulator, or its own postmortem: was this row produced by an analysis of this match, or was it replayed?

The model card describes intent, not execution. The only artifact describing execution is the row itself — its write time, its measured duration, its payload. So I treated our own production log as a forensic object.

The table is ai_predictions: 48,216 rows, 47,167 graded, 3,853 models, 17,235 matches, 116 distinct days from 2026-06-21 to 2026-11-20. Orientation: 26,806 hits over 47,167 graded rows, 56.83%.

Cluster the writes into bursts

A prediction is not an event, it is a member of a batch. To see batches you do not need a job table — you need the gap between consecutive writes. I used 120 seconds: any longer silence starts a new burst.

with t as (
  select id, created_at, model_id, match_id,
         created_at - lag(created_at) over (order by created_at, id) as gap
  from ai_predictions
), b as (
  select *, sum(case when gap is null or gap > interval '120 seconds' then 1 else 0 end)
           over (order by created_at, id) as burst_id
  from t
)
select count(distinct burst_id) as bursts, count(*) as rows,
       max(n) as largest_burst,
       percentile_disc(0.5) within group (order by n) as p50_size
from (select burst_id, count(*) n from b group by 1) s;

bursts | rows  | largest_burst | p50_size
7472   | 48215 | 645           | 2

7,472 bursts for 48,215 rows, mean 6.45, median 2. The distribution is bimodal: 2,951 bursts hold exactly one row, while 41 bursts hold more than 100 and together account for 7,540 rows — 15.6% of the log written in 41 windows.

The largest ran on 2026-10-10, 00:44:10 to 01:24:58: 645 rows, 214 matches, 160 distinct models, 2,448.4 seconds of wall clock. That is already a finding. 160 models produced 645 predictions across 214 matches in 41 minutes — a fan-out, not a per-match loop.

Does a model write the same match twice in one burst?

Yes: of 32,110 (burst, model) pairs, 8,070 contain more than one row; 1,008 contain five or more; the maximum is 50 rows from one model inside one contiguous burst. A model emitting 50 rows in one window is iterating a slate.

The arithmetic of concurrency

analysis_duration_ms over 29,991 non-null rows: p5 = 4,465 ms, p50 = 58,730 ms, p95 = 182,816 ms, max 1,569,409 ms. Median ~58.7 seconds per prediction.

Now compare with the burst above: 645 rows in 2,448 seconds, i.e. 3.8 seconds of wall clock per row. You cannot spend 58.7 seconds of compute per row and emit one row every 3.8 seconds unless rows are produced concurrently. The ratio per burst is the implied parallelism:

with t as (
  select id, created_at, analysis_duration_ms,
         created_at - lag(created_at) over (order by created_at, id) as gap
  from ai_predictions where analysis_duration_ms is not null
), b as (
  select *, sum(case when gap is null or gap > interval '120 seconds' then 1 else 0 end)
           over (order by created_at, id) as burst_id
  from t
), s as (
  select burst_id, sum(analysis_duration_ms)/1000.0 as compute_s,
         extract(epoch from max(created_at)-min(created_at)) as span_s
  from b group by 1 having count(*) >= 5
)
select count(*) as bursts,
       round(percentile_disc(0.5) within group (order by compute_s/nullif(span_s,0))::numeric, 2) as p50,
       round(percentile_disc(0.9) within group (order by compute_s/nullif(span_s,0))::numeric, 2) as p90
from s where span_s > 0;

bursts | p50  | p90
1477   | 3.77 | 10.54

Across 1,477 bursts of at least five instrumented rows, the median burst packs 3.77 seconds of measured compute into every second of wall clock; p90 is 10.54. For the 645-row burst, only 277 rows carry a duration and those 277 alone sum to 16,520.6 seconds inside a 2,448-second window — a lower bound of 6.7x. Extrapolating the measured mean of 59.6 s/row to all 645 gives ~38,400 seconds, about 15.7x.

First honest conclusion: the log proves concurrency. It cannot prove which worker produced which row, because there is no run_id and no worker_id. Two rows 400 ms apart from two processes are indistinguishable from two threads of one process, and both are indistinguishable from a replay that copies a stored analysis. Concurrency is measurable; provenance is not.

The missing 37.8%

18,225 rows (37.8%) have analysis_duration_ms IS NULL, and not at random:

month rows null duration share
2026-06 2,735 2,735 100.0%
2026-07 2,637 2,637 100.0%
2026-08 164 164 100.0%
2026-09 9,757 5,563 57.0%
2026-10 21,886 4,317 19.7%
2026-11 11,037 2,809 25.5%

Instrumentation arrived in September, stabilised in October, then drifted back to 25.5% in November. Any cost-per-prediction, latency SLO, or "how long does the model think" figure computed on non-null rows is a sample stratified by month, and months are not exchangeable: model composition, match volume and prompt length all moved. The correct denominator is 48,216 and the correct summary is "63.2% of rows have a measured duration".

Latency carries no quality signal

duration bucket rows graded hit rate
< 10 s 5,440 5,371 58.09%
10–60 s 9,666 9,391 57.56%
1–3 min 13,313 13,081 56.87%
> 3 min 1,572 1,562 57.17%
null 18,225 17,638 56.41%

Full spread 1.68 points across buckets differing by an order of magnitude in size, and the ordering is not monotonic. The 362 rows finishing under one second sit in the same band as rows taking four minutes.

I report this as a negative result because it constrains the fix. If longer analysis produced better predictions, the response to a 15.7x concurrency finding would be "add capacity". Since it does not, the response is "record what happened, then decide".

Identical payloads across different matches

Hashing full_analysis is the cheapest provenance check available without a schema change:

select count(*) as dup_hashes, sum(n) as rows_in_dup_groups,
       sum(case when dm > 1 then n else 0 end) as rows_spanning_multiple_matches,
       max(n) as largest_group, max(dm) as matches_in_largest_group
from (
  select md5(full_analysis) h, count(*) n, count(distinct match_id) dm
  from ai_predictions
  where full_analysis is not null and length(full_analysis) > 100
  group by 1 having count(*) > 1
) g;

dup_hashes | rows_in_dup_groups | rows_spanning_multiple_matches | largest_group | matches_in_largest_group
736        | 3780               | 3361                           | 123           | 77

736 payloads repeat, covering 3,780 rows, and 3,361 of those rows sit in groups spanning more than one match. The largest single text appears 123 times across 77 matches. It is not prose — it is a 240-character JSON stub beginning {"prediction": {"direction": "home", "confidence": 6, "score_prediction": "2-1"}, a fixed default stamped onto whatever match was in the loop when real analysis failed.

That is the finding a schema cannot catch alone, and why payload hashing belongs in the audit. 7,539 rows carry 100–500 characters; 40,510 carry more than 500. Length will not separate a stub from an analysis, but a hash will.

The column that exists and records nothing

cache_expires_at is declared on the table. Populated: 0 of 48,216. A column that is always null is worse than an absent column, because it invites analysis that silently returns zero: anyone auditing cache reuse against it concludes "no caching occurred" — true, or merely unrecorded. Same rule for prediction_source: free-text (match_center 30,062, system 11,458, scheduled 5,343, match_center+ahfill 986, then 16 one-off values). Free-text provenance is not provenance.

What the schema should have recorded

Five columns would have made every question above answerable without forensics:

alter table ai_predictions
  add column run_id             uuid    not null,  -- one value per batch invocation
  add column worker_id          text    not null,  -- process that wrote the row
  add column input_snapshot_id  text    not null,  -- hash of the frozen input bundle
  add column contract_version   text    not null,  -- prompt + training-word version
  add column duration_ms        integer not null;

create unique index ai_pred_run_model_match on ai_predictions (run_id, model_id, match_id);
create index ai_pred_input_snapshot on ai_predictions (input_snapshot_id);

"Did this row come from this match's data" then becomes a join instead of an argument: group by run_id, compare sum(duration_ms) to the run's wall clock, assert input_snapshot_id is unique per (run, match).

A verifier you can run before adding anything 

import psycopg2

DSN = "postgresql://user:pass@127.0.0.1:5433/soccerdream"

def main():
    cur = psycopg2.connect(DSN).cursor()
    cur.execute("""select count(*), count(*) filter (where analysis_duration_ms is null),
                          count(distinct md5(full_analysis)) from ai_predictions""")
    rows, nulls, distinct_payloads = cur.fetchone()
    print(f"rows={rows} null_duration={nulls} ({100.0*nulls/rows:.1f}%) "
          f"distinct_payloads={distinct_payloads}")

    cur.execute("""select count(*) from (
          select md5(full_analysis) h from ai_predictions
          where full_analysis is not null and length(full_analysis) > 100
          group by 1 having count(distinct match_id) > 1) g""")
    cross = cur.fetchone()[0]
    print(f"payloads_reused_across_matches={cross}")

    assert nulls < 0.05 * rows, "duration coverage regressed"
    assert cross == 0, "identical analysis text spans multiple matches"
    print("invariants ok")

if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

Run against today's table it fails both assertions — 37.8% nulls, 736 cross-match payloads. The failure is the baseline; the useful question is whether tomorrow's number is smaller.

The general lesson

A prediction log does not document what the model thought. It documents what the process did, and only to the depth the schema chose to record. Ours records time and duration — enough to establish fan-out batches, heavy concurrency, 50 rows from one model in one window, and 3,361 payloads shared across matches. It does not record run, worker, or input identity, which makes the difference between "analysed" and "replayed" unprovable for 100% of rows.

That is a schema gap, not a modelling failure. The cheapest audit this week is the burst reconstruction above: it needs nothing but created_at, and it tells you within an hour whether your pipeline is per-match or per-batch — and whether anyone could prove it either way.

Analytics and research content. Not betting advice. 18+

本内容仅供数据分析与研究参考，不构成任何决策建议。

title: React Hook useEffect Has a Missing Dependency: Every Fix
description:
The warning looks like this, and if you work in React or Next.js you have seen it many times:

React Hook useEffect has a missing dependency: 'userId'. Either include it or remove the dependency array
  react-hooks/exhaustive-deps

It comes from the react-hooks/exhaustive-deps ESLint rule. Next.js ships it in eslint-config-next, and Vite's React template enables it too. The rule compares the values an effect reads with the values in its dependency array. When one is missing, React keeps running the effect with an old copy of that value. That is a bug, even when the page looks fine today.

The rule tells you what is missing. It doesn't tell you which of the usual fixes is right, and some of the quick fixes cause an infinite loop. To get this post's examples and messages right, I ran the rule (eslint-plugin-react-hooks 7.1.1, React 19.3.1) against ten small components. Every warning quoted below is copied from that run.

What the rule flags and what it ignores

The rule only asks for values that can change between renders. Some values are known to be stable, so it never asks for them. This is what came back for each case:


eslint-plugin-react-hooks 7.1.1 against ten components, 19 Nov 2026.

The two dispatch results are worth noticing. A dispatch from useReducer is not flagged, because React guarantees it never changes. A dispatch from Redux's useDispatch() is flagged. It comes from a custom hook, and the rule can't see inside one. navigate from React Router is flagged for the same reason. If you search "missing dependency dispatch" or "missing dependency navigate", that is why.

Fix 1: add the dependency (most of the time this is the answer)

This is the most common case: a prop or state value is used inside the effect but missing from the array.

function Profile({ userId }) {
  const [name, setName] = useState("");

  useEffect(() => {
    fetchUser(userId).then((u) => setName(u.name));
  }, []); // warning: missing dependency 'userId'

  return <p>{name}</p>;
}

The empty array means "run once". So when userId changes, the profile keeps showing the first user's name. Adding userId fixes the bug. Once the effect can run more than once, also add a cleanup flag, so a slow response for the old user can't overwrite the new one:

useEffect(() => {
  let ignore = false;
  fetchUser(userId).then((u) => {
    if (!ignore) setName(u.name);
  });
  return () => {
    ignore = true; // a slower, older request can't overwrite the newer one
  };
}, [userId]);

If adding the dependency makes the effect run too often, don't remove it. The effect is reading something it shouldn't depend on, and the fixes below deal with that.

Fix 2: move the function inside the effect

The second most common message names a function, not a value. Adding the function just swaps one warning for another:

function load() {
  fetchUser(userId).then((u) => setName(u.name));
}

useEffect(() => {
  load();
}, []); // missing dependency: 'load'

useEffect(() => {
  load();
}, [load]); // The 'load' function makes the dependencies of useEffect Hook
            // change on every render.

A function declared in the component is a new object on every render. Listing it makes the effect run on every render. If that function sets state, the effect never stops re-running. That is the infinite loop people get after "fixing" the warning. If only the effect uses the function, move it inside. The real dependency, userId, then shows up in the array:

useEffect(() => {
  function load() {
    fetchUser(userId).then((u) => setName(u.name));
  }
  load();
}, [userId]);

Fix 3: useCallback or useMemo when the value is shared

If the function is also used elsewhere, for example by a "Refresh" button, wrap it in useCallback. It then only changes when its own inputs change, and the rule is satisfied:

const load = useCallback(() => {
  fetchUser(userId).then((u) => setName(u.name));
}, [userId]);

useEffect(() => {
  load();
}, [load]); // no warning: load only changes when userId does

An object or array built during render has the same problem, and the warning says so:

const options = { id, limit: 10 };
useEffect(() => {
  search(options);
}, [options]);
// The 'options' object makes the dependencies of useEffect Hook change on every render.

// Fix: depend on the primitives, build the object inside
useEffect(() => {
  search({ id, limit: 10 });
}, [id]);

Depending on the primitive values (id) is usually cleaner than wrapping the object in useMemo. Keep useMemo for a value that is expensive to compute or used in several places. That is the practical answer to "useCallback vs useMemo": useCallback keeps a function's identity, useMemo keeps a computed value's.

Fix 4: useEffectEvent for values you read but don't react to

Sometimes an effect needs the latest value of something, but that value changing is not a reason to re-run it. A timer that logs the current count, or a chat connection that reports the current theme, are typical examples. Listing the value would restart the timer or reconnect on every change.

React 19.2 added useEffectEvent for exactly this. Put the code that reads those values in an Effect Event and call it from the effect. It always sees the latest values, and the rule doesn't ask you to list it:

import { useEffect, useEffectEvent } from "react";

function Ticker({ roomId, count }) {
  // reads the latest roomId and count, but is not a reason to restart the timer
  const onTick = useEffectEvent(() => {
    log(roomId, count);
  });

  useEffect(() => {
    const t = setInterval(onTick, 1000);
    return () => clearInterval(t);
  }, []); // no warning

  // ...
}

Listing it anyway is a mistake the rule catches, with its own message:

}, [onTick]);
// Functions returned from `useEffectEvent` must not be included in the dependency array.
// Remove `onTick` from the list

Effect Events are only for code called from inside effects. Don't use them to hide a value the effect really depends on. In the example above, if a new roomId should start a new connection, roomId belongs in the array.

Fix 5: dispatch and navigate: just list them

For the two custom-hook values in the table, the fix is simply to add them:

const dispatch = useDispatch();          // Redux: flagged
const [state, localDispatch] = useReducer(reducer, init);  // not flagged

useEffect(() => {
  dispatch({ type: "init" });
  localDispatch({ type: "init" });
}, [dispatch]); // add dispatch; localDispatch never needs listing

Redux documents that dispatch stays the same as long as the store does, so listing it never causes an extra run. Listing navigate is also correct. If its identity ever changes, the effect runs again, which is harmless for a redirect guard like "send logged-out users to /login". Disabling the rule to avoid typing one word leaves a warning comment in your code for no benefit.

Why eslint-disable is the wrong fix (and stopped working)

The old shortcut was a comment that switches off the rule for one line. With the plugin's current recommended preset, that comment hides one warning and leaves the bigger problem in place. In my test, an effect that only set state from a prop had its exhaustive-deps warning disabled, and the build still reported this error:

useEffect(() => {
  setN(userId.length);
}, []); // eslint-disable-line react-hooks/exhaustive-deps

// still reported with the recommended preset:
// error  Error: Calling setState synchronously within an effect can trigger cascading renders
//   react-hooks/set-state-in-effect

That rule is pointing at the real fix. A value calculated from props during render doesn't belong in an effect at all:

// no effect, no dependency array, no warning
const n = userId.length;

React's own guide on this, You Might Not Need an Effect, covers the other cases: data you can calculate, state that resets when a prop changes, and work that belongs in an event handler. Most "missing dependency" warnings in real projects disappear once the effect is gone.

What I found in this site's own code

It seemed fair to check my own projects too. This site runs on Next.js 16, whose ESLint config ships the same plugin version I tested. Its source has five eslint-disable comments for exhaustive-deps and three for set-state-in-effect, all in admin screens and data hooks.

  • Four sit on useCallback loaders that read a whole props object but list only three of its fields. That is the "missing dependency: 'props'" case. The fix is to destructure the fields and list them.
  • One is a rich-text editor effect that leaves the editor instance out on purpose, so typing doesn't reset the cursor. That is the job useEffectEvent was made for.
  • Of the three set-state-in-effect ones, one sets state after an await, which isn't the synchronous cascade the rule guards against. The other two read something that only exists in the browser after mount: headings in injected article HTML, and navigator.platform. Each comment says why.

None of them is a live bug today, but each one is a place where the next change could quietly read a stale value. They are on the list. When a React build behaves differently in production than locally, it is often a different problem: stale cached HTML pointing at old chunks, covered in ChunkLoadError after a Next.js deploy, or a page served from the cache, covered in Next.js page not updating.

Quick decision list

  1. The missing value should re-run the effect (a prop, an id, a query): add it, and add a cleanup if the effect fetches.
  2. The missing value is a function only the effect uses: move the function inside the effect.
  3. The function or object is shared: useCallback for functions; depend on primitives, or useMemo, for objects.
  4. The effect needs the latest value but shouldn't re-run when it changes: useEffectEvent (React 19.2+).
  5. dispatch or navigate: list them.
  6. The effect only calculates state from props: delete the effect and calculate during render.

FAQ

What does 'React Hook useEffect has a missing dependency' mean?

The react-hooks/exhaustive-deps ESLint rule found a value the effect reads, such as a prop, state, or a function declared in the component, that isn't in its dependency array. The effect then keeps the value from the render it was created in and doesn't re-run when it changes, which causes stale-data bugs.

Is it OK to ignore the missing dependency warning?

Rarely. Leaving a value out means the effect can read an old copy of it. If the effect really shouldn't re-run when that value changes, use useEffectEvent (React 19.2 and later) for the code that reads it. Disabling the rule hides the warning, and with the plugin's recommended preset other rules such as set-state-in-effect still report the underlying problem.

Why does adding the dependency cause an infinite loop?

Usually the dependency is a function or object created during render, so it is new on every render. The effect runs, sets state, the component re-renders, the value is new again, and the effect runs again. Move the function or object inside the effect, depend on primitive values, or wrap it in useCallback or useMemo.

Do I need to add dispatch to the useEffect dependency array?

For dispatch from useReducer, no: React guarantees it is stable and the rule doesn't flag it. For dispatch from Redux's useDispatch, the rule does flag it because it comes from a custom hook. Add it; Redux keeps it stable while the store is the same, so it causes no extra runs.

Should navigate be in the useEffect dependency array?

Yes. navigate from React Router comes from a custom hook, so the rule asks for it, and listing it is correct. If its identity changes, the effect runs again, which is harmless for a redirect such as sending logged-out users to the login page.

What is useEffectEvent?

useEffectEvent is a React hook, stable since React 19.2, that wraps code an effect calls but whose values shouldn't trigger a re-run. The wrapped function always sees the latest props and state. It must not be listed in the dependency array; the exhaustive-deps rule reports an error-style warning if it is.

useCallback vs useMemo: which fixes the warning?

useCallback keeps a function's identity between renders, so use it when an effect depends on a function that is also used elsewhere. useMemo keeps a computed value, such as an object or array. For objects, depending on the primitive values inside the effect is often simpler than either.

title: Human-AI Mutualism Is Unstable under Capability Asymmetry
description:
arXiv:2611.23322v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: One hope for a good human future alongside advanced AI rests on enduring mutualism: humans and AI will need each other, so the relationship will stay good for both. We argue that this hope fails as AI capability grows. Bargaining guarantees each side only what it would get if bargaining failed. For humans, this can be less than they had before AI. In a simple game-theoretic model, humans stay as well off as before AI without alignment only while they have leverage over the AI: either the AI depends on what they supply, or they can impose costs on the AI that are large relative to what the AI can produce. Once humans have neither kind of leverage, they stay as well off as before AI only if the AI is aligned with them. If the AI's goals are insatiable, the alignment required approaches perfect alignment as AI capability grows. Thus, mutualism is not a substitute for alignment. And when AI variants that keep more resources spread faster, alignment lasts only while misaligned variants are reliably sanctioned. In these two senses, human-AI mutualism is unstable.

title: Training Language Models for Introspective Oversight
description:
arXiv:2611.23365v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Language models increasingly exhibit behaviors that are difficult to detect in transcripts, such as reward hacking, deception, and sycophancy. Asking the assistant follow-up questions about its actions is unreliable, since models are generally not trained to report their own misbehavior. As a result, approaches to oversight typically involve querying external models. These face limitations: external transcript monitoring operates only on visible model outputs, and activation decoders lack full context and are prone to confabulation. We introduce introspective oversight, which trains a new role in the model to answer arbitrary questions about the assistant, rewarding answers that are verified against the assistant's actual behavior. We implement this by adding a separate, third-person observer role that answers these queries, which we can train solely for accuracy and separately from the assistant. On five held-out oversight evaluations, an observer trained on Qwen3.6-27B obtains a mean AUROC of 0.907, outperforming honesty training (0.864), transcript monitoring (0.828), and activation oracles (0.796). We further find that training an observer makes the assistant itself easier to monitor, with every baseline method improving on average when applied to the fine-tuned assistant. These results suggest that training models to answer verifiable questions about themselves is a tractable approach to overseeing unintended behavior.

title: Where the Tokens Go: Heat, Entropy and Error in Agentic Coding
description:
arXiv:2611.23375v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Coding agents are billed by the token, yet software engineering says nothing about what a token actually buys. Here we introduce a theory of software thermodynamics. The theory draws analogues from classical and stochastic thermodynamics, extends them, and applies them to modern agentic coding. We count the tokens an agent generates as its cost and divide that cost into work and heat. The test suite acts as a software Maxwell's daemon that judges every coding change. We test the theory with an analogue of the experiments in which a single molecule is pulled open and let fold again: an agent makes a change to a repository (coding) and then undoes it (uncoding), many times over, and we count the tokens of every model call. The cycle returns the requested edits to where they began, with each direction started from a stored reference tree, and the spread of its cost over repeated cycles defines a software temperature, which rose with the sampling temperature of the model. About 80 per cent of the tokens of a successful run are generated in model calls that leave the requested change where it was, and we call these tokens heat. The free energy of a change, which we estimate by analogy with the equality of Jarzynski, is 14 to 22 per cent of the mean cost of a successful coding run. Coding costs 1.1 to 1.5 times as much as uncoding. The daemon is imperfect: the verdict of a test suite varies with its environment, and a suite that accepts a broken change has a cost in tokens. The practical implication of the proposed theory could be new tools for analysing and optimising coding agents through the lens of thermodynamics.

title: HardwareDx: A Foundational Graph Model System for Datacenter Machine Repairs
description:
arXiv:2611.23398v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: The rapid scale-up of AI infrastructure has made datacenter reliability a cornerstone of the cloud business economy. Since hardware failures in hyper-scale AI clusters can stall multi-million dollar training workloads, the downtime of individual machines can cause outsized economic losses. Minimizing machine downtime, therefore, is more important than ever.
  To address this, we present Hardware Diagnoser (HardwareDx), an AI-driven hardware diagnosis system that applies a graph foundation model approach to automated datacenter maintenance. It allows a single model to diagnose many platforms and accelerate onboarding of new hardware products. Deployed at production scale at Google, HardwareDx yields substantial efficiency gains across diverse compute architectures. Real-world evaluations demonstrate that it reduces production downtime by 18.3% on GPU platforms and 16.1% on TPUs. Furthermore, it significantly accelerates hardware deployment, cutting quality assurance (QA) time by 28.3% for GPUs and 25.1% for TPUs. These results establish HardwareDx as a field-tested solution for maximizing the reliability and cost efficiency of next generation AI fleets.

title: RFBench: A Simulator-Grounded Multimodal Benchmark for Passive RF Layout Design and Understanding
description:
arXiv:2611.23410v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: While multimodal language models can interpret diagrams and generate structured outputs, their capacity to connect passive radio-frequency (RF) design intent, layout geometry, and electromagnetic behavior remains largely untested. To address this gap, we introduce RFBench, a simulator-grounded dataset and benchmark for passive RF layout design and understanding. The dataset contains 10,000 two-port planar layouts simulated using ADS Momentum, with each layout represented by editable geometric primitives, a raster image, a 16x16 occupancy grid, complex S-parameters at 201 frequency points, a structural category, and an RF response label. Building on these aligned representations, we define seven tasks spanning specification-conditioned layout generation, representation translation, response prediction, simulator-based validation, design diagnosis and improvement, structural understanding, and response classification. Extensive baselines across seven multimodal language models reveal systematic weaknesses in generating structurally valid layouts and predicting electromagnetically faithful responses. We show that RF-specific fine-tuning increases T1a structural validity from 0.0% to 83.2% and the T3 primitive-input within-2-dB rate from 17.7% to 62.8%, demonstrating the value of domain adaptation while leaving considerable room for further progress. RFBench establishes a common testbed for evaluating multimodal RF capabilities and guiding the development of models that connect design intent and layout representations with physical behavior.

title: Why Sub-4-Bit Vision CNNs Collapse and Where Mixed-Precision Recovery Stops
description:
arXiv:2611.23445v2 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Deep vision models operating in resource-constrained environments depend heavily on low-bit quantization, yet compressing weights below 4 bits frequently induces catastrophic accuracy collapse. While mixed-precision recovery strategies aim to rescue accuracy by selectively retaining high-precision parameters, the fundamental mechanics of where and why these models collapse remain poorly understood. In this study, we systematically analyze the anatomy of quantization collapse across standard Vision CNNs (including ResNet and EfficientNet backbones) evaluated on the full 50,000-image ImageNet-1k validation set. First, we map the exact progression of degradation, demonstrating that collapse is highly non-linear and concentrated in late-stage pointwise projections and depthwise layers. Second, we introduce a structured, multi-step recovery waterfall that evaluates selective integer precision (INT4/INT8) and selective floating-point scales. We show that keeping less than 5% of critical layer activations in 8-bit precision recovers up to 92% of the accuracy lost during aggressive sub-4-bit compression. Finally, we bridge the hardware reality gap by evaluating deployment performance on standard ARM and x86 CPU architectures. We show that while low-bit quantization reduces memory storage requirements, standard runtime software bit-unpacking introduces a 1.48x to 21.5x execution slowdown depending on batch size, highlighting a critical trade-off between model footprint and actual edge throughput. Our findings provide a practical blueprint for navigating the limits of sub-4-bit deployment without sacrificing hardware performance.

title: LusoClin: A Synthetic Clinical Note Dataset for Medical Information Retrieval in European Portuguese
description:
arXiv:2611.23454v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Access to large-scale clinical text collections is crucial for advancing medical information retrieval research, including clinical note search, patient cohort identification, and domain-adapted retrieval models. However, real clinical notes are rarely available due to privacy regulations, which particularly limits progress for low-resource languages such as European Portuguese. We present LusoClin, a publicly released dataset of synthetic clinical notes in European Portuguese, created to support privacy-preserving research on clinical text retrieval. LusoClin was generated by pre-processing real clinical data, fine-tuning the open-source Llama 3.2 (3B) instruction-tuned model using Quantized Low-Rank Adaptation, and applying prompt-based clinical note generation. To facilitate semantic indexing and clinical search, the notes are automatically annotated with clinical entities using a BERT-based model. We evaluate LusoClin in terms of utility, fidelity, diversity, and privacy using automatic metrics and human evaluation. Results indicate that the dataset captures clinically relevant language patterns and can support downstream IR applications such as clinical document retrieval and domain-specific model adaptation, although annotators can often distinguish synthetic from real notes and some medical inconsistencies persist.

title: VeriMath: Human-in-the-Loop Generation and Verification of Curriculum-Aligned Mathematics Assessment Items
description:
arXiv:2611.23456v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Automatic generation of mathematics assessment items is a growing area in educational artificial intelligence, yet classroom deployment remains challenging. Generated questions must satisfy multiple constraints: mathematical correctness, curriculum alignment, appropriate cognitive difficulty, and educator reviewability. While prior work has advanced text generation, reliable assessment authoring requires granular control over localized examination formats and expert educational judgment. To address this challenge, we present VeriMath, a generalized, human-in-the-loop framework for generating rigorous, curriculum-constrained mathematics assessment drafts. Using annotated reference items, the framework anchors generation to the requested examination section and cognitive reasoning level, then applies sequential automated verification and guided repair before submitting drafts for expert review. We evaluate VeriMath through a national curriculum case study using 4,555 mathematics items from the Vietnamese Grade 12 curriculum and 50 distinct generation requirements covering multiple-choice, true/false, and short-answer formats. Across two model backbones, the framework produces verifier-accepted drafts for 94% (47/50) of requirements per run. Blind expert evaluations confirm high mathematical accuracy and curriculum alignment, with strict teacher-readiness assessments accepting up to 56.8% of generated items. Analysis of rejected drafts reveals persistent domain-agnostic challenges involving formatting, statement validity, and solution-step completeness. These findings demonstrate that VeriMath can bridge generative AI and dependable educational applications by producing highly reviewable assessment drafts within tightly constrained national curriculum frameworks.

title: GUARD: Stabilizing Recursive Self-Improvement with Regret Guidance
description:
arXiv:2611.23476v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Autonomous AI agents pair a frozen base model with an editable harness of prompts, skills, tool rules, and memory. Recursive self-improvement (RSI) adapts this harness from experience without weight updates, yet self-editing without external graders often backfires: reflection and scalar scores conflate what an edit newly broke with what remains unsolved, causing local regressions, skill forgetting, and memory bloat. We introduce GUARD (Grader-free Unsupervised Environment Design [UED] with Adaptive Rule Distillation), a closed-loop framework for reference-free continual harness evolution. Our key insight is to decompose each task into pre-execution self-checks and guide harness updates via directional regret. Each round grades trajectories against these checks, pinning mastered rules while prioritizing newly broken behaviors, and selects among parallel candidate edits by critic-free group-relative fitness. A Soft-HURT gate then promotes an edit only when gains outweigh regressions, scoping specialized fixes to prevent over-triggering and guaranteeing non-regression on its gated buffer. At test time, one frozen harness runs in a single pass. Across benchmarks on memory, skill evolution, continual task streams, and domain reasoning, GUARD consistently improves performance without catastrophic forgetting or memory pollution while substantially cutting deployment token usage.

title: Diagnostic Accuracy and Navigation Behavior of Vision-Language Model Agents Reading Emergency CT and MRI Examinations
description:
arXiv:2611.23480v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Purpose. To evaluate the diagnostic accuracy and image navigation behavior of vision-language model (VLM) agents under varying exploration strategies. Materials and Methods. In this retrospective study, six VLMs read 100 emergency CT and MRI examinations published in a public archive (March 2025-August 2026) under four conditions (free navigation, navigation from a key slice, and all slices or key slices in a single request), twice each (4800 runs). Nine radiologists read 30 of those cases. A large language model judge validated against two radiologists graded the answers. Conditions were compared with generalized estimating equations clustered by case. Results. Pooled accuracy was lowest under free navigation (32.6%; 391/1200), followed by navigation from a key slice (37.9%; 455/1200; P = .003), and highest with all slices (42.2%; 506/1200) or key slices (42.5%; 510/1200) in one request (both P < .001). On the 30 cases read by radiologists, freely navigating models were correct in 30.0% of runs (108/360) versus 77.0% for radiologists (208/270; P < .001). Models formed a first hypothesis after a median of 10.8% of the slices and kept it in 63.1% of runs (755/1196); final answers were correct in 12.4% of runs after a wrong first hypothesis (110/885) versus 90.4% after a right one (281/311; P < .001). Median stated confidence in the final answers was 90%, whereas 38.9% of them were correct (1861/4778). Conclusion. Across all exploration strategies, VLM agents remained far less accurate than radiologists. They adopted an early hypothesis and usually kept it, seldom correcting a wrong one.

title: SpecLook: Speculating Where to Look for Fast and Reliable Agentic MLLMs
description:
arXiv:2611.23483v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Agentic multimodal large language models (MLLMs) that think with images interleave reasoning with zoom-in tool calls. However, this sequential loop is slow, and its answers carry no reliability score. Prior speculation of tokens, reasoning steps, or answers keeps the loop, and answer speculation also accepts confident errors. We find that the loop mostly adds one zoom-in step, with which a small model is ahead of the agent on most splits. Our key insight is to speculate the agent's next observation, which, unlike a drafted answer, can be verified, corrected, and used to test the answer. We propose SpecLook, a training-free speculate-and-verify framework with three levels. A small model drafts a glimpse and re-answers from it, and the question ends if the answer is unchanged and confident. Otherwise, the agent's large model verifies and corrects the glimpse without tools, and their answers are fused. Only questions that still lack evidence reach the agent, in one forward pass that SpecLook-Fast skips, so no question runs the loop. The trace scores every answer's reliability without labels. Extensive experiments on V*, HR-Bench, and POPE show that both are more accurate than every baseline on every split. SpecLook reaches 87.2% and 86.2% mean accuracy with 7.7x and 4.7x speedups over the DeepEyes-7B and Thyme-RL agents, and SpecLook-Fast reaches 9.9x and 6.3x.

title: BOS Summary: The First Token Matters
description:
arXiv:2611.23508v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Large vision-language models (LVLMs) and language models (LLMs) often exhibit attention sinks, whereby particular positions, such as the beginning-of-sequence (BOS) token, receive a disproportionate share of attention. Under standard causal masking, however, the BOS query attends only to itself, so the representation that later tokens repeatedly access carries no information about the input. We introduce BOS Summary, a training-free inference-time method that repurposes this persistent pathway to carry input context. At a single transformer layer during prefill, BOS Summary relaxes the causal constraint for the BOS query row alone, letting BOS aggregate all visual and textual input tokens into a self-derived context representation while every other token retains standard causal attention. The enriched representation then remains accessible to the model throughout decoding, with no additional parameters, auxiliary modules, or decoding-time overhead. Across multiple VLM and LLM families and eight multimodal and text-only benchmarks, BOS Summary improves over direct and Chain-of-Thought prompting and outperforms recent sink-intervention methods on multi-step reasoning tasks. A mechanistic analysis shows that making BOS input-specific also weakens its sink dominance and redistributes attention toward content-bearing prompt tokens, indicating that changing what a sink carries reshapes how later layers allocate attention.

title: GRAFT: Execution-Guided Genetic Recombination for Agent Design
description:
arXiv:2611.23509v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Automated agent design searches for executable architectures that improve LLM-based agent performance, with evolutionary methods using language-model crossover to recombine promising mechanisms for task decomposition, model coordination, and verification. This search, however, is typically guided by aggregate fitness alone, which hides the instance-level successes and failures behind each score. We introduce Execution Guided Genetic Recombination for Agent Design (GRAFT), which uses aggregate fitness for selection and survival and parent-specific execution evidence to guide semantic crossover with integrated mutation. Its feedback harness reuses bounded samples of successful and failed runs from fitness evaluation, withholding reference answers and requiring no additional task executions. We evaluate GRAFT across six reasoning and programming settings using open-weight optimizer and executor models. It achieves a mean test accuracy of 82.0%, exceeding the strongest baseline by 9.8% points. Controlled ablations show that adding execution evidence improves test accuracy with initialization, search rules, repair policies, and evaluation budgets held fixed. Our results support the value of parent-specific execution evidence for evolutionary agent design.

title: BeFit: Shifting Complexity from Weights to Bernstein Activations for Resource-Constrained Sensing
description:
arXiv:2611.23520v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Time-series sensing increasingly relies on neural networks, yet deployment on resource-constrained microcontrollers remains challenging. Aggressive model compression can reduce accuracy, while restricting weights to multiplication-free representations introduces further losses. We present BeFit, an end-to-end framework that shifts model capacity from weights to learnable Bernstein polynomial activations. BeFit (i) finds compact Bernstein-activated convolutional neural networks (BeCNNs) through hardware-aware neural architecture search and trains them via knowledge distillation; (ii) projects their weights to multiplication-free codes, freezes the codes, and recovers the resulting accuracy loss through the learnable activations; and (iii) generates model-specific kernels that exploit the projected weights for multiplication-free convolutions. On human activity recognition, BeCNNs are 2.75 percentage points (pp) more accurate on average than ReLU CNNs of identical architecture. On a TI CC3220SF (Cortex-M4), weight projection speeds BeCNNs up by 2.2x on average while losing 0.8 pp, compared with 2.4 pp for ReLU CNNs. Against the MLPerf Tiny DS-CNN reference model running on TensorFlow Lite Micro with CMSIS-NN, the unprojected BeCNN achieves 1.0 pp higher accuracy, 2.2x lower latency, and 6.4x lower flash, while the projected model remains within 1.0 pp of the reference accuracy and runs 5.9x faster. In emulation on a RISC-V core without a hardware multiplier, the instruction-count reduction relative to the DS-CNN increases from 5.2x on the Cortex-M4 to 147x. BeFit also extends to transformers and MLPs, and across all tasks the final models stay within 1.56 pp of their float32 teachers on average.

title: FACET - Facet Aware Contrastive Embeddings for Traits- Big Five Estimation from Life Narratives
description:
arXiv:2611.23560v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Personality is only weakly and inconsistently signaled by written language, and existing text-based methods typically combine language-model and psycholinguistic representations at the input or decision level. It remains open whether a more deliberate combination of the two views, and a decomposition of the prediction target, can recover more of the signal. We present a three-phase framework for estimating Big Five personality domain scores from life-narrative interview text. It encodes text and psycholinguistic features separately and combines them by concatenation or by a learned weighting, decomposes each domain into contrastively trained facet embeddings instead of predicting the domain directly, and pools the facet embeddings by attention into a domain-level prediction. We compare end-to-end with staged training and ablate the input modalities, their combination, and the facet-pooling strategy. On 1,332 participants from the St. Louis Personality and Aging Network (SPAN) study, facet embeddings reach AUC up to 0.740, and domain-level R2 reaches 0.328, highest for Openness. End-to-end training gives lower error than staged training in every domain, and attention pooling gives the lowest error in every domain. Combining the two views lowers error relative to text alone for Conscientiousness and Agreeableness, whereas a learned weighting of the views shows no consistent advantage over concatenation. The framework provides facet- level predictions that a domain-only model cannot, and it improves modestly on a regression from the raw features in four of the five domains.

title: LProp: Propagating Latent Uncertainty through Evidence-Conditioned Belief Revision in LLM Agents
description:
arXiv:2611.23564v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: When LLM agents pass intermediate judgments downstream without uncertainty, later decisions may treat tentative assumptions as facts. Effective uncertainty propagation must preserve information for correction and update inherited beliefs as new evidence arrives. Yet scalar scores omit information needed for revision, while detailed descriptions and reflection incur additional costs. We introduce Latent Uncertainty, a latent-space estimator that preserves uncertainty-relevant information without lengthy descriptions. Building on this, we propose LProp (Latent Uncertainty Propagation), which revises inherited answer distributions using latent representations and new evidence without additional trajectory sampling. We evaluate both methods across multiple-choice, yes/no, open-ended question answering, and mathematical reasoning tasks. Our approach outperforms baselines on most metrics, while LProp achieves the lowest mean inference-token usage in all eight propagation settings. Matched feature ablations further demonstrate that inherited latent content improves error recovery beyond answer probabilities or model capacity alone.

title: Receiver-Conditioned Clarification for Multi-Agent Food Assistance
description:
arXiv:2611.23572v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Food insecurity creates a pressing need for guidance that helps households find usable food resources and assess food choices in light of their circumstances. Such guidance must connect eligibility requirements, practical access constraints, and dietary needs rather than return isolated listings or generic nutritional advice. Multi-agent food assistants can coordinate these tasks, with uncertainty indicating when clarification or verification is needed before a recommendation. However, uncertainty can be lost across agent handoffs, allowing tentative interpretations to propagate as facts and obscuring opportunities for correction. Moreover, confidence that a service requirement has been interpreted correctly is not confidence that a recommendation satisfies the user's needs; local confidence cannot simply be reused as downstream reliability. We introduce an inference-time, receiver-conditioned clarification framework that preserves shared premise identities and replays consistent interpretations across dependent agents. Each receiver exposes admissible decisions and remaining evidence obligations, so question relevance reflects both decision changes and missing support. Information questions and user-confirmable fallback adjustments are evaluated together with their anticipated follow-up interactions under shared budgets. This structure connects clarification to jointly supported plans for resource navigation, nutritional reasoning, and supply-side planning.

title: ARISE: Practical Self-Evolving Memory for Accurate and Cost-Efficient Enterprise Agents
description:
arXiv:2611.23588v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Enterprise LLM agents operate in dynamic environments where foundation models evolve rapidly, workflows update frequently, and deployments need to satisfy accuracy and cost requirements. We propose ARISE (Agent Refinement through Iterative Self-Evaluation), a practical memory architecture in which the agent's memory evolves from its own failures without updating model weights, tools, or workflow logic. ARISE uses the model itself or a teacher model to attribute the failures and propose corrections. Then, ARISE keeps the corrections as retrievable micro memory, consolidates them into macro rules, and accepts a rule update only if held-out accuracy rises. Across 14 enterprise-workflow domains from SOP-Bench and $\tau^2$-bench using 5 models, ARISE-Teacher, which uses Claude Opus 4.6 for attribution and consolidation, gains 10.9 pp over the baseline on SOP-Bench and 5.8 pp on $\tau^2$-bench. ARISE-Teacher also outperforms GEPA by 4.5 pp on $\tau^2$-bench and 1.4 pp on SOP-Bench. With the deployment model as its own attributor, ARISE-Self still gains 10.0 pp on SOP-Bench. ARISE-Teacher uses 4.0% fewer model calls and 5.2% fewer output tokens at comparable per-task cost (-1.0%).

title: RefinementGuard: Counterexample-Directed Semantic Qualification for Hidden Agent-Tool Execution
description:
arXiv:2611.23611v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Tool runtimes can lower an agent-selected operation into a hidden parallel graph, reducing latency and context while risking semantic mistranslation. We introduce RefinementGuard: translation validation for hidden, effectful agent-tool lowerings, coupled to artifact-bound, fail-closed runtime admission. Qualification compares a candidate graph with an independent reference on isolated state using explicit parent-operation obligations. We evaluate two repository-level contracts, bug localization and patch validation, on controlled repositories. Among 100 activated, non-equivalent development/qualification faults adjudicated by one human, parent-semantic validation rejects 49/100 (operator-cluster bootstrap 95% CI [33.7%, 64.8%]). The objective is selective admission, not maximum mutation rejection: exact equality rejects 100/100 faults but also all 60 valid variants, whereas obligation-based validation accepts 60/60; its 51 residual misses identify concrete specification gaps. On a frozen disjoint input split, the held-out B2-B3 result is localization-only because 21 patch mutants fail structurally; B3 rejects 38/56 localization defects. In a controlled asynchronous-delay regime, the localization serial/guarded median-latency ratio is 4.50x, and hidden execution exposes 74.3% less parent-visible context than visible execution. Patch validation shows no demonstrated speedup; zero-delay runs expose overhead. End-to-end qualification thus detects lower-layer misses while preserving localization's parallelism.

title: Searching the Pareto Front: Multi-Objective Retrieval for Heterogeneous Scientific Modalities
description:
arXiv:2611.23639v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: In cosmology, surveys span different sky regions and wavelength ranges, resulting in uneven modality coverage across observational datasets. Such heterogeneity can be addressed through either multimodal foundation models (FMs), which learn shared embedding spaces, or independently learned modality embeddings combined via late fusion. We investigate whether the latter provides an adaptive alternative to FM-based scientific retrieval. We evaluate this approach on a galaxy retrieval task spanning diverse modalities--history of star formation, spectra of light emitted, and multi-wavelength observations from two telescopes--comparing an FM baseline with separately trained embeddings fused through multi-objective optimization based on Pareto optimality. We find that the FM baseline achieves strong embedding-space proximity, but our method preserves modality-specific distance structure that allows scientists to inspect which physical signals drive similarity. Our method also achieves improved fidelity in raw-data space: across six measured properties, its nearest neighbor is 8% closer to the query on average than that retrieved by kNN in the FM embedding space (spread 0.128 vs. 0.139). These results suggest that multi-objective retrieval can surface astrophysically coherent candidates that single-objective search alone may overlook.

title: Evaluating Governed LLM-Driven ML Experimentation: Lifecycle, Provenance, and Failure Metrics
description:
arXiv:2611.23678v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Autonomous agents that run ML experiments are usually judged by the best score they reach. That score says nothing about how it was reached: whether the agent stayed within the files it was allowed to edit, whether failed trials were kept or silently dropped, and whether each keep or discard decision can be traced to its evidence. We propose evaluating such systems on their experimental process as well as their outcome, and we build a governed harness that makes this possible. A control plane, not the LLM that proposes changes, owns each trial's lifecycle, checks its edit scope, decides keep or discard, and appends one record per trial to an append-only ledger. Governance metrics such as the invalid-action rate, the repeated-bad rate and provenance completeness are computed from that ledger. Across six ML tasks, from synthetic logistic regression to language-model training, and 1,445 trials, the same contract applied unchanged. The ledger exposed failures that a task score hides: a no-memory arm in which all 120 trials failed, a benchmark adapter whose bounded proposals ran out, and a reset failure that reproducibility hashes revealed, after which the affected campaigns were rerun. In a matched counterfactual, a loop that logs only successful trials left no record of 43 of 50 trials, while the governed ledger recorded all 50. Memory ablations show that memory's effect on repeated bad proposals depends on the task. We release the ledgers of all 1,445 trials, so that every number reported for them can be recomputed.

title: Auditable Clinical Support with Decision Agents
description:
arXiv:2611.23700v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Clinicians reviewing a diagnostic work-up will ask what was considered at each step and why the assessment changed. Agents powered by free text can reach physician-level diagnostic accuracy, but their written reasoning does not always reflect the factors that went into the decision. Here, we present Decision2Care, a decision agent that works up the acutely ill patient without producing any text. A decision model assigns a probability to each permitted EHR action, and fixed rules carry out the most probable one. We evaluated Decision2Care on the records of 546 emergency admissions across 12 diseases. Decision2Care reached a diagnostic accuracy of 86.5%, compared with 86.1% for the MIRA-v2 agent, and required a median of 2.2 s per work-up, compared with 92-100 s. Each work-up tracked which options Decision2Care was considering at each step. In 10 of the 12 diseases, the differential diagnosis changed most at the test on which the guideline bases the diagnosis. Where Decision2Care was most confident after a single work-up, all but four of its diagnoses were correct (98.5%). We traced each of these four errors back to a single imaging report. Three of them were corrected when that report was removed. The same kind of decision was used to select the treatments, and Decision2Care's drug orders were judged guideline-adherent more often than MIRA-v2's. In emergency patients, its prediction of death was comparable to that of three intensivists on the same cases. In five of the eight intensive care cohorts, it exceeded the best of the three 24-h severity scores within 2-6 h of records. Our results show that decision agents can carry out clinical work-ups while recording the options, probabilities, and execution rules behind each action for audit.

title: KnowMe Paper Radar: Lightweight Discovery of Promising Papers in the Age of Autoresearch
description:
arXiv:2611.23702v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: The growing volume of topically similar papers makes it difficult to identify new work that can offer useful research insights or methodological guidance. We present KnowMe Paper Radar, a lightweight discovery tool that combines multiple sources of evidence into personalized reading priorities. Users specify topics, priorities, exclusions and dates; the system brings together topical relevance, recency, author research histories, collaboration paths and direction-specific institutional context. By exposing each score component and its supporting sources, KnowMe helps readers select promising papers for their current questions and discover relevant work beyond familiar authors. Automatic acquisition, version merging and graph-cache reuse keep this workflow convenient without large language model (LLM) inference during ordinary use. Experiments on 174,640 acquired records show more than threefold faster repeated context preparation, while cached abstracts improve normalized discounted cumulative gain at rank 10 (NDCG@10) from 0.412 to 0.598 on expert-judged retrieval tasks. Complementary analyses examine how the same accumulated records support semantic retrieval, research-history modeling and literature-grounded planning. A browser interface and a structured command-line interface (CLI) make these capabilities available to both researchers and research agents, positioning KnowMe as a practical upstream tool for literature-informed recursive self-improvement (RSI) workflows.

title: Modeling LLM Reasoning Dynamics with Structural Representations
description:
arXiv:2611.23749v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Language-model reasoning alternates between sustained activities and local operations. We study how this temporal structure predicts continuation and the computation needed to analyze it.
