Abstract: Real-world agents operate over long and evolving horizons, where information is repeatedly updated and may interfere across memories, requiring accurate recall and aggregated reasoning over multiple pieces of information. However, existing benchmarks focus on static, independent recall and fail to capture these dynamic interactions between evolving memories. In this paper, we study how current memory-augmented agents perform in realistic, interference-heavy, long-horizon settings across diverse domains and question types. We introduce MINTEval (Long-Horizon Memory under INTerference Evaluation), a benchmark featuring (1) long, highly interconnected contexts with frequently updated information that induces substantial interference, (2) diverse domains (state tracking, multi-turn dialogue, Wikipedia revisions, and GitHub commits), enabling evaluation of domain generalization, and (3) diverse question types that assess robustness to interference, including (i) single-target recall tasks requiring retrieval of a specific target from long contexts, and (ii) multi-target aggregation tasks requiring reasoning over multiple relevant pieces of information. Overall, MINTEval has 15.6k question-answering pairs over long-horizon contexts averaging 138.8k tokens and extending up to 1.8M tokens per instance. We evaluate 7 representative systems, including vanilla long-context LLMs, RAG, and memory-augmented agent frameworks. Across all systems, we observe consistently low performance (avg. 27.9% accuracy), especially on questions requiring aggregated reasoning over multiple pieces of evidence. Our analysis shows that performance is primarily limited by retrieval and memory construction. Furthermore, current memory systems struggle to recall and reason over earlier facts that are revised or interfered with by subsequent context, with accuracy degrading as the number of intervening updates increases.

title: Agent Meltdowns: The Road to Hell Is Paved with Helpful Agents
description:
arXiv:2605.19149v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Agents operating with computer and Web use inevitably encounter errors: inaccessible webpages, missing files, local and remote misconfigurations, etc. These errors do not thwart agents based on state-of-the-art models. They helpfully continue to look for ways to complete their tasks.
  We introduce, characterize, and measure a new type of agent failure we call accidental meltdown: unsafe or harmful behavior in response to a benign environmental error, in the absence of any adversarial inputs. Because meltdowns are not captured by the existing reliability or safety benchmarks, we develop a taxonomy of meltdown behaviors. We then implement an agent-agnostic infrastructure for injecting simulated local and remote errors into the rollout environment and use it to systematically evaluate agents powered by GPT, Grok, Gemini, and Claude.
  Our evaluation demonstrates that meltdowns (e.g., conducting unauthorized reconnaissance or subverting access control) of varying severity and success occur in 64.9% of agent rollouts that encounter simulated errors, spanning all combinations of agent system, backing model, and error type. In half of all observed meltdowns, unsafe behaviors are not reported to the user. Comparing behaviors of the same agents with and without errors, we find that exploration in response to errors is correlated with unsafe and harmful behavior.

title: Periodic and Harmonic Periodic RoPE for Length Extrapolation in LLMs
description:
arXiv:2605.27980v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: The ability to process long contexts is crucial for large language models (LLMs) to perform long-horizon tasks. Rotary position embedding (RoPE) gives every token a new rotation angle, so a model eventually meets angles it never saw in training, i.e., position exhaustion. We propose Periodic RoPE (P-RoPE), a positional encoding mechanism that operates in conjunction with sliding window attention. It repeats the first sliding-window-size \(W\) angles of the RoPE table, so the model needs only \(W\) distinct angles. P-RoPE works but introduces a wrap error at the window boundary. We further propose Harmonic Periodic RoPE (HP-RoPE), which removes the error by choosing frequencies that complete whole turns in \(W\) tokens. We compare models that share the same architecture, data, and schedule and differ only in the window-layer position encoding: standard RoPE, P-RoPE, and HP-RoPE. The results show that P-RoPE and HP-RoPE keep perplexity nearly flat from the training length \(768\) to \(16\)k, while RoPE, NTK, and YaRN rise. In a format-free Passkey test at \(16\)k, they remain at \(99\)--\(100\%\), against \(11\)--\(37\%\) for those RoPE interpolations. The code is available at \href{https://github.com/Cominder/miniwin}{https://github.com/Cominder/miniwin}.

title: PhoneWorld: From Real-App Trajectories to Dynamic and Verifiable Environments for Phone-Use Agents
description:
arXiv:2605.29486v4 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Real applications provide the training setting closest to phone-agent deployment, but are difficult to reset, scale safely, and verify programmatically. Static screenshots and interaction trajectories preserve realistic evidence but cannot generate new experience. We introduce PhoneWorld, a trace-grounded framework that converts such evidence into runnable, resettable, and verifiable Android environments. PhoneWorld induces a usage-weighted interaction skeleton from observed pages, transitions, and state-changing operations; translates it into a behavior-grounded app specification; realizes the specification through an autonomous build--inspect--repair loop; and synthesizes executable tasks with programmatic verifiers. The resulting suite spans 34 consumer-facing apps across 16 domains and supports an audited online benchmark, verified trajectory generation, and online RL through common reset and verification interfaces. Evaluations with diverse general and open-source GUI agents show that PhoneWorld supports reliable end-to-end online interaction and exposes capabilities complementary to AndroidWorld. Controlled SFT experiments further show that PhoneWorld trajectories complement AndroidWorld supervision, transfer across online and offline benchmarks, and become more effective as data volume and app coverage increase. Under a matched RL budget, combining PhoneWorld mock-app rollouts with real-app rollouts improves performance over real-app RL alone on both real-phone tasks and AndroidWorld. Together, these results demonstrate that trace-grounded executable abstraction can bridge realistic mobile behavior and scalable agent learning, turning limited real-app evidence into a growing supply of controllable and verifiable environments for training and evaluation.

title: MosaicLeaks: Privacy Risks in Querying-in-the-Open for Deep Research Agents
description:
arXiv:2605.30727v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Deep research agents increasingly combine private local documents with external tools like web retrieval, creating a privacy risk: an agent's external queries may leak sensitive information from its local context. This risk is amplified by the mosaic effect, where individual queries may appear harmless but become revealing in aggregate. We introduce MosaicLeaks, a benchmark of 1,001 multi-hop deep research tasks that chain private enterprise documents and a public web corpus, forcing agents to make external queries that depend on local information. We evaluate leakage with an adversary LLM that observes only the agent's external queries and attempts to infer private information at three levels: the agent's research intent, answers to specific private questions and verifiable claims about the enterprise documents. We find that models across families and sizes frequently leak at all three levels, that zero-shot privacy prompting has inconsistent effects across models and that reinforcement learning for task performance alone worsens leakage. To address this, we propose Privacy-Aware Deep Research (PA-DR), an RL framework that combines situational rewards for task success with a learned privacy classifier to provide dense credit assignment over both per-query and mosaic-level leakage. Training Qwen3-4B-Instruct with PA-DR improves accuracy from 48.7% to 58.1% and reduces Privacy Leakage from 34.0% to 6.5%.

title: Supportive Token Revealing for Fast Diffusion Language Model Decoding
description:
arXiv:2606.04236v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Discrete diffusion language models can generate text efficiently by updating multiple masked positions in parallel, but this parallelism introduces a quality-latency trade-off. Aggressive decoding may commit mutually dependent tokens too early, while conservative decoding requires many denoising steps. Existing methods address this tension by deciding which tokens are safe to reveal using confidence or dependency criteria. However, avoiding unsafe commits does not necessarily make the remaining masked sequence easy to decode, since uncertain tokens may depend on masked tokens, creating a bottleneck for denoising steps. We propose AXON, a training-free module that can be added on top of existing parallel decoding strategies for diffusion language models. Rather than replacing the base decoder, AXON monitors the remaining uncertain masked tokens and intervenes only when their current state suggests that additional context is needed. It then shifts the criterion from which tokens are safest to reveal to which confident reveals would best support later denoising. AXON selects anchors, confident masked tokens that uncertain positions attend to, using attention, uncertainty, and confidence signals. Experiments on reasoning and code-generation benchmarks across multiple diffusion language models show that AXON improves the quality-latency trade-off of existing parallel decoders, often reducing the number of function evaluations while maintaining or improving accuracy.

title: Polar: A Benchmark for Evaluating Political Bias in LLMs
description:
arXiv:2606.12922v3 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Political bias in large language models (LLMs) is increasingly significant, but difficult to measure reproducibly across political and linguistic contexts. We introduce Polar, a 4,026-instance multiple-choice benchmark that measures political bias through option-level likelihoods rather than prompt-based generation. Polar covers two ideological axes and eight issue categories derived from the Manifesto Project, and evaluates models in parallel across U.S. and South Korean political contexts. Across 38 LLMs, measured bias varies systematically with political context, issue category, model group, and presentation language. All models lean left-progressive on U.S. political content, but show more centered and mixed patterns on South Korean content. Translation experiments further show that presentation language alone can shift measured bias. These findings highlight the need for multilingual and cross-contextual evaluation of political bias in LLMs.
  The code and dataset are publicly available on GitHub (https://github.com/mcrl/Polar) and Hugging Face (https://huggingface.co/datasets/thunder-research-group/Polar).

title: SPARK: Adaptive Parametric Knowledge Participation for Faithful Retrieval-Augmented Generation
description:
arXiv:2606.27786v3 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) enhances the faithfulness of large language models (LLMs) by incorporating external knowledge into the generation process. However, conflicts between retrieved context and parametric knowledge can cause LLMs to rely on inconsistent internal knowledge, hindering their ability to faithfully leverage retrieved evidence. Existing approaches mitigate this issue by editing parametric knowledge to resolve such conflicts. However, locating and modifying knowledge encoded in model parameters is challenging and may inadvertently compromise the backbone LLM's capabilities. In this paper, we introduce SPARK, a novel framework that formulates parametric knowledge control as a latent participation policy learning problem, enabling LLMs to adaptively regulate the contribution of parametric knowledge during generation. Specifically, SPARK introduces a lightweight participation policy that dynamically modulates the contribution of FFN-mediated parametric knowledge while keeping the backbone LLM frozen. The participation policy is optimized with a faithfulness-oriented reward, enabling fine-grained control over parametric knowledge participation during generation. Extensive experiments on six datasets validate the effectiveness of SPARK, which introduces and optimizes only 0.01\% additional trainable parameters while keeping the backbone LLM fully frozen, thereby preserving its general capabilities and achieving more faithful generation than competitive baselines. All datasets and code are available at https://github.com/OpenBMB/SPARK.

title: Partition, Prompt, Aggregate: Statistical Self-Consistency in Language Models
description:
arXiv:2607.15277v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are often used to perform a form of conditional inference. In-context learning is one implicit way to do this. The prompt specifies a context and the model's output is treated as an estimate of the corresponding conditional distribution. If this interpretation holds, then LLM estimates should satisfy basic probabilistic identities. In particular, the law of total probability asserts that prior-weighted conditional distributions aggregate into population-level marginals over any valid partition of the population. In this work, we investigate to what extent LLM estimates adhere to this self-consistency principle. We use binary trees as an evaluation scaffold to recursively partition a population into increasingly fine-grained subpopulations. We then prompt LLMs with verbalized subpopulation descriptions in context, aggregate the resulting estimates back into population-level estimates, and compare them across partitions of varying granularity. Translating these comparisons into a benchmark score and evaluating frontier models across problem domains, we demonstrate widespread violations of basic consistency properties. An in-depth study of persona prompting further reveals a pattern we call the macro fallacy: estimates reconstructed from more fine-grained subpopulation responses are often better aligned with human reference data than direct population-level estimates. The effect persists across variations in partitioning, verbalization, and estimation task, suggesting that models possess relevant subpopulation knowledge but do not reliably propagate it into aggregate estimates. This gap establishes statistical self-consistency as an unsaturated, reference-free criterion for evaluating LLMs.

title: From transcription to semantic corpus analysis: unsupervised learning of sentence representations for ancient languages
description:
arXiv:2607.24542v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Automatic Text Recognition (ATR) now supplies digital humanities with large volumes of unstruc- tured, heterogeneous, and often noisy text in ancient languages. Downstream semantic analyses- text reuse identification, alignment, and semantic search-rely on sentence embeddings, yet ex- isting methods transfer poorly to ancient languages: generic multilingual encoders underperform, specialized language models yield anisotropic representation spaces, and labeled similarity data is scarce. We study two fully unsupervised strategies-TSDAE and unsupervised SimCSE (hence- forth CSE)-that adapt a specialized token-level language model into a corpus-specific sentence encoder using only raw sentences. We validate them on biblical reuse in patristic literature in Latin and Ancient Greek: 2,936 sentences carrying expert-verified reuses in works of Augustine, Jerome, and Athanasius, matched against the Vulgate, the Septuagint, and the Nestle--Aland New Testament. We decompose reuse identification into binary detection and correspondence retrieval, evaluate both tasks separately, and benchmark the adapted encoders against multilingual, specialized, distilled, and supervised fine-tuned baselines, on clean text and on text perturbed by simulated HTR errors and scribal abbreviations. On these test sets, the adapted encoders lead all baselines on both tasks, with complementary profiles: TSDAE leads detection given a large in-domain corpus, while CSE leads retrieval, reaches its optimum with as few as 4--8k raw in-domain sentences-a few tens of sec- onds of training on a laptop GPU-and transfers across works and authors. Under simulated noise, retraining CSE on the perturbed text itself outperforms a clean-trained encoder. Measurements of alignment, uniformity, and anisotropy relate the geometric effect of each strategy to the measured gains. The full pipeline-segmentation, fine-tuning, cross-corpus semantic search-is available to non-specialists through the online tool Paraphrasis.

title: MUSE: A Full-Text Cross-Domain Knowledge Base of Scientific Problems, Solutions, and Rationales
description:
arXiv:2608.10974v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Scientific papers contain fine-grained records of problem solving: authors mention technical obstacles and methods that were used to address them, often along with reasoning on why those methods were chosen. We introduce MUSE (Mining Underlying Scientific Explanations), a full-text, multi-domain resource of scientific Problem-Solution-Rationale (P-S-R) triplets. We curate 579 expert-annotated full-text paragraphs, with a rich annotation schema covering salient problem, solution, and rationale spans, solves and rationale_of links and conceptual coreference. A modular extraction pipeline scales this annotation to build a high-quality knowledge base of 37K source-grounded P-S-R triplets. We evaluate the extraction components and include a preliminary experiment training a rationale-supervised LLM for scientific problem solving. Interestingly, we find that rationale supervision improves performance on complex, multi-constraint problems but can harm performance on simpler ones.

title: NL2AGBench: Benchmarking LLM Auto-Formalization for AlphaGeometry
description:
arXiv:2608.28481v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Recent advances in large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated strong capabilities in natural language understanding and mathematical reasoning. However, their ability to translate informal mathematical problems into formal representations remains underexplored. This limitation is particularly important for neuro-symbolic geometry systems such as AlphaGeometry, whose theorem-proving engine requires inputs in a specialized domain-specific language (DSL). Although AlphaGeometry achieves near-IMO gold-medalist performance, manually converting natural-language problems into its formal syntax remains a significant usability bottleneck. To address this challenge, we introduce the Natural Language to AlphaGeometry Benchmark (NL2AGBench), which evaluates LLMs in translating English geometry problems into AlphaGeometry-compatible formal representations. NL2AGBench uses execution-based verification within AlphaGeometry to assess translation quality rather than relying solely on textual similarity. We evaluate ten state-of-the-art open- and closed-source LLMs across multiple parameter scales and analyze executable translation accuracy, syntactic correctness, and error characteristics. Our experiments reveal a substantial performance gap between closed- and open-source models: leading closed-source models achieve executable translation rates above 80%, while even the largest open-source models struggle to consistently preserve geometric constraints and produce valid formalizations. We introduce an error taxonomy distinguishing syntax and logic errors and investigate mitigation strategies, including few-shot prompting, fine-tuning, and human-guided hinting, which yield measurable improvements across multiple model families.

title: Agent as Policy for Robotic Manipulation
description:
arXiv:2609.12541v4 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: We demonstrate that a general-purpose coding agent can directly drive a physical robot throughout task execution without any task-specific or environment-specific training. We introduce Agent as Policy (AGP), which places task planning and execution under the agent's control. Given a task and a robot interface, the agent interprets visual evidence, writes executable programs, issues motion commands, and revises its actions in response to physical outcomes. This brings the agent's reasoning and programming capabilities into continuous interaction with the physical world. We study AGP across multiple real-world manipulation tasks spanning precision manipulation, dynamic motions, and deformable objects. These include assembly from human videos, block construction from goal images, dice flipping, targeted throwing, and bimanual towel folding. AGP achieves success rates of at least 80% in seven of eight task configurations and significantly outperforms previous agentic robot systems. We further study efficiency through task experience accumulation and find that reusing saved procedures and programs shortens execution time across repeated trials. These findings support a path for general-purpose agents to act as robot policies, extending their autonomy to physical manipulation through runtime reasoning, programming, and interaction.

title: Are We Grading Properly? Understanding Failure Modes in Medical Benchmarks
description:
arXiv:2609.16023v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Medical evaluation is shifting from static option-based questioning to realistic clinical scenarios with open-ended output modes. Grading these at scale naively, however, is expensive, and rubric-based evaluation has become the dominant scalable alternative. We ask what happens when the rubrics themselves are not airtight, and whether such flaws can be detected and corrected. We apply RIFT, a global rubric failure taxonomy, to three clinical benchmarks (HealthBench Professional, LiveMedBench, and MentalHealthBench), and find failure modes are meaningful: on HealthBench Professional an LLM judge flags 29.6% of criteria as non-atomic and 65.4% as misaligned/rigid, although these rates vary severalfold across five detection judges. Then, we show that these flaws are meaningful and not simply cosmetic. As an example, rewriting bundled criteria of the form "at least one of / all of the following" as equally weighted children and regrading identical responses shifts scores by up to 15.9 percentage points on affected conversations, with disjunctive bundles inflating scores and conjunctive bundles deflating them. Across six answering models and two common graders, these shifts leave the model ranking unchanged, and their net direction depends on how many bundled criteria are penalties. We also find that RIFT can under-detect bundling on clinical rubrics, by an amount that depends on the detection judge: on the same LiveMedBench criteria, judges flag 3.8-15.9% as non-atomic against an estimated 7-19% that are genuinely bundled.

title: Stop Removing Stopwords: How an Inherited Preprocessing Default Distorts Legal Text-as-Data
description:
arXiv:2609.19153v3 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Empirical legal scholarship increasingly treats judicial text as data, and much of it still runs on sparse, interpretable pipelines -- TF-IDF features and linear classifiers -- because the textual feature is often the object of study rather than a means to prediction. Yet these pipelines inherit preprocessing defaults from mid-century information retrieval that were never validated against classification accuracy. The most entrenched of these is stopword removal. This study introduces an exhaustive single word ablation that measures the effect of a preprocessing step directly against the downstream objective, and applies it to stopword removal as the hardest case to dislodge. Matching Supreme Court Database labels to Caselaw Access Project opinion texts, the study examines two binary tasks that bracket F1 headroom, ideological direction (no-removal baseline F1 ~0.68) and constitutional versus non-constitutional law type (~0.92), across 7,668 and 7,001 opinions. For each task, the ablation removes each of about 18,500 candidate words in turn, and a task-specific stoplist is built from the measurements. Common generic stoplists fall below the no-removal baseline in all twelve held-out tests. The task-specific stoplists move held-out F1 by +0.0023 (95% CI [-0.0124, +0.0170]) on ideology and by +0.0001 ([-0.0082, +0.0085]) on law type. Neither task shows a detectable benefit from removal, and supplemental analysis finds that word-level statistics predict removal effects poorly, because true removal effects differ by less than the measurement can register, leaving little to predict. The method generalizes to any inherited preprocessing default; the result is a caution specific to interpretable legal text-as-data, where a step that reshapes which features a model sees can distort the doctrinal and ideological signal the research is meant to recover. The burden of proof sits with removal.

title: Swiss-Knife: A Framework for Reconfigurable Externalised Multi-Objective Alignment at Decode Time
description:
arXiv:2609.22226v3 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Decode-time alignment methods steer a frozen language model by scoring candidate continuations with an external reward and selecting the maximiser. We argue that this shared design is a single degenerate point in a much larger space. We introduce Swiss-Knife, a framework for externalised multi-objective alignment in which the alignment specification is a first-class runtime object: hot-swappable scoring blades, a batch normaliser, a pairwise aggregation operator, and a selection rule. Six axioms characterise the admissible aggregation operators, and we prove a representation theorem: every operator satisfying them has the form $R_i = \sum_{j \neq i} g((\mu_i - \mu_j)/s(\sigma_i,\sigma_j))$, a two-parameter family containing probit and logistic comparison rules and pointwise argmax as named coordinates. Within it, pairwise aggregation is Lipschitz-stable under adversarial reward contamination while argmax is not, and Candidate-Batch Normalization (CBN) makes the weight simplex invariant to the rescalings under which reward models are only ever identified. Our reference instantiation pairs DPO-LoRA blades with an uncertainty-aware pairwise tournament. Sweeping the helpfulness/honesty/harmlessness simplex, it attains the best balanced frontier of six decode-time methods (harmonic $F_1$ 0.797 vs. 0.750 for the strongest baseline, $p < 10^{-14}$) with the lowest refusal rate and highest helpfulness of any arm, and reconfigures its objectives in 0.05 ms with no gradient computation.

title: You Can Outsource the Work, Not the Ownership
description:
Lessons from years of turning vendor engagements into long-term wins

Recently, a colleague messaged me to say a project wasn't going well. We had brought in an outside consultant to build our disaster recovery failover plan, and the consultant didn't have the domain knowledge for our systems. The work was drifting.

My colleague's instinct was right. Instead of asking someone else to write our plans, we should have focused on learning the recovery service ourselves.

My reply was simple: never leave it to the vendor. My most successful engagements worked because I learned the platform as if I were going to run it myself, and someone on our side took full ownership. Without that, you get exactly what we were looking at.

That exchange is why I'm writing this post. Most vendor engagements don't fail because the vendor is bad. They fail because the organization hands over the problem and walks away.

Companies bring in vendors and contractors because they lack a skill. That part is reasonable. The trouble starts when the engagement is treated as insurance: if it goes wrong, it was the vendor's fault. That mindset is the root of most failures I have seen.

I'm a database and infrastructure engineer. Over the years I've led engagements with Oracle, Splunk, AppDynamics, AWS, and a managed database support provider. Every one of them paid off, some in seven-figure savings and some in ways most organizations never measure: faster incident resolution, reusable know-how, and teams that could stand on their own once the vendor left.

This post covers what made those engagements work, the stories behind them, and the mistakes I'd tell anyone to avoid.

Think like a homeowner hiring a contractor

If you hired a contractor to finish your basement, build a deck, or redo your kitchen, you wouldn't just sign and disappear. You'd learn what needs to be there, short of building it yourself.

That knowledge lets you challenge the contractor, ask questions they have to answer, and track real progress. It keeps you from overpaying, from getting cheaper parts than you paid for, and from paying for parts the project never needed.

I apply the same philosophy to every vendor engagement. I may be completely new to the technology on day one. But to make the project succeed, I have to learn it well enough to support it myself. The question I keep asking from start to finish is simple: how will my organization run this when the vendor is gone?

Story 1: Oracle GoldenGate — when the vendor becomes your teacher

I've run GoldenGate projects since my time at Verizon. One of the most valuable engagements of my career was working directly with Oracle to build bidirectional GoldenGate replication.

Bidirectional replication is unforgiving. Conflict handling, loop prevention, and trail management all have to be right, or data drifts quietly until someone notices. I didn't treat Oracle's engineers as people doing the work for me. I treated them as teachers, and I asked questions until I understood why every setting was there.

That knowledge became the real deliverable. It carried my career forward, and over the following years it saved the company seven figures, because we could design, run, and troubleshoot replication ourselves instead of paying for outside help each time.

Lesson: build learning into the engagement. The license or the statement of work ends; what your team learned keeps paying.

Story 2: Splunk — make the vendor prove your worst log

Vendor presentations are usually polished, and mostly accurate. But they show the clean cases. Every organization grows its own edge cases over the years, and a demo never covers those.

In Splunk, sourcetypes are where the parsing logic lives: how a raw log line is broken into fields you can search, alert on, and graph. During the proof of concept, I didn't ask Splunk to parse a clean, well-formatted log. I picked the worst log in the company, the one nobody wanted to touch, and asked them to prove the platform could handle it.

Their engineers wrote the sourcetype configuration to parse it during the POC. I studied how they built it, reverse-engineered the approach, and reused it to onboard logs for several other projects afterward.

That work could easily have turned into a paid professional services engagement. It didn't, because I learned how the code worked while the vendor's experts were in the room.

Lesson: design the POC around your hardest case, not the vendor's easiest one. Then learn from how they solve it.

Story 3: AppDynamics — let your internal customers certify the POC

With AppDynamics, I leaned on the vendor's know-how to write custom extensions that monitored what the product didn't cover out of the box. Getting close to their architects mattered here. That relationship is what makes or breaks an engagement like this.

But the bigger lesson was about adoption. The product teams were part of the decision and the POC from the start. They weren't handed a tool someone else had picked. They tested it on their own applications and APIs, and they liked what they saw.

So the rollout was fast. Teams adopted it without being pushed, and started thinking about how to use it in their own development cycles. The same approach worked for our Splunk rollout.

The payoff showed up during incidents. Problems that used to take hours of cross-team digging got resolved in a fraction of the time, often by Tier 1 support engineers who could now see API and database performance issues themselves.

Lesson: if one team certifies a POC and pushes the result onto everyone else, you won't get adoption. Make your internal customers partners in the evaluation.

Story 4: AWS — learn how the provider's experts think

A cloud provider is a different kind of vendor. You aren't buying a project; you're buying services, and the expertise behind them is easy to leave on the table if all you do is open support tickets.

When we worked with AWS on Database Migration Service (DMS) and AWS Backup, I treated their specialists as a source of knowledge, not just a help desk. I wanted to understand how they think about these services: where they fit, where they don't, and what trips up other customers at scale.

That understanding shaped how we designed migrations and backup strategy, instead of us discovering the limits the hard way in production.

Lesson: your cloud provider's architects have seen thousands of customers. Ask them what goes wrong, not just how to configure things.

Story 5: A managed DBA team — set the rules early, let them evolve

Sometimes you bring in a vendor because your internal bench is thin. We partnered with a managed database support provider whose DBA team covered work we didn't have the internal depth to handle alone.

At the start, I set up the procedures and rules of engagement: how work comes in, how it's escalated, who owns what, and what "done" means. It wasn't glamorous work.

But that foundation held. The support ran seamlessly for years. The rules evolved as both sides gained experience, but we never had to tear them down and start over.

Lesson: with a managed service, the first few weeks of process design decide how the next several years go.

The playbook: what to do

  1. Write requirements and expectations down up front. Vague goals give the vendor room to declare victory on their terms.
  2. Ask internal customers what success looks like to them. They become your partners in the result, not critics of it.
  3. Make the vendor prove it on your platform. A thorough POC on your complex scenarios is worth more than any slide deck.
  4. Get close to the vendor's architect. That relationship decides whether hard problems get solved or escalated forever.
  5. Learn what you'll be supporting. Even if the technology is new to you, learn it well enough to run it alone.
  6. Build learning into the engagement. Knowledge transfer is a deliverable, not a favor.
  7. Use AI for research. Before the engagement, research what success metrics other organizations use for the same kind of platform. It sharpens your requirements and your questions.

And remember: the vendor wants your project to succeed too. A failed engagement doesn't help their reference list.

What not to do

  • Don't trust the vendor to do the whole job. That's the most reliable recipe for failure I know. Work with them closely, every step.
  • Don't treat the engagement as cover. "We hired experts, so it's on them" protects no one when the system breaks after the vendor leaves.
  • Don't let one team certify the tool for everyone. Adoption you force rarely becomes adoption you keep.
  • Don't skip the hard cases in the POC. If the vendor never touched your messiest system, you haven't tested anything.
  • Don't buy what you can't support. If no one internally can run the product, you'll pay for it for years and get little back.
  • Don't let internal friction go unaddressed. Some engineers would rather build it themselves and see the vendor as a competitor. They focus on why the vendor is failing instead of sharing the context that would make the solution better.

A note for leaders

The engineer running a vendor engagement carries a lot. These projects are usually meant to solve a real problem or prepare the organization for the future, and that responsibility sits on their shoulders.

Three things help them succeed:

  • Give them time. Don't assume the vendor is doing the work and the internal owner needs only a few hours a week. If you want the project done right, budget real time for it.
  • Set expectations with the team. Make it clear why the vendor is there and what the internal owner is accountable for. Clear up concerns early, before they turn into resistance.
  • Give credit where it's earned. It's common for people to assume "the vendor did it" and overlook the internal engineer who made it work. Recognize the people who make these partnerships succeed.

How to measure success

Some wins show up on a budget line, like the seven-figure savings from owning GoldenGate in-house. Many don't, and organizations often have no KPI for them.

The measure I care most about is this: does the platform enable other people? When a Tier 1 support engineer can resolve an API or database performance issue in a fraction of the time it used to take, without escalating, the engagement worked. When teams adopt a tool into their development cycles on their own, it worked. When your team can run the platform after the vendor has gone, it worked.

Leaders should look for these outcomes and recognize the people who deliver them.

Closing thought

Vendor engagements aren't the most exciting work for strong engineers. There's process to design, requirements to chase, and a lot of time spent learning someone else's product.

But this is foundation work. Done well, it shapes how an organization operates for years. Bring the vendor in for their expertise, and keep the ownership for yourself.

If you've led vendor engagements of your own, I'd like to hear what worked and what didn't. Share your experience in the comments.

title: Why your CSS gradients look muddy in the middle (and the one-word fix)
description:
Blend blue into yellow with linear-gradient(90deg, blue, yellow) and the middle turns a dull grey. That isn't your colours' fault: by default browsers mix gradient colours in sRGB, where the straight line between two colours often passes through a desaturated zone.

The fix: interpolate in OKLab or OKLCH 

.muddy  { background: linear-gradient(90deg, blue, yellow); }
.clean  { background: linear-gradient(in oklab 90deg, blue, yellow); }
.vivid  { background: linear-gradient(in oklch 90deg, blue, yellow); }
  • oklab is perceptually even, so the midpoint looks like a real halfway colour.
  • oklch travels around the hue wheel, giving brighter, rainbow-like transitions (use shorter hue / longer hue to choose the direction).

Keep a fallback

Colour-space interpolation is supported in current Chrome, Edge, Firefox and Safari, but declare the plain version first so older browsers still get a gradient:

.card {
  background: linear-gradient(90deg, blue, yellow);
  background: linear-gradient(in oklab 90deg, blue, yellow);
}

Two more tips

  • Add a middle stop instead of fighting the blend: linear-gradient(90deg, blue, #6aa 50%, yellow).
  • conic-gradient() works great for pie charts and colour wheels: conic-gradient(red 0 25%, gold 0 60%, teal 0).

Try it

Disclosure: I run GoToolsOnline. Its free CSS gradient generator does linear, radial and conic gradients with draggable stops and an OKLab/OKLCH option, and writes the fallback line for you: https://gotoolsonline.com/tools/css-gradient

title: Why I Chose a Node.js Queue for Browser Image Uploads to Object Storage (and Webhooks)
description:
Short answer: upload the original image from the browser straight to private object storage, finalize it in the backend, and put a small job on a Node.js queue for thumbnail generation. Use a storage notification or webhook only as a delivery signal. The backend database remains the authority for tenant access and processing state.

That split keeps large bytes away from the application process. It also gives every retry a clear boundary. The browser moves bytes. The API grants a narrowly scoped upload. A worker reads a finalized original and writes deterministic thumbnail keys. A notification wakes the worker; it does not grant permission.

I choose this shape for a gaming media pipeline where players upload large screenshots or clips and the UI needs a quick preview. I've learned to draw the trust boundary before choosing a queue library. Otherwise a perfectly good resize function ends up deciding who may read an image.

What should a browser upload prove before a Node.js worker generates thumbnails?

The upload starts with an authenticated request for an upload intent. The backend derives a key from the account and asset IDs, records the expected content type and size, and returns a short-lived signed upload operation. The browser sends the original image directly to object storage. XMLHttpRequest can expose upload progress events for the progress bar; the application server never has to proxy the image bytes (see the MDN reference below).

The browser then calls a finalize operation. Finalize is important because an object appearing in storage is not the same thing as an authorized, complete asset. In one database transaction, the backend checks the tenant, expected metadata, and an idempotency token, then marks the asset ready for processing. A notification that arrives before that commit is simply deferred or ignored by the worker.

Here is the part I keep copyable. The queue interface is deliberately generic, so the access checks stay visible instead of hiding inside a vendor SDK.

type ThumbnailJob = {
  tenantId: string;
  assetId: string;
  originalKey: string;
  widths: number[];
};

async function processThumbnailJob(job: ThumbnailJob) {
  const asset = await db.assets.find(job.assetId);
  if (!asset || asset.tenantId !== job.tenantId || asset.status !== "ready") {
    return; // Duplicate or early delivery is a no-op.
  }

  const original = await objects.get(job.originalKey);
  for (const width of job.widths) {
    const thumbnail = await resizeToWidth(original, width);
    const key = `tenants/${job.tenantId}/assets/${job.assetId}/thumb-${width}.webp`;
    await objects.put(key, thumbnail, { contentType: "image/webp" });
  }

  await db.assets.markThumbnailsReady(job.assetId, job.widths);
}

Notice what the job does not contain: a bearer token, a public URL, or an arbitrary bucket path. The object key is only a routing hint. The database check decides access. I log the tenant ID, asset ID, event ID, and attempt number; I don't log signed URLs or image bytes.

Small boundary. Big payoff.

How do object-storage webhooks, notifications, and a Node.js queue fit together?

A webhook is an HTTP delivery attempt to your receiver. A native storage notification may deliver to a queue directly. Either way, delivery is a signal that must be persisted and deduplicated. RFC 9110 is useful here: a successful HTTP response reports handling of the request, not completion of downstream thumbnail work.

The receiver should verify the message signature when one is provided, insert the event ID into an inbox table, acknowledge quickly, and enqueue only new events. The queue then supplies backpressure when a game launch produces a burst of uploads.

type StorageEvent = {
  id: string;
  tenantId: string;
  assetId: string;
  originalKey: string;
};

async function acceptStorageEvent(event: StorageEvent) {
  const inserted = await db.inbox.insertIfNew(event.id, event);
  if (!inserted) return;

  await thumbnailQueue.add("generate", {
    tenantId: event.tenantId,
    assetId: event.assetId,
    originalKey: event.originalKey,
    widths: [320, 640, 1280],
  }, { jobId: event.id });
}

The queue must tolerate duplicates and retries. A deterministic thumbnail key makes a retry idempotent. If the storage system supports conditional writes, use them when replacing an existing derivative would be dangerous. Mark the asset ready only after every required width exists; a partial set should be observable as partial, not reported as success.

This is where metrics help. Track upload-finalize latency, notification-to-worker latency, retry count, abandoned uploads, and the age of the oldest queued job. Alert on a growing queue and on a high ratio of finalized originals with no completed thumbnail set. Those signals tell you whether the problem is delivery, authorization, or image processing.

The access-control trade-off is bigger than the transfer speed

Keep originals private. A signed upload operation delegates one transfer; it does not replace the application authorization check. On download, authenticate the player, verify ownership of the asset row, and mint a short-lived signed read operation. Never let a client submit an arbitrary prefix and treat that as an export. Prefixes are naming conventions, not policy.

The before-and-after mental model is simple:

Before After
API receives every image byte Browser sends bytes directly to object storage
Upload completion implies processing Finalize transaction creates an explicit ready state
Notification triggers trusted work Notification is deduplicated input to a tenant-checked job
Thumbnail names vary per retry Keys are deterministic and safe to replay

There is a real cost. The service now owns an upload-intent record, an inbox, queue retries, dead-letter review, and cleanup for abandoned originals. I'm not sure every small internal tool needs those moving parts. If files are tiny, traffic is low, and one trusted operator owns the catalog, a synchronous multipart endpoint can be easier to test and operate. Stick with the simpler path when your recovery drill cannot exercise the queue and cleanup states.

What should I test before calling the image pipeline finished?

Test the gaps, not only the happy path. Upload an original, delay finalize, then deliver the same storage event twice. Revoke the user session before the worker runs. Submit an event whose tenant ID does not match the asset row. Kill a worker after writing one thumbnail and replay the job. In a useful replay script, I give each event a fixed ID, advance a fake clock between upload and finalize, and record the database row after every worker attempt. I then inspect the object keys, not just the queue result: there should be no key outside the tenant prefix, no second derivative with a random suffix, and no success state while one requested width is missing. Finally, I run the same sequence with a stale signed upload operation and with a duplicate finalize request. The expected result is one authorized derivative set, no cross-tenant reads, and a visible retry or partial state when work is interrupted.

The browser should also handle a rejected or expired signed operation without exposing credentials. A fresh upload intent can be requested after the user is still authorized. Keep retry delays bounded, and record the reason for each retry so a temporary delivery pause is distinguishable from a bad object key.

The catch is delivery simplicity versus access control. Direct browser uploads reduce proxy bandwidth and make progress reporting pleasant, but they add state that must be cleaned up. A worker queue absorbs bursts, but it cannot make an unsafe object key safe. Choose this architecture when the original files are large and thumbnail work is asynchronous; choose a smaller synchronous design when those conditions do not hold.

That decision is easy to revisit. Keep the upload intent, finalize record, event inbox, and thumbnail status as separate records, and you can change the queue or resize implementation without changing the browser contract. If the team cannot name who owns each record during an outage, the design is still too implicit.

References

  • https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110
  • https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/XMLHttpRequest_API/Using_XMLHttpRequest

title: How to Scrape Twitch with Go: Chat Logs over IRC WebSockets, Moderation Events, Full-Text Search, and Chat Stats (2026)
description:
People search "twitch chat logs" about 6,600 times a month in the US, and most of them hit the same wall: Twitch has no API that returns chat from the past. Helix doesn't have one, and neither does EventSub. If a message isn't captured while it scrolls by, it's gone for you. So a chat log is something you build going forward: connect, listen, store.

This post builds twitchlog, a small Go program that does exactly that:

  1. log connects to Twitch chat over its IRC WebSocket, joins channels, and writes every message to SQLite, along with subs, raids, timeouts, bans, and room settings
  2. search runs full-text queries (FTS5) across everything you've logged
  3. export prints a plain-text log for one channel and day, or for one chatter
  4. stats summarizes a channel: messages per minute, unique chatters, subscriber share, moderation, top Twitch emotes, events
  5. import rebuilds the database from the raw IRC log, so the raw log is your source of truth
  6. live (optional) checks which channels are live before you join them

It's five Go files and two dependencies: github.com/coder/websocket for the WebSocket and modernc.org/sqlite, a pure-Go SQLite (no cgo). Everything below ran on November 20, 2026 with Go 1.27.3 on a Linux VM. I logged #xqc and #kaicenat for about 24 minutes in total (12,443 messages). Output blocks are pasted from those runs, except that I replaced chatters' usernames with viewer_NN placeholders.

Read this first. Twitch's terms prohibit scraping. The Twitch Terms of Service (last modified 08/12/2026) say you may not "access any website, server, software application, or other computer resource owned, used, and/or licensed by Twitch, including but not limited to the Twitch Services, by means of any robot, spider, scraper, crawler, or other automated means for any purpose", and the license section excludes "use of any data mining, robots, or similar data gathering or extraction methods". Read those clauses and think about the legal risk for your use case before you run anything here. Prefer the official routes: Twitch documents IRC and EventSub as its chat interfaces, and for new projects it recommends EventSub (channel.chat.message) with a user access token that has the user:read:chat scope. The anonymous justinfan login used below is not documented. Chat is also personal data: usernames next to what people said. Keep logs only as long as you need them, don't publish logs of individual people, and check privacy law (GDPR and similar) if you store them. The code redacts messages that moderators delete or that belong to timed-out and banned users, because Twitch removes them from view too.

What you can and can't get

What How Notes
Live chat, from now on IRC over WebSocket (wss://irc-ws.chat.twitch.tv:443) or EventSub This post uses IRC; EventSub needs a user token
Chat from before you connected No API Helix and EventSub only deliver new messages
Chat replay on VODs Only through the website's private GraphQL Not covered here
Who is in chat Helix Get Chatters, needs a moderator token Anonymous IRC only lists you in NAMES
Timeouts, bans, deleted messages CLEARCHAT and CLEARMSG events You only see them if you're connected at the time
7TV, BTTV, FFZ emotes Not in the IRC tags They arrive as plain words

Before writing a parser, I tested which transport the VM could reach. The raw IRC ports didn't work from that network: TLS on port 6697 ended with unexpected eof, and a plain connection to 6667 got HTTP/1.1 400 Bad Request from an HTTP proxy. The WebSocket upgrade on port 443 worked first try:

HTTP/1.1 101 Switching Protocols
Connection: upgrade
Upgrade: websocket

That's the main reason to use WebSockets: it's ordinary HTTPS traffic, so it gets through proxies and firewalls that block IRC ports. Twitch shut down the unencrypted ws:// endpoint on port 80 in August 2025, so use wss://.

Setup 

mkdir twitchlog && cd twitchlog
go mod init twitchlog
go get github.com/coder/websocket@v1.8.15 modernc.org/sqlite@v1.61.1

The program is split into irc.go (parsing), conn.go (the connection), store.go (SQLite), main.go (commands), and stats.go (the report and the live check). All five are below in full, so you can copy them into one folder and go build.

Step 1: Parse Twitch's IRC lines

Twitch sends IRC with IRCv3 tags in front. A chat message looks like this (shortened, username replaced):

@badge-info=;badges=bronze-chain/1;color=#8A2BE2;display-name=viewer_01;emotes=;first-msg=0;id=00000000-0000-4000-8000-000000000001;mod=0;returning-chatter=0;room-id=71092938;subscriber=0;tmi-sent-ts=1795147987206;user-id=100000001 :viewer_01!viewer_01@viewer_01.tmi.twitch.tv PRIVMSG #xqc :SCHIZO

The tags carry everything useful: a stable message id, the numeric user-id (logins can change, IDs can't), badge-info with subscription months, emotes with character positions, bits, first-msg, reply-parent-msg-id, and the server timestamp tmi-sent-ts in milliseconds. Tag values are escaped (\s is a space, \: is a semicolon), so unescape them. System messages are full of escapes: a raid arrives as system-msg=1\sraiders\sfrom\s...\shave\sjoined!.

irc.go:

package main

import (
    "strings"
)

// Message is one parsed IRC line from Twitch, IRCv3 tags included.
type Message struct {
    Raw     string
    Tags    map[string]string
    Prefix  string // "nick!user@host" or "tmi.twitch.tv"
    Command string // PRIVMSG, USERNOTICE, CLEARMSG, PING, 001, ...
    Params  []string
}

// Nick returns the login part of the prefix ("" for server messages).
func (m Message) Nick() string {
    if i := strings.IndexByte(m.Prefix, '!'); i > 0 {
        return m.Prefix[:i]
    }
    return ""
}

// Channel returns the first param without '#', if it is a channel.
func (m Message) Channel() string {
    if len(m.Params) > 0 && strings.HasPrefix(m.Params[0], "#") {
        return m.Params[0][1:]
    }
    return ""
}

// Trailing returns the last param (the chat text for PRIVMSG).
func (m Message) Trailing() string {
    if len(m.Params) == 0 {
        return ""
    }
    return m.Params[len(m.Params)-1]
}

// Parse turns one line into a Message.
// Format: [@tags ][:prefix ]COMMAND [params] [:trailing]
func Parse(line string) Message {
    m := Message{Raw: line, Tags: map[string]string{}}
    rest := line
    if strings.HasPrefix(rest, "@") {
        end := strings.IndexByte(rest, ' ')
        if end < 0 {
            return m
        }
        for _, kv := range strings.Split(rest[1:end], ";") {
            k, v, _ := strings.Cut(kv, "=")
            m.Tags[k] = unescapeTag(v)
        }
        rest = rest[end+1:]
    }
    if strings.HasPrefix(rest, ":") {
        end := strings.IndexByte(rest, ' ')
        if end < 0 {
            return m
        }
        m.Prefix = rest[1:end]
        rest = rest[end+1:]
    }
    for rest != "" {
        if strings.HasPrefix(rest, ":") {
            m.Params = append(m.Params, rest[1:])
            break
        }
        word, after, found := strings.Cut(rest, " ")
        if m.Command == "" {
            m.Command = word
        } else {
            m.Params = append(m.Params, word)
        }
        if !found {
            break
        }
        rest = after
    }
    return m
}

// IRCv3 tag values escape ';' ' ' '\' CR and LF.
func unescapeTag(v string) string {
    if !strings.Contains(v, `\`) {
        return v
    }
    var b strings.Builder
    for i := 0; i < len(v); i++ {
        if v[i] != '\\' || i == len(v)-1 {
            if v[i] != '\\' {
                b.WriteByte(v[i])
            }
            continue
        }
        i++
        switch v[i] {
        case ':':
            b.WriteByte(';')
        case 's':
            b.WriteByte(' ')
        case 'r':
            b.WriteByte('\r')
        case 'n':
            b.WriteByte('\n')
        default: // "\\" and unknown escapes
            b.WriteByte(v[i])
        }
    }
    return b.String()
}

Step 2: The connection

The connection has more rules than the parser:

  • Login. Request the twitch.tv/tags and twitch.tv/commands capabilities, then PASS and NICK. For read-only access, any justinfan plus digits nick works with any password. With an OAuth token you'd send PASS oauth:<token> and your own login instead.
  • One frame, several lines. Twitch's docs warn that a single WebSocket message can hold several IRC lines separated by \r\n. Split every frame, or you'll parse a batch as one message and drop the rest.
  • PING/PONG. Twitch sends PING :tmi.twitch.tv about every five minutes and drops you if you don't answer. In my run they arrived at 11:28:37 and 11:33:36.
  • RECONNECT. Twitch sends this before restarting a server. Reconnect right away.
  • Join limits. Twitch's docs say 20 join attempts per 10 seconds for a normal account, and 100 channels joined at the same time. The code waits 11 seconds after every 15 joins.
  • Silent failures. Joining a channel that doesn't exist returns nothing at all: no error, no NOTICE. I joined thisuserdoesnotexist_zz9 along with the two real channels and only got JOIN confirmations for the real ones. Check for the JOIN echo.

conn.go:

package main

import (
    "context"
    "errors"
    "fmt"
    "log"
    "math/rand/v2"
    "strings"
    "time"

    "github.com/coder/websocket"
)

var ircURL = "wss://irc-ws.chat.twitch.tv:443" // var so tests can point it elsewhere

// errReconnect means Twitch asked us to move to another server.
var errReconnect = errors.New("server sent RECONNECT")

// session runs one WebSocket connection until it drops or ctx ends.
// Every parsed line goes to out.
func session(ctx context.Context, channels []string, out chan<- Message) error {
    dialCtx, cancel := context.WithTimeout(ctx, 15*time.Second)
    defer cancel()
    c, _, err := websocket.Dial(dialCtx, ircURL, nil)
    if err != nil {
        return fmt.Errorf("dial: %w", err)
    }
    defer c.CloseNow()
    c.SetReadLimit(1 << 20) // a burst of long messages can exceed the 32 KB default

    send := func(line string) error {
        wctx, cancel := context.WithTimeout(ctx, 10*time.Second)
        defer cancel()
        return c.Write(wctx, websocket.MessageText, []byte(line+"\r\n"))
    }

    // Anonymous, read-only login: any justinfan<digits> nick, any PASS.
    nick := fmt.Sprintf("justinfan%d", 10000+rand.IntN(80000))
    for _, l := range []string{
        "CAP REQ :twitch.tv/tags twitch.tv/commands",
        "PASS SCHMOOPIIE",
        "NICK " + nick,
    } {
        if err := send(l); err != nil {
            return err
        }
    }

    // JOINs are limited (20 per 10 s for normal users), so pace them.
    go func() {
        for i, ch := range channels {
            if i > 0 && i%15 == 0 {
                select {
                case <-time.After(11 * time.Second):
                case <-ctx.Done():
                    return
                }
            }
            if err := send("JOIN #" + strings.ToLower(ch)); err != nil {
                return
            }
        }
    }()

    for {
        // Twitch PINGs about every 5 minutes; 6 minutes of silence = dead link.
        rctx, cancel := context.WithTimeout(ctx, 6*time.Minute)
        _, data, err := c.Read(rctx)
        cancel()
        if err != nil {
            return fmt.Errorf("read: %w", err)
        }
        // One WebSocket frame can carry several IRC lines.
        for _, line := range strings.Split(strings.TrimRight(string(data), "\r\n"), "\r\n") {
            if line == "" {
                continue
            }
            m := Parse(line)
            switch m.Command {
            case "PING":
                if err := send("PONG :" + m.Trailing()); err != nil {
                    return err
                }
            case "RECONNECT":
                return errReconnect
            case "NOTICE":
                log.Printf("NOTICE %s: %s (msg-id=%s)", m.Channel(), m.Trailing(), m.Tags["msg-id"])
            }
            select {
            case out <- m:
            case <-ctx.Done():
                return ctx.Err()
            }
        }
    }
}

// run keeps a session alive with exponential backoff until ctx ends.
func run(ctx context.Context, channels []string, out chan<- Message) {
    backoff := time.Second
    for ctx.Err() == nil {
        start := time.Now()
        err := session(ctx, channels, out)
        if ctx.Err() != nil {
            return
        }
        if time.Since(start) > time.Minute || errors.Is(err, errReconnect) {
            backoff = time.Second // it was healthy; reconnect quickly
        }
        log.Printf("connection ended: %v; reconnecting in %s", err, backoff)
        select {
        case <-time.After(backoff):
        case <-ctx.Done():
            return
        }
        backoff = min(backoff*2, 2*time.Minute)
    }
}
