Step 3: Store messages, and honor deletions

This is where most chat loggers are sloppy. Three things deserve care.

Moderation. CLEARMSG means a moderator deleted one message (target-msg-id). CLEARCHAT with a target-user-id is a timeout (when ban-duration is present) or a ban, and Twitch hides that user's recent messages. CLEARCHAT with no target clears the whole chat. The code keeps the row (time, user, channel) but empties the text and records why. In 22 minutes of logging I saw 74 CLEARCHAT events and no CLEARMSG at all. Timeouts are how these chats get moderated: 375 of 7,360 #xqc messages (5.1%) ended up redacted.

Emote positions are code points, not bytes. The emotes tag says 425618:2-4 and means characters 2 to 4. With an emoji earlier in the message, slicing the UTF-8 bytes gives you garbage. Slicing a []rune is correct. I checked all 1,702 emote ranges from my first two runs: 3 of them would have come out wrong with byte slicing, all in one message that started with ✌🏾. That's rare, and it's exactly the kind of bug that slips through testing.

Invisible characters. Twitch rejects the same message sent twice in a row, so chat clients append an invisible character to get around it. In my first two runs, 219 of 11,662 messages ended in U+034F (combining grapheme joiner) and 22 in U+E0000. Strip them before storing, or "KEKW KEKW" and "KEKW KEKW\u034f" count as different messages and searches miss.

Twitch's docs also say the server "may also send a message multiple times" if it thinks you didn't get it, so the message id is the primary key and inserts use INSERT OR IGNORE.

store.go:

package main

import (
    "database/sql"
    "strconv"
    "strings"
    "time"

    _ "modernc.org/sqlite"
)

const schema = `
PRAGMA journal_mode=WAL;
CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS messages (
  id TEXT PRIMARY KEY, channel TEXT, room_id TEXT, user_id TEXT, login TEXT,
  display_name TEXT, text TEXT, sent_at INTEGER, badges TEXT,
  sub_months INTEGER, bits INTEGER, first_msg INTEGER, reply_to TEXT,
  emotes TEXT, deleted TEXT);
CREATE INDEX IF NOT EXISTS messages_chan_time ON messages(channel, sent_at);
CREATE INDEX IF NOT EXISTS messages_user ON messages(user_id);
CREATE VIRTUAL TABLE IF NOT EXISTS messages_fts USING fts5(
  text, content='messages', content_rowid='rowid');
CREATE TRIGGER IF NOT EXISTS messages_ai AFTER INSERT ON messages BEGIN
  INSERT INTO messages_fts(rowid, text) VALUES (new.rowid, new.text);
END;
CREATE TRIGGER IF NOT EXISTS messages_au AFTER UPDATE OF text ON messages BEGIN
  INSERT INTO messages_fts(messages_fts, rowid, text) VALUES ('delete', old.rowid, old.text);
  INSERT INTO messages_fts(rowid, text) VALUES (new.rowid, new.text);
END;
CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS events (
  id TEXT PRIMARY KEY, channel TEXT, kind TEXT, login TEXT, system_msg TEXT, text TEXT,
  sent_at INTEGER, months INTEGER);
CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS roomstate (
  channel TEXT PRIMARY KEY, room_id TEXT, slow INTEGER, followers_only INTEGER,
  emote_only INTEGER, subs_only INTEGER, updated_at INTEGER);`

func openDB(path string) (*sql.DB, error) {
    db, err := sql.Open("sqlite", path)
    if err != nil {
        return nil, err
    }
    db.SetMaxOpenConns(1)
    if _, err := db.Exec(schema); err != nil {
        return nil, err
    }
    return db, nil
}

func atoi(s string) int { n, _ := strconv.Atoi(s); return n }

func sentAt(m Message) int64 {
    if ts, err := strconv.ParseInt(m.Tags["tmi-sent-ts"], 10, 64); err == nil {
        return ts
    }
    return time.Now().UnixMilli()
}

// subMonths reads "subscriber/14" out of badge-info.
func subMonths(badgeInfo string) int {
    for _, b := range strings.Split(badgeInfo, ",") {
        if k, v, ok := strings.Cut(b, "/"); ok && (k == "subscriber" || k == "founder") {
            return atoi(v)
        }
    }
    return 0
}

// emoteNames maps the emotes tag ("25:0-4,6-10/1902:12-16") to names.
// Positions count Unicode code points, not bytes, so index into []rune.
func emoteNames(tag, text string) []string {
    if tag == "" {
        return nil
    }
    runes := []rune(text)
    var names []string
    for _, e := range strings.Split(tag, "/") {
        _, ranges, _ := strings.Cut(e, ":")
        for _, r := range strings.Split(ranges, ",") {
            a, b, ok := strings.Cut(r, "-")
            s, t := atoi(a), atoi(b)
            if !ok || s < 0 || t >= len(runes) || s > t {
                continue
            }
            names = append(names, string(runes[s:t+1]))
        }
    }
    return names
}

// clean drops the invisible characters chat clients append to get past
// Twitch's "identical message" check (U+034F, U+E0000), plus trailing spaces.
func clean(s string) string {
    s = strings.NewReplacer("\u034f", "", "\U000E0000", "").Replace(s)
    return strings.TrimSpace(s)
}

// apply writes one IRC message into the database inside tx.
// Returns true if it stored a chat message.
func apply(tx *sql.Tx, m Message) (bool, error) {
    switch m.Command {
    case "PRIVMSG":
        text := clean(m.Trailing())
        // /me messages arrive wrapped in CTCP ACTION.
        if strings.HasPrefix(text, "\x01ACTION ") {
            text = "/me " + strings.TrimSuffix(strings.TrimPrefix(text, "\x01ACTION "), "\x01")
        }
        res, err := tx.Exec(`INSERT OR IGNORE INTO messages VALUES
            (?,?,?,?,?,?,?,?,?,?,?,?,?,?,NULL)`,
            m.Tags["id"], m.Channel(), m.Tags["room-id"], m.Tags["user-id"], m.Nick(),
            m.Tags["display-name"], text, sentAt(m), m.Tags["badges"],
            subMonths(m.Tags["badge-info"]), atoi(m.Tags["bits"]), atoi(m.Tags["first-msg"]),
            m.Tags["reply-parent-msg-id"], strings.Join(emoteNames(m.Tags["emotes"], m.Trailing()), " "))
        if err != nil {
            return false, err
        }
        n, _ := res.RowsAffected() // 0 when Twitch re-sent a message we already have
        return n == 1, nil

    case "USERNOTICE": // sub, resub, subgift, raid, announcement, ...
        months := atoi(m.Tags["msg-param-cumulative-months"])
        text := ""
        if len(m.Params) > 1 {
            text = m.Trailing()
        }
        _, err := tx.Exec(`INSERT OR IGNORE INTO events VALUES (?,?,?,?,?,?,?,?)`, m.Tags["id"], m.Channel(),
            m.Tags["msg-id"], m.Tags["login"], m.Tags["system-msg"], text, sentAt(m), months)
        return false, err

    case "CLEARMSG": // a moderator deleted one message
        _, err := tx.Exec(`UPDATE messages SET text='', emotes='', deleted='deleted'
            WHERE id=?`, m.Tags["target-msg-id"])
        return false, err

    case "CLEARCHAT":
        reason := "ban"
        if m.Tags["ban-duration"] != "" {
            reason = "timeout"
        }
        if uid := m.Tags["target-user-id"]; uid != "" {
            // Twitch hides a timed-out or banned user's recent messages; do the same.
            _, err := tx.Exec(`UPDATE messages SET text='', emotes='', deleted=?
                WHERE user_id=? AND channel=? AND sent_at<=? AND deleted IS NULL`,
                reason, uid, m.Channel(), sentAt(m))
            return false, err
        }
        _, err := tx.Exec(`UPDATE messages SET text='', emotes='', deleted='clear'
            WHERE channel=? AND sent_at<=? AND deleted IS NULL`, m.Channel(), sentAt(m))
        return false, err

    case "ROOMSTATE": // full state on JOIN, partial updates later
        _, err := tx.Exec(`INSERT INTO roomstate VALUES (?,?,?,?,?,?,?)
            ON CONFLICT(channel) DO UPDATE SET
              slow=COALESCE(excluded.slow, slow),
              followers_only=COALESCE(excluded.followers_only, followers_only),
              emote_only=COALESCE(excluded.emote_only, emote_only),
              subs_only=COALESCE(excluded.subs_only, subs_only),
              updated_at=excluded.updated_at`,
            m.Channel(), m.Tags["room-id"], optInt(m, "slow"), optInt(m, "followers-only"),
            optInt(m, "emote-only"), optInt(m, "subs-only"), time.Now().UnixMilli())
        return false, err
    }
    return false, nil
}

// optInt returns nil when the tag is absent, so partial ROOMSTATE updates
// don't overwrite the other settings.
func optInt(m Message, k string) any {
    v, ok := m.Tags[k]
    if !ok {
        return nil
    }
    return atoi(v)
}

The FTS5 table uses content='messages', so the text isn't stored twice. The update trigger keeps the index in sync when a message is redacted, so a deleted message stops showing up in search.

Step 4: The commands

main.go wires it together. The logger buffers messages and writes them in one transaction per second, or every 1,000 messages. A commit per message adds a disk sync per message, which gets expensive in a busy chat: #kaicenat peaked at 814 messages in one minute during my run.

With -raw, every IRC line also goes to a text file. That file is worth keeping. import replays it into a fresh database, so you can change the schema or fix a bug and rebuild everything. Because of INSERT OR IGNORE, importing the same file twice adds nothing.

main.go:

// twitchlog: log Twitch chat to SQLite over IRC WebSockets, then search,
// summarize and export it. Usage:
//
//  twitchlog log    -db chat.db -channels xqc,caedrel [-for 30m] [-raw raw.log]
//  twitchlog search -db chat.db -q 'NEAR(gta mall, 10)' [-channel xqc] [-user name]
//  twitchlog stats  -db chat.db -channel xqc [-since 60m]
//  twitchlog export -db chat.db -channel xqc|-user name [-day 2026-11-20] [-tz Asia/Saigon]
//  twitchlog import -db chat.db -raw raw.log   (rebuild from a raw log)
//  twitchlog live   -channels xqc,caedrel   (needs SCRAPEATLAS_API_KEY)
package main

import (
    "bufio"
    "context"
    "database/sql"
    "flag"
    "fmt"
    "log"
    "os"
    "os/signal"
    "strings"
    "syscall"
    "time"
)

func main() {
    if len(os.Args) < 2 {
        fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, "usage: twitchlog log|search|stats|export|live [flags]")
        os.Exit(2)
    }
    cmd, args := os.Args[1], os.Args[2:]
    fs := flag.NewFlagSet(cmd, flag.ExitOnError)
    dbPath := fs.String("db", "chat.db", "SQLite file")
    channels := fs.String("channels", "", "comma-separated channel logins")
    channel := fs.String("channel", "", "one channel login")
    dur := fs.Duration("for", 0, "stop after this long (0 = until Ctrl-C)")
    raw := fs.String("raw", "", "also append raw IRC lines to this file")
    q := fs.String("q", "", "FTS5 query")
    user := fs.String("user", "", "filter by login")
    since := fs.Duration("since", time.Hour, "stats window")
    day := fs.String("day", "", "export one day (YYYY-MM-DD, in -tz)")
    tz := fs.String("tz", "UTC", "time zone for export/search output")
    fs.Parse(args)

    loc, err := time.LoadLocation(*tz)
    if err != nil {
        log.Fatal(err)
    }
    if cmd == "live" {
        if err := cmdLive(split(*channels)); err != nil {
            log.Fatal(err)
        }
        return
    }
    db, err := openDB(*dbPath)
    if err != nil {
        log.Fatal(err)
    }
    defer db.Close()

    switch cmd {
    case "log":
        err = cmdLog(db, split(*channels), *dur, *raw)
    case "import":
        err = cmdImport(db, *raw)
    case "search":
        err = cmdSearch(db, *q, *channel, *user, loc)
    case "stats":
        err = cmdStats(db, *channel, *since)
    case "export":
        err = cmdExport(db, *channel, *user, *day, loc)
    default:
        err = fmt.Errorf("unknown command %q", cmd)
    }
    if err != nil {
        log.Fatal(err)
    }
}

func split(s string) []string {
    var out []string
    for _, c := range strings.Split(s, ",") {
        if c = strings.TrimPrefix(strings.ToLower(strings.TrimSpace(c)), "#"); c != "" {
            out = append(out, c)
        }
    }
    return out
}

func cmdLog(db *sql.DB, channels []string, dur time.Duration, rawPath string) error {
    if len(channels) == 0 {
        return fmt.Errorf("-channels is required")
    }
    ctx, stop := signal.NotifyContext(context.Background(), os.Interrupt, syscall.SIGTERM)
    defer stop()
    if dur > 0 {
        var cancel context.CancelFunc
        ctx, cancel = context.WithTimeout(ctx, dur)
        defer cancel()
    }
    var raw *os.File
    if rawPath != "" {
        f, err := os.OpenFile(rawPath, os.O_CREATE|os.O_APPEND|os.O_WRONLY, 0o644)
        if err != nil {
            return err
        }
        defer f.Close()
        raw = f
    }

    msgs := make(chan Message, 4096)
    go func() { run(ctx, channels, msgs); close(msgs) }()

    // Batch writes: one transaction per second instead of one per message.
    tick := time.NewTicker(time.Second)
    defer tick.Stop()
    var batch []Message
    var stored, total int
    flush := func() error {
        if len(batch) == 0 {
            return nil
        }
        tx, err := db.Begin()
        if err != nil {
            return err
        }
        for _, m := range batch {
            ok, err := apply(tx, m)
            if err != nil {
                tx.Rollback()
                return fmt.Errorf("%s: %w", m.Command, err)
            }
            if ok {
                stored++
            }
        }
        batch = batch[:0]
        return tx.Commit()
    }
    report := time.Now()
    for {
        select {
        case m, ok := <-msgs:
            if !ok {
                err := flush()
                log.Printf("done: %d lines, %d chat messages stored", total, stored)
                return err
            }
            total++
            if raw != nil {
                fmt.Fprintln(raw, m.Raw)
            }
            switch m.Command {
            case "JOIN":
                log.Printf("joined #%s", m.Channel())
            case "PING":
                log.Printf("PING from server, answered with PONG")
            case "PRIVMSG", "USERNOTICE", "CLEARMSG", "CLEARCHAT", "ROOMSTATE":
                batch = append(batch, m)
            }
            if len(batch) >= 1000 {
                if err := flush(); err != nil {
                    return err
                }
            }
        case <-tick.C:
            if err := flush(); err != nil {
                return err
            }
            if time.Since(report) > time.Minute {
                log.Printf("%d chat messages stored so far", stored)
                report = time.Now()
            }
        }
    }
}

// cmdImport replays a raw IRC log into the database. INSERT OR IGNORE on the
// message id makes it safe to run twice or over overlapping logs.
func cmdImport(db *sql.DB, rawPath string) error {
    f, err := os.Open(rawPath)
    if err != nil {
        return err
    }
    defer f.Close()
    tx, err := db.Begin()
    if err != nil {
        return err
    }
    sc := bufio.NewScanner(f)
    sc.Buffer(make([]byte, 64*1024), 1<<20)
    lines, stored := 0, 0
    for sc.Scan() {
        lines++
        ok, err := apply(tx, Parse(sc.Text()))
        if err != nil {
            tx.Rollback()
            return fmt.Errorf("line %d: %w", lines, err)
        }
        if ok {
            stored++
        }
    }
    if err := sc.Err(); err != nil {
        tx.Rollback()
        return err
    }
    log.Printf("imported %d lines, %d new chat messages", lines, stored)
    return tx.Commit()
}

func cmdSearch(db *sql.DB, q, channel, user string, loc *time.Location) error {
    if q == "" {
        return fmt.Errorf("-q is required")
    }
    rows, err := db.Query(`
        SELECT m.channel, m.login, m.sent_at,
               snippet(messages_fts, 0, '[', ']', '…', 12)
        FROM messages_fts JOIN messages m ON m.rowid = messages_fts.rowid
        WHERE messages_fts MATCH ? AND (?='' OR m.channel=?) AND (?='' OR m.login=?)
        ORDER BY m.sent_at DESC LIMIT 50`, q, channel, channel, user, user)
    if err != nil {
        return err
    }
    defer rows.Close()
    n := 0
    for rows.Next() {
        var ch, login, snip string
        var ts int64
        if err := rows.Scan(&ch, &login, &ts, &snip); err != nil {
            return err
        }
        fmt.Printf("%s #%s %s: %s\n", time.UnixMilli(ts).In(loc).Format("2006-01-02 15:04:05"), ch, login, snip)
        n++
    }
    fmt.Printf("%d matches (newest first, max 50)\n", n)
    return rows.Err()
}

func cmdExport(db *sql.DB, channel, user, day string, loc *time.Location) error {
    if channel == "" && user == "" {
        return fmt.Errorf("-channel or -user is required")
    }
    from, to := int64(0), int64(1<<62)
    if day != "" {
        d, err := time.ParseInLocation("2006-01-02", day, loc)
        if err != nil {
            return err
        }
        from, to = d.UnixMilli(), d.AddDate(0, 0, 1).UnixMilli()
    }
    rows, err := db.Query(`SELECT sent_at, channel, login, text, deleted FROM messages
        WHERE (?='' OR channel=?) AND (?='' OR login=?) AND sent_at>=? AND sent_at<?
        ORDER BY sent_at`, channel, channel, user, user, from, to)
    if err != nil {
        return err
    }
    defer rows.Close()
    for rows.Next() {
        var ts int64
        var ch, login, text string
        var deleted sql.NullString
        if err := rows.Scan(&ts, &ch, &login, &text, &deleted); err != nil {
            return err
        }
        if deleted.Valid {
            text = "<message " + deleted.String + ">"
        }
        fmt.Printf("[%s] #%s %s: %s\n", time.UnixMilli(ts).In(loc).Format("2006-01-02 15:04:05"), ch, login, text)
    }
    return rows.Err()
}

Step 5: Stats, and checking who's live

stats.go has the channel report and the optional live command. Emote counts come from the emotes tag, so only Twitch-native emotes are counted. 7TV, BTTV, and FFZ emotes (OMEGALUL, KEKW, ICANT, and friends) are plain words in the text. You could count them by matching against those services' emote lists, but that's a separate project.

Joining channels that aren't live wastes join slots and fills your database with nothing. IRC can't tell you whether a channel is live, and Helix needs an app token for that. I used ScrapeAtlas* for this check. It's a scraping API that covers 50 platforms, and its GET /v1/twitch/profile/basic?handle=... returns isLive and currentViewersCount. If you already have a Helix app token, Get Streams does the same job.

stats.go:

package main

import (
    "database/sql"
    "encoding/json"
    "fmt"
    "net/http"
    "net/url"
    "os"
    "sort"
    "strings"
    "time"
)

func cmdStats(db *sql.DB, channel string, since time.Duration) error {
    if channel == "" {
        return fmt.Errorf("-channel is required")
    }
    from := time.Now().Add(-since).UnixMilli()
    var n, chatters, subs, firsts, bits int
    var t0, t1 sql.NullInt64
    err := db.QueryRow(`SELECT COUNT(*), COUNT(DISTINCT user_id),
        COALESCE(SUM(sub_months>0),0), COALESCE(SUM(first_msg),0), COALESCE(SUM(bits),0),
        MIN(sent_at), MAX(sent_at)
        FROM messages WHERE channel=? AND sent_at>=?`, channel, from).
        Scan(&n, &chatters, &subs, &firsts, &bits, &t0, &t1)
    if err != nil {
        return err
    }
    if n == 0 {
        return fmt.Errorf("no messages for #%s in the last %s", channel, since)
    }
    mins := max(float64(t1.Int64-t0.Int64)/60000, 1)
    fmt.Printf("#%s, last %s: %d messages from %d chatters over %.1f min (%.1f msg/min)\n",
        channel, since, n, chatters, mins, float64(n)/mins)
    fmt.Printf("  from subscribers: %.1f%%   first-time chatters: %d   bits cheered: %d\n",
        100*float64(subs)/float64(n), firsts, bits)

    var peakMin int64
    var peak int
    db.QueryRow(`SELECT sent_at/60000 AS m, COUNT(*) c FROM messages
        WHERE channel=? AND sent_at>=? GROUP BY m ORDER BY c DESC LIMIT 1`, channel, from).Scan(&peakMin, &peak)
    fmt.Printf("  busiest minute: %s UTC with %d messages\n",
        time.UnixMilli(peakMin*60000).UTC().Format("15:04"), peak)

    rows, err := db.Query(`SELECT COALESCE(deleted,'kept'), COUNT(*) FROM messages
        WHERE channel=? AND sent_at>=? GROUP BY 1 ORDER BY 2 DESC`, channel, from)
    if err != nil {
        return err
    }
    var parts []string
    for rows.Next() {
        var k string
        var c int
        rows.Scan(&k, &c)
        parts = append(parts, fmt.Sprintf("%s=%d", k, c))
    }
    rows.Close()
    fmt.Println("  moderation:", strings.Join(parts, " "))

    // Top chatters.
    rows, err = db.Query(`SELECT login, COUNT(*) c FROM messages
        WHERE channel=? AND sent_at>=? GROUP BY user_id ORDER BY c DESC LIMIT 5`, channel, from)
    if err != nil {
        return err
    }
    parts = parts[:0]
    for rows.Next() {
        var login string
        var c int
        rows.Scan(&login, &c)
        parts = append(parts, fmt.Sprintf("%s (%d)", login, c))
    }
    rows.Close()
    fmt.Println("  top chatters:", strings.Join(parts, ", "))

    // Top Twitch emotes (from the emotes tag, so third-party emotes are not counted).
    counts := map[string]int{}
    rows, err = db.Query(`SELECT emotes FROM messages
        WHERE channel=? AND sent_at>=? AND emotes<>''`, channel, from)
    if err != nil {
        return err
    }
    for rows.Next() {
        var e string
        rows.Scan(&e)
        for _, name := range strings.Fields(e) {
            counts[name]++
        }
    }
    rows.Close()
    type kv struct {
        k string
        v int
    }
    var top []kv
    for k, v := range counts {
        top = append(top, kv{k, v})
    }
    sort.Slice(top, func(i, j int) bool {
        if top[i].v != top[j].v {
            return top[i].v > top[j].v
        }
        return top[i].k < top[j].k
    })
    parts = parts[:0]
    for i := 0; i < len(top) && i < 8; i++ {
        parts = append(parts, fmt.Sprintf("%s %d", top[i].k, top[i].v))
    }
    fmt.Println("  top Twitch emotes:", strings.Join(parts, ", "))

    // Events (subs, gifts, raids...).
    rows, err = db.Query(`SELECT kind, COUNT(*) FROM events
        WHERE channel=? AND sent_at>=? GROUP BY kind ORDER BY 2 DESC`, channel, from)
    if err != nil {
        return err
    }
    parts = parts[:0]
    for rows.Next() {
        var k string
        var c int
        rows.Scan(&k, &c)
        parts = append(parts, fmt.Sprintf("%s=%d", k, c))
    }
    rows.Close()
    fmt.Println("  events:", strings.Join(parts, " "))
    return nil
}

// cmdLive asks ScrapeAtlas which channels are live right now and prints
// them comma-separated, so you can feed them to `twitchlog log -channels`.
func cmdLive(channels []string) error {
    key := os.Getenv("SCRAPEATLAS_API_KEY")
    if key == "" {
        return fmt.Errorf("set SCRAPEATLAS_API_KEY")
    }
    var live []string
    for _, ch := range channels {
        req, _ := http.NewRequest("GET",
            "https://api.scrapeatlas.com/v1/twitch/profile/basic?handle="+url.QueryEscape(ch), nil)
        req.Header.Set("x-api-key", key)
        res, err := http.DefaultClient.Do(req)
        if err != nil {
            return err
        }
        var p struct {
            DisplayName         string `json:"displayName"`
            IsLive              bool   `json:"isLive"`
            CurrentViewersCount *int   `json:"currentViewersCount"`
            Failure             *struct {
                Code string `json:"code"`
            } `json:"failure"`
        }
        err = json.NewDecoder(res.Body).Decode(&p)
        res.Body.Close()
        switch {
        case err != nil:
            return fmt.Errorf("%s: %w", ch, err)
        case p.Failure != nil:
            fmt.Fprintf(os.Stderr, "%-16s %s\n", ch, p.Failure.Code)
        case p.IsLive:
            fmt.Fprintf(os.Stderr, "%-16s live, %d viewers\n", ch, *p.CurrentViewersCount)
            live = append(live, ch)
        default:
            fmt.Fprintf(os.Stderr, "%-16s offline\n", ch)
        }
    }
    fmt.Println(strings.Join(live, ","))
    return nil
}

Running it

Build it and check who's live:

$ go build -o twitchlog .
$ export SCRAPEATLAS_API_KEY=...
$ ./twitchlog live -channels xqc,caedrel,kaicenat,zackrawrr,shroud,jynxzi,thisuserdoesnotexist_zz9
xqc              live, 32822 viewers
caedrel          offline
kaicenat         live, 30218 viewers
zackrawrr        offline
shroud           offline
jynxzi           offline
thisuserdoesnotexist_zz9 not_found
xqc,kaicenat

Status goes to stderr and the live list goes to stdout, so you can pass it straight in: ./twitchlog log -channels "$(./twitchlog live -channels ...)".

Log for 12 minutes:

$ ./twitchlog log -db chat.db -channels xqc,kaicenat -for 12m -raw raw2.log
2026/11/20 11:24:07 joined #xqc
2026/11/20 11:24:07 joined #kaicenat
2026/11/20 11:25:05 250 chat messages stored so far
2026/11/20 11:26:05 755 chat messages stored so far
2026/11/20 11:27:05 1174 chat messages stored so far
2026/11/20 11:28:05 1711 chat messages stored so far
2026/11/20 11:28:37 PING from server, answered with PONG
2026/11/20 11:29:06 2411 chat messages stored so far
2026/11/20 11:30:07 3106 chat messages stored so far
2026/11/20 11:31:08 3704 chat messages stored so far
2026/11/20 11:32:09 4427 chat messages stored so far
2026/11/20 11:33:09 4994 chat messages stored so far
2026/11/20 11:33:36 PING from server, answered with PONG
2026/11/20 11:34:09 5398 chat messages stored so far
2026/11/20 11:35:09 6106 chat messages stored so far
2026/11/20 11:36:05 done: 7279 lines, 7188 chat messages stored

The first run lasted 10 minutes (4,474 messages) and the second one 12 minutes (7,188). Notice the gap: the first run ended at 11:23:05 and the second one joined at 11:24:07, so about a minute of chat is missing from my logs for good. Nothing can fill it in later. For a real logger, run it as a service and leave it running.

The stats report, with chatters' usernames replaced:

$ ./twitchlog stats -db chat.db -channel xqc -since 3h
#xqc, last 3h0m0s: 7360 messages from 1374 chatters over 26.4 min (279.2 msg/min)
  from subscribers: 36.7%   first-time chatters: 22   bits cheered: 800
  busiest minute: 04:31 UTC with 574 messages
  moderation: kept=6982 timeout=375 ban=3
  top chatters: viewer_02 (94), viewer_03 (78), viewer_04 (78), viewer_05 (75), viewer_06 (68)
  top Twitch emotes: LUL 71, xqcL 40, BatChest 32, DinoDance 9, xqcEZ_TK 9, DinoBusted 8, Kreygasm 8, JinxLUL 7
  events: resub=7 viewermilestone=2 sub=2
$ ./twitchlog stats -db chat.db -channel kaicenat -since 3h
#kaicenat, last 3h0m0s: 5083 messages from 1536 chatters over 26.3 min (193.1 msg/min)
  from subscribers: 25.8%   first-time chatters: 135   bits cheered: 1000
  busiest minute: 04:35 UTC with 814 messages
  moderation: kept=4952 timeout=128 ban=3
  top chatters: viewer_07 (107), viewer_08 (65), viewer_09 (52), viewer_10 (49), viewer_11 (48)
  top Twitch emotes: kaicFireMGM 448, <3 62, kaicQM 53, NeedHeal 42, BleedPurpleHD 36, kaicMGM 35, kaicHeart 27, WutFace 24
  events: resub=9 sub=8 raid=5 submysterygift=2 subgift=2 viewermilestone=1

The two chats differ in clear ways. #xqc is busier and more of its messages come from subscribers (36.7% vs 25.8%), and moderators hand out a lot of timeouts. #kaicenat has six times as many first-time chatters, more raids, and one channel emote, kaicFireMGM, accounts for about a third of all Twitch emotes used there (448 of 1,370). The "busiest minute" is in UTC (04:35 UTC is 11:35 in Asia/Saigon, where I ran this).

Full-text search uses FTS5 syntax: phrases in quotes, * for prefixes, NEAR(a b, 10) for words close together.

$ ./twitchlog search -db chat.db -q '"gta 6"' -channel xqc -tz Asia/Saigon | tail -6
2026-11-20 11:21:00 #xqc viewer_12: [gta 6] and 2000s youtube in one stream, nice
2026-11-20 11:20:25 #xqc viewer_13: have you seen that mall in [gta 6] yet
2026-11-20 11:17:08 #xqc viewer_14: the [gta 6] has that gta 5 driving wobble screen thing, i…
2026-11-20 11:14:12 #xqc viewer_15: [GTA 6] is kinda mid compared to gta 5
2026-11-20 11:13:19 #xqc viewer_14: why is forsen not streaming [gta 6] yet :(
12 matches (newest first, max 50)
$ ./twitchlog search -db chat.db -q 'NEAR(gta mall, 10)' -tz Asia/Saigon
2026-11-20 11:20:25 #xqc viewer_13: have you seen that [mall] in [gta] 6 yet
1 matches (newest first, max 50)

Pass user input through as-is and FTS5 will choke on punctuation:

$ ./twitchlog search -db chat.db -q 'gta 6?'
2026/11/20 11:42:19 SQL logic error: fts5: syntax error near "?" (1)

If the query comes from users, wrap each word in double quotes before you pass it on.

Exports print one line per message. Redacted messages keep their place in the timeline, so the log stays honest about what happened without repeating what was removed:

$ ./twitchlog export -db chat.db -channel xqc -day 2026-11-20 -tz Asia/Saigon
[2026-11-20 11:20:53] #xqc viewer_16: glass in front
[2026-11-20 11:20:53] #xqc viewer_17: jewelry
[2026-11-20 11:20:53] #xqc viewer_18: All that for 300
[2026-11-20 11:20:53] #xqc viewer_19: <message timeout>
[2026-11-20 11:20:54] #xqc viewer_20: Glass
[2026-11-20 11:20:54] #xqc viewer_21: jewlery
[2026-11-20 11:20:54] #xqc viewer_22: meow
[2026-11-20 11:20:55] #xqc viewer_23: jewelry💎!!
[2026-11-20 11:20:55] #xqc viewer_24: EZ
[2026-11-20 11:20:55] #xqc viewer_25: Omds break the front
[2026-11-20 11:20:55] #xqc viewer_26: smash the glasses
[2026-11-20 11:20:55] #xqc viewer_27: Merch drop #3 is out https://xqc.store/ EZ

Storage is small. The raw logs for all 12,443 messages came to 4.9 MB, and the SQLite file, FTS index included, to 3.4 MB. That's about 400 bytes of raw IRC per message, and a chat at 280 messages a minute would produce roughly 160 MB of raw log per 24 hours of streaming. Compress old raw logs with gzip.

Pitfalls, in one list

  • There's no backfill. Every minute your logger is down is lost. Neither IRC nor EventSub has history.
  • Raw IRC ports may be blocked. Port 443 WebSockets got through where 6667 and 6697 didn't.
  • Split frames on \r\n. One WebSocket message can carry several IRC lines.
  • Answer PING, or you get dropped. It comes about every 5 minutes, and a read deadline a bit longer than that catches dead connections.
  • A nonexistent channel fails silently. Confirm each JOIN echo.
  • Emote ranges are code points. Slice []rune, not bytes.
  • Strip U+034F and U+E0000 before storing or comparing messages.
  • Deduplicate on the message id. Twitch can send the same message twice, and replays will too.
  • Use user-id, not the login, to group messages by person. Logins can be renamed.
  • Timeouts redact more than one message. Store the reason, and keep the CLEARCHAT timestamp so a replay doesn't redact messages sent after it.
  • Batch your writes. A busy chat broke 800 messages a minute.
  • Third-party emotes are invisible to the tags.
  • Join limits: 20 joins per 10 seconds, 100 channels at once on a normal account.

Wrapping up

  • Twitch chat logs are forward-only. You build them by being connected; no API gives you yesterday's chat.
  • IRC over wss:// on port 443 is the simplest way to read chat, and the anonymous login needs no app registration. EventSub is the documented route Twitch recommends.
  • Treat moderation as data. Timeouts and deletions arrive as events. Honoring them keeps your log in line with what Twitch shows, and it's the decent thing to do.
  • Keep the raw log. With import, it's a full rebuild whenever your schema changes.

What would you track in a chat? Emote trends across a season, moderation load per stream, how raids change a chat? If you've built a Twitch chat logger with EventSub instead, I'd like to hear how it went.

*I build it.

title: Calibrating 1σ Error Bars for Mountain Snow Forecasts (6 NWP Models + USDA SNOTEL)
description:
As everyone in AI jokes right now, open = close. By symmetry, close = open.

After enough ski friends nudged me, I built CloseSnow (close-snow.clifan.com), a 100% free, zero-paywall 15-day mountain snow forecaster covering all 120 Ikon and Epic Pass resorts.

Why single-number snow bars lie

Most snow apps show a single crisp integer on every day of a 10- or 15-day chart. To a skier planning PTO, 8" on Wednesday and 8" next Thursday look identical. Physically, they aren't even the same species of number:

  1. Snow-to-liquid ratio (SLR) swings 4× across storms. Half an inch of liquid water (0.50" SWE) falling through a saturated -15°C dendritic growth zone in Little Cottonwood Canyon stacks up to 9" of cold smoke (18:1 SLR). That same 0.50" SWE in a 31°F atmospheric river at Palisades Tahoe settles into 4" of sierra cement (8:1), or turns to rain at base lodge elevation.
  2. Ensemble spread explodes with lead time and marginal temperatures. At Day 2, high-resolution convection-allowing models like NOAA HRRR (3 km) and NBM v4.2 often agree within an inch. By Day 9, or whenever wet-bulb temperature sits within 1.5°C of freezing, global models routinely span 0" to 14". Hiding that variance behind a single mean tricks people into chasing phantom storms.

What CloseSnow computes instead

CloseSnow pulls live pressure-level profiles (850, 700, 600, 500 hPa) across six NWP models—NOAA HRRR 3km, NBM v4.2, ECMWF IFS 9km, ECMWF AI AIFS, DWD ICON, and GFS 16-day—at Base, Mid-Mountain, and Summit elevations for 120 resorts:

  • 3D Cobb/Alcott microphysics: Weights vertical motion through the -12°C to -18°C dendritic growth zone, penalizes 50+ mph ridge-top wind riming, and applies resort-specific 700 hPa canyon alignment multipliers.
  • Color-matched ±1σ I-beam error bars: Every bar displays a calibrated ±1σ range (5 ± 1", 7 ± 3", 6 ± 4"). Uncertainty grows monotonically with lead time and 0°C wet-bulb phase risk while staying physically non-negative.
  • Live USDA SNOTEL ground truth: 41 US mountain resorts pair directly with hourly USDA NRCS SNOTEL ultrasonic snow-pillow telemetry so you can check what actually fell over the past 15 days.

Out-of-sample SNOTEL & HRRR backtest

Before sharing it publicly, I evaluated the model out-of-sample (live Accuracy Lab):

  • Atmospheric sounding test (N = 7,863 held-out HRRR 3km soundings, 2,829 mountain events ≥1,500m, trained strictly on 31,178 ERA5 soundings): CloseSnow reached 3.23 SLR MAE on mountain snow events, compared to 3.91 for Kuchera, 5.12 for OpenSnow's temperature heuristic, and 5.43 for fixed 10:1.
  • Real 48-hour mountain storms (N = 221 held-out USDA SNOTEL storm cycles from Jan 16 – Apr 15, 2025 across 20 Ikon/Epic resorts):
    • CloseSnow ($0): 2.37" MAE (52.9% within ±2", 72.4% empirical ±1σ storm coverage)
    • Bergfex / MeteoBlue Pro ($25/yr): 3.21" MAE
    • OpenSnow ($49.99–$99.99/yr): 4.01" MAE
    • pow.fyi / Fixed 10:1 ($0): 4.14" MAE

Honest scope limits

Extended Days 11–15 reflect synoptic storm-window probabilities across ECMWF IFS, AI AIFS, and GFS rather than exact inch counts—which is why their ±1σ whiskers stretch wide. Also, SNOTEL snow pillows cover 41 US mountain resorts and sit in sheltered clearings; non-US resorts use Open-Meteo reanalysis for past-15-day history.

It is a solo, zero-ad, zero-login public-good build. Expect rough edges and bugs—if you spot a resort with weird canyon physics or mobile layout quirks, send feedback my way. Fixes ship between laps.

  • Live App: https://close-snow.clifan.com/
  • Overview & Architecture: https://clifan.com/close-snow/
  • Live Accuracy Lab: https://close-snow.clifan.com/?view=methodology

title: Cutting out a background colour with a canvas pixel loop: what I learned building Color to Transparent
description:
A few months ago I needed one boring thing: a logo on a white background that had to sit on a transparent one. Every online tool I found wanted an account, a watermark, or an upload of a file I would rather not send anywhere. So I wrote the loop myself, and it turned into Color to Transparent, a free browser tool that removes one chosen colour from an image and makes it transparent.

The core is shorter than you think

Every pixel is four numbers in a Uint8ClampedArray. Once you have the background colour you want gone, the rest is a distance check:

function keyOut(ctx, width, height, target, tolerance) {
  const img = ctx.getImageData(0, 0, width, height);
  const d = img.data;
  const [tr, tg, tb] = target;
  const limit = tolerance * tolerance * 3;

  for (let i = 0; i < d.length; i += 4) {
    const dr = d[i] - tr, dg = d[i + 1] - tg, db = d[i + 2] - tb;
    if (dr * dr + dg * dg + db * db <= limit) d[i + 3] = 0;
  }
  ctx.putImageData(img, 0, 0);
}

That is the whole idea. Everything else in the tool exists because the naive version looks bad.

Four details that decide whether it looks finished

Picking the colour from the edge. Asking people to type a HEX value is friction. A click on the image is faster, so the tool reads the pixel under the pointer and uses it as the target — and it can sample from the border by default, because the background is usually what touches the frame.

Tolerance needs to be a small number and a big one. A pure white background is not uniform once a JPEG has touched it: compression leaves bands and ringing. Too little tolerance leaves a soft grey halo; too much eats into the subject. A 0–100 slider that maps to a squared RGB distance is easy to reason about for both the user and the code.

Halo cleanup is separate from keying. Pixels blended between subject and background keep a hint of the old colour. Removing the old colour from them is a blending problem, not a threshold problem, and it is worth doing as a second pass.

The connected-area option saves a lot of retries. If a logo also happens to contain the background colour — white letters on a white page, for instance — a global key destroys them. Restricting the removal to the region connected to the click keeps the interior intact.

Per-pixel work belongs on the main thread only briefly

A 6,000 px image is 36 million pixels. For loops over typed arrays on that scale are fast enough in practice, but they are still long enough to drop frames. What helped most was keeping the preview at screen resolution and applying the same settings to the full-size image only when exporting, so nothing feels laggy while you drag a slider.

That is also why the files never leave the device: the browser reads the image, runs the loop, and hands back a PNG or WebP with an alpha channel via canvas.toBlob(). No queue, no storage, nothing to clean up.

What I would tell anyone building the same thing

  • Put the tolerance slider and the colour picker side by side; people adjust them together.
  • Offer an undo brush early. One bad tolerance value is usually all it takes.
  • Export PNG by default. There is no point in a transparent background you cannot keep.
  • Test with a JPEG, not a PNG. Real-world white is almost never white.

The tool itself is free, needs no sign-up and has no watermark, so if you want to see the finished version of this loop you can try it at colorremoverfromimage.com. If you are writing your own keying code, the two things I would invest in first are tolerance control and a connected-area mode — they are what turn a ten-line demo into something people can actually use.

title: Export Mailchimp Data with the API: A Node.js Script
description:
Export your Mailchimp data with the API and you get something the dashboard export doesn't give you: a repeatable, scriptable backup you can run whenever you like and feed straight into another system. With Bending Spoons agreeing on November 19, 2026 to buy Mailchimp from Intuit (closing is expected in early 2027), plenty of teams want a complete copy of their data on their own disk. Nothing has changed yet. This is just good practice.

This guide walks through a single Node.js script that:

  1. lists every audience in the account,
  2. exports every contact in each audience, by status (subscribed, unsubscribed, cleaned and the rest), with merge fields and tags,
  3. saves the HTML of every sent campaign, and
  4. optionally loads your subscribed contacts into Cresca, an AI email marketing and transactional email platform, through its contacts API.

Mailchimp API details below come from Mailchimp's developer documentation, checked on November 20, 2026. For the business side of the deal, see Bending Spoons acquires Mailchimp: what it means for you.

What the Mailchimp API export covers (and what it doesn't)

Data API Dashboard export
Contacts with status, merge fields and tags Yes: GET /lists/{list_id}/members Yes, one CSV per status
Merge field definitions Yes: GET /lists/{list_id}/merge-fields Column headers only
Sent campaign HTML Yes: GET /campaigns/{campaign_id}/content Yes, in the account data export
Template HTML No documented endpoint returns full template HTML Custom-coded templates only, or the account data export
Open and click history Reports endpoints Campaign report exports

For templates, use the dashboard: Account, Settings, Manage my data, Export Data puts the HTML of your templates in a Templates folder. You can run that export once every 24 hours.

Step 1: Get a Mailchimp API key and your server prefix

In Mailchimp, open your profile, then Extras and API keys, and create a key. A Mailchimp API key has full access to the account and doesn't expire, so treat it like a password, keep it in an environment variable and delete it when you're done.

The key ends in a dash and your data centre, for example -us6. That suffix is the server prefix in the API URL: https://us6.api.mailchimp.com/3.0.

Authentication is HTTP Basic, with any string as the username and the API key as the password. Bearer tokens work too.

export MAILCHIMP_API_KEY="your-key-us6"
# Optional, for step 5:
export CRESCA_API_KEY="cr_live_..."

Step 2: A small Mailchimp API client with pagination

Mailchimp's list endpoints return at most 1,000 items per call. You page through them with count and offset, and each response includes total_items. The API allows 10 simultaneous connections per user and returns 429 TooManyRequests above that. This script makes one request at a time, so it stays well under the limit, and it retries on 429 just in case.

// export-mailchimp.mjs (Node.js 18 or later, no dependencies)
import { mkdir, writeFile, appendFile } from 'node:fs/promises';

const KEY = process.env.MAILCHIMP_API_KEY;
if (!KEY || !KEY.includes('-')) throw new Error('Set MAILCHIMP_API_KEY (it ends in -usN)');
const SERVER = KEY.split('-').pop();                 // e.g. "us6"
const BASE = `https://${SERVER}.api.mailchimp.com/3.0`;
const AUTH = 'Basic ' + Buffer.from(`export:${KEY}`).toString('base64');
const OUT = './mailchimp-export';
const sleep = (ms) => new Promise((r) => setTimeout(r, ms));

async function mc(path, params = {}) {
  const url = new URL(BASE + path);
  for (const [k, v] of Object.entries(params)) url.searchParams.set(k, String(v));
  for (let attempt = 1; ; attempt++) {
    const res = await fetch(url, { headers: { Authorization: AUTH } });
    if (res.status === 429 && attempt <= 5) { await sleep(attempt * 2000); continue; }
    if (!res.ok) throw new Error(`Mailchimp ${res.status} on ${path}: ${await res.text()}`);
    return res.json();
  }
}

// Yields every item of a paginated collection, 1,000 at a time.
async function* all(path, key, params = {}) {
  const count = 1000;
  for (let offset = 0; ; offset += count) {
    const page = await mc(path, { ...params, count, offset });
    yield* page[key];
    if (offset + count >= page.total_items) return;
  }
}

Step 3: Export every contact, by status

A full backup needs more than your subscribers. The unsubscribed and cleaned contacts are your record of who must not get marketing email again, so the script exports every status Mailchimp documents for this endpoint. Each audience gets a JSON Lines file with the complete member objects, so nothing is lost, plus a simple CSV of subscribed contacts for importing elsewhere.

const STATUSES = ['subscribed', 'unsubscribed', 'cleaned', 'pending', 'transactional', 'archived'];
const slug = (s) => s.toLowerCase().replace(/[^a-z0-9]+/g, '-').replace(/^-|-$/g, '');
const csvCell = (v) => `"${String(v ?? '').replace(/"/g, '""')}"`;

async function exportAudiences() {
  await mkdir(`${OUT}/audiences`, { recursive: true });
  const subscribedByAudience = {};

  for await (const list of all('/lists', 'lists')) {
    const name = slug(list.name) || list.id;
    const dir = `${OUT}/audiences/${name}`;
    await mkdir(dir, { recursive: true });

    // Merge field definitions (FNAME, LNAME, and your custom fields)
    const fields = [];
    for await (const f of all(`/lists/${list.id}/merge-fields`, 'merge_fields')) fields.push(f);
    await writeFile(`${dir}/merge-fields.json`, JSON.stringify(fields, null, 2));

    const subscribed = [];
    for (const status of STATUSES) {
      const file = `${dir}/${status}.jsonl`;
      await writeFile(file, '');
      let n = 0;
      for await (const m of all(`/lists/${list.id}/members`, 'members', { status })) {
        await appendFile(file, JSON.stringify(m) + '\n');
        n++;
        if (status === 'subscribed') {
          subscribed.push({
            email: m.email_address,
            first_name: m.merge_fields?.FNAME || '',
            last_name: m.merge_fields?.LNAME || '',
            tags: (m.tags || []).map((t) => t.name).join('|'),
          });
        }
      }
      console.log(`${list.name}: ${n} ${status}`);
    }

    const header = 'email,first_name,last_name,tags';
    const rows = subscribed.map((r) => [r.email, r.first_name, r.last_name, r.tags].map(csvCell).join(','));
    await writeFile(`${dir}/subscribed.csv`, [header, ...rows].join('\n'));
    subscribedByAudience[list.name] = subscribed;
  }
  return subscribedByAudience;
}

On a very large audience (hundreds of thousands of contacts), consider Mailchimp's batch operations endpoint (POST /batches) instead. A batched GET without a count pages through the whole collection on Mailchimp's side, and you download the results as a gzipped tar file.

Step 4: Save the HTML of every sent campaign

GET /campaigns lists campaigns, and GET /campaigns/{campaign_id}/content returns the campaign's html and plain_text. That gives you a permanent archive of every email you've sent, including the drag-and-drop designs you can't export as templates.

async function exportCampaigns() {
  await mkdir(`${OUT}/campaigns`, { recursive: true });
  let n = 0;
  for await (const c of all('/campaigns', 'campaigns', { status: 'sent' })) {
    const content = await mc(`/campaigns/${c.id}/content`);
    const date = (c.send_time || '').slice(0, 10) || 'unsent';
    const base = `${OUT}/campaigns/${date}-${slug(c.settings?.subject_line || c.id)}-${c.id}`;
    if (content.html) await writeFile(`${base}.html`, content.html);
    if (content.plain_text) await writeFile(`${base}.txt`, content.plain_text);
    n++;
  }
  console.log(`Saved ${n} sent campaigns`);
}

Step 5: Load your subscribers into Cresca (optional)

If you want to try a different tool while your Mailchimp account keeps running, the same script can load your subscribed contacts into Cresca. Cresca's POST /contacts endpoint takes up to 1,000 contacts per request, creates the list if it doesn't exist, and never duplicates a contact. Imports are limited to 120 requests per 15 minutes, which is up to 120,000 contacts.

Only subscribed contacts are sent. Unsubscribed and cleaned addresses stay in your backup, where they belong.

const CRESCA = 'https://api.cresca.xyz/api/v1';

async function importToCresca(listName, contacts) {
  for (let i = 0; i < contacts.length; i += 1000) {
    const chunk = contacts.slice(i, i + 1000).map((c) => ({
      email: c.email,
      ...(c.first_name && { first_name: c.first_name }),
      ...(c.last_name && { last_name: c.last_name }),
    }));
    const res = await fetch(`${CRESCA}/contacts`, {
      method: 'POST',
      headers: {
        Authorization: `Bearer ${process.env.CRESCA_API_KEY}`,
        'Content-Type': 'application/json',
      },
      body: JSON.stringify({ list_name: listName, contacts: chunk }),
    });
    if (!res.ok) throw new Error(`Cresca ${res.status}: ${await res.text()}`);
    const { summary } = await res.json();
    console.log(`${listName}: +${summary.created} new, ${summary.updated} updated, ${summary.rejected} rejected`);
  }
}

// Run everything
const audiences = await exportAudiences();
await exportCampaigns();
if (process.env.CRESCA_API_KEY) {
  for (const [name, contacts] of Object.entries(audiences)) {
    await importToCresca(`${name} (from Mailchimp)`, contacts);
  }
}
console.log(`Done. Files are in ${OUT}`);

Run it:

node export-mailchimp.mjs

You end up with a folder like this:

mailchimp-export/
  audiences/
    newsletter/
      merge-fields.json
      subscribed.jsonl
      unsubscribed.jsonl
      cleaned.jsonl
      pending.jsonl
      transactional.jsonl
      archived.jsonl
      subscribed.csv
  campaigns/
    2026-11-14-black-friday-early-access-abc123.html
    2026-11-14-black-friday-early-access-abc123.txt

To get a Cresca API key, create a free account (30 days, 250 contacts, 1,000 emails, no credit card) and create a key with full access. The add contacts API reference has the full request and response format. Cresca's contacts API stores email, first name and last name. Your other Mailchimp merge fields stay in the JSON backup.

Step 6: Send your first campaign from Cresca

Once the import finishes, your Mailchimp audience is waiting in Cresca. Here's how to send to it, from sign-up to report:

1. Verify your sending domain

Open Sending Domains, add your domain and add the DNS records Cresca shows (ownership, DKIM and MAIL FROM/SPF), each with a copy button. When the domain shows as Verified, add your sender address.

2. Find your imported list

Open Contacts, then Contact Lists. The script named each list after its Mailchimp audience, with "(from Mailchimp)" at the end.

Contact Lists in Cresca (sample data).

3. Describe the email to Cresca AI

Open Templates and type a brief in the Message Cresca AI box, for example "Welcome email for new subscribers with the code HELLO10 for 10% off". The AI agent designs the whole email in your brand, and you can refine it in the same conversation or in the editor.

Cresca AI designing a welcome email from one brief (sample brand).

4. Create the campaign

In Campaigns, choose New Campaign. Pick your sender, the template and the imported list, then send now or schedule it.

Scheduling a campaign in Cresca (sample data).

5. Check the results

on the dashboard or in Delivery logs: deliveries, bounces, complaints and unsubscribes. Hard bounces and complaints are suppressed automatically.

What to do with the backup

  • Store it somewhere safe and private. It contains personal data, so treat it under the same privacy rules as your live list.
  • Re-run it before any big change, such as a plan change, a migration or the deal closing.
  • Keep the unsubscribed and cleaned files for as long as you keep sending email. They're how you avoid emailing people who opted out.
  • Delete the API key when you're finished, because Mailchimp keys never expire on their own.

Why developers like Cresca

If your product sends both marketing and transactional email, Cresca puts them in one account, on your own domain:

  • a REST API for transactional email at https://api.cresca.xyz/api/v1, included on every plan, with templates, batches of up to 100 emails, scheduled sends and idempotency keys;
  • an AI agent that designs your marketing campaigns from a one-line brief, so nobody on the team has to hand-code newsletter HTML;
  • guided SPF and DKIM setup, one-click unsubscribe and automatic bounce and complaint suppression.

Email automation workflows are launching soon in Cresca. Campaigns, the AI agent and the transactional API are available today. Start with the quickstart, or try Cresca free for 30 days.

FAQ

Can I export Mailchimp contacts with the API?

Yes. GET /lists/{list_id}/members returns up to 1,000 contacts per call with count and offset for paging, and a status filter for subscribed, unsubscribed, cleaned, pending, transactional and archived contacts.

Does the Mailchimp API export templates?

No documented endpoint returns a template's full HTML. GET /templates/{template_id}/default-content returns only the editable sections. Use the account data export, which includes template HTML files, or export custom-coded templates from the dashboard.

What are the Mailchimp API rate limits?

Mailchimp allows 10 simultaneous connections per user and times out calls after 120 seconds. Going over the connection limit returns a 429 error.

Is my Mailchimp data changing because of the Bending Spoons acquisition?

No change has been announced. The deal is expected to close in early 2027, and neither company has said anything about plans, prices or data. A backup simply means you have a complete copy whatever happens.

title: CADCraft: Free Rust-Based 2D CAD for Technical Drawing
description:
CADCraft is a free, open-source 2D CAD application built in Rust for accurate drafting and technical documentation. It provides a familiar command-line workflow with precision editing, layers, dimensions, hatches, plotting, and support for DWG, DXF, PDF, SVG, and PNG.

The application runs on Windows, macOS, Linux, FreeBSD, and the web through WebAssembly. It is designed for architects, engineers, students, educators, makers, and technical designers, with no subscription or account registration required.

CADCraft also includes MCP, JSON, and headless CLI interfaces for AI-assisted automation: agents can create drawings, inspect entities, render screenshots, convert files, and verify results. The project is released under the MIT or Apache-2.0 licenses and is still in active development.

Learn more at CADCraft.

title: AWS Cloud Quest: Cloud Practitioner Badge - How to Earn It
description:
A beginner's guide to earning the free AWS Cloud Quest: Cloud Practitioner badge on AWS Skill Builder, with steps, benefits and next steps.

tags: aws, cloud, beginners, learning

vishalcloudjourney

Learning cloud from videos and notes alone can feel dry. AWS Cloud Quest: Cloud Practitioner on AWS Skill Builder takes a different route: you learn AWS by playing a game. I earned the AWS Cloud Quest: Cloud Practitioner (Trained) badge, and in this post I'll cover what it is, how to earn it, its advantages, and how it can help you grow.

What Is AWS Cloud Quest?

AWS Cloud Quest is a 3D, role-based learning game on AWS Skill Builder. You play through a virtual city and solve problems using AWS services. Each assignment teaches a concept and then asks you to apply it.

The Cloud Practitioner role is aimed at beginners and needs no prior cloud experience.

Topics You Practice

The badge grounds you in foundational concepts like compute, storage, networking and security. Assignments include areas such as core security concepts, file systems in the cloud, a first NoSQL database, auto-healing and scaling applications, and highly available web applications. Services you work with include EC2, S3, VPC, RDS, DynamoDB and IAM.

How to Earn the Badge

Step 1: Create a free account. Register for a free AWS Skill Builder account. You may also be asked to set up an AWS Builder ID.

Step 2: Find Cloud Quest. Go to Skill Builder, search for Cloud Quest, and open AWS Cloud Quest: Cloud Practitioner.

Step 3: Choose the free role. During the onboarding tutorial you pick a role. Choose Cloud Practitioner, which is the free one.

Step 4: Complete every assignment. The Cloud Practitioner course has 12 free hands-on assignments. To earn the official badge, you complete every assignment in the role.

Step 5: Claim and share your badge. Badges are shareable on Credly and on your Skills Profile. Add yours to LinkedIn, your resume and your portfolio.

Good to Know

  • It's free. Cloud Practitioner is one of the free roles.
  • The labs are real AWS work. They are done in the AWS console, so you build real things.
  • It is a training badge, not the certification. The AWS Certified Cloud Practitioner certification requires passing the official exam.
  • Requirements can change. Check the official Skill Builder page for the latest details.

My badge: View on Credly

Advantages of Earning This Badge

  1. Hands-on experience, not just theory. You practice building real solutions instead of only watching videos.
  2. Free to start. Anyone can begin without paying.
  3. Beginner-friendly. Each assignment explains the concept first, then lets you apply it.
  4. Official, shareable proof. Easy to add to LinkedIn, your resume and your portfolio.
  5. Builds core knowledge. You touch compute, storage, networking, databases, security and scaling, the foundations of almost every AWS role.
  6. Supports certification prep. It prepares you for the AWS Certified Cloud Practitioner exam.
  7. Keeps you motivated. The game format makes it easier to stay consistent than passive learning.
  8. Stands out as a student. It shows initiative and real learning, which helps with internships, cloud clubs and community programs.

How This Badge Helps You Grow

A badge is a starting point, not the finish line.

  1. Build confidence. Finishing real labs proves to yourself that you can work with AWS.
  2. Take the next learning steps. Try the AWS Cloud Essentials Knowledge Badge, the free AWS Cloud Quest: Generative AI Practitioner, and the AWS Well-Architected basics.
  3. Prepare for certification. Use the badge as a base, then move on to exam prep for the AWS Certified Cloud Practitioner (CLF-C02).
  4. Create your own projects. Set up a billing alarm, host a static site on S3, or launch an EC2 instance, then write about it.
  5. Share your journey. Posting on AWS Builder Center, dev.to and LinkedIn builds your portfolio and helps other beginners.
  6. Join the community. Engage with AWS communities, student groups and programs like AWS Community Builders.
  7. Grow toward a career. These skills lead naturally toward roles like cloud support, DevOps and cloud engineering, one step at a time.

Tips for Beginners

  • Don't rush. Read each explanation before starting the lab.
  • Take short notes on each service as you meet it.
  • Retry a lab if you get stuck. Repetition helps.
  • Connect each service to a real example, like S3 for file storage.
  • Pair it with the official Cloud Practitioner Essentials course for a fuller picture.

Key Takeaways

  • Cloud Quest turns AWS learning into a hands-on game, and the Cloud Practitioner role is free.
  • Complete all assignments to earn an official, shareable badge.
  • The badge shows hands-on training, and it is a strong first step toward the certification.
  • Badge by badge, lab by lab, that's how you grow. Keep learning, keep building, keep sharing.

Connect with me

  • LinkedIn: vishalpatil-devops-aws
  • dev.to: @vishal_patil_aws
  • GitHub: VishalPatil-DevOps-AWS
  • Portfolio: vishalpatil-devops-aws.github.io/portfolio

vishalcloudjourney #AWS #AWSCloudQuest #CloudPractitioner
