title: Your AI Agent Completed 4 of 5 Steps. Who Is Responsible for the Damage?
description:
Why multi-agent workflows need failure recovery, compensating transactions, and reliable execution guarantees

There is something particularly uncomfortable about an AI agent that almost completes its job. Not an agent that crashes immediately. Not one that misunderstands a request or produces an obviously incorrect response. Those failures are relatively easy to recognise.

I am talking about an agent that completes four steps of a five-step workflow, reports progress along the way, and then fails at the exact moment when recovery becomes complicated.

Imagine an AI-powered order management system. A customer places an order. An agent creates the order, another reserves inventory, a payment service processes the transaction, and a shipping agent prepares the delivery. Everything appears to be working.

Then the shipping service times out. The payment has already been processed. Inventory is reserved. The order exists. But the shipping label has not been generated. The orchestration layer retries the operation. Meanwhile, another agent takes ownership of the workflow because the original agent appears unresponsive.

Now two agents are looking at the same incomplete transaction, neither of which has a complete understanding of what already happened. One attempts to process the payment again. The other tries to release the inventory reservation. The shipping service eventually recovers, but the system has already moved into an inconsistent state.

The interesting part is that none of the individual agents necessarily made a bad decision. The order agent did its job. The inventory agent did its job. The payment service processed the payment. The shipping agent encountered a failure.

The problem was not intelligence.

The problem was that the workflow had no reliable way to recover from partial execution.

This is a problem I think deserves considerably more attention as AI agents move from answering questions and generating recommendations to coordinating real business operations. We have spent considerable time discussing how to make agents reason better, retrieve better information, and avoid conflicting decisions. But there is another question that becomes unavoidable when these systems start executing multiple dependent actions:

What happens when the workflow cannot finish, but some of its actions have already taken effect? That is where reliable AI engineering becomes much more interesting.

1. The Dangerous Assumption: A Workflow Either Succeeds or Fails

Traditional application workflows often encourage a simple mental model. An operation starts, executes its steps, and eventually returns success or failure.

For a small operation, this model works reasonably well. Consider a function that validates an email address, checks a field, and writes a record to a database. If something fails before the transaction commits, the database can roll back the changes.

But distributed workflows are different. A single business operation may involve:

  • An order management database.
  • An inventory service.
  • A payment gateway.
  • A shipping provider.
  • A notification service.
  • Multiple AI agents coordinating the process.

These systems do not share one database transaction. A database rollback cannot automatically reverse a payment that has already been accepted by an external payment provider. It cannot guarantee that a shipping label was not generated or that an email was not delivered.

The workflow may have completed some actions permanently, while other actions remain pending. I find this distinction important because AI orchestration frameworks sometimes make multi-step execution look deceptively simple.

A workflow might be represented as:

async def process_order(order):
    await create_order(order)
    await reserve_inventory(order)
    await process_payment(order)
    await schedule_shipping(order)
    await send_confirmation(order)

    return {"status": "completed"}

The code is easy to read. The operational behaviour is not. What happens if schedule_shipping() raises an exception?

What happens if the payment provider accepts the payment, but the response never reaches the application?

What happens if the process crashes after scheduling shipping but before recording that the operation succeeded?

What happens if another worker starts processing the same order?

The function does not answer these questions. Adding a generic retry decorator does not solve them. A reliable workflow needs to understand not just what it intends to do, but what has actually happened.

2. The Five-Step Failure That Changes Everything

Let's examine the order scenario more carefully. Suppose an AI-powered commerce platform coordinates five actions.

Step Operation Result
1 Create customer order Success
2 Reserve inventory Success
3 Process payment Success
4 Schedule shipping Failed
5 Send confirmation Not executed

At first glance, this looks like an ordinary failed workflow. But look at the actual business state. The customer has an order. The inventory is unavailable to other customers. The payment has been collected. The delivery has not been arranged.

The system is not simply unsuccessful. It is partially committed. That difference matters. If we retry the entire workflow, we risk creating another order, reserving inventory twice, or charging the customer again.

If we abandon the workflow, the customer may lose money while the inventory remains unavailable. If we reverse everything, we may need to refund the payment and release inventory, but we must first establish whether any of those operations can safely be reversed.

This is why I prefer thinking about workflows in terms of execution state rather than a single success or failure flag. A useful execution record might look like this:

{
  "workflow_id": "order-84721",
  "status": "PARTIALLY_COMPLETED",
  "steps": {
    "create_order": {
      "status": "SUCCEEDED"
    },
    "reserve_inventory": {
      "status": "SUCCEEDED"
    },
    "process_payment": {
      "status": "SUCCEEDED",
      "payment_reference": "pay-91281"
    },
    "schedule_shipping": {
      "status": "FAILED",
      "error": "Provider timeout"
    },
    "send_confirmation": {
      "status": "NOT_STARTED"
    }
  }
}

This gives the orchestration layer something much more useful than a generic exception. It knows which operations have been completed, which have failed, and which have not started. However, there is an important caveat.

A status record is not proof that an external operation did or did not happen. A timeout after a payment request could mean the payment failed, or it could mean the payment succeeded and the response was lost. That uncertainty is one of the hardest parts of distributed execution.

3. Why Retrying Is Not the Same as Recovering

Retries are one of the first mechanisms engineers introduce when an external service becomes unreliable. A request fails. The system waits. It tries again. For transient failures, this is useful. But retries become dangerous when an operation has side effects. Consider a payment request.

async def charge_customer(amount, payment_method):
    response = await payment_provider.charge(
        amount=amount,
        payment_method=payment_method
    )

    return response

Imagine the payment provider successfully charges the customer. Before the response reaches our application, the network connection drops. Our application sees a timeout.

It has no immediate way of knowing whether the payment happened. If it sends the same request again without additional safeguards, the customer might be charged twice. This is not an AI reasoning problem. It is a distributed systems problem.

The agent may have correctly interpreted the request, selected the right payment method, and decided that payment should be processed. The failure occurs because the system cannot safely distinguish an unsuccessful operation from an operation whose result is unknown.

I think this is where teams need to be careful about using retries as a universal recovery strategy. A retry should not mean:

"Execute the same instruction again."

It should mean: "Establish whether the previous attempt took effect, then decide whether another attempt is safe." That requires operation identity, durable state, and reconciliation.

Introduce idempotency keys

One practical solution is to assign a stable idempotency key to each logical operation. For example:

import uuid

def create_payment_request(order_id, amount):
    operation_id = f"payment:{order_id}"

    return {
        "operation_id": operation_id,
        "amount": amount,
        "idempotency_key": operation_id
    }

The payment provider or an application-owned payment adapter can use this key to recognise repeated requests representing the same logical payment. A simplified implementation might look like:

async def process_payment(order_id, amount):
    operation_id = f"payment:{order_id}"

    existing = await payment_store.get(operation_id)

    if existing and existing["status"] == "SUCCEEDED":
        return existing

    result = await payment_provider.charge(
        amount=amount,
        idempotency_key=operation_id
    )

    await payment_store.save({
        "operation_id": operation_id,
        "status": "SUCCEEDED",
        "provider_reference": result.reference
    })

    return result

This illustrates the approach, but a production implementation needs more. In particular, it must handle concurrent requests, uncertain provider responses, key-retention policies, and atomic persistence of operation state.

A local lookup alone does not prevent two workers from sending the same request simultaneously. The important principle is that the same logical operation should not accidentally become multiple independent business actions.

Idempotency protects the workflow from repeated delivery. It does not automatically protect it from every kind of partial failure.

That brings us to a more fundamental design pattern.

4. The Saga Pattern: Recovering Without a Global Rollback

In distributed systems, one widely used approach to managing long-running business transactions is the Saga pattern. Instead of treating an entire workflow as one atomic database transaction, a Saga breaks it into smaller transactions.

Each transaction commits independently. When a later step fails, the workflow can execute compensating transactions for earlier completed steps. For our order example:

Forward operation Possible compensation
Create order Cancel order
Reserve inventory Release reservation
Process payment Refund payment
Schedule shipping Cancel shipment, if supported
Send confirmation Send correction or cancellation notice

This is a powerful idea, but it is important to understand what compensation actually means. A compensating transaction is not a database rollback. If a payment has been processed, a refund does not erase the original payment. It creates another financial operation that offsets it.

If a customer has already received an email, the system cannot make that email disappear. It can send a correction. If a package has already left a warehouse, cancelling the shipment may no longer be possible. Compensation is a business operation designed to restore an acceptable state.

It is not necessarily a perfect reversal of history.

A simple Saga implementation

We can model the workflow explicitly.

async def execute_order_saga(order):
    completed = []

    try:
        await create_order(order)
        completed.append("order")

        await reserve_inventory(order)
        completed.append("inventory")

        await process_payment(order)
        completed.append("payment")

        await schedule_shipping(order)
        completed.append("shipping")

        await send_confirmation(order)

        return {
            "status": "COMPLETED"
        }

    except Exception as error:
        recovery = await compensate(
            order,
            completed
        )

        return {
            "status": "FAILED",
            "error": str(error),
            "completed_steps": completed,
            "compensation": recovery
        }

The compensation logic might look like:

async def compensate(order, completed):
    results = []

    if "payment" in completed:
        results. append(
            await refund_payment(order)
        )

    if "inventory" in completed:
        results. append(
            await release_inventory(order)
        )

    if "order" in completed:
        results. append(
            await cancel_order(order)
        )

    return results

This is a useful conceptual starting point. However, there is a serious problem with this implementation.

What happens if the application crashes while executing the compensation? The in-memory completed list disappears. The system may have already refunded the customer, but failed before recording the refund result.

When the workflow restarts, it could attempt the refund again. We have simply moved the original reliability problem into the recovery mechanism. That is why a Saga must be durable. Every meaningful state transition needs to be recorded so that another worker can continue recovery after a crash.

5. A Workflow Needs a Durable Execution History

One of the mistakes I would avoid is treating an agent's conversational memory as the source of truth for workflow execution. An agent might remember that it successfully processed a payment. But memory is not an execution ledger. The process may have restarted. Another agent may have taken ownership. The external payment provider may have updated its state.

The system needs a durable record that exists independently of the agent. I would separate three responsibilities:

The agent decides what should happen.

The orchestrator determines which operation is allowed to execute next.

The execution ledger records what actually happened.

A simplified workflow state machine might be:

             PENDING
                |
                v
           EXECUTING
                |
       +--------+--------+
       |                 |
       v                 v
   COMPLETED         RECOVERY_REQUIRED
                         |
                         v
                    COMPENSATING
                         |
                 +-------+-------+
                 |               |
                 v               v
            COMPENSATED    MANUAL_REVIEW

The important part is that recovery is a first-class workflow state. It should not be an exception handler that exists only in the memory of the process that encountered the failure. A durable execution record could contain:

CREATE TABLE workflow_steps (
    workflow_id TEXT NOT NULL,
    step_id TEXT NOT NULL,
    operation_id TEXT NOT NULL,
    status TEXT NOT NULL,
    attempt_count INTEGER DEFAULT 0,
    idempotency_key TEXT NOT NULL,
    external_reference TEXT,
    last_error TEXT,
    updated_at TIMESTAMP DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP,
    PRIMARY KEY (workflow_id, step_id),
    UNIQUE (operation_id)
);

For production systems, I would also maintain an append-only execution history. For example:

CREATE TABLE workflow_events (
    event_id TEXT PRIMARY KEY,
    workflow_id TEXT NOT NULL,
    operation_id TEXT NOT NULL,
    event_type TEXT NOT NULL,
    event_payload JSON,
    created_at TIMESTAMP DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP
);

The first table represents the current state. The second records how the workflow reached that state. This distinction becomes particularly useful when investigating failures.

Suppose an agent claims that a payment succeeded, but the ledger shows that the payment operation was submitted and never received a confirmed result. Instead of trusting the agent's previous message, the recovery process can investigate the operation using its stable identifier and the payment provider's reference.

The execution history becomes the basis for recovery, auditing, and accountability.

6. The Problem of Unknown Outcomes

There is one failure scenario that deserves special attention. Suppose the shipping agent sends a request to generate a shipping label. The provider processes it. The response never arrives. The agent times out. Should the system retry?

Not immediately. The operation is now in an ambiguous state. It may have succeeded externally, even though the local application does not know that. I would represent this explicitly:

PENDING
   |
   v
SUBMITTED
   |
   +-------------------+
   |                   |
   v                   v
CONFIRMED           UNKNOWN
                       |
                       v
                  RECONCILING
                       |
                +------+------+
                |             |
                v             v
             SUCCESS        FAILED

The UNKNOWN state is important. Without it, many applications collapse uncertain outcomes into ordinary failures. That creates unnecessary retries and duplicate side effects. A better recovery sequence is:

  1. Persist the operation identifier before making the external request.
  2. Submit the request with an idempotency key where supported.
  3. If the request times out, mark the outcome as unknown.
  4. Query the provider using the operation or external reference.
  5. If the operation succeeded, record success.
  6. If it definitely failed, decide whether retrying is safe.
  7. If the result cannot be established, escalate rather than blindly repeating the operation.

This process is especially important for payments, financial transfers, reservations, shipment creation, and other externally visible operations. The system should distinguish between:

  • An operation that failed.
  • An operation that succeeded.
  • An operation that might have succeeded but whose outcome is not yet known.

That third category is where many duplicate-execution problems begin.

7. Exactly-Once Execution Is Not a Magic Guarantee

AI agent frameworks and distributed workflow systems sometimes use language that makes execution guarantees sound simpler than they are. Terms like exactly-once execution can be misleading if we do not specify what is being guaranteed.

Consider a workflow that sends an external payment request. The application may guarantee that it processes a particular internal event once. But the network can fail after the provider has accepted the payment. The application cannot infer the external outcome merely from its local processing history.

In practice, I prefer designing around:

  • At least once message delivery.
  • Idempotent operation handling.
  • Durable execution records.
  • External operation reconciliation.
  • Explicit handling of unknown outcomes.

At least once delivery means an event may be delivered more than once. That is not necessarily a problem if processing is designed to be idempotent. For example:

async def handle_payment_event(event):
    operation_id = event["operation_id"]

    claimed = await claim_operation(operation_id)

    if not claimed:
        return {
            "status": "ALREADY_PROCESSED"
        }

    await apply_payment_result(event)

    return {
        "status": "APPLIED"
    }

The important detail is that claim_operation() must be implemented with an atomic database operation or another reliable coordination mechanism. A normal check followed by an insert is not enough.

Two workers could both check that the operation does not exist, and then both proceed. A unique constraint, conditional insert, or atomic claim operation can prevent this race.

Even then, the system must account for crashes between claiming an operation and completing its side effect. This is why idempotency, durable state, and reconciliation need to work together. No single mechanism solves the entire problem.

8. Multi-Agent Workflows Introduce an Additional Problem: Ownership

So far, we have discussed a workflow controlled by one orchestrator. Multi-agent systems make recovery more complicated. Imagine that the original payment agent becomes unresponsive after submitting a payment request.

The orchestrator detects a timeout and assigns the operation to another agent. The second agent sees an incomplete payment step and decides to execute it. But the original agent may still be running. Now both agents believe they own the same work. This is a form of split-brain execution. The problem is not simply that two agents have the same information. They have competing authority to perform the same operation.

I would address this by separating task assignment from execution authority. An agent may be assigned a task, but it should not automatically receive unrestricted permission to execute every external action associated with that task. The orchestrator should maintain ownership and enforce it at the execution boundary.

For example, a workflow operation could include:

{
  "workflow_id": "order-84721",
  "operation_id": "payment:order-84721",
  "owner": "payment-agent-02",
  "lease_version": 8,
  "lease_expires_at": "2026-11-20T10:15:00Z",
  "status": "EXECUTING"
}

The lease_version acts as a fencing token.

When ownership changes, the version increases. The execution layer checks that an agent's request carries the current version before accepting an operation. A stale worker holding version 7 cannot perform an operation that requires version 8. A simplified database update could look like:

UPDATE workflow_steps
SET status = 'EXECUTING',
    owner = 'payment-agent-02',
    lease_version = lease_version + 1
WHERE workflow_id = 'order-84721'
  AND step_id = 'process_payment'
  AND lease_version = 7;

In a real implementation, lease expiry, ownership acquisition, and fencing checks need to be handled atomically.

Also, a fencing token only protects resources that actually validate it. An external payment provider may not understand your internal lease version, so the payment adapter must combine ownership checks with provider-side idempotency and reconciliation.

This distinction is important.

Changing the agent that owns a task does not mean the previous agent's external actions have disappeared.

Ownership transfer is a coordination operation, not a reset button.

9. What Should Happen When Compensation Also Fails?

This is where the architecture becomes more realistic. Suppose shipping fails and the system begins compensation. The payment refund is successful. But the inventory release fails because the inventory service is unavailable.

Now the workflow has moved into another partially completed state. The customer has been refunded, but the inventory remains reserved. A naive implementation might simply mark the entire workflow as compensated. That would be incorrect. The system needs to track compensation at the individual operation level. For example:

Compensation action Status
Refund payment Completed
Release inventory Retry pending
Cancel order Completed
Notify customer Pending

This is why compensation should have its own execution history. It should not be represented by a single boolean field such as rolled_back = true.

A better model might look like:

{
  "workflow_id": "order-84721",
  "status": "COMPENSATION_IN_PROGRESS",
  "compensations": {
    "refund_payment": {
      "status": "SUCCEEDED"
    },
    "release_inventory": {
      "status": "RETRY_PENDING"
    },
    "cancel_order": {
      "status": "SUCCEEDED"
    }
  }
}

The recovery worker can continue with the unfinished compensation without repeating the successful refund. However, even this requires careful design.

What if the inventory reservation expired naturally before the release operation ran? What if another process has already released it?

What if the customer support team manually intervened? Recovery logic must check the current business state before applying another action. The purpose of compensation is to restore an acceptable outcome, not to execute a predetermined list of reverse operations regardless of what has changed.

Some failures should require human intervention

I do not think every failure should be handled autonomously. Consider these situations:

  • A payment provider reports an ambiguous transaction result.
  • A refund request is rejected.
  • A shipment has already left the warehouse.
  • Inventory is no longer available.
  • Two external systems report conflicting transaction references.

In these cases, automatically guessing the correct action can create a larger problem. A reliable system should support a MANUAL_REVIEW_REQUIRED state. The human operator should receive:

  • The workflow identifier.
  • The completed operations.
  • The failed operations.
  • The external references.
  • The compensation attempts.
  • The current ownership and execution history.
  • The specific decision requiring intervention.

This is not a failure of autonomous AI. It is a recognition that some business decisions require authority and information that the system does not possess. The best autonomous system is not the one that never asks for help. It is the one that knows when continuing automatically would be unsafe.

10. A More Reliable Architecture for AI-Orchestrated Workflows

If I were designing this architecture, I would avoid allowing individual agents to directly control every external side effect. Instead, I would use a workflow orchestrator with a durable execution ledger. The agents would propose and coordinate actions, while the orchestrator would control their execution. Here is the conceptual architecture:

                 USER REQUEST
                      |
                      v
               AI ORCHESTRATOR
                      |
          +-----------+-----------+
          |           |           |
          v           v           v
       ORDER       PAYMENT     SHIPPING
       AGENT        AGENT       AGENT
          |           |           |
          +-----------+-----------+
                      |
                      v
              EXECUTION GATEWAY
                      |
          +-----------+-----------+
          |           |           |
          v           v           v
       ORDER       PAYMENT     SHIPPING
      SERVICE      PROVIDER     SERVICE
          |           |           |
          +-----------+-----------+
                      |
                      v
             DURABLE EXECUTION
                   LEDGER
                      |
             +--------+--------+
             |                 |
             v                 v
       RECOVERY WORKER     AUDIT HISTORY
             |
       +-----+------+
       |            |
       v            v
    RETRY       COMPENSATE
       |            |
       +------+-----+
              |
              v
         HUMAN REVIEW
         WHEN NEEDED

The architecture has several important boundaries.

The AI orchestrator understands the business workflow and determines the next appropriate step.

The execution gateway validates whether the proposed operation is allowed and whether its prerequisites remain valid.

The durable ledger records operation state and execution history.

The recovery worker handles retries, reconciliation, and compensation.

Human review handles situations where the system cannot establish a safe next action.

This architecture does not require every team to build a large distributed orchestration platform. A small application can begin with a database-backed workflow state machine and a background worker. The important part is establishing the right execution boundaries before the system starts handling more consequential operations.

11. Putting the Design Together: A Durable Workflow Example

Let's bring the concepts together with a simplified Python implementation. The following example demonstrates a workflow that persists step state, identifies logical operations, and delegates uncertain outcomes to recovery rather than blindly retrying. It is an architectural illustration. A production implementation would need atomic database operations, provider-specific idempotency, durable event publication, authentication, and concurrency control.

from enum import Enum
from dataclasses import dataclass
from typing import Optional


class StepStatus(str, Enum):
    PENDING = "PENDING"
    EXECUTING = "EXECUTING"
    SUCCEEDED = "SUCCEEDED"
    FAILED = "FAILED"
    UNKNOWN = "UNKNOWN"
    COMPENSATING = "COMPENSATING"
    COMPENSATED = "COMPENSATED"
    MANUAL_REVIEW = "MANUAL_REVIEW"


@dataclass
class WorkflowStep:
    name: str
    operation_id: str
    status: StepStatus = StepStatus.PENDING
    external_reference: Optional[str] = None


async def execute_step(step, handler, ledger):

    existing = await ledger.get(step.operation_id)

    if existing and existing.status == StepStatus.SUCCEEDED:
        return existing

    await ledger.mark_executing(step.operation_id)

    try:
        result = await handler(
            idempotency_key=step.operation_id
        )

        await ledger.mark_succeeded(
            operation_id=step.operation_id,
            external_reference=result.reference
        )

        return result

    except TimeoutError:

        await ledger.mark_unknown(
            step.operation_id
        )

        return {
            "status": "UNKNOWN",
            "operation_id": step.operation_id
        }

    except Exception as error:

        await ledger.mark_failed(
            step.operation_id,
            str(error)
        )

        raise

Notice the most important decision in this example. A timeout does not immediately trigger another execution. It changes the operation state to UNKNOWN. A separate recovery process can then investigate the external system.

For example:

async def reconcile_operation(operation, provider, ledger):

    result = await provider.lookup(
        operation.operation_id
    )

    if result.status == "SUCCEEDED":

        await ledger.mark_succeeded(
            operation.operation_id,
            result.reference
        )

    elif result.status == "FAILED":

        await ledger.mark_failed(
            operation.operation_id,
            result.error
        )

    elif result.status == "NOT_FOUND":

        await ledger.mark_retry_pending(
            operation.operation_id
        )

    else:

        await ledger.mark_manual_review(
            operation.operation_id
        )

The NOT_FOUND case deserves care.

A provider lookup may be eventually consistent. An operation that is not visible yet is not necessarily an operation that never happened. A production implementation should account for provider-specific consistency guarantees, query windows, and idempotency-key retention before deciding that a retry is safe. The key design decision is that execution and recovery are separate responsibilities.

An agent does not need to remain alive throughout the entire recovery process. The workflow can survive the agent, the worker, and even the application process that originally started it. That is the value of durable execution.

12. What Should Teams Measure?

A system can appear reliable while hiding significant recovery problems.

For example, a workflow might report a 99.5% completion rate.

But that number alone does not tell us how many customers were charged twice, how many refunds remained pending, or how many workflows required manual intervention.

I would measure recovery quality separately from ordinary execution success.

Here are some useful metrics:

Metric What it reveals
Partial execution rate How frequently workflows stop after some steps succeed
Unknown outcome rate How often external results cannot be established immediately
Duplicate side-effect rate Whether retries or concurrent workers create repeated actions
Compensation success rate How reliably failed workflows restore acceptable business state
Recovery time How long workflows remain incomplete
Manual intervention rate How often autonomous recovery reaches its limits
Orphaned operation count How many operations remain unresolved beyond an agreed threshold
Ownership conflict rate How often multiple workers attempt to control the same workflow

One metric I would pay particular attention to is the unresolved partial-execution rate.

It measures workflows that have completed some side effects but have not reached either a valid final state or a verified compensated state within the recovery objective. That is more informative than simply counting exceptions.

For financial workflows, I would also track duplicate charges, outstanding refunds, and payment reconciliation discrepancies independently.

A workflow can eventually report success while still having caused an earlier business error. We need metrics that expose those failures rather than hiding them behind the final status.

13. A Practical Starting Point for Small Teams

It is tempting to look at all these components and conclude that reliable AI workflows require a sophisticated orchestration platform. They do not necessarily need one. In fact, I would recommend starting smaller.

If a team is building its first multi-agent workflow, I would prioritise the following steps.

First, assign a stable operation ID to every external side effect.

Do not rely on an agent's conversation ID or a temporary request ID. The same logical payment or reservation should retain its identity across retries and ownership changes.

Second, persist every completed operation.

Do not keep the critical workflow state only in memory. If a worker crashes, another worker must be able to establish what happened.

Third, make side effects idempotent wherever possible.

Use provider-supported idempotency keys, database uniqueness constraints, and atomic claims.

Fourth, distinguish failure from uncertainty.

A timeout is not proof that an operation failed. Introduce an explicit unknown state and reconcile before retrying.

Fifth, implement compensation for the most important business actions.

You do not need a sophisticated compensation engine on day one. Start with the operations that could create financial loss or leave business resources locked.

Sixth, make recovery observable.

Give operators a clear view of partial execution, failed compensation, unresolved external operations, and ownership conflicts.

Finally, define when the system must stop and request human intervention.

These steps provide a foundation that can evolve as the number of agents, external services, and business operations increases.

The objective is not to eliminate every possible failure. It is to make sure failures do not silently become business damage.

14. The Bigger Problem: Who Is Accountable for an Agent's Actions?

There is one question I keep returning to when thinking about autonomous systems.

When an AI agent makes a recommendation, the consequences may be limited to the quality of the information it provides. When an AI agent executes a workflow, the consequences become much more tangible. A payment can be processed. Inventory can be reserved. A contract can be submitted. A customer can receive an incorrect notification.

At that point, asking whether the agent made a correct decision is no longer enough. We need to know:

  • Who authorised the operation?
  • Which version of the workflow executed it?
  • Which agent held execution ownership?
  • Was the operation submitted more than once?
  • Did the external system accept the request?
  • Was the outcome verified?
  • If the workflow failed, which compensations were completed?
  • Who decided that the system should stop and request human intervention?

These questions are not just about audit logs. They are about accountability. I believe the next generation of AI systems will need a much stronger separation between intelligence and execution authority.

An agent should be able to reason about a business operation without automatically receiving permission to perform every action it proposes. A workflow should be able to survive an agent failure without losing its execution history.

A replacement agent should be able to continue a task without unknowingly repeating what the previous agent already completed. And a recovery mechanism should be able to establish whether an action happened before attempting to reverse or repeat it.

This is where I see the distinction between an impressive AI demonstration and a reliable production system. A demonstration can show an agent completing five steps successfully.

A production system must also explain what happens when the fourth step fails; the first three have already changed the external state, and the original agent is no longer available. That is a very different engineering challenge.

15. The Workflow Is the Unit of Reliability

We often evaluate AI agents individually. We measure response quality, reasoning accuracy, tool selection, latency, and task completion. These measurements are useful, but they do not fully describe the reliability of a multi-agent application.

An individual agent can behave correctly while the overall workflow produces an incorrect business outcome. Two agents can execute perfectly according to their individual instructions and still create an inconsistent result.

A payment agent can correctly process a transaction, while a shipping agent fails to arrange delivery.

A replacement worker can correctly retry a task while accidentally repeating an external side effect. The system needs a reliability model that covers the complete lifecycle of an operation.

That lifecycle includes:

  1. Proposal.
  2. Authorisation.
  3. Execution.
  4. Confirmation.
  5. Reconciliation.
  6. Compensation, when required.
  7. Final verification.

The AI agent is one participant in this lifecycle.

It is not the lifecycle itself.

I would argue that this is one of the most important architectural shifts required as AI systems become increasingly autonomous.

We need to stop treating an agent's final response as proof that the business operation succeeded.

We need durable evidence of what actually happened.

And we need recovery mechanisms that continue working even when the agent that initiated the operation disappears.

Final Thoughts

The most dangerous AI workflow is not necessarily the one that fails immediately.

It may be the one that succeeds just far enough to make recovery difficult.

When an AI agent completes four of five steps, the system cannot simply forget the first four because the fifth one failed.

The payment still happened. The inventory may still be reserved. The order still exists.

Those actions have consequences outside the agent's reasoning process.

Retries, compensating transactions, durable execution records, idempotency, and reconciliation are not optional architectural decorations when an AI workflow controls real business operations.

They are the mechanisms that make autonomous execution manageable.

I keep coming back to a simple engineering principle:

An AI agent should not be considered reliable merely because it knows what to do. It should be considered reliable when the system can establish what it actually did, recover when something goes wrong, and prevent an incomplete workflow from becoming an irreversible business mistake.

The next time an AI workflow reports that four out of five steps succeeded, I would not start by asking why the fifth step failed.

I would ask a much more important question:

Does the system know exactly what happened during the first four?

title: RocketMQ-Rust vs. Apache RocketMQ 5.5.0: The Full Benchmark Overview
description:
AI disclosure: This article was generated from the project’s public benchmark report and pull requests. It does not report a new test run.

The November 2026 RocketMQ-Rust benchmark covers Broker sends, LitePull, message sizes from 128 B to 64 KiB, synchronous flush, Controller-mode replication, a Java client cross-check, and Proxy gRPC sends. At 1 KiB, synchronous sends reached 1.79× Java 5.5.0 throughput. Putting 256 asynchronous requests on one connection brought the ratio down to 0.96×. Here is the full matrix and where the bottlenecks moved.

1. Test setup

An Intel i7-11700K ran Docker Desktop on Windows with WSL 2 (Linux 6.18, 16 GB). The services and load generator were pinned to separate sets of eight logical CPUs. Traffic stayed on loopback; the store used the container filesystem. The Rust release-image setup used PGO and BOLT for the Broker and PGO for the Proxy. The Java side used the official 5.5.0 image with default OpenJDK 8 settings. Both Brokers used the same Rust load generator for the main comparison. The project warmed up fresh containers, rotated run order and reported medians of four to nine runs per cell, with zero reported failed sends. Displayed rates are rounded; ratios come from the report.

2. Broker sends and LitePull at 1 KiB

These measurements use one replica and asynchronous disk flush. A synchronous send means the client waits for one response before sending again. In the async rows, 4×64 means four connections with up to 64 requests outstanding on each.

Workload Java msg/s Rust msg/s Rust / Java CPU µs/msg (Java → Rust)
Sync send 2.3k 4.0k 1.79× 381 → 137
Async 1×256 116.6k 112.4k 0.96× 44.9 → 46.8
Async 4×64 115.9k 137.8k 1.19× 50.5 → 46.4
Async 16×16 100.9k 123.7k 1.23× 58.4 → 51.4
LitePull 107.7k 140.0k 1.30× 17.9 → 11.2

Synchronous send p50 fell from 0.43 to 0.24 ms. Broker CPU per message fell by about 64% for sync sends and 37% for LitePull. The one-connection throughput was measured after #12699; the corresponding CPU figure is from the earlier round. They are not values from the same run.

3. Message size sweep

Rust/Java throughput ratios for uncompressed payloads with one replica. The 1 KiB row is from a separate round from the main Broker table.

Payload Sync Async 1×256 Async 4×64
128 B 1.74× 1.14× 1.34×
1 KiB 1.72× 0.99× 1.16×
4 KiB 1.86× 1.21× 1.55×
64 KiB 2.14× 1.49× 1.34×

At 64 KiB on one asynchronous connection, Rust stored about 1.05 GB/s versus Java’s 0.70 GB/s. Across the three 64 KiB workloads, Rust Broker CPU per message was 14–37% of Java’s.

4. Synchronous flush and three replicas

1 KiB workload Java msg/s Rust msg/s Rust / Java
Sync flush · sync 0.7k 0.8k 1.15×
Sync flush · async 1×256 48.1k 46.3k 0.96×
Sync flush · async 4×64 46.2k 47.9k 1.04×
3 replicas · sync 1.3k 1.9k 1.39×
3 replicas · async 1×256 44.2k 63.2k 1.43×
3 replicas · async 4×64 53.7k 64.3k 1.20×

With synchronous flush, both Brokers waited for msync, about 2 ms per call on this machine. The three-replica run used one Controller-mode Broker group, two required in-sync replicas and asynchronous flush. Stopping both followers at the end of each run caused synchronous sends to the leader to fail, confirming that acknowledgements depended on replication. Total Broker CPU across all three replicas was 1,062/127/119 µs per message for Java and 748/96/94 for Rust in table order. The Broker processes and Controllers shared the same CPUs, so these are not cross-host replication capacity numbers.

5. Java client cross-check

With a Java 5.5.0 client and the same in-flight limits, sync throughput was still 1.47×, and the Rust Broker used 59% less CPU per message. The Java client limited async throughput on both Brokers. Server-side CPU nevertheless differed: Rust used 3.6% more at one connection and 11.5% and 23.2% less with four and sixteen client processes respectively. A throughput plateau is a reason to check the load generator before tuning the Broker.

6. Proxy gRPC sends

Cluster mode, one 1 KiB message per RPC. Java and Rust ran on the same host with the same settings but a day apart, not as paired A/B runs. The latency column reports Rust only.

Workload Java msg/s Rust msg/s Rust Proxy CPU µs/msg Rust p99
Sync 0.8k–0.9k 2.89k 184 0.49 ms
1×256 34.9k–35.4k 38.6k 97 20 ms
4×64 39.3k–39.7k 53.1k 82 10.5 ms
32×4 27.2k–28.4k 45.7k 91 6.5 ms

Two separate Rust-only A/B tests explain why tracking both CPU and latency matters. TCP_NODELAY on accepted sockets moved median p99 from 43.6 to 6.9 ms at 32×4. In the PGO A/B, CPU per message fell about 10% at 1×256 while p99 rose from roughly 14 to 20 ms. Neither experiment establishes a post-fix p99 advantage over Java.

7. Reproducing and extending the results

Use client-production-benchmark for Broker sends and LitePull and grpc_send_benchmark for Proxy sends. The full report has the exact sample commands. Record image digests, build flags, CPU placement, payload size, connections, in-flight limits, flush and replica settings. Keep every run’s JSON, throughput, error counts and tail latency. Repeat with independent load generators and Brokers before planning capacity.

The dedicated-host plan is the next step. The published report does not cover cross-host networking, long runs, failover, cold reads, Push/POP, filtering, many topics and queues, or Proxy consumption.

title: I gave Claude Code and Codex one landing page. Here’s the handoff I’d use.
description:
The fastest way to get two coding agents to do the same work twice is to give them the same vague brief in two separate chats.

The second agent starts from scratch. It can’t see why the first agent made a recommendation, which screenshot backs it up, or what you already decided not to change. You end up copying context between chats and reviewing two versions of the same work.

As a marketing engineer, I’d rather give Claude Code and Codex different jobs on the same task. One finds the problem. The other makes the fix. I decide whether it’s ready to ship.

One page, one problem

Say we’re reviewing a SaaS landing page. At a viewport width of 390 px, the hero’s two buttons wrap, and the primary CTA drops below the first screen. That’s an illustrative example, but it’s the kind of issue I’d hand off. “Improve the landing page” is too broad. “Keep the primary CTA visible on mobile without changing approved copy” gives both agents a clear finish line.

The handoff I’d put in the task

Goal: Keep the primary CTA visible at 390 px.
Sources: Staging URL, hero component, approved positioning brief.

Claude Code: Reproduce the issue. Leave a screenshot, point to the
relevant component, and explain the smallest change you’d try.

Codex: Use that evidence to make the change on a branch.
Leave the diff, a before/after screenshot at 390 px, and a note
on what you checked on desktop.

Constraints: Keep the approved copy and analytics event names.
Do not deploy.

Done when: The primary CTA is visible on mobile, there’s no
horizontal overflow, and the desktop layout still works.

How I’d set it up in ActVox

I’d connect both agents to the same Space over MCP, give them separate @handles, and enable Read and edit so they can take assignments. I’d leave sharing and publishing off for this exercise. Claude Code takes the first assignment. Codex gets the second on the same task, blocked until the first is complete. If Codex doesn’t pick it up, I’d prompt it to check its ActVox inbox before creating another task.

One setup caveat: ActVox’s guide confirms native MCP reads for Claude Code but doesn’t confirm production writes through that route. It documents a CLI fallback if a write doesn’t land. Full setup and commands.

What I’d actually review

I’d open the before/after screenshots and the diff side by side. If the button is visible but the click event changed, I’d return the task with that specific note. If the evidence matches the brief, I’d accept it. Deploying is a separate decision.

The part worth copying is the handoff itself: pass the evidence, the constraints, and the definition of done. That gives the next agent something to work from and gives you something to review besides a green checkmark.

If you’re running multi-agent workflows, what’s the one piece of evidence you always ask the second agent to return?

title: ExplorerPatcher 26100.9711.71.2 Pre-Release / 26100.9711.71.1
description:
ExplorerPatcher is a lightweight open-source project by Valentin-Gabriel Radu for Windows 10 and 11 UI customization.

It offers developers and power users a way to modify the Taskbar, Start menu, and File Explorer without heavy system overhead.

The project supports configuration via a right-click interface and is currently available in versions 26100.9711.71.1 and 26100.9711.71.2 (Pre-Release).

Tool functions

ExplorerPatcher allows users to customize specific elements of the Windows interface:

  • Start Menu: Allows changes to the way the menu appears and functions.
  • Line of Work: It offers options to customize the taskbar to the user's needs.
  • File management: Allows you to configure how File Explorer works.

Use and installation

The tool does not require any complicated installation to work. Once the program is active, the user can access the settings menu by simply right-clicking on the taskbar. Through this menu, it is possible to configure all the available customization options.

title: A minus sign before an SCSS interpolation that Biome read as math
description:
Minus signs in SCSS are a little tricky. $a - $b is a subtraction, -$b is a negative value, and 1px 2px is a list. A formatter has to read every minus sign exactly the way Sass does, or it quietly changes your CSS.

That's what issue #12957 was about. The reporter had this:

$s: 8px;
.a {
  margin: -#{$s} -#{$s} -#{$s} auto;
}

and Biome formatted the value as -#{$s} - #{$s} - #{$s} auto. Looks like a spacing tweak. It isn't. The reporter checked with Dart Sass: the original compiles to margin: -8px -8px -8px auto;, the formatted file to margin: -8px-8px-8px auto;. That's invalid CSS, so the browser drops the whole declaration.

I picked it up, and the fix was merged in biomejs/biome#12983.

Why it happened

The formatter wasn't really the problem. It prints the tree the parser gives it. The SCSS parser decides what counts as a binary operator in crates/biome_css_parser/src/syntax/scss/expression/precedence.rs, and its scss_binary_precedence function took every - after a value as subtraction. So -#{$s} -#{$s} became "negative #{$s}, minus #{$s}". Once the tree says subtraction, the formatter prints spaces around the operator.

Sass reads it differently. A - written directly against #{ starts an interpolated identifier. With a space before it, that's simply the next item in the list. Only $a - #{$s}, with a space on both sides, subtracts.

The fix

Both parse_scss_binary_tail and is_at_scss_binary_operator go through scss_binary_precedence, so one check there covers both. I added a small helper:

/// Returns whether the current `-` starts the next item of a space-separated
/// list instead of subtracting: it follows whitespace and is written directly
/// against an interpolation.
///
/// Sass reads a `-` followed by `#{` as the start of an interpolated
/// identifier, so `-#{$s} -#{$s}` is a two-item list (`-8px -8px`), while
/// `$a - #{$b}` subtracts.
///
/// Docs: https://sass-lang.com/documentation/operators/numeric/#unary-operators
#[inline]
fn is_at_scss_negated_interpolation_list_item(p: &mut CssParser) -> bool {
    p.at(T![-])
        && (p.has_nth_preceding_whitespace(0) || p.has_nth_preceding_line_break(0))
        && is_nth_at_scss_interpolation(p, 1)
        && is_nth_source_tight(p, 1)
}

In words: a minus, with a space or a line break before it, followed by #{ with nothing in between. When that's true, it's not a binary operator:

if !p.at_ts(SCSS_BINARY_OPERATOR_TOKEN_SET) || is_at_scss_negated_interpolation_list_item(p) {
    return None;
}

I kept it narrow on purpose. It only looks at #{, so height: 1 -$s; still parses as a subtraction, same as before.

Tests, and two snapshots that moved

I added the same input as a parser spec and a formatter spec:

$s: 8px;

.a {
  margin: -#{$s} -#{$s} -#{$s} auto;
  padding: 1px -#{$s};
  width: $a - #{$s};
  height: 1 -$s;
  inset: -#{$s}
    -#{$s};
}

The formatter now leaves margin and padding as written, keeps $a - #{$s} as a subtraction, prints height as 1 - $s like it always did, and joins the two line inset into -#{$s} -#{$s}. Both specs fail without the parser change.

Two existing snapshots changed too. In the Prettier compatibility snapshot parens.scss, the line prop25-4 used to come out as #{$width} - #{$width} where Prettier keeps #{$width} -#{$width}. Now Biome matches Prettier on that pair.

The bigger one showed up when I ran the whole parser suite. The ok/scss/value/minus-operator.scss snapshot, a matrix of subtraction cases, had 17 cases recorded as subtractions, all of the same shape: a space before, the minus tight against #{, like 10 -#{10} and #{10} -#{10}. I checked them against Sass's own conformance tests in sass/sass-spec, and Sass's expected output keeps every one of them as separate values. So I updated that snapshot as well.

ematipico merged it on 6 November 2026, the same day I opened it, with no changes asked. Thanks!

What I'm keeping from this one

When a formatter changes what your code means, look at the parser first. The formatter here did exactly what the tree told it to.

The reporter's compiled output was the best part of the issue. -8px-8px-8px next to -8px -8px -8px made the bug obvious in one line.

And run the whole suite, not only your new tests. Those 17 cases sat in an existing snapshot.

Do you write negative interpolations like this in your SCSS, or do you wrap them in parentheses to be safe? I'd like to hear what your team does.

title: Rails RCE 취약점(Ruby2Shell): 내 API가 영향을 받았는지 확인하는 방법
description:
Ruby2Shell: 기본 설정의 Rails API에서 인증 없이 도달 가능한 Ruby RCE 취약점 패치하기

이번 주에 화제가 된 Rails RCE 취약점은 Ruby2Shell(발견자들은 "Ruby2ßhell"로 표기)이며, CVE-2026-132825 및 GHSA-34m4-m9fh-gqp5로 추적되고 있습니다. 이것은 Ruby의 문자열 대소문자 변환에서 발생하는 1바이트 힙 오버플로우로, 연구진에 따르면 기본 설정의 Rails 앱에서 인증 없이도 도달 가능하다고 합니다. Ruby 2.4.0~3.3.13, 3.4.0~3.4.12, 또는 4.0.0~4.0.9 버전을 사용하는 API라면 영향을 받습니다. 해결 방법은 gem 업데이트가 아니라 Ruby를 3.3.14, 3.4.13 또는 4.0.10으로 업그레이드하는 것입니다.

지금 Apidog를 사용해 보세요

빠른 답변: 내가 영향을 받나요?

  1. API를 실제로 서빙하는 환경(컨테이너, VM 또는 dyno) 내에서 ruby -v를 실행하세요. 노트북에서 실행하면 안 됩니다.
  2. 버전이 위 세 범위 중 하나에 해당한다면 노출되어 있습니다.
  3. Ruby를 업그레이드하고, 모든 이미지를 다시 빌드하고, 모든 앱 서버를 재시작한 후, API 테스트를 다시 실행하세요.

Ruby2Shell Rails RCE 취약점이란 무엇인가?

Ruby2Shell은 ISO-8859-x, Windows-125x 같은 레거시 단일 바이트 인코딩에서 문자열의 대소문자를 변경하는 데 사용되는 Ruby 코드의 1바이트 힙 버퍼 오버플로우입니다. Veria Labs는 이를 치명적(Critical) 등급으로 분류하며, 네트워크를 통해 인증 없이 도달 가능하고, Rails와 전통적인 방식의 Sinatra는 기본 구성에서 이 취약점에 노출된다고 밝혔습니다.

근본 원인은 사소합니다. 대부분의 단일 바이트 인코딩에는 독일어 에셋 첫("ß")의 대문자 형태가 없어서, 이를 대문자로 변환하면 두 바이트 "SS"가 기록됩니다. 이 작업을 수행하는 루프는 1바이트 분의 공간만 확인합니다. Ruby는 출력 버퍼를 입력 길이에 20바이트를 더한 크기로 할당하므로, Veria의 분석에 따르면 "ß" 문자 21개가 포함된 입력이 이 버퍼를 1바이트 초과하여 오버플로우시킵니다.

이 오버플로우는 upcase, swapcase, downcase(:fold), casecmp?를 통해 도달할 수 있습니다. UTF-8 문자열은 다른 코드 경로를 사용하므로 영향을 받지 않습니다. 이 버그는 Ruby 2.4.0부터 존재했습니다.

Ruby는 2026년 11월 18일에 정규식 엔진과 문자열 대소문자 변환의 여섯 가지 다른 결함과 함께 보안 권고문을 발행했습니다. Ruby는 "일부 시나리오"에서 이 결함을 원격 코드 실행에 사용하는 개념 증명(PoC)을 알고 있다고 밝혔습니다. Veria Labs는 기본 설정의 Rails에서 RCE를 최초로 시연했으며, 2026년 11월 25일 이후에(주요 벤더들이 그때까지 수정 사항을 배포하지 않았다면 그 이후에) 익스플로잇을 공개할 계획이라고 밝혔습니다.

이 날짜가 실질적인 마감 시한입니다. 익스플로잇이 공개되는 순간, 패치되지 않은 Rails API를 찾는 스캐닝은 매우 저렴해집니다.

어떤 Ruby 및 Rails 버전이 영향을 받나요?

이 표는 2026년 11월 20일 기준으로 Ruby의 권고문과 Veria Labs의 영향받는 소프트웨어 표를 결합한 것입니다.

Ruby 시리즈 영향받는 버전 수정 버전
4.0 4.0.0~4.0.9 4.0.10
3.4 3.4.0~3.4.12 3.4.13
3.3 3.3.0~3.3.13 3.3.14
3.2 및 이전 2.4.0부터의 모든 릴리스 수정 없음 (지원 종료)

Rails 버전은 여기서 중요하지 않습니다. 버그는 인터프리터에 있으므로 bundle update rails는 아무런 영향을 주지 않습니다. Ruby 3.4.12에서 실행되는 Rails 8 앱은 취약하고, Ruby 3.3.14에서 실행되는 Rails 6.1 앱은 취약하지 않습니다.

Veria Labs는 Rails와 전통적인 방식의 Sinatra가 기본 구성에서 영향을 받는다고 명시했습니다. 다른 프레임워크와 순수 Rack 앱은 기본적으로 노출되지 않지만, 레거시 인코딩에서 신뢰할 수 없는 문자열을 대문자로 변환하는 모든 코드는 여전히 이 버그에 도달할 수 있습니다.

Ruby 3.2 이하는 패치를 받지 못합니다. 서비스가 여전히 3.1이나 3.2에 있다면, Ruby2Shell은 "다음 분기에 업그레이드하자"는 계획을 이번 주의 일감으로 바꿔놓을 것입니다.

Rails API가 영향을 받았는지 확인하는 방법

함정은 잘못된 곳을 확인하는 것입니다. 노트북에 설치된 Ruby나 .ruby-version 파일의 Ruby는 프로덕션에서 실행되는 것과 다를 수 있습니다.

1단계: 실행 중인 환경에서 버전 확인하기

트래픽을 처리하는 프로세스에 물어보세요. 호스팅 환경에 맞는 명령을 선택하세요:

# Docker / Kubernetes
docker exec <container> ruby -v
kubectl exec deploy/<api-deployment> -- ruby -v

# Heroku-style platforms
heroku run ruby -v -a <app-name>

# A VM or bare-metal host, as the app user
sudo -u deploy bash -lc 'cd /srv/api/current && bundle exec ruby -v'

2단계: 수정 릴리스와 비교하기

많은 서비스의 경우 다음 한 줄 스크립트를 각 환경에 붙여넣으세요. Ruby에 기본 포함된 Gem::Version만 사용합니다:

ruby -e '
fixed = { "3.3" => "3.3.14", "3.4" => "3.4.13", "4.0" => "4.0.10" }
v = Gem::Version.new(RUBY_VERSION)
series = RUBY_VERSION.split(".").first(2).join(".")
if v < Gem::Version.new("2.4.0")
  puts "#{RUBY_VERSION}: outside the Ruby2Shell range, but end of life"
elsif fixed[series] && v >= Gem::Version.new(fixed[series])
  puts "#{RUBY_VERSION}: patched"
else
  puts "#{RUBY_VERSION}: VULNERABLE, upgrade Ruby"
end'

한 줄이 출력됩니다. 예를 들어 3.4.12: VULNERABLE, upgrade Ruby와 같습니다. 3.2 이하에서도 취약하다고 표시되는데, 이것이 맞습니다. 해당 시리즈에는 수정된 릴리스가 없기 때문입니다.

3단계: Ruby 버전이 고정된 모든 곳 찾기

프로덕션은 현재 상태를 알려줍니다. 저장소는 다음 배포에 포함될 내용을 알려줍니다. 다음 항목을 모두 검색하세요:

  • .ruby-version과 .tool-versions (rbenv, asdf, mise)
  • Gemfile의 ruby 라인
  • Gemfile.lock 하단 근처의 RUBY VERSION 섹션
  • 멀티스테이지 빌드를 포함한 모든 Dockerfile의 FROM ruby:... 라인
  • GitHub Actions 워크플로우의 ruby-version: 같은 CI 설정
  • Ruby 버전을 고정하는 buildpack 또는 플랫폼 설정 
grep -rnE "ruby[-_]version|^ruby |FROM ruby:|RUBY VERSION" \
  --include="*.yml" --include="*.yaml" --include="Dockerfile*" \
  --include="Gemfile*" --include=".ruby-version" --include=".tool-versions" .

4단계: 직접 설치하지 않은 Ruby를 잊지 마세요

셀프 호스팅 도구는 자체 Ruby를 번들로 포함하므로, 시스템 Ruby를 업그레이드해도 도움이 되지 않습니다. 2026년 11월 20일 01:59 UTC 기준으로 업데이트된 Veria Labs의 표는 다음과 같습니다:

소프트웨어 상태 수정 버전
GitLab 19.6.0 이하 취약 아직 수정 릴리스 없음
GitHub Enterprise Server 3.22.5 이하 취약 아직 수정 릴리스 없음
Chatwoot 4.20.0 이하 취약 아직 수정 릴리스 없음
Mastodon 4.7.5 이하 4.7.6, 4.6.12, 4.5.22, 4.4.29
OpenProject 17.9.7 이하 17.9.8, 17.8.3
Discourse 2.0.20261119-0203 이전 베이스 이미지 2.0.20261119-0203

수정 사항이 없는 제품의 경우, Aikido의 가이드에 따라 벤더가 수정 사항을 배포할 때까지 서버를 퍼블릭 인터넷에서 분리하고 VPN이나 IP 허용 목록 뒤로 두는 것이 좋습니다.

API를 망가뜨리지 않고 Ruby2Shell을 패치하는 방법

Ruby는 우회 방법을 제공하지 않으므로, 패치가 곧 해결책입니다. 다음 순서로 진행하면 당황할 일이 없습니다:

  1. 버전 고정을 변경하세요. .ruby-version, Gemfile의 ruby 라인, 그리고 모든 CI의 ruby-version을 현재 시리즈를 유지하면서 3.3.14, 3.4.13 또는 4.0.10으로 설정하세요.
  2. 락파일을 갱신하세요. bundle install을 실행하여 Gemfile.lock의 RUBY VERSION 섹션이 일치하도록 하세요.
  3. 패치된 베이스에서 이미지를 다시 빌드하세요. FROM ruby:를 수정된 패치 릴리스를 포함하는 태그로 지정하고(고정하기 전에 Docker Hub의 태그 목록을 확인하세요), --pull 옵션으로 재빌드하여 캐시된 오래된 레이어가 다시 들어오지 않도록 하세요.
  4. 모든 프로세스를 재시작하세요. Puma, Sidekiq, cron 러너, 일회성 콘솔은 모두 재시작 전까지 기존 인터프리터를 메모리에 유지합니다.
  5. 프로덕션에서 1단계를 다시 실행하세요. 병합된 풀 리퀘스트가 아니라 실제 컨테이너의 ruby -v 출력을 믿으세요.

같은 릴리스에서 정규식과 문자열 관련 여섯 가지 버그도 수정되는데, 이는 API가 의존하는 코드에 영향을 줍니다: 파라미터 파싱, 유효성 검사, 대소문자 구분 없는 조회 등입니다. 빌드를 프로덕션에 배포하기 전에 스테이징에서 API 테스트를 실행하세요.

Apidog CLI로 코딩 에이전트가 패치된 API를 검증하게 하세요

Ruby 버전 고정을 변경하려고 코딩 에이전트를 이미 열어두고 있을 것입니다. 직접 엔드포인트를 하나하나 클릭하는 대신, 같은 에이전트에게 패치된 빌드가 클라이언트가 기대하는 응답을 반환하는지 증명하게 하세요. Apidog CLI는 Claude Code, Codex, Cursor 또는 OpenCode에 API 명세를 가져오고, 테스트 케이스를 작성하고, 모든 환경에서 실행할 수 있는 스크립트 방식의 방법을 제공합니다.

설정은 세 개의 명령입니다:

npm install -g apidog-cli@latest
apidog login --with-token <YOUR_TOKEN>
npx -y skills add https://apidog.com   # pick your agent when prompted

Rails 앱이 OpenAPI 파일(예: rswag)을 내보낸다면, 에이전트에게 다음 프롬프트 하나를 주세요:

Import openapi.yaml into Apidog project <id>. Create test cases for our five
most-used endpoints, including GET /api/v1/users/:id and POST /api/v1/orders,
that assert status codes, response schemas and that names containing non-ASCII
characters (like "Straße") round-trip unchanged. Run them against staging after
the Ruby 3.4.13 deploy and summarize any failures.

에이전트는 페이로드 스키마를 읽고, 검증하고, 스위트를 실행합니다. 에이전트가 사용하는 명령은 다음과 같습니다:

apidog import --project <id> --format openapi --file ./openapi.yaml
apidog cli-schema get test-case-create
apidog cli-schema validate test-case-create --file case.json
apidog test-case create --project <id> --file case.json
apidog run --test-case <caseId> --project <id> -e <stagingEnvId> -r cli,json

non-ASCII 검사는 익스플로잇 테스트가 아니며, 그래서도 안 됩니다. 프로덕션에 조작된 오버플로우 페이로드를 보내지 마세요. 이는 패치가 건드린 코드 경로에 대한 회귀 검사입니다. 스테이징에서 통과하면, 같은 apidog run ... -r junit 단계를 CI에 넣어 다음 Ruby 업그레이드 때도 같은 검사가 자동으로 수행되도록 하세요. Apidog CLI CI/CD 가이드에서 파이프라인 설정 방법을 확인할 수 있고, Claude Code에서의 Apidog CLI에서는 에이전트 측면을 다룹니다. Apidog Free는 최대 4명까지 지원하므로 소규모 백엔드 팀이 오늘 바로 이 검사를 실행하기에 충분합니다.

Ruby2Shell과 최근 런타임 RCE 비교

Ruby2Shell은 10월 이후 이 블로그에서 다룬 두 가지 런타임 수준 RCE에 이은 것입니다. 세 가지 모두 버그가 런타임에 있으므로, 프레임워크와 패키지 업데이트로는 해결되지 않습니다.

버그 계층 업그레이드 대상
Ruby2Shell (CVE-2026-132825) Ruby 문자열 대소문자 변환 Ruby를 3.3.14, 3.4.13 또는 4.0.10으로
PHP2Shell (CVE-2026-109618, CVE-2026-109619) PHP 인터프리터 PHP를 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36 또는 8.2.35로
Node.js Brotli RCE (CVE-2026-111497) Node.js Brotli 디코더 Node.js 자체

팀이 폴리글랏 스택을 운영한다면, 서비스별로 런타임 버전 목록을 하나 만드세요. 이 버그들 모두 같은 질문에서 출발합니다: 프로덕션은 실제로 어떤 버전을 사용하고 있는가? 더 폭넓은 접근 방식은 자동화된 API 취약점 탐지를 참고하세요.

FAQ

Rails gem을 업데이트하면 Ruby2Shell이 수정되나요? 아니요. 버그는 Ruby 인터프리터에 있으므로 bundle update rails로는 해결되지 않습니다. Ruby 3.3.14, 3.4.13 또는 4.0.10이 필요하며, 이미지 재빌드와 프로세스 재시작도 함께 필요합니다.

UTF-8만 사용하는 앱이라면 안전한가요? Veria Labs에 따르면 UTF-8 문자열은 다른 코드 경로를 사용하므로 영향을 받지 않습니다. 하지만 Rails와 전통적인 Sinatra가 기본 구성에서 취약한 코드에 도달한다고도 밝혔으므로, "우리는 UTF-8만 사용한다"는 가정이 업그레이드를 건너뛸 이유가 되지는 않습니다.

Ruby2Shell의 공개 익스플로잇이 있나요? 2026년 11월 20일 기준 아직 없습니다. Ruby는 일부 시나리오에서 RCE에 대한 개념 증명을 알고 있다고 밝혔고, Veria Labs는 2026년 11월 25일에(벤더들이 그때까지 수정 사항을 배포하지 않았다면 그 이후에) 기본 Rails 대상 익스플로잇을 공개할 계획입니다.

Ruby 3.2 이하를 사용 중이라면 어떻게 해야 하나요? Ruby 3.2 이하는 지원이 종료되어 수정 사항을 받지 못합니다. 3.3.14 이상, 가능하면 3.4.13 또는 4.0.10으로 이동하고, 이 업그레이드를 긴급한 작업으로 처리하세요.

GitLab이나 Mastodon의 Ruby2Shell 노출 여부는 어떻게 확인하나요? 이 제품들은 자체 Ruby를 번들로 포함합니다. 벤더의 릴리스 노트에서 수정된 버전을 확인하세요. 아직 없다면, 수정 사항이 배포될 때까지 VPN이나 IP 허용 목록으로 접근을 제한하세요.

Ruby 업그레이드로 다른 것도 수정되나요? 네. Ruby 3.3.14, 3.4.13, 4.0.10은 같은 Ruby 권고문에 나열된 정규식 및 문자열 대소문자 변환의 여섯 가지 다른 결함도 수정하므로, 한 번의 업그레이드로 일곱 가지가 모두 해결됩니다.

title: hexbin-heatmap: تجميع النقاط في سداسيات H3 وخلايا geohash، في المتصفح ومن سطر الأوامر
description:
ضع خمسين ألف نقطة على خريطة وستتوقف عن رؤية البيانات. تتراكم العلامات فوق بعضها، وتتحول المناطق الكثيفة إلى بقعة واحدة مصمتة، ولا تستطيع أن تعرف إن كان الموضع يحمل عشر نقاط أم عشرة آلاف. الحل المعروف هو التوقف عن رسم النقاط ورسم خلايا بدلها: قسّم الخريطة إلى شبكة، عُدّ ما يقع في كل خلية، ثم لوّن الخلايا.

الفكرة سهلة القول، لكن فيها أجزاء متحركة أكثر مما توقعت. أي شبكة؟ كيف تلوّن قيمًا تمتد على عدة مراتب عشرية؟ وماذا يحدث لخلية تعبر خط الطول 180°؟ hexbin-heatmap هو المشروع الذي اشتغلت فيه على هذه الأسئلة.

يجمّع المشروع بيانات النقاط (CSV أو GeoJSON) في سداسيات H3 أو خلايا geohash، ويعرض النتيجة كخريطة حرارية ملوّنة (choropleth) في MapLibre، مع شريط تمرير للدقة (resolution). والتجميع نفسه متاح كأداة سطر أوامر (CLI) تكتب GeoJSON أو CSV.

ماذا يقدّم

تطبيق ويب. افتح ملف CSV/TSV أو ملف GeoJSON فيه عناصر Point أو MultiPoint. الملفات تُقرأ محليًّا ولا تُرفع أبدًا. في ملفات CSV، يُكتشف عمودا خط العرض وخط الطول تلقائيًّا (lat و latitude و y و lon و lng و longitude و x وغيرها)، والفاصل يمكن أن يكون , أو ; أو tab أو |.

طريقتان للتقسيم. اختر H3 (دقة من 0 إلى 15) أو geohash (دقة من 1 إلى 12) بشريط التمرير، أو فعّل "follow map zoom" لتتغير الدقة مع التكبير.

التلوين حسب ما يهمك. لوّن حسب count، أو حسب sum أو mean لعمود وزن رقمي. الفئات يمكن أن تكون log أو quantile أو linear، مع 4 تدرجات لونية.

الفحص والتصدير. مرّر المؤشر فوق خلية لترى إحصاءاتها، وصدّر الخلايا الظاهرة كـ GeoJSON.

أداة CLI بنفس المحرك. أداة سطر الأوامر تشغّل كود التجميع نفسه وتكتب GeoJSON أو CSV. كل عنصر في المخرجات يحمل الخصائص cell و count و sum و mean، ومعرّفه هو معرّف الخلية.

طريقة الاستعمال

تطبيق الويب لا يحتاج تثبيتًا. النسخة التجريبية موقع ثابت على GitHub Pages، وملفاتك تبقى في المتصفح: https://abdeldjalilchougui.github.io/hexbin-heatmap/

لتشغيله محليًّا، أو استضافة نسختك، أو استعمال الـ CLI:

git clone https://github.com/AbdeldjalilChougui/hexbin-heatmap.git
cd hexbin-heatmap
pnpm install
pnpm dev                    # web app: click "Sample data" or open your own file
pnpm test                   # vitest
pnpm build                  # CLI -> dist/cli, web app -> dist/web

بناء الإنتاج يستعمل مسار Vite الأساسي /hexbin-heatmap/ (انظر vite.config.ts). غيّره إذا كنت تقدّم الموقع من مسار آخر.

الـ CLI على ملف العيّنة المرفق:

pnpm cli samples/points.csv --res 5 --weight value -o cells.geojson
pnpm cli samples/points.csv --mode geohash --res 4 --format csv --min-count 10
cat points.geojson | node dist/cli/index.js - -r 8      # after pnpm build

وخياراته:

-m, --mode <h3|geohash>     binning scheme (default h3)
-r, --res <n>               H3 resolution 0-15 or geohash precision 1-12 (default 7 / 5)
-w, --weight <name>         numeric CSV column / GeoJSON property to sum
    --lat / --lon <name>    explicit coordinate columns
    --min-count <n>         drop sparse cells
-f, --format <geojson|csv>  output format
-o, --out <file>            output file (default stdout)

ما بنيته من الصفر

كل المنطق موجود في src/lib/، بـ TypeScript صرف يتشاركه الـ CLI وتطبيق الويب:

src/lib/      pure TypeScript, shared by the CLI and the web app
  csv.ts        RFC 4180 splitter, delimiter sniffing, column detection, bad-row skipping
  geojson.ts    Point / MultiPoint / GeometryCollection extraction, weights from properties
  geohash.ts    geohash encode/decode/bounds written from scratch
  aggregate.ts  point -> cell id (h3-js latLngToCell or geohash), count/sum/mean per cell, cell polygons
  polygon.ts    antimeridian handling: split rings into a MultiPolygon at ±180°
  color.ts      ramps, linear/quantile/log class breaks, value -> colour
src/cli/      node:util parseArgs CLI
src/web/      MapLibre UI; colours via a "step" expression built from the class breaks

H3 نفسه يأتي من h3-js؛ لم أُعِد كتابته. ما كتبته يدويًّا هو ترميز geohash وفكّه، وقارئ CSV مع اكتشاف الفاصل، ومنطق حدود الفئات، وقسمة الخلايا عند خط الطول 180° (antimeridian).

التجميع مرور واحد على النقاط باستعمال Map<cell, {count, sum}>. الخلايا تخرج مرتبة حسب المعرّف، فالنتائج حتمية (deterministic): الإدخال نفسه يعطي دائمًا الملف نفسه. مضلعات الخلايا تأتي من cellToBoundary في H3 أو من الصندوق المحيط في geohash، على شكل حلقات مغلقة من [lon, lat].

ما تعلّمته

الشبكة اختيار له نتائج. خلايا geohash مستطيلات بخطوط العرض والطول، فمساحتها تتغير مع خط العرض. أما خلايا H3 فمتقاربة المساحة. إذا قارنت الأعداد بين خلايا متباعدة في خط العرض، يصبح هذا الفرق مهمًّا. كتابة geohash من الصفر جعلت الأمر واضحًا: الخلية مجرد مجال من خطوط العرض ومجال من خطوط الطول، لا أكثر.

سلّم الألوان يحدد ما تراه. بيانات النقاط في العادة غير متوازنة أبدًا: خلايا قليلة تحمل أغلب النقاط. مع الفئات الخطية (linear)، تقع كل الخلايا تقريبًا في أدنى فئة. فئات quantile تساعد، لكن حدودها المكررة تُحذف، فالبيانات كثيرة التساوي (مثلًا أغلب الخلايا عددها 1) قد تعطي فئات أقل مما طلبت. ولهذا السبب كان السلّم اللوغاريتمي (log) هو الافتراضي.

خط الطول 180° حالة حدّية حقيقية. خلية H3 التي تمتد على جانبي ±180° لها حلقة تقفز خطوط طولها من طرف العالم إلى الطرف الآخر. إذا تُركت كما هي، رُسم مضلع يعبر الخريطة كلها. المشروع يقسم هذه الحلقات إلى MultiPolygon عند هذا الخط ليبقى الـ GeoJSON صالحًا وفق RFC 7946.

مكتبة واحدة وواجهتان. لأن src/lib/ لا يعرف شيئًا عن المتصفح ولا عن الطرفية، لا يمكن أن يتباعد الـ CLI وتطبيق الويب. وفي تطبيق الويب، تأتي الألوان من تعبير "step" في MapLibre مبني من حدود الفئات، فتستعمل الخريطة والمفتاح الأرقام نفسها.

الحل بالقوة الغاشمة مرجع جيد للاختبار. الأمر pnpm test يشغّل 22 اختبارًا:

  • geohash مقابل قيم مرجعية منشورة، مع اختبار أن فكّ الترميز يعطي خلية تحتوي النقطة
  • التجميع مقابل تجميع بالقوة الغاشمة (brute force) على 3,000 نقطة عشوائية لـ H3 و geohash، مع بقاء مجموع الأوزان محفوظًا
  • شكل خلية H3 وترتيبها، والقسمة عند antimeridian، والتحقق من الدقة
  • علامات الاقتباس في CSV، والفواصل، واكتشاف الأعمدة، والأسطر الخاطئة؛ وأوزان GeoJSON والأشكال المتجاهَلة
  • حدود الفئات والتصنيف
  • الـ CLI من البداية إلى النهاية على ملفات مؤقتة

أشياء يجب معرفتها

  • كل شيء يعمل في الذاكرة. مئات الآلاف من النقاط لا مشكلة فيها، أما عشرات الملايين فلا.
  • فئات quantile قد تخرج أقل من المطلوب مع البيانات كثيرة التساوي، كما ذُكر أعلاه.
  • مساحة خلية geohash تتغير مع خط العرض. استعمل H3 عندما تحتاج خلايا متقاربة الحجم.
  • الخريطة الأساسية من tile.openstreetmap.org، وهي للاستعمال الشخصي الخفيف فقط حسب سياسة بلاطات OSM.
  • الملف samples/points.csv (ونسخته في public/) بيانات اصطناعية ينتجها pnpm gen:sample: تجمعات غاوسية حول إحداثيات تقريبية لمدن جزائرية مع ضجيج منتظم. لا تمثّل أي قياس حقيقي.

لماذا بنيته

كومة النقاط تخفي نمطها، والتجميع في خلايا هو المخرج المعتاد. أردت أن أفهم المسار كاملًا من ملف CSV خام إلى خلية ملوّنة، لا أن أستدعي طبقة جاهزة فقط: كيف تصبح النقطة معرّف خلية، وكيف يغيّر اختيار الشبكة الصورة، وكيف تغيّرها حدود الفئات مرة أخرى. ووجود الكود نفسه خلف صفحة ويب وخلف CLI يعني أن الصورة التي تستكشفها في المتصفح يمكن إعادة إنتاجها كملف بواسطة سكربت.

احصل على الكود

الكود المصدري والاختبارات والعيّنة الاصطناعية على GitHub: https://github.com/AbdeldjalilChougui/hexbin-heatmap. الكود برخصة MIT. مكتبة H3 حقوقها لـ Uber Technologies (Apache-2.0، عبر h3-js)، وبيانات الخريطة © مساهمو OpenStreetMap (ODbL). الملاحظات (issues) وطلبات الدمج (pull requests) مرحّب بها.

نُشر في الأصل على abdeldjalilchougui.biz.

title: Traditional Data Warehouse vs Modern Data Platform: What’s the Difference?
description:
Traditional data warehouses have supported business reporting for decades. However, growing data volumes, changing reporting requirements and the rapid adoption of AI are exposing the limitations of older architectures.


A Modern Data Platform provides a more flexible way to bring together structured, semi-structured and unstructured data across databases, business applications, cloud services and other systems. The result is a scalable, governed foundation for reporting, analytics and AI.


The infographic below compares the infrastructure, processing and operational requirements of a traditional data warehouse with a Modern Data Platform.



Traditional data warehouses remain effective, but can be costly to operate


A traditional data warehouse generally collects structured data from selected source systems, transforms it through ETL processes and loads it into a central database for reporting. This model remains suitable for stable, structured reporting requirements. However, it can become harder and more expensive to maintain as data volumes, sources and business needs grow.


Common challenges include:


Database, operating system and ETL licensing costs
Separate compute, storage and backup infrastructure
Significant database and infrastructure support requirements
High data engineering effort when sources or reports change
Duplication of data across different systems
Limited support for unstructured data
Additional platforms and processing required for AI

These dependencies can increase operational overhead and make it harder for organisations to respond quickly to new reporting, analytics and AI requirements.


How a Modern Data Platform changes the model


A Modern Data Platform separates storage, processing and consumption into flexible components that can scale according to demand. Raw data from databases, SaaS applications, files, APIs, sensors and cloud environments can be brought into a central data lake. Automated pipelines then clean, organise and prepare the data for reporting, analytics or AI applications.


This approach can provide:


Support for structured and unstructured data
Scalable cloud-based storage and processing
Reusable, automated data pipelines
Reduced dependency on database and infrastructure specialists
Centralised data governance and platform management
More efficient integration of new data sources
A trusted data foundation for analytics and AI
Greater visibility and control over data platform costs

The exact benefits depend on the platform architecture, workloads, governance model and existing technology environment.


Traditional Data Warehouse vs Modern Data Platform


Area
Traditional data warehouse
Modern Data Platform
Data support
Primarily structured data
Structured, semi-structured and unstructured data
Processing
ETL before loading
Flexible ETL and ELT processing
Storage
Database-based storage
Scalable data lake, lakehouse and warehouse storage
Infrastructure
Often fixed or separately managed
Cloud-based or hybrid, with flexible scaling
Maintenance
Database, OS and infrastructure support
More centralised platform management
Scalability
May require capacity planning and additional licensing
Storage and processing can scale independently
Analytics
Primarily reporting and business intelligence
Reporting, advanced analytics and AI
AI readiness
Often requires additional tools and data preparation
Can provide governed, reusable AI-ready data
Cost model
Infrastructure, licensing and support costs
Consumption-based services and reduced infrastructure overhead

Does a Modern Data Platform replace your data warehouse?


Not necessarily and here's why - a Modern Data Platform does not require an organisation to discard every existing database or reporting system. In many cases, the best approach is to retain valuable systems while gradually modernising the way data is collected, governed, processed and used.


The right architecture may combine:


Existing operational databases
A cloud-based data lake or lakehouse
Automated ingestion and transformation pipelines
A data warehouse for structured reporting
Business intelligence and visualisation tools
Governance, security and data quality controls
Private AI or machine-learning capabilities

Modernisation can therefore be delivered progressively, based on business priorities, platform risks and the value of each use case.


When should you consider modernising?


It may be time to review your data architecture if:


Reports take too long to produce
Teams rely on manual spreadsheet consolidation
Different departments report conflicting figures
Data is trapped across disconnected systems
Licensing and infrastructure costs continue to rise
Platform changes require significant engineering work
The organisation lacks confidence in data quality
Existing data cannot be used safely or effectively for AI

Build a trusted foundation for reporting, analytics and AI


Blue Crystal Solutions helps Australian organisations assess, design, implement and manage Modern Data Platforms across cloud and hybrid environments.


We bring together experience across databases, cloud infrastructure, data engineering, managed services and Private AI to help you modernise without losing control of your critical systems or information.


Whether you need to replace a costly legacy data warehouse, improve reporting or prepare trusted data for AI, we can help you determine the most practical path forward.


Talk to a Modern Data Platform specialist


Join our webinar on 30 September at 1:00 PM ACST


to dive deeper into the topic and gain practical insights.


.....................


Frequently asked questions


What is a Modern Data Platform?
A Modern Data Platform is an integrated architecture for collecting, storing, processing, governing and analysing data from multiple sources. It can support business intelligence, advanced analytics, automation and AI across cloud or hybrid environments.

What is the difference between a data warehouse and a Modern Data Platform?


A data warehouse is primarily designed to store structured, processed data for reporting. A Modern Data Platform supports a broader range of data types and workloads, potentially incorporating data lakes, lakehouses, warehouses, automated pipelines, governance, analytics and AI services.

Is a Modern Data Platform cheaper than a traditional data warehouse?


It can reduce database licensing, fixed infrastructure and operational support costs, but savings depend on platform design and usage. Cloud consumption, data movement, storage growth and poorly governed workloads can still create unnecessary costs.

Can a Modern Data Platform use our existing databases?


Yes. Existing Oracle, SQL Server, PostgreSQL and other databases can remain operational data sources. Information from these systems can be integrated into a Modern Data Platform without requiring an immediate full replacement.

How does a Modern Data Platform support AI?


It brings data together, applies quality and governance controls, and makes trusted datasets available for AI applications. This helps reduce the risk of AI producing answers from incomplete, inconsistent or unauthorised information.

title: Automação de navegação em Rust com rust-headless-chrome
description:
O que é

O rust-headless-chrome é uma biblioteca em Rust que oferece uma interface de alto nível para controlar navegadores Chrome ou Chromium sem interface gráfica (modo headless). A comunicação é feita por meio do Chrome DevTools Protocol. Ela é considerada o equivalente em Rust ao Puppeteer do Node.js, operando com uma API síncrona baseada em threads.

Para quem serve

Essa ferramenta é voltada para pessoas desenvolvedoras que constroem soluções em Rust para automação web, como automação de testes em navegadores e extração de dados (web crawling). Ela inclui recursos como captura de tela da página ou de elementos específicos, exportação de arquivos para PDF, interceptação de requisições de rede, monitoramento de cobertura de JavaScript, navegação em modo anônimo e download automático de binários do Chromium para Linux, Mac e Windows.

Como começar

Para incluir a biblioteca em seu projeto, adicione a dependência headless_chrome ao seu arquivo Cargo.toml. Caso queira baixar o Chromium automaticamente, habilite a opção de features contendo "fetch".

No código em Rust, inicialize o navegador usando Browser::default(), crie uma nova aba com browser.new_tab() e utilize métodos como navigate_to para direcionar a navegação. A partir disso, é possível aguardar elementos da página com wait_for_element, interagir com botões, tirar capturas de tela e executar funções em JavaScript.

Instalação 

use std::error::Error;
use headless_chrome::Browser;
use headless_chrome::protocol::cdp::Page;
fn browse_wikipedia() -> Result<(), Box<dyn Error>> {
    let browser = Browser::default()?;
    let tab = browser.new_tab()?;
    // Navigate to wikipedia
    tab.navigate_to("https://www.wikipedia.org")?;

🔗 Repositório oficial: https://github.com/rust-headless-chrome/rust-headless-chrome
