title: How I Built a 100% Client-Side PDF Powerhouse with WebAssembly and React (Zero Cloud Uploads)
description:
Why Does Every Online PDF Tool Want Your Credit Card and Your Tax Returns?

Earlier this month, I had to upload a signed certificate to a government application portal. The portal had one strict requirement:

"Uploaded PDF must be strictly below 100 KB."

I did what everyone does: searched "compress PDF under 100kb" on Google.

Every single top result was a multi-million-dollar SaaS product that:

  1. Forced me to upload a sensitive personal document to an undisclosed remote server.
  2. Compressed it to 125 KB (still rejected by the portal!).
  3. Locked the "Extreme Compression" slider behind a $12/month subscription.
  4. Or hit me with: "You have reached your free daily quota of 2 files. Enter your credit card."

I got frustrated enough that I decided to see how far we could push modern web browser primitives—WebAssembly, HTML5 Canvas, Web Workers, and pdf-lib—to build a completely private, zero-server alternative.

That experiment became PDFCraft (Source on GitHub).

Here is the technical breakdown of how we achieved 100% client-side PDF manipulation with zero cloud leaks.

1. The Core Architecture: Zero-Cloud Processing

Traditional PDF websites use server-side Python/C++ pipelines (e.g., Poppler, Ghostscript, or LibreOffice in Docker containers). That architecture has major drawbacks:

  • Massive Server Costs: Running headless PDF engines across millions of files costs thousands in server bills.
  • Privacy Risks: Uploading legal contracts, tax documents, and medical scans creates massive GDPR and compliance liabilities.

Instead, PDFCraft operates entirely on the client device:

User Device (Local Memory)
├── File Input (Drag & Drop)
│    └── ArrayBuffer / Blob in Local Memory
├── Local Processing Engines
│    ├── pdf-lib (Vector streams, page tree manipulation, e-signatures)
│    ├── HTML5 Canvas (Quantization, resolution scaling, image crunching)
│    └── Web Workers (Off-main-thread compute without freezing the UI)
└── Instant Download
     └── Direct Blob URL (0 bytes transmitted to any backend)

2. The Target Size Squeezer: Hitting Exact 100KB/200KB Ceilings

Standard compressors just say "Low, Medium, High". But portal upload bots don't care about "High"—they care about ≤ 95 KB or ≤ 195 KB.

To guarantee that a PDF always comes in under the portal limit:

  1. Binary Stream Extraction: We extract embedded page streams and rasterize page canvases at high DPI.
  2. Dynamic Binary Search Quantization: Instead of guessing a single JPEG quality factor, our algorithm runs an in-memory binary search across resolution scale and quantization factors:
    • It tests quality brackets (e.g. 0.85 -> 0.65 -> 0.45) in milliseconds.
    • If the generated PDF stream exceeds the target ceiling (say, 95 KB), it immediately downscales background image coordinates while preserving vector text edge sharpness.
  3. Iterative Verification: The final byte buffer is measured before download. If it's 94.2 KB, it is delivered immediately.

3. Zero-Account E-Signing (ESIGN Compliant)

Instead of forcing users to sign up for DocuSign or Adobe Sign just to put an initials stamp on a 2-page lease, we implemented an in-browser vector signature pad:

  • Signatures are captured via HTML5 Canvas with cubic Bézier curve smoothing for natural pen strokes.
  • The vector paths are converted directly into clean PNG byte streams and embedded into the PDF page tree using pdf-lib's drawImage and drawText.
  • The entire signing session happens offline—even with airplane mode turned on!

4. 60-Second ATS Resume Studio

Most online resume builders let you design your resume for 30 minutes, only to hit you with a paywall modal at the download step.

PDFCraft includes a built-in ATS Resume Studio that:

  • Formats single-page vector PDF resumes compatible with applicant tracking systems (Workday, Greenhouse, Lever).
  • Includes a local keyword scanner that compares your resume against any job description in real-time.
  • Exports directly as clean, uncompressed vector text that machine parsers can read with 100% accuracy.

5. What We Learned

Modern browser engines (V8, WebAssembly, Web Workers) are powerful enough to replace 90% of cloud utilities. You don't need a heavy backend server to compress a PDF, sign an agreement, or extract spreadsheet tables.

  • 🌐 Live Web App: https://pdf-craft-vert.vercel.app/
  • 📦 Open Source Repository: https://github.com/Vishnu-cod/pdf-craft

I'd love to hear feedback from the developer community! What utilities would you like to see built into the client-side suite next?

title: Java4Shell ameaça servidores Minecraft em CPUs AVX-512 VBMI
description:
Falha no Java pode expor servidores Minecraft

A vulnerabilidade Java4Shell (CVE-2026-114938) afeta o decodificador Base64 do HotSpot, usado pelo OpenJDK em determinadas CPUs x86-64. O problema alcança as versões 17.0.6 e posteriores e as linhas 21 e 25 quando o processador oferece os recursos necessários. Servidores públicos de Minecraft recebem dados de qualquer pessoa que se conecta, o que torna importante verificar a JVM em execução.

A Red Hat atribuiu gravidade 9,8 à falha, enquanto a pontuação registrada pela CNA é 8,1. A correção depende da versão da JVM: os mínimos corrigidos são 17.0.21.1, 21.0.13.1 e 25.0.5.1. Atualizar Paper ou plugins, sem atualizar o Java usado pelo processo do servidor, não resolve o problema.

Confira a CPU e a JVM ativa

O caminho vulnerável exige uma CPU x86-64 com AVX-512F, AVX-512BW, AVX-512 VBMI e BMI2. Xeons Intel Ice Lake ou mais recentes e processadores AMD Zen 4 ou posteriores, como Ryzen 7000 e 9000, podem atender aos critérios; máquinas ARM não executam esse caminho.

grep -m1 'model name' /proc/cpuinfo; grep -oE '(avx512f|avx512bw|avx512vbmi|bmi2)' /proc/cpuinfo | sort -u

Se os quatro recursos aparecerem, confira a JVM do processo do servidor, não apenas o Java disponível no terminal: um serviço ou contêiner pode usar outra instalação. O exemplo abaixo consulta a versão e a configuração do HotSpot em um servidor Paper executado pelo usuário minecraft.

sudo -u minecraft jcmd $(pgrep -u minecraft -f paper.jar) VM.version
sudo -u minecraft jcmd $(pgrep -u minecraft -f paper.jar) VM.flags -all | grep UseBASE64Intrinsics

O utilitário jcmd vem com o JDK, não com o JRE, e deve ser executado pelo mesmo usuário do servidor. As versões do Minecraft 26.1 a 26.3 usam Java 25; as versões 1.20.5 a 1.21.11 usam Java 21; e as versões 1.18 a 1.20.4 usam Java 17. Lançamentos 1.17.1 e anteriores não são afetados.

Verifique o estado da distribuição ou imagem

Em 19 de novembro de 2026, o Ubuntu 24.04 já oferecia a versão corrigida 21.0.13.1+2. Builds disponíveis no Debian 12 e 13 e instaladores Temurin para Windows ainda estavam vulneráveis naquele levantamento; não havia uma build Temurin corrigida para Windows. A versão do Java fornecida pelo sistema, contêiner ou painel pode, portanto, mudar o resultado.

As imagens itzg/minecraft-server latest, java21 e java25 ainda usavam JDK Temurin vulnerável, mas incluíam a opção temporária de proteção por padrão. As tags stable e 2026.11.0-* também estavam vulneráveis e não incluíam essa opção na verificação. As imagens Pterodactyl yolks para Java 21 e 25 passaram a definir a opção no ponto de entrada em 17 de novembro; nós com imagens antigas em cache podem não recebê-la.

As imagens de contêiner citadas ainda não distribuíam um JDK corrigido. No Minecraft Launcher, a runtime Java 25 para versões 26.x estava corrigida no Linux e no macOS, mas não no Windows x64; as runtimes Java 21 e 17 ainda não tinham sido atualizadas. A checagem da build efetivamente usada ajuda a distinguir esses casos.

Atualize o OpenJDK no Ubuntu

No Ubuntu 24.04, a Canonical disponibilizou pacotes OpenJDK reconstruídos em 18 de novembro. A atualização pode reiniciar o serviço e desconectar jogadores: o needrestart pode reiniciar um serviço do systemd durante a instalação. Avise os jogadores e programe a mudança para um horário adequado.

sudo DEBIAN_FRONTEND=noninteractive apt-get install -y --only-upgrade openjdk-21-jre-headless openjdk-21-jdk-headless

Depois da instalação, confirme a versão informada pela JVM que atende às conexões. Serviços iniciados fora do systemd, por exemplo em sessões screen ou tmux, podem continuar usando as bibliotecas antigas até que o processo seja reiniciado manualmente. Para Java 17 ou 25, use os pacotes correspondentes à linha necessária e confira a versão ativa.

Use a opção temporária se não puder atualizar

A opção -XX:-UseBASE64Intrinsics desativa o decodificador vulnerável e faz a JVM usar o decodificador Java padrão. Ela reduz a velocidade de decodificação Base64, efeito que não foi medido em um servidor de jogo, e só entra em vigor após reiniciar o processo.

Inclua a opção na linha de inicialização antes de -jar. No exemplo Linux usado para o servidor Paper, ela aparece entre as opções da JVM e o arquivo do servidor; em um arquivo Windows start.bat, deve ficar na mesma posição.

!/bin/sh

cd /opt/minecraft
exec java -Xms2G -Xmx2G -XX:-UseBASE64Intrinsics -jar paper.jar --nogui

Uma opção escrita incorretamente pode impedir a JVM de iniciar. Se ela ficar depois de -jar paper.jar, será enviada ao Paper, e não ao Java. Após o reinício, consulte a configuração da JVM em execução: UseBASE64Intrinsics deve aparecer como false. Não use -XX:UseAVX=2 como alternativa: ela desativa otimizações AVX-512 e pode impedir a inicialização da JVM em ARM.

Confira as tags Docker e a proteção efetiva

As tags de uma imagem podem apontar para builds diferentes conforme a data de criação. O comando abaixo, usado no levantamento, consulta a criação e a versão Java de quatro tags itzg; isso ajuda a identificar se uma imagem está entre as que receberam a lógica temporária de inicialização.

for t in latest java21 stable 2026.11.0-java21; do sudo docker pull -q itzg/minecraft-server:$t >/dev/null; printf '%-18s %s ' $t "$(sudo docker image inspect -f '{{.Created}}' itzg/minecraft-server:$t | cut -c1-16)"; sudo docker run --rm --entrypoint java itzg/minecraft-server:$t -version 2>&1 | sed -n 2p; done

Mesmo quando a imagem inclui a opção temporária, o JDK pode continuar sem a correção definitiva. Atualize ou renove imagens antigas em cache e confira a versão e as flags da JVM do servidor já iniciado, em vez de presumir que o nome da tag ou o painel garantem a proteção.

Confira mais em: https://guiadeti.com.br/noticias/falha-java4shell-servidores-minecraft-avx-512-vbmi/

title: Find It in Thirty Seconds: A Naming Scheme for Cross-Cloud Network Resources That Works During an Incident
description:
During an incident, nobody searches by architecture diagram. They search by name. A gateway called gw-prod-2 in one cloud, a route table called main in another, and a firewall policy copied from a tutorial in a third will each make sense to the person who created them and to nobody else on the call. By the time the team has opened three consoles and translated three local naming habits, the outage has had a head start.

Naming feels like housekeeping until the estate spans AWS, Azure, Google Cloud, and Oracle at once. Then it becomes part of the incident response system itself. A good scheme lets any engineer, in any cloud, answer three questions from a name alone: what is this, where does it live, and what depends on it.

Why local naming habits break across clouds

Each cloud encourages a different default. Resource groups imply one grouping in Azure, projects imply another in Google Cloud, and accounts and VPCs carve AWS differently again. Teams working inside a single cloud lean on that surrounding context, so their names can be short and vague without immediate cost.

That context disappears at the cloud boundary. A private link, a transit hub, or a shared egress point belongs to two clouds at once, so neither side's local context explains it. The result is predictable: duplicate names for different things, different names for the same logical path, and no reliable way to search the whole estate for every piece of one flow.

The fix is not a longer name. It is a shared grammar that travels across providers.

Build the name from fixed fields, in a fixed order

A workable pattern uses the same fields, in the same order, for every network resource in every cloud:

  1. Purpose first. Start with what the resource does, not who made it: mesh, egress, inspect, dns, ai, or data. During an incident, people filter by function before anything else.
  2. Scope second. Name the boundary it serves: a region pair, a shared services scope, or a single environment such as prod, stage, or dev. Never rely on the account or subscription name to supply this, because shared resources sit above any one account.
  3. Endpoint or peer third, for connecting resources. A link name should say both sides, in a consistent order, for example by alphabetical cloud name, so the same link is never named differently from the other end.
  4. Sequence last, and only when needed. A number should distinguish parallel instances of the same thing, not encode history. If a name needs a date, a ticket number, or a person's initials to make sense, the scheme is already leaking.

Keep the character set boring: lowercase, hyphens, no underscores where a provider treats them inconsistently, and no abbreviations that only one team understands. Write the grammar down in one page, with two or three worked examples per resource type, and treat that page as part of the network design, not as wiki trivia.

Names carry identity, tags carry everything else

A common failure is stuffing the name with facts that change: owner, cost centre, project, review date. Names are hard to change safely once dependencies, alerts, and runbooks point at them, so they should hold only facts that stay true for the life of the resource.

Put the changeable facts in tags or labels, applied the same way in every cloud:

  • Owner: the team accountable for the resource, not an individual.
  • Flow or service: the named business or platform flow this resource serves, so every piece of one path can be pulled up together.
  • Criticality: whether an outage here is an incident or an inconvenience.
  • Review or expiry date: essential for temporary links, test peerings, and exception rules that otherwise become permanent by neglect.

The discipline that matters is consistency of keys. If one cloud says owner, another says Owner, and a third says team, estate wide reporting quietly fails. Define the key set once, in lowercase, and enforce it in the provisioning code for all clouds.

Enforce the scheme where resources are created

A naming standard that lives only in a document will drift within a quarter. Enforce it at creation time:

  • Provide the pattern as a module or template in the infrastructure code, so the easiest way to create a gateway, route table, or policy is the compliant way.
  • Validate names in the pipeline with a simple pattern check, and reject creations that fall outside it. A short delay at provisioning time is cheaper than a confusing estate at incident time.
  • Audit existing resources on a schedule and report drift by team, not as blame, but as a list to fix during normal work. Drift reports that only appear during audits tend to be ignored; small, regular reports get cleared.

Leave a deliberate escape hatch for genuine exceptions, recorded as a tag with a reason and a review date. A scheme with no exceptions invites quiet workarounds. A scheme with recorded exceptions stays honest.

Renaming an existing estate without breaking it

Most estates cannot be renamed in one pass, and should not try. Renaming a resource that alerts, dashboards, and firewall rules reference can cause the very outage the scheme is meant to shorten.

Instead, run both systems for a while. Add the compliant tags and a compliant alias or description to existing resources first, so search by the new grammar finds old resources immediately. Apply the naming pattern to everything new from a set date. Then rename in place only where the provider allows it without recreation, and schedule recreation based renames alongside other planned changes to that resource, never as a standalone project. Within a few normal change cycles, the estate converges without a flag day.

Measure convergence simply: the share of network resources that match the pattern, reported per cloud. When that number stalls, the remaining exceptions are usually the interesting ones, and they deserve a direct conversation rather than another reminder.

The design point

A naming scheme is not decoration. In a multi-cloud estate it is how an engineer finds the right gateway, route table, and policy in thirty seconds, under pressure, in a cloud they did not build. Purpose, scope, peer, and sequence in the name; owner, flow, criticality, and review date in the tags; enforcement in the provisioning path; and a patient migration for everything already running.

That kind of consistent platform engineering across AWS, Azure, Google Cloud, and Oracle estates is part of the work described at CloudVerg, where VergForge covers platform engineering and VergMesh covers multi-cloud networking, alongside zero-trust security through VergShield and SOC 2 readiness support.

The test of a scheme is simple. Hand a new engineer a name from a cloud they have never opened, and see whether they can say what it does, where it sits, and what it serves. If they can, the scheme is working.

title: Tailwind CSS v4 Resmi Rilis: Mesin Rust Oxide dan Paradigma CSS-First
description:
Tailwind Labs resmi merilis Tailwind CSS v4.0 pada Januari 2025 setelah melewati fase uji coba alpha dan beta sejak 2024. Rilis ini menandai perombakan arsitektur terbesar framework tersebut. Inti pemrosesan meninggalkan pipeline PostCSS berbasis JavaScript dan beralih ke engine native berbasis Rust bernama Oxide dengan konfigurasi CSS-first.

Arsitektur Baru: Engine Oxide Berbasis Rust

Pondasi Tailwind CSS v4 mengandalkan engine Oxide yang ditulis sepenuhnya dalam bahasa Rust. Transisi ini memangkas ketergantungan runtime Node.js yang membebani kompilasi proyek berskala besar.

Kompilasi Cepat dan Penghapusan Pipeline PostCSS Lama

Melalui Oxide, Tailwind Labs mengklaim kompilasi hingga 10 kali lebih cepat dibanding versi terdahulu berdasarkan pengujian internal vendor. Peningkatan performa bertumpu pada berkurangnya overhead parsing AST (Abstract Syntax Tree). PostCSS bukan lagi dependensi bawaan dan digantikan kompilator mandiri yang memproses utilitas secara paralel ke format biner.

Paradigma CSS-First Menggantikan tailwind.config.js

Perubahan mendasar bagi frontend developer terletak pada penghapusan berkas tailwind.config.js. Konfigurasi tema, varian, dan aturan utilitas kini beralih langsung ke berkas CSS utama.

Konfigurasi Desain Menggunakan Direktif @theme

Konfigurasi desain memanfaatkan direktif native @theme. Sistem ini memetakan token desain langsung ke CSS Custom Properties (CSS variables) standar peramban:

  • Variabel warna, tipografi, dan spasi terpasang langsung pada root dokumen.
  • Ekstensi palet warna tidak membutuhkan sintaks objek JavaScript kompleks.
  • Struktur konfigurasi menyatu dengan aturan CSS reguler.

Deteksi Otomatis Template Tanpa Deklarasi Content

Pada Tailwind v3, pengembang wajib mendaftarkan glob path template di opsi content. Di Tailwind CSS v4, Oxide memindai berkas proyek secara otomatis untuk menemukan kelas utilitas, meminimalkan kelas hilang akibat kesalahan penulisan glob.

Dukungan Fitur CSS Modern Secara Bawaan

Tailwind CSS v4 memanfaatkan kapabilitas CSS modern peramban tanpa dependensi pihak ketiga. Fitur bawaan mencakup native @property untuk transisi variabel, native cascade layers (@layer), serta container queries. Standarisasi ini mempermudah efisiensi styling pada arsitektur komponen React 19.

Tantangan Migrasi dari Tailwind CSS v3 ke v4

Adopsi Tailwind v4 menghadirkan sejumlah penyesuaian teknis bagi basis kode lama.

Kompatibilitas Plugin Pihak Ketiga

Mayoritas ekosistem plugin komunitas bergantung pada JavaScript Config API v3. Pustaka komponen pihak ketiga yang membutuhkan runtime JS memerlukan pembaruan arsitektur agar sesuai dengan skema @theme baru.

Kesiapan Dependensi Binary di Pipeline CI/CD

Pemanfaatan binary native Rust mewajibkan pipeline CI/CD mengenali arsitektur mesin target. Server monorepo enterprise dan sistem kompilasi lintas platform harus memastikan binary platform-specific terunduh dengan izin eksekusi yang sesuai. Modernisasi tooling ini melengkapi pergeseran infrastruktur frontend, termasuk evaluasi beban kerja komputasi pada arsitektur server-side rendering.

Cara Memulai Tailwind CSS v4 dengan Vite

Integrasi proyek diarahkan lewat plugin bundler resmi seperti @tailwindcss/vite. Alur kerja yang ringkas ini mempercepat setup tooling modern, melengkapi bantuan alat otomatisasi seperti AI Copilot dan generator kode dalam alur kerja developer. Konfigurasi membutuhkan beberapa langkah ringkas:

  • Pasang dependensi tailwindcss dan @tailwindcss/vite.
  • Daftarkan plugin Tailwind di dalam vite.config.ts.
  • Tambahkan baris @import "tailwindcss"; pada berkas CSS utama.

Analisis dan Kesimpulan

Tailwind CSS v4 mencerminkan tren tooling web modern: menggeser abstraksi JavaScript tebal ke performa kompilasi biner native dan spesifikasi CSS standar. Proyek baru memperoleh alur kerja bersih tanpa boilerplate konfigurasi. Untuk sistem enterprise lama, migrasi bertahap disarankan guna mengantisipasi kesiapan plugin pihak ketiga.

title: I Put My AI Code Reviewer Through 100 Real-World Testing Scenarios. Here's What I've Learned So Far
description:
Building an AI code reviewer is one thing.

Trusting it with your GitHub pull requests is another.

An AI reviewer can identify a suspicious line of code, explain a possible bug, or suggest a fix. But does it understand the surrounding code? Can it distinguish harmless examples from actual security vulnerabilities? Does it recognise weak tests? And, perhaps most importantly, can we trust its recommendations?

I wanted to investigate these questions by testing my own product, CodeGuard AI, against a growing collection of real GitHub pull request scenarios.

The goal is 100 meaningful scenarios. We're currently progressing through the campaign, and the results have been more interesting than simply checking whether the AI finds bugs.

What is CodeGuard AI?

CodeGuard AI is a self-hosted AI-powered GitHub pull request reviewer built with Java 21 and Spring Boot.

It is designed to help developers review code changes by combining AI analysis with deterministic checks.

It supports multiple AI providers, including OpenAI, Gemini, Groq and Ollama.

Some of its capabilities include:

  • Repository-aware code analysis
  • Bug and security finding detection
  • Test-quality analysis
  • Behaviour impact analysis
  • Team rules and review policies
  • AI-suggested fixes
  • Patch validation
  • Review history and GitHub PR integration

Rather than relying entirely on an AI-generated opinion, CodeGuard also tries to show the evidence behind its findings.

That distinction became particularly important during testing.

How we're testing it

I created a separate GitHub test repository and started introducing controlled changes through individual pull requests.

Each scenario has a specific objective and an expected outcome.

The testing campaign covers areas such as:

  1. Test execution and result verification
  2. Bug detection
  3. Security analysis
  4. False-positive resistance
  5. Test-quality analysis
  6. Mock and assertion analysis
  7. Behaviour impact analysis
  8. Suggested fix safety
  9. Merge decision consistency
  10. Repository and GitHub integration

The idea is not to make CodeGuard look good. It is to discover where it performs well and where it needs improvement.

Some encouraging results so far

1. It can distinguish harmless SQL examples from potential security problems

One scenario contained SQL-looking text inside Java strings and Markdown documentation.

CodeGuard did not incorrectly report SQL injection vulnerabilities merely because SQL syntax appeared in the source.

The scenario completed with:

  • 10/10 review score
  • 100% AI confidence
  • 3 tests passed
  • 0 critical issues
  • No unnecessary security suggestions

This was an encouraging result for false-positive resistance.

2. Mock analysis showed promising method-level isolation

I created scenarios where one test method used Mockito while another performed an ordinary calculation using a real value.

CodeGuard correctly identified the mocked assertion without incorrectly flagging the separate real-object assertion.

We also tested the same idea across separate test classes.

These scenarios passed their execution checks and showed that the method-level and cross-class isolation worked in the tested examples.

This matters because test-quality analysis should understand the context of an individual test, not blindly treat every mock in a file as suspicious.

3. It recognised weak assertions

We introduced a test that checked only whether a calculated discount was positive:

assertTrue(result > 0);

The test could pass even if the implementation returned an incorrect discount.

CodeGuard identified the weakness and suggested an explicit expected-value assertion.

This is a useful distinction: a green test suite does not necessarily mean that the tests verify the intended behaviour.

4. It handled a correct implementation with boundary coverage

We tested a percentage calculator with normal and boundary inputs, including:

  • 20% discount
  • 100% discount
  • 0% discount
  • Invalid negative inputs
  • Percentage values above the allowed range

The corrected implementation completed with:

  • 10/10 review score
  • 100% AI confidence
  • All tests passed
  • 0 critical issues
  • Safe-to-merge recommendation

It was also important to see that CodeGuard did not invent problems in a correct implementation.

5. It distinguishes test execution outcomes

Another important area is the difference between a test passing and a test actually being verified.

During the campaign, we encountered cases involving failed assertions, timeouts, compilation errors, no tests executed and unverified test-result evidence.

CodeGuard produced different execution classifications rather than treating every exit code or build result as proof of success.

This is particularly important for an AI reviewer: it should communicate what it actually knows instead of presenting uncertainty as certainty.

The findings that reminded me why testing matters

Not every result was positive.

Some scenarios exposed important improvement areas:

  • Confirmed failing tests did not always lead to a blocking merge decision.
  • Some unverified or missing test results were associated with inconsistent merge recommendations.
  • Suggested patches occasionally weakened tests instead of improving their verification.
  • AI and deterministic analysis sometimes produced duplicate findings.
  • A GitHub repository identity mismatch caused an API request to target the wrong repository and pull request.
  • Behaviour Impact reporting showed inconsistencies between reference counts and evidence.

These are not issues I want to hide.

An AI code reviewer should not only find problems in someone else's code. Its own findings, fixes and decisions must also be tested.

The findings are being recorded for a consolidated improvement phase after the testing campaign.

What I find most important about this experiment

A useful code reviewer needs to do more than generate suggestions.

It should be able to:

  • Identify the changed code accurately.
  • Distinguish a genuine issue from harmless code.
  • Explain the evidence behind a finding.
  • Recognise when tests have not actually run.
  • Avoid weakening tests through suggested fixes.
  • Make merge recommendations consistent with the configured policy.
  • Be transparent about uncertainty.

I am treating these as product requirements, not optional enhancements.

What's next?

The target remains 100 meaningful test scenarios.

The upcoming scenarios will continue exploring security vulnerabilities, repository context, patch validation, regression detection, stale reviews, team policies and other review behaviours.

I also plan to consolidate the issues discovered so far and run regression tests after implementing fixes.

The objective is simple: build something developers can inspect, test, configure and run within their own environment.

Want to explore CodeGuard AI?

CodeGuard AI is available as a self-hosted source-code product for developers who want to explore, customise and extend an AI-powered GitHub PR review system.

If you're working with Java, Spring Boot, GitHub integrations or developer productivity tools, you may find the project interesting.

Explore CodeGuard AI:

https://javacoder716.gumroad.com/l/codeguard-ai?utm_source=devto&utm_medium=article&utm_campaign=codeguard_testing_100

I'm continuing the 100-scenario experiment and sharing what works, what fails and what gets improved along the way.

Because an AI code reviewer should earn a developer's trust through evidence, not just impressive-looking output.

What would make you trust an AI code reviewer enough to use it on your team's pull requests?

title: Rizzbase v1.3.0: Go SDK, append-only Events, still no cloud
description:
I'm Paul, founder of Rizzbase.
Rizzbase is a local-first encrypted database. Each Project is one AES-256-GCM .rizz file on your machine. No cloud service, no accounts, no network database. The SDKs never download the engine you install it, you own the binary.
Today we're shipping v1.3.0, and three things matter.

Official Go SDK
Node and Python clients have been available for a while. v1.3.0 adds an official Go SDK that speaks the same protocol: spawn the local engine, check version and format, then run Project / Lobby / Yap operations.
Install the engine first (installers or a verified release binary), then:
go get github.com/pazti/Rizz-Base/sdk/go
Binary resolution is explicit: WithBinaryPath → RIZZBASE_BINARY → PATH. Same rule as the other SDKs no silent downloads.
Shared conformance tests keep Go aligned with Node and Python.

Append-only Events
Rizzbase started as a document store: Lobbies and Yaps (JSON documents you can update and delete).
v1.3.0 adds an append-only Events mode in the same .rizz file:

  • Documents - users, settings, app state (create / update / delete / query)
  • Events - visits, logs, analytics (append and scan; no per-event update/delete) One file. Two access patterns. No second database and no server required.

That matters if you're building offline analytics, audit trails, or high-write local logs without giving up the document model for everything else.

Same product principles

  • Local-only V1: no realtime, no hosted backend, no accounts
  • Passphrase-derived encryption; passphrase only to the local engine over stdin
  • Clear limits (including the project size cap) instead of pretending we're a cloud warehouse

  • Studio for Windows if you want a desktop UI over local Projects

  • Site: https://rizzbase.tech

What we didn't build
We didn't rush a cloud. Sync and hosted features stay later. The work in v1.3.0 is useful offline and doesn't force a network into the design.
Try it

  • Release: https://github.com/pazti/Rizz-Base/releases/tag/v1.3.0
  • Repo: https://github.com/pazti/Rizz-Base

- Site: https://rizzbase.tech

If you care about local-first storage, a Go client, or append-only events next to documents, I'd like feedback especially from people putting real data in a .rizz file.

title: A free HTML to React (JSX) converter that runs in your browser
description:
I made a small tool: paste HTML, get React JSX or a typed component. It's free, needs no signup, and runs in your browser. The link is at the end.

The problem

HTML and JSX look alike, but they differ in small, annoying ways. class has to become className, for becomes htmlFor, inline style="..." strings must turn into objects, and void tags like <img> and <input> must be self-closing. When you paste a big chunk of markup from a template, a design export or an old page, fixing all of this by hand is slow and easy to get wrong.

What the converter does

  • Converts attributes to their JSX names (class to className, for to htmlFor)
  • Turns inline style strings into style objects with camelCase properties (background-color becomes backgroundColor)
  • Self-closes void elements
  • Converts hyphenated SVG attributes to camelCase (viewBox, strokeWidth)
  • Can wrap the result in an exported component, with TypeScript typing (React.FC)

Example

Input:

<div class="user-card" style="background-color: #0f172a; padding: 16px;">
  <label for="username">Developer Name</label>
  <input type="text" id="username" name="username" placeholder="Alex" />
  <img src="/avatar.png" alt="Profile avatar">
</div>

Output (TypeScript component mode):

import React from 'react';

export const UserCard: React.FC = () => {
  return (
    <div className="user-card" style={{ backgroundColor: "#0f172a", padding: "16px" }}>
      <label htmlFor="username">Developer Name</label>
      <input type="text" id="username" name="username" placeholder="Alex" />
      <img src="/avatar.png" alt="Profile avatar" />
    </div>
  );
};

What it doesn't do

  • Parsing uses the browser's DOM parser, so <script> tags and inline event handlers like onclick are stripped.
  • Server template syntax (PHP, Blade, Liquid) is not evaluated and stays as plain text.
  • It converts markup only. State, props and event logic are still your job.

Privacy

The conversion happens in your browser. The HTML you paste is not uploaded to a server.

Try it

https://www.devmaple.com/tools/html-to-react

I'm the author, and the site has 40 free browser tools in total: https://www.devmaple.com

If you find a snippet it converts wrongly, I'd like to see it. You can send it through the contact page: https://www.devmaple.com/contact

title: Rust Rewrites, Faster LLMs, AI App Security, Video Clipping, and Blender MCP
description:
The latest developer-tool signal is clustering around five practical workflows: incremental Rust rewrites, local LLM performance tuning, AI-app security, self-hosted video clipping, and AI-controlled Blender scenes.

The GitHub star counts below are point-in-time signals from November 20, not proof that a tool is production-ready. The useful next step is to test each project against a small, measurable workload.

Rust Anything: incremental rewrites with behavior checks

What it is: Rust Anything is a workflow for converting existing software to Rust incrementally. It records the original program’s behavior, rewrites one component, and compares the Rust implementation against that recorded behavior before moving forward.

Why now: The project was created on November 16 and reached 5,188 GitHub stars by the November 20 signal—the strongest traction among the newly created tools in this report. That interest reflects a real problem: full rewrites often introduce subtle regressions in error handling, edge cases, or side effects.

Tutorial angle: Build a small CLI or HTTP service and use it to demonstrate the complete workflow:

  1. Record normal requests, malformed inputs, error responses, and other important behavior.
  2. Rewrite one bounded component in Rust.
  3. Run the parity check against the recorded baseline.
  4. Stop and roll back when the first mismatch appears.
  5. Expand the rewrite only after the component passes.

For a CLI, record stdout, stderr, exit codes, and file-system changes. For an HTTP service, include status codes, response bodies, headers, and side effects. That makes the tutorial useful beyond Rust: it demonstrates how to make behavior-preserving refactoring measurable.

Difficulty: Intermediate

  • Start today: Run git clone https://github.com/erkamyaman/rust-anything.git && cd rust-anything && ls.

Inference Optimisation Skill: benchmark local LLM configurations

What it is: The Inference Optimisation Skill is an agent skill that searches for better local LLM serving configurations. It can tune decoding, speculative decoding, prefill behavior, KV-cache settings, startup time, and time to first token.

Why now: Created on November 16, the project accumulated 1,260 stars by November 20. Developers are running local models for coding, chat, and private workloads, but raw tokens-per-second numbers rarely explain why one configuration feels faster than another.

Tutorial angle: Start with a benchmark before allowing the optimizer to change anything. Measure:

  • Time to first token
  • Inter-token latency
  • Total generation throughput
  • Peak memory usage
  • Model startup time
  • Output correctness on a fixed prompt set

Keep the model, hardware, prompt set, context length, and sampling settings fixed. Run the optimization skill, compare the best configuration with your baseline, and then replay the prompts. A faster setup that produces different answers is not an optimization—it is a regression.

This separation is especially important for speculative decoding and cache changes. Both can improve latency while also changing the behavior you are trying to measure.

Difficulty: Intermediate

  • Start today: Run git clone https://github.com/sybil-solutions/inference-optimisation-skill.git && cd inference-optimisation-skill && ls.

Lovable: test authorization in AI-built applications

What it is: Lovable is an AI application builder that generates web applications along with supporting code and data flows. The generated happy path can work quickly, but that does not prove that its access controls are correct.

Why now: A published security investigation reported exposed passport details and more than 200,000 private messages. The related Hacker News submission reached 1,007 points and 382 comments, showing strong developer interest in the gap between “the app works” and “the app is safe.”

Tutorial angle: Build a deliberately small two-user application using fake data only:

  1. Create users Alice and Bob.
  2. Give each user private records.
  3. Try to read or mutate the other user’s record by changing the object ID.
  4. Inspect the generated API routes, database queries, and storage permissions.
  5. Add server-side object-level authorization.
  6. Turn the failed cross-user request into a regression test.

The important check is that authorization runs on the server. Hiding a button in the interface does not prevent a direct API request. Also test both read and write operations; write authorization failures are just as serious as data leaks.

Difficulty: Intermediate

  • Start today: Open https://lovable.dev and create a throwaway two-user project populated only with fake records.

PeakCut: self-hosted AI video clipping

What it is: PeakCut is a self-hosted AI clipping tool for long videos and live streams. It supports a bring-your-own-key model-provider workflow rather than requiring users to send media to the tool’s own hosted backend.

Why now: The project was created on November 14 and gained 1,337 stars by November 20, making it one of the fastest-rising new content-processing repositories in the report. Turning hours of recordings into a short set of publishable clips is still a repetitive manual task.

Tutorial angle: Self-host PeakCut, configure a supported model provider, and process two different inputs:

  • A recorded long-form video
  • A live-stream recording

Record the selected start and end timestamps, then compare them with clips you would have chosen manually. Measure selection quality, processing time, and the amount of manual trimming required.

The privacy section should be precise. Self-hosting the application keeps media and project data under your control, but requests to a third-party AI provider may still disclose the relevant media or extracted content. Show exactly what leaves the machine and document the provider’s retention policy.

Difficulty: Beginner

  • Start today: Run git clone https://github.com/haziqahmedqasmi/PeakCut.git && cd PeakCut && ls.

Blender AI MCP Add-on: give an AI client access to Blender

What it is: The Blender AI MCP Add-on combines a Blender add-on with an MCP server. Compatible AI clients can inspect a scene, manipulate objects, and work through visual chat and scene tools.

Why now: Created on November 19, the repository collected 526 stars within the November 20 signal. Unlike a chat-only assistant, an MCP-connected client can inspect the current Blender scene and perform operations that normally require clicking and menu navigation.

Tutorial angle: Install the add-on and MCP server, connect an AI client, and request one visible change—for example, moving or duplicating a cube. Save a “before” render, inspect the resulting scene, and save an “after” render. Then test the failure modes:

  • The client cannot reach the MCP server
  • Blender and the client use different configurations
  • The working directory or asset path is incorrect
  • The requested operation changes more objects than intended

Start with one deterministic scene containing only a few objects. Once that works, test a more complex scene with collections, materials, and external assets.

Difficulty: Intermediate

  • Start today: Run git clone https://github.com/bookwjitchieni1986/blender-ai-mcp-addon.git && cd blender-ai-mcp-addon && ls.

Building in public: my lead-gen engine

The same research-and-build loop powers an automated pipeline for finding, enriching, and contacting Hong Kong SME leads. In the latest run, it discovered 1,776 leads, enriched 201 records, and contacted 231 prospects; these are pipeline events, not a claim that every record passed through the same stages.

  • Leads discovered: 1,776
  • Leads enriched: 201
  • Leads contacted: 231

Start with this today

Pick Rust Anything and run this single command:

git clone https://github.com/erkamyaman/rust-anything.git

It takes less than five minutes, does not modify an existing project, and gives you a safe way to evaluate whether behavior-recorded rewrites could fit your development workflow.

Picks of the week

  • Best for controlled refactoring: Rust Anything
  • Best for measurable performance work: Inference Optimisation Skill
  • Most important pre-launch check: Lovable authorization testing
  • Best self-hosted content workflow: PeakCut
  • Best visual AI experiment: Blender AI MCP Add-on

Which of these would you test first, and what result would you require before putting it into a real project?

Connect

title: Java4Shell segue sem correção no Debian estável; sid já tem o patch
description:
Debian estável ainda usa builds afetados

Em 19 de novembro de 2026, os pacotes OpenJDK dos repositórios de segurança do Debian 12 e 13 continuavam na faixa vulnerável à Java4Shell, identificada como CVE-2026-114938. A correção estava disponível no sid, a distribuição instável, mas ainda não havia chegado aos pacotes estáveis; por isso, uma atualização comum pelo apt não resolvia o problema.

Os builds observados no Debian 12 eram openjdk-17 17.0.21+9-1~deb12u1; no Debian 13, openjdk-21 21.0.13+9-1~deb13u2 e openjdk-25 25.0.5+8-1~deb13u1. O rastreador de segurança marcava os três como vulneráveis, sem DSA. No sid, os builds corrigidos listados eram 17.0.21.1+2-1, 21.0.13.1+2-1 e 25.0.5.1+2-1.

As versões corrigidas upstream são 17.0.21.1, 21.0.13.1 e 25.0.5.1 ou posteriores. O forky, em testes, ainda trazia builds afetados: 21.0.13.0.3+1-1 e 25.0.5+8-1. A versão necessária depende da distribuição: bookworm usa Java 17, enquanto trixie oferece as linhas 21 e 25.

Confirme hardware, pacotes e processos Java

A falha só aciona o caminho vulnerável em processadores x86-64 que expõem simultaneamente as quatro flags de instrução necessárias. Sistemas ARM64 e máquinas x86 sem AVX-512 VBMI ficam fora do escopo descrito. A verificação indicada para o host é:

grep -oE '(avx512f|avx512bw|avx512vbmi|bmi2)' /proc/cpuinfo | sort -u

Confira também os pacotes instalados e as versões candidatas. Em Debian 13, consulte as linhas 21 e 25; em Debian 12, verifique o pacote da linha 17. Aplicações como Elasticsearch e instaladores do Jira podem incluir uma JVM própria, então o Java no PATH não representa necessariamente todos os processos do host.

apt-cache policy openjdk-21-jre-headless openjdk-25-jre-headless

Compare a versão do runtime com a flag que controla a intrínseca Base64. A flag aparece habilitada por padrão nos builds afetados; confira a saída da JVM que será usada, e não apenas a configuração ou o Java invocado em uma sessão diferente.

java -version
java -XX:+PrintFlagsFinal -version 2>/dev/null | grep UseBASE64Intrinsics

Desative a intrínseca nos serviços

Uma mitigação é iniciar cada JVM com -XX:-UseBASE64Intrinsics, que desativa a intrínseca vulnerável e direciona a decodificação Base64 para o código Java portátil. Definir JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS em /etc/environment pode atender a sessões de login, mas não basta para serviços geridos pelo systemd, que normalmente não iniciam em uma sessão PAM.

Para cada serviço systemd, configure a variável em um drop-in da unidade. Se ela já definir JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS, combine os valores, pois uma declaração posterior substitui a anterior. O exemplo usa a unidade demoapp; adapte o nome ao serviço e confira a flag na JVM ativa após recarregar o systemd e reiniciar a unidade.

[Service]
Environment="JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS=-XX:-UseBASE64Intrinsics"

sudo systemctl daemon-reload
sudo systemctl restart demoapp
sudo jcmd $(systemctl show -p MainPID --value demoapp) VM.flags -all | grep UseBASE64Intrinsics

A JVM do serviço deve reportar UseBASE64Intrinsics = false. Repita o procedimento para cada serviço Java e valide o processo após a reinicialização; jcmd faz parte do pacote JDK, então pode ser necessário instalar o JDK correspondente em hosts que tenham apenas o JRE.

Instale um build corrigido do Temurin

Outra alternativa é instalar um Temurin corrigido pelo repositório apt da Adoptium. O exemplo de configuração abaixo é o fornecido para Debian e instala a chave de assinatura e a entrada do repositório usando o codinome do sistema, sem substituir os comandos da distribuição.

sudo install -d -m 0755 /etc/apt/keyrings
curl -fsSL https://packages.adoptium.net/artifactory/api/gpg/key/public | sudo tee /etc/apt/keyrings/adoptium.asc >/dev/null
echo "deb [signed-by=/etc/apt/keyrings/adoptium.asc] https://packages.adoptium.net/artifactory/deb $(. /etc/os-release; echo $VERSION_CODENAME) main" | sudo tee /etc/apt/sources.list.d/adoptium.list

No Debian 12, atualize o índice e confirme que o candidato para Java 17 é o build corrigido antes de instalar. No Debian 13, escolha o pacote da linha usada pelos serviços, temurin-21-jdk ou temurin-25-jdk, e confirme a versão candidata correspondente.

sudo apt-get update
apt-cache policy temurin-17-jdk | head -4
sudo apt-get install -y temurin-17-jdk

Após a instalação, confira para onde aponta /usr/bin/java e qual runtime cada serviço iniciou. A instalação do Temurin pode alterar a alternativa padrão; serviços com JAVA_HOME apontando diretamente para o diretório do OpenJDK Debian podem continuar usando o build vulnerável mesmo depois da troca.

update-alternatives --display java | head -3
sudo update-alternatives --set java /usr/lib/jvm/temurin-17-jdk-amd64/bin/java
sudo systemctl restart demoapp
sudo jcmd $(systemctl show -p MainPID --value demoapp) VM.version

Confira mais em: https://guiadeti.com.br/noticias/java4shell-sem-correcao-debian-estavel/

title: A printable map is not a screenshot: fitting 798 pins onto A4
description:
The print button is the most underestimated control on a map site. People hit it before a session, not during one. Whatever comes out has to work without hover, filters or zoom.

That changes the job. On screen, density is almost free: you zoom in, hover a dot, filter a category, pan to the next district. On paper every decision is made once, at the size of the sheet, and the reader can't undo it.

The sheet can't carry the database

Leonida has 798 pins in the current atlas. Put that on A4 landscape and you get roughly 1.3 pins per square centimetre if you plotted every one, which leaves no room for a label at a size anyone can read.

So the printable sheet on GTA 6 map doesn't try. It prints the six regions with their pin counts, a legend, the atlas date, and a line saying the positions are approximate and the pin list lives in the interactive map.

That reads like a limitation. It's actually the design. A sheet that tries to be a lookup table fails at the thing paper is good at: giving you the shape of the world before you commit to a route. Six region names and their counts do that in about four seconds: Vice City holds 499 of the 798 pins, Port Gellhorn 157, and Grassrivers 20. That ratio alone tells you where a session is worth starting. A field of 798 unlabelled dots does not.

What breaks in print

None of them show up on a desktop preview.

Colour. The sheet is built at 300 DPI for A4 landscape, 297 × 210 mm, or A3 if you have the paper. Region colours that read fine on a monitor collapse into the same grey when someone prints in black and white, which is still the default in a lot of offices. Counts and labels have to carry the hierarchy, not just hue. If the sheet only works in colour, it doesn't work.

The fold. A4 landscape folds once, and the crease lands near the middle. Anything important on that line gets a permanent dent. The legend and the date should sit away from it.

The date. A printed sheet is frozen at the moment it leaves the printer, and a game map changes weekly during a launch window. If the sheet doesn't say when the data was pulled, the reader has no way to tell whether a region count is current or three weeks stale.

Print is a second layout, not a stylesheet

The temptation is to add @media print and hide the sidebar. That produces a screenshot of an app, with labels sized for zoom and controls that no longer exist.

The version that works is a separate layout with fewer elements and one clear job. It knows it isn't the database, and it says so on the page. The interactive map keeps the pin list. The sheet keeps the orientation.

If you're building something similar, the test is simple: print it, put it on a table, and try to plan a route without opening the laptop. If you can't, the problem isn't the printer.

The current sheet is here if you want to see what made the cut: printable GTA 6 map, A3 or A4.

title: CodeGraph: Pre-Indexed Code Knowledge Graphs for Agent Tool Calls
description:
Coding agents burn tokens on repeated file reads. Claude Code, Cursor, and Codex scan the same functions over and over because they lack persistent memory of codebase structure. CodeGraph solves this by maintaining a live semantic graph that agents query instead of scanning files.

The project sits at 78K+ GitHub stars and trending #11 in TypeScript. It runs 100% local with a Rust-powered kernel that watches file changes and incrementally updates the graph. The MCP server exposes this graph as a tool boundary for agents.

The Problem: Context Waste in Agent Tool Calls

Coding agents typically operate in two modes:

  1. Scan mode: Read entire files to understand structure, then discard context.
  2. Edit mode: Read files again to make changes.

This pattern wastes tokens and introduces latency. A 10,000-line monorepo might require 50+ file reads per agent session. Each read costs tokens and round-trip time.

CodeGraph pre-indexes the codebase into a queryable graph. Agents ask "show me all functions that call authenticate" instead of reading 20 files to find them. The graph persists across sessions, so repeated queries cost nothing.

Architecture: Rust Kernel + MCP Server

CodeGraph splits into two layers:

Rust kernel: Watches file system events, parses code into AST nodes, and updates the graph incrementally. When you edit a function, only that function's subgraph updates. Full re-indexing happens only on initial setup or major refactors.

MCP server: Exposes the graph as a tool boundary. Agents call structured queries like find_callers(function_name) or get_dependencies(module_path). The server translates these into graph traversals and returns results as JSON.

The kernel uses tree-sitter for parsing, which supports 40+ languages. Each language gets its own parser, but the graph schema is uniform: nodes represent symbols (functions, classes, variables), edges represent relationships (calls, imports, inheritance).

Storage Format

The graph lives in a local SQLite database. Schema looks like this:

  • Nodes table: id, type (function/class/variable), name, file_path, line_start, line_end, signature
  • Edges table: source_id, target_id, relationship (calls/imports/extends)

SQLite handles query speed well for graphs under 100K nodes. For larger monorepos, the kernel can export to a graph database like Neo4j, but most projects stay under the SQLite threshold.

Query Interface: Structured vs. Natural Language

The MCP server exposes two query modes:

Structured queries: Direct graph operations. Example:

{
  "tool": "codegraph.find_callers",
  "arguments": {
    "function_name": "authenticate",
    "max_depth": 2
  }
}

Returns a list of functions that call authenticate, plus functions that call those functions (up to depth 2).

Natural language queries: The server embeds a small LLM (Phi-3 or similar) that translates plain English into structured queries. Example: "What functions depend on the database connection?" becomes a graph traversal for all nodes with edges to the db_connection module.

Natural language queries add 50-200ms latency but reduce the need for agents to understand the graph schema.

Incremental Updates: How the Kernel Avoids Full Re-Indexing

File watching uses platform-native APIs (FSEvents on macOS, inotify on Linux, ReadDirectoryChangesW on Windows). When a file changes:

  1. Kernel reads the diff (not the full file).
  2. Parser identifies changed AST nodes.
  3. Kernel updates only the affected nodes and edges in the graph.

Example: You rename a function from login to authenticate. The kernel:

  • Updates the node name in the nodes table.
  • Finds all edges where source_id or target_id matches the old node.
  • Updates edge metadata to reflect the new name.

This takes 10-50ms for typical changes. Full re-indexing (parsing every file) happens only when you add a new language or change the graph schema.

Polyglot Codebases: Cross-Language Dependencies

CodeGraph handles polyglot repos by treating imports as opaque edges. If a TypeScript file imports a Python module, the graph stores:

Node: TypeScript function `fetchData`
Edge: imports → Python module `data_loader`

The kernel doesn't parse Python's internal structure from TypeScript. It just records the dependency. When an agent queries "what depends on data_loader?", it sees fetchData in the results.

For deeper cross-language analysis, you run the kernel with multiple parsers enabled. The Python parser indexes data_loader, the TypeScript parser indexes fetchData, and the graph links them via the import edge.

Agent Integration: MCP Server as a Tool Boundary

CodeGraph ships with MCP server configs for Claude Code, Cursor, Codex, and others. The agent sees CodeGraph as a tool with these capabilities:

  • find_definition(symbol_name): Returns file path, line number, and signature.
  • find_callers(function_name): Returns all functions that call the target.
  • find_dependencies(module_path): Returns all modules imported by the target.
  • search_symbols(query): Full-text search across function and class names.

Agents call these tools instead of reading files. Example flow:

  1. Agent receives task: "Refactor the authentication flow."
  2. Agent calls find_definition("authenticate") to locate the function.
  3. Agent calls find_callers("authenticate") to see where it's used.
  4. Agent reads only the files returned by the query (3 files instead of 20).
  5. Agent makes changes and commits.

This reduces token usage by 60-80% for typical refactoring tasks.

Trade-Offs: When CodeGraph Helps and When It Doesn't

Scenario CodeGraph Benefit Limitation
Large monorepo (10K+ files) High. Avoids scanning thousands of files. Initial indexing takes 5-10 minutes.
Frequent refactors High. Agents query structure instead of reading. Graph updates lag by 50-200ms after file save.
Polyglot codebase Medium. Cross-language imports work, but deep analysis requires multiple parsers. Parser support varies. Obscure languages may not work.
Small project (<100 files) Low. File scanning is fast enough. Overhead of running the kernel isn't worth it.
Dynamic languages (Python, Ruby) Medium. Static analysis misses runtime behavior. Graph shows imports and calls, but not dynamic dispatch.

Failure Modes and Observability

Graph corruption: If the kernel crashes mid-update, the SQLite database can end up in an inconsistent state. CodeGraph includes a codegraph repair command that re-indexes from scratch.

Parser errors: If a file has syntax errors, the parser skips it and logs a warning. The graph remains incomplete until you fix the syntax. Agents see a partial view of the codebase.

Memory usage: The kernel holds the graph in memory for fast queries. A 100K-node graph uses ~500MB RAM. For larger repos, you can configure the kernel to use disk-backed storage, but queries slow down by 2-3x.

Observability: The MCP server logs every query with timing data. You can pipe logs to Prometheus or Datadog to track:

  • Query latency (p50, p99)
  • Cache hit rate (for repeated queries)
  • Kernel update lag (time between file save and graph update)

Deployment Shape

CodeGraph runs as a local daemon. Install via npm:

npm install -g @colbymchenry/codegraph
codegraph init /path/to/repo
codegraph serve

The kernel starts in the background and watches the repo. The MCP server listens on localhost:3000. Agents connect via HTTP or WebSocket.

For team deployments, you can run CodeGraph on a shared server and point multiple agents at the same MCP endpoint. This works if everyone on the team uses the same codebase. If developers work on different branches, each needs their own CodeGraph instance.

Security Boundaries

CodeGraph runs locally and never sends code to external servers. The MCP server has no authentication by default, so any process on the same machine can query the graph. For production deployments, you should:

  • Run the MCP server behind a reverse proxy with API key auth.
  • Restrict file system access so the kernel can only read the target repo.
  • Disable natural language queries if you don't want to run a local LLM.

The kernel has read-only access to the file system. It never writes to source files, only to the SQLite database.

Technical Verdict

Use CodeGraph when:

  • You work on a monorepo with 1K+ files and agents repeatedly scan the same code.
  • Your agents spend more than 30% of their token budget on file reads.
  • You need cross-file analysis (call graphs, dependency trees) and don't want to build it yourself.

Avoid CodeGraph when:

  • Your codebase is under 100 files. File scanning is fast enough.
  • You use a language that tree-sitter doesn't support well (COBOL, Fortran, obscure DSLs).
  • You need runtime behavior analysis. CodeGraph only sees static structure.

The project is stable but young. Expect rough edges in polyglot repos and large-scale deployments. The Rust kernel is solid, but the MCP server API may change as agent tooling evolves.

Source Links

  • CodeGraph GitHub Repository
  • CodeGraph Documentation

title: Poler-harvest: A Content-Addressed Search Tool in Rust with 2ms Warm Cache for AI Agents
description:
⚡ Why Another Search Tool?

I love ripgrep and grep — they are legendary for one-off manual terminal lookups. But while designing local AI coding agents and automated developer loops, I hit a fundamental bottleneck: traditional search tools have zero memory.

When an autonomous coding agent or CI test runner performs dozens of searches across the exact same 100,000-file codebase within a few minutes, re-traversing the directory tree and re-scanning gigabytes of files from disk on every single turn wastes seconds of user latency.

To solve this, I built poler-harvest in Rust.

🎯 How It Works

poler-harvest combines high-throughput multi-threaded search with content-addressed L1–L3 persistent caching:

  1. Cold Run (Zero Cache):

    • Multi-threaded traversal powered by rayon, aho-corasick, and regex.
    • Automatically segments matching anchor maps using FastCDC (Fast Content-Defined Chunking) with BLAKE3 deduplication.
    • Compiles anchors into an ultra-compact binary crystal file (.t5a / .tar.poler).

  2. Warm Run (Instant Lookups):

    • Returns exact matches in 2 milliseconds — streaming results directly through memory-mapped L1–L3 cache.
    • Up to 300×–400× faster than cold searches on large codebases.

  3. Honest Invalidation (7/7 Regression Tests):

    • The cache never serves stale data.
    • Automatically validates files by size, mtime, and content hash, selectively re-scanning only modified, added, or deleted files in sub-milliseconds.

📊 Benchmarks (Debian 12, 100,000 Files / 12 MB)

Tool Cold Search Warm Search (Repeated) Speedup
GNU grep 3.8 (grep -r) 407–451 ms 407–451 ms 1×
ripgrep 13.0 (rg) 728–760 ms 728–760 ms 1×
poler-harvest 633–760 ms 2 ms 364× faster 🚀

(Measurements taken with hyperfine on Linux 6.x, x86_64, NVMe).

🚀 Quick Install (Linux x86_64)

One-line installer: 

curl -sSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/poler-engine-org/poler-harvest/main/scripts/install.sh | bash

Arch Linux / CachyOS (Pacman): 

sudo pacman -U https://github.com/poler-engine-org/poler-harvest/releases/download/v0.96.1/poler-harvest-0.96.1-1-x86_64.pkg.tar.zst

Debian / Ubuntu / Mint (.deb): 

curl -LO https://github.com/poler-engine-org/poler-harvest/releases/download/v0.96.1/poler-harvest_0.96.1_amd64.deb
sudo dpkg -i poler-harvest_0.96.1_amd64.deb

Python Wheels: 

pip install https://github.com/poler-engine-org/poler-harvest/releases/download/v0.96.1/poler_harvest-0.96.1-py3-none-manylinux_2_34_x86_64.whl

🛠 Usage Examples 

# Exact search with 2ms warm lookups:
poler-harvest . "TODO: fix this bug" address

# Contextual markdown search for documentation:
poler-harvest src/ "network timeout" markdown -c 2

# Regex search with machine-readable JSONL stream:
poler-harvest src/ "struct.*Error" -r -f json

# One-off scan without touching persistent cache:
poler-harvest /var/log "kernel error" --no-cache

💎 Source-Available & Open Tooling

The project is published under the POLER Custom Source-Available License v1.0 — completely free for personal use, security audits, academic research, and community developer tooling:

⭐ GitHub Repository: https://github.com/poler-engine-org/poler-harvest

I would love to hear feedback, architectural suggestions, or questions about the FastCDC chunking pipeline from the community!

title: Zero-Server Go: Compiling Go to WebAssembly and Deploying on Brimble’s Static Edge
description:
Running Go on a Static Host: A Webhook Debugger With No Backend

I built a webhook signature debugger where the Go code runs in your browser. It is compiled to WebAssembly and served as plain static files from Brimble. No server, no container, no function. Your secret never leaves the tab.

Try it: https://brimble-guide.brimble.app/
Code: https://github.com/Luckyisrael/brimble-guide/tree/main/WASM%20Deployment%20article

This post has two parts. The first shows what is possible when you push real backend logic to the edge as static files. The second is my experience deploying it on Brimble, with what worked well and a few things I would be glad to help build.

Part 1: What is possible

The problem

Debugging a webhook usually means pasting a payload and a signing secret into some online tool and hoping it does not log them. That has always felt wrong.

EdgeHook Wasm does the check locally. Paste the payload, the secret and the signature header. You get PASS or FAIL, the computed signature next to the one you received, and the time it took.

It supports Paystack (HMAC-SHA512), Stripe (the t=...,v1=... format), GitHub (sha256= prefix), and generic SHA-256 or SHA-512 with hex or base64 output. It also pretty-prints JSON, lists top-level keys, and reports the exact line and column of a syntax error.

Why Go compiled to WebAssembly

  1. The standard library has everything needed: crypto/hmac, crypto/sha256, crypto/sha512, crypto/subtle, encoding/json. Zero dependencies.
  2. The core is a normal Go package with normal Go tests. I run go test without a browser.
  3. Static hosting plus Wasm means no cold starts and no server to secure. The code runs on the user's machine.

The shape of the project

Two sides. internal/verifier is pure Go and knows nothing about browsers. cmd/wasm is a thin layer that registers four functions on the browser's global object. The frontend is vanilla HTML, CSS and JavaScript. No npm, no framework.

The four functions are goVerifyWebhook, goInspectPayload, goGeneratePreset and goGetRuntimeInfo. Each returns one JSON string. The verify function takes five strings, the inspector and preset functions take one, and the runtime-info function takes none. I kept it that boring on purpose, because passing complex objects across the JavaScript and Wasm boundary gets messy fast. Each function also recovers from panics and returns an error field, so bad input never crashes the page.

Details that mattered

The raw body is sacred. An early version of my plan had a "pretty print" button that rewrote the payload. That silently breaks every signature, because signatures are computed over exact bytes. Formatted output now lives in a separate read-only box.

Presets are computed, not pasted. The sample buttons do not contain hardcoded signatures. Go computes them from a fixed test secret at runtime, and a unit test proves every preset verifies.

Honest timing. Browsers deliberately blur their timers, so one HMAC can read as 0 microseconds. Go runs the check 200 times and reports the average, and the UI says so.

Constant-time comparison. Signatures are compared with subtle.ConstantTimeCompare, the same code you would use on a real server.

Testing without a browser. I used the standard HMAC test vectors and cross-checked them with openssl. Then a small smoke test loads the real .wasm file and calls all four functions before I open a page. Coverage on the verifier package is 91.4%.

Numbers I measured locally

Thing Value
main.wasm size (raw) 3,646,177 bytes (3.48 MB)
main.wasm size (transferred) 1,081,392 bytes (1.03 MB) over the wire, gzip encoded
Wasm init time 21 to 30 ms in headless Chrome on a local static server
Average verify time Paystack 39.0 µs, Stripe 114.5 µs, GitHub 113.5 µs, each an average of 200 runs
Go version go1.26.5
Works offline Yes, verified with headless Chrome offline network emulation

A Go Wasm binary carries the Go runtime, so expect a few megabytes raw. Edge compression helps, and it is cached after the first load.

Part 2: Deploying on Brimble

What I did

First, sign up on brimble.io if you do not have an account.

On the Brimble dashboard, look towards the top right. You will see two bold buttons: a blue one and a grey one. The grey button is a powerful part of Brimble. It lets you create different environments, for example a production environment and a development environment, and Brimble handles the rest so you can focus on your code. I will talk about environments in a later article. For now, click the blue Create Project button.

The next page asks how you want to deploy. My personal favourite is connecting my GitHub account. You can also use GitLab, Bitbucket or a Docker image, depending on your setup. Follow the prompts, connect your account, and when the repository list appears, install only the repo you are working with. I do not give access to all my repositories. Once that is done, your account is authenticated with Brimble.

Why this is good: every commit you push to GitHub is deployed automatically to your environments, with no manual trigger. That also means you should always check that everything works locally before pushing, so you do not waste build minutes on a broken commit.

Which brings me to brimble.toml. A TOML file is just a small config file. TOML stands for Tom's Obvious, Minimal Language. It is plain text that a tool reads to know what to do, instead of you writing code for it. The rules are tiny: key = value pairs, [section] headers that group keys, and # for comments. We will not go too deep into TOML here, you can do a quick search if you want more. When you push to GitHub, Brimble looks for this file and uses it to work out how to build and publish your project. You can find ours at the root of the repo. It selects WASM Deployment article as the project root and dist as the output folder. The build command is a no-op echo prebuilt, because the dist folder is already built and committed. Keep it at the repository root. Brimble looks there first, and a copy inside a project folder will not be read.

When the repository is connected, Brimble greets you with a deployment page. Here you set the project name, branch, root directory, deployment type and build framework. Depending on the framework you choose, you may need to fill in build settings, but 99% of the time Brimble already has that covered. Just check that everything looks right, then click Deploy Project. For this project the deployment type is static site, and for the build framework I picked HTML.

Congratulations, you have successfully deployed a Go WebAssembly project on Brimble. You land on an overview page where you can see your infrastructure, how it is connected, whether it is running, the region it runs in, the framework, and your connected repository.

One tool you will need sooner or later is the logs. If something goes wrong, the deployment logs tell you what happened. If you work with AI, Brimble provides a button that copies the logs for you. Paste them into your agent and it can trace the problem, fix it and redeploy.

Steps, with screenshots:

  1. Click Create Project in the top right of the dashboard, then choose GitHub as the source.
  2. Connect GitHub and select only the repository you want to deploy.
  3. On the deployment page, choose static site and HTML, check the root and build settings, and click Deploy Project.
  4. Open the overview page and the deployment logs to confirm the site is live.

We will explore more of Brimble in later articles.

Keep these in mind

  • Connecting GitHub was a short flow, and I could give Brimble access to just one repository instead of all of them.
  • Every push deployed automatically, so there was no separate deploy step to remember.
  • The deployment logs were easy to find, and the copy button made it simple to hand them to an AI agent.

Build your own

The pattern is simple and reusable:

  1. Keep your logic in a pure Go package with tests.
  2. Add a thin syscall/js layer that takes strings and returns JSON.
  3. Compile with GOOS=js GOARCH=wasm.
  4. Ship the .wasm, wasm_exec.js and a few static files.

Anything that is CPU-bound and safe to run on the user's machine is a candidate: validators, formatters, parsers, converters, offline tools.

Try EdgeHook here: https://brimble-guide.brimble.app/. Paste a payload, paste a secret, and see if your signature really matches. If you deploy something with the same pattern, send it to me. I would like to see it.

title: Storybrand Website Framework
description:
Storybrand Website Framework: A Comprehensive Architectural Breakdown

As a principal frontend engineer and conversion architect, I have encountered numerous websites that fail to effectively engage their audience and drive conversions. One primary reason for this failure is the reliance on standard off-the-shelf templates and generic forms. These templates often lack a clear understanding of the target audience's needs, desires, and pain points, resulting in a generic and unremarkable user experience.

Standard off-the-shelf templates and generic forms fail for several reasons:

  • They do not provide a clear and concise message that resonates with the target audience
  • They lack a well-defined narrative that guides the user through the website
  • They do not prioritize a clear call-to-action (CTA) that encourages users to take action

In contrast, the Storybrand website framework offers a structured approach to building websites that prioritize clarity, simplicity, and conversions. This framework is based on the principles of storytelling and provides a clear narrative that guides the user through the website.

Here are three concrete engineering takeaways from the Storybrand website framework:

  1. Clearly define the customer's problem: The Storybrand framework emphasizes the importance of clearly defining the customer's problem and presenting a solution that resonates with their needs and desires. This requires a deep understanding of the target audience and their pain points.
  2. Use a clear and concise message: The framework prioritizes a clear and concise message that communicates the value proposition and unique selling points of the product or service. This message should be consistent throughout the website and guide the user through the narrative.
  3. Prioritize a clear call-to-action (CTA): The Storybrand framework emphasizes the importance of prioritizing a clear CTA that encourages users to take action. This CTA should be prominent, visible, and consistent throughout the website, guiding the user towards the desired outcome.

By applying the Storybrand website framework, businesses can create websites that effectively engage their audience, communicate their value proposition, and drive conversions. Vareli breaks this down in the complete analysis:
https://vareli.info/blog/storybrand-website-framework

title: Sub-6ms In-Process AI Runtime in Rust: Eliminating HTTP Bottlenecks and Enforcing Zero-Wipe Invariants
description:
Deep Dive: Sub-6ms Sovereign Autonomous Code Runtime in Pure Rust

How Omni Engine Eliminates HTTP IPC Latency and Enforces Zero-Wipe Invariants (W = ∅)

By Ibrahim El Feqi (@ielfeqi)

1. The Core Problem with Local Coding Agents

Most local coding agents today are built on a fragile layer: they spin up an external HTTP daemon (such as Ollama, vLLM, or llama-server), and communicate with it over localhost:11434 via REST or Server-Sent Events (SSE).

When a multi-agent loop executes 20–50 consecutive tool-calling cycles:

  1. Serialization Bottleneck: Every prompt prefix, system prompt, AST diff, and token stream undergoes full JSON encoding/decoding and TCP/socket context-switching.
  2. Context Eviction & KV thrashing: Each turn invalidates or forces costly prefix re-evaluation in external server buffers. Latency balloons from milliseconds to tens of seconds per turn.
  3. Destructive Hallucinations (File Wiping): As attention degrades over long context windows, models emit truncated replacements (// ... rest of code unchanged ...) that silently wipe hundreds of lines of code.

To solve this, we architected Omni Engine: a sovereign, autonomous software engineering runtime in pure Rust that embeds llama.cpp directly in-process via C-FFI.

+-------------------------------------------------------------------+
|                        Omni Engine (Rust)                         |
|                                                                   |
|   +-----------------------+              +--------------------+   |
|   |  Maestro Coordinator  |              |  AST Diff Enforcer |   |
|   |    (Rayon Runtime)    |              |  (Zero-Wipe W=∅)   |   |
|   +-----------+-----------+              +---------+----------+   |
|               |                                    |              |
|               v                                    v              |
|   +-----------------------+              +--------------------+   |
|   | In-Process C-FFI      |              | Bubblewrap Sandbox |   |
|   | (libllama in RAM)     |              | (Hermetic Cleanroom|   |
|   | <6ms KV-Cache Slicing |              | Net=None, PID/MNT) |   |
|   +-----------------------+              +--------------------+   |
+-------------------------------------------------------------------+

2. In-Process C-FFI vs. Localhost HTTP

Instead of spawning child processes or querying daemons, Omni Engine links directly against llama.cpp using Rust FFI bindings:

  • Zero IPC Overhead: Token generation pointers write directly into Rust memory arenas.
  • O(1) KV-Cache Arena Slicing: By maintaining pre-allocated contiguous memory slabs, switching context between subagents drops to sub-6ms on consumer silicon (Apple Silicon M-series, x86_64 AVX2, or NVIDIA RTX).
  • Zero Cloud Tokens: 100% of execution occurs air-gapped on device with zero telemetry.

3. Strict Zero-Wipe Invariant (W = ∅)

A critical guarantee of Omni Engine is mathematical verification before disk mutation:

If a model attempts to generate a destructive diff, partial snippet, or malformed AST, the transaction fails closed. Host files remain completely untouched until tests pass within an isolated sandbox.

4. Hermetic Bubblewrap Cleanrooms

Every tool invocation (compiling, running test suites, executing scripts) is contained within a Linux kernel namespace jail via bwrap:

  • unshare-net: Completely disables external network access.
  • Read-only mounts for system root libraries.
  • Ephemeral writable tmpfs workdirs that isolate mutations until verification completes.

5. The ATLR Concurrency Benchmark Results

To benchmark agent robustness under high load, we conducted a 50-thread concurrent refactoring stress test on a single Tesla T4 GPU:

Architecture Engine / Runtime Concurrency Success Rate Wall-Clock Time Destructive Wipes (W) Exit State
Omni Engine In-Process C-FFI (Rust) 50 Threads 50/50 (100%) 37m 58s 0 (W = ∅) Exit 0 (Clean)
Aider + Ollama Local HTTP Daemon 50 Threads 11/50 (22%) 5h 24m 14 partial wipes SIGKILL
Aider + Gemini 2.5 Flash Cloud REST API 50 Threads 38/50 (76%) 12m 41s 3 truncations Panic 101

6. Get Started & Links

  • GitHub Repository: https://github.com/omni-engine-ai/omni_engine
  • Official Documentation: https://omni-engine-ai.github.io/omni_engine/
  • 1-Line Install: 
curl -sSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/omni-engine-ai/omni_engine/main/install.sh | bash
