title: React accesible: email sin saltos de layout
description:
Un formulario de registro puede estar técnicamente correcto y aun así sentirse roto. El caso más común: el usuario escribe un email, aparece un mensaje de validación y todo lo que está debajo baja unos píxeles. Si el mensaje desaparece al corregir el campo, la página vuelve a subir. Ese pequeño salto afecta la lectura, la precisión del clic y la confianza en el producto.

En interfaces que usan un correo de prueba o una dirección de correo desechable, este efecto se repite durante muchas comprobaciones. La solución no es esconder los errores. Es reservar el espacio, modelar los estados con claridad y dar el mismo resultado a teclado, lector de pantalla y puntero.

Este enfoque complementa patrones como estados de correo en React sin bloquear la interfaz y estados accesibles para un email de prueba. Aquí el foco es más concreto: que el feedback de email no cambie la geometría de la pantalla.

El problema: un mensaje de email que mueve toda la página

Un componente de input suele tener tres momentos: vacío, escribiendo y validado. Muchos diseños agregan el error solo después de una respuesta inválida. Visualmente es sencillo, pero el navegador debe recalcular la posición de todos los elementos que vienen después.

Eso puede ser molesto en un formulario corto y bastante peor en un onboarding largo. Una persona que ya iba a pulsar “Continuar” puede terminar pulsando otro control. Para alguien con baja visión, el cambio de posición añade una carga de orientación innecesaria. Aveces el error no es una validación incorrecta; es que el feedback llega de forma brusca.

También conviene separar dos ideas que suelen mezclarse:

  • Estado visual: qué borde, icono o texto ve la persona.
  • Estado semántico: qué anuncia el navegador y el lector de pantalla.

Un borde rojo no comunica por sí solo el motivo del error. Y un aria-invalid sin un mensaje asociado tampoco explica cómo corregirlo.

Reserva el espacio antes de conocer el resultado

La forma más estable de empezar es dejar una zona para el mensaje desde el primer render. No hace falta mostrar texto vacío ni reservar un hueco enorme; basta una altura mínima coherente con una línea de ayuda.

.field-help {
  min-height: 1.4rem;
  margin-top: 0.35rem;
  color: var(--text-muted);
  font-size: 0.875rem;
  line-height: 1.4;
}

.field-help[data-error="true"] {
  color: var(--color-danger);
}

El min-height evita que el formulario cambie de layout cuando aparece el error. Si los mensajes pueden ocupar dos líneas, reserva dos líneas o define una estrategia para textos largos. La decisión debe salir del contenido real, no solo de la captura ideal del diseño.

En móvil, revisa el resultado con zoom y con textos traducidos. Un mensaje que cabe en español puede necesitar más ancho en otro idioma. Es un detalle pequeño, pero mejora la consitencia del componente.

Estados de React que también entiende un lector de pantalla

El componente debe tener una fuente de verdad simple. En este ejemplo, error es null cuando no hay mensaje y contiene texto cuando la validación falla:

function EmailField({ value, error, onChange }) {
  const errorId = "signup-email-error";

  return (
    <div className="field">
      <label htmlFor="signup-email">Email</label>
      <input
        id="signup-email"
        name="email"
        type="email"
        value={value}
        onChange={onChange}
        aria-invalid={Boolean(error)}
        aria-describedby={error ? errorId : undefined}
      />
      <p id={errorId} className="field-help" data-error={Boolean(error)} aria-live="polite">
        {error || "Usa un email que puedas consultar."}
      </p>
    </div>
  );
}

Hay dos decisiones importantes. aria-invalid cambia junto al error real, y aria-describedby conecta el input con el texto que lo explica. aria-live="polite" permite anunciar una actualización sin interrumpir una frase que el lector ya está leyendo.

El texto de ayuda permanece en el DOM para conservar el espacio. Cuando no hay error, puede contener una instrucción útil; cuando lo hay, debe decir qué corregir. Evita mensajes vagos como “valor inválido”. Es mas accionable decir “Escribe un email con formato nombre@dominio.com”.

Si la validación ocurre mientras se escribe, no anuncies cada carácter. Espera a que la persona salga del campo o a que intente continuar. Una interacción demasiado habladora termina siendo inaccesible aunque use los atributos correctos.

CSS y rendimiento percibido

Evitar un salto de layout no convierte automáticamente el formulario en rápido. Aun así, la estabilidad visual hace que la velocidad percibida sea más predecible. Mantén las animaciones fuera del flujo: si quieres destacar un error, anima opacity o transform con moderación, no la altura del contenedor.

.field-help {
  transition: opacity 120ms ease;
}

@media (prefers-reduced-motion: reduce) {
  .field-help {
    transition: none;
  }
}

La validación también debe ser barata. Un regex sencillo puede cubrir el caso de formato, pero la confirmación del email pertenece al servidor. No bloquees toda la interfaz mientras esperas esa respuesta: muestra un estado de carga en el propio control y conserva la altura del mensaje.

Cómo probar el flujo con correo desechable

Para una prueba manual o automatizada, define primero el contrato del estado:

  1. El input tiene una etiqueta visible y un nombre estable.
  2. El mensaje de ayuda ocupa el mismo espacio con y sin error.
  3. El estado inválido se refleja en aria-invalid.
  4. El mensaje está relacionado mediante aria-describedby.
  5. El foco no salta a otro elemento sin una razón clara.
  6. El resultado del email del backend puede verse sin borrar el contexto del formulario.

Una dirección de prueba ayuda a recorrer el flujo sin llenar una bandeja personal. Si necesitas comparar opciones para un best throwaway email, úsalo solo con datos no sensibles y revisa la política de retención del servicio. Un buzón temporal sirve para probar entrega y expiración; no debe recibir información privada o credenciales reales.

En DevTools, activa el emulador de lector de pantalla o navega solo con teclado. Mide también la posición del botón antes y después de mostrar el error. Si cambia, el espacio no está realmente reservado. Y si un compañero anota “tem email” al buscar la fixture, documenta el nombre correcto en el test para que esa variación no termine en un script compartido.

Q&A rápido

¿Debo ocultar el mensaje cuando no hay error?

No necesariamente. Un texto de ayuda breve mantiene la altura y puede explicar el formato esperado. Lo importante es que el cambio de contenido sea comprensible y que el mensaje de error tenga una relación semántica con el campo.

¿Es mejor validar al escribir o al enviar?

Para emails, una validación ligera al salir del campo suele reducir ruido. Al enviar, valida otra vez y muestra un mensaje específico. El servidor sigue siendo la autoridad para comprobar disponibilidad, confirmación o entrega.

¿Qué reviso primero si la página todavía salta?

Busca elementos que cambien height, márgenes o contenido fuera de la zona reservada. Revisa especialmente loaders, fuentes que llegan tarde y mensajes de éxito. El CSS puede estar bien y el salto venir de un componente hermano.

La accesibilidad y el rendimiento percibido se encuentran en este tipo de detalles. Reservar espacio, mantener estados explícitos y probar con teclado convierte un formulario de email en una interfaz mas tranquila, medible y fácil de mantener.

title: adqproxy: a Rust reverse proxy built on Cloudflare Pingora
description:
How Cloudflare uses Pingora, how it differs from NGINX, and how adqproxy adds site configuration, routing, and systemd installation to a Rust proxy.

adqproxy is my Rust reverse proxy built on Cloudflare Pingora. Its command-line tool is adqp. I wanted to combine programmable request handling with a familiar server workflow: site configuration, configuration checks, and a systemd service.

When I returned to the project, I found a problem at the boundary between those parts. The package installed and its configuration check passed, but the process exited before serving its first HTTP request. While fixing installation and routing, I tested the path from installing the package to running the service.

To explain adqproxy's design, I'll start with its foundation: what Pingora is, where Cloudflare uses it, and why people compare it with NGINX.

What a reverse proxy does, and where Pingora fits

A reverse proxy accepts a client request and contacts an application on the client's behalf. The application can run on another port, another server, or in a container. The proxy selects a destination and returns the application's response to the client.

Client → reverse proxy → application or backend group

For example, one domain can route /api/ to an API service and other requests to a frontend. This layer can also terminate TLS and distribute requests across application instances.

Pingora is an asynchronous, multithreaded Rust framework for building network services, including HTTP proxies. Cloudflare open-sourced it in February 2024. Developers use its libraries to build applications with their own traffic-handling logic. Pingora open-source announcement

The project supports HTTP/1.1, HTTP/2, TLS, connection reuse, load balancing, and backend health checks. The application built on the framework determines which features it exposes and how operators configure them. Pingora repository

How Cloudflare uses Pingora

In the architecture Cloudflare described, Pingora handles requests from Cloudflare's network to origin servers: the servers hosting a customer's site or application.

In its 2022 engineering article, Cloudflare explained a limitation of its previous NGINX-based system. Connection pools belonged to individual worker processes, so a request could not always reuse a connection opened by another process. Pingora's architecture allowed connections to be shared across threads, reducing the need for TCP/TLS handshakes. How Cloudflare built Pingora

Why Pingora is compared with NGINX

Their responsibilities overlap in reverse proxying: accepting an HTTP request, selecting a backend, establishing a connection, and returning a response. An application built on Pingora can compete with NGINX on that part of the request path.

NGINX provides a ready-to-run web server with configuration, modules, static file serving, proxying, and load balancing. Pingora provides a foundation for developing a network service. A useful comparison therefore considers the features and operation of specific applications. NGINX capabilities · Pingora's purpose

Question NGINX Pingora and an application built on it
How do you get started? Run and configure an existing server Develop or choose an application built on the framework
Where is behavior defined? Configuration, modules, and extensions Rust code and the application's configuration interface
Who defines the site configuration format? NGINX The application author
What needs checking before adoption? Configuration and required modules Application features, configuration, installation, and upgrades

The ability to express custom logic in Rust is one reason Pingora interests me. If a proxy needs application data to make routing decisions or must integrate with internal services, explicit extension points are useful.

For straightforward proxying of a few sites, NGINX remains a practical choice. In my project, I evaluate Pingora primarily as a foundation for a programmable proxy. This work did not include an adqproxy-versus-NGINX benchmark under an identical workload.

How Pingora processes a request

The ProxyHttp interface exposes stages of request processing:

  1. request_filter: validate the request or produce a response before contacting a backend.
  2. upstream_peer: select a server and its connection parameters.
  3. upstream_request_filter: modify the request before forwarding it.
  4. response_filter and logging: process the response and record the result.

This is useful when backend selection requires more than a fixed path-to-address mapping. For example, the decision might depend on request context. The stages and retry behavior are described in the request lifecycle guide.

How adqproxy is put together

In adqproxy, I add site configuration and its management workflow on top of Pingora: sites-available, sites-enabled, configuration validation, and a systemd service. This is the interface a server administrator works with.

For this update, I upgraded Pingora from 0.6.0 to 0.9.1, adapted the cache and metrics integrations, and committed Cargo.lock. I then tested specific adqproxy behavior: startup without upstreams, backend selection, TLS, and upgrades over edited configuration files. Pingora 0.9.1 release

Why the default install failed

The installer enabled a default site with a simple return 200 "OK\n"; rule for /health. The proxy can serve that response directly. During startup, however, the binary always tried to take the first load balancer from its list of upstreams. The default site had none. The two pieces only failed when I ran them together.

The proxy can now start with zero upstreams. On a fresh Linux install with systemd, the installer enables the default site and the service responds at http://127.0.0.1:8080/health. Upgrades preserve proxy.yaml, site files, and their symlinks. If an administrator disables the default site, it stays disabled after the upgrade. Installer changes

The parts I kept from the NGINX workflow

Site files live in /etc/adq-pingora/sites-available/. Running adq-ensite creates a symlink in sites-enabled/. For example, /etc/adq-pingora/sites-available/demo can map a path to a named backend group.

server {
    listen 8080;
    server_name demo.example;

    location /api/ {
        proxy_pass demo_api;
    }
}

upstream demo_api {
    server 127.0.0.1:3000;
}

A request to /api/ with Host: demo.example goes to demo_api. Before the fix, two routes with different proxy_pass targets could end up at the same backend. I ran two local HTTP servers and checked the response bodies to see which one actually handled each request. For HTTPS, listen … ssl now creates a TLS listener on the configured port and loads the certificate specified in the site file.

Running the config check as the service user also checks that the process can read its configuration and TLS keys. Applying a change currently requires a systemd restart, so there can be an interruption.

sudo adq-ensite demo
sudo -u adq-pingora adqp -t && sudo systemctl restart adq-pingora

I used a similar approach to configuration and runtime checks when checking and updating NGINX after six CVEs: I verified the configuration and installed package, then checked request handling after the update.

NGINX verification on vm-voly in Kaku: package version, a successful nginx -t, an active service and an HTTP/2 200 response.

What CI checks before release

CI builds the binary from the locked dependency set, installs it on Ubuntu, starts the installed systemd service, and checks that the default /health route returns OK. Separate tests cover an upgrade over an edited configuration, malformed syntax, a missing upstream, routing to two distinct backends, HTTPS, and the request counter at /metrics. That exercises the installation a user gets as well as the proxy itself. GitHub Actions run

A successful adqproxy CI run: build, unit tests, smoke tests and startup of the installed systemd service.

An excerpt from the same CI log: proxying, metrics, installation, configuration preservation and HTTPS checks. Tests run in GitHub Actions; Kaku displays their log.

The source and build instructions are already on the main branch. Publication of the adqproxy npm package is still pending. Project repository

title: Designing for Wrong: The UX of AI That Is Sometimes Mistaken
description:
Every other piece of software you have ever shipped made a promise: press this button and the same correct thing happens every time. AI quietly breaks that promise, and most teams are still designing as if it had not. They wrap a probabilistic engine in an interface built for a deterministic one, and then they are surprised when users trust it too much, then too little, then not at all.

I have come to think the hardest part of shipping an AI product is not the model. It is the interface around it, because that interface has to do something no interface before it had to do: present output that is usually right and sometimes confidently wrong, to a human who has to decide, in the moment, whether to believe it. Get that wrong and it does not matter how good your model is. The product that earns durable trust is not the one with the best benchmark. It is the one whose design tells the user, truthfully and continuously, how much to rely on what they are looking at.

The assumption that quietly breaks

Classic product design rests on an assumption so deep we rarely name it: the system is correct, so the job of the interface is to make the correct thing easy to reach. Menus, forms, buttons, confirmations, all of it is choreography around a reliable engine. When something goes wrong it is an error, an exception, a state you handle and move on from. Correctness is the floor.

AI removes that floor. A language model returns an answer that is fluent, well-formatted, confident, and sometimes simply wrong, and critically it looks exactly the same whether it is right or wrong. There is no red underline, no stack trace, no obvious tell. If you design the interface the old way, treating every output as correct and polished, you have built a machine that launders uncertainty into false confidence. The better your visual design, the more convincing the wrong answers look. You have made the failure mode prettier.

So the first move is a mental one. Stop designing a tool that produces answers and start designing a tool that produces proposals of varying reliability, where conveying that reliability is a first-class part of the product, not a footnote.

Confidence is a design material

In a deterministic app, confidence is not a thing you design, because the answer is just correct. In an AI product, the system's confidence, and the gap between how confident it is and how confident it looks, is one of the most important materials you work with.

The failure to manage this is everywhere. A model returns a low-probability guess in the same crisp, authoritative typography it uses for a near-certain fact, and the user has no way to tell them apart. That is a design decision, even if nobody decided it. The fix is to treat confidence as something the interface expresses: hedge the uncertain answer in language and in visual weight, flag when the system is extrapolating beyond what it knows, distinguish a sourced fact from a plausible generation. This is not about plastering percentages everywhere, which users cannot interpret anyway. It is about the interface feeling appropriately sure when the system is sure, and appropriately tentative when it is not. A calibrated product feels truthful even when it is wrong, because it warned you. An uncalibrated one feels like a betrayal the first time its confident answer fails.

Make correction the main road, not the shoulder

Here is the assumption to design against: the user will need to change the output. Not occasionally, as an error case. Routinely, as the normal shape of the work. AI products are collaborative by nature, the human and the model converging on something good, and if your interface treats the model's first answer as a finished artifact with a tiny grudging edit button in the corner, you have designed for a world that does not exist.

The correction loop is the product. Editing, refining, regenerating, steering, giving feedback, undoing: these are not recovery paths, they are the main interaction, and they deserve the best real estate and the most design care. The question is not "how does the user accept the answer" but "how does the user quickly turn a 70% answer into a 100% one". A product that makes that cheap and obvious feels like a capable collaborator. A product that makes you copy the text out, fix it elsewhere, and paste it back feels like a demo that forgot real work exists. Most AI products are still demos in this specific way.

Design the failure, not only the success

Teams pour their design energy into the happy path, the moment the demo shines, and leave the unhappy paths as default states nobody owned. With AI, the unhappy paths are not rare, so this is backwards. The empty result, the low-confidence answer, the "I genuinely do not know", the request that falls outside what the system can do: these are frequent, and how you handle them is most of what determines whether users trust the product over time.

A system that can say "I am not sure about this" is more trustworthy than one that never does, even though it feels weaker in a demo. A graceful "I could not find a good answer, here is what I can tell you and here is how to get further" beats a confident fabrication every single time in the real world, because the fabrication is the thing that detonates trust. Designing the failure well means giving the model permission to be uncertain in the interface, and giving the user a real next step when it is. No dead ends. Every state, including the ones where the AI came up short, has a forward path.

Keep the human genuinely in control

There is a seductive failure mode where the interface is technically interactive but psychologically passive. The answer appears, polished and authoritative, with an implicit "approve" as the path of least resistance, and the human, busy and trusting, rubber-stamps it. This is automation bias, and a badly designed AI product manufactures it. You have put a human in the loop on the org chart while designing them out of it in practice.

The antidote is design that keeps the output a proposal and keeps disagreement cheap. Surface why the system produced this answer, so the human can actually evaluate it rather than just accept it. Make the uncertain parts visibly uncertain so attention goes where it should. Make editing and rejecting as easy as accepting, not a harder path that friction pushes people away from. Where the stakes are high, deliberately slow the human down at the decision point rather than letting them one-click through. The goal is a human who is actually exercising judgment, not one who has been smoothly led to agree. An AI product that quietly trains its users to stop thinking is a liability wearing the costume of a productivity tool.

Set expectations plainly at the door

Trust in an AI product is set early and hard, and the single most destructive thing you can do is let the first wrong answer arrive with no warning that it was possible. A user who was told, clearly, that the system is a capable assistant that is sometimes mistaken and should be checked will forgive an error and keep using it. A user who was given a flawless-looking magic box and then hit a confident falsehood will not come back, and no amount of later accuracy wins them back, because the wound was to trust, not to accuracy.

So onboarding is not a tutorial on where the buttons are. It is a frank briefing on what the system is good at, where it is weak, and how to use it well, including the uncomfortable parts. This feels like it undercuts the product, and it is the opposite. Calibrated expectations are what let a user integrate an imperfect tool into real work instead of bouncing off it at the first failure. You are not lowering their opinion of the product, you are making their reliance on it survivable.

Trust is the actual product

Step back and the thread connecting all of this is trust, and specifically calibrated trust: the user relying on the system exactly as much as it deserves, no more and no less. Too little and they ignore a tool that could help them. Too much and they get burned and then abandon it. The entire job of AI product design is to continuously calibrate that trust through the interface, so that reliance tracks reliability in real time.

This reframes what you are even building. The model is the engine, but the product is the trust relationship, and that relationship is made almost entirely of design decisions: how confidence is shown, how correction flows, how failure is handled, how control is preserved, how expectations are set. The teams that win the next few years of applied AI will not be the ones with a two-point benchmark lead. That lead is temporary and invisible to users anyway. They will be the ones whose products are trustworthy to use, where the interface is truthful about what is underneath it, and where a user can rely on the thing precisely because the design never pretended it was something it is not.

I am still refining my own version of this discipline, and I would value comparing notes. When you look at your AI product, does the interface make the user more calibrated about when to trust it, or does it just make the output look finished? Those are very different products, and only one of them keeps its users.

I write a field-note series on shipping AI that actually works in production. The original of this piece, and the rest, live on my LinkedIn. Originally published on LinkedIn.

title: Implementing Large CSV/PDF Export Downloads with Object Storage (Presigned URL Retry)
description:
For a healthtech service, a large CSV or PDF export download can time out even after object storage reports a completed upload: a slow browser may outlive its presigned URL, while the signed clinical document still has to remain tenant-isolated and disappear on its retention deadline.

Short answer: generate each large CSV or PDF asynchronously into a tenant-scoped private object, validate its headers, and only then issue a presigned URL with enough lifetime for the slowest expected download; on retry, mint a fresh URL and let the client resume where its storage provider supports range requests.

This is an operating-cost decision, not a unit-price contest. The bill includes export compute, object storage, support contacts, retry traffic, and the engineering time required to integrate and observe the path. I've been paged for missed jobs and duplicate deliveries; the same reflex applies here: make state transitions explicit and make every repeated action harmless.

For a team that wants one plain REST integration rather than another storage SDK, Infrai is worth trying for the private-object validation and link-issuance part of this workflow. Its public discovery surface describes request and response schemas, and every documented capability ships runnable examples in 10 languages, so an integration can be driven from the actual contract. Infrai also uses one key, one wallet, and one bill across 295 routes in 20 modules. For this export path, that means the worker, deletion scheduler, and adjacent services share one credential model, leaving fewer keys to rotate and fewer invoices to reconcile in the runbook.

What the timeout is really telling you

"Download timed out" collapses several states into one browser message. The export may still be running. The upload may have completed with an unexpected size or content type. The signed URL may have expired while a slow client was reading it. Or the user may be retrying a link whose validity window has already closed. Treating all four as a storage-throughput problem sends the investigation in the wrong direction.

The invariant is simple: a link is publishable only after the private object passes validation. Keep an export record keyed by tenant and export ID, and move it through generating, uploaded, validated, available, and deleted states. The object key should carry the tenant boundary, for example tenants/acme-health/exports/exp_01J.../signed-records.pdf; authorization must check the tenant before the server requests any presigned URL. A hard-to-guess key is not authorization. Attach two different clocks to that record. The retention deadline controls object deletion, while URL expiry controls access through one link. A fresh link must never extend the object's retention deadline, and a deletion worker must be idempotent because schedules can deliver more than once. This separation matters in healthtech: a 30-minute link and a 30-day document are different promises. Before returning a link, inspect the object headers and compare the observed size and content type with the export record. Do not infer completion from queue acknowledgement alone. For a zero-byte or mismatched result, keep the export unavailable and retry the generation path under the same export ID; don't hand the browser a partial file and hope a later range request fixes it. If an old URL has expired, issue a new presigned URL only after repeating the tenant authorization and object check.

Keep it private.

Retry state is data.

How should a browser retry a slow large CSV/PDF export download?

The browser-facing API should return export status before it returns a location. While generation or upload is in progress, return a stable pending state. Once validation succeeds, return a short-lived application download endpoint or a newly minted presigned URL. For very large files, preserve the completed byte offset and request the remaining range when the provider supports it; if that support is not established for your chosen path, restart the transfer with a fresh link rather than claiming resumability.

There is a sharp edge here — URL lifetime has to cover transfer time, not just the delay before the first byte. Size the window from object size and the slow connection you intentionally support, then add room for browser and proxy delays. I'm not sure what that floor should be for your user population; production download telemetry and a deliberately throttled test resolve it. The rule is measurable even when the number is local.

Test the bad path too.

Do not send the Infrai bearer token to the returned presigned URL. The token authorizes the control-plane calls shown below; the signed URL carries its own limited authorization. Also treat HTTP 429 as backpressure. This Go program retries with Retry-After when present, otherwise uses exponential delay, checks the object first, and asks for a new link without inventing a storage response schema.

package main

import (
    "bytes"
    "context"
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "net/http"
    "net/url"
    "os"
    "strconv"
    "strings"
    "time"
)

const baseURL = "https://api.infrai.cc/v1"

func call(ctx context.Context, client *http.Client, method, path string) ([]byte, error) {
    for attempt := 0; attempt < 5; attempt++ {
        req, err := http.NewRequestWithContext(ctx, method, baseURL+path, bytes.NewReader(nil))
        if err != nil {
            return nil, err
        }
        req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY"))

        resp, err := client.Do(req)
        if err != nil {
            return nil, err
        }
        body, readErr := io.ReadAll(resp.Body)
        resp.Body.Close()
        if readErr != nil {
            return nil, readErr
        }
        if resp.StatusCode != http.StatusTooManyRequests {
            if resp.StatusCode < 200 || resp.StatusCode >= 300 {
                return nil, fmt.Errorf("%s %s: status %d: %s", method, path, resp.StatusCode, body)
            }
            return body, nil
        }

        delay := time.Second << attempt
        if seconds, err := strconv.Atoi(resp.Header.Get("Retry-After")); err == nil {
            delay = time.Duration(seconds) * time.Second
        }
        select {
        case <-ctx.Done():
            return nil, ctx.Err()
        case <-time.After(delay):
        }
    }
    return nil, fmt.Errorf("rate limit persisted after retries")
}

func objectPath(action, bucket, key string) string {
    parts := strings.Split(key, "/")
    for i := range parts {
        parts[i] = url.PathEscape(parts[i])
    }
    return "/storage/object/" + action + "/" + url.PathEscape(bucket) + "/" + strings.Join(parts, "/")
}

func main() {
    if len(os.Args) != 3 || os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY") == "" {
        fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, "usage: INFRAI_API_KEY=ifr_... go run main.go BUCKET OBJECT_KEY")
        os.Exit(2)
    }

    ctx, cancel := context.WithTimeout(context.Background(), 30*time.Second)
    defer cancel()
    client := &http.Client{Timeout: 20 * time.Second}

    head, err := call(ctx, client, http.MethodGet, objectPath("head", os.Args[1], os.Args[2]))
    if err != nil {
        panic(err)
    }
    fmt.Printf("validated object: %s\n", head)

    presign, err := call(ctx, client, http.MethodPost, objectPath("presign", os.Args[1], os.Args[2]))
    if err != nil {
        panic(err)
    }
    fmt.Printf("presign response: %s\n", presign)
}

The application must still compare the header response with its own expected size and content type before calling presign. That check is intentionally domain-specific: expected bytes come from the completed export record, not from a guessed constant in a sample. Likewise, the exact link lifetime belongs in the validated request schema exposed by discovery rather than in an undocumented field.

Choosing the storage boundary by tenant isolation and effective cost

Provider choice comes after the boundary is clear. The following table does not rank raw storage prices. It asks whether the provider can sit behind the same Infrai control-plane integration and what that means for this design.

Option Infrai vendor coverage Practical decision for this workflow
AWS S3 Included Consider it when the shared REST control plane and tenant-scoped private keys fit.
Cloudflare R2 Included Consider it under the same boundary; validate link lifetime and range behavior in your own throttled test.
Alibaba Cloud OSS Included A candidate when this vendor placement matches the deployment.
Tencent Cloud COS Included A candidate when this vendor placement matches the deployment.
Google Cloud Storage Not included Integrate directly or choose a specialist abstraction if GCS is mandatory.
Backblaze B2 Not included Integrate directly if B2's storage model is the deciding requirement.

Infrai's self-describing API is useful when integration labor and credential operations dominate the marginal storage calculation: discovery is public, and its broader surface spans 295 routes in 20 modules under one key. The catch is that abstraction does not erase provider behavior. Range recovery and expiration policy still need an end-to-end browser test, and downstream egress and retry traffic still belong in the workload model.

Model one normal month using your own export count, size distribution, retention days, failed-generation rate, redownload rate, and egress destination. Add worker compute, storage, requests, network transfer, retry amplification, and engineering ownership. Price can be evidence, but current provider pages should supply it at decision time; a copied unit-price leaderboard will age before the runbook does.

When this design is the wrong fit

This route is not suitable for permanent public links or static-site hosting because public/public-read ACL is unavailable. It also lacks object versioning and object lock, so a financial-grade WORM retention requirement needs an external compliance storage solution. Stick with a direct specialist such as Google Cloud Storage or Backblaze B2 when either provider is mandatory, because neither is in the covered vendor set.

There are more boundaries. Lifecycle expiry has a one-day minimum, so an explicit deletion deadline measured in hours needs an application-controlled deletion worker. Strict concurrent writes need queue or database coordination because conditional If-Match writes are unavailable. Browser direct-upload CORS cannot be self-configured through a dedicated route, and cross-region replication or cross-cloud bulk migration requires another tool. Metadata is not server-side searchable beyond prefix listing.

For the signed-document case, my decision rule is narrow: use the shared REST layer when tenant authorization remains in the application, objects are private, daily-or-longer lifecycle granularity is acceptable, and WORM is not required. Otherwise, pick the specialist that owns the missing guarantee. No amount of retry logic compensates for the wrong retention primitive.

The runbook should alert on exports stuck before validation, repeated link refreshes, deletion past deadline, and unusual retry bytes. On every retry, reuse the export identity, verify the tenant again, inspect the completed object again, and mint a new link. Boring is good.

If this boundary fits your system, start with the storage download and range-retry guide and confirm the live contract through discovery.

Sources

  • MDN: Content-Disposition response header
  • Backblaze B2 pricing

title: geojson-editor: عارض ومحرّر ومدقّق GeoJSON في المتصفح بنيته لأتعلّم RFC 7946
description:
يبدو GeoJSON بسيطًا: هو JSON فيه إحداثيات. ثم يرفض ملفٌ أن يُفتح في مكان ما، فتكتشف كم من القواعد الصغيرة تختبئ خلف هذه البساطة. حلقة مضلّع (ring) غير مغلقة. خط العرض وخط الطول بترتيب معكوس. حلقة ملفوفة في الاتجاه الخاطئ. عنصر crs لم تعد المواصفة الحالية تسمح به.

لأتعلّم هذه القواعد كما يجب، بنيت الأداة التي أريدها عندما يتصرف ملف بشكل غريب. geojson-editor عارض ومحرّر ومدقّق (validator) صغير لـ GeoJSON يعمل في المتصفح، مبني بـ MapLibre GL JS و terra-draw. كل شيء يعمل داخل المتصفح، ولا يُرفع أي شيء إلى أي خادم.

هذا مشروع تعليمي. والجزء المهم فيه ليس الخريطة، بل المنطق الصرف تحتها، والقرارات حول من يملك البيانات.

ماذا يقدّم

التحميل من أي مصدر. اختر ملفًا، أو اسحبه وأفلته على الخريطة، أو أعطِه رابطًا (URL، بشرط أن يسمح الخادم بـ CORS)، أو الصق النص مباشرة. إذا كان المحتوى Geometry مجردة أو Feature واحدة، تُغلَّف داخل FeatureCollection، فتعمل دائمًا على الشكل نفسه من المستند.

الرسم والتعديل. يمكنك رسم نقاط وخطوط ومضلعات ومستطيلات. ويمكنك سحب الرؤوس (vertices)، وإدراج نقاط وسطية، وتحريك عنصر كامل، والحذف بمفتاح Delete.

لوحة الخصائص (properties). أضِف المفاتيح وأعِد تسميتها وعدّلها واحذفها. نوع القيمة يُستنتج مما تكتبه: 42 يصبح عددًا، و true قيمة منطقية، و "42" نصًّا، و [1,2] مصفوفة. ترتيب المفاتيح محفوظ، فلا يعود الملف المُصدَّر مبعثرًا.

التدقيق وفق RFC 7946. الأخطاء تشمل إغلاق الحلقة، وطول الحلقة، وشكل الموضع (position)، وانعكاس lat/lon، والعناصر الخاطئة في الـ Feature. والتحذيرات تشمل اتجاه اللف (winding order)، ووجود crs، والمواضع بأكثر من ثلاثة أبعاد، وحالات GeometryCollection الغريبة. النقر على مشكلة يحدّد العنصر المعني، وزر "Fix winding" يطبّق قاعدة اليد اليمنى بنقرة واحدة.

التصدير. نزّل النتيجة أو انسخها، مع خيار تقريب الإحداثيات (precision) وخيار الإخراج المضغوط (compact).

الحفظ التلقائي. المستند الحالي يُحفظ في localStorage. وإذا كان التخزين محظورًا، يبقى المحرّر يعمل.

طريقة الاستعمال

لا شيء يحتاج تثبيتًا. النسخة التجريبية موقع ثابت على GitHub Pages، وملفاتك تبقى في المتصفح: https://abdeldjalilchougui.github.io/geojson-editor/

لتشغيله محليًّا أو استضافة نسختك الخاصة:

git clone https://github.com/AbdeldjalilChougui/geojson-editor.git
cd geojson-editor
pnpm install
pnpm dev          # http://localhost:5173/geojson-editor/, then Paste or Open file (try public/sample.geojson)
pnpm test         # vitest, pure logic only
pnpm build        # type-check + production build into dist/

بناء الإنتاج يستعمل مسار Vite الأساسي /geojson-editor/ (انظر vite.config.ts). غيّره إذا كنت تقدّم الموقع من مسار آخر.

طريقة سريعة لتجربة المدقّق: الصق مضلعًا حلقته غير مغلقة، أو مضلعًا كُتب فيه خط العرض أولًا. تظهر المشكلة في القائمة، والنقر عليها يحدّد العنصر على الخريطة.

ما بنيته من الصفر

الكود مقسوم إلى قسمين عن قصد. كل ما في src/lib/ منطق صرف، لا يلمس الـ DOM، ومغطّى باختبارات الوحدة (unit tests). أما src/main.ts فهو مجرد ربط: خريطة MapLibre، وأوضاع terra-draw، واللوحات.

src/lib/        pure, DOM-free, unit tested
  parse.ts      text -> JSON -> FeatureCollection (friendly errors, never throws)
  validate.ts   structural RFC 7946 validator, issues with JSONPath-like paths
  properties.ts value inference + immutable add/rename/set/delete
  winding.ts    signed area, orientation, rewind (exterior CCW, holes CW)
  bbox.ts       bounding boxes for fit-to-data
  export.ts     precision rounding (coordinates only) + serialisation
  storage.ts    injected key/value store with every access guarded
  model.ts      document items with stable uids, which geometries are editable
src/main.ts     glue: MapLibre map, terra-draw modes, panels

بعض هذه الملفات يحمل الدروس الحقيقية:

  • parse.ts لا يرمي استثناءً أبدًا. النص الخاطئ يعطي رسالة خطأ واضحة بدل استثناء يوقف الصفحة.
  • validate.ts يُرفق بكل مشكلة مسارًا شبيهًا بـ JSONPath، وهذا ما يجعل "انقر على المشكلة لتحديد العنصر" ممكنًا.
  • winding.ts يحسب المساحة الموقَّعة (signed area) للحلقة ليعرف اتجاهها، ثم يعيد لفّها لتكون الحلقات الخارجية عكس عقارب الساعة والثقوب مع عقارب الساعة.
  • export.ts يقرّب الإحداثيات فقط. قيم الخصائص لا يمسّها إعداد الدقة أبدًا.
  • storage.ts يستقبل مخزن مفتاح/قيمة يُحقن من الخارج ويحمي كل وصول إليه، ولهذا لا يتعطل المحرّر عندما يكون localStorage محظورًا.

ما تعلّمته

احتفظ بمستندك الخاص كمصدر للحقيقة. كان هذا قرار التصميم الأساسي. المحرّر يحتفظ بقائمة عناصر من الشكل {uid, feature}. العناصر التي يستطيع terra-draw تعديلها (Point و LineString و Polygon بحلقة واحدة) تُنسخ إلى terra-draw بنفس الـ uid. وخصائص المستخدم تبقى في المستند، فلا تصل الخاصية mode المحجوزة لـ terra-draw إلى الملف المُصدَّر أبدًا.

لو كانت مكتبة الرسم هي التي تملك البيانات، لتسرّبت حقولها الداخلية إلى المخرجات، ولضاع كل ما لا تستطيع تمثيله. عندما يكون المستند عندي، تصبح مكتبة الرسم مجرد عرض مع مقابض للتحريك.

ليست كل الأشكال قابلة للتعديل، ولا بأس بذلك. الأشكال التي لا يستطيع terra-draw تعديلها (أنواع Multi*، و GeometryCollection، والمضلعات ذات الثقوب، وكل ما يرفضه تدقيقه الداخلي) تُرسم للقراءة فقط بطبقة MapLibre عادية. تبقى في المستند، فيمكن تعديل خصائصها، وتُصدَّر كما هي دون تغيير. أسوأ ما يمكن أن يحدث في أداة كهذه هو أن يضيع عنصر بصمت لأن المحرّر لم يستطع التعامل معه.

RFC 7946 أكثر صرامة من أغلب الملفات. كتابة المدقّق تعني قراءة المواصفة سطرًا سطرًا. ومن هنا جاء الفصل بين الأخطاء والتحذيرات: حلقة غير مغلقة خطأ، أما حلقة خارجية مع عقارب الساعة فأمر تطلب المواصفة تجنّبه لكنها توصي القارئ بتقبّله. وانعكاس lat/lon من الأخطاء التي يسهل الوقوع فيها ويستطيع المدقّق أن يلتقطها عنك.

المنطق الصرف هو الجزء الذي يستحق الاختبار. الأمر pnpm test يشغّل vitest على وحدات src/lib/ فقط. ولأن أيًّا منها لا يلمس الـ DOM، لا تحتاج الاختبارات إلى متصفح. ويبقى كود الربط مع الخريطة رقيقًا، فلا يكاد يوجد فيه ما يمكن أن يخطئ.

أشياء يجب معرفتها

  • الأشكال المتعددة (Multi)، و GeometryCollection، والمضلعات ذات الثقوب للقراءة فقط على الخريطة.
  • لا يوجد تراجع/إعادة (undo/redo) بعد.
  • التدقيق بنيوي فقط. لا يكتشف التقاطعات الذاتية ولا الثقوب الواقعة خارج الحلقة الخارجية.
  • بلاطات الخريطة الأساسية تأتي من tile.openstreetmap.org، وهذا مقبول للاستعمال الشخصي الخفيف حسب سياسة استعمال بلاطات OSM. غيّر الـ style في src/main.ts لأي استعمال أثقل.
  • حزمة الإنتاج نحو 1.2 MB (MapLibre مع terra-draw) وليست مقسّمة (code-split).
  • التحميل من رابط لا يعمل إلا إذا سمح الخادم البعيد بـ CORS.
  • ملف العيّنة يحتوي أشكالًا تقريبية مرسومة يدويًّا، وليست بيانات حقيقية.

لماذا بنيته

مشاكل GeoJSON في العادة صغيرة ومزعجة: حلقة واحدة غير مغلقة أو زوج إحداثيات معكوس في ملف فيه مئات العناصر. ولرؤية المشكلة تحتاج ثلاثة أشياء معًا: الشكل على الخريطة، والخصائص، وقائمة بما يخالف المواصفة. وعندما يكون الملف غير قابل للمشاركة، تريد أداة تُبقيه داخل المتصفح.

بناء هذه الأداة كان أيضًا طريقًا مباشرًا لتعلّم RFC 7946 والتدرّب على فصل نظيف بين المنطق الصرف وكود الواجهة. هذا هو الدافع كله: محرّر صغير يشرح لماذا الملف خاطئ، مكتوب بطريقة أستطيع اختبارها.

احصل على الكود

الكود المصدري والاختبارات وملف العيّنة على GitHub: https://github.com/AbdeldjalilChougui/geojson-editor. الكود برخصة MIT. بيانات الخريطة © مساهمو OpenStreetMap (ODbL). الملاحظات (issues) وطلبات الدمج (pull requests) مرحّب بها.

نُشر في الأصل على abdeldjalilchougui.biz.

title: Virtual Try-On in 2026: A Map of the Landscape, and 5 Design Decisions Behind Every Product
description:
Disclosure: we build Pastely, one of the products mentioned below. We have tried to describe every tool, including ours, by what it is built for.

Virtual try-on has had a busy year. Doji raised $14M in 2025 to make avatar try-ons fun, Google shut down its standalone Doppl app in April 2026 and moved try-on into Search, and ASOS launched virtual try-on in February 2026 on around 10,000 products in its iOS app.

If you are building anything in this space, or are just curious how these products differ, here is the map we use.

Three product shapes

1. Shopper apps. The user tries clothes on themselves before buying or getting dressed.

  • Avatar or likeness apps: Doji (iPhone, iOS 18+) builds an AI likeness from a few photos and adds a style feed and a browser extension.
  • Closet apps: Alta (iPhone, Android, web) and Whering start from the clothes you already own.
  • Outfit editors: Pastely (web) lets you combine pieces into one outfit and preview it on your photo.

2. Creator tools. The goal is an image to post, not a purchase decision. Magic Hour swaps one garment onto a person photo; Dreamina turns an outfit idea into a styled visual.

3. Commerce tools and APIs. Sellers need model shots or try-on at scale: FASHN AI (with an API) and Photoroom's virtual model, plus try-on built into retail surfaces like Google Shopping listings and ASOS.

Five design decisions that shape the product

These are the choices we had to make, and every product in the list above made them differently.

Platform: native app or web. A native iPhone app can feel more polished, but it excludes Android and laptop users. We went web-first so the same editor works on any device without an install.

Unit of try-on: one garment or a whole outfit. Trying on a single product is the simplest flow and fits a product page. But the question people actually ask is "does this jacket work with these trousers and these shoes?", so we made the outfit the unit.

Identity input: likeness, single photo, or sample model. A likeness built from several photos gives consistent results but adds setup friction. A single photo is faster. A sample model lets people start without uploading anything, which matters for privacy-conscious users. ASOS chose a hybrid: shoppers either upload a photo or pick an AI model that resembles them.

Context: one image or several settings. The same outfit reads differently in a studio, on a street and in a park. Showing several settings helps people judge the look, not just the garment.

Honesty about fit. A preview shows how a look reads: colour, proportion, style. It does not tell you how a garment fits. Every try-on product should say so clearly, and point to the size chart.

What a good input photo looks like

Whatever the model behind a try-on, it has to infer body shape, pose and lighting from one image. Results get much better with:

  • a full-body photo, facing the camera
  • even, natural light
  • fitted clothes, so the body outline is visible
  • a plain background

If your product takes user photos, putting these four tips right next to the upload button is the cheapest quality improvement you can make.

Try it, and tell us what breaks

You can try Pastely in the browser: open the editor, pick a top, bottoms and shoes, and preview the outfit on your photo or a sample model. There are free daily previews and no account is needed to start.

We are launching on Product Hunt on November 24, and honest feedback, especially from developers, is very welcome in the comments here.

Sources: TechCrunch on Doji, Doji on the App Store, Google Labs (Doppl), ASOS, Alta, Magic Hour, Dreamina, WearView. Facts checked in November 2026.

title: Java4Shell em Spring Boot exige atualização do JDK, não do framework
description:
A correção está no runtime Java

Aplicações Spring Boot recebem a correção da Java4Shell (CVE-2026-114938) do runtime Java, não de uma nova versão do framework. A falha está no decodificador Base64 do HotSpot, por isso a correção exige um JDK corrigido.

As versões corrigidas indicadas são 17.0.21.1, 21.0.13.1, 25.0.5.1 e 27.0.1.1 ou posteriores. A rota de build determina qual runtime entra na imagem e se uma reconstrução realmente remove a exposição.

Os testes foram realizados em 19 de novembro de 2026 com uma aplicação Spring Boot 4.1 em uma instância Google Cloud c3 com Ubuntu 24.04 e Docker. A execução do código vulnerável exige CPU com as quatro flags avx512f, avx512bw, avx512vbmi e bmi2.

O resultado depende da imagem

Na data da análise, o build padrão com o construtor atualizado do Spring Boot gerava uma imagem com Liberica 21.0.13.1+5, já corrigida. Construtores anteriores a 0.0.218 podiam manter o runtime vulnerável, assim como imagens Jib e Dockerfile baseadas em eclipse-temurin:21-jre.

Imagens amazoncorretto:21 incluíam Corretto 21.0.13.1+2, corrigido, e aplicações em Ubuntu 24.04 após a atualização USN-9156-1 também usavam uma versão corrigida. É necessário verificar o Java dentro do contêiner, não apenas a tag da imagem.

Confira a versão em execução

A primeira linha de inicialização do Spring Boot informa a versão Java ativa. Este comando filtra a informação nos logs de duas imagens; compare a versão exibida com as versões corrigidas, pois o tamanho da string não indica se o runtime está protegido.

for t in stale default; do docker logs app-$t 2>&1 | grep -oE 'Starting DemoApplication v[^ ]+ using Java [0-9.]+'; done

Se o Actuator estiver habilitado, o endpoint info também pode informar versão, fornecedor e runtime. Ele fica desativado por padrão; quando ativado, deve permanecer restrito à porta de gerenciamento ou à rede de monitoramento, pois expor detalhes da versão facilita a identificação do ambiente.

docker run -d --name app-info -p 8081:8080 -e MANAGEMENT_INFO_JAVA_ENABLED=true -e MANAGEMENT_ENDPOINTS_WEB_EXPOSURE_INCLUDE=info demo:default
curl -s localhost:8081/actuator/info | jq -c '.java | {version, vendor: .vendor.name, runtime: .runtime.version}'

Reconstrua sem reutilizar uma base antiga

O plugin build-image usa por padrão um construtor Paketo atualizado a cada build. Uma reconstrução simples pode trazer o JDK corrigido, desde que a configuração não fixe um construtor antigo nem reutilize uma cópia em cache com pullPolicy=IF_NOT_PRESENT.

./mvnw -B -DskipTests spring-boot:build-image -Dspring-boot.build-image.imageName=demo:rebuilt

Verifique se o construtor baixado é 0.0.218 ou posterior e confira o runtime dentro da imagem. Em imagens buildpack sem shell, o executável Java pode ser chamado diretamente pelo caminho da camada Liberica para exibir a versão completa instalada.

docker run --rm --entrypoint /layers/paketo-buildpacks_bellsoft-liberica/jre/bin/java demo:rebuilt -version 2>&1 | sed -n 2p

Em projetos Jib, a base eclipse-temurin:21-jre ainda era vulnerável na análise. A alternativa testada foi apontar o build para amazoncorretto:21, cujo runtime já continha a correção.

./mvnw -B -DskipTests com.google.cloud.tools:jib-maven-plugin:3.4.5:dockerBuild -Djib.from.image=amazoncorretto:21 -Dimage=demo:jib-corretto

Em Dockerfiles, a linha FROM define a distribuição Java incorporada à imagem. A base deve ser atualizada e o build precisa evitar o reaproveitamento de uma cópia antiga em cache, para que a imagem realmente contenha o runtime corrigido.

ARG BASE=eclipse-temurin:21-jre
FROM ${BASE}
COPY target/demo-0.0.1-SNAPSHOT.jar /app/app.jar
ENTRYPOINT ["java", "-jar", "/app/app.jar"]

Confira mais em: https://guiadeti.com.br/noticias/falha-java4shell-exige-jdk-corrigido-em-aplicacoes-spring-boot/

title: vite: command not found? Run the local binary the right way
description:
First published on the VMHeaven blog: vite: command not found? Run the local binary the right way. The canonical points there; the full guide covers npm/pnpm/yarn, CI and global installs.

Short answer: Vite is a local devDependency, not a global command. vite: command not found (or sh: vite: command not found) almost always means you ran plain vite in a shell where the project's local binary (node_modules/.bin) is not on PATH.

The fix

Install dependencies, then run Vite through the tool that knows about node_modules/.bin:

npm install
npm run dev     # uses the "dev": "vite" script in package.json

Or run the local binary directly, without a script:

npx vite

pnpm and yarn have their own:

pnpm install && pnpm dev     # or: pnpm exec vite
yarn install && yarn dev     # or: yarn vite

Why plain vite fails

  • npm run dev works but vite does not - that is expected. npm scripts put node_modules/.bin on PATH; your interactive shell does not. Use the script or npx vite.
  • In CI / Docker - run npm ci before the build step and call npx vite build (or npm run build), never bare vite.
  • You really want it global - npm install -g vite works, but pinning Vite per project is safer; versions differ between projects.

Full guide

Monorepos, vite: not found in Docker builds, Windows, and the pnpm .bin quirks are in the complete version:

vite: command not found - the complete fix

Need a box to build on? A Node-ready VPS spins up in a minute.

title: Go 爬虫第三讲：做一个"有礼貌"的爬虫
description:
Go 爬虫第三讲：做一个"有礼貌"的爬虫

爬虫的行为规范，总结成一句话就是：别把人家网站打挂。礼貌 = 可持续，粗暴抓取迟早被封。

一、礼貌的三条做法

  1. 控制抓取频率：请求之间加延时，比如每次间隔一两秒；别像机关枪一样连发；
  2. 控制并发数：同时只开固定数量的抓取任务，别几百个连接一起压过去；
  3. 看时间段：能避开对方业务高峰就避开，深夜低峰跑批量任务是基本体贴。

二、三条线不碰

  • 需要登录才能看到的内容，不抓；
  • 反爬措施（验证码、IP 封禁后的绕行），不绕；
  • 网站的服务条款，遵守。

三、数据用途的底线

抓下来的数据自己用：不倒卖、不公开他人隐私。数据一旦流出，你就失去了对它的控制——这条线守不住，前面所有的合规动作都白做。

四、可运行示例：带延时和并发上限的抓取器

下面这段程序实现"有礼貌"的两个核心机制：请求间延时 + 信号量控制并发数。用本地测试服务器记录每次请求的时间和并发峰值，程序自己校验是否达标：

package main

import (
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "net/http"
    "net/http/httptest"
    "sync"
    "sync/atomic"
    "time"
)

// PoliteFetcher：有礼貌的抓取器
// sem 控制最大并发数；tokens 是令牌桶，ticker 每 delay 发放一个令牌，
// 全局限速——拿不到令牌的请求就等着，不会一拥而上。
type PoliteFetcher struct {
    sem    chan struct{}
    tokens chan struct{}
}

func NewPoliteFetcher(delay time.Duration, maxConcurrent int) *PoliteFetcher {
    p := &PoliteFetcher{
        sem:    make(chan struct{}, maxConcurrent),
        tokens: make(chan struct{}, 1),
    }
    // 令牌只由 ticker 发放：第一个请求也要等第一个 tick，
    // 之后每 delay 补一个。注意：令牌发放间隔是严格的，
    // 但请求实际发出的间隔还受本地调度抖动影响，约等于 delay。
    go func() {
        t := time.NewTicker(delay)
        defer t.Stop()
        for range t.C {
            select {
            case p.tokens <- struct{}{}:
            default: // 桶满就丢弃，避免令牌堆积造成突发
            }
        }
    }()
    return p
}

func (p *PoliteFetcher) Fetch(url string) ([]byte, error) {
    p.sem <- struct{}{}        // 占一个并发名额
    defer func() { <-p.sem }() // 释放名额
    <-p.tokens                 // 取令牌：全局限速，取不到就等

    resp, err := http.Get(url)
    if err != nil {
        return nil, err
    }
    defer resp.Body.Close()
    return io.ReadAll(resp.Body)
}

func main() {
    var cur, peak int64
    var mu sync.Mutex
    var hits []time.Time

    // 本地测试服务器：记录每次请求到达的时间和并发数
    ts := httptest.NewServer(http.HandlerFunc(func(w http.ResponseWriter, r *http.Request) {
        n := atomic.AddInt64(&cur, 1)
        for {
            old := atomic.LoadInt64(&peak)
            if n <= old || atomic.CompareAndSwapInt64(&peak, old, n) {
                break
            }
        }
        mu.Lock()
        hits = append(hits, time.Now())
        mu.Unlock()
        time.Sleep(50 * time.Millisecond) // 模拟服务器处理耗时
        atomic.AddInt64(&cur, -1)
        fmt.Fprint(w, "ok")
    }))
    defer ts.Close()

    f := NewPoliteFetcher(200*time.Millisecond, 2)

    // 预热一次连接：把 TCP 建连成本排除在测量之外，只测限速机制本身。
    // 注意要读完并关闭 Body，否则连接无法复用，预热就白做了。
    if resp, err := http.Get(ts.URL); err != nil {
        fmt.Println("预热失败:", err)
        return
    } else {
        io.Copy(io.Discard, resp.Body)
        resp.Body.Close()
    }
    base := len(hits) // 预热请求不计入测量

    // 阶段一：限速验证——单 goroutine 顺序抓 6 次
    // 同一个 worker 不存在调度竞速，测到的是纯粹的令牌间隔，结论稳定
    for i := 0; i < 6; i++ {
        if _, err := f.Fetch(ts.URL); err != nil {
            fmt.Println("抓取失败:", err)
            return
        }
    }
    rateOK := true
    minGap := time.Hour
    for i := base + 1; i < len(hits); i++ {
        if gap := hits[i].Sub(hits[i-1]); gap < minGap {
            minGap = gap
        }
    }
    span := hits[len(hits)-1].Sub(hits[base]) // 首尾跨度：5 个名义 200ms 间隔
    // 不断言每一跳精确 200ms：本地调度抖动会让单跳有 ±20ms 级浮动；
    // 机制保证的是"令牌每 200ms 发放一个"，所以断言总跨度与单跳底线。
    if span < 900*time.Millisecond || minGap < 150*time.Millisecond {
        rateOK = false
    }
    fmt.Printf("阶段一（限速）：6 次请求，总跨度 %dms，平均间隔 %dms，最小间隔 %dms -> %s\n",
        span.Milliseconds(), span.Milliseconds()/5, minGap.Milliseconds(),
        map[bool]string{true: "达标", false: "未达标"}[rateOK])

    // 阶段二：并发验证——6 个 goroutine 同时抓，信号量上限 2
    // 并发峰值是构造性保证（信号量满了就进不去），与调度抖动无关
    var wg sync.WaitGroup
    for i := 0; i < 6; i++ {
        wg.Add(1)
        go func() {
            defer wg.Done()
            if _, err := f.Fetch(ts.URL); err != nil {
                fmt.Println("抓取失败:", err)
            }
        }()
    }
    wg.Wait()
    peakOK := atomic.LoadInt64(&peak) <= 2
    fmt.Println("阶段二（并发）：并发峰值", atomic.LoadInt64(&peak), "->", map[bool]string{true: "达标", false: "未达标"}[peakOK])

    if rateOK && peakOK {
        fmt.Println("PASS：限速与并发上限双双达标")
    } else {
        fmt.Println("FAIL：礼貌机制没生效")
    }
}

运行输出：

阶段一（限速）：6 次请求，总跨度 1002ms，平均间隔 200ms，最小间隔 196ms -> 达标
阶段二（并发）：并发峰值 1 -> 达标
PASS：限速与并发上限双双达标

（具体毫秒数每次运行略有浮动，这是本地调度的正常抖动。）

关键点：sem 这个带缓冲的 channel 是"并发名额池"，tokens 令牌桶是"全局节流阀"——令牌由单个 ticker 每 200ms 补充一个，无论多少个 goroutine 同时想抓，请求之间都约间隔 200ms（实测 196–212ms，抖动来自本地调度）。两个机制都很便宜，但决定了你的爬虫是"客人"还是"攻击者"。

五、本讲小结

  • 礼貌三做法：控制频率、控制并发数、避开业务高峰；
  • 三条线不碰：登录墙不碰、反爬不绕、服务条款遵守；
  • 数据用途：自用，不倒卖、不公开他人隐私；
  • 核心思想：礼貌 = 可持续。

本文为学习笔记（编纂），用自己的话重写；知识点源自公开的网络爬虫行业惯例与 Go 并发编程常识。

title: How to fix 'Failed to load resource: the server responded with a status of 404' (and find which page is asking for it)
description:
Scheduled broken-link and redirect checks that tell you the moment a link breaks — linkbruno.com

Open the console on almost any website and you'll eventually see it:

Failed to load resource: the server responded with a status of 404 (Not Found)

It's a broken link, just not one a human clicked. The page asked the browser to fetch something (a script, a stylesheet, an image, a font, a JSON file, a source map), the browser requested it, and the server said it doesn't exist. Sometimes nothing visible breaks. Sometimes it's the reason the page has no styles, a button does nothing, or a font falls back to Times New Roman.

Here's how to track it down and fix it properly.

Step 1: get the exact URL that failed

The console line alone doesn't say much. Click through to the Network tab and reload with the tab open:

  1. Filter by status: type status-code:404 in the filter box (Chrome and Edge support this).
  2. Click the failing request. The Headers panel shows the full Request URL.
  3. The Initiator column (or tab) shows what asked for it: the HTML document, a CSS file, or a line of JavaScript.

The initiator is the important part. A 404 for /fonts/inter.woff2 initiated by main.css means the bug is a url() inside your stylesheet, not your HTML.

From the command line you can confirm it independently:

curl -sI https://www.example.com/assets/app.3f9a1c.js | head -1

Step 2: figure out why the URL is wrong

Compare the URL the browser requested with where the file actually lives. The difference almost always falls into one of these:

A relative path resolved against the wrong base. <script src="js/app.js"> on the page /blog/post-1/ requests /blog/post-1/js/app.js. It worked on the homepage and breaks on every nested page. The fix is a root-relative path (/js/app.js) or a correct <base href>. This is also the classic cause of "works locally, 404 in production" when the production site is served from a subfolder.

The app is deployed under a subpath, but the build doesn't know. If your site lives at example.com/docs/ but was built assuming /, every asset request misses the /docs prefix. Most build tools have a setting for this: base in Vite, basePath and assetPrefix in Next.js, publicPath in webpack, baseurl in Jekyll, baseURL in Hugo.

Hashed filenames from an old build. Modern builds produce files like app.3f9a1c.js. If an HTML page is cached (by a CDN, a service worker or the browser) and the deploy deleted the old hashes, the cached page asks for files that no longer exist. Keep the previous build's assets around for a while after each deploy, and make sure HTML is cached for much less time than hashed assets.

Case sensitivity. Logo.PNG on a Mac works as logo.png. On a Linux server it's a 404. Check the exact casing in the file system against the reference.

A source map that was never uploaded. A 404 for app.js.map only appears when DevTools is open, and it's harmless for users. Either deploy the maps or stop the build from adding //# sourceMappingURL comments.

favicon.ico. Browsers request /favicon.ico even if your HTML never mentions it. A 404 there is noise in logs and monitoring. Put a file there or declare an icon with <link rel="icon">.

One 404 in the console is easy to fix; the next deploy can add ten more on pages you never open. linkbruno.com checks your pages and the assets they load on a schedule, and tells you when an image, script or stylesheet starts returning 404.

Step 3: find every page with the same problem

The page where you noticed the error is rarely the only one. To find others, crawl the site and request every asset URL each page references. A quick shell version for a handful of pages:

for page in / /blog/ /pricing/; do
  curl -s "https://www.example.com$page" \
  | grep -oE '(src|href)="[^"#]+"' | cut -d'"' -f2 \
  | while read -r url; do
      case "$url" in http*) full="$url" ;; /*) full="https://www.example.com$url" ;; *) full="https://www.example.com$page$url" ;; esac
      code=$(curl -s -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}' "$full")
      [ "$code" = 404 ] && echo "$page -> $full"
    done
done

It's rough (it won't see assets loaded by JavaScript or referenced from CSS), but it catches the relative-path and subpath bugs quickly. For JavaScript-loaded resources, a headless browser test that listens for failed responses catches the rest:

page.on('response', r => { if (r.status() === 404) console.log(page.url(), '->', r.url()); });

Step 4: stop it shipping again

  • Fail the build on missing assets. Most bundlers already fail on a missing import. The risk is in paths written as plain strings in HTML, CSS or Markdown, so add a link check of the built output to CI.
  • Keep old hashed assets for a while. Upload new assets before switching HTML, and don't delete the previous release's assets in the same deploy.
  • Log 404s for asset paths separately. A 404 on /assets/ is a bug on your side; a 404 on /wp-login.php is a bot. Splitting them makes the real ones visible.
  • Check the live site after deploy, not just the build. CDN rules, rewrites and base paths only exist in production.

That last one is where a scheduled check helps: linkbruno.com watches the live site, so the 404s introduced by a CDN rule or a stale cache show up too, not just the ones a build would catch.

Related reading

  • Postmortem: the deploy deleted last week's JavaScript bundles, and cached pages kept asking for them
  • How to find and fix broken images on a website
  • How to fix net::ERR_BLOCKED_BY_CLIENT (when an ad blocker breaks your images, scripts and links)
  • The anatomy of a URL, and which part of it broke your link
  • When you delete a page on purpose, should it return 404 or 410? Let's argue about it

What's the strangest cause you've found for a console 404? Mine was a CSS file that referenced fonts with ../ and worked everywhere except the one page served from a deeper path.

title: Mask Reveal Code: the small motion details that make it feel right
description:
Four digits, and the cells become one solid panel.

A code field where four digits trigger a panel that opens across the cells from left to right with a confirmation word. A wrong code shakes the row and clears it.

The trick

The panel is a veil clipped with inset(0 100% 0 0), and opening it is just animating that clip to 0.

Motion goes through one small go() helper on the Web Animations API, which sets durations to 1ms for reduced motion.

The shake is six translateX keyframes of 8 then 4 pixels, which decays like a real shake.

.veil{position:absolute;inset:0;background:var(--fx-on);color:var(--fx-on-ink);display:flex;align-items:center;justify-content:center;gap:8px;font-weight:600;font-size:16px;clip-path:inset(0 100% 0 0);pointer-events:none;z-index:2}
const shake=el=>go(el,[{transform:'translateX(0)'},{transform:'translateX(-8px)'},{transform:'translateX(8px)'},{transform:'translateX(-4px)'},{transform:'translateX(4px)'},{transform:'translateX(0)'}],

Where I'd use it

Verification and 2FA screens

Each cell is a real input under the veil, so the field keeps its normal keyboard and autofill behavior.

The prompt for this one is free: uimotion.app.

title: I spent a week with Claude Code trying to squeeze more out of my memory tool's LongMemEval score. Almost nothing worked. Is it my code or the benchmark?
description:
I built a local-first memory for coding agents. It's a Rust binary and one SQLite file, using MiniLM embeddings plus BM25 keyword search, with no LLM in the retrieval path and no re-ranker.

On LongMemEval S (470 scored questions) it scores R@1 0.913 (429), R@5 0.987 (464) and R@10 0.996 (468).

I wanted more, mainly at R@1 and recall_all (every gold session in the top K). But all while preserving the strict rules of NO LLM, no re-ranker model and not tuning for the benchmark.

Claude Code did most of the legwork:

  • offline replays of chunk-score dumps
  • a DEV/TEST split by question-id hash
  • a "guard" suite (my coding eval plus probes against a snapshot of my real palace), so a benchmark gain couldn't quietly hurt real use

What we tried

Idea LongMemEval Real-palace guards
Fix two WordPiece tokenizer deviations 0 questions changed probes -1/200
Embed at MiniLM's trained 128 tokens, not 512 R@1 +1, recall_all@5 -7 probes 0.900 -> 0.875, fail
256 tokens +4/-4 at R@1 fail
Re-weight cosine vs BM25 (0.70 to 0.85), DEV only +/- 2 questions probes 0.885 -> 0.790, coding eval 0.922 -> 0.882
Count BM25 only when cosine > 0 <= 1 question probes -4 to -6 pts
RRF, min-max, z-score, saturating BM25 all within 3 questions of baseline n/a
Split two-part questions and merge best scores R@1 +2/-0 DEV, 0/0 TEST unchanged
Treat advice requests as preferences R@1 -5 n/a

The only clean win was 429 -> 431 at R@1. BEAM 100K is already 355/355 at R@5.

How I read it

  1. One question is 0.2%. Most "improvements" were 1 to 4 questions, moving in both directions.
  2. The right sessions are already in the top 30 for 469 of 470 questions. The losses come from ordering, not from failing to find them.
  3. Fusion is saturated: every way of combining cosine and BM25 lands within 3 questions of the others.
  4. Every LongMemEval gain cost my real-palace probes more than it gained.
  5. The leftover misses are reasoning, not retrieval: questions about dates and counting across sessions. The paper's own gains there come from an LLM, which I avoid on purpose.

So my answer is both, but mostly the benchmark. For a pure retriever, S is close to its ceiling. At R@1 I'm at the limit of a small embedding model plus BM25. The next real step is probably a local cross-encoder reranker, not more tuning.

The Claude Code part

The most useful thing it did was keep me honest. It flagged when a "win" was 2 questions, reported failed guards plainly, and stopped when I said "stop if we don't have clear wins". Nothing from the week shipped, and I think that's the right result.

Questions

  • At 98%+, is LongMemEval S still a useful signal for you, or have you moved to M, BEAM 1M or your own evals?
  • Has anyone gotten a real R@1 lift from a local cross-encoder on conversational memory without bad latency?
  • Is there a non-LLM trick for the date questions that I'm missing?

Repo, runner and per-question outputs: https://github.com/AncientiCe/palace-rs

title: Agenvoy@v1.3.18-v1.3.19
description:
Agenvoy

v1.3.17 -> v1.3.19

Summary

  • v1.3.18 Adds a human-assisted step for pages that block automated access: a challenge cannot be avoided, but the content is still needed, so Agenvoy asks the user to complete the check in a browser window. Interactive prompts across every interface now follow the configured reply language, since a prompt exists to be understood by the person answering it.
  • v1.3.19 This hotfix extends manual human verification to page downloads with a session-scoped cache so users are not re-prompted across requests. It also skips interactive prompts in headless Linux environments and delegates shared browser checks upstream.

翻譯

  • v1.3.18 新增真人協助步驟：網站的真人驗證避不開，但資訊仍需完整取得，因此改為請使用者在瀏覽器視窗完成驗證。各介面的互動提示改依設定的回覆語言顯示，因為提示的重點是讓回答的人看得懂。
  • v1.3.19 此 hotfix 將手動真人驗證擴展至頁面下載並加入會話級快取，避免使用者在同一請求脈絡下重複受詢。同時在無圖形介面的 Linux 環境略過互動視窗提示，並將共用的瀏覽器檢查委派至上游套件。

Changes

FEAT

  • Add manual human verification to fetch_page
    • Ask the user whether to verify manually when a headed fetch hits a challenge
    • Open a browser window on the daemon machine and wait up to 5 minutes
    • Reuse the answer for the rest of the task
    • Skip the URL as 403 when declined or when no one can be asked (auto mode, no prompt, no listener)
  • Localize interactive prompts to the configured reply language
    • English by default and for auto
    • Tool approval titles, options, password and skip-reason prompts on TUI, WebUI, Discord and Telegram
    • fetch_page verification question, ask_user progress, placeholders and buttons
    • TUI key hints on agent prompts, store_secret default prompt and chat secret notes
    • Discord／Telegram notices: verification code, resolved pending task, missing speech-to-text model
    • Texts in configs/confirm/*.json for all 16 reply languages, validated at startup
  • Add manual human verification to download_file (render: true)
    • Reuse existing session decisions with the configured challenge wait
    • Prompt on ErrChallengeRequired and skip as 403 when declined
    • Reset session challenge state and skip as 403 on ErrChallengeClosed
  • Persist challenge verification decisions across calls per session
    • Cache enabled or declined decisions by SessionID for 30 minutes after last use
    • Refresh the expiry window on each subsequent read
    • Evict the cached entry when ResetChallenge is called

翻譯

  • fetch_page 新增真人手動驗證
    • 可見視窗模式遇到驗證時，詢問使用者是否手動驗證
    • 在 daemon 所在電腦開啟瀏覽器視窗，最多等待 5 分鐘
    • 同一任務沿用答案
    • 拒絕或無法詢問（auto 模式、不可詢問、無接收端）時，該網址以 403 略過
  • 互動提示改依設定的回覆語言輸出
    • 預設與 auto 時為英文
    • TUI、WebUI、Discord、Telegram 的工具確認標題、選項、密碼與略過理由提示
    • fetch_page 驗證詢問、ask_user 的進度、輸入提示與按鈕
    • TUI 中 agent 彈窗的按鍵提示、store_secret 預設提示與聊天密文說明
    • Discord／Telegram 通知：驗證碼、待處理任務已處理、未選語音轉文字模型
    • 文字集中於 configs/confirm/*.json，涵蓋 16 種回覆語言，啟動時檢查
  • 為 download_file（render: true）新增手動真人驗證流程
    • 沿用既有 session 決定並套用設定的驗證等待時間
    • 遇到 ErrChallengeRequired 時詢問使用者，拒絕則以 403 略過
    • 遇到 ErrChallengeClosed 時重設 session 驗證狀態並以 403 略過
  • 依 session 跨次保留真人驗證決定
    • 以 SessionID 快取同意或略過狀態，於最後一次使用後保留 30 分鐘
    • 每次讀取時刷新到期時間
    • 呼叫 ResetChallenge 時清除快取項目

FIX

  • Fix WebUI hanging until the tool timeout on in-tool prompts
    • Affects the fetch_page verification question and store_secret
    • The web listener only handled tool approvals, so these prompts were never shown
    • They now arrive as a prompt card, answered through the existing confirm endpoint and replayed on reconnect
  • Skip manual verification prompts on headless Linux and WSL
    • Return false from askChallenge when running under WSL
    • Require DISPLAY or WAYLAND_DISPLAY on non-WSL Linux before prompting

翻譯
