title: My Build Tool Reached 35ms. Here's Why I'm Not Celebrating Yet.
description:
Inside Ionify — A story about verified reuse, unexpected correctness bugs, and the engineering work behind a hotfix that isn't ready to ship.

There's something satisfying about seeing a production build complete in 35 milliseconds.

Especially when you've spent months building a tool designed to eliminate redundant work.

But there's also something uncomfortable about that number.

A fast build doesn't tell you whether the engine made the right decisions.

That's the lesson I'm being reminded of while working on Ionify 0.1.39.

What Started as Two Bugs Became Something Bigger

Ionify is an open-source frontend build engine built around a simple principle:

Don't repeat work that has already been verified, unless something relevant has changed.

To support that idea, the engine preserves information about previous computations and their dependencies.

The goal is to determine what can be safely reused instead of treating every build as a completely new problem.

But while investigating warm-build behavior, we found two opposite failures.

Sometimes the engine reused work that should have been invalidated.

Other times, it recomputed work that was still valid.

One threatened correctness.

The other wasted time.

And both challenged the same architectural assumption: that the engine knew precisely which previous results it could trust.

When Memory Becomes a Liability

Persistence is one of Ionify's most important architectural ideas.

A build engine that remembers previous work can potentially save substantial time across repeated builds.

But memory introduces responsibility.

A previous result may have been correct when generated.

That doesn't necessarily mean it remains correct after a source file, dependency, configuration, or compiler-related input changes.

The engine needs to understand the relationships behind that result.

Otherwise, persistence can become a source of stale outputs.

And the danger is that stale reuse can look like excellent performance.

The build completes quickly because it skipped work.

But it skipped work that was actually necessary.

The fastest incorrect build is still an incorrect build.

The Investigation Kept Expanding

What initially appeared to be a warm-build issue expanded into several areas of the engine.

We found problems with stale dependency reuse.

We investigated CSS and Tailwind correctness gaps.

We uncovered cases where output was recomputed unnecessarily.

And faster compression exposed a native memory-ownership bug.

These weren't all identical failures.

Some involved the engine's decisions about dependencies.

Others involved compilation behavior or lower-level resource management.

But they collectively reinforced the same lesson.

A persistent build engine cannot optimize reuse in isolation from correctness and resource safety.

Then We Reached 35ms

During the investigation, we measured a no-change production build on a real React application with approximately 1,900 modules.

The result was:

35ms, deploy-ready, in a local run.

That's encouraging.

But it only answers one question:

How quickly can the engine complete a production build when nothing relevant has changed?

It doesn't answer the more difficult question:

What happens when something does change?

Source mutations still expose performance bottlenecks we're not satisfied with.

And that matters more to me than celebrating one impressive number.

The Importance of Causal Locality

I've been thinking about this through a principle I call causal locality.

The idea is straightforward:

The amount of work a build engine performs should follow the consequences of the change, not the size of the project.

If a leaf module changes, unrelated modules shouldn't automatically require recomputation.

If a widely shared dependency changes, broader work may be necessary.

The engine should distinguish those situations correctly.

That means the best result isn't always the smallest amount of work.

It's the smallest amount of work that still produces the correct output.

And that distinction is harder than simply optimizing a hot path.

The Unexpected Challenge of Upgrades

There's another reason this hotfix is taking careful validation.

Ionify doesn't forget everything between builds.

It preserves build knowledge inside .ionify.

That means upgrading the engine isn't the same as starting from a clean environment.

The new version may encounter artifacts created under previous correctness or invalidation rules.

What should it do with them?

Trust them all?

Delete everything?

Neither option is particularly satisfying.

The goal is to retain valid knowledge while safely invalidating anything that can no longer be trusted.

And ideally, developers should be able to upgrade without manually deleting .ionify or clearing their caches.

That's the experience we're working toward.

But it has to be proven through upgrade testing, not assumed.

Why 0.1.39 Isn't Released Yet

The hotfix is still under validation.

We're checking how the new behavior handles existing caches, dependency mutations, CSS changes, output recomputation, and native memory ownership.

I'm not interested in publishing a release that improves a benchmark while leaving correctness questions unanswered.

And I'm not interested in presenting a fast no-change build as if it tells the entire performance story.

The source-mutation paths need to improve too.

That's why I'm treating three principles as non-negotiable.

Correctness. Causal locality. End-to-end performance.

Building in Public Means Showing the Unfinished Work

It's easy to share a performance improvement.

It's harder to explain why you haven't released it yet.

But I think that's an important part of building open source.

A useful engineering update isn't always an announcement that something is finished.

Sometimes it's an explanation of what went wrong, why it matters, and what evidence is still missing.

This hotfix has become one of those moments.

The 35ms result is promising.

The newly discovered bugs are real.

And the remaining validation work matters just as much as the optimization.

The Principle I Keep Returning To

Ionify exists because I believe build tools can avoid repeating more work than they do today.

But I don't want to solve that problem by blindly trusting cached results.

The engine should remember.

It should reuse.

And it should know when its previous knowledge is no longer valid.

That's the engineering challenge I'm continuing to work through.

Stop recomputing verified work. But never reuse work without proof.

Inside Ionify — Rethinking Frontend Build Architecture

Ionify is open source:

https://github.com/ionifyjs/ionify

Feedback, independent testing, and critical questions are always welcome.

When should a build engine choose to recompute rather than trust its previous results?

title: Nightly Reconciliation for Node.js Email and Webhook Failures: Idempotent Queue Recovery
description:
Short answer: For a B2B SaaS service sending user reminders while reconciling a payment provider overnight, choose a queue whose operational recovery is explicit, then make the consumer idempotent, bound retries, and preserve every uncertain send as an auditable state rather than treating a successful acknowledgement as proof of delivery.

The queue is a transport mechanism. The reconciliation record is the authority. That distinction matters when a worker sends an email, receives no response, and dies before it can acknowledge the job: the next worker must be able to recover without either silently losing the reminder or sending it twice.

Evaluate Node.js user reminder queue recovery

At 02:00, the useful question is not whether the queue reports healthy. It is whether the team can explain every reminder that was due, attempted, accepted, retried, quarantined, or left uncertain. Start the nightly run with a resumable comparison against the payment provider, checkpoint the provider cursor or comparison range, and emit repair commands only for state differences that the local ledger can justify. A useful run record includes the reconciliation window, the last provider cursor, the deployment revision, the number of commands emitted, and the number of records deliberately held for review; without those fields, a rerun can look complete while quietly examining a different slice of the provider's data. The recovery operator should be able to distinguish “no differences found” from “comparison stopped after page 18,” because those states demand opposite actions even though both can leave the process with no new queue messages.

Record counts for matched, missing, disputed, retried, and manually reviewed items. Alert on the age of the oldest unprocessed item and on dead-letter growth. A green scheduler metric can coexist with a queue full of work that nobody can safely redrive.

This operational view changes the queue decision. The winning design is the one the team can recover at 02:00, during an incomplete deployment, with an uncertain provider response and a clear audit trail.

Delivery data belongs in a ledger

Start with a durable delivery identity. For a reminder, use a key built from the reminder ID, delivery revision, and channel, such as rem-1042:v3:email. Store that key with an attempt record and enforce uniqueness in the database. A read followed by an insert is not enough under concurrent delivery; two workers can observe the same empty state. A unique constraint, conditional write, or transactionally claimed state gives one worker the right to proceed.

The send itself creates an uncomfortable interval. The provider may accept the request while the worker is unable to record the response. No queue can remove that ambiguity. The application needs an explicit unknown or needs_reconciliation state, a later check against provider evidence where available, and an operator-visible audit trail that connects the command, idempotency key, attempt, response, and final business decision.

That's the boundary.

In a payment reconciliation workflow, the nightly job should compare provider records with the local ledger and emit repair commands for missing or disputed reminder state. It should not infer that a missing local acknowledgement means a missing external send. Reconciliation is a second path to the same state machine, not a second permission to send. Keeping those paths convergent prevents an overnight repair job from becoming a duplicate-notification generator.

package main

import "fmt"

type Delivery struct {
    Key   string
    State string
}

// A database unique constraint must enforce this invariant in production.
func accept(d Delivery, seen map[string]bool) bool {
    if seen[d.Key] {
        return false
    }
    seen[d.Key] = true
    return d.State == "ready"
}

func main() {
    seen := map[string]bool{}
    delivery := Delivery{Key: "rem-1042:v3:email", State: "ready"}
    fmt.Println(accept(delivery, seen))
    fmt.Println(accept(delivery, seen))
}

This small program demonstrates duplicate suppression, not exactly-once external delivery. The production equivalent must make the durable claim atomic and must define what happens if the provider call succeeds between the claim and the attempt record. Compliance requirements also vary: a queue retention period is not automatically an acceptable audit retention period, so the ledger and attempt history need their own policy.

Can dead-letter, webhook, and email failures share one policy?

Classify the result before choosing the next action. A timeout after an outbound request is an uncertain result, a temporary provider rejection is retryable, and an invalid destination is terminal. HTTP 429 means the sender is being rate limited; when Retry-After is present, use it, because immediate retries create more pressure at the exact moment the remote service is asking for less.

Use bounded exponential backoff with jitter, and put an attempt number and next eligible time in durable state. A dead-letter queue is a quarantine and review path, not a trash can. It should retain the original idempotency key and enough context to explain why the message stopped progressing, while redrive must preserve that key instead of creating a fresh identity.

Webhooks have a second acknowledgement problem. The receiving endpoint should validate the request, persist the event or delivery key, and return success only after the duplicate check is durable; the downstream work can then proceed asynchronously. Email providers work in the opposite direction from a webhook receiver: the application initiates the call and must keep a local attempt ledger. Both flows need the same state discipline even though their network boundaries differ.

Which queue design supports nightly recovery?

Choose the smallest operational surface that preserves the needed recovery behavior. The following comparison is about failure handling, not feature-count theatre.

Design Useful when Trade-off
Database work table Reminder state and delivery claims must share one transaction boundary Polling, backoff, dead-letter handling, and cleanup belong to the application
Managed queue The team wants broker operations handled by its infrastructure platform Send state, reconciliation, and duplicate protection still belong to the application
Redis-backed job queue The service already has mature Redis operations and a job-oriented workload The job record must not become the only audit record
Broker with routing Multiple destinations and routing rules are central to the system Broker topology and recovery become an operational responsibility

PostgreSQL can be a reasonable starting point for a modest reminder volume. Workers claim rows with FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED, commit that claim, and perform the provider call outside the transaction. This keeps a slow network request from holding database locks, although it means the state machine must explicitly handle a worker that disappears after claiming work. A dedicated queue is a better fit when backlog isolation, independent scaling, or broker-level routing is more important than transactional proximity.

The catch is that neither choice is suitable when the real requirement is a replayable event history consumed independently by several teams. Use an event-log design for that job, and use workflow orchestration when the process needs joins, timers, or long-running human decisions. A reminder queue should not quietly become all three systems.

Roll out reconciliation with checkpoints

Define the delivery states and idempotency key before creating the queue. Then test the dangerous transitions: duplicate delivery, a timeout after provider acceptance, a worker crash after a durable claim, a 429 response, an invalid address, and a dead-letter redrive. Each test should assert both the externally visible send count and the ledger or audit record that explains it.

For the overnight reconciliation, make the run resumable by checkpointing the provider cursor or comparison range. Record counts for matched, missing, disputed, retried, and manually reviewed items. Alert on age of the oldest unprocessed item and on growth of the dead-letter population; a green scheduler metric can coexist with a queue full of work that nobody can safely redrive.

Node.js is a perfectly viable worker runtime, but the runtime does not decide the delivery semantics. Go is used below to keep the example concrete, and the same state transitions apply in a Node.js process. Your mileage may vary on the right queue boundary: team ownership, database topology, provider limits, and compliance policy matter more than language preference.

The final decision rule is plain: select the queue your team can recover at 02:00, keep send authority in a durable idempotency state machine, and let reconciliation repair evidence rather than replaying delivery blindly.

References

  • https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Reference/Status/429
  • https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/sql-select.html

title: AWS Marketplace now supports agentic payments with AgentCore
description:
AWS Marketplace now supports agentic payments over the x402 protocol, so AI agents can discover and buy select products and pay per request in US dollars through AgentCore payments, part of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore. Agents often need paid APIs, data, or content mid-task, but access usually requires a person to sign up, add a payment method, and create an API key. With agentic payments, customers skip that per-seller setup, and charges settle on their existing AWS bill with no crypto wallet required.

Customers enable the AWS Marketplace payment connector in AgentCore payments, then they or their agents find listings through the AWS Marketplace connector in AgentCore Gateway. For example, a research agent can buy a single web search, or a coding agent can call a paid guardrail service. Customers can set spending limits, approved sellers, and guardrails before agents transact, Private Marketplace policies still apply, and transactions appear in AWS CloudTrail and AWS Cost Explorer.

AWS Marketplace sellers can charge AI agents per request without building a sign-up flow or billing system. They register with AWS Marketplace, configure agentic payments for their listings, and integrate the AWS Marketplace x402 SDK. AWS Marketplace collects customer payments and pays sellers through their AWS Marketplace seller disbursements, like other AWS Marketplace transactions.

The capability is available in all AWS Regions where AgentCore payments is available. To learn more, see AWS Marketplace and the Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Developer Guide. To list as a seller, see the AWS Marketplace Seller Guide.

title: PNG, JPG or WebP? A developer's rule of thumb for picking image formats
description:
Most image-format bugs I see in code review aren't exotic. A logo ships as a 900 KB JPG with fuzzy edges. A hero photo ships as a PNG that weighs more than the rest of the page combined. A product cut-out loses its transparency and shows up on a white box over a dark theme. All three come from the same gap: picking a format by habit instead of by what the pixels are.

Here's the rule of thumb I actually use.

First, know what you're compressing

A 1920×1080 image is 2,073,600 pixels. Stored raw with an alpha channel (4 bytes per pixel), that's 8,294,400 bytes — about 8.3 MB before any compression. Every format below is a different strategy for shrinking that number, and each one is good at a different kind of image.

  • PNG is lossless. It reproduces every pixel exactly and supports full alpha transparency. It compresses well when the image has large flat areas and repeated patterns — UI, text, diagrams, icons.
  • JPG is lossy. It throws away detail the eye is bad at noticing, which works beautifully on photos with gradients and noise. It has no alpha channel at all.
  • WebP can do both: a lossy mode for photos and a lossless mode for graphics, with alpha in either. For most web delivery it's the format to reach for first.

The decision, in three questions

1. Does it need transparency? If yes, JPG is out. Use PNG for a source asset you'll keep editing, WebP for what you actually serve.

2. Is it a photo or a graphic? Photos (people, landscapes, product shots on a background) → JPG or lossy WebP. Graphics (screenshots, logos, charts, anything with sharp text) → PNG or lossless WebP. JPG's compression smears hard edges, which is why a screenshot saved as JPG gets that halo of artifacts around every letter.

3. Where does it end up? If an upload form, email client or legacy CMS only accepts JPG, the decision is made for you — convert and move on.

What happens when you convert PNG to JPG

Two things change, and both are worth knowing before you script it.

First, the alpha channel has to go somewhere. JPG can't store it, so transparent pixels get flattened onto a solid background — usually white. A logo designed for a dark header will suddenly sit on a white rectangle. If that matters, don't convert to JPG; convert to WebP and keep the alpha.

Second, quality is a dial, not a switch. Around 85–90 is the usual sweet spot for photos: visibly identical, much smaller. Pushing below ~70 starts to show blocky artifacts in skies and skin tones. And every lossy re-save compounds the damage, so keep your lossless original and always export from it.

Common mistakes

  • Serving PNG photos because "PNG is higher quality." Lossless doesn't mean better-looking on a photo — just heavier.
  • Saving screenshots and UI as JPG and wondering why the text looks dirty.
  • Converting a transparent asset to JPG without noticing the new white background.
  • Re-compressing the same JPG over and over instead of exporting once from the source.

I wrote a longer walkthrough of the PNG-versus-JPG trade-off — when a conversion is worth it and when to leave the file alone — on the Toolonium blog. When you just need the conversion done, there's a free PNG to JPG converter that runs in your browser, so the image never leaves your machine.
